Quick Summary: Mighty No 9 is a side-scrolling 2-dimensional shooter game with some tricky air dash platforming (no wall jumping), challenging bosses, and a cheesy story. It plays extremely similarly to the small handful of Megaman X games that I played on the Super Nintendo.
You play the title character Mighty Number 9 (AKA Beck) a kid-shaped robot with a gun in one hand and the ability to absorb the “xel” of other robots. The story doesn’t really explain what xel is, but it seems to be some kind of energy that gives robots their power. Unfortunately for Beck and the rest of the world, a mysterious enemy has appeared with the same xel absorption power, and it’s using this ability to turn all the world’s robots hostile, including the other Mighty Numbers (1-8).
Just like the Megaman games, the campaign of Mighty No 9 is broken up into individual levels that you can choose to play in any order (except for the tutorial and final levels). Each of the levels has a boss (one of the Mighty Numbers) that you must beat and absorb their xel. After doing so, you gain that boss’s special attack. For example beating the boss with fire powers will give you a fire attack. By pressing a button on your controller (I used an xbox 360 controller) you can switch between your collected weapons for whatever best fits the situation. Most of the bosses have a weapon that they’re weak against, so you may want to choose your levels in a specific order to take advantage of it. For example, the ice boss is weak against fire, so don’t play the ice level until after you’ve beaten the fire boss and have the fire attack in your arsenal.
By the way, the xel absorption mechanic is not just for bosses, it actually applies to all your enemies (though you don’t take their powers). Every time you shoot an enemy a few times, they start flashing and you need to “dash” into them to absorb their xel. This instantly destroys the enemy. If you don’t press the dash key you’ll take damage from touching them, even though the enemy is “stunned” and will just die in a few seconds anyway. This absorption mechanic is kind of annoying to be honest, especially against bosses where you need to absorb their xel multiple times during the fight (or they heal). Get used to the dash key because the game has no double jumps or wall climbs, so most of your movement will involve dashing around.
You should play Mighty No 9 if:
+You enjoyed the gameplay style of the old Megaman games and you have a decent controller. Dashing while shooting and avoiding spike zones would be a challenge to play with keyboard. You don’t use the mouse because you don’t “aim” your shots. They just go horizontally across the screen.
+You’re looking for a challenge. Most of the game is semi-easy, but they really ramp up the difficulty for the end. I wasn’t able to beat the final boss, and just moved on to another game. Also, there are a lot of instant death threats in the game, like spikes and bottomless pits. Unlike Megaman, if you misjudge a jump, you cannot wall jump/climb out, you just fall in and die.
You should NOT play Mighty No 9 if:
-You’re looking for an easy breezy game. Some of the levels (like Countershade’s) are a pain in the butt.
-You’re looking for an exciting or fresh story. Mighty No 9’s story is really generic and predictable. Seriously, you’ll know what’s coming right from the beginning.
Overall I enjoyed the game, but I would have liked an option to turn down difficulty at the end so I could actually finish the story after trying/dying a bunch of times. Some of the bosses are a nightmare with all the projectiles flying around, and I’m not proficient enough with a game controller to quickly switch between forms in the heat of combat. The game has a mixed rating on Steam, some of which seems to come from high expectations based on the game’s Kickstarter beginnings, and some from people who aren’t able to get the game to work at all. I had absolutely no technical problems with my 6 year old computer. Also the game has a ton of Steam achievements (100+), many of which are very difficult to obtain, if that makes any difference to you potential buyers.

I am one of the KickStarter Backers, and as of this week I finally decided to play the game.
The game is 100% designed around can you guess it.... Speed Running. Yes everything about this game screams speed running. Even how the game bonus features are unlocked, they all revolve around speed running. The game has a “high” frustration level and rarely rewards you, unless you are looking for a “top score” or “top speed run”.  PLEASE READ before you buy. P.S. this isn't a bad game just know what you are getting, I wouldn't have backed it or purchased it if I would have known. But I know plenty of others would really enjoy this game. Thus I'm giving it a thumbs up.
(1) This game is nothing that we actually were hoping for when we backed the project in Kickstarter, but what is this game.
Do you like these following games that have these mechanics or sections?
“Super Meat Boy” (all of it)
“Battle Toads” (Instant Death Portions)
“Mega Man” (Instant Death Portions)
“Ninja Gaiden” (Jump monster hits you then fall to instant death portions)
If you said yes, than you will like this game.
Don't get me wrong I feel this game is a bit more forgiving since you can have 9 lives, and restart from the beginning of the level. I beat the game in 10 hours (not including the DLC). Around 2 ½ hours of that was the final boss stage. Which then goes into my next portion of the review.
Some mechanics or functions in the game that either just don't work well, or you may not like;
(a) One does press jump+Dash work some times, but then it won't work other times. You have to time several things just perfectly not even a sliver/pixel of error allowed. This is why it took me 2 ½ hours at the final boss stage, on the final boss second form. I knew the patterns of attack I just couldn't... can you guess it... jump over the “head”. p.s. Look on YouTube you'll see others being able to do it.
(a) Your alt attack; It is never used, nor is it valuable to use.... EVER
(b) The down slide, not only is it never truly explained, but you rarely use it unless if you are forced to. Yes on a few bosses you can use it to dodge things, but you can always do something different.
(c)Your newly acquired boss equipment.... IS ALMOST NEVER USED. I mean never, zero balance there is one “boss equipment” I used almost through the entire game & no it wasn't the “swords”.
(c1)Majority of the time it's easier & more valuable to use your buster gun, including on bosses.
(c2) Just a hint use the boss equipment that does High Damage & is AOE (ease mode)
(d)Many portions of the game you can just run/dash, no need to kill a single enemy unless you are looking for that “high score”.
(e) Tons of Instant Kill locations & I mean a ton. This game brings me back to the NES days.
(f) Most “secret” locations when you find them you are punished, or are not actually rewarded for going to them
(g) Game play that revolves around you getting hit. Some times it's just 100% easier to get hit.
(g1) towards the end of the game the final stage I could reach the final boss with almost full health & all my lives. Yet around ¼ of the game I kept getting hit & ignored the enemies. P.S. It really didn't make a difference “game play wise” to really hit/dash/absorb the enemies.
(h) So you don't have a new equipment piece aka the “AOE Damage weapon”, well a large amount of the levels are set up so unless you received a power up you can't weaken all the monsters in a group & will receive some damage
(i)You will fail, you will die, you have to... this game is designed around repeating the stages just so you can learn how the stage works.
Again it isn't a “bad” game I just feel those who were looking for a “Mega Man” like game didn't receive it. Again for those of you who like the mechanics/area's listed in the other games I highly recommend you buying this game.  I actually enjoyed the dashing system & the absorbing but! I didn't feel the game was designed around it.
DLC: RAY, RAY is a very cool unique character the character you can play as gives you an incentive to "kill" the enemy. but the difficulty sky rockets, the game just feels like it isn't designed for close combat. Considering RAY loses life continuously it makes it so you have to "speed" through the runs but kill every enemy. Again reinforcing this game was designed around speed running.

It was a couple of summers ago. A friend and I had nothing to do, and we got bored of the usual few games that we engage ourselves with: Left 4 Dead, Team Fortress 2 and so on. We ran out of things to play with empty wallets as well. We were students, merry, but poor, and then we saw this new free-to-play game on steam known as Alien Swarm. No harm giving it a try, right? Little did we know that we will be spending the whole of our summer rolling around a blue-themed spaceship setting aliens ablaze.
Alien Swarm is not a big project or game in particular, or so to speak. There is only one campaign of 7 maps to choose from, and the game itself gets repetitive in the long run. Still, what makes this game fun and captivative is the co-operative nature of this game and the array of weapons the game offers. Choosing the right class and weapon will be highly beneficial for the game play as having the right setups will shorten or lengthen the gameplay by up to 10 minutes, and there will be a drastic difference in reward as well. Since this game uses a leveling system, it will mean that one of the best case scenario is to look for a map where you can do quick runs (in a minute or two) over and over again so as to accumulate the largest amount of experience in the shortest time possible.
One thing I am found of for free-to-play games developed and published by valve, especially Alien Swarm in particular, is that there are no micro-marketing. Meaning, every single item in game are attainable through a little bit of hard work and grinding. It’s free, and if you have the time to spare, what’s your reason for not trying?

Alien Swarm is a Third-Person shooter game where you use tactics and teamwork to get to the end of each amazing level. Up to 4 people Co-Op games, and epic close-encounters with Aliens! Equipt attatchments to your weapons, drop ammo, explosives, chainsaws, flamethrowers, I love this game!

This is a morbidly charming game that appears simultaneously mobile-esque simple and simulation-level complex. Fortunately, Plague Inc meets somewhere in the middle.
You'll find yourself balancing competing variables: how fast can I infect everyone without raising the world's alarm so that they don't create a cure in time, how deadly should I be (heaven forbid you kill people faster than you can infect them... at least at first), or how exactly do you infect Greenland, use your DNA points, and so on. There is a surprising number of concepts to juggle for such a simple game. On top of that, the different types of plagues (bacteria, virus, fungi, etc.) all play differently and there are random events that keep you on your toes so that games aren't rinse, wash, repeat.
That isn't to say that there isn't a rythm to the game (at least on Normal difficulty--I'm no genius and I've won 4 of my 6 games so far) or that certain strategies seem to work better.
There are some mobile-esque quibbles that might cause an aneurism if you're a diehard PC master race proponent. There are clickable bubbles to get points, for example.
For all the apparent replayability, a multiplayer mode I haven't even touched, and a fascinating strategy game that ends in human extinction all for a fairly low price, this game is worth it.

Even in it's simple state, Dead State is the zombie game i've been waiting for. What State of Decay should've been: A zombie survival game that places emphasis on "Survival". An XCOM-State of Decay hybrid, I'd recommend this game to anyone whose a fan of strategy and/or survival games. This game oozes originality and fun gameplay, you'll be immersed very quickly into a tense atmosphere where one wrong step can land you knee deep into a horde of Zombies. The only downside is it lacks a character creation, an element that would help bolster the RPG aspect of the game. Other then that, a solid game. Can't wait for it's release.
***EDIT***
Since the game has come into beta, I've pumped a bunch more hours into the game and have only scratched the surface of the game's depth and content. However, one issue that I was unaware of was the travelling system; whilst the game is better then a lot of triple A games nowadays, if you go beyond 12PM whilst travelling back to camp, you die. Now, that seems quite harsh, especially with the games lack of an autosave feature, relying on you to spam that F5 every few minutes. The character creation has been implemented, but it's relatively bare right now, a lot of the features being locked and still being worked on. I imagine we'll be seeing more updates to it within the next few updates.
That being said, the game oozes style and creativity, and whilst state of decay was a poor comparison with this game, it's a breed on it's own; a XCOM and Walking Dead lovechild. If you love strategy, and you love RPG's that you can make your own story to, then this is the game for you.
Can't wait for more updates and more content.

If Diluvion’s gameplay was tighter, with less frustrating meandering and more direction, even the most vague of directions, it’d be a sure-fire diamond in the rough. I understand that the developers wanted the player to take their own time, and I appreciate the effort made to encourage the player to explore. It’s just that there’s just too much time wasting in between. The lulls in gameplay are not exceeded by the thrills of exploration, with the excitement outweighed by the slow, unrelenting crawl the player goes through to get there. It’s a really neat experience… but not a fantastic game.
Pros:
+ Fantastic feeling of being in an ocean. The dark waters are legitimately awe-inspiring.
+ Looks and sounds fantastic.
+ Really interesting game-world, I want to know more about the lore.
+ Landmark and compass-based navigation is a breath of fresh air.
Cons:
- Frustrating movement that often spins out when turning too quickly.
- Docking sometimes works, often doesn't.
- Lack of direction means lots of tedious back-tracking.
- Little bugs ruin immersion and make it a frustrating experience
- Very slow, with bland combat.
- Crew management ultimately adds very little to the experience.

Very cool game, but I might not be as enthusiastic about it as the everyone else.    It has some amazing mechanics, but it also has some parts that get stale.   I'll get right to the pros and cons.
PROS
Very amazing self sustaining system.   It blew my mind when I figured out how you could make something be to the point to where you don't have to do anything is you build it smart.
Amazing ideas for not only having ideas for creating polution, but polution morphs your alien enemies and makes them stronger.   Also that you can avoid this by creating cleaner solar energy.   It is important to note that it still causes polution, but significantly less.   The developers deserve a high five for coming up with this concept.
The world's coolest logistic problems that you can figure out multiple ways to figure out.   This is the game's greatest strength, because in most games there might be 2 or 3 right ways to do something.   In this game, the amount of ways you can do something are endless.    There always seems to be a slightly better way to organize your items and inventory.  A better way to get items from point A to point B.   In truth, it is more like a way to get from point B to C, E, G, H, R, T and Z.   It gets pretty crazy when you have machines that demand so much of 1 material.   How do you get a material there, but evenly distribute it so point G, H and R aren't starved of that resource?   I think I figured out a really good strategy for it and I am pretty pround of thinking of it.   I feel pretty accomplished for coming up with it, because it took me several attempts to wonder how I could do it better.
CONS
Because of early development, AI for aliens is stale.   They spawn, they attack, you eventually kill them, you rebuild what they broke, the end.   It might be nice to get items from them?
Buggy power steam generators
Crafting becomes a little stale.    It is cool that you need parts to make some stuff, but it gets a little....annoying?  cumbersome? needy?   I started getting a little bored because it was demanding so much attention to get what is required to create it.   This should become a strength of the game, because I think the logistics problems are fun to figure out.  It eventually becomes a nuisance and extreamly demanding to craft some parts.   A good example of this complaint, is that it required about 3-5 minutes to automate something easy in the beginning.  Towards the end of the game, it was taking me upwards of 40 minutes to automate crafting one item.  I know it gets even more demanding too.
CONCLUSION
I am a very patient person, but this might demand a little to much patience.   It is worth it if you want a cool game for about 40-50 hours.   After that it might become stale.    I would still recommend, but it might not be worth playing to beat it unless you are a very patient person....   I wasn't willing to invest that much time to make that little of progress.

I understand the bad reviews of this game, which mostly revolve around disappointed expectations. Because I read the reviews, my expectations were more realistic, and so I was pleasantly surprised when I bought it during a sale.
The Good
This game evokes Megaman. It has a fairly steep challenge with an acceptable curve. Some of the challenge is not fun (like when your character won't do what you want it to), but it is a good challenge for a game like this. It's not as hard or unforgiving as the OG NES Megaman games, but it is tougher than Megaman X series games. I like the difficulty level. It took me 20 hours to beat all the levels with both playable characters.
The Boss fights are actually pretty good. Some are more challenging than others and none of them require you to use their "weakness" to beat them. Although for a few, I would have had a VERY tough time without the expoiting weapon. Some of the boss fights are more long/obnoxious than difficult, and a few had a very high difficulty level and took multiple game overs and level repeats to beat (that's a good thing).
The Art is pretty good. It really feels like a cool game universe and everything is consistent and immersive.
The playable characters each go through the same level but offer fairly different gameplay experiences. This makes repeating levels with the other character pretty fun/different which is good for replayability.
The Bad
The Controls are mushy. Some of the bosses and technical jumps in the game require pinpoint accuracy and quite frankly, the controls are not precise enough to do something accurately 100% of the time. I would blow my brains out trying to play this on 1-hit death mode. For instance, trying to slide-dash as you land from a jump will sometimes work, and sometimes just do a normal dash. Sometimes when hanging from a ledge and trying to jump, your character will just let go and fall instead of jumping or pulling himself up. Again, usually the character will do what you want, but not always.
The Story is top-to-bottom absolute garbage. The voice acting fails. They don't bother to make the speaking characters mouths move. The writing is simultaneously confusing and juvenile. It honestly seems like the plot was thrown in at the last minute as an afterthought.
The Mechanics that are unique-ish to this game seem pointless. For some reason the enemies are easily weakened and then you "absorb" them or something with a dash. There seems to be no reason for this for the main character. For the secondary character, its actually a VERY cool mechanic that I dig completely, but you have to play the game for a long time before you get to that point. Again, it doesn't make sense and for the main character doesn't jive with the plot or anything.
The Scoring system at the end of levels doesn't really offer any explanation or way to improve. Some levels I would get a D after killing every enemy and taking no damage while beating it without dying. Other levels I would die multiple times and skip some enemies and get a B. I don't think I ever got an A. No idea how it works. Game also doesn't encourage me to care.
Overall, I recommend this game if you get it on sale. Its a fun little nostalgia piece for any old school gamer's collection.

I did not back the Kickstarter.  When the game came out, I heard the flood of bad reviews and was disappointed enough to never get it.  I've been playing Mega Man since I was 4 (now 29) and have played all of them many times.  Hearing the bad news, I left it alone until a friend of mine gifted this to me a while after it came out.
I went into the game thinking "Here goes nothing"  rather than "Alright!  A new Mega Man game!".  This might have saved the experience for me.  To other who may play the game, I recommend, if possible, that you forget that this was advertised a successor to Megaman.  I have now played the game on Normal and Hard modes and have found a lot to like abot the game.
At it's core, it does have many similarities to Mega Man, but when playing the game, it feels much more like Doom 2016.  If you play it simply to pass levels, it might be dull.  The game is meant to be played at a frantic pace where you constantly push the timer.  And I felt it did very well at this.
The way the power-ups and weapons work, it allows players to adopt a weapon and playstyle they like.  For example, playing well and using the dash mechanic is intended allows me to switch off of "buster" mode and use an alternative weapon for the entire level should I choose to do so.
The way the life works also complements the game well as you can gain an "energy tank" of sorts by doing good combos, meaning that playing slick is more important than not getting hit.
I will admit that there is a lot of polish missing.  There are limitations that I don't understand why they were put in the game.  Weapons are not very well balanced (some are next to useless where I use others more than I use the basic weapon).  The difficulty fluctuates a lot more than it should.  Some levels, or parts of levels are a breeze, where others require very precise movements.  The last boss is much harder than the rest of the game and the game doesn't provide tools to accomodate players not ready for the steep slope.  In a lot of ways, they would have been better off not trying to make this game like Mega Man and do what fits the game best.  As opposed to Mega Man history, the music in the game is entirely forgettable.
Megaman was a game universally accepted in it's time and the series still appeals to a pretty broad group.  This game fits into a much tighter, hardcore audience that enjoys pushing their skills, besting their times or putting themselves on leaderboards.
I think this game would have been received much better if it had not been marketed as a Mega Man follow-up.  Put Mega Man out of your mind and give the game a try

Based on a quick play:
The game is a squad based JRPG with main two phases to combat - Movement & Attack.  Each character's move is planned separately, but all moves are actioned at once. You have to guess where the enemy will go.
The attack phase is based on agility rating and how active your character is. If you have a low agility character in a green glowing square you can pull off a co-op attack with a higher agility character; both must still pay the action point cost to attack. Characters who don't move can perform more attacks than those who ran across the map. The quicker and more violently you win a battle the better your rewards will be.
All world movement is done via a map with travel nodes; you can't freely wander where-ever you feel like unless you're in a quest dungeon.
This is when the game expects you to know that you can jump to clear obstacles in a quest dungeon, as you never have to jump at any other time. The other main flaw with the game is the non-obvious undo/go-back option in the menus. You'll probably look for an exit option, but there isn't one. You right cick to undo or go up a menu level.
The gameplay is mainly mouse with some keyboard keys used outside of battle.
The currencies are G (gold), TP (trade points), PP (profile points), EP (equipment points). TP is for crafting, PP is to enhance sats, EP is for upgrading items to a better quality.
Most of the DLC is items and resources (pay to win style boosts), not extra levels/characters etc, so it's your choice to acquire (during a sale) or ignore. All voices are Japanese only, the subtitles are in English. So far a tidy game from 2010-ish.

This is one of those games structured around a couple of key boss fights, in between which you explore moderately dangerous environments looking for upgrades to your health and abilities while occasionally fighting weak enemies. This means there's very little filler - it gets straight to the point of fighting Jotuns, for the most part, which is great. Combat is simple and fairly intuitive while also being challenging during the Jotun fights, and all the abilities you've gained will prove themselves useful at one point or another. The difficulty curve isn't strictly ascending- the hardest boss fight in my eyes was one of the middle ones, with things getting easier after that.
The game is also excellently drawn and animated, has a well-done soundtrack that perfectly fits the setting, and is bound together by really excellent voice acting in Icelandic that does a huge amount to set the tone and teach you a bit more about Norse mythology as well. For example, I learned about Ratatoskr, the messenger squirrel who runs along the branches of Yggdrasil, provoking other mythical beings by relaying slanderous gossip. Now I know what I'll name that pet squirrel I've always dreamed of.

Plague Inc: Evolved is a well made and enjoyable casual game of strategy with a lot of developer support and expansions, originally not recommendable due to the price, but the content has steadily expanded to better justify it.
As a simulation it has a couple of problems. First the there is the whole human immune system which historically has created far more "cures" to disease than medical science. As a disease percolates in hosts without killing them there should be a rising chance for a natural immune system cure to emerge leaving part of the population immune thus requiring mutation to revitalize its ability to affect hosts who have previously encountered it and will have a leg up on defeating it. Kind of like how the flu comes back every year.
The second more nitpicky problem being that the "goal" of any "disease" is to reproduce. Not to destroy its host. Successful diseases become symbiotic with their hosts. This is touched on in a few scenarios in the game, but is generally in opposition to the main goal. It would have been nice to see other goals such as destruction of a region or set of nations for the bioweapon rather than kill all humans.
The third and most nitpicky issue is with port closings which are the biggest threat to your disease's success and have historically been almost completely useless at stopping the spread of disease.

Pros:
-Interesting (highly linear) story.
-A twist on match-3 mechanics that is enjoyable and strategic.
-Combat system has more depth than meets the eye and player skill MATTERS.
-Failing to complete a run leads to unlocks which make the next run easier.
Cons:
-SHORT. Starved for content and story. It takes 5-10 hours to beat if you're playing at a decent skill level.
-Some mech/pilot combinations are a lot stronger than others
-Random node generation CAN make or break a run at times, but not as much of a big deal as people might claim. Skill still matters more.
-"Only" 4 pilots / 4 mechs. (This is nice considering the indie nature of the game, but in reality doesn't provide variety)
I don't really like the comparison to FTL that some people (including TB) are making. Once you play through the game a few times you can tell that missions repeat themselves a lot more than they do in FTL, and there is no exploration to speak of.
The most successful way to play is to learn the harder missions and how to best equip yourself for them, and to milk out experience and scrap from easy missions by beating them as close to the final turn as possible without taking too much damage.
If you stick to game-winning principles and use a strong pilot-mech combo you shouldn't even fail the first boss theoretically unless you get horrible node generation. The second (final) boss is harder but even so you can beat it with average gear and no mech upgrades what-so-ever. The story ends as soon as the final boss is killed which is frustrating.
I feel this game could've used more dev time poured into its storyline and maybe some more variety in weapons, pilots and mechs. Everything is extremely same-y and somewhat wastes a fantastic foundation in terms of mechanics and replayability potential.

I really want to play this game, a lot. It has a nice theme, it has progression, it has match three elements, the steampunk setting works, and it's fun to watch the machines duke it out.
However, I got bored of dying every three games mainly because there are no ammo, no energy, no coolant, no chance, etc. It feels like I'm supposed to die until my global level is something ridiculously high. I don't feel like there is much I can do to improve my chances of winning any one match, and every match has the odds stacked against me.
If you think flipping a coin enough times to get 20 heads in a row is fun, then I'd suggest doing just that as it only costs you the coin, and even that only if you happen to lose it while flipping.
The UI is also lacking. I can't easily check my own machine's stats during combat, so I need to remember my max ammo slots, energy slots, coolant slots, and repair slots. I can't easily skip the texts that I've seen, as I first need to read a few lines to see if they are new or old. The UI makes me wait stuff, when I just want to get to the next screen already. Effectiveness of projectiles, energy weapons, etc against different opponents is best done by trial and error, since you'll be doing that (=dying) a lot anyway.
Pretty much anytime I happen to get a rare blueprint I'm guaranteed to die the next round when I have that piece on the machine. I've only done maybe 20 matches, and I'm mostly frustrated. I've tried upgrading my guns first, I've tried upgrading my shields first, I've tried upgrading my drives first. I usually die first.
So, I just don't get this type of "rogue like". What is the point of just dying constantly based on a biased flip of a coin? "For every 100 times you fail, your base success rate is increased by 1% point, from the initial 1%, up to a maximum of 49%"?
I play games that are fun and engaging. This is only fun for the first 3-4 fights, and then you die. After the third or fourth death, the fun goes away but you have not learned much that would help you survive any longer.
For some, this might be worth 10-15 euros, but to me this is a 1 eur failure. Hopefully, they'll add an easy mode or tune the numbers to increase the odds, or add mechanics that I could grasp and use.

Oh.My.God. It is like Puzzle Quest had a lovechild with a steampunker. Just started playing, but it is already one of the main reasons I want to get home from work. The sound effects, the music (during the boss batle there is a really grim variant of the La Marseillaise - gave me a braingasm), smooth and simple graphics with a visual style that is really up-to-date, even if it is simple. Everything is just what it should be.
As for the negative reviews concerning the change from the classical match3 gampelay mechanics: Yes, it is frustrating that you can not see what the opponent is matching. BUT, I never felt cheated. It is a cruel game, sometimes you will have an all-you-can-eat-buffet of tiles, sometimes you will cry for at least ONE MORE COOLANT. But it was never unfair. If you stick along with it for a while, you will understand and learn to love its system. I was beaten like a little child the first time I played the boss, but I gained 5 global levels getting to it, so the next time around it was easier (still a bi***, though and still a fail, but I will keep on reaching for the stars).
For all of you lovers of Puzzle Quest like games, and definitely for steampunk lovers (I myself was not one before this game), this is a must buy at an RSP of around 10 EUR during the current sale. The story is more than elaborate and definitely more than can be expected of this genre.

As a big fan of the Halo franchise, I've played pretty much all of the games in the series. I decided to immediately pick this up as soon as I saw it for sale, as I enjoyed the last game, Halo: Spartan Assault.
Spartan Strike's story has you playing as an unnamed orange SPARTAN-IV, tasked with the goal of hunting down the Conduit, an ancient Forerunner object from the Covenant. The first part of the game takes place in a simulation of Battle of New Mombasa during the events of Halo 2, with the rest taking place after Halo 4. The story isn't anything special, but I enjoyed it quite a bit. The gameplay remains the same from Spartan Assault, but with the additions of a new UNSC vehicle called the Kestrel, and the Prometheans as an alternative enemy to the Covenant. As with the Steam release of Spartan Assault, there are no microtransactions ingame, as additional weapons and abilities can be bought with ingame currency gained from completing missions. There is no multiplayer sadly, which is disappointing.  The music(composed by Tom Salta) is one of the best parts in this game, as it sounds closer to original trilogy's soundtrack compared to Halo 4's.
If you enjoy the Halo franchise and/or like top down shooters, I recommend this game, especially at it's current price.

Explore the wonderful world of PLC programming. As a newbie engineer for one of the Chinese engineering company you should design logic boards and write the logic of microcontrollers they use in pseudo assembly language.
I've been lost to this world for three days playing this game, if you're a programmer this is really really addictive game.
If you're not this is your chance to actually learn something. Of course this game won't make you a real engineer but it will give you basic understanding about what really happens inside your electronic gadgets.
You can also compete with other players for less power usage, cheaper chematics or less lines of code.
A bit of criticism for the developers: this is a game. Yes, it comes close to real life programming but it's a game nevetheless, so, please, add the datasheets and descriptions to the parts into the game itself. Alt-Tabbing back and forth can be really annoying.
And I don't know whether the fact that the parts of manuals written in Chinese is intentional to add 'the fun' or we'll have full English manuals some time soon.
My rating 4/5 (for not providing English manuals).

Yes, it's really that bad!
I thought I would give the game a try. I mean, surely it's not as bad as peoplare saying, right? Well, I was wrong! Thanks to the "absorption" mechanic, the game is practically unplayable.
How does this mechanic work? Well imagine any game you like to play. Now imagine the necessity to "capture" every enemy (yes, all of them!) as you defeat them. Now imagine that you aren't actually rewarded for this, aside from a few temporary bonuses. Sounds bad, right? Well it is. You'll be fighting groups of enemies and unable to hit those in the back because those in the front are blocking your shots until you "absorb" them, and absorbing them will often send you headfirst into the enemy just behind them. You'll pretty much end up taking damage that you normally wouldn't in this type of game (and, again, for no reward).
I would also like to point out that there are a LOT of insta-kill moments in this game. In most Mega Man clones it's usually just the spikes you have to look out for, and you can usually depend on a reprieve if you got hit first. Not so in Mighty #9! That "exploit" is a thing of the past! Now enjoy enemies knocking you backward into insta-kill zones. There are also moments where you'll be forced to rush past enemies, smashing yourself into them just to get past a falling bridge that DOES NOT come back (leaving you no option other than jumping to your inevitable demise).
Some other minor details that aren't as bad, but I will point them out anyway. The voice acting is super cringy (but that's to be expected I suppose. If only they hadn't bothered at all...). There are so many instances where you really wish they wouldn't talk at all (since when do the regular Mega Man bosses need?), such as Pyro.
I haven't really played the game much, aside from getting to Pyro (and failing, thanks mostly to his seemingly insta-death bear hug attack). I then played the next stage (ice, but it was underwater at the start, oddly) and decided to stop after getting pushed into insta-death "spikes" by an enemy's attack.
Well I hope some of you are able to enjoy this game, but it's just not playable for me. I would highly recommend other games of this style, like the original Mega Man games (they're on Steam now, so get those instead). If you really want the best then I would suggest Mega Man X1, 2, and 3. (thankfully no voice acting, unlike the rest of the series).
As for Mighty #9, well I would rather pretend it doesn't exist at all.

This title does make good use of several well-established mechanics and has a high level of polish with artwork and music. With that being said, it would be a weak argument to say it brings anything new to the table. The level up system is grindy and gives me odd feelings of idle clicker games. I'll explain more on that in a bit.

It's not all that difficult.
That system is grindy and feels like an idle clicker. It's grindy for the sake of being grindy. You get rewarded regardless of how you fair (yeah, amount of reward changes, but still). I also get feelings of
because it is quite common to enter a room and then fight a few waves of enemies. Success is in getting to know the enemy patterns.
Another review stated something to the effect that deaths are not enlightening like in titles such as
- instead they are a result of a series of minor reflex errors. You get ground down slowly. Yeah, that's true.
+Even after what I said above - it is fun. I will grind away at this slowly, I am sure.
+Music is top-notch
+Pixel art is really well done BUT I do have a hard time noticing the traps and where the background begins and foreground end (I am horribly colorblind, so maybe that's part of it?). Also I frequently overlook door handles. I think they should be a different color.
+Game loops are short for quick play sessions.
+Controls feel tight and it's fun to zip around.
+I like the RPG-leveling up elements and character building.
-Why do enemy bullets not hurt other enemies? Odd design decision that leaves out potential strategy.
-Enemies in bubbles are annoying because your hook auto-grabs onto any number of the other background hooks (and there are a lot of them - just look at nearly any screen shot).
-Colors/artwork make distinguishing between things difficult at times.
-Grindy in a idle clicker kind of way (maybe I'm not explaining this correctly, but yeah). Another way to think of this is the upgrades - awesome! Now you are more powerful... But so are the enemies. It scales 1:1 almost, which can just artificially inflate game length. Or at least that's how it feels in clicker games, and here too.
It doesn't do enough new to merit really existing - BUT I still recommend in the sense that it is a fun game, and if you are on the fence - go for it.

This game is so damn juicy, I am trying really hard to like it.  The developers really know what they're doing; the roguelite loop has been extremely well crafted.  There is such a good game in here.
Unfortunately, if you're playing w/ a controller, there's a fundamental control scheme flaw that completely hamstrings the design.  I can't recommend it unless you play mouse + keyboard.  Too frustrating.
See, the conceit of the game is that you're constantly moving around swinging on these hooks -- its really fun and good.  But it also means your character is spending the majority of his time airborne.  With mouse + keyboard your gun's aim is independent from your character's movement, but on controller the devs have decided to use the main thumbstick for aiming AND movement.  This means that if youre aiming at an enemy while airborne... you're also falling straight into him.  And yeah, you don't wanna run into enemies.  The fact that the initial range of your gun is very short exacerbates this issue since you need to be pretty close to them.
I think the control scheme can be fixed by moving AIM to RIGHT THUMBSTICK.  HOOK goes to LEFT TRIGGER and SHOOT goes to RIGHT TRIGGER.  This leaves SLOW TIME unbound.  I think it would be best turned into a toggle effect and moved to the LEFT THUMBSTICK BUTTON (you know, when you press the stick in).
My other minor gripes are 1) that backgrounds, enemies, and bullets don't have sufficient color saturation differences; it can be hard to pick out important elements during a hectic firefight. And 2) missing or insufficient aim assist for controller.
I hope these things get addressed.  I am sure it wouldn't be a big effort.  Even if it doesn't replace the default I would love it to be added as an alternative control scheme.

It has a lot of inconsistencies that feel 'off' as well - you never quite know what kinds of bullets and enemies can fly through the terrain, what range or vibe they'll have,  and this isn't strange in an exciting or interesting way - it's just frustrating.
All of the stuff in it - the art, the audio, and even the theoretical concept of it - are good.
But the gameplay itself does not captivate.

I'm very satisfied with this game, even after only having played it for 2 hrs. I've always been a fan of Norse Mythology so I thought this game looked like it would be an interesting diversion; it ended up being so much more.
Pros:
+simplicity in control means concise and idiomatic gameplay
+no tutorials or handholding
+first level "teaches" player how to play simply through design
+story unravels in snippets, neither overloading the player with information nor leaving them completely in the dark, which also makes for good pacing
+boss fights require observation and strategy; however, it is clear what can/needs to be done to win.
+consistent, pleasing art style that is conducive to play and that makes bosses somehow more terrifying than they already are
+incredible "camera" work that follows the player perfectly, panning out at points to show beautiful scenes, larger areas, end goals, or to foreshadow events
+Norse Mythology
+excellent, natural voice acting
+well-crafted/composed music
+coherent, game-enhancing general sound design
Cons:
-unable to roll/dodge diagonally
-power move takes sliiiightly too long
-environs/player interactions seem a tad empty (perhaps intentionally?)
-No sprint option. There was no issue with this at first, but at a couple spots a fair amount of backtracking was required and it would have at least felt better to be able to go a little faster.
Neautral/Double Edged Aspects:
=Maps are over simplified and do not show player position. I liked this because it kept me from over-reliance of the map and required me to observe the area and the map to figure out where I was, meaning using the map was engaging rather than tiresome. I could easily see how some would find this confusing and tedious, however.
=Moves are stiff and committal. Maybe this is to promote timing attacks/when to run, or maype to prevent movement exploits. Perhaps I just really like to move while attacking.
=All voices speak in some sort of Scandinavian dialect (sorry, I can't tell which one, or if it's a fabricated language) and there are English subtitles to go along. I personally prefer subtitles while listening to other languages, but I understand some may find this distracting. I honestly think that this way just feels right, as though the words would have less impact or meaning if they were spoken in English with some sort of faux-European accent.
I'm sure there are some points I'm missing here, but this about covers everything important. I definitely would say this game is worth the $15 it costs; and, if you got it for free, I would consider supporting the developers by buying the game for a friend and sending it to their steam account as a gift. As a whole picture or a complete product of visual and aural art, this piece is definitely a breath of fresh air.

Jotun is a great experience and although not perfect, it is definitely worth your time, provided you like boss-rush games.
About half of the game focuses on exploration, which is mandatory to progress the game. You will traverse various levels that are wildly different thematically and although there are no enemies to fight and no end goal to reach, the art, the soundtrack and the various events/puzzles/hazards you encounter are definitely enough to maintain your interest.
The other half of the game is fighting the bosses. The combat unfortunately is a bit shallow and clunky at times, but not a deal-breaker. The bosses are challenging enough that you have to attempt them at least a few times before you manage to beat them, but not hard enough to make you feel overwhelmed.
Overall, the art and general atmosphere of the game is something you shouldn't miss. Even if you will find parts of the game bad, a playthrough takes only 4-5 hours, so it is unlikely that you will be fed up before you reach the end.

Flinthook is a terribly scrambled game with no identity.
Movment is both the center feature and the most problematic part
-The room are far too small
Many rooms, while featuring a large amount of hooks and platforms, also contain walls (I'll get to that later), enemies that deal contact damage, and traps you cant ever get rid of. this slows down the pace of the game and will often lead to unaviodable damage as your "Acrobat" is unable to dodge a bullet without flinging themseles into a spikeball, and speaking of the players hook...
-Hooks and bubbles
The hook works great and is satisfying to use, I love running around empty rooms with it. however it is ruined by putting it into almost any dangerous situation. There exist bubbles enemies that require you to attack them with your hook to make them vulnerable, this isint so bad, a bit redundant as the range of your hook and gun are almost the same but the problem comes in when a bubbles enemy moves over a grapple point, if you attempt to pop their bubble then you will often find yourself flying towards the creature an into other potential damage, I remember one time this happen to me three times on the same enemy as I didnt have the room to readjust myself. This could be fixed by simply making bubbled enemies immune to sub weapons which seems to be the intent as the bubbles protect them from bombs and skulls.
-Momentum and grapple points
The hook features the ability to fly cross gaps and towards enemies so you may shoot them, however this feature is almost broken as you are unable to properly control your momentum, even in bullet time. There is no option to simply hang from a grapple point, let alone dangle or swing, you MUST be rocketed past the grapple point as part of your hooks move, this  may be the first thing most people try and was for me. While options for intracting with grapple points arent part of the design of rooms they would greatly improve the depth of the game, as combat is shallow and looted gold is worthless unless you luck out on a shop. This game starts out well but ultimateally lacks momentum.
-Lack of upgrades
You have 3 real options to spend your pp, Health, Gun upgrades, and bullet time upgrades, Too many upgrades seem to do nothing intresting, some help you surve or give you more nearly worthless gold/xp. the only intresting upgrades are the ones that make your gun better as it starts very lacking and the sun weapons are both rare and weak.
-Monster variety
There is a depressing lack of intresting monsters, most monsters act as stationary turrest or killable versions of the bouncing spiked balls. At the bottom is a list of some monsters and my problems or compliments for them
-Walls.
Walls are a big problem in this game, all floating floors in combat areas should have been platforms that you can shoot and fall through, as it stands players will find themselvs unable to move freely around areas as not only are they facing supressing fire, but they are unable to take cover as enemy bullets and fireballs travel through walls/floors. this could have also been fixed by simply stoping any bullet when it comes into contact with a wall.
-Traps.
Traps are mostly unfair, floor spikes trigger far too fast and most traps blend into the background animations, just unexceuable in a game where healing is hard to come by. this could have been fixed by tinting all damage sources red and reducing the damage you take by traps to half so that your run dosen't end because of a difficult (but rare) hook puzzle.
-The standard enemies:
1:Pirate with gun
This enemy stands still and fires through walls, most of the time he is either above or below you, allowing you to get hit with cheap shots while he enjoys the comfort of cover
2: Pirate without gun
This is a "enemy" that will damage you if you contact it and dies very fast, cannon fodder that you see too much of.
3:Mage
An enemy that shootd bursts of wall penitrating fireballs, good idea, and the inly enemy that makes sence to be able to hit you through walls, though I would have rather just had him do 5 more damage to make him fit the theme of mage better.
4:Exploding bird
These enemies needed to not explode if you kill them, your gun simply dosent have to range to reliably kill them while dodging other enemies, the current fix seem to be that the game simply never spawns birds along with other enemies
-Closing statement
Despite my complaints this is a great game and I dont regret buying it, I hope updates can fix some of the bigger issues and bring more depth or replayability to the table.

Surprisingly fun match-3 game that adds strategy and tactics, oh, and you also get to control stempunk mechs.  With roguelite mechanics every run is different as wel as global advancement so each time you finish a game you become a little bit stronger, or unlock new mechs.

I normally don't like steampunk:  I find the genre overly pretentious (which may actually be the point, I suppose).  But I do love me some giant robots, and you can't deny the addictive simplicity of a match three puzzler.  Add in the strategy of resource management and chance, rogue-like elements of permadeath, random missions, and gear drops, and you have an intriguing game experience.  Ironcast is certainly more than the sum of its parts.
I may not have a lot of time in on it yet (I am bad at it, and only play in short stints), but I have not enjoyed a match three as much as this in quite a long time.

Here's the short of it:
+Simple match-3 puzzle game feeds into complicated mech battles.
+Roguelike gameplay ensures a different experience for each playthrough.
+New unlocks on subsequent playthroughs encourage experimentation.
-Limited Visuals
Here's the really short of it:
Ironcast is fun in small doses, challenging in the long haul.

Pros:
1. It works. I've had no crashes, freezes, performance issues, or game-breaking bugs so far.
2. Art style is nice. Victorian Steampunk.
3. Match 3+ but with limited number of matches per turn, makes you think before matching.
4. Replayability.  As long as you don't rage quit, the game by design is very replayable.
Cons:
1. Frustrating. Be prepared to die every time you play. But each time you die, you usually unlock something new to help you in your next playthrough. You'll often feel like you're never making progress though.
2. I honestly didn't care what was being said between battles.
I'm probably not going to play this a lot.  It doesn't overly appeal to me. I'd rather play Puzzle Quest.  But it's hard to thumbs down a game that works properly, doesn't have microtransactions and tons of DLC, and doesn't appear to pander to Social Justice Warriors.

The premise of Cranium Conundrum is pretty simple, it's a side-scrolling platformer reminiscent of all our old favourites with levels that are user-created as well as a campaign. This lends itself to a lot of charm and endless possibilities, and given the abundance of choices in the level editor and sandbox, it would be easy to re-create levels that are nostalgic and challenging.
I don't want to be negative with this game as there is a lot of potential to be had here. The UI is easy to use and nicely polished. The graphics are a nice nod to console gaming with that refined touch that a lot of ‘faux pixel’ games seem to have these days. The main character (you) is a lot like Rayman. The other beautiful part of Cranium Conundrum, is the ability to co-op. Like in true platformer fashion.
This is a game to watch. If you want to support the developer, and maybe have a little play around at creating some levels (and sharing them on the workshop) then it's a nice purchase. But don't expect a fully polished, ready to play game. There is no story/campaign mode yet.

Having spent a few fun hours playing Ice Lakes, and seeing this game being played by some of my Steam buddies, I've decided to give it a shot. Due to my squeamish nature, I would never consider real life fishing. I would also never kill a person, but you don't see me stray away from ultra violent games (and enjoying A LOT OF THEM). Therefore, onto fishing.
The first ten minutes getting accustomed to game's UI made me realize I am staring at mobile platform / social network game gone Steam. I've asked in global chat why doesn't this game have a better Steam implementation and three or four variations of 'what is Steam?' made me realize I will be playing with mobile phone owners and Facebook Gameroom users mostly. Let it be known, I am no PC elitist nor I will scorn a mobile platform games if they're good. For example, I've played hundreds of hours of Plague Inc. on my mobile phone, way before the game was released on PC. You won't see me complaining. If it's good, it's good.
However, The Fishing Club 3D manages to avoid just a few negative aspects of mobile games. The rest - it's all in there and it's bad.
Let's start with something positive: The Fishing Club 3D looks and sounds pretty. No way it's AAA title, but the graphics makes you wonder how did we get from Space Impact and Sttack Attack to this on mobile devices. Sound is also pretty nice. Music can get irritating, but SFX sounds are relaxing; those of water and buzzing insects help set the mood. The Fishing Club 3D is missing any 'energy' obstacles. I approve of and support this decision - you can fish for as long as you like without the need to spam your buddies for energy which allows you to play some more.
Game mechanics are simple. Way too simple. So simple that after one hour of playing you get bored. Don't get me wrong, simplicity is sometimes a way to go: take a look at Timberman, for example. The Fishing Club 3D only allows you to bait the hook and once the fish is on, you need to reel it by keeping reel meter in the optimal zone, by pressing and releasing the left mouse button. However, game simplifies even this challenge, because at later stages you're only in danger of snapping the line when you're catching larger fish without the proper equipment.
By playing and catching fish you level up, by leveling up, you unlock different locations and equipment (hooks, lines, baits, rods and gadgets). You can buy equipment using premium currency or in-game money. Some of the items (better ones, of course) are only available for purchase with premium currency (goldfish) which you're getting (in minimal amounts) by completing missions (catch x amount of this fish...) or paying real money. You probably know how the game economy works... by promising you a 'relaxing experience', game devs are actually pointing out you will need to change your artistic name to Sir Grind-A-Lot if you want to manage anything without shelling out real cash.
Multiplayer actually doesn't allow any interactions with the exception of joining leaderboards as individual angler or a member of the fishing club.
If you're a casual player looking for overly simplified time killer and you don't mind mobile platform mechanics and economy, The Fishing Club 3D could prove interesting. I am also not recommending it for the same reasons: it's way too simple and there's no real challenge to be found in these waters.

If you've played a Zach game you know what you're getting in to. This is a well-designed and polished programming puzzle game. The solution space is massive and then it's all about grinding out optimizations versus your friends or world histograms. Hours of fun if that's what you're in to!
It looks most like TIS-100, but it functions very differently. In this you use threads that sleep and wake up on timed or interrupt schedules. Your process must sleep between frames, but otherwise there’s no time restriction on how much processing it does in a frame. You’re given a grid to assemble various processors and parts connected by ribbon cables (similar to Spacechem pipes). Your goals are cost (each processing part has different prices), power (each instruction run counts), and total lines of code.
The story is simply that you’re a programmer at a Chinese engineering company. Company emails set up the product goals and then you build the products. Some products have in fiction reference specs which come in the form of the printable PDF. The characters are great and there’s fun bits of trivia and scifi sprinkled throughout. There’s also a solitaire minigame which is pretty fun.
This is one of the most difficult Zach games, but once I wrapped my head around the hardware limitations the challenges became very interesting. High scores can really take some creativity and it fun gloating about a crazy exploit you found while friends believe your score is impossible. Sometimes people ask if this is a good way to learn programming. I don’t think so. Maybe start with Spacechem or Infinifactory.

I usually avoid early access games like the plague. However, with this being my second most played game on steam, right behind Warframe and just ahead of Civ5, I don't think I need to specify how much I like this game.
This game is very much for the lazy man. You make things to make things to do things for you. Automation is the point of the game, and the challenge is setting up your factory in such a way that it can do everything you need it to with you doing as little as possible to keep it going.
Setting up your factory is one big math and logic puzzle. You have to figure out how the parts fit together, and what's the best way to do so.
I can't stand playing Minecraft (or any survival sandbox game for that matter) solo anymore because of this game. Gathering resources is a waste of time that is better allocated to machines.
Also, the dev team is extremely active. They push updates frequently. They post on the dev blog every friday to inform the community about future stuff. They even interact with the community on the factorio subreddit. These guys care about making a good game.
At the time of writing, I'm 425 hours in. I just installed Bob's mods and Angel's mods which together make the game 100,000,000,000x more complicated and I'm loving it.
It's not for everyone though. If you played any significant amount of Minecraft and never made a wheat auto-harvester, you probably won't have a good time with Factorio.

Ironcast has proven me quite wrong.  A very solid, deeply strategic dual-axis gameplay experience.  The puzzle board gathers the resources used for the RNG-based mechanized combat. (Caution: RNG is the core of the combat experience)  All this overlayed on a steampunk Victorian-esque wartime setting for an entertaining, though skippable story.
Decent pricing and gameplay combine for an easily recommened purchase with a single caveat: you MUST be OK with dying.  The rogue-lite element added by the devs means that sometimes the RNG WILL just plan screw you, and you start all over again when you fail.  And you WILL fail, at least once.
Final rating: Buy on Sale

On my second try, I beat the game after around 4 hours and I had lots of fun and some very tense moments. On my third try, I used a newly unlocked officer, a newly unlocked Ironcast, and I didn't really have all that much fun anymore. Even though I had unlocked a bunch of stuff with all the exp from my second try, it just felt like I was doing more of the same and there was nothing interesting waiting anymore, my new officer for example was only the different picture and one different ability. In the game's defense: I get bored of games that have nothing new to offer anymore quicker than most people. So you might get more hours out of this than I did. But where a game like Risk of Rain or FTL or BoI have tons of random abilities and encounters and classes that are very different from each other, here every playthrough feels too much like the ones before it, since barely anything changes.
tl;dr: Generally recommending the game, it's quite beautiful and fun, but there is not enough stuff mixing up your playthroughs, so you might not keep hitting that retry button as much as you would in other rogue-lites.

In combat you are using the match3 system to gather 3 chains of resources like ammo or energy. You have to think what you will need the most and in what order to gather them. Get more energy to power my shield? or maybe ammo and try to finish off enemy mech? or maybe stock up some repair anticipating that one of your systems will be disabled?
Game is using global leveling system to unlock new mechs, pilots and abillities.
I can recommend this game to everyone who playe and liked games like FTL or Bionic Dues.

What bothers me about this game is having level up your global level until you're at a point where you can stand on even footing with the final boss.
In FTL you play, you fail and you learn from it and you get better. You tell yourself you'll do tings differently next time. In Ironcast it's like you're smashing your head in to a brick wall until the wall breaks. You rely way too heavily on the random number generator to give you favorable gems to match.
I found that it's best to try to end a fight as soon as possible because if you don't then the gem board tends to become unmanagable where you can hardly match anything, like there's a bunch of gems stuck at the bottom of the board that you can't do anything with.
What would have been more beneficial to this game would be to have more board manipulation abilities (like Puzzle Quest) so you don't end up with an unmanageable board.
I have a strong feeling the devs only tested this game for bugs but never tested it to see if it was any fun.
I think they could have done something more intuitive with the "target enemy parts" panel. Does it really need to cover the entire enemy ironcast?

And it glitches.
So, I can't recommend playing this game until they fix the save model. If you must, remember to back up your game save (if you can find it) before every mission. Assuming that works -- I didn't do it, and now it's too late for me.

I don't typically write reviews, but where do I begin with this one...
I didn't enjoy this at all. I had times when I almost enjoyed it and thought "oh, I could see some fun gameplay potentially...wait no...I'm still bored."
Pros
-The transformation "Brandish" was kinda neat.
-A few (only a few) of the character designs were nice.
-Some of the voice actors were decent, but even the good performances were undermined by bad scripts.
-Some of the music and sound effects were actually pretty decent...But there was also a con to this, see below.
BTW: I really had to think hard about the pros.
Cons
-Dash mechanic doesn't work well. I want to run and gun darnit! I want to feel like I'm destroying these robots, not take the time to figure out when they become vulnerable enough to dash through. It's an unecessary chore the game nearly forces you to partake in. Without it, your health reserves won't fill up.
-Speaking of health reserves, they vanish the moment you die! So if you're having a tough time with a boss, good luck, because it you didn't nail it the first time with your health reserves, you won't have any for your second or third attempt.
-Character names: Beck? It's fine as a person's name or a pet name, but come on! Beck is way too plain an ordinary for what is supposedly the spiritual successor to Megaman X! The female robot that just feels...lifeless...her name is "Call". I don't even know how to critique that other than it's horrible. Why not a more interesting name? And I know what you're thinking - robots (as we know them today) are in fact "lifeless", but even siri and google assistant have more pep in their voices. And this is supposed to be the future! Couldn't doctor White (don't even get me started with that name) add more emotion to Call's voice?
-The stage you play as "Call": what an awful stage. I freakin hated this. It was like busy work, felt like the team got desperate and wanted to add some content and had no idea what to do. This stage did not save the game from mediocrity. I nearly gave up on beating the game because of this.
-Maniac mode: the only game mode I can use the "retro" skin. Well I certainly am not masochistic enough to put myself through this garbage again on a mode that only take one hit to die. Again, lazy as hell - they must have thought, how can we make a game mode that is more challenging. Lets not bother to manipulate enemy stats and maybe add some "new moves" to the enemy arsenol. We will just make Beck as fragile as burnt bagel...Give me a break.
-Story wasn't very unique, but I wasn't expecting much.
-Voice acting was mostly bad. Even the good performances were annoying due to poor scripting (Dr. Sanda). Sometimes I just wanted to punch that loveable bag of fluff in the face.
-The graphics were lazy as all hell. They look like Nintendo Mii's. From the charactor models to the lazy expressions on their face.
-The sound (music and sound effects) were pretty good but served as a slap in the face to Megaman games (some of which I consider masterpieces). This is because the game makes you feel like it is trying to be megaman, you start getting hyped, and then you realize the game sucks....what a kick in the pants. Also I feel like certain sounds and level tracks were ripped out of megaman games, almost like they used the megaman games for more than just "inspiration".

Megaman, a massive game franchise spreading over many series like the original series, X series, Zero series, and a few others. Needless to say this game is classic and is good enough to have those extended series. Now we have mighty number 9... I will be going over the game in a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.
Pro:
The main menu song is pretty ok. This one song is the only song that is somewhat passable as ok, it is no MMX 5 main menu but it is the only good thing the game has for it. There....happy game?
Con:
No animation in cutscenes. The game has fully voiced cutscenes which is a cool idea...on paper but the execution is very very poor. No animations makes these cutscenes jarring and unpolished for a game that has 8 million dollar budget. Ether have cutscenes with animations or dont have cutscenes. Those old school X5 cutscenes were ok with those 2d stil images, which would be good. Many visual novels do that and i find them an ok way to provid narrative.
Voice acting is awful. The voices are just that awful. They have no emotions and sound phoned in. If there was no voice acting, that would be ok. I dont mind reading text dialogue. Old megamans had that and it worked just fine.
The game is hard as hell. It is not hard for the right reasons, rather it is hard because poor mechanics or bad level design. For starters we will talk about these poor mechanics, the sub tanks. Normally in megaman games like the x games the sub tanks remain filled until used and to refill them all that needs to be do is grind up the extra hp. Here they return but are not fixed to work right. A sub tank can be filled by grinding blue EX but on death all subtanks are lost. Had that maxed out sub tank well too bad you loose it on death. Another bad mechanic is the exposition in the middle of a boss battle. All the enemies have attacks tied  to audio clues. When any exposision during a boss fight occures it drowns out the bosses voice which can lead to more deaths. Good job developers. Finally lets talk about bad level design. Through the game it is full of instant death traps like spikes, some levels have way more than any level in the megaman series and there are quite a few moments of leaps of faith that more than often leads to unexpected death. Why would people make levels on par with super meat boy level design in a megaman game? If that does not top it then enemy placement is awful too. Some enemies are placed at the edge of the platform you need to jump to which slows down pace to shoot the enemy up some and continue or there are moments where enemies are specifically placed to do damage. Those moments are unavoidable and really defines this game.
Conclusion:
I could certainly talk more about cons of the game and how the flow of the game is crap but i think i hit some pretty decent points. Needless to say i think mighty number 9 is an awful game and in the gameplay itself you can see that even the game doesnt want to be played. With its poor level design, poor mechanics the game is in an unplayable, unenjoyable state. The irony is that the developers if they cared about their game, could save it by fixing issues but that will never happen. The failure that is mighty number 9 does more than damage fans of a beloved franchise for believing that megaman is no a dead or dying franchise because capcom is not doing anything with the character but also hurts people on kickstarters both future developers and donators. As a game with a $8 million budget, this game was a huge failure and i can not reccomend the game to anyone.

I didn't follow this game through the Kickstarter hype, and I did see all the bad review, so my expectations were low.
I think the game is amazing. I have no idea what else the Megaman fanboys wanted--probably something like "a grown-up version of Megaman." Except that's impossible--Megaman was a tween-friendly, brightly colored romp with a dorky story and even dorkier enemies in super hero costumes. It'd be like trying to make the ninja turtles "dark and edgy." Mighty No 9's problem is being TOO faithful to its source, except with better graphics and voice acting, so the dorkiness is much more obvious. It feels like a Saturday morning cartoon (abso-freaking-tootly!).
The difficulty is about on par with the early Megaman games, but much easier than MM9. The hardcore Megaman guys are going to find it way too easy, because this game is aimed at kids. You can crank the difficulty (one-hit-death? Really?), but I was never that hardcore, so I turn it down to keep it playable. It usually takes me 5-10 runs at a boss before I can kill them. Easily worth what I paid.

Running the gamut, EHM takes what's good about Be A GM mode in EA's NHL series and turns it up a level. Despite the minimalistic animations of the game, which essentially consist of watching 10 dots with small sticks running around the ice,  the clear meat of the game is within the management aspect of the game, hence the title.
From assigning individual scouts to scour specific countries, leagues, teams or even individual players, to keeping up to date and managing contracts on an annual basis. You will need to continuously conduct scouting missions in order to have information on upcoming prospects, if not, come the annual draft you will find yourself staring at barebone details regarding individual players. When it comes to contracts, be sure to re-sign and add free agents or claim players from waivers as needed, you'll regret it down the line if you forget to re negotiate with one of your star players.
Players in EHM do not have a single 'overall' skill number and instead have over 25 different skills ranging from things like Slapshots, Flair, or Stamina. As well, the coaching staff, including physiotherapists are also ranked with a number of different skills.
This is a great hockey management simulation, at a very reasonable price. However I almost wish I never discovered EHM, because now I have no life.

This is possibly the best game that I have that I refuse to play.
It's fantastic, all-around. Great soundtrack, great art design, all the mechanics are a whole lot of fun and I really want to play it.
It's just that everything about it seems to scream at the top of its lungs that it was designed to be played with a controller... and it *doesn't* have controller support.
What the hell?
The aiming feels awkward with a mouse, it contains your cursor within a certain scope around the character which is roughly the distance the hook and your shots can reach, and it looks and feels like a mechanic that was designed with a right analog stick in mind. I looked at the videos for the game and that's literally the first thing I thought to myself, "Oh, you do this with the right stick, that's cool." - no. No you don't. The game doesn't allow it.
Literally everything about the game's look harkens back to a time when you'd be sitting on the floor in front of a big CRT TV with your face a foot from the screen and your mom yelling at you that you're gonna go blind, but you can't hear her because you're busy timing jumps and dodging enemy pellets WITH THE CONTROLLER IN YOUR HAND.
I just don't get it. At all. What kind of thought process was the developer going through when they thought of making side-scrolling pixel-art platformer and then just slapped keyboard-mouse controls into the plans with a control scheme that begs to be used with analog sticks? It honestly breaks my heart.
I guess I can try to use my Steam controller and see how that works? Or Xpadder and a 360 controller? But why should that even be a thought that I have to have? Why is this not the default? My review should've been something like, "It's neat how they gave mouse-and-keyboard users the option to play it like that if they didn't have a controller handy, but I feel bad for them because the aiming mechanics obviously call for the controller it was designed for. Luckily I have one! I'm gonna go play the game now! It's a lot of fun!"
Instead, I'm sitting here whining about it instead of playing it. The only reason I'm still recommending the game is under the assumption that it will, at some point, be given controller support.

I supported this title expecting the same level of dedication to quality was one finds in Football Manager (not that FM is without it's issues - but it is a very good game); but this - EHM, is not anything like its sports management brother.
This game is apparently a product from developed back in 2007. And it looks like it. Important features are buried behind menus and different screens and navigating to them is far from intuitive. So your left blindly clicking hoping to find what you need. To make matters worth, some buttons are links without a hover state. So it doesn't look like a button or link, and doesn't behave like one until clicked. I discovered some features this way be accident. You can filter some lists, but I've always found this buggy.
Then there's how data is laid out, which is in a busy, packed manner. Wheres FM lays things out in easy to look at, well spaced datas, organized in a pleasing and logical layout; in EHM you have glaring or just poorly chosen colors that either flash or blend with the games background. And did I mention that to date you're going to play this in windowed mode in a display resolution harkoning back pre-1080p monitors? Yes. This game doesn't know what 16:9 is.
The actual games are laid out on a 2d, with stick-figure hockey sticks glued to little circles. Albeit this is better than OOTPs rendition, but its a laugh-out-loud insult to those who enjoy the live 3d action of FM.
I could go on, but, to end on a positive is the community. There are update rosters and all kinds of nuggets of info to be found at
.
To be fair, to date I've put in 10hrs and aside from the horrific UI - when you get the hang of it I did have fun. But I just find the interfaces learning curve to much work that it sucks all the joy out of what could be a really fun game.
Honestly, if you're a hockey fanatic get this on a massive steam sale. If not, move along.

Flinthook is so beautiful and full of character and polish and love... but I just didn't have any fun.
Perhaps it's because I'm a cranky old man who hates everything.
The challenges are designed to annoy you with minor mistakes and keep poking you until your health pool depletes - instead of dying because of big, game-changing mistakes like in Spelunky, for example.
I find this makes me feel increasingly impatient and annoyed while playing - dying is never fun. It feels like the result of a lot of minor reflex mistakes, not one big thing that I can get better at and give me that feel of "just one more run!".
Also
- I found the running and gunning underwhelming.
- The rooms are too small to allow the fun hooking mechanic to shine.
- Too many empty rooms, or with just busywork, and a lot of backtracking.
- A lot of backtracking.
- Sloppy level design in SOME (only some!) of the rooms, with platforms and traps that don't quite match jump height and hook impulse power.
- The absolutely adorable animations between the actual gameplay get old fast, and are very, very long.
- Boss fights are♥♥♥♥♥♥br>
And I think that's it. If all of these (honestly minor) complaints above sound insignificant to you, by all means buy this game. It is a very charming and well-crafted game. I just don't feel like playing it anymore after barely an hour with it.
