Mighty No. 9 is a game that seeks to style itself after Rockman 1 and 2. Do not let anything else you have read, heard, or seen fool you, Mighty No. 9 is incredibly similar to the first two Rockman (Megaman for us North Americans) games both thematically and mechanically. The visuals do escape the Rockman 1 and 2 comparison, however, being more similar to Rockman Legends and the Rockman X games - wouldn't want to get all our inspiration from a single source!
It might appear to be praise, and on one level it is, but in a different capacity, it's a very harsh criticism. Rockman 1 and 2 are extremely fun games to play, and I really enjoyed both of them, but neither is particularly well designed by modern standards. And the same can be said of Mighty No. 9.
Let me talk about what I liked first. Mighty No. 9 is fun to play in much the same way as the 8-bit Rockman games are. The characters are great. Each of the "Mighty Numbers" has their own kind of personality and brings that across in their boss mechanics, voice, visual design, and the special weapon mode No. 9 can absorb from them. The whole experience has a fun kind of Saturday Morning Cartoon feeling to it. The sound track is also pretty good, providing a good backdrop to the world. I've had no technical issues or crashes, either, with the exception that the game didn't want to detect my controller the first couple times I booted it.
However, for a game that supposedly had industry veterans at the helm, it makes a number of incredibly stupid mistakes. The game's checkpoint system is practically antique, using finite lives and forcing a stage restart if they're depleted. Enemies do NOT drop powerups, only temporary boosts when defeated using Beck's dash move, and any stored energy tanks are lost on death. This gives the game a painfully randomized feel.
The dash itself is purposed as a kind of all-function tool, the game expects the player to use the dash to cross gaps in the terrain, defeat weakened enemies, speed across open spaces, evade attacks, and re-position during boss fights using it. Beck is NOT invulnerable while absorbing an enemy's "Xels," however, and it's very possible to take damage from the very boss you're dashing to stack damage on. The game is also designed to trick the player into dashing into off-screen enemies while trying to cross bottomless pits frequently. Sections of some stages that expect the player to navigate mazes of instant-death spikes using the dash are not always designed with the fixed distance the dash travels in mind, causing a lot of incidental deaths that feel like the game's fault, instead of my own.
I didn't pay attention to the Kickstarter drama, because the resulting game is all I'm really concerned with. However I did notice that there's no small amount of mention that the game is heavily influenced by fan input. I think Mighty No. 9 is at least as useful as an educational study on what happens when you let the fans have too much say in a project.
In summary, I can see why people were disappointed, because for a game that had industry veterans at the helm it makes an overwhelming number of amazingly avoidable mistakes that anyone with some knowledge of gameplay design would be able to catch and correct. However I still have to say that the gameplay IS fun, so grab this when it goes on sale. Just don't expect to beat it, if you're anything like I am, you'll need to flip a table and bash your head against a wall to alleviate the frustration first.

Played 8 levels and few challenges. Used gamepad. Wasn't kickstarting. Wasn't expecting much. Loved it. Not a full price purchase though.
Cute graphics. Silly characters. Great level design. Nice enemy design. Responsive and enjoyable controls, with proper precision levels. Game doesn't need you to be pixel-perfect on your jumps and shots but will punish you for sloppiness. No cheap deaths, no struggling with controls. Every time i died i knew that i was careless and messed up. Average difficulty, peaking randomly at some bosses and some levels. Some people might hate that, i liked it because you can never make the game which will be equally challenging for everyone.
Pretty decent speedrunning capabilities in main levels as well as challenges. Mechanic of unlocking weapons feels nostalgic. Using them can be fun, at times - open secrets or kill tricky enemies. Although game could've used a lot more of those situations where i needed special weapons. Some weapons are pretty generic, some are fun to use. Bosses are enjoyable, but nothing out of the ordinary.
All in all its a solid, short, responsive, above average platformer with decent graphics and varied difficulty. At a solid discount its a good buy for a platforming fan, especially if you don't expect it to be some kind of genre revolution.

My opinions on the series conclusion aside, did I enjoy the rest of the show?
The jokes were at least a little fresh but I wouldn't call them great and I wish that the use of fujoshi-inspired humour had kept up a more consistent degree of creativity than mostly limiting itself to sporadic moments of apparent homosexuality and then at other times Akane just geeking out over her two favourite shows - I've seen worse in Genshiken, but it still gets bland very quickly.
The character development is virtually non-existent. Of the main 6 cast only 2 characters undergo a basic development, neither of whom are the main character who stays just as selfish from the beginning of the story to the end.
That's another point, because the series basically boils down to
- Akane is a friendly, chubby girl who hides her true nature from the boys who appreciate her kindness
- Akane is suddenly very pretty all of a sudden, and all those boys finally take an interest in her now that she's more appealing to them
- Akane tries and fails to continue hiding her nature, but fails within the first few episodes. The boys now have to swallow two bad situations at the same time, that Akane loves anime much more than she values actual people and that they have several rivals to contend with.
- The rest of the series never has Akane forced out of her shell ever again and instead follows the disastrous trail of her dragging the boys around to do things that she enjoys, so that they can reluctantly also enjoy themselves in the process.
That kind of selfishness is mostly what led to why I can't like Akane as a character and a major part of why I don't like the show and its messages.
I've wasted my money on things that were a lot more disappointing than a biased comedy about a nerdy girl but I still wouldn't recommend picking this up. For funny, spazzy girl antics you should instead go look for Nichijou: My ordinary life, or Chio-chan no tsuugakuro.

Way more than your average match three game that is actually a lot more focused on the actual combat and decision making than the matching.  Unlike similar match three games that fuel a combat system (something like Puzzle Quest where matches result in instant actions), with Ironcast the matches simply provide resources used in making combat decisions.  This is what I loved about the game as it prevented it from being mindless fun and offered something more.
Having multiplayer would have been a nice touch, but there is still plenty of fun to be had in the game's sole single player mode considering the amount of randomization and the Global Progression leveling system (experience earned in each playthrough carries into a global exp bar that unlocks new perks, Ironcast, pilots, and passive boosts) which keeps things interesting even after you beat the game.  On the negative side, this type of progression system does mean the difficulty is tuned in a way that it doesn't feel meant to be completed in your first try which may turn away some players.
If you are on edge about I purchase I personally recommend it as if the game sees enough success it is likely we will see more updates and possibly even the addition of a multiplayer mode.

I've been trying to figure out what bugs me about this game. In theory, it should be perfect for me. Permadeath, resource management, strategic match-three gameplay, steam-punk aesthetic: it all sounds tailor-made for me. And yet, I don't enjoy it nearly as much as I'd hoped.
The game apes FTL: Faster than Light a fair bit too, but misses a few key design decisions. FTL has a limited timeframe to build up your vessel to handle the end-boss just like this does, but taking risks with your time management can yield great rewards there. Here, there's no risks to take with your turn timer, the strategy only comes through during the actual games, in between those there's little to no reward for good play.
The other big gripe I have is the meta-progress. The end-boss is horrifically overpowered (again, just like in FTL), but in FTL, you get better at the game the more you play it, until you beat the boss. In this game, the boss will pound you into a pulp until you've leveled up your "meta level" enough to stand a chance. That isn't fun. t first, I really liked this desgin choice: when a run goes awry on the last boss in FTL, you feel like you've thrown away 2 hours of your life with nothing to show for it and Ironcast remedies that with its meta-progression. At the very least, you've made subsequent runs easier. But these meta-levels feel like requirements to have a chance against the boss. I doubt the boss is killable on your first playthrough, you have to grind out some levels to make it a fair fight and that is just annoying as sin.
TL:DR Get FTL instead, unless you're really dead set on seeing what these folks did to the match-3 genre. It's not a bad game, as such, but slips on a few crucial points that result in a frustrating game. And that's dispite all its charm, which it has in spades.

Ironcast.
Surprisingly good strategic match-3 game set in a steampunk world with great atmosphere, art, and gameplay.
In the game, there are many different pilots and mechs/Ironcasts to choose from, with most of them unlockable through dying.
How does dying help? Every time you lose, your XP gets transferred to a global level bar which gives you bonuses for your next runthroughs of the game.
As for gameplay, it basically is match-3, except there's no cascading and does require you to think ahead and strategize due to resources being limited. These resources, like Ammo and Energy, are needed to shoot the opponent, raise shields, repair equipment, and move to dodge projectiles.
Story? There is some, and it's pretty interesting. Simply put: Mecha-France wages war against Mecha-Britain and you're the only pilot that can stop the giant mech headed towards the heart of Britain.
Replayability? Yes. Global unlocks, special rare drops, different skills every time you level up, and making your own strats.
Verdict: 8/10. Solid Match-3. Definitely would recommend to anybody looking for a fun puzzler, especially if you like steampunk.

Received the game free from their recent promotion, and while it has some pacing issues overall I would still recommend this game to anyone interested in it. The visuals and soundtrack are excellent, the boss fights are very satisfying, and the adventure through norse mythology is executed in an interesting way. The combat may be an issue to some people but it's very deliberate and I didn't have an issue with it, you feel slow because your foes and their attacks are massive, the attacks have a wind up but you're often given openings to use them, it's not a lightning fast battle system like you might find in DMC or Furi but it still feels satisfying and solid. The biggest issue is the pacing, the levels leading up to the boss fights look nice and often have interesting bits of lore that you pass through and learn about, but often times they feel too empty and too long. Most of them have hazards or traps you're dealing with that aren't really that satisfying to overcome, and even the ones with enemies aren't often that fun to fight, they just exist to slow down the game and pad out the length instead of give you something satisfying to do. Overall because of those pacing issues I feel like 15 dollars may be a bit much, but if you can get the game on sale I do feel the great boss encounters and overall visuals and theme still holds the game together well enough to recommend.

Was looking forward to this and I currently have a mixed reception of the game.
The Controls
-Initially i started with a controller but could not handle moving and aiming with the same stick.
-Moving to M+K is much better, more fluid, would strongly reccomend.

The Visuals

The Music
-Great soundtrack, sound effects are good.
Upgrades
-Very dissapointing. Getting packs makes you somewhat excited, until you understand that the cards themselves are not worth much. You'll just click through the packs you get, might as well not have this, which sucks.
-The permanant upgrades are by far the most important, you feel like they somewhat matter. Very grindy to collect tokens for permanant upgrades.
Bosses
-I have fought 3 of the bosses, not much to them. A little disspointing as well.
Replayability
-Would not even consider putting more than 15-20 hours into the game, there just isnt enough of a difference through each run to warrant that much time

Overall I believe they could have done a bit better at expanding what goes on in the game. Each run of a rogue-like should feel pretty different (especially if you take different upgrades), but with this is feels the same.

I played this game months ago, and the experience has never left me.
Big words, but true.
This is a visually stunning, emotionally mature, big-picture-of-humanity game. It won't be for everyone - action fans will probably lament the amount of time spent just walking around and the lack of a big payoff at the end - but playing this game left me feeling not only as though I'd just spent months in the great outdoors instead of 5 or so hours at my laptop, but as though I'd read a really profound novel.
Make no mistake, this game is a masterpiece of unpacking the human condition. It is by turns beautiful, suspenseful, desperately sad, and unfailingly cliche-busting in the way the story unfolds. I don't want to say too much about the plot or the gameplay, but I unwaveringly recommend anyone to give this game a red-hot go.
The writing and voice acting are just superb - incredibly naturalistic and engaging. If you can't empathise with Henry and Delilah, well - someone should probably tell your parents that they failed to raise a fully-rounded human being.
This is an experience that doesn't cater to infants. It's a tremendous achievement in interactive storytelling, and although I played it more than 6 months ago, it has stuck with me ever since. And that's a sign of a truly Great Game.

Okay, this is a strategy-rpg, and it's a genre I love, I buy any game on Steam as long as it's a strategy-rpg. If you want to sell a game to me, just give it the 'strategy-RPG' tag, along with 'turn-based combat' and I'll buy it instantly.
But it's not like your grandfather's Final Fantasy Tactics, or your great-grandfather's Shining Force, instead it has five generations, each of which is -- mostly the same. The first generation is quite fun. I can't say I didn't like playing through the first generation, because more or less I did, it felt like a good game at that point.
Then you play the second generation and it feels like basically the same game over again, starting from the beginning -- same enemies, same character types, just a slightly different story. Okay, then they expect me to repeat that three more times? No, at that point I got bored. I can play the same game once. I can even play it twice. But to put the same game five times in one game and call it five games in one when in fact it's just one game cloned five times... um, fool me once, shame on you, fool me five times... you can't fool me five more times!
Additionally, the game tries to sell you so-called pay to win DLC. Why should I pay extra money to make an already easy game even easier? To get through the boredom of the five repetitive games faster? It's a decent trick, but again it's a trick.
I don't think strategy-rpgs should rely on tricking the player. They're one of the few noble genres left in the world, less touched by corruption than most game genres. So it's sad to see such tricks creep their way even into this genre. Especially when there are so very few games in this genre on Steam (sure there's a whole slew of western-style tactical RPGs like Xcom and Shadowrun Returns, and they're great, but they just aren't quite the same genre as Disgaea or Tactics Ogre to me).
Bottom line is, the first thirty hours of this game are actually quite fun. Then they ask you to play those same 30 hours over again, five times. And they expect you to pay them more money so it won't feel as boring to do so. That's literally what this game is doing. That more people don't realize this is a mystery.

I think the decision to buy this game pretty much boils down to three questions, if you're on the fence.
1.) Do you like the Halo franchise?
2.) Did you enjoy Spartan Assault?
3.) Do you mind playing more of the same, with some new content and a fresh coat of paint?
Of course, it's not always that simple. Spartan Strike might appeal to people who haven't played much of the Halo franchise, sure. The gameplay is basic, but satisfying. Thanks to the 'Skull' system in this and its predecessor, you can custom-tailor your difficulty to a degree, as well as limitedly changing up a some of the gameplay mechanics.
If you're looking at the game from a value standpoint, my opinion is that it's worth the money... if the gameplay is your cup of tea. I haven't finished the game yet, but I can tell it's most likely going to be short. I don't have a problem with that, considering the reasonable price tag. Honestly, $6 feels like a sale price already, especially considering that the aforementioned Skulls can add some challenge and a bit of replayability.
Now, for fans of Halo, this game succeeds in capturing a bit more of the large scale feel of the previous Halo games a lot better than Spartan Assault, at least in the beginning. That doesn't mean it's got huge levels with divergent paths and a whole lot of room for creativity in your runs, it just means that the actual scale of things is better. There are background events you can pay attention to going on above or below your field of play; the second level even had the huge bridge from Halo 2 down below, with what I assume to be Master Chief in a Scorpion tank blowing up Ghosts. It was a nice touch.
I can't speak for the state of the port. Honestly, I haven't had any issues playing the game. The game looks reasonably pretty, though I might not be the best metric for that. I thought Dark Souls I looked good on PC. Performance is solid, even on my relatively low-end PC, but that's to be expected from what's basically a side-by-side PC and mobile game. Luckily, there aren't any of the microtransactions the mobile version undoubtedly has, which is always refreshing.
All in all, I'm enjoying my time with Spartan Strike. If you like Halo and don't mind a bit of rehashing, give this game a try. Then again, if you like Halo, you have to have a pretty good tolerance for rehashing. If you like twin-stick shooters, this is a pretty decent one.

I don't usually write reviews, but this game is already so good and still has such great potential, coming from a die hard hockey fan, I love this game.
Pros:
Scouting - Scouting mission details can be changed like player age, position, or ignore well known players/prospects, and it really helps you find the players you need, whether you're playing as Arizona stocking up on talent, or Detroit looking for a diamond in the rough, or Montreal and you are looking for some proven foreign skill to boulster your roster for the cup run, you can find the players you need. You can also generalize the scouting by assigning a scout to a continent, or country/nation, or you can assign him to individual leagues, you can even assign a scout to a particular player if you'd like.
Game simulation- You can choose to simply speed up games to get it over with, or you can watch the game real time and make tactical changes, line changes, etc.
Line Changes/team tactics/unit tactics/player tactics- Wow. Just great. You can change defensive zone strategies, neutral zone defensive strategies/positioning, neutral zone offensive strategies/positioning, forecheck, breakout strategies, offensive zone strategies, and of course special team units like PP and PK. You can choose which player is le playmaker of the line, choose who takes faceoffs (which is great I'll explain further in), etc you have absolute control of your lines. You can also change individual tactics, so if you have two offensive players and a power forward on your first line, you can change the line to not body check often or hard, and not be aggressive, then go to your power forward individually and make him check hard, play aggressively and with a high tempo to balance out your line, or set a defensive type of player to shadow an opposing player and keep him in check.
You also have control over practice so you can train what coaches do what (coaches have attributes like coaching defensive players at 17/20, but then he might have 11/20 for coaching forwards and a poor goalie stat as well, so make him only handle defeinsive training. I believe it helps, clarification would be nice though. You can make certain player focus on an area of the game that maybe he is weak at, or boost what he's good at even more. You can have signing bonuses for games played, points, shut outs, etc.
Those are a few things that stuck out that I liked

Standpoint is a first-person puzzle game that allows you to manipulate gravity and the world's orientation to overcome obstacles.
I currently have around 26 hours in the game and it's easily one of the best puzzle games I've played this year. It's simple to pick up but deceptively challenging. The game has around 20 chapters that mix up the mechanics as you progress. The more you play, the more you learn how to manipulate the world effectively. It can get pretty difficult as you move further in to the game but nothing too crazy as StandPoint does a good job of preparing you for the later levels.
StandPoint's puzzles offer a good balance of reflex based solutions and thinking solutions. The chapters offer enough variety to keep you interested to the end and despite getting frustrated at times trying to figure out a solution, actually realizing what the solution was and executing it became really rewarding.
I'd say my favourite parts of the game were the hidden "secrets" as they offered a completely new challenge to the game and required a lot of creative thinking to find and aquire them. These secrets along with time trials and challenging achievements definitely give you your money's worth and make this game a sure recommendation.
I'd pick up this game for sure if you like games like Antichamber, Relativity and Portal (obviously) as StandPoint offers something unique and interesting enough to keep you playing until the end. The dev is a cool guy and listens to all player feedback and fixes any bugs in a timely manner too. StandPoint is a great puzzler that offers interesting mechanics with a supported underlying narrative that brings it all together.

Victor and Olivia are back! While they're wanting just some rest, they find themselves on a land where Olympus Gods are reigning... or more important, they were reigning as the land is in disarray. Olivia got sucked into another world, captured by a demon, leaving Victor to embark on a journey to save his wife.
Weather Lord: Legendary Hero follows Following the Princess. However, the game has new mechanics and new graphics.
The gameplay brings back the deck of the three weather elements, which is better as you don't have to find them anymore on the level. While workers are still collecting ressources, now, you don't have trees or fields or mines. You have to build a grain mill to have fields to harvest, a sawmill for trees to chop and mines to get gold. Improving these buildings will allow you to increase your production. In other words, two gameplay mechanics from previous games were fusionned in one. However, you can still collect these ressources thanks to bushes or obstacles or shipwrecks or treasures. Besides, now, you don't have to build an house anymore for more workers, you can hire them from the wagon. As the game has also a seaside landscape, you'll get buildings to restore which will give... ressources: gold, food and wood. However, a new type of ressource appears and replaces the crystals: the fame, the only ressource that can't decrease. You can earn it by building arenas or fountains, defeating wild boars or even by speaking to natives (and restoring their houses). Also, you have traders to exchange ressources. Also, fairies houses can be used to make money when you can't build a mine or an archaeologist's tent.
The weather elements are these ones: wind (for mines, dissipating fogs or make trolls fly), rain (for flames, grain mills and sawmills), wave (for pushing vases with ressources to the ground, for leading aways turtles or shells, for fisherman's hut and archaeologist's tent), sun (for drying roads or puddles and for corral houses), thunder (for drying lava or destroying barricades), rainbow (for restoring portals, dissipating mirages and uncast a spell on fairies). These elements can also be used to drive away enemies, replacing the warriors from previous game, whether directly on them or by building a tower. Also, for some actions, like inflating balloons for trolls, you need a stronger element than given at the beginning of the level: you have to restore altars.
Also, you have also bonuses that you can use during the level: hire a temporary worker, stop time, more wood, food or gold, working faster.
The artifacts gameplay has also carried over: you can use three per level and they're varied: more wood, more food, more gold, longer bonus, elements getting resplenished faster, more ressources after using an element, etc..
As you can see, Legendary Hero, while true to the Weather Lord series, is also changing some aspects and making the game easier, at least for me - apart for one of the levels.
Also another major change is the design: it's more cartoonish now and more in 3D. While the magma golem and ghosts are still the same, the goblins changed, the workers changed and well, the ressources changed. It's a nice improvement. The music is still enjoyable.
You have also bonus levels and Collector's Edition levels, which can help for the ingame achievements, way more easier to achieve than in the previous games.
My only negative point is Olivia being a damsel in distress (yeah, I've played Royal Holidays where she is contributing, it's kind like of Megara in 12 Labours of Hercules).
The whole Weather Lord series is worthy (I didn't play the two first games that aren't set in this universe), so yeah, I can recommend the game.

Ironcast is nice little gem in the vast sea of games.
It is a Roguelike mech fighter where you can get your resources from making connections in a classic gem matching game. You have 2 offensive and 2 defensive systems on your mech each can have an augmentation. Your hero and your mech warrior can also have augmentations, 4 each.
The game is fairly challenging and actually it requires you to understand your opponent. You can't just go crazy and shoot without any consideration. You want to target specific sub systems of the enemy mech to make your fight easier. Sometimes ignoring hints or even direct orders from your command can cost you the mission or even the game. (Remember, it's a Roguelike, if you die, it's game over. You have to start from the beginning.)
The story is interesting and I also liked the ending. I love that fact that you have a global XP, meaning even if you die, you have gained something for your next game (a little bit of extra HP per level ups, more augmentations to choose from, new heroes or mechs, etc).
The graphics is nice, the sound is nice.
Only thing I found as a negative is the text. Sometimes I miss the voice acting, but what I mean is the dialogues are sometimes messed up. The displayed text is not checked and contains word duplication, inconsistencies (mission description says different than in the actual mission). These are just minor thing and I found only 2 or 3 of these in my the play time.
If you like mechs and gem matching and you are not scared of a roguelike and enjoy a decent challenge, this game is for you. Especially when it is on sale.

the addictiveness of match3, the fun of turn based combat, the style of steampunk and the awesomeness of mechs.

If you were to create a Steampunk mech-like setting, toss in RPG elements and turn-based strategy, and then use Match-3 mechanics for the combat while implementing Roguelike permadeath, you'd have Ironcast. Unfortunately, there's a lot wrong with it, so much so that it overshadows the game's good qualities.
First, the game mechanics: you have a choice of four pilots (you start off with one), all of whom have different bonuses attached to them. Likewise, you'll eventually gain four different ironcasts (which I'll refer to as "mechs" from here on out), but only start with one.
You can usually choose between three or so missions every round, after which you'll appear in the hangar to repair your mech and purchase new weapons, drives or shields/armor. Every time you level up you'll also get a chance to pick a new active or passive ability (the choice is randomized, so there's really no telling what you'll be offered).
The combat is a little different from typical Match-3 games in that you don't click on each individual node (different colored pieces that represent ammo, energy, coolant, and repair), but instead click on one node and hold down the mouse button, connecting a line between the nodes you want. This works a lot smoother than most Match-3 styles, plus it also manages to avoid the constant cascades of new pieces that plague many Match-3 games.
Now then... I said there are quite a few problems with Ironcast, all of which I shall detail below:
1. The game only saves when you're in the hangar. If you need to leave the game for ANY reason during combat, your entire campaign will be deleted. Got a real commitment? Too bad. You're going to lose all of your progress if you need to quit.
To make matters worse, this includes errors like crashing to the desktop, your PC freezing up (and needing a reboot or you've got to kill the Steam process), or a power surge. So even a situation that's beyond your conrol could cost you your entire campaign.
The above isn't a hypothetical either. Someone in the forums had a technical problem and in the end, the game deleted his progress.
2. Ironcast claims to be based around strategy and while there definitely is some in the game, the single greatest factor is luck.
How well you do in the campaign is directly tied to your mech's capabilities, which stem from three different systems (weapons, drives, shields/armor) and any active/passive abilities you have.
The problem is that what abilities and weapons, drives and shields/armor you end up finding is completely randomized. If you're lucky and you get some really good abilities and systems early on, you'll probably do well, but if you don't, you're pretty much doomed from the start.
In addition, the Match-3 gameboard can make or break you in a heartbeat. Say you need more coolant or energy nodes, but the game doesn't give them to you. Now you've got to waste turns getting rid of crap on the board you don't want while at the same time being unable to fire your weapons, raise shields, or even move.
3. Combat always starts off unfairly. When the first round begins, you can't shoot, but your opponent can. This means that the enemy effectively gets a free shot at you, so unless the AI does something really dumb (and it has before), it WILL score a few good hits before you can even think of returning fire.
The in-game explanation is that it takes a round to "charge up your weapons." This begs the question, "Why would anyone enter combat without being able to fight immediately?"
Oddly enough, you can still move and activate shields just fine, so apparently your pilot is smart enough to think about defending himself or herself, but couldn't properly prepare to do any damage.
4. Repair costs are insane. It's not uncommon to spend 50% or more of your earnings on simply repairing your mech. This makes purchasing new weapons, drives, and shields/armor extremely difficult as those items are very expensive.
So what's good about the game? It's a neat fictional universe, and if you like the Steampunk setting at all, you'll probably find something to enjoy. If you're looking for a more casual game (like Puzzle Quest) don't bother, as the Roguelike game mechanics will infuriate you.
All in all, I'd suggest buying it if and when it's under five dollars. At anything above that, it's simply not worth it (as of this review), but maybe that'll change at some point in the future.

Don't let my play time fool you, I have played this game on the Xbox 360. I have beaten this game once and by the gods, this is by far my favorite J-RPG.
J-RPGs are known for being tedious grind sessions, great story elements, and of course, great 'plot'. This series has it all to be quite frank, and I love every bit of it! The visual novel aspect of this game makes it different from most other J-RPGs, and even get the chance to romance with 3 woman for the first 4 generations is pretty limiting, but it's enough!
This game is not for the faint of heart, it has moments where you will feel for a character, and you will want to keep playing. My only bad nag about this game is that there is sometimes a long point-to-point battle system. However, the ability to return to these already battle-fought points for grind makes it easy for grinding and material hunting.
This game is long, overly long for a J-RPGs to take place, however, the endings makes it worth while. I have only ever gotten the neutral ending, and I plan to play this to get te true ending!

Going to start this review by simply saying, this is a grind heavy JRPG with an incrementally harder learning curve as you go on. If you don't enjoy having to grind a lot, and you don't enjoy the general concept of a JRPG, I strongly believe this is not a game for you.
With that out of the way, this is my first Agarest game I have played, and I did truly enjoy the experience. I found the art and soundtrack to be very well done all-in-all. This game has a dating sim portion to it, and that much I could have personally done without, though it isn't really that bad. The game has easily a hundred hours of content if you care to do every little thing.
I find that this game tried to standout as a good and strong stand-alone JRPG, but it failed that to an extent and made it into a pretty generic one. Furthermore, I believe the story itself is also quite generic, and has been done many times before. The story itself, although generic, can be captivating. The game tries to make you feel as though you can change the story based on your choices, though they do very little beyond forcing you to take the shorter or longer path.
To conclude, this game is a roughly generic JRPG, but it comes with countless hours of gameplay and a very strong value for the cost of the game. I recommend this purchase to anyone who's a fan of JRPG's and is looking for something along the lines (especially at it's price)!

1. The plot.

This is an anime JRPG (like we didn't already have enough of them). You can have 6 characters at your disposal at once to do your dirty work (and killing batmans) when you go into characters menu, which will always at the end be the 5 main characters and Plum. StandPoint is a Fps puzzle platformer that forces you to master gravity and spatial thinking.
The gameplay of StandPoint on paper is rather simple. When you point towards a wall with you'r cursor and click the left mouse button, you change the characters own personal gravity and make that wall into an floor.
Using this one mechanic you must navigate through these levels while trying to figure out the right course of actions on how to get through them.
At the start it's just changing the gravity to the roof to avoid an obstacle, but rather quickly the game's difficulty starts to spike up as it brings elements into the levels that affect you and the level itself in number of ways.
Like moving deathrays and such that you must avoid (hence the name deathray), surfaces that do not allow the change of gravity and walls that let you through only if you are on particular gravity level/plain/field?
There is also a story in the game which is at least intriguing if nothing else. Mostly a female voice narrates about something that has happened to her or perhaps to the player itself, not really clear as of yet to me.
The voice also changes it's tone depending on the stage where you are at.
The stages are separeted into themes following the 5 stages of loss and grief.
In the denial stages the narrator is indeed very much so in denial and as you advance to anger she gets really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of at everything.
The visuals also reflect the emotional stages very well and help you to set yourself into that particular mood.
The music fits and there's nothing else really about it to say except that it has the same effect with you're movement speed like in Portal. That was cool.
You'll get some replay value from this by trying to beat you'r previous time records and trying to find all the secrets of the game which give you some more tiny story bits.
All and all a good puzzle platformer, but I'd still prefer portal with its humor, then this psychoanalysis of humans but its still interesting.
Do check my video out if you are on the fence about you're possible  purchase or just watch it anyway.

Alien Swarm is still my favorite multiplayer co-op game and is also the reason I created my Steam account.  In its current state, you will have to find friends to play this game with as the community is basically empty. However, back in the day, before TF2 went free to play, there were only 4ish free games on Steam and Alien Swarm was one of them. Alien Swarm could often be seen as the second most played game right after Football Manager 2011 it was da bomb and for good reasons besides being free. After Team Fortress 2 became free to play, and Valve's new Free to Play category soon after Alien Swarm slowly saw a decline in players until it had finally reached the barren state it currently is in. So if you plan on playing this, get some friends or hope that you will find a game during steam primetime.
Alien Swarm can be very punishing if you make a mistake. It requires its players to stay focused, move quickly, and keep together as a team. This makes the game very difficult to new players trying to figure out how to be successful, and I've seen players never figure out how to work together and drop the game.
However, when playing with other good players and finding out what you do best in the team Alien Swarm can become an extremely fun game that ends up being one of the best co-op games that I happen to know about.

This was one of those games that looks really promising. A strategy game like Civ with unlimited potential and real time strategy where every move you made would make an impact. That is certainly what Plague Inc evolved tries to be, atleast.
After almost 10 hours in this game I've come to the sad realisation that there is very little depth to it. You gain DNA points -the points used to upgrade your disease - overtime as you infect/kill more people, and also from occassionally clicking on little pop up bubbles on screen. You can then use these to add Symptoms to your disease, manners for it to spread and to increase its resistances to certain climates or being cured by the humans. This may seem interesting at first, but once you figure out which upgrades to use the game really has little strategy involved and is more so based on probability and luck.
It is also worth mentioning that this game leads you to believe that there is much more content than it actually has, in the main singleplayer, that is. You start off with Bacteria and can see that there are other disease types you can unlock once you beat certain difficultues with Bacteria. Now you may think that these other disease types would have much different gameplay to them, making the game diverse and complex. Wrong! Every disease type is practically the same with a few minor adjustments.
To give this game some credit though, it is fun for the first 5-8 hours or so when you don't really understand the game's underlying mechanics. You can sit there and be an evil mastermind, watching humanity crumble before you as you upgrade your plague. Not to mention its hillariously amusing to name your disease after something stupid due to the in-game pop up's you can get.
Is it also important to mention that this game does have Steam Workshop, and thus there is a surplus of player content to go through. The player created levels are far more entertaining that the ones the game gives you (and a lot more creative!).
If you're buying this expecting a strategy game with the depth of Civ you're going to be disappointed. If your intent with this game is to just have a good time laughing at popups like: "Furries to Eradicate Humanity!" then I would say go ahead and buy this. I just do warn that this game isn't that entertaining after awhile, and I would advise buying it on sale rather than at full price. It's definitely not a "must have" game for your Library.

-Unique Scenarios that depict real life plagues or something completely random to occupy you after you beat the core game.
-The ultimate feeling that will please all sadists knowing you are killing off all of humanity.

-I really dont have other cons personally, if I play this game more and I find some other things personally tedious, I will add them.

I finally finished Mighty No. 9 (on Steam/Windows). I have to say, the game is as challenging as people have made it out to be and even I felt frustrated at several points in the game. However, I felt the same way when I had such difficulty when I first played Mega Max X4 on Playstation One when it first came out. It didn't play the same as the SNES version for X1-X3 and both my brother and I had difficulty with that game. I tend to compare that difficulty at the time to how Mighty No. 9 handled in that respects.
That being said, part of what lead to my initial frustrations was realizing that with only three lives that, once lost, you had to start from the beginning again. I found out that in options you can increase it to 9. I wish I knew that at first. What helped me through the games at times were videos and walkthroughs only when I needed them (such as who to go after first and how to beat the last boss). Otherwise, I learned on my own. Thankfully, I knew the eight bosses' weaknesses thanks to Mighty Gunvolt Burst which uses the main character and the eight bosses from Mighty No. 9 so that made things a bit easier.
Many of the backers tend to bash this game since it was crowdfunded due to several issues which I won't go into here (they already know what the issues were). However, playing this after it went on sale and from the standpoint of a non-backer, it does have its points of frustration and I understand that if you have been used to how Mega Man games have gone. But this game is NOT Mega Man. It may have a similar feel to it but it tries to make itself unique in ways that Mega Man was not. I may have been frustrated playing through it at times but those times eventually passed. In the end I would say that it was enjoyable to play and was a different experience than what I have been used to.

Growing up playing ther original Homeworld game, I had to pick up Deserts of Kharak as soon as I saw it. Nostalgia may have led me to buy the game, but that isn't what ept me playing it.
DoK is an interesting prequel to the series. Taking place in the titular deserts of the planet Kharak, you lead a carrier and her science officer through the desert to locate an anomaly and find out the fate of a prior expedition. Along the way, you are hounded by a hyper religious group of desert nomads trying to stop you from completing your goal, seeing your use of technology as sacreligious. The character of Rachel S'Jet (the science officer and protagonist) is very one-dimensional, but her lack of depth doesn't take away from the story. After all, this isn't a deep story game, but a strategy game with a small story to lead you from one battle to the next. While that sounds like admonishment, it's not meant to be; merely it is an observation. The story is decent and kept me entertained enough to actally listen to it.
The visuals are phenominal though. I loved the art style of the story cutscenes. It was a unique choice to go with what are mostly painted stills telling the story through voiceover. They mixed surprisingly well with game engine footage of units moving during other cutscenes and added to the enjoyment of the otherwise mediocre story. The actual units in the map looked great as well. The Coalition forces use wheeled tanks and rovers for their armies against the hovercraft of the opposing Gaalsien. Though I did prefer the sleeker, more advanced look of the Gaalsien over the rough-and-tumble look of the Coalition, I did learn to like the less refined look of Coaltion forces, especially since it fit with their losing war of attrition against the antagonists. The only complaint is that each map looked almost the exact same as the other map. I get it's a desert, but more variety in maps would have been nice.
The only other complaint I have is in the "strategy" part of a strategy game. Namely, there isn't any. Overwhelming force in your friend, underwhelming force will make you lose. Load up on railguns and missle boats and you'll be fine. I won most levels by spamming railguns with a handful of missle boats for air defense. Throwing in a couple assault units to mop up the strike craft made it a walk in the park. Don't go into this looking for any depth to your strategy. You won't get it.
With that, I do recommend this game. It's good. Not great, but I enjoyed every second I played and definitely got my money's worth. Other than the caveat of strategy-lite on this, it is a decent play if you enjoy strategy games. If you only kinda like strategy games though, I'd stay back. The grind to build up your forces can get dull since all you have to look at is sand and a blue radar screen.

Thank you to the developers for a recent update, almost two years after launch, that provides some nice upgrades, in particular "tactical pause" also called "free pause".  This has revived my play of this game.  Why?  A problem for me with RTS games is there can be too many things happening to control at once, especially mid or late in the game or mission.  I enjoy pausing when it is getting too hectic, analysing the situation, and issuing orders to my units.  I don't enjoy feeling majorly rushed to control lots of units at the same time.  I enjoy taking in the gameplay without the rushed feeling.
Let me immediately say that yes, I know many RTS players believe that tactical pause spoils the "real time" aspect of RTS.  My answer to that is, if you don't like tactical pause, don't use it.  There is no harm to you from this feature.
My other comments would be that the RTS basics of this game are good.  The gameplay is good, the user interface is good, the graphics are good. The graphics (the setting) are very atmospheric -- the games is set in a desert planet, and it feels like it.  There are not only cut scenes before a campaign mission, but also cut scenes are triggered during missions, which makes the story stronger.
(My comments at this time are based on playing the campaign, which I have returned to now that tactical pause has been added.  Tactical pause adds just enough, on top of the game's other merits, to push the game up and over its competitors into my "play" list at this time.)
If you enjoy sci-fi RTS, there's a good chance you will enjoy this game.

I just finished this game, and right now I'm like wow. Not because the story is grand (it isn't) or because you love the characters  (I don't) but because this is a terribly hard game. To the point where I would say it's unbalanced.
So Agarest Generations of war is a strategy RPG, like say Disgaea but not as good. The game is divided into different chapters, where in each generation you get a different protagonist (the son of the prior one) and a couple of different party members. Mostly females, as candidates to become the mother of the son for the following generation.
So don't put too much grinding in certain characters, because they won't be available in the next generation. Because of this, I didn't use the main character or his possible wives in my party, because I would need to grind to get their levels on par with the rest of my team.....only to lose them again at the end of the chapter. If you think that already makes for a tougher game; one of your characters who might very well be one of your best ones, becomes a traitor and ends up leaving your group. Yeah, I loved it when that happened.
Now that just makes the game harder, but it's not necessarily the reason I think the game is unbalanced. Keep in mind that the pc version of the game gives you a couple of uber weapons from the start. This gives you an unbeatable edge in the first 2 chapters, however things soon will change once you go further into the game. As your party members die left and right in even a random fight. So not against a boss, just a simple random fight.
For me, and I'd say I'm far from a novice when it comes to (S)RPGs, it became impossible later in the game to proceed from certain fights. So I bought the dlc to give my character stats a boost. So now I have the uber weapons, and the padded stats. Thankfully the late game becomes doable at this time......untill you meet the final boss. Holy mother of God, even despite all the extra buffs this fight was next to impossible. To the point where I wonder how players defeated this game without it, because uber weapons and super stats be damned, that thing killed my party easily multiple times.
It makes me wonder either if I'm doing something wrong, or if the game is unnecessarily difficult to make people buy the dlc. At any rate, be aware that this game is hard. I kept playing because of the challenge, but just barely. As mentioned above the story is rather fluff, and the characters pretty bland. So the challenge and the fact I like SRPGS are basically the only +s for Agarest. I would say it's above average. Worth a buy when it's on sale if you're into these types of games.

If you enjoy turn-based combat RPGs with a subsystem-based damage model, alongside a link-based Match-3 system for gathering your resources, I do insist that you consider putting this in your shopping trolley. Though you may end up being screwed by bad luck from time to time, in the form of your attacks missing your moving adversary, ending up with a sub-optimal board and so-on, the non-random mechanics of the combat are still very much solid, allowing you to repair damaged subsystems while ensuring you have enough Coolant, Energy and Ammunition to doll out punishment and minimize your injuries.
But what of the progression system in the game? Well, at the end of each mission you acquire Scrap, Experience and War Effort, alongside system blueprints and sometimes even intact enemy systems, all of which play an important role in the battle for Great Britain. Scrap is generally used to convert blueprints into various weapons and defensive systems for your Ironcast mechanical walker, and can also be spent on increasing your health and the capacity of your resource tanks. For each War Effort point, the forces of Great Britain will be able to deal a point of damage to the massive enemy Ironcasts that serve as the game's bosses, so if you gain a great deal of War Effort before the boss fight you will stand a better chance at defeating the gargantuan interlopers that threaten Queen and Country.
As for Experience, it functions as you would expect in most RPGs in that it will drive you to level up and become even more powerful. However, rather than flat statistical increases or allowing you to progress further down a skill tree, each level grants you a Skill Point and makes you choose one out of three different Abilities or Augmentations. Excluding the Core Ability and Core Augmentation granted by your initial choice of Ironcast and Pilot, you will be able to equip three Ironcast Abilities, three General Augmentations, two Weapon Augmentations, one Shield Augmentation and one Drives Augmentation, all of which can be switched out in the Hangar to customize your Ironcast as you see fit.
Speaking of the Ironcasts and their Pilots, when you first start playing the game you have access to 1 Pilot, Lady Aeres Powell, and 1 Ironcast, the Dunraven, but later Pilots and Ironcasts will be unlocked as your Global Level increases. In the spirit of modern roguelite progression, the experience you earn during the campaign will be added up at the end, most likely when your Ironcast has been blasted to Timbuktu, and cause your Global Level to increase while unlocking new options in a linear succession. For the most part, this is a vital system for any roguelite title nowadays, as each time you play you are guaranteed to have unlocked something new when the campaign is concluded, whether it be the stalwart Sir William Beechwood, the Energy-focused Arundel-class Ironcast, new Abilities/Augmentations to be introduced to the pool, or even simply starting with more health. But while it ensures that you are always making progress, the depth of Global Levelling seems shallower than the main levelling system, in that you do not have the same element of choice when your Global Level increases.
All in all, I would say Ironcast is a jolly good show, but rather than expose you to a base and primitive numerical score to sum it up, I will instead give it "achievements" in a similar fashion to a Mr Ross Scott, citing prominent points of the game in a more concise manner.
-Every Run Earns You Something
-Rather Replayable
-Wonderful Aesthetic
-Good Customizability
-Big Stompy Mechs
-Beautifully British
-Compelling Combat

Initially I was really excited: A new match-three kind of game with strategy and meaningful matching!
But now after having played it a bit, I feel somehow disappointed.
First of all, the enemy is not playing with the same rules which makes it kind of meaningless and disconnected opponent. "Oh, he fixed shields. Oh, he fired weapons. I guess he had resources for it". The only thing you see is the coolant. This gives you a strong feeling that the enemy is playing some other game, and it also makes your token matching less exciting. You don't need to worry about enemy stealing some resources you'll about to need soon - instead you need to worry not to match too much (see below). The fear of enemy making good moves was the essence of Puzzle Quest. This a major buzz killer for me.
I do like the fact that when you die, you get this campaign XP that gives you unlocks. But I still miss the way Puzzle Quest or 10000000 worked. I could keep on trying, find alternative routes, improve your stats etc.
My third issue is a pure UI/UX issue. Not being to able to see my max stats for bullets, energy, coolant or repair is just stupid. You have to memorize that "ok I can get 8 bullets max" and then when matching you need to calculate in your head whether the match will go over or not - because everything over the max cap is just wasted. I wish the game would display the max cap and somehow inform when the match is going to be wasteful.
It's a gorgeous looking and sounding game, but I don't think I have desire to play it much further...

I don't write reviews, but I felt as this game deserves one.
Firstly, I do not recommend this game or not recommend it, but rather I recommend this game to those who may be interested in the specific core mechanics and gameplay which are the defining factors between a good game and a bad game. I also do not recommend this game to those who may want more depth in combat, length, or are generally frustrated with the core mechanics.
To put briefly, this game has exetremely basic mecahnics. Being essentially a match 3, they spice it up with overload and link buffs that can be matched with any color and provide a specific bonus. Nontheless, it is very very simply. This is not at all a bad thing but it can dissuade potential buyers (not saying that your natural inclination is wrong, but that if you honestly dislike or hate match 3, then be wary of purchase). Also, If you find yourself having a distaste for match three, you will not like this game if the second part of the mechanics does not 'wow' you.
As for the second part of the mechanics, the resources gained from the match three provide action and detailed analysis of how your mech interacts. Though you don't control the mech per se, you are more of dealing with possibilities, potential outcomes, and weighing risk with reward. This gives a sense of commandering that shows a mind's ability to assess and impliment.
Now this all sounds cool, in part because it is and I enjoy it, but the game's depth is not shallow as some reviews claim or deep. Instead, this game is amazing for the $10 starting price or $15 when it goes off sale regarding mechanics and replayability. Expect 10 to 20+ hours with this game, which in my book, is more than what you will get from most triple AAA titles that cast 6x-4x more.
TL;DR -- Game is great, functions properly, synthesizes a combat and management, but uses a simple formula that some dislike.

An excellent Puzzle Quest style game with FTL style (rogue-like) progression.  In addition there's a bit of Rogue's Legacy where you earn global XP for every run which gives you global unlocks, slowly making you a bit more powerful every time.
The gameplay is quite fun: you match tiles to build up your meters, and then raise your defenses and unlesh hell on your enemy!  Watching your massive cannons turn your enemy into a fiery ruin never gets old. :)
On the diffuculty of the game: there's definely strategy to be learned, but a lot depends on luck.  Not just the tiles that you get to match against, or missing your target, but also the weapons, shields and enhancements you receive.  If RNG is hating on you, then it's going to be rough.  If you get lucky, things can really go your way.  That's at least part of why some people feel this game is too easy and some feel it's too hard.  For me, it's just about right.
Summary: 9/10, definitely worth the money.

Monday: Day 1
At 0600 Hours Patient Zero contracts an unknown contagion.
At 0720 Hours, a public hospital located Shanghai, China, is quarantined and an hour later, health authorities immediately issue a travel warning regarding travel in China's most populated city.
Tuesday: Day 2
At 0330 Hours, what appears to be a highly virulent strain of tropical rabies begins appearing throughout Shanghai and neighboring cities. Symptoms include a serve headache, coughing, excess saliva and mucus forming at the mouth and nose. Sensitivity to noise and movement is also heightened, mild aggression is also being reported. Within the hour, police respond to over 18,600 calls, all of which describe paramedic casualties resulting from the hostile sick.
At 0520 Hours, another health emergency is issued and all flights in and out of the Shanghai, and her neighbor cities has been suspended until further notice. The number of infected tops a million and a half hours later: the number of deceased has yet to be confirmed, even the media doesn't know.
At 0945 Hours, the Chinese Government requests assistance from the CDC, a leading health institution of the USA. The Chinese Government informs the North American institution that all cases reported outside the "Epicenter for the Outbreak" have been quarantined, and that all of whom who may have come into contact with an infected person are under a mandatory isolation. Furthermore, all emergency procedures implemented into preventing the spread of disease, have been activated with a 24/7 curfew placed in Shanghai.
The CDC team begin their analysis of the infected persons under isolation. By this stage, the mystery contagion has caused a mild necrotic breakdown of its host’s tissue, extreme hemorrhaging and a serve migraine bordering extreme aggresion. The streets of Shanghai remain calm for now, the police stationed at checkpoints throughout the city keeping a cautionary eye out...nothing like this stays calm for long...
Of the 24.1 million, a micro-handful of individuals who are asymptomatic (Unable to show symptoms) were on thirteen different travel routes before the Flight Cancellation Procedure was activated. Twenty four individuals, that's all that's required to bring modern civilization to its knees and palms...
Day 3 sees the "Previously contained outbreak" spiral out of control as protesters march the streets. Quickly, China's biggest ever riot quickly forms and within hours, Molotov’s are being hurled, riot police beat their shields with their batons as they represent supperiority, all the while the contagion is being actively transmitted from person to person, the infected becoming cannibalistic in nature. The national press gets whiff in the Chinese media storm of the CDC team being evacuated after a serious altercation with the patients they were tending too.

Close only counts with hand grenades, and Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak is so close to being great it is painful. It's more of a mediocre game than a bad one, which makes it all the more disappointing. I really wish Steam had a neutral "meh" option because that is what I would rather give than a thumbs down (or up!).
It is unquestionably a Homeworld game in spirit, keeping the essential feel and atmosphere of its predecesors, even with the switch to a 2D, desert setting. The story, voice acting and general presentation are very compelling and I was really enjoying it. There are a number of great touches, like how the unit chatter includes conversations about leaky drive trains and how to improve vehicle performance. I laughed out loud when a communications officer had to chew out a unit for not having their sensors turned on. It's small stuff, but it really helps make the world feel alive.
At mission 6, just under halfway through the game, it started to sour on me. The stuff I mentioned above? Great. The actual mechanics of the game? Not so much. It's the worst kind of bad mechanics, where everything works just enough to be functional, but not well enough to make playing the game easy. And it's a lot of little things that just kept piling on top of each other.
The camera doesn't zoom out quite far enough, so with a decently large group of units, you will be able to see all of your guys...but often not what they are shooting at. There badly needs to be a minimap, since going out to the map view takes just long enough that whatever game event you want to look at will be mostly finished by the time you find it. Some units have too many special abilities and some abilities should not be special at all. Coalition assault cruisers, for example, have 3 distinct abilities, but the game doesn't have a good way to queue up anything more complication than move actions. The battlecruiser, on the other hand, needs to research indirect firing, but instead of being a useful passive ability you have to trigger it every time. Want to use airstrikes? You can't rebind those key commands, so you have to first select the carrier, then the type of airstrike you want, then the attack location.
The units feel like they are made out of construction paper, not armor, and every single enemy unit does a ton of damage. Even cruisers go down in a couple of seconds to only a couple of anti-armor units. When I build a battlecruiser, it would be nice if it felt like an accomplishment, instead of a disposable nothing. Units respond incredibly slowly to movement orders, making it almost pointless to order units to retreat when they are under fire. Either you'll win the fight or you'll have to rebuild the entire attack force. Possibly both.
Units can't see far enough away to make scouting viable/fun, and both your and enemy units attack ranges almost exactly match their sight ranges, so I lost track of how many units I lost/destroyed pretty much the instant they came into view.
Worst of all, in the campaign, the enemy spawns units infinitely out of thin air. In the 8th mission, I was clearing out a group of turrets and the game kept spawning in an attack cruiser in the middle of my attack force. Not, like, from a production carrier. Just POP! New enemy. It turns the tense resource & fleet management of Homeworld into a farce.
I could go on, but hopefully that illustrates why I am considering giving up in the middle of the penultimate level. I will definitely go onto YouTube to watch the final cutscenes and see how the story ends. I don't think I will fight the game to get to that ending.

As I said, the game is ugly, honestly it would have done better to have knocked down some of the shaders and made it cell shaded. But even then the game's art design just isn't there. It feels like so much of it was thrown together instead of designed and worked on. But graphics aren't everything right? Nevermind the slowdown, many Mega Man titles have slowdown and they're well loved! Well let's move on...
The mechanics are a mess, they're unoffensive for most of the game as they're not directly required to beat the game- what I'm talking about specifically is where you absorb enemies. This will buff your buster gun in various ways including penitration. This isn't a permenant upgrade and fades in a short span.  Why is that important? In 1 section if you do not use the ability you might not realize you have acquired you will be unable to proceed and be crushed to death. The biggest problem is it's never really needed to do anything. It's never important enough to be needed  nor can I say it's made the game any better but randomly at 1-3 parts it is.
Things just are not laid out and are left to being killed to learn from. There's a sniper level which is open, you go right or left and try to hunt the boss down. It's goofy and weird...and if you die (there are 1 hit kills in this part) you have to start the whole section over again and find him 3 times. Comically having beat the game I still have NO idea how the Energy Tanks work in this game. All I know is if you die, you lose them. Yup. So did you want to go into a boss with half health and learn the pattern before comitting energy tank power? Too bad. Use it the first time or you waste it. Die just before the boss? Gone. I have NO idea how to even acquire them to begin with but they just annoyed me with how they worked anyway.
The presentation is not great, voice acting is not good in english and I've read comments on twitter from Japenese speakers that they didn't fair any better. Why is this so noteworthy to point out? Because you have support characters that constantly talk in mission. None of it is important and if you don't have it in english you're forced to read the text- but if you don't want either of those you're still left with the dialog boxes coming up.
Powers are unbalanaced and bosses can just be down right annoying to fight. The best weapon in the game from what I can tell is the sword, you can zip right up to most bosses and omni-slash their stupid faces off faster than most other guns.
Level design is alright for the most part I guess, but there's some sections that are SO UNFORGIVEABLE (see the screenshots for the big red circular blade) where you have to get Beck's face buried in the blade for you to be able to dash and survive getting under it. The above portion I mentioned where you're being chased and need a specific power.
The mechanics really clash and don't help the gameplay at all. The absorption should have been a means of score & or multipliers because as it is it's too finnicky to depend on.
If you want a good platformer, there's plenty other better ones out there. This game isn't great but I wouldn't even reccomend it to Megaman fans. The PC version is apparently the definitive version and it's not even great.
Mighty Gunvolt a little 8-bit spinoff is vastly better despite it's simplicity, there's another game like this currently only on Switch that hopefully hits steam featuring Beck and Gunvolt that was even better than that.
Other games to look at vs this mess: Freedom Planet, Sonic Mania, Shadow Complex, Axiom Verge, Mega Man collections.

I usually avoid early access games like the plague. However, with this being my second most played game on steam, right behind Warframe and just ahead of Civ5, I don't think I need to specify how much I like this game.
This game is very much for the lazy man. You make things to make things to do things for you. Automation is the point of the game, and the challenge is setting up your factory in such a way that it can do everything you need it to with you doing as little as possible to keep it going.
Setting up your factory is one big math and logic puzzle. You have to figure out how the parts fit together, and what's the best way to do so.
I can't stand playing Minecraft (or any survival sandbox game for that matter) solo anymore because of this game. Gathering resources is a waste of time that is better allocated to machines.
Also, the dev team is extremely active. They push updates frequently. They post on the dev blog every friday to inform the community about future stuff. They even interact with the community on the factorio subreddit. These guys care about making a good game.
At the time of writing, I'm 425 hours in. I just installed Bob's mods and Angel's mods which together make the game 100,000,000,000x more complicated and I'm loving it.
It's not for everyone though. If you played any significant amount of Minecraft and never made a wheat auto-harvester, you probably won't have a good time with Factorio.

I wanted to like this despite not being a fan of 2D platformers.   Most 2D platformers have low effort, low quality graphics and are just used by untalented developers as a get-rich-quick-on-Steam plan, so the market is flooded with these.  Not so here!  The graphics look great and the game runs well in 4K which should be a clear indicator that there's a hope of a good quality game.
Unfortunately the controls are a bit janky, there's no mouse pointer so it's a complete pain to set up the keyboard.  The game works with KB+M but practically demands you play with a controller - don't tell me what to do, console porting developers, when you don't develop for PC first, you're second class when it comes to Steam reviews!
Gameplay hammers the nails into the coffin lid.  While intended to be a spiritual MegaMan successor, the gameplay is painfully difficult due to poor level design decisions - it's not fun.  Unavoidable damage, unforgiving pixel precise jumps.  Voice acting is also painful.
It's easy to give a thumbs down to a thoroughly bad game.  It's harder to give one to a game that should have been good but the developers have snatched defeat from the jaws of victory here.
Just not worth your money. Story is terrible and had the voice acting to match. Dissapointing to see a classic inspired game turn out so boring.

Ugh, this game is stressful. It's incredibly frustrating, nostalgic, and too close to home.
So why did I recommend it?
Because, I like it since it IS stressful, frustrating, and too relatable. I feel like everyone who uses some form of online messaging should experience this game... particularly people who have online friends or are no longer able to hang out 'irl' with old friends. This game brings out conflicting emotions, "should I do this?," "do I tell her?," "what do I say?" that we all have experienced before. You might as well call this game, "Online Rejection Simulator - Now with 'Hate Yourself' DLC!" But, I want other people to experience how just staring at a screen of text can stir your emotions. How difficult is it to confess your feelings to someone you barely see in person? This game is going to spit in your face and tell you it's hard. The game will push you into situations that you aren't prepared for. It's just like life in that aspect. But, maybe this game is teaching us a lesson. Don't have yourself an Emily and keep your feelings locked up. Don't stop yourself from expressing your love. Go for it, or else you'll end up like this poor guy who hasn't gone over his high school crush. And if that doesn't go well, leave that behind. High school left, so why can't your high school crush?

I strongly recommend this game if you are a tactics fan.
You move your characters like any tactics game but when you move, so does the enemy, meaning you gotta move to see how your enemy reacts. Long ranged units try to avoid you while hitting you from far away and melee units try to bash on you up close.
The trick is you can set your characters on spaces that are set by a passive skill every character has that links them all together when they are in spots that are set by each character. Every character can be linked with another character and more than one but what this link does is let you cast more than one skill on another characters turn, the trade off being that those characters might have to move to get in range both helping you put your melee units into the fight but also removing the link most of the time. Those spots are also linked to the way the character is facing and you'll have to keep an eye out for that as well.
You can also do what you normally would with these games, set units, change items etc etc. Normal stuff you'd find in any tactics games.
The next interesting part to the game is the fact that you are going down the generation line of the main character, meaning the character stats change and so does their weapons and armor. Meaning you need to find out who gives what and plan well cause you might end up with a tank character but have two other characters who are well built as tanks as well.
When i first played this i didn't think much of it from the first few mintues but as the game goes on it gets better and better and after a while it became my favorite tactics game. It might not be for everyone who likes these style of games but this one will really get you thinking about your unit placement more than any other game.

Never thought I'd play a tactical RPG I didn't like, but there's a first time for everything.
looks grandiose from the description and screenshots, but it utterly fails to deliver.
The story's fairly cliche, but that by itself wouldn't kill it.  What does kill it is that it doesn't even do justice to the cliches it uses.  The protagonist of the first generation is a soldier who decides that his own country is in the wrong and turns traitor.  It's been done before, but it's been done with a decent setup, showing the protagonist playing the part of the loyal soldier with his comrades, questioning his loyalty as he witnesses assorted warcrimes, and eventually turning traitor as things come to a head in a scene of extreme pathos.  Here, we fast-forward through all that, with Leonhardt, who somehow has a reputation as a war hero, turning around and unhesitatingly attacking his buddies at the drop of a hat right at the start of the game.  That sets a low bar for a game that continues to deliver shallow plot with shallow characters.
But is the gameplay worth it?  Well, no, the dev managed to botch that as well.  For starters, the DLC that comes with the base game lets you start with equipment that's seemingly endgame-quality, which cheapens the game.  I've been playing on hard, and overkilling everything I encounter in one hit.  I suppose I could toss the OP materiel and continue, but A) it really shouldn't be there in the first place, and B) the battle system's clearly not great anyway.  Unusually for a tactical RPG, the battle field is always small, completely flat, and free of obstacles - though, after a while, the game does introduce fields with squares that arbitrarily increase or decrease stats for units standing on them.  In a typical battle, on the first turn, you and the enemy charge each other, and then it's just an all-out melee in which positioning sort of matters, but in ways that either don't require much thought or can't be controlled reliably because you and the enemy move simultaneously.  One wonders why it's a tactical RPG at all.  Standard JRPGs have battle systems that are about as deep as this one is while feeling less cumbersome.
10 hours in, I'm still on the first of five generations, and that's where I'll stop.  Between the story and the gameplay, I'm bored to tears, and don't want to slog through another 100+ hours of this.
Fun to play and can recommend this for anyone that likes these types of RPGs.
