This tactical strategy JRPG is a fun mix of turn-based fighting and dating simulation, featuring suggestive anime-style art.
The game puts you on a map where your path takes you from spot to spot, only occasionally breaking the linear momentum.  Each spot upon which you stop will either be a battle, a discussion where choices are made, or a town where one can go shopping and fiddle with stats (among other activities).
The fighting is different but still familiar, for myself at least as a person who has only played a few JRPGs.  Your party of six will start the battle with a movement round upon a gridded battlefield.  Each character has a certain type of movement he or she can perform.  One downside is that you move first and cannot know where the enemy party will choose to move.  So your positioning is an eduscated guess at best.  Yet movement is also important where your party members are concerned, because based on appropriate positioning your party members may link to perform combo attacks for extra damage.  The visuals for these attacks are a nice break from the norm, as the screen goes dark and lots of bright colors burst forth.  I am easily impressed by pretty lights.  The battle system is turn-based after that, with spells for some and swords for others.  You get a healer and potions and you all know the routine.  Not bad fighting I say.
I bought the game and its DLC.  When I started to play, I saw that the DLC provided me with super weapons and a vast wealth in gold.  Now I enjoy feeling like a badass as I plow through enemies and loot their corpses, but I can't help but wonder what this took away from the game, as early on the effort required to win was quite minimal.
Rolled into this JRPG is a dating sim that has a visual novel feel.  The game is divinded into five parts, or Generations.  The player creates a new main character at the end of each generation, or during the generation as it all depends upon which of the game's heroines you were able to win affection from.  Whichever girl wins your heart, her traits and yours combine to create the next Generation's main character, both in terms of visually and stats.  Through a variety of choices in-game you become good or evil (light/dark) and your love interest's opnion of you is altered.  Be careful because the results of your choices are not always obvious.  You may end up offending the girl who has captured your heart.
The music is a bit of a trial.  I turned it off.  The voices are all in Japanese, which is really cool except you can hardly hear them unless you turn the speaker volume up.  Even with the music off this is a problem.  The graphics are anime-style and the stills look great during conversations.  The graphics during fights are okay and what you except from JRPGs but nothing to get excited about.  One thing TO get excited about is the abundance of scantily-clad anime girls, all somehow having found themselves in dignity-compromising postures.  If you like that sort of thing, your sad urges will be satiated.
May not be a game for everyone but, Agarest: Generations of War is a fun play, especially on sale for under ten bucks.

Most roguelikes, even the great ones, seem to put a priority on exploration, items and mystery over a solid gameplay foundation. But Flinthook has all of that, plus fantastic presentation AND excellent traversal. It feels fun just to *move around in the levels* with the grappling hook, much less weaving between enemies and bullets and lasers and traps and laser traps.
The progression system doles out plenty of upgrades in the early going, and you rarely feel like your run was totally for nothing. There are definitely heavy consequences for death, but Flinthook doesn't go out of its way to suck your lifeforce away with every big loss.
I'd definitely recommend this for fans of roguelikes and great platformers.

EDIT: I initially stated here that I thought Flinthook was a good game with some bad controls getting in the way. I still think the game has wonderful aesthetics, but it has some questionable design decisions in addition to the poor controls.
Some areas have jumping challenges that don't involve the grapping hook, and they are made even less fun by the controls. Some rooms have spikes or pits immediately when you enter them. Most rooms are filled with visual clutter. It makes the game look great, but it interferes with your ability to see projectiles, traps, and hazards.
The mouse and keyboard controls have two primary problems. The first is the inability to rebind keys. The options menu has a few presets to switch between, but keys can't be individually rebound. I found the settings file that has the controls listed, but I haven't I tried manually changing them yet. The second, and much larger, issue is that your aiming reticle is locked in a set radius around your character. This distance is the same as the range of your hook and attacks, and it is reasonable for a controller. I don't care if my shots are only going to travel a quarter of the screen; I want to move my cursor freely throughout the screen when using a mouse. It feels incredibly awkward and counterintuitive as is.
It seems like the game was built around using a controller because that method feels more natural in motion than M&K. The controller has both aiming and movement tied to the left stick, which is rather strange. Ideally, you'd move with the left stick and aim with the right stick, but I guess that would have required more controls, like jumping and shooting, on the triggers than face buttons. This scheme feels like it was chosen for the sake of simplicity rather than because it is the best setup for the game.
Even if they do fix the control related issues, I wouldn't recommend this game.

+ Clean and polished; I didn't see anything that seemed to be a bug or "not as intended".
- I would perhaps wish for something like an endless mode or other non-campaign plays.
- Multiplayer would be excellent, I suspect.
- It can be a bit irksome when the AI gets a good turn and you sometimes suspect the game of cheating (since their board is invisible to you); perhaps an option to show the AI board for those who find it constantly aggravating might be worthwhile.
+ Quite a bit of fun; each match is a few minutes, and the campaign is just about the right length.
+ Mission variety is there, but there's often clear choices as to which to pick, which is a bit of a detriment in my mind.
+ The match-three mechanic variant used is a fairly relaxing strategic one, with the balancing of clearing the board/getting match XP and saving a string of tiles you can't currently use but could use later.  There are three 'special' nodes, one allowing you to jump from one tile type to another, one being a wildcard that gives a boost to your next action and one being a 'collectible' wildcard that's a mission objective in some of the missions.
- I feel like the defensive options aren't quite balanced; I keep using shields all the time, with drives only when I have plenty of spare energy and coolant.  Perhaps the latter's cost could creep down a bit more, or the dodge chance increased.
+ You can set up a *very* satisfying turn, firing lots of shots and completely devastating an enemy mech or train, which feels pretty good.  The 'feel' of the actions is pleasant - relevant sound and graphical assets are excellent.
All in all, a really solid game, in my opinion.  It doesn't over-reach and focuses on polishing a smaller area, and it shows.  I'd like to see more pilots and mechs (perhaps there's more to unlock in later global levels) though.

Ironcast is a piece of class.

Resources are then spent on turn based combat between giant mechs in a steampunk universe where France has invaded England.
Between missions you spend cash on upgrading/customising your machine and deciding between a choice of special abilities. The campaign involves completing 10 or so randomised missions before facing the boss (there are two bosses, a bit limited but then in the perfect FTL there is only one.). Lots of luck but with fairly taxing gameplay where your decisions are the biggest factor.
Except for some minor quirks with displaying information and perhaps a shortness of the campaign - it's a near flawless offering.  Really pleased to have found this.

This game is a bit difficult to summarize, but here goes.
It's a Turn-Based Roguelite RPG with Match Three mechanics, set in a steampunk Victorian England where you play as a mech pilot and go around blowing up other mechs. This is why I initially bought the game, and as it turns out it was pretty damn good!
The gameplay is tactical and challenging and this game borrows Ziggurat's best mechanic, where every time you level up you are offered a choice of three unique and special passives or abilities. The item progression is mostly just linear stats, but there are quite a few different varieties of weapons, and rare items often offer higher-than-average power with a drawback.
Including the one you start with there are four Ironcasts and four pilots. Each Ironcast has different strengths and weaknesses (one is a beast with a lot of health, one is really good at dodging et cetera) and come with a unique ability, such as a missile battery or a temporary damage reduction. Each Pilot also gives you a passive ability. The only problem is that some of the pilot abilities are quite rubbish, and you are better off sticking with the first pilot.
The story is nothing special, really. There are some funny conversations with your superior officer, but mainly it's just "this is the reason why we are murdering this mech".
Performance should not be an issue unless your computer is literally a potato - I ran this on a dell laptop with an i3 and it ran just fine. This game makes me so angry. I honestly, despite 440 hours of mostly enjoyable gameplay, can't recommend this game to anyone.
This game is so full of bugs it's stupid and what's worse is that the developer has seemingly abandoned the game altogether. When I first downloaded the game about a year ago everything was great. The dev released very frequent updates and bug fixes and everything was peachy. The game ran super fast and smoothly and while there were small problems there was nothing major that had a big effect on gameplay.
These frequent updates continued until the game was finally released until December 1st, 2015, when the game was taken out of Early Access and given a full release. As a huge fan of the game I was super excited for this new "EHM 1". There were a lot of cool new features added and it was the biggest update I had seen thus far. Unfortunately EHM 1 would be the beginning of the steep decline in the quality of EHM. This 1.0 update was so full of bugs it was actually unplayable for a large portion of players. Myself and a ton of other users had to spend days combing online forums and google searches for solutions to the problems we faced. I remember being so frustrated that this huge update came out on December 1st but I actually couldn't play it until mid December, and even then I just kept playing a save game from an earlier version of the game because the new version was so messy.
As if this disaster of an update wasn't bad enough, a lot of these bugs have gone totally unfixed even now on May 29th, 2016. Since the 12/1 full release, there have been only 3 updates to the game, the last coming out more than 3 months ago on February 17th. These updates were two minor bug fix updates and then a 1.1.1 update that added some new content to the game. The game is still in shambles, and the developer hasn't touched the game in more than 3 months. He used to release updates on a weekly basis, and now he doesn't release updates at all.
Let me break down a couple of the major bugs that have made me want to pull my hair out, and keep in mind that this isn't all of them.
- You can't minimize this game. If you minimize the game, or if some pop-up automatically minimizes the game you can't open the game back up. You better hope that you saved recently because all of your progress will be lost. This bug has been around since the December 1st update, and has been unsolved for almost 6 months now.
- The in-game clock was completely ruined by the December 1st update. In EHM you can't play the games, you just simulate all of them. You can mess with the in-game clock settings to make it slow, medium, or fast. I can't speak for everyone, but my friends and I and a lot of other people I've seen on the online forums play the game on the fastest clock settings. We do this because we don't want to sit and watch a simulated game for a long period of time, we'd rather it just be over with as fast as possible. Before the December 1st update you could simulate a game in under 30 seconds and it was absoulutely tremendous. Being able to fly through games so fast meant that you could finish entire seasons relatively quickly and your manager's career would progress at a nice pace. The December 1st update made the clock much much slower than it was before, even on the fastest settings. That quick 20 second game suddenly took almost a minute or more to simulate. I get that a 50 second game still doesn't seem like much, but when all you can do is just sit there and watch a screen for 50 seconds you get bored really quickly. This bug actually frustrated me to the point where I just stopped playing the game completely for almost a month. It's a really boring game when you have to stare at your screen for a collective two hours and do nothing just to finish one season. Luckily I found a fix to that bug by tinkering with the settings, and I was able to play the game with a super fast clock again, until earlier today. My clock is now super slow again, and there is NOTHING I can do about it. I've already tinkered with the settings as much as I can and my clock is super slow. I'm sick about it.
- The bug I talked about earlier that kept most players from playing the new update for a few days after the 1.0 release is still around for a lot of new players. Whenever you start up the game you get some error message that breaks the game. You can't open the game, you can't do anything until you go into the game's properties and change all of the resolution settings, just so you can finally open the game and change the in-game resolution settings, before you go back and reset your computer's resolution settings. You have to do all of this annoying tinkering just to be able to play the game! Come on Riz!
This game is super fun, don't get me wrong. I've played more than 400 hours. Unfortunately this is a game I cannot recommend to anyone, as it is just a giant headache.
I'm sure the developer Riz is working on other games, and I'm sure he's very busy. He's the only developer of this game and while I'm very thankful for all of the work he's done the fact of the matter is that this game is abandoned right now. There hasn't been an update in MONTHS, not even a tiny bug fix!! I don't understand why the guy would just let this game that he worked so hard on sit and rot.
TL:DR
This game right now is a buggy pile of mush. Before it was taken out of early access it was absoulutely brilliant, but now that it has been fully released it has been completely abandoned by the developer. Only buy this game if you want to deal with a bunch of problems before you can really enjoy the game. Don't buy this game unless it's on sale.

Plague Inc. Evolved is a really sick idea that has the potential to be an interesting strategy game. I'm really not into the bubble clicking thing but this can be removed later in the game: I still feel this may turn off more "serious" strategy gamers with it's free mobile app feel and that really I don't think that it adds anything in terms of game-play: I suspect it's there to add a sense of urgency and to keep the player's attention focused, but I really think that it would be better replaced with something that feels a bit less cheap.
That being said, there's clearly a lot of depth here. The game ramps up the difficulty pretty quickly and there are a good few options for altering the core game pretty significantly.
I've not felt particularly interested in sustained gameplay: it hasn't totally grabbed me in all honesty. Personally I find that the fact you can play through a single player game in a half hour or less very appealing. I recommend the game on this basis, that it's a good quick strategy fix. I'll be putting more hours into this
But it's pretty unique as far as I can tell and it's a worthwhile addition to any strategy gamer's collection.
EDIT:
I've noted the comments below and edited this review accordingly: further proof that you should probably research something before low-rating.

As for the inaccuracy of troops I'm from the days of old school PnP RPGs and I've seen the dice make enough mockery of statistics to not even flinch when my troops appereantly forget to load their weapons with live ammo and seemingly just fires randomly into the air anyway. However, it's not my experience that the enemy faction is any better off. It's just blind luck at times which can be frustrating to some but for me it kinda' works (seeing the same thing on my analog 40k battlefields all the time anyway).
So to sum up a short review... it's ugly, it's simplistic, and it's fun!

Once upon a time Mideval Engineers (ME from here on out) was a game which was largely a copy of Space Engineers - Well those days are gone...Now we have a game where albeit loosely resembles SE ultimately falls into a unique game experience.
Let Me explain some of the more "major" Developments - then I'll get to pros and cons.
Planets Update: This happened some time ago and was the initial "branch off" from SE - it took a playfield that was rather small and devoid and created an entire world to explore - complete with fast travel and area ownership.
Farming Update: Added Mideval-based Farming so you no longer have to scavenge or hunt for food/resources of an organic nature.
Iron Update: Added the Resource to the game called "iron" and expanded the scope to include basic smithing.
Shovels Update - This took place before I got back into the game but essentially it added the ability to dig up ground to find stones/dirt/iron.
Now that you have a firm grasp of the History Let me share some pros and cons.
Pros:
+The game is largely Era Accruate, realistic and moderately configurable.
+The Building System allows for adaptation and modification on the part of the player even without Mods
+The Game is moddable
+Machinery can eventually be developed that is nearly complete automation for age appropriate devices (ie windmills, basic farming wagons etc)
Now for the...
Cons:
- The Game has very little multiplayer population despite obviously being modelled after a MMO-style idea.
- The Mods that exist are largely blueprints - very few block mods in comparison.
- You have to "Research" higher level building blocks - which is kinda a time-sink.
- For the love of god, there is NO WAY to play this game past iron's introduction unless you are completely non-colorblind and very observant - or know how to check the forums for a guide.
- Only Poor Iron Deposits can be mined with the shovel - anything higher requires an iron pickaxe (naturally made of iron itself)
- Although you can "drag" wagons - they are fundamentally not self-propelled and therefore do NOT have seats which you can ride on; this is kind of age inaccurate as they would've had Horses for this in that age,  and as a result carriages. (Hope it changes with a future patch but knowing keen they'll ignore the idea)
- Update History has been sparatic at best - While currently they update about once a week - they had taken several months off development just before the planets update - which meant they posted "dev blogs" instead of "updates" - upsetting a great deal of the vocal populace in the action.

It's intense, it's immersive; it's a Homeworld-game even if it's not located in space.
You can tell by all the small and bigger details, that developers of the original homeworld were working on this:
Be it the atmosphere, the interface or vehicle style.
But you'll also notice, the remaining elements of its roots, back when it was intended to be a mere spiritual spin-off to homeworld, called Shipbreakers.
Now, my guts tell me, the game would have worked even better, if it would have been this spin-off instead of a direct prequel but that's pure speculation on my end.
Even if you're not familiar with the whole lore of homeworld, you'll know how the mainplot will work out in the end. But while you're in-game, it will still grab you by the angles.
In terms of gameplay, even with the physical limitation of land-based movement, the game takes differences in height into full account and you'll make use of it beyond just holding choke points.  Unit balance is extremly good: even on the last mission, the smallest units can be vital assets and the progression system makes a huge part of it:
Units gain experience, get more health & damage ... and you'll keep them between missions.
Having an LAV from Mission 1 all the way through gives you an immense feeling of accomplishment.
But there's one down-side, that hampers the whole experience:
It's short.

UPDATED REVIEW AT THE BOTTOM:
I have always been a fan of metroidvanias, Megaman, and roguelikes. This is a perfect combination of all three. Fast and fluid controls, simple but extremely fun hook mechanic, and a great look, feel, and the sound and music is amazing. I cannot tell you how good it feels to hook your way through a long corridor with the ring sfx whenever you hook and the animation of you plunging into the next room.
The only problem I have is that it's crashed a few times when playing it and that's pretty frustrating (but it does save things you've acquired like EXP and relics but you lose your run). I don't know if it's just me. Running on OSX and with big picture mode using a steam controller.
Highly recommend this game. It's just the platformer I've been looking for.
UPDATE 6/3/17
Okay so having played it about 40 hours now, I can say that I still love this game. However, the end game is in dire need of some work, a lot of the game still needs a lot of polish. I have a screenshot on my account where you can see enemies that spawn (with invincibility bubbles) that you CANNOT avoid damage from, in order to get to the enemy you need to hit (once that enemy is killed, the bubbles protecting the other enemies are removed.)
Spikes have a bigger hit box than it shows. If you are standing on a box and the left side of that box has spikes, be sure not to walk past that threshold because the spikes will damage you as they extend beyond their side. The same goes for spikes that are on a slightly higher plane than you. Floor pressure traps are extremely hard to see. They are two pixels wide and stay out for several seconds. You will get hit two, maybe three times in some cases before you can escape them because they can be anywhere.
I've seen a vertical column I had to climb by jumping between the left and right wall, except they're covered with pressure plate spikes. Like, four huge plates that you can't avoid needing to jump to/fom in order to climb up this wall. There's no rings, you just take the hits and keep moving. These spikes stay out for 2-3 seconds which, again, lasts a lot longer than your invincibility frames which are very short.
Even with a perk to increase the timer, it feels like it lasts less time than Megaman's frames last by a long time so you'll be hit multiple times off of invinicible enemies, unavoidable or unseen traps. Seriously, a lot of the background imagry has better signalling than some of the things you are suppose to interact with in the foreground. This game has a lot of visual clutter as it feels they prioritize the art direction more than playability.
The perks are helpful but they are not descriptive enough. For a roguelite, they really don't want to give you any help with understanding what your benefits or penalties are. You need to keep notes or use a wiki or data mine the game files to find out. And there are so many duplicates and you get them at random. I was level 91 before I got the perk for rolling, an ability you know about right from the beginning because there's a button for it on the controls. I had to get 20+ hours into the game to even find out what it was.
Binding of Isaac has a lot of the same "Here's a thing, figure it out", but at least that game has a stat screen so you have some frame of reference. You jump to ships not knowing what challenges you're facing, getting perks without knowing what they do.
The enemies are pretty repetative. You'll have seen all of them by the time you get to the first boss likely, and then it's just more of them in a wider variety of combinations. You never face -new- challenges. They just feel like they make them cheaper and more unforgiving in unfun ways. The same ship on 2 skull difficulty might be 4 enemies, but on 5 skull difficulty you'll have them being invincible and the shield generator pirates are behind them so you have to get around them to have a chance of hitting them, except they'll also have missiles spawned now or electricity shooting from nodes (these missles and notes also can spawn from fights but be really easy to miss; again, really bad signalling.)
These aren't 'harder' fights any more than sending the same enemy with ten times more HP isn't harder, it's just tedious. The difference between regular enemies and the green 'elite' versions are pretty small, and beyond that, they're either bubbled (so you need to pop it) or magically bubbled (and you have to find who is bubbling them). And that's the game play, which is fine, but it never evolves. They just throw more of it at you and say it's harder. It's just more frustrating.
As I'm editing my review, I see that the reviews went from "very positive" to "mixed" recently and I totally understand. My crashing bug is still not fixed and it's really only starting to be understood (the devs in the forums have been hard at work on it and it seems to be a very strange bug. Seriously, not being sarcastic, they've been wonderful.)
The late game is really where this game suffers. They give you over a hundred levels to grind through but there's no reason for it. They give you expensive things to buy in the black market but it's really pointless. You can grind to find treasure but that is a small joy.  I haven't tried it myself but people on the forums say the hard mode of bosses (you have to pay a lot to unlock for, by the way) are just the same bosses with more HP. And that's really the problem with this game. It doesn't build up and evolve, it just kind of gives you more of the same until you're overwhelmed.
I've literally walked into rooms and see a wall of free floating spike balls and turrets and froze because (a) I don't know where the spikes are going and (b) I don't know where the turrets are shooting. I have a split second to decide what to do before being hit multiple times trying to get into a safe space and to look at the room, only to find that it goes to a dead end with a key door that I don't have a key for yet.
Oh yeah, keys. They felt exciting in the beginning but again, now they're just tedious. Especially because half of the treasure rooms behind them are ridiculously hard and not worth going for. Really, for a game about fast paced combat and exploration, they made me sigh when I see new challenge rooms a lot. The harder ships don't test your skill as much as they test your patience. You aren't playing an action platformer anymore, you're playing a deadly maze.
Oh, last thing. The hook has a bit of auto-aim which I can appreciate. But they have some really strange prioritizing. Spike balls seem to be a higher priority than rings are so often, I find myself hitting a spike ball three or four times as I'm falling and not being able to hit the ring RIGHT next to it. Sometimes, this means getting hit so many times I just quit the run. The same is true for bubbles you can pop on enemies. Usually I want to pop the bubbles but I still grab the hook behind them sometimes and fly into them and take more damage and put myself in a bad position. This is not fun.
I say "No" to recommending this game only because I feel that it has such a solid start and has such an uninteresting ending. I won't spoil it but the last boss was so boring; way easier than every other boss in the game. I was so let down.

The Good:
- Absolutely gorgeous pixel art. Beautifully stylized and full of character, Flinthook is some of the best modern pixel art around. If you're famliar with the technical side of creating good pixel art - Flinthook is a masterclass example.
- Wonderful animations, characters, world design, etc. A very unique take on the space pirate theme.
- Movement, especially when using the grappling hook, just feels good. They nailed the thrill of hooking around each stage (when the stage allows for it).
- Tons of things to collect: perks, relics, lore pages, new modes, sub-weapons, etc.
- UI design that's full of character. It isn't perfect (some things aren't quite as clear as they could be, such as the Perk Equip menu which I find to be a bit confusing as to which perks are equipped/unequipped, etc) I appreciate them going for something more bold as it's rare to see UI as fun and jolly as Flinthook's.
The Not-So-Good
- There isn't enough distinction between the background and foreground elements, resulting in situations where it's incrediblydifficult to digest whats happening on screen. Many background elements are also animated, creating more visual noise.
- Obstacles that are a danger to the player aren't sufficiently highlighted. Enemies are usually fairly easy to see - but almost every single trap is muted in color and hard to pin-point with a quick visual sweep of the room. They blend in easily with the tiles, so you don't realize you've triggered a trap until it's too late - resulting in frustrating losses of life.
All in all, a fun experience! If you're into difficult, rogue-like games, or just fantastic pixel art, Flinthook is definitely for you.

I remember back when I was younger how I used to play the old Megaman games, I loved them and the variety to the levels and most of all I loved how it was challenging to an extent. Once you defeated a boss you got a special ability in which you could use when facing another, just choose one boss you want to fight first and off you go!
Sadly...the game 'Mighty Number 9' does not stand up to what it is trying to reproduce, while it seemed fun for the first twenty minutes I started to notice flaws in its system. The graphics were pretty good and the game was responsive of course...but the big hole that had staring at me♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. The difficulty was spiked way too high for a game of this sort!
Yes I know what you're thinking 'It's an arcade shooter, it's meant to be difficult' and I agree with you on that part! But there is a difference between the reasonable (And most likely when playing these games) "The boss has killed me for the tenth time of my first level, ♥♥♥♥ing hell what is this!" and the reaction that I had "I haven't even made it through the first level in an hour! where is the boss? Jesus christ this is HARD!"
Okay now for the sake of my sanity i'll step back and ignore the difficulty of the fights within this, let's say that it's simply hard to get through the game because they designed the enemies as such. But once I do that I notice the next problem I had, specifically level design.
Just to be sure it wasn't just me I went through and tried each...single..level! Of course I didn't make much progression through them but that was not the point, if it's this difficult to get across a gap because an enemy has been placed in such a way that not only do I need to be on the other side to defeat him...but he is actually blocking my path to do so!
Again let's say that I manage to look over this little flaw because every game has its bad moments of course...oh hey a miniboss let
Oh! I'm on ice so I slide around and the pattern the piece is taking is random, not only that but there are things that can freeze me in place? Alright..what do you mean that I have to defeat both sides AND avoid the ice drops AND avoid the bouncing balls AND try and do it on a slippery surface...ugh.
Look, the point is that they tried. They tried to make this a good game and I do not blame them because it almost caught the essence of its grandfather 'megaman' But please...this game looks like it's designed for kids and I couldn't do a level in an hour. Difficulty be damned I do not like this game.
HOWEVER...I am NOT saying that you should not play it and hell I could just suck at this so badly that my nephew can do this better than me (He's five By the way). I'm just saying that the rage inducing level design is not really worth it if you want to re-live the megaman experience.

Plague Inc. Evolved is a really sick idea that has the potential to be an interesting strategy game. I'm really not into the bubble clicking thing but this can be removed later in the game: I still feel this may turn off more "serious" strategy gamers with it's free mobile app feel and that really I don't think that it adds anything in terms of game-play: I suspect it's there to add a sense of urgency and to keep the player's attention focused, but I really think that it would be better replaced with something that feels a bit less cheap.
That being said, there's clearly a lot of depth here. The game ramps up the difficulty pretty quickly and there are a good few options for altering the core game pretty significantly.

Personally I find that the fact you can play through a single player game in a half hour or less very appealing. I recommend the game on this basis, that it's a good quick strategy fix. I'll be putting more hours into this

Recommended - with some reservations for those expecting a game, and not a novel.
Rarely does a game come along where I feel the need to actually take the time to write a review - but even rarer still does something as simple as a game have the power to instantly transport me almost 20 years - short of heading to GOG, of course.
If you spent any significant portion of your life in front of a clicking Windows XP box, chatting over AIM, _everything_ about this title will rocket you back to a distant memory in a way that only Q could rival.  From the perfectly executed windowsXP login screen, to the dings and doors of AIM, to the buddy icons and song lyrics in profiles and the ability to set your type to an unreadable blue-on-red, to the whirring of fans...
Superb.  Simply put - the 'feel' of this is masterfully executed.
The tone and syntax of the writing is so spot on that I found myself actually remembering conversations with my then-girlfriend, now-wife as if it were just yesterday, and not two decades ago.  If you didn't 'grow up' with AIM in this context, you won't get it, and I'm truly sorry for your loss.  If you did, however, prepare to be astonished at how well Emily Is Away captures what is likely a forgotten, but very important, part of your life.
For the first playthrough, at least.
And here's the reservations: There's not much replayabilty, as much of it is significantly scripted, but honestly, that's to be expected with such an expertly crafted tone to the words. HOWEVER, as it's more of an interactive novel with a story to tell, emotions to evoke, and commentary to make, I cannot fault it for this - it's lasting impact would be vastly damaged if you could alter the outcome in any way.
THAT SAID: This game is free, and it is totally, unequivocably, worth the price of admission, and more.  If you can afford it, donations to the author are completely justified.

When I played this game I was expecting to have a friend relationship with Emily. However, it seems that our protagonist has desires for a romantic relationship with Emily. I only played through the game twice and it appears that you have no choice about whether you and Emily remain together (whether in a romantic way or simply in a friendly way.) Overall the whole story-based chatbox concept I found cool, and the fact that actual, real Steam friends who are online show up in the buddy list. I also liked the choice of icons based off of the years.
It would have been nice if you could salvage some type of relationship with Em, but I believe I understand the message of the game fairly well: Sometimes in life, things are just not meant to be. My wife and I love to play cribbage.  I wanted to get a computer cribbage game for those times when I need my crib fix and my wife isn't up for a game.  This serves that purpose.  It's decent, but not fabulous.
Pros:
-- Game runs in full screen.
-- Seems to be totally bug-free (at least cribbage and gin rummy...I haven't had a chance to play the other games yet).
-- The AI is alright.
-- Some of the other reviewers seemed upset because, apparently, the AI avatars and voices in this version are inferior to previous installments (or something).  I dunno...I had an older version of Hoyle's card games on my old computer several years ago, and I personally don't remember the AI's "personality" being anything even remotely memorable.  I honestly don't give a rat's behind about any of that.  I just want to play crib, and this game lets me do it.  I guess it's important to some other players, but it wasn't an issue for me.
Cons:
-- The soundtrack is atrocious elevator music.  Fortunately, it can be turned off.
-- The game uses rookie scoring methods for cribbage.  Anyone who plays crib knows that a pattern of cards like the following, JQQK or 4456 for instance, is known as a "double-run" and is worth 8 points.  But the AI scores it like a noob, counting it as two runs (3 points each) and a pair (2 points).  Here's another example: in crib, a three-of-a-kind is known as a "pair royal" and is worth 6 points, but the AI counts it as 3 seperate pairs, worth 2 apiece.  Why does this matter, you ask?  Well, first of all, it's totally annoying to veteran players who are used to the standard scoring practices.  And, secondly, because one of the best parts of cribbage is watching your opponent overlook something as they count up their hand, and then stealing those points for yourself!  It's known as the "muggins rule".  The game does give you the option of playing with the muggins rule enabled...but, jeez, I can't imagine any better way to suck the fun out of it and make it a tedious ordeal, than by using the rookie scoring methods the AI employs.  I mean, I guess for someone learning cribbage for the first time the scoring MIGHT be helpful...but they could have at least given the player an option in the options menu to choose between "veteran scoring" and "beginner scoring".  Meh... :P
Conclusion:
6/10.  When push comes to shove, it gets a thumbs up...barely.  It sucks compared to a real opponent, of course.  But the lame crib scoring methods and the sound issues are what really drag it down.  I got it on sale for 75% off, so I'm happy with the purchase overall.  I would have been disappointed had I paid full price.  Wait for it to go on sale.

This game is trashed upon beyond hell and is treated as if it's worse than Bugsy 3D. The reality is, this is just a standard bad Mega Man game. Remember we got those before? Those Mega Man games that just weren't good? They existed before this.
The main problem (outside of 3D graphics on 2D gameplay, I HATE when games do this) is the levels themselves are frustrating. Most of the difficulty comes from unfun insta-death that feels like a medusa head hit me when I'm standing on a thin platform. Rarely, you'll die because your HP hit 0.
Outside the annoying levels, the physics and controls are fine. The game no longer pauses when switching weapon which can be annoying when you need time to think which one you want to equip, especially since you have to scroll through them. The dashing into dead enemies seems like it could be cool if it mattered. It seemed unnecessary in this game other than as a "finisher"
The bosses are mostly well-done, they all play different and have nice attack patterns, the way you use some of your weapons makes the game feel different a little.
Unmemorable music. Other than the main menu song (which isn't that great, just overplayed throughout the game), I can't remember a single song.
I don't care about story in a robot fighting game so I won't comment, but it seemed like Mighty No. 9 sequel would've had a interesting plot based on how this game ended.
Steve Blum could do a better job.
It's not a horrible game, but you have to go through horrible moments to get to the decent parts, and for that I wouldn't really recommend it. Especially when Mega Man 1-10 are on Steam now and other great(?) Mega Man clones such as 20XX, MetaGal, Rosenkreuzstilette,and the Gunvolt games (hopefully more to come on Steam)

I played lots of Mega Man titles with my friends... starting on NES, later Game Boy versions up to Mega Man X on the SNES. Those games were tough but rewarding. We spent hours and hours on different battles and situations, we improved and finally beat them all.
This game wants to be the "spiritual successor" and they tried hard but failed quite badly - which is a pity, really. It tried hard and that's why I give it a "thumbs up" rating despite many flaws.
On the good side, there is a new and interesting mechanic: You don't kill enemies but instead weaken them until they change their colour and then dash through them to absorb them. Depending on how fast you are at absorbing your enemies, you are granted higher score and bonuses like increased damage or speed - though I never found them really useful. You also absorb Boss enemy abilities like Mega Man does.
So what's bad about it, then? Well... Mega Man was tough. I sometimes felt Might No. 9 is outright
.
There are tricky jumps? Well, that's OK. But if you chain a dozen of those and if you fail you insta-die and then have to do all the crazy stuff again? That's too much. And they set the levels up in a way that basically
contains such an unfair situation. Very often you don't even know how to handle them because the tutorial lacks some fundamentals and new weapons sometimes have extremely useful and necessary abilities that are not shown to you but that you have to manually look up. Why they didn't include a quick tutorial about each weapon is beyond me...
In any case, I have stopped playing twice because I died at an unfair location too often... I just asked myself: why on earth am I doing that to me? I finished them, later... but that kind of frustration is the wrong kind. It may drive away some players.
New weapons have auto-recharging energy which is nice to have but honestly I liked the MM system much better. It was also easier to switch to a required weapon in MMX, you simply hit the shoulder buttons - here you also use 2 shoulder buttons but have to confirm the switch which slows you down. Bosses are "weak" to specific weapons but I found not a huge difference like e.g. in MMX where you could completely change Boss fights using the "correct" weapon.
The new mechanic sounds all nice and fancy but in reality it doesn't always work out as expected... maybe I'm just too stupid but I often ended up dashing into enemies who weren't weak enough and screwed up my combo or got pushed into an abyss or a one-hit trap (and there are plenty). It also creates an unpleasant air of pressure. I know some will like that and share their speedruns proudly but I absolutely hate that "need for speed".
It's nice that there are cutscenes
you cannot skip single lines but only the whole scene. I always hate it when a developer does that! I read much faster than you speak but I still want to get the whole story - why isn't that possible?!
The music was OK but never really got to me... if you can, boot up a copy of MMX and you will immediately feel enthrilled by the soundtrack, you know it's about the future, robots, fights - but here it was just... well, it was just playing along. Not in a bad way but not really good, either. Some "pixelated" music from the past would have been awesome :)
About the price: about 20€ is too much. I got it in a Humble Bundle and that was OK. I have just finished it in under 5h and I have no intention to play it again. There is a lot of stuff that you can do, Boss rush, online ranking about speed and skill - but neither do I like stuff like that in general nor do I like the game enough to play them and it does of course not justify the price.

if you like hectic platforms you have probably found a game for you. I'd definitely recommend to get it during a sale, though.

// Quick Look
Flinthook is a charming rogue-lite that manages to provde a good challenge and plenty to unlock. I'd recommend it for those - like me - that love tight platformers and super crunchy pixel graphics. I'm almost tempted to say the game is worth it's price alone just to look at the art.
// Gameplay
The levels in Flinthook take the form of randomly generated space-pirate-ships made up from a selection of hand-crafted rooms. You - as the daring Captain Flinthook - must delve into these floating space labyrinths to recover what I only assume are some kind of space ghost.
A brief tutorial at the beginning of the game teaches you how to use the 'tools of the trade'. The trade here being space-ghost-hunting-space-ghost-pirate. These tools consist of the Blasma Blaster - a short range 'blasma' cannon that can be aimed freely and used whilst slinging yourself around the levels, The Quickhook/Hookshot - a grappling hook that allows you to zip around the levels using specific anchor points and THE BELT OF TIME (TM) - Whilst i'm not entirely sure what the actual name of the magic belt is, it's incredibly helpful if you want to slow things down for a couple of seconds to take stock of your situation.
Whilst navigating the levels with your new found weapons and fabric-of-reality-warping garments you'll be sure to come across a wealth of shiny coins and collectibles that can be used to make your journey easier, or spent at the black market to buy things that make your journey easier. The Black Market functions as an upgrade shop, where the Player can spend their hard-earned coins on permanet upgrades for captain Flinthook.
Many of the upgrades simply increase the Captain's health whilst others grant you extra abilites such as being able to lock yourself in place while aiming. The game also features a perk system that allows you equip perks in the form of cards that will provide you with boons on your intergalactic ghost hunt. These perks are only interchangeable at the start of a 'run', so choose wisely!
// Controls
I've been playing with a 360 controller and so far the controls are nigh-on perfect! My only nitpick is that aiming is done using the left thumbstick, so you're constantly on the move even when you want to try and line a shot up. Luckily the devs had the fore-sight to put the ability to lock yourself in place into the game as a - admittedly pretty cheap - and immediately available upgrade.
// Sound
The soundtrack is probably one of my favourite parts of the game so far, it really complements the art style and puts you in the mood for some 2D platforming.
There isn't much I can say really! If you enjoyed the music from the trailer, then you'll enjoy the sound track!
// Replay Value
The 'rogue-lite' genre is normally synonomous with games that have bucket loads of content. Whilst I don't doubt that Flinthook will keep me entertained for hours to come, I do wonder what it's long-term appeal will be. The time you'll get from the game will largely depend upon your own ability and how quickly you pick up the controls. At the rate i'm going, I can't see my first full run through happening before the ~10hr mark.
Flinthook boasts a large amount of collectibles in the form of relics, perks and lore that can all be accessed from the main menu - along with percentage counters for how much you've collected! Whether or not these will be enough to draw me back in after my first play through remains to be seen, though at the moment I find myself exploring every inch of the randomly-generated levels to ensure I don't miss anything!
Speaking of the levels, I'm afraid this is where the game may stagnate to point of deterring long-term play. Having only played 1.5 hrs, I've seen frequent repeats of room layouts and enemy placements. It is with hesitation I would complain about this at this point - I've just defeated the first boss and there seems to be some variation in level setting and scenery.
I will update the review with regards to level-generation once I've sunk a few more hours into it!
// Overall
Would I recommend Flinthook? Absolutely.
The platforming is tight and satisfying and the art/music is gorgeous.
Is it worth the price? For me, yeah, without a doubt! Though if you're someone that looks for an hour per penny when buying games - especially rogue-lites - then it will be largely down to your skill and willing to hunt collectibles that will determine how long you play the game for.
If you have any questions about the game, ask away! I'll be happy to answer :)

At the time of this edit I've just beaten the final boss for the first time, so I'm adding a bit to my original review. My opinion is pretty much unchanged: This game is going to go down as one of my favorite roguelites, and I'll likely be trying to get 100% on it.
Everything from the music to the spritework to the soft color palette is superb. I originally disliked the controls on controller, but after some experience I've come to understand why it was done the way it was. Most people seem to share my original sentiment, many of them opting to use keyboard and mouse instead because it allows for independent movement and aim, but I think it's because we just didn't get it. Everyone switches to KB&M in the first hour or two and goes "wow, this is so much better!" because it seems that way when you don't know what you're doing, it's more familiar. The game is heavily structured around the Chronobelt -- a device that slows time for a short period, for the uninitiated -- and I've seen so many people, including myself, completely ignore it. It feels like a last resort, like a Blank in Enter the Gungeon, but there are numerous loading screen tips and posts by the developers urging you to USE IT. It's very important to the core of the game, that's why it recharges so quickly! You're intended to leap towards an enemy, slow time, aim and launch a volley of shots, and then hook or dive away as the effect ends. But anyway, I digress! Let's get on to the good stuff.
This is where things get more in-depth, so if you want to go in blind, look away now! The game goes a bit like this: Before setting out on your journey, you pick a set of perks -- things like a health boost or longer hook range or faster movement speed -- each of which is allocated by your "perk points." You can get new perks as rewards from playing the game and ranking up, and expand your maximum perk points at the Black Market. The Black Market gives the game a progression system of sorts, similar to Rogue Legacy, where you can upgrade your ghost-headed fella so he has a chance of lasting a little longer than last time. After choosing which bad guy you're going to take down, each of which increases in number of "levels" and difficulty, you're given a list of ships to raid. Each ship has a difficulty level and modifiers that tell you what types of things you'll find on the level: Nice things like libraries, which let you piece together the lore of the universe, or warnings of stronger enemies. The goal is to go from room to room to find your way through the level, collecting gold and spending it on temporary perks or healing items along the way, defeat the miniboss (which often just takes the form of a harder room of enemies), take what is basically a piece of a boss key, and fly to the next ship to repeat the process until you've located the big bad guy.
Your equipment includes your "blasma" pistol, which can fire in any direction and has a somewhat limited range; your quickhook, which is similar in use but allows you to hook onto stationary rings scattered about every room for quick movement and evasion; your time belt, which lets you slow down time for a few precious seconds; and various subweapons, unlockable one-use items like throwable bombs and a trio of spinning skulls that help take out enemies when you're in a pinch.
Unfortunately, there are a few problems with the game. I don't exactly consider the control scheme to be an issue, more of an uncommon design choice that works once you get a handle on it. Occasionally enemies will be surrounded in a bubble that requires the quickhook to pop, but from my experience there's a very strange threshold where the hook decides it's going to latch onto a nearby ring instead, pulling you into the enemy and causing you to take damage. Cutscenes are completely unskippable. I've pushed every button on my controller and none of them do anything, not even bring up a menu, so every time I beat Baron Von Guu I have to sit through the introduction of the final boss. There also seems to be somewhat of a lack of animation quality towards the end. Several animations don't quite line up during certain parts of the final area, and some are reused. I know expecting unique animations for everything is asking a lot, but it kind of detracts from the experience of the final boss.
That being said, definitely give Flinthook a chance. The positives FAR outweigh the negatives, and I don't think you'll be disappointed.

So I spent ~80$ in the Steam sales and the game I'm the most happy about having purchased so far is the one that didn't even have a discount. You know. That's how I roll.
Soft Body is fun and engaging and well-designed.
It's also quite difficult to describe. Its official website says the game is "a meditative action game where you control two beautiful, gooey snakes at the same time." I've seen people naming it a "bullet hell" multiple times. And technically, you could call it that; but for me, it doesn't feel right. I can't relate to the word "hell" when it comes to this game. This isn't hell. This is different.
The thing is: I'm occasionally bad at games, and always terrible at losing them. Seriously. I'm an awful loser. I get mad. I shout at the screen. I ragequit. I'm not proud of it, but most of the time, that's how it goes: it doesn't sit well with me when a game forces me to do the same thing all over again with little to no reward.
In Soft Body I enjoy getting hit and dying because that means I get to experience the level again from the beginning. I get so caught in the flow of each level I just wish I could experience it on loop mode, with enemies constantly respawning.
The order in which the levels are presented kind of feels arbitrary at first, and sometimes you may find yourself finishing a stage and wondering, "that's it?". But it's also key for the experience. Some of them are more organic - not necesarily easy, but more "natural" to play and move - and some of them are kind of merciless, forcing you to be in a constant state of tension. The juxtaposition of the "easy" levels and the harder levels is perfectly planned to equilibrate the moments when you're keeping your guard up, playing very quietly and carefuly, and the moments in which you're just relaxing and wandering, watching the two little snakes painting the world around you in vibrant colors.
It's the perfect game for those times when you don't want to think about anything, and the days you want to think about everything, too. I'm currently struggling a bit with the hard mode ♥
tldr; Really cool immersive artsy experience. I love it.

First, let me say that I never got the chance to play this game when it first came out, so my review isn't coming from a place of nostalgia. Rather, this is my first time getting to enjoy the game.
And I have to say that other than a few slight gameplay issues, I'm really enjoying it so far.
Anybody who complains about the graphics is probably just a millenial piece of trash who thinks looks are more important than story. While it's true that some characters have a clubbed hand for their main hand, it does not detract from the rest of the game's asthetics.
The complaints I have for the game are the camera and the party AI. First of all, the camera can be difficult to manage, especially in situations where you need to look up. The camera doesn't pitch far enough, which caused me a bit of problems during the Path of Cain maze when I needed to use the symbols on the doors to figure out which path to take.
As for the party AI... umm... they're a bunch of idiots. I'll just tell you right now to not give them ranged weapons, because they will hide behind corners and literally fire straight into the wall, using up whatever precious ammo you've found / bought for them. Melee weapons are the way to go. Just be careful not to get funneled into choke points. Also, make a point to double check the party's stance before entering the streets. Because if you have them set to offensive, they will attack everybody in sight, which draws the town guards and you'll find your humanity dropping like a rock as they start racking up innocent victims.
As for the rest of the gameplay, it's arguably better than Masquerade Bloodlines. There are A LOT of supernatural powers you can get your hands on. Some of which have pre-requisite stats in order to learn, use, or master them. You can also diablerize your fellow vampires, a feature which was sadly missing in the subsequent game.
The game is fully voice acted, at least when it comes to the story, and each of the recruitable party members feels unique. Sadly, most of them end up being temporary party members by the time you come to the end of the game, so I recommend keeping the best tomes and equipment inside your vault until you know who is sticking around for the long haul. Then load up your remaining party members and go take on the big baddy!
The story spans from the medieval to the modern era, culminating at the end of 1999, when everybody thought the world was going to end. Though at the time, we were more afraid of self launching nukes than evil vampire gods.
SO yeah, I played this game without nostalgia goggles and still found it to be a fun ride. So I would recommend purchasing it for your library. Besides, it's only like $6, anyways, so you aren't blowing your cash if you decide you don't like it.

Vampire: The Masquerade – Redemption is a game past its prime. The character models are downright rudimentary, even sporting a literal hamfist at the end of their arm. The poor pathing often results in characters getting trapped behind objects or each other. The party, or coterie, commands, meant to mitigate the latter issue, never seemed to work for me. I would say this rendered the coterie useless, but that's mostly because I was afraid to take control of them directly. There isn't a pause and issue commands system, so the AI takes over your main character as soon as you switch to another. The AI is eager to spend blood constantly and frivolously, so as soon as it has him, he'll start using up his blood and consumables right away. The ability to transfer blood between your coterie – preferably out of combat when they are more docile – does help to manage this propensity for waste a little bit.
The combat, which accounts for the majority of game time, however, seems flawed even by the standards of its day. A handful of enemies have attacks that can and will lock you into a recovery animation until the character is knocked straight into torpor. These situations lend themselves to cheap solutions, which is fine because there are so many abilities ripe for that sort of exploitation. That lack of combat balance as well as casual references to information you'd only have if you'd chosen the other of the two dialogue paths leaves the game feeling a little like a first draft.
At this point you might be wondering why I'm recommending you play this game. It's because the narrative design outweighs all the above. Christof's journey spans from the Dark Ages to the oh-so modern age of 1999 as he seeks to deal with what it means to be damned as a vampire. The soundtrack perfectly sets the mood for each disparate area, from the eerie dissonant chords of the Tzimisce haven to the vampire-themed rap of New York City. And even though I caught dialogue being rearranged to include the maximum number of thous and thees more than once, the voice acting is spot on as well. However, the real magic starts when all those elements combine with those moments that result from Christof's unavoidable moral crisis.
There's a lot to slog through here and a lot to forgive, but I haven't stopped thinking about this game since I first played it a decade ago, and this more recent playthrough didn't ruin that memory for me. I'd say that alone means it's worth the effort.

Is this game worth playing? Absolutely.
Is this game worth getting all the achievements in? No.
Jotun is a hard game that simply refuses to hold your hand. Does that mean the game as a whole is hard? No. There are two kinds of levels, puzzle/exploration levels and boss fights.
The puzzle and exploration bits of the game are extremely easy and serve not so much as a test of your skill but merely to introduce you to some mythology. Thora narrates a bit about every now and again to explain what's going on lore-wise. Besides that, you can find golden apples which boost max health and god powers which are your abilities. These levels, while rich in knowledge, can be boring and sometimes feels like filler. There's simply long stretches of time where nothing happens. Enemies are scarces, only appearing in a few levels, and even then they pose little threat. The puzzles are also painfully easy at times so you don't feel challenged. However, that all changes during the boss fights.
This is where the game truly shines and it's a shame the other levels aren't as exciting. The boss fights are brutal, ranging from satisfying tough to "THE GAME DEVS ARE SADISTS" but in a good way. First off, this game lets you challenge any boss (besides the last) at the start. Kinda like a Mega Man game. If you can beat the boss, you can beat the boss, no prerequisite powers required, just beat the two levels to unlock it. While the bosses can be tought, the game is built around using everything you got at them and learning from your many, many mistakes. To boot, the bosses don't punish you for using your powers early. I'd go far as suggest using your powers ASAP to kill the bosses faster. This is way better than clinging tightly to your abilities for when the boss is staggered. Just hammer them. Now, I will say these bosses definitely can be frustruating but nowhere near impossible.
Combat is uh, good. Not particular varied but what we got is great. Thora swings her axe with some weight so it's satisfying to attack. Your light attacks work well for chip damage and the heavy attack is gratifying to land. Your powers are easy to use and all feel unique and useful. Even the Loki one, despite being gimmicky and kinda meh, was still useful during the final boss.
My one big critique is just how slow puzzles can be. While some puzzles work light attacks most of them require you to use heavy attacks to progress. Why is this an issue? Well, it just takes longer and you feel as though your light attack is useless. I'm not sure if you can use light attacks for puzzles if you simply attack enough times but it just feels useless at times. During boss fights, your light attack is your consoloation prize if you know you don't have the time to use a heavy attack. I just never felt like it was as useful as the heavy attack in combat or while exploring. Even worse, since it's a heavy attack, it takes a second to charge... oh boy, the time I could save using light attacks.
Story? Eh, it was fine. I liked Thora, she was badass. The mythology was cool too, didn't know much of this. All I knew was that I got really excited when I saw Nidhogg. I was in it for the gameplay mostly.
So yeah, definitely worth playing. I'm not sure you'd want to get all the achievements because they're going to be brutal to get but it's worth beating. This game has impressed the gods.

Recommended - with some reservations for those expecting a game, and not a novel.
Rarely does a game come along where I feel the need to actually take the time to write a review - but even rarer still does something as simple as a game have the power to instantly transport me almost 20 years - short of heading to GOG, of course.
If you spent any significant portion of your life in front of a clicking Windows XP box, chatting over AIM, _everything_ about this title will rocket you back to a distant memory in a way that only Q could rival.  From the perfectly executed windowsXP login screen, to the dings and doors of AIM, to the buddy icons and song lyrics in profiles and the ability to set your type to an unreadable blue-on-red, to the whirring of fans...
Superb.  Simply put - the 'feel' of this is masterfully executed.
The tone and syntax of the writing is so spot on that I found myself actually remembering conversations with my then-girlfriend, now-wife as if it were just yesterday, and not two decades ago.  If you didn't 'grow up' with AIM in this context, you won't get it, and I'm truly sorry for your loss.  If you did, however, prepare to be astonished at how well Emily Is Away captures what is likely a forgotten, but very important, part of your life.
For the first playthrough, at least.
And here's the reservations: There's not much replayabilty, as much of it is significantly scripted, but honestly, that's to be expected with such an expertly crafted tone to the words. HOWEVER, as it's more of an interactive novel with a story to tell, emotions to evoke, and commentary to make, I cannot fault it for this - it's lasting impact would be vastly damaged if you could alter the outcome in any way.
THAT SAID: This game is free, and it is totally, unequivocably, worth the price of admission, and more.  If you can afford it, donations to the author are completely justified.

Since this is currently my longest played games on Steam and maybe you won't find a person with a longer hours count in the review section, I think I am kind of obligated to give this game a bit of review.
1.
Don't let my hours count fool you. I spent at least 50+ hours on researching for all the tricks, crafting and story route on Wikia.  And this is very typical of your old-school RPG or JRPG in general. You need to do homework, you need to do research. The hours you spent outside the game is MUCH MUCH more important than your gaming hours. If you are the kind of person who just go and immerse yourself in the game world and you don't care much about research game mechanics, this is bad for you.
2.
Again, don't let my hours count fool you, my actual human controlled play time is only about 200 hours, the rest? I left a keyboard-simulator to auto-grind for EP, money and materials when I went out to hang around  (And you can find guide about this on Wikia, it even works in Xbox 360 version). I have seen many people complain about grind, I have to say, sorry you did it wrong. It is true for the true end bosses you need to grind for the ATTACK+999 items which is more nightmarish than hell, but other than that, there are smart ways of doing it. Still, if you don't like the sound of it, perhaps you would like to stay way.
3.
Again and again, don't let my hours count fool you, my first play through on easiest difficulty took me around 250 hours, and I used a trainer to modify save files, and yet I got demolished by the true end bosses. This is again your old-fashioned RPG or JRPG, difficulty choice is just bullsh*t. If you are doing it right, using the right method, utilising all the game mechanics, even hell feels like kindergarten. But if you are doing it wrong, even easiest difficulty feels like an upfront sandbagging to you. The in-game description says easy difficulty is for players only to view the story which is motherf*cking lying. If you don't like the taste of this, don't try this game.
4.
, which is understandable, as this game is quite old since it first came out. Many things are considered sub-standard even by anime game standard. Characters are just a piece of cardboard with no animation.
The best music cannot withstand 700 hours listening, trust me.
5.
The grid are there to fool you, the real strength lies within linking. Contrary to many other games, the casual mobs on the streets are just as dangerous as the boss fights. So in mid to late game every fight needs you to focus, in the end, this plus the endless repetition takes out the fun that you used to have on the battle field. Of course I apreciate the absurd diffculty of this game, the feeling of each battle win is good even though it is repetitive. But if you don't, the battle can bore you to death.
6.
And there are differences in the culture which I think western audience may find it awkward or even offensive. Since I played a lot of anime games, I know this is the norm, but as a review, I think I need to point this out.
Overall, after I got smashed in easy difficulty with trainers on the first run, I decided I ought to give a try the second time and I really wanna beat it on the hardest difficulty. In the end, I did. The process is quite satisfying, especially when you watch the final boss got beaten by you like a kid, it was so easy if you put in time. And I don't regret the decision to purchase this game a single bit. But I think I don't have any energy left to beat this game again, or to try any other agarest games on my steam account...

I honestly tried my best to complete this game, but it's truly just beyond me. It's an insult to anyone that plays it, assuming that our lives are so empty and devoid of meaning that we'd be content to slog through over a hundred hours (and that's if you cheat to avoid grinding) of bland, tedious, uninteresting drivel. The story is so much generic anime it should get its own commercials on Crunchyroll, all dark gods and contracts with enigmatic magic women, and if there's anything new or interesting about the plot, it's buried so deep into the game that no reasonable person should expect a player to ever reach it. The characters are absolute stock archetypes, which might be forgiven if they were given anything interesting to do or talk about, but as you might surmise by this point, they're not. The vast majority of the game's dialog is just the characters droning on about nothing in particular as they travel from point A to point B.
The gameplay manages to combine the long setup and playtime of strategy RPGs with the constant random battles of normal RPGs, with a bonus of having to grind endlessly for various types of points and currency in order to get the best gear, like a bad MMO. The only value or potential for enrichment to be found in this plodding, pointless waste of code is as a first-hand lesson on what it must be like to be Sisyphus. After over thirty hours, even seeing it in my Steam library causes me to cringe, the game feeling more like homework than a leisure activity. I don't know what we ever did to the developers for them to decide to so insultingly waste our time, but I hope that this review will spare others from sharing that fate.

[Music - bad]: The music did not help with the tedium of grinding because it had (what felt like) 8 songs to cover the entire game and ended up bleeding together. I've liked just about every JRPG soundtrack I've ever heard but this game is one of the few that felt shallow and irritating to listen to. Just remembered that the game does have voice-acting in the story parts of the game and in at least some parts of combat... obviously it wasn't that memorable since I only just remembered it when I was about to finish my review.
[Combat - good]: I liked the combat, it's a turn-based, isometric-grid system that utilizes team combo attacks that can be chained together to kill foes very quickly. The game also has a Pokemon-like system that lets you capture and use enemies in your party or merge them with other captured enemies to make a stronger one. Your combat effectiveness depends on the equipment which is where the gameplay hits a bump and leads to...
[Gameplay - bad]: All the good items, skills and equipment is either crafted, stolen, dropped from a boss, equipped on captured enemies, transmuted from captured enemies or an overkill bonus drop. Basically every enemy in the entire game has stuff to be stolen which means you have to have a party member that can steal with you at all times. Most of them also have overkill bonus items which means you have to empty their entire health bar and then do enough extra damage to fill up the health bar with overkill damage in order to get the bonus item, this is a pain in the butt on boss fights. To capture enemies you have to whittle their health bar to a sliver in order to even use the capture skill which also means you have a dedicated capture user in your party.
So, all of the above ultimately revolves around having materials you need in order to unlock new skills and make new equipment. There are hundreds of things you will have to craft and you will need to use the Agarest Wiki crafting pages to have a chance at finding all the materials, I ended up having like 6 tabs full of lists and charts to keep track of it all. The only saving grace is that some of the crafted items and skills can be purchased from the item shop once you've made them once... But not all of them, which means lots of grinding and farming and farming and grinding and-*ragequits*
[Story - average]: The storytelling comes via the visual novel style and has voice-acting for every character. It also has the somewhat cool quirk of progressing over the span of 100 years while following 5 generations of main characters. Starting in Generation 2, the main character's appearence, stats and weapon options are determined by who the main character chose to marry in the previous generation. Standard with any visual novel style game, is the multiple choice events that will determine which girls you can marry, optional party members and the ending. But, every time I started getting immersed in the plot and characters, I'd get smacked in the face with more stuff to grind.
[Difficulty - average]: The game offers several difficulties but there's a catch. You can only get the game's true ending by playing on hard or higher. There's no benefit to playing on any of the lower difficulties because the new game+ feature doesn't let you take anything important to a higher difficulty than the one you initially beat it on or lower. So you get to do even more grinding.
[Replayability - Why?]: You might as well just google the "True Ending" because even a few wrong choices during the multiple choice questions can cause you to get a different ending.
[Overall - average]: I'll be nice and give it an average because there are people out there that can tolerate the grinding insanity and enjoy the game... As hard as I tried to stay interested and enjoy the game like I wanted to, I just couldn't... That is a huge feat and not in a good way.

As someone who has an Iron Warriors army dedicated to the Tallarn war, this was basically an instant-buy for me.
Gameplay wise, it's okay.
I highly suggest going for the How to Play the moment before you begin, so you know the basics of how the game plays. But, if you played 40k, most of the tank combat carries over. Firing at your targets from the side or rear has a higher chance at dealing damage, so positioning and movement are perhaps even more important than shooting. (Except for Contemptor Dreads, who basically one-shot everything with their power fists). The AI is competent, and will give you a run for your money especially on hard.
My major complaints are the sound, music and sprite department, which really could use some work. It sounds like it's a PC game from the early 90s, and that's when there's music that plays. Most of the time, it's just silence during gameplay. The poor sound, mediocre sprites and effects doesn't really help the cheap iOS feel that the game has from time to time.
As an app, I wouldn't be as critical. But on PC, I'm expecting a few upgrades at the very least. Especially at the asking price.
Finally, I wish there were some ease-of-life fixes. For example, make it easier to rotate your tank. Fix the rotation button instead of making figure out which pixel is okay to click on. As well, even with a tutorial telling me how to navigate the clunkiness of the game, it's far too easy to make mistakes with the current interface. It's easy to make mistakes when figuring out which weapon you're going to fire. It's easy to mess up your movement and shooting because a friendly unit got in the way of your firing arc. It's easy to underestimate how long it takes to climb a hill, messing up your unit's movement.
And it's this clunkiness that makes it hard for me to recommend thus far. As it stands, it's hard for me to recommend it. I like it, and I want to like it more. I love the setting, I love the factions in play, and I love the 40k universe, and I'm going trudge through another few hours, and hope things turn out for the better.
