I was seriously pumped when I saw this game on my discovery queue. Looked absolutely awesome and, for the first few games, it totally was. The art is nice, the music gets repetitive and the theme is awesome. But after a few more games, I started to realise a few things:
1. This game is short. REALLY short. Compared to FTL's 9-ish zones and ~10-ish encounters per zone, you're looking at a total of less than 10 encounters in the whole game! Final boss included!! The whole game can, if you're fairly lucky, be completed in around 1.5-2 hours.
2. Continuing on from 1, because the game's so short, much of the character, mech etc. development becomes essentially worthless. In a single game, there's absolutely no possibility of being able to put more than 3/4 upgrades into anything and, unless you want to play with level 1 equipment all game, it's pretty clear which areas are going to get upgrades and which will have to be ignored right from the start. In EVERY game.
3. Again, unlike FTL, the number of potential encounters are seriously limited. After 4-5 games, you'll pretty much have seen every encounter that can possibly happen.
4. Again, again, unlike FTL, the game seems to be designed to be impossible at the start. It's got a cross-game character development thing going on, meaning that as you play more and more games, you'll start with more HP, better stuff etc. and the balancing seems to be built around this - you'll have to play 10+ games with a 95%+ probability of losing, so that you can collect enough upgrades to have a reasonable shot at the end boss.
All in all, I'm fairly disappointed in this game. While I'm still glad I got it, even on a sale price of £7, I think it's significantly overpriced. YMMV.
[edit] Two more things I'm starting to really hate:
1 - Salvage missions require the collection of an undamaged part. If the enemy overuses his stuff and overheats (dealing damage to his parts) you auto-fail the mission. Hooray for stupid design!
2 - Mission timers. Every single mission has a timer (max no of turns). Pull a couple of bad hands, and the mission is completely impossible, regardless of your planning, skill, equipment etc. It's the equivalent of telling a L20 character that they lost a fight with a L1 character because it was going to take them 10 seconds to kill the L1 rather than 8. Complete BS. [/edit]
Overall, I'm starting to actively dislike the game, and am now playing only to complete the achievements.

In a nutshell:
An awesome game for the lovers of the Puzzle Quest/FTL kitbash genre. The game has the randomness of the FTL and the strategic thinking of PQ WITHOUT the randomness factor. This is just huge. While it is still a bit luck based, strategic thinking while connecting the available resources on your board ill lead to victory.
Not a TL;DR In-depth:
1. The Game in general.
1. Like FTL: Make your own vehicle from a bunch of given presets, upgrade and augment it with stuff you find on the battlefield and go for victory.
2. Like FTL: randomness and replayability at its best.
3. Like FTL: varying encounters with different goals to go for.
4. Like Puzzle Quest: you have a board with gems - here you have resources.
5. Like Puzzle Quest: you need to match the resources, with the difference that you can go diagonally.
6. Like Puzzle Quest: There is still some randomness.
7. You lose, you die. Simple.
8. UN-like 90% of FTL: you have intel (unless you have FTL info of the map which is rare), and you can prepare.
9. UN-like 60% of FTL: you know what the mission's all about. Not just "there is an enemy starship in this area"
10. UN-like Puzzle Quest: you have your own board and you can plan ahead. You can even strategicaly make a huge 12-tile chain just to open up more board space.
11. UN-like Puzzle Quest: the enemy can't foil your plans with your own pieces. Only bad luck can - or yourself, for that matter.
12. UN-like Puzzle Quest: The is no luck factor to enemy beating you using your own board and making you smash your screen.
13. UN-like both of them: you have way bigger control over what happens in a mission.
The Battles:
1. Enemies vary, and are interesting - you need to examine an enemy and attack it in a specific manner.
2. Simple mouse clicking is your doom. Using your brain wins battles.
3. The various ironcasts have different abilities. Play to the advantage or detriment of those.
4. Battle variety is huge, with boss battles every 10 turns thrown in for good masure.
5. You have shields, movement, evasion, hull, everything you need to defeat the enemy. Or lose.
The Rest:
Is mediocre. Gameplay makes this game good.

If you love games that sound amazing and feel good to play, this is probably your game of the year. It's a bullet hell like no other; a game where you don't shoot your enemies but try to get close enough to touch them without getting shot. And you do it by controlling two snakes at once, one with each hand.
Getting good at Soft Body is like a form of meditation. As you start to get better at it, you stop focusing on controlling one snake at a time, and you wind up controlling both simultaneously, not looking at either one. Then the game starts to throw challenges at you where you need to be moving and dodging and attacking with both of them at once.
This is a bigger game than people sometimes realize - Hard Mode isn't just a difficulty tweak, it's a whole new set of levels and mechanics.

A review at 10 hours for the benefit of fellow 2016 summer sale shoppers.
I've been playing JRPGs since Final Fantasy 4 (though back then it was labeled "2").
This game's music, art, leveling/stat progression, graphics, battle system...it works for me.
Audio: If "RPG music" is a genre of music you have actively sought after at some point, this game could add several tracks to that rotation. It's about as enjoyable as the Valkyrie Profile soundtrack. Game also has full Japanese voice acting, none that I recognize enough to put a name to yet, but there's talent to appreciate. My hearing sense is pleased.
Visual: Graphics are.... "nostalgic". Or maybe if you'd rather look at Doom or Fallout 4, they're just bad. I find them enjoyable though. The anime character drawings are nice to look at, the backgrounds are kinda pretty.
Gameplay: Hilariously overcomplicated. It was throwing tutorials at me for far longer than expected. When I was 14 I might've sat and memorized it all before going forward, but at this age, I choose to just learn as I go, and the game hasn't punished me for doing so yet (it presented me with easy-normal-hard at the start, I chose normal). The myriad mechanics are pretty fun once I started learning them, though I still haven't mustered the patience to stop moving the plot forward and find an optimal battle loadout. All in time I suppose.
I recommend that DLC be disabled, since it hands you game-breakingly overpowered items in your starting inventory, items with stat numbers like 1700 when starting stats are something like 200. If it's an additional playthrough the DLCs kind of make sense, speed things along and save oneself the grind. I went back to the "select DLC" at the new game screen to note what all the items were and then discarded them in-game on the save I had been playing, which also worked fine.
The plot is...okay! I've seen better, I've seen worse, it's enough to keep me playing. So far it's just war, war, war.
Now lastly, the topic I haven't touched yet. This is a game made for a heterosexual male demographic. The term "male gaze" was invented for the costumes the female characters in the game wear (or lack of costumes, or whatever). The plot has some familiar devices from the anime harem genre. Partly I find this sort of thing funny, partly I enjoy it for what it is, and, another part of me acknowledges that it's pretty stupid. This paragraph is just a warning that there is such a theme to this game, which isn't for everybody.
Anyway, not beating myself up over spending the sale price, since I'm enjoying the game for the time being.

A fairly straightforward translation to 2D. The game follows the same formula, even story-wise, as the original but makes some good minor tweaks in how the game plays. It is probably more accessible than the original and streamlines and balances some aspects of the original without dropping them (capturing is a good example).
There is no revolution, just gentle polishing, and for me that worked well - I loved Homeworld 1, and this game is more of the same, just tuned and more accessible (which it did not need to be for me, but it probably does not hurt for a general audience).
Gameplay is good, story is unsurprising and serviceable (which is fine - I am very happy with this approach of telling a story familiar to us from HW1 without "improving" it), but where the game excels is its atmosphere - I am impressed and delighted that the developer understood that this always was the series' main strength. The music is expertly implemented, following the strong musical Homeworld tradition. Together with the graphical style and details, background chatter, story and gameplay this all helps to achieve a degree of immersion few RTS titles manage.
I have a small nitpick in what I dub "carrier inflation" in the story - after the thrilling multi-mission chess-battle of the Sakala & you against the the Ashoka, you then kill another carrier in the next battle... and two more in the battle after. Luckily this was not followed by four carriers, but you get the idea: Tellingly I cannot recall the other carriers' names, and the game wisely did not introduce their commanders as it did with Khagaan (whom I found to be a subtly portrayed, strong character). I thought the Ashoka section was expertly done to create a tense atmosphere and fantastically-realistic portrayal of the Gaalsien and their supposed desert superiourity; murdering three more carriers in two more missions somewhat cheapened the experience. Rachel and her personal sidequest also fell a little flat for me; I did not really felt they fitted well into the scope of the series, though I can see what was trying to be achieved, and think it was executed competently.
But to end on a high note, I also appreciated the effort (not always the execution) of portraying some moral ambiguity of the inter-Kiith conflict.
So, yeah, solid recommendation. Solid game and a solid option if you wish to spend another 12 hours or so in the Homeworld universe. Do play "classic" difficulty if you are familiar with Homeworld's emphasis on unit preservation, resource husbandry and unit capture.

The Homeworld series has a special place in my heart. The original series is in my top RTS favorites of all-time. Deserts of Kharak shares some of the great strengths of the original series, namely compelling story-telling, diverse strategic scenarios, and a foreboding atmosphere of isolation and self-reliance. The unit design is well done, the attacks, movement, and overall gameplay I would say is very satisfying.
Though they are few, I also have significant complaints.
1.  Really inconvenient camera views -- you just can't zoom out far enough to avoid scrambling between units; particularly whilst trying to micromanage strike fighters and bombers, keeping them from flying too far behind enemy lines while simultaneously managing ground units.
2. No pause functionality. Self-explanatory. The style of gameplay in Homeworld and DoK means that there are GREAT benefits of micro-managing your fleet (i.e. explicitly telling each unit where to stand guard or flank enemy units even within smaller command-groups) since, left to their own devices, your command groups will cluster together making them easier targets and less tactically effective. When you have multiple command groups, and possibly multiple battles occuring at once, it is simply not feasible to give that level of detailed attention to each group in real-time.
Honestly, if the devs really want to keep the game real-time and avoid pausing, then they could've made the map more accessible by not restricting the camera views so much. Alternatively, the camera views would be workable (albeit annoying) if the game had pause functionality so as to not loose too much time traversing between sectors. Neither of these makes the game unplayable on its own, but the combination is extremely inconvenient and unnecessarily restrictive on playstyle. I mean, if you are master and commander over a warzone, you would want to have a detailed but high-level view of said battlefield, no? Otherwise you would not be a very effective leader. I prefer an RTS that removes such stops blocking the way to effective commanding.
3. And this is a big one too -- once your main objective is completed, you move on to the next challenge whether or not you were able to collect the available resources beforehand. This means I have reloaded old saves and postponed completing the mission just to finish exploring the map and collecting everything I can. This really impedes gameplay on certain missions, such as the airborne resupply mission. Again, if it were possible to pause the game and issue commands to your dispersed fleet, devs could get away with this. But as-is, you have to make a choice about how much time you are willing to budget for keeping salvagers productive at the expense of protecting your fleet and engaging the enemy.
There are other minor things, like salvagers needing constant attention to keep them on-task, and forcing some weird key-bindings on the end-user, but the game itself is so good that I don't even care about those things.
4. Autosave ridiculousness -- is it just me, or do the autosaves regularly occur at awful times? I frequently will go back to an autosave just to realize it saved my progress precisely AFTER a successful attack was launched on the salvagers that I forgot to redirect to a new resource field, or some such event. Combined with the fact that I cannot save on my own without making a custom name each and every time (no automatic time-stamp file names defaulted), it means that my saves are fewer and farther between and I cannot rely on autosaves whatsoever. Several missions started over for this reason.
Like I said before, it's the combination of restrictive design-choices that make it almost too much to bear. Ultimately I recommend the game to anyone who enjoyed Homeworld OR is a real RTS fan. The game's quality, judged on its own, stands up.

As an NES/GBA MegaMan speedrunner, I expected to love this game; It seemed like everything I loved about Legends, X and the classic series combined, with some design elements from the visuals of Battle Network and Zero. This... is not the game I thought it was, even after setting my expectations low from the multiple delays, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ reviews from big and no name reviewers alike, and playing the demo build released to backers. (I am not a backer. I am just a man who loves MegaMan.)
The character designs are unlikable in every way, at least for the main cast. They aren't ugly-cute. They aren't cute. They aren't 90's-trying-to-be-badass or trying to recapture or reimagine what classic 2D platformers could look like and feel like. (That could describe a lot of this game. I'll get to that.) There's a stereotypical dork white dude named DOCTOR WHITE, and his fat friend Dr. Sanda. The Mighty No.s are more interesting, better looking, and have better voice actors, but for the most part are boring. Shoutout to Dynatron and Countershade for having interesting stages and character designs, I almost thought this game was good until I tried to play the rest of the stages.
The visuals are bad, but not in the way that people publicized on Youtube videos and clickbait articles. It's bad in that I have tried to create 3D models with textures mapped to them and done horribly, DISGUSTINGLY bad, but that I'm fairly sure if I was given the time that Comcept was given, I would be able to put something better out. They do have pretty visual effects on certain things to try to make something lazy look like it's not, such as Beck's dash.
Signposting (the art of letting your player know through subtle signs what they're supposed to do, for those unfamiliar) is terrible in this game. There are mechanics and abilities that are either barely explained or only explained to you once you are punished for not knowing them. (Crouch-Dash, anyone? What absorption does and how enemy type or combat proficiency affects it?) Zelda had better signposting, and that game is notorious for having that as a fatal flaw. It is unforgivable to leave the player clueless in so many ways. One of the only 'good' stages (Intro, Countershade, Dynatron, but Countershade is what I'm referencing) also has several flaws that make it insufferable.
1. The entire stage is just a bossfight.
2. Most of the stage is in a single corridor that is a uniform size.
3. You are expected to find the boss, but there is no way you are told or shown how to find them. Maybe there's a way through watching the sniper fire in some way, but I couldn't detect it, as it was fairly linear AND ON A 2D SPACE. How do you figure out how far a sniper is from you in 2D space?
The fact that this is one of the only good things I have to point out here as someone who loves and eats up anything MegaMan should tell you a lot. Call is emotionless and boring, seems like her only reason for existence is to remind people of Roll, since her callouts and info are borderline useless 90% of the time.
I guess that the jumping and shooting themselves feel good (minus the omission of the charge shot) but the horrible level design ruins that bit for you, and the wonky animations they chose for Beck running make it pretty difficult to tell where you're supposed to place yourself for precise jumps (not that those come often, and not that you can't just dash past everything.)
IN SHORT: It's bland, unattractive, and reminds me of the 4kids versions of popular anime. Maybe if you've never seen One Piece or Naruto unedited, you can enjoy the horrible voice acting, disjointed plot, and soulless feel since some of the charm the creators put in originally shines through like a tiny hole to the surface in a dark dungeon thousands of meters underground. Fantastic metaphor for this game. Do not buy it. I got it as part of a Humble Bundle for $5 with Deadlight and a bunch of Saints Row games AND Killer is Dead, and I still have that dirty feeling you get when you waste your money on something  you were completely sure you were going to fall in love with. The only reason I still have this game installed or have any additional playtime past the hour I played before writing this review is because I'm considering streaming it as part of a series of bad games including Husk and Team Indie. Take a look at those if you want an idea of how much quality was put into this.

(note: I have more hours on this than shown - played at a friend's house) It's one thing to pay homage to source material.  It's another to copy/paste the code and gameplay, and then throw in some freshman collage era 3D and circa 1998 textures.  This game is a blatant ripoff of a beloved franchise - Dr. White?  Seriously?  Kid sister robot girl in red?  Pyro and Cryo etc Man?  This is a game that could have easily reinvigorated the fan base of Megaman, and had such potential to open the doors to new gameplay that could have synergized marketing with old fans as well as new ones.
It falls short on almost every level - the story is the same ridiculous 'robots go crazy, we must stop them' gibberish.  It's devoid of any heart or soul(which is a bummer, because the BOX artwork is fantastic and brimming with personality).  The platforming elements are either nearly freeform as you can air-dash infinitely, OR you get to parts where you have to wait AGES for the fire/electric/ice/whatever barriers to sloooowly turn enough for you to continue the slog through the level.  I was digging the dash mechanic at first, expecting it would give a nice kind of rhythm to the levels, but those are immediately dispelled when enemies and barriers are introduced into the mix(so, about 30 seconds into the first level).  And no matter what robot ability you absorbs from the other Mighty #'s, the blaster is by far more useful than most of what they have to offer - and usually, the others are rendered absolutely worthless except in extremely specific situational events.
I think, bottom line, if they would have done something more... engaging?  With the dash attack, this game could have been fun.  Maybe the dash is geared towards speedrun players?  I'm not sure - it's the only time the game starts to feel fluid and tactical, but that's over in literally less than a second.  If you could use the dash to build momentum, or to charge abilities, or point the dash in 8/analog directions, or use it to go *through* enemies and attack from behind, etc - anything would have been better than what was given.
If you want to play a shovelware, kiddie version of the original Megaman from 1987, have at it.  Otherwise, play Owlboy, Azure Striker Gunvolt, Flinthook, Axion Verge, or any of the bajillion retro inspired games that really put thought and effort into their gameplay and look.

Silly camera.

But dont be afraid. The game manages to ease you in. Over the course of the (very well written) story, which glues the puzzles together, you gain access to more and more parts to use.
The game would suit you if you like puzzle solving. Its a plus to have some fundamental understanding how computer are working (even if it is greatly abstracted within the game), and to have heard about assembler languages.
After I've bought it I had an all-nighter. Juste one more design and just one more tweak to get it working with fewer assembler instructions or components used.

Essencial a sequal to TIS-100 takes the simple idea of writing a assembley like code to solve puzzels and adds electronics and circuit design to the mix. Its also got a fun little variation of solitare thown in.

If you are into programming, especially low-level programming, this is the right game. Unlike its prequel (well, I guess I can call TIS-100 this way), SHENZEN actually has some kind of story to move you.
If you are not into programming, this is a great game to decide if it's yours thing. I love to recommend it to people that are yet to decide their life and career path.
If you like programming, you will like this game!

More than a great puzzle game, SHENZEN I/O is a great concept.
It's hard. Especially when you're a programmer and are obsessed with optimization.
But it's, like SpaceChem, Infinifactory or TIS 100, near perfection when you manage to beat a puzzle and feel even smarted afterward.
Really a great game if you like to tinker.
Very clever and a worthy successor to Spacechem and TIS-100.

Medieval Engineers is in its early stages as I write this review.
Have you ever played block building games and felt the need to place foundations and build buttress, even though the game physics don't require it? Ever looked at a floating building with despair?
Then THIS is the game for you. Composite building and structural integrity mean you can build a realistic building where the design matters far more than in any other game of this kind.
I have clocked quite a few hours on this so far, and I can see myself whiling away a good chunk of my spare time here. I love the way you can build structures from deep basements to towering watchtowers that will collapse if I do it wrong!
Don't get me wrong, the physics aren't too punishing. You won't have your buildings falling apart every five minutes. It's just a relief to build structural supports where they actually have an effect.
The potential of this game has only just begun to be realized. I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys building. Also, to anyone who loves to destroy and test the strength of a tower.
[Addition] After a couple of months, I do find a degree of frustration with this game. Lag and frame drop are a very real issue everytime you know down a building. As I see much of the fun of this game in the destruction of what I build, this has become a real disappointment. I also love the idea of playing multiplayer, and running through a building my friend is destroying. Again though, lag is intense when destroying things, making this an almost unplayable feature.
It is my hope that this game will improve, but it might be worth waiting a while.

Recommended up to a point.
People looking for the new Puzzle Quest will be disappointed, because it lacks many of the crucial features that made PQ such a success.  But on its own terms, it is a terrific little filler that is intended to be played in short bursts and works well in that form.
The biggest problem of Match-3 games remains: the sheer random nature of the drops means that resource management becomes a case of crossing your fingers rather than feeling as though you are planning ahead - and this applies to the level upgrades as well.  Having said that, there is a surprising variety of approaches that seem viable, and the Global Unlock notion is a neat way of encouraging replayability whilst having to put up with the same encounters over and over (although I'm sure some new ones may well follow in time.)
Personally, I like the low-key graphics; they don't distract from the core gameplay but they give the right atmosphere, which is important here.  As others have noted, there are some UI issues, especially on the actual resources side, but they feel minor enough that they don't spoil things.
In the end, this feels a bit too much like a tablet game.  That's not a criticism in the slightest, but as soon as I can play it on a tablet I will probably uninstall it from my PC.

This review is of the Early Access edition of the game.
Having been a Football Manager addict for many years, I was extremely pleased to see that Eastside Hockey Manager was back. Having played hockey myself for many years, this is the ultimate sports sim. The tactical options on display gives a multitude of options in terms of implementing the game plans you have in mind from individual players all the way up to the team as a whole. Line matching could be a bit more transparent and flexible, but by and large all the necessay tools are there to make your guys play the way you want them to.
Graphically the 2D engine does a good job of representing what's happening on the ice, and while I would like to see and option of chosing between 3D and 2D just as in Football Manager, I'm more than content to settle for the current model as it serves it purpose really well. So if you like hockey and manager games, get this. You won't be sorry.

9.5/10, almost the perfect simulator
I have to say, this is the best hockey simulator out there, by far. This goes way more in-depth than any other hockey GM simulator I have ever played and it is by far the most realistic of any hockey simulators I have played. The strategies mean a lot in this. In my first year of Tampa, Ben Bishop was terrible: 3.43 GAA and a .878 save percentage. I made lots of strategy changes that made more players defensively-minded and it raised Bishop's stats to a 2.75 GAA and a .902 save percentage. In EA's be a GM mode, the strategies mean nothing. You can't decide how a player plays, you can't coach the players, you only assign what lines the players are on and that is it. In EHM, you decide where the player plays, the length of his shifts, his shoot/pass ratio, his practice, almost everything. Overall, it is incredibly addictive. I only have two games on Steam: TF2 and Eastside Hockey Manager. I have played more TF2 than Eastside Hockey Manager, but Eastside Hockey Manager has almost completely gotten me away from NHL 15's GM mode. When you compare the two, EHM is by miles better, and it's still in beta. Bravo to the developers for making such an amazing game.
Wishlist/Gripes:
*The ability to edit players. No matter what simulator I play, there will always be tweeks needed to the rosters. For example, Cam Talbot has worse stats than Robin Lehner in this game which I highly disagree with. In NHL 15 on current gen, you are able to edit players and make the sim even more realistic. I would like to see a player editing option because I still find that there are players who are rated too high or too low.
*More casual options. I think options like injuries, waivers, and an assistant coach rotate goalies option would all be welcome in my opinion. I feel that waivers make it a little too easy and they need some fixes. I have seen the following players in years one, two, or three get placed on waivers:
*Marian Hossa
*Jiri Sekac
*Brandon Saad
*Dustin Brown
If options like this are available then I'm stupid, just saying.
*More simple simulation. I find it frustrating that when I go on a vacation the assistant GM completely takes over. I think there is an option that can turn him off, but it is still very annoying when I'm a cap team and my assistant GM brings in Marian Gaborik. And the coach will also make lineup changes when there is no injury which is annoying. I wish the simulation way more like EA's but at least it isn't a major problem.
*About the injuries, sometimes it feels like the injuries do get way out of hand. I always see like one or two or tears a month and those are four month injuries. I remember on my Edmonton play through in year two I had an injury every other game it felt like. All were minor (thank god), but it got to be very annoying. I think injuries can stay because they add a lot of challenge (like when I lost Jason Demers to a damaged spine which is essentially a year-long injury), but turning down the frequency of the injuries would be welcome.

Appropriately enough Bad Company 2 begins by kicking the doors in and unloading a shotgun blast of thrills in your face. Following a brief, straightforward prologue you’re pitched into the snowy wastes of Alaska (not to mention 24-style intrigue) as the Bad Company boys stumble across a Russian plot involving a terrifying experimental weapon. Given that almost every gun you can pick up here doubles as a grenade launcher, that’s quite a threat.

While some of the quips between the protagonists are fun, the overall experience with the singleplayer mode is rather boring. There's only few variety and the linearity of the levels is terrible. This becomes especially noticeable in forest levels.
Graphically it can't even compare to Battlefield 3 and later, however especially the textures of the clothes still look quite detailed. And this game is a bit older, after all.
Of course the most important part in a Battlefield game is the multiplayer mode. Besides the server list, which I had problems with, this game is still a lot of fun. However, it only has one thing that is better than in Battlefield 3: it has smaller maps and thus it feels more action-oriented. For anyone who likes a more realistic experience though, I would recommend Battlefield 3.

tl;dr: HIGHLY reccommend getting this game. Ignoring the mediocre campaign and occasional server frustrations, this is probably the best fps I've ever played.
Even though I moved to a rural area and can no longer play it's muliplayer, I still regard this game very highly. If you have the money to spare, I can almost guarantee that you won't be disappointed. I have no idea what the servers are like these days, but back when I played it, the minor hiccup with the punkbuster service was overshadowed by the dedicated server support. Even the campaign is a fun playthrough for the first couple of times.
What it does right: Where to begin. This is what an fps should feel like. The guns are satisfying to shoot, and kills are an amazing gratification in multiplayer. Everything is smooth and works well, with nothing seeming out of balance if you know which situation to use it in. The massive maps and inclusion of vehicles pretty much necessitates that every match of conquest or mcom needs to be a team effort, and makes this easy with the squad system. The endless unlocks and medals in the multiplayer ensure you always have a goal to work for, and make sure you never stick with one playstyle long enough to get bored with it.
The multiplayer was the most fun I think I've ever had with an fps. The maps are always just the right size to ensure that you can't miss out on the action if there's a full lineup on the server, and with all the variables on each map there's never a dull moment, and every match is a different experience.
Moving away from multiplayer, the singleplayer campaign was surprisingly enjoyable as well. The typical 'russians invading the world' plot bores me to death, but with the likeable characters at the forefront, and throwing out the traditional sense of taking everything way too seriously, this campaign was much more enjoyable than others of the same type. Most COD or even later battlefield games just take themselves too seriously, and the constant quips from the characters and such make it so that's never a problem.
What it does wrong: EA has never been very good at dealing with customers, and the punkbuster service is no exception. Not only is it an extra account that has to be logged into every time you want to play multiplayer, but sometimes it doesn't even work for multiple attemtps. It can get really frustrating when I just want to play the game. I've heard it was to curb piracy and hacking in the game, but all it really does is inconvenience the actual paying customers. It wasn't a good design choice, especially if EA stops checking up on the servers entirely. I would hate to see an entire game broken because of the lack of consideration by the publisher, but with who we're talking about, it wouldn't be surprising.
Another complaint might be the campaign. I know I said it was good, but especially on later playthroughs it can get really repetitive at times. The varied locations are nice, but there's really no reason to play through the campaign to find intel or something once you've beaten it once. This game really shines in the multiplayer, but that doesn't mean some features couldn't have been added to the offline side to make it more enjoyable. Like, you know, a skirmish mode to play against bots. That would've been nice. I don't get how earlier games had this, but DICE just decided to stop doing it all of the sudden. It would've been a godsend when the sign in service was acting up.
The campaign could've done with some weapon customization or unlocks or something to make it worth playing more than once anyway.
So overall, it's a really great game in the multiplayer side of things, and even still enjoyable in singleplayer. I would definitely recommend that everyone give it a try. It has definitely been one of the best experiences I've had in the gaming world.

What I think is not good are:
我觉得不够好的是：
1. Unlike the classic Homeworld 2 and the Homeworld Remastered, this game does not auto-collect resources when one mission finishes. Worse, in this game, a mission ends immediately once all objectives are complete. Therefore, what I chose to do was just like how I did in the classic Homeworld 1 many years ago -- to collect all resources manually before the last objective is complete. I don't want to miss any collectible resources.
1. 与原版《家园2》及《家园》重制版不同，这个游戏在关卡结束时不会自动收集资源。而且，游戏中，一旦任务目标完成，关卡立刻结束。于是，我只能像以前玩原版《家园1》那样，手动收集所有资源，而且故意留着最后一个任务目标不去完成。我就是不想浪费任何一点资源。
2. Unlike all previous Homeworld series (either the classic or the remastered), this game does not auto-save when one objective completes in a mission. I really do not like this. What I did was to manually save the game whenever I completed one objective in any mission.
2. 与之前所有的《家园》游戏都不同，这个游戏，每关的任务目标完成后不会自动保存一下。这就很要命了。如果我不手动保存，那从头到尾就只有一个自动保存的最近保存点，极其崩溃。
3. The game has some bugs unpatched. For example, in some cases, one group of fighters launched from the carrier are not three but two, but what I saw on the Carrier control panel was three fighters. Another example is in the final mission, when I destroyed the Gaalsien super carrier, the Gaalsien leader made his last speech. However, the speech was made without any background music or sound effect. I guess this is a bug, too.
3. 游戏有一些bug还没修补。比如，有些情况下，母舰里出来的同一批次战斗机只有2架而不是3架，但母舰控制面板上显示的却是3架战机。另外，最后一关把Gaalsien的超级母舰打爆后，Gaalsien领袖带着哭腔发表了一段“失败感言”。这段感言说的时候，游戏的背景音乐及特效声音都没了，只剩下人说话的声音。
4. This game removes many familiar short keys in Homeworld series. For example, I can't order Salvagers to collect resources by pressing "H" key. This makes resourcing inconvenient.
4. 游戏取消了《家园》系列中的一些快捷键。比如，采集资源的快捷键H就没有了。每次采集资源都要手动点击资源，很不方便。
5. The final cutscene is too short. I really hope I can see the mothership under construction. However, there was only space. But the background music is familiar -- the one played in Homeworld 1 Mission 1.
5. 最后一段过场动画太短。我本来还希望能从那段动画里看到正在建筑中的母舰，结果除了星空什么也没有。不过背景音乐倒是《家园1》第一关的音乐。
Overall, this game is good. I think I can play for many times to try different tactics. I really hope some bugs can be fixed. I also hope we can see Homeworld: Cataclysm (or Homeworld: Emergency) Remastered and Homeworld 3 (and 4, 5, 6, ...)
总体来说，游戏不错。我觉得还可以再多玩几次，尝试下不同的战术。我希望上面所说的bug能修复一下，然后希望能看到《家园：惊世活动》的重制版，以及《家园3》（以及4、5、6……）。

This is a very competent RTS that leans a bit too heavily on the Homeworld brand- I honestly would have rather seen what Blackbird did without the IP from gearbox.
The unfortunate thing is that nearly two years after release it is still being sold for $49.99- killing any chance of any userbase growth, community, or real multiplayer presence. Which seems counter intuitive and a bit tone deaf considering how much multiplayer DLC is tacked on. This game should be $15 at this point, and $12 on sale- but at this point it's a waste of potential.
For a niche game in a niche series you really can't afford to not go all in on getting as many people as possible to play it, because you can't depend on all your sales coming from fans who have been pining for a decade for a sequel- you need to attract fresh blood. You can't sell it on the same model as a AAA game- all that will do is get you to convince yourself that there is no money to be made in a series like this, which is wrong.
This is a fine game that never had a chance in hell of having any sustainability because of mishandling.

I tried to enjoy this game, I really did. It has great deal of potential and it's heartbreaking to see it wasted. This game has so many features - complex battle system, monster hunting and catching, crafting and enhancing, dating elements, generations of characters just to name few, yet many of them feels not needed or rushed. Game doesn't make you want to use them at all. I can't call Agarest the worst game I ever played, I can't call it a very bad game either, but it's certainly not a game I can recommend to anyone.
Story is interesting, but characters are rather flat. Not bad, but they feel unfinished. You have huge team of people, yet can hardly say anything about the character or reasons others have to travel with you. In most cases it isn't hard to guess who's good and who's bad, good guys look innocent and noble, bad ones cunning and evil. Cute girls look cute, brave girls look brave. Everything is so obvious, you hardly ever feel surprised by the turn of events. Main antagonist and his heirs all seem to suffer from Mary Sue complex and many of their partners are flattened to the role of brainless, boobs showing dolls - most of them doesn't feel real at all. There are few interesting characters out there, but in the end the lack of deepness is a biggest flaw of the game, most of the characters is not memorable at all. I spent nearly 80h in this game and I can't remember even 30% of characters that are traveling with me.
Combat system was interesting at first, but gets repeatable very fast. I hardly see it as a flaw, but this game is too long in general. I felt like doing same stuff over and over again. Each battle is the same like earlier one. Of course the game has something for people, who are a bit tired of killing and want to enjoy the story mode - the autobattle system, that is supposed to play combats for you, while you prepare your favourite tea. However, don't be fooled by it. Your AI controlled characters have an IQ of a potato and will keep dying all of the time. You have a healer in the party? Great. Just don't expect it to stay in the last line and support others. It will act like a first line tank and die first. You're fighting against fire elemental? Expect party members to throw fire spells in it like there is no tomorrow. Suddenly a fight you could easily finish yourself turns into a slaughter of your team. In fact it's best not to watch those battles at all, unless you enjoy face palming every few seconds.
The world and environment are another very disappointing element. Everything is empty and dull. Dungeons are big empty spaces you just run through, many of them are just slightly altered versions of earlier dungs. Even though you're visiting different continents and places in each generation, all maps and towns look the same. Same npc's, same spaces, there is no variety that would make the world feel truly alive. Music is just generic sounds that play in the background that hardly anyone will want to hear again after the game ends, in fact I got sick and tired of it after second generation.
Many small things are annoying. Lack of possibility to resurrect outside of battle, characters that are not in the party will not gather exp which makes them useless in the long run, crafting is much more complicated than it should, even though game forces battle spots (battles are not random most of time) on you, you still have to grind exp in the end. Nothing in this game is memorable or makes you want to go back to playing it again.
Thing I liked the most? Battle customization of the characters. Even though each character has default class, you're the one deciding what skills they use and those can be changed almost anytime. You need one more healer? Conver your fire casting mage into one just for the boss battle. Or give a ressurect to your tank to support team in hardest moments. You decide. Of course this brings yet another flaw of the game - there is no preset system that would allow you to save different sets of skills and equipment. You need to change everything manually each time you need different skills or items for battle.
Pros:
- The overall story.
- Great customisation of your character's set of skills.
- Has this old-school jrpg feeling to it.
Cons
- Repetitiveness.
- Even more repetitiveness.
- Too long.
- Empty, dead world.
- Dull and boring maps.
- Grind.
- Too much boobs, too little attitude in the characters.
- Story and characters just don't make up for all the cons.

Agarest: Generations of War is a JRPG with a rather interesting concept.  The game takes place over several generations.  It would have been nice to see the world evolve as time passes.  Unfortunately, that never happens and the world is very much static despite the hundred year gap from start to end (give or take, the game never really mentions how much time passes).  The whole generations thing boils down to the ability to determine the stats/abilities of the main hero of each generation through which brides you pick.
The rest of the story isn't much to speak of.  It is all fairly generic stop the evil forces plot.  This isn't helped by the characters that are all one-note and there are no surprises along the way.  Most of the characters even completely lose their reason for joining in the first place once the generation they join in is over; most of them follow you to further generations because "reasons."  The brides of each generation aren't helped that you know the second they join that their purpose is to fall for the hero (the degree of which depends on mostly dialogue choices) to create the next hero.
The combat could make up for all of that but it has its own issues.  At the start of the game you begin with some end game items for whatever reason that trivialize the first couple generations.  If used, you won't get the chance to understand how to fully use the combat, but if not used battles can take forever to finish (I played on Hard).
To properly fight in this game, you need to constantly use your links.  Basically, every character has link spots in set patterns from where they are.  If another character is on that space, you can attack with them when either character's turn comes up plus you can combine their abilities for considerably more damage.  You can link your entire team like that and this becomes mandatory later on, especially for bosses.  It gives the game some strategy but enemies can counter the entire mechanic by killing characters (easily done in single attacks on Hard) or using abilities with knock back, both of which can ruin your links.
There was a lot of potential going into this game but every aspect of the story falls flat and the combat can take forever even discounting enemies ruining your big damage moves.  At least grinding isn't necessary (unless you want to level up a previously unused character which isn't too bad) and once things are properly set up in battles, you can take out bosses in one giant attack.

I've played many Jrpg's in my time from the well known final fantasy, dragon quest, kingdom hearts and soon Legend of Heroes:Trails in the Sky. Let me say this first if you are reading this never having played a jrpg, or any kind of rpg for that matter. Stop what you are doing and think if a game that most likely will be spent grinding experience, currency for weapons or armour, etc... is what you want.
That out of the way anyone with experience with Jrpg's should pick up this game especially when on sale for what $4.99? Jrpg fans should already know what they are getting into. The story is while not it's strongest suit, is somewhat linear, and anime trope heavy, but it is still very satisfying in my opinion. The story is  delivered in a visual novel presentaion with some choices(routes to take, people to marry).  The combat style is reminiscent of games like Disgaea, and Final Fantasy Tactics. The music, oh the music, this alone is what probably kept me going through this game. This Ost is one of my favorites in gaming. The fast beat tracks kept me on edge, the slower solemn tracks were able to create a great atmosphere.
All in all this is a great game that delivers in practically every place needed. If you are still undecided, then i believe you should wait until a sale for the game to arrive, but do not skip this game.

Don't be scared off by the "Early Access".   Iknow the tag has been abused by many devs in recent memory, but this is not really a new franchise.
EHM is a game series that has been around since 2004 with EHM: Franchise Edition, and in spirit since 2001 when the original freeware EHM was released.  After EHM:FE, SI Games released EHM 2005 and then EHM 2007.  The fan community has kept 2007 alive and updated since then.  So this is not a brand-new, from scratch game.  This is a game built on an already successful core from EHM 2007.  Riz and the SI guys are not new at this, and SI is the company behind the super-popular, long-running Football Manager series.  EHM:EA marks essentially the 4th release in the EHM series after a hiatus of many years,
There is not a more-detailed, in-depth hockey management simulation game available on the market, period.  As with any sports management sim there is a learning curve.  But once you get it, you'll be willingly sinking a whole lot of time into it.

Let's assume you've never played the EHM-series and you like hockey. In that case - the game is just for you! You can make your own God-awful decisions like an actual Oilers GM! How cool is that!
Well.. kinda cool. Yeah.
The EHM-series was created by the Finnish Risto "Riz" Remes and picked up by the SI Games (Sports Interactive - Football Manager [the ol' Championship Manager] and OOTP-baseball-manager-thingye). That's how it's been for about fifteen years or so. And it's awesome that the few that enjoy manager-games that are just basically Excell-sheets with a bit of graphic.
The game is awesome as it was in the year 2006 (?) when EHM-07 was released. And quess what? IT'S STILL THE SAME DAMN GAME! The engine is the same and the mechanics work the same way. It even has the same glitches (the junior players refuse to sign to the team, the international games happen at the same time as the European leagues etc). Ok. The year is now 2015 in the game or something like that, but nothing much.
Don't get me wrong - I love the game. I actually bought it three times when it was the crappy Sega-distribution that allowed you to install it three times and three times only. (So when you must re-install Windows - there goes one licence. Oh yay). Now it's yours eternally when you buy it from Steam but that's prolly the biggest change in the game.
I know it's still an early release (though 10 years old), but I really hope that the developing theam has the courtesy to update the game A LOT or it's just a cheap way to make some money.
Summary: You like hockey? You hate the way EA handles the managing-bit? Bored of Maso Hockey Manager? Yeah. This is for you. Prepare to be annoyed, though. The game has a few bugs (ok. new bugs that weren't in the earlier version, so that's a feature for the old-timers) and a cheap feel to it, but as a managing game of hockey made in the UK - it's pretty ok. Worth your money, but hopefully offers a lot more in the future.

I played this game at Pax East 2015 was impressed that it was a day 1 purchase for me.
I bought it day 1 and got to see all the extra features that I did not get to try at the convention was really impressed.
Gameplay: I can see the similiarites from FTL and from a typical match 3 gem game. You have two weapons and two defensive moves that can be used every round. Both kind of devices use different resources (minus coolant as that is used for both) you also get to do 3 matches on the gem board to gather resources for said skills.  Do you match some ammo gems and shot a few rounds and then use the next two matches to get more? Or do you go for a more balanced approach and try to keep your defenses at their top tier every turn.
Once you get the basics down they introduce active and passive abilities, special gems to match and also the ability to target specific parts of the enenmy.
After every mission you go back to your hanger where you spend salvage to repair or upgrade your mech.
Graphics: Not sure how to describe them, but they do the job. Simple but perfect for what this game is.
Music: Love it.
Story: Simple but enjoyable. You get to make choices for the missions which adds to the rogue-lite feel of it. An enemy cargo ship oftered their cargo to spare their life. I agreed and I got the choice to still turn on them and kill their ship for salvage. Simple choice system but really enjoyable.
Final Thoughts: Great game, if you enjoyed Puzzlequest or games like that it is a must buy. The staff is also very friendly speaking with them directly at Pax and also on the forums.

You are the pilot of a Mech, or Ironcast, in a Steampunk world engaged in a desperate war between England and France. As  an Ironcast pilot, you need to gather ammunition to fire at opponents, energy to drive your mech forward and power shields, coolant to prevent overheating,  repair points for your repair pool and even extra scrap for currency between missions. All of these resources are spread around a match-3 style board, and are collected by swiping through them in the usual fashion, as per this genre of game.
The catch: You can only swipe through one resource type per action you take, and you only get 3 actions per turn. Will you choose coolant to prevent overheating, or swipe some ammo and spend the ammo and what coolant you have to fire off another volley? Maybe collect repair points or energy for shields?
These decisions arise every single turn. All the while you collect XP to drive unlocks that can customize your mech, change your play style, and even help you build new weapons, shields, drives and other customizations. And in completing missions, your XP also goes toward global unlocks which will add additional content such as new perks, mechs, commanders, etc to future playthroughs.
Oh yeah...when you die - and you will - its game over. But dont let that discourage you. This just might be the best Match 3 I have ever played and if you are a fan of the genre, for this price, you owe it to yourself to play this tough but fun title right now.

YES, for the odd non-believers EVERY other Homeworld game had Tactical Pause, yes I see people arguing they didn't somehow as if you can't just play the games to check. That said IDK why it is so hard for the Devs to simply add a simple OPTION. That one tiny little check box in the game menu (that way those super cool hardcore "true" gamers could turn it off) would turn my thumb from down to up in a heartbeat.
"Why would it have that it's called an RTS". The previous games were also concidered RTS. Here's why I believe it only makes sense to have one in a game like this. I, as the player, am actually taking on the role of many many people. I, as a human being with one brain, cannot simultaneously make 5 command decisions and carry them out within 1 second. Having the tactical pause allows me to role play as it were and put myself into each units pilot and make decisions for each as if I was in each unit for that second whereas otherwise I could not.
On top of that I LOVE the art design. I love zooming in on a unit and watch it fire or take hits or whatever. Without pause there simply is no time to appreciate anything. If you aren't fully zoomed out or even in tac map your gonna be screwed. This relegates you to looking at little dots. ???
I simply can't understand how implementing the option could hurt anyone since you could just turn it off or just not use it. I'm not alone, do a google search and you'll see sooo many people are asking for this. If I thought it could be modded in I'd hope for that but can't see how that could be done then again I'm no coder and since the Devs have come on the forums and stubbornly persisted this mindset of making their customers unhappy for some stupid conviction...let's not forget the franchise is known for it. Then I won't help them sell it.
So, sorry favorite franchise of all time (pretty much) I can't recommend. BTW it's the only game I have ever done so. Sad.

For the record, I've not beaten this game. And I doubt I ever will. I'm just not enjoying myself when I play it. I'm not an angry kickstarter backer who's annoyed by how poorly handled the whole thing was, I'm just someone who picked the game up on the cheap.
I've been a fan of 2D platformers for a long time, and while I would not put the Mega Man series as my favourite platformers, I still enjoy them. So I was interested in giving Mighty No. 9 a try, despite the negative press it was getting. Now I see why it was getting so much negative press. Kickstarter drama aside, this is just not a good game.
They really dropped the ball on this one. The graphics look cheap. As in the kind of low budget game you would expect to get as advertisement cheap. Things lacks detail, and everything just looks so lifeless. Most of the levels that I've seen reminds me of how levels tend to look when they're still work in progress, and they've not added all lighting, clutter objects, and interesting little tidbits that make them look distinct.
The character design does not help. Most of the characters just look bland. The ones I've seen have no personality, they're not memorable, and they just help the game look even more cheap. What happened here? The concept art, while not stellar, had some personality, but what we got was one of the blandest looking games I've seen in years.
And the sound. It's not good. The music is non-intrusive, but it's not good, with the tunes just being there. Nothing is memorable about the music in Mighty No. 9. It's, like the graphics, just bland.
The sound effects are at least alright. You get a good feel for what's going on with the sound effects. They're not outstanding, but the sound effects might be the best thing about this game. They work, and they work well.
As for the voice acting, let's just say that it sounds phoned in. The voice actors sound bored, like they don't want to be there. It's not inspiring, and it's another thing that adds to the feeling of cheapness of the entire game. It might have been better to just not have any voice acting at all.
In the future, there are robots. Some of them go bad, and you need to figure out why. There's some more to the story, but a combination of the phoned in voice acting, and how boring they made things sound made me not pay attention. Robots are supposedly not allowed to fight outside the robot arena, but something bad happens, and suddenly a group of mighty robots turn on humanity. Mighty No. 9, your character (also known as Beck) seems to remain good, as does Call, your sidekick (who looks a bit like Roll from Mega Man).
The story is not told particularly well. You either get big chunks of story dumped on you, told in a really uninspired way, or story gets told mid level, with characters trying to talk over the action. It's quite hard to focus on what the characters say when you're busy trying to dodge enemy attacks. At least they don't completely stop the action, like in Duck Tales.
At its core Mighty No. 9 is a Mega Man clone. You move through the stages, usually from left to right, fight enemies, and avoid stage hazards. After a short tutorial level you get to pick from 8 different levels to play, all with their own theme and boss. Beat the boss and you get a new weapon.
New to the formula is a dash mechanic that allows you to dash mid-air. This is central to the game as you need to dash through enemies once you've shot them a few times, in order to fully destroy them. Stage bosses & mid-level bosses require you to do this more than once in order to beat them. And I'm going to be controversial and say that it's not a bad idea. At times it's even quite fun. During sections of some levels enemies will be spread out in such a way that finding an optimal way to hurt & dash through them is quite tricky, and this is where the game is at its best. You get a nice sense of momentum during these sections. These mechanics would make for a great score attack game, that's less focused on platforming than Mighty No. 9 is.
Sadly the level design is uninspired. It's hard to explain, but apart from those few sections where they take proper advantage of the dash mechanic, the levels are just boring. The controls don't feel precise enough for the platforming to be particularly fun, and the way stage hazards are placed often make them feel more cheap than challenging. The levels feel like they would belong in some poorly put together ROM hack rather than a commercially released game.
And the final nail in the coffin for Mighty No. 9 is the hit detection/hitboxes. While it usually works, I ended up just dashing straight through enemies on a few occasions, and on some other occasions I was hit by things that did not look like they were touching me. It's inconsistent.
Mighty No. 9 is quite simply not a good game. Bad level design, uninspired graphics & sound, and a novel mechanic that's not put to good use makes this a game I simply can't recommend. It's not the worst game ever, there are far worse platformers on Steam, but it's one of the most boring platformers I've ever played. Boring and utterly forgettable.

Tl;dr  Deepest tactical battle system out there, many characters, excellent growth, weapons/armor/accessories, weapon and item crafting, separate adjustable passive ability system, monster capture, in game performance rewards, great end-game difficulty.  "Real" ending is impossible to achieve without min/maxing.   Play once blind.  10/10 for the port.  9/10 for the game
This is a great game if you like anime and turn based tactical RPGs.   I'm pretty indifferent to anime and I thought it was awesome.  Just tons of different characters with different specialties.  Each generation builds on the last, so you tend to feel more connected to the characters from early than late, since they've been around for so long.  And contrary to the way they advertised the game, it has very little to do with sex.  The main story is about developing relationships, but there are easter eggs for the horn-balls.
The battle system is as deep a system as you could dream.  You can choose your fields to maximize your play style and capture monsters.  Skill attacks, team skill attacks, special attacks, and ultimate attacks.  A hundred different attack/magic types, with weapon specialties.  Adjustable passive skills with armor and accessory usage.  And a growth system that is a great blend of feeling actual progress without giving the farm away after lvl 1.
Assuming you play on "hard," the difficulty curve is a bit unusual, though.  The very beginning is hard because you have so few options.  Once you get to 2nd gen, though; the difficulty drops significantly until the end of the 4th generation.  After that, and through the end of the game, you can no longer power your way through with grinding.  It is mandatory that you develop effective tactics to deal with the punishment that the enemies will unleash.
I strongly recommend you play the  game blind, and take your time.  You will get 100's of hours out of this game that way.  Once you've beat it once, it's good for a min/max playthrough to get the best ending.  After that, the combat is fun enough to come back to occasionally; but like most games, once you figure out the most powerful attacks, it can be hard to stop using them.
There's an in game rewards system for certain accomplishments (getting $1 mil, 500 hits in one turn, having every weapon, etc), which is actually pretty fun to go after (if you are not trying for the good ending).  The alchemy/weapon/armor/accessory building system is deep.  Not only can you build different (1000's) of weapons, armor, accessories, and items -- each with their own strengths and weakensses; but you can level those weapons up, and even break them down into ingredients necessary for the most powerful weapons and armors.  It's truly a system that requires a great amount of planning to get the most out of.
And for those who like the capture aspects of games, this game has it.  Many of the advanced monsters you can get are actually worthwhile.  I can't say much about this, as I'm not a big fan of capturing monsters in general; but it is an excellently implemented system.
And finally, there are tons of easter eggs.  Not only the sexy kind, but additional dungeons, and uber enemies to challenge once you feel like a master.

The only thing I don't like about this game is how to get the "right" ending.   I liken it to Chrono Cross.  You either had to get the knowledge from an external source, or go through the game a dozen times to figure out how to get the ending that actually ends the game.  And worse, you cannot procede with the relationships that are most obvious, or appeal to you the most if you want to see the ending.  And you have to rush the game in order to see the actual ending.  You have to finish each generation in less than so many turns.  Don't get me wrong, you can do all those things, you just won't get the ending that actually ends the game.
Honestly, there's not a lot to not like about this game.  Add to it that you can tranfer your data directly to the two sequels and you have a whole lot of game for your buck.  I beat these games years and years ago on consol, so I know them much better than my 152 hours would suggest.
The port is fine.  I really have had 0 issues with it at all.  10/10 for the port, and 9/10 for the game.

This game is actually a really good game despite some of the negative reviews here. Most of these negative reviews are because the game runs kinda slow. However there is a really easy tweak for making the game run super smooth.
Go into the folder where you installed the game. Locate the Agarest.ini file. ( Might have to run the game once for it to appear. )
Find this line : LockWindowFrameRate=30.000000
Change the value 30 to 60 and save and exit.
I have played with this setting for 70 hours and have NOT encountered a single issue. I do however have a pretty decent computer and therefore it might not work on old systems. But for me the game runs really great after doing this!
So if u like SRPG games and turn based strategy. Get this game and do this simple tweak and enjoy a truly great story with beautiful characters, dialogues, battle system, artwork and hundreds of hours of gameplay.

Let me preface this by saying that I am not good at this game.
I mean, I get the way the game works, and I'm not hopeless, but as of this writing, I've put in nearly 100 hours and still haven't unlocked cheats.  And while that is largely due to the fact that I don't want to try Bioweapon again, it is also illustrative of why I recommend this game so highly.  You don't have to be good at Plague Inc. to play it and have fun with it.
At its core, Plague Inc. is a casual game.  You pop bubbles with your finger or mouse, tap or click to choose how your disease progresses, and that's it.  However, where this game differs from most casual games is that the developers have created layers of strategy and complexity over that basic framework, layers that individual players can freely embrace or ignore as they see fit.  If you don't particularly care about factors like how many uninfected countries have dry climates as opposed to wet climates or how to best target the countries that are advancing cure research, then you can simply ignore them, play on casual, and evolve whatever you feel like.  However, if you are looking for more challenge and depth than the average casual gamer, then you can crank up the difficulty to normal. brutal, or even mega-brutal, and carefully plot out which combinations of symptoms, transmission vectors, and other abilities will lead you to victory.
In short, Plague Inc. has something for everyone, from the most casual of casual players ro the hardest of hardcore gamers, and I highly recommend it.

Last Day of June is a game developed by Ovosonico and published by 505 Games
Last Day of June kinda reminds me of Groundhog Day, you repeat the same day over and over, from differemt perspectives, making minor adjustments to try and get the outcome your character desires
The different perspectives interact with each other; leave a gate unlocked from one perspective, and the other perspectives can see it. It's not a real-tme switch; you play one character's entire day, resulting in some outcome, and only after you receive that outcome can you switch to another character and the outcomes, together, determine the result
It's actually a pretty cool way to tell a story, if not somewhat repetitive. I've never seen it done quite this way and the game is distinctive and reasonably pretty
The only issue I had with Last Day of June is that the game has these little mini cut-scenes that are repated way too many, many times and that you cannot fast-forward or skip and each time there is like 30-60 seconds of unskippable cut-scenes which if you're playing in one whole sitting can get pretty annoying and repetitive
And then, at the end of each day for each character, you're forced to watch the entire outcome, over and over and over again. This is a LONG cut scene, that you can't skip, and if you're going back and forth between 2 or 3 characters it adds a lot of repetitiveness and frustration
I would have enjoyed the game a lot more if you could either skip the cutscenes entirely or if they didn't make you repeat certain unnecessary parts
However, overall, Last Day of June sums up a wonderful, beautifully aesthetic story that should not be missed. Just relax, don't let the overall repetitiveness of the game get to you and enjoy the wonderful story Last Day of June has to offer

DO NOT BUY IF YOU ARE EXPECTING GAMEPLAY.
This is a story based game, and it damn well pulls it off.

"What would you do to save the one you love?"
The dramatic question warns you about the emotional subject which Last Day of June brings to the table.
With its simple, cute art style and its atmosphere you can tell the game really tries to get the player to feel sad, upset and emotionally involved in the grim story.
Unfortunately, as hopeful as I was when I bought it, Last day of June really didn't manage to leave me as heartbroken as it probably wanted. I have to say the non verbal interactions don't really work as well as they might have thought they would, and the repetitive puzzle just gets more frustrating everytime instead of making the plot darker, which was probably the original intention.
The story is indeed upsetting, but because of the game mechanics you tend to feel almost bored, like you just want to get to the end so you can stop doing the same thing over and over again, instead of growing some form of attachment to the characters.
Many people were left sad, some say they cried, but I'm genuinely sorry to say that the game did not really manage to strike a chord. You can see what the developers were aiming for, but it was just poorly executed.
I would recommend the game on sale, and if you're easily satisfied by short animated novels.
Otherwise, to me, Last Day of June is just a missed opportunity, that could have been a
heartbreaking story.

After several hours of playing Eastside Hockey Manager: Early Access Edition I can say that it is one of the most enjoyable and addictive simulation games I have ever played.  I always enjoyed various football (soccer for us in N. America) simulations but I love hockey and am so glad that a game developer has introduced (in this case re-introduced) a simulation for hockey fans.
Pros: The game offers a variety of setting which allow you to establish how many hats you want to wear when managing the team you take over.  You can just manage (draft, develop prospects, sign free-agents, trade players, hire and fire coaches, scouts and other personnel, salary cap) while analyzing endless statistics or micro-manage every aspect of your team by adding coaching responsibilities to your portfolio and establish in-game tactics and select game-day rosters.  The game has an active modding community.  You can download NHL player rosters or other professional league players and team logos for a more realistic experience.
Cons:
- The game could offer higher resolution settings than the 1024 x 768.
-  Also while the lower resolution does not detract from game play I have found that when I quit a game the default      resolution setting on my Windows desktop sometimes reverts to the 1024 x 768 resolution setting that the game uses (from my normal desktop resolution of 1920x 1200). Not a big deal to change resolution back to 1920 x 1200 but a nuisance.
- In rare instances some of the historical statistics do not tally correctly.
-  Some statistics do not export correctly to a file or printer
Game Improvement:
- I would like to see some graphical updates made to the game as some of the 2D graphics seem a little dated like when watching individual games.
- Also would like to see when winning a cup or when a player I manage wins an individual trophy,  it would be nice to have a graphic of a newspaper where headlines highlight the achievement like I have seen in other sports sims.
Recommendation:  The game for an early access product is well developed and if no further development of the game was offered would still represent extremely good value.  There are some small tweaks that need to be made with the game which is to be expected with an early access product.  With that said I can say without hesitation that if you enjoy sports simulation games, you will not regret purchasing this title.

This game seems like it should be good, but it isn't.
The combat system is uninteresting and has really binary outcomes - you either win easily or lose totally. There is no way to flee from a losing battle like you can in FTL, which is frustrating.
The game is very RNG focused in loot/upgrades disribution and in battles. It's annoying when you lose what should be an easy battle because you aren't drawing the right tiles on the board. It reminds me of getting mana screwed/mana flooded in a CCG like Magic, except there are no skills/abilities in this game to help you avoid that.
The tile matching gameplay isn't as fun as in match-3-style games like puzzle quest as there are no cascades. You don't have to think hard as to your move, but actioning your plan it is pretty time consuming and tedious compared to similar games.
The game is a roguelike in that when you die you have to start again, and it starts to feel repeatitive and grindy fast. The campaign is the same every time, and there is not much variation possible in the build/tactics used by your mech.
On the plus side, the presentation of the game is good and it is bug free. The writing is pretty solid and while the storyline is light, it works well for its purpose. The setting (19th century steampunk mechs) has been done before but not that often, so its still kind of fresh.
I wouldn't recommend this game. Try something like Puzzle Quest or Puzzle Kingdoms for a better strategy/tile matching game, or FTL for a more entertaining rogue-lite.

I'm sure that for me at least it has a lot to do with the vehicle designs. I loved how varied and exotic some of the ships were in the series, with form taking a pretty large precedent over function. DoK is inundated with very generic looking and forgettable unit designs, and they just are not satisfying to command or spectate in battle. I can understand this is partly due to the ground setting (the types of vehicles used that is) but the unoriginality in their aesthetics is so boring. That's what strikes me most: this game is boring. The AI can be routed with ease and forced into submission with simple tactics, and I never feel a real sense of challenge from the campaign. I honestly would only recommend picking DoK up on deep discount, and as a huge fan of the prior games please set your expectations a little lower.

I was keen on persisting through this game, however much to my disgust its PC port is a mess as well as a certain crucial element of the gameplay.
First, the controls; they are really counterintuitive. Functions share a key that shouldn't and ones that should don't. An example is to fire the gun. Under the default controls, you would have to hold "f" to aim down sight and "g" to fire. Left mouse is bound exclusively to attack and asssassinate. Functions you can do neither of when aiming down sight. Right mouse button is bound to heavy attack, a completely redundant attack and even more redundant by how little anyone would dare to use the appalling mess of a combat system.
If you rebind the controls you can get around this. However by the time you realize how ludicrous the default controls are you'll be half way through a mission. That wouldn't be an issue for any other game, however in this game you have to be in the main menu to change the controls, or even to turn on subtitles.
Navigating the main menu is a pain. Remember how normally you'd press escape to leave a submenu, well now that's backspace. Every single time I have instinctively pressed escape trying to close a menu. You'd think they'd be above this problem by the third game in the series.
Second, the graphics settings. This is probably the least damning concern. But at some point my eyes start to hurt from the lack of anti-aliasing. The graphics settings are as follows. Vsync, fullscreen, resolution and that's it. This isn't a techinically demanding game. However if the game doesn't have any anti-aliasing by default, it should at least have it as an option. The absence of any graphics settings shows how roughly this game was ported from consoles.
Thirdly, is the skills section. The game constantly criticises you for slipping up even slightly. You get less points if you get seen, or if you asssassinate people (Because god forbid you do that). These points go towards getting skills, the only meaningful progression through this game other than getting accustomed to the controls. However their gated behind a judgemental god that expects absolute perfection.
I carelessly rushed through a few of the levels because I didn't really feel the need for the skills (And the gameplay is long since tedious by the end of the tutorial). Then I came across a skill I do want, gated behind getting a perfect score in all regards. One of the conditions was to loot a chest behind some landmines. To get through this without sacrificing your perfect passifist creed gameplay, you must have had the fast looting skill from the tutorial. And you can't repeat the first level without overriding your save from that point onward.
The game also has set a few difficutly settings. It has 3 of them and at the start only the first one is able to be selected. Meaning they expect people to be playing through this game 3 times and not throwing up. I'm gonna finish this game because I did pay for it, however I would not recommend anyone else buy this. It somehow ended up with more problems than the first game in the series, or maybe I am noticing more because they should be gone by this point. Either way I still can't recommend it.
This game could have been worthwhile if the developers payed the slightest bit of attention to the community throughout the three games. And secondly by gating skills behind completing the levels, instead of playing it their way. Obviously "Open ended levels" do take away from the challenge, however terrible gameplay can be tolerable if you can have some freedom. Instead of taking away skills for killing, they need to make killing generate it's own challenge. Make the guns louder, melee takedowns harder. You can't balance the game by sternly yelling at the player for doing things the easy way.
EDIT: From what it seems I won't be finishing this game
