I learned a valuable lesson playing this game. That is - Never, ever listen to a general consensus about what is or isn't a good game.
This was one of those games that I had heard time and time again over the years that it was, quite frankly, a bad game. I heard a lot of "It's not as good as Bloodlines (the other Vampire the Masquerade game)", or "It's more of a Diablo-style RPG", which funnily enough is usually used as a coded insult to say the game is "dumbed down" or is just mindless hacking and slashing.
While this game certainly has some Diablo influences like many other RPGs did in that era, it's also a very, very unique RPG. I am trying to pinpoint what game it is most like out of the hundreds of RPGs I've played, and I really can't think of any other game that is quite like it. It's sort of like a real-time Neverwinter Nights in some ways, maybe with a dash of Dungeon Siege and, surprise surprise, even a lot of Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, the other (and generally better-known) game in the World of Darkness setting.
So, the game is unique. But what makes it good? Well, there are a lot of great elements in the game. First, the combat is not a great great element, but it is real-time and you can do things like use spells or Vampire Disciplines to incapacitate foes in various ways. You can buff various stats to make you hit harder or more often, or debuff an enemy in some way, heal yourself and so on. You can use scrolls as well which are handy in a pinch when you aren't that skilled in the Disciplines themselves, or chuck a bottle of holy water in a vampire's face, which is always fun. There are also more creative Disciplines as well, and you will have to Feed as a vampire to regain your ability to use these Disciplines, since they require Blood to activate. The combat is basic but the best thing is that the entire game uses a pen-and-paper-style implementation for mechanics, and that means dice-rolls and all the lovely character building using stats and numbers. The game surprisingly has 9 main stats you can increase, with 3 for melee, 3 for magic and 3 more conversation skills, and they are meaningful in that it is possible to create a "bad" character, so you'll want to mind that and build your character in a clever enough way.
Beyond combat, there are many choices to make as to how to handle things, and the game actually considers these choices and gives different results based on them. I'm not all that far into the game yet but already I can see there are opportunities to join different Vampire clans and make some pretty interesting decisions that will change the game, and perhaps change the endings of the game as well. It's interesting in that regard, and some of the decisions seemed quite consequential.
There's also loot to find, some unidentified stuff and what not, and in this regard it's a bit like Diablo, but a bit more more "low fantasy". Also, there isn't a huge overload of loot like the Diablo games, and that is an important distinction to make. So while the inventory and look of the inventory is a bit Diablo-esque, you aren't going to be picking up endless amounts of magical items and trash items. There is still a lot of hand-placed good stuff to find, unique items, quest items and so on.
You also meet colorful characters and the writing is on point. Very on point. And the lore already goes without saying, it's great. Gritty, old-school vampire stuff with a gothic edge. It's a dark world, often creepy, and mixes both real-world locations and settings with the gritty vampire and undead fiction. There are many vampire clans and they are in an endless war with each other. There's a lot of underworld politics, conspiracy and intrigue in this world and that makes it continuously awesome to play and explore as you learn about various undead and the nefarious underworld. It also mixes in religious overtones and plays on the real history of that as well. There is also a very unique aspect in the game where you start in 1100 A.D. and eventually make your way to modern times! So the game actually takes place over the span of hundreds of years.
Oh, and it has full voice acting! Not bad for an older CRPG like this. The voice acting is great, but in that old-school voice acting kind of way. If you've played and enjoyed the Gothic series you'll be right at home here. The medieval prose early in the game is ofttimes very cute and campy, and it's made me smile a lot so far. It's probably not going to be as "technically" great as a modern game with the voice reading, but it's got a ton of charm and character, which is way more important to me anyway.
There are some quirks as well. Like any older RPG, you will have to get used to the game. It's different and requires actually playing for awhile to get the hang of it. The camera takes a lot of getting used to and the controls in general take time to learn. You will also have to look up what the character stats do so you get a better idea of how to build your character. But beyond that it is classic CRPG goodness. The barrier to entry is not nearly as high as other old-school CRPGs like the Wizardry series or what have you, so I'm fairly sure anyone would be able to figure this game out if they have a bit of knowledge in pen-and-paper style RPGs.
I am playing the game with my own Steam Controller configuration that you can find in the community section for the game. Look for Fluent Controls - Vampire: The Masquerade - Redemption to give it a shot. It works quite well.
All in all, it's a really good game so far. I'd deifnitely recommend it. It has more Bloodlines in it than I expected, and I learned the important lesson that it is always best to investigate yourself to see what something is about rather than listening to others. If you like classic CRPGs you should really give this one a shot.

Too Long, Didn't Read: This fails to capture the feeling of old MegaMan games, and fails at basic game design, story-telling, and visuals.
When I saw that Keiji Inafune (co-creator of MegaMan) put up Might No. 9 on KickStarter, I decided to back it because Capcom wasn't planning on doing anything with MegaMan.  After waiting a while (couple of years I think), I finally got my keys, and played the game.  I didn't play long, because of its unintuitive design choices, uninteresting characters, and lack-luster visuals.
First, anyone who has ever played a MegaMan game (or any side scroller with guns) knows that you just shoot the enemy until they're dead.  That is not how it works in this game.  What you do, is shoot an enemy until they're stunned, and then dash at them.  I didn't know this right away, because the message stating this in the tutorial only appeared for half a second, and then disappeared.  I was trying to figure out why I was stuck on the screen, and why the enemy was still there.  I finally figured it out by accidentally dashing into the dazed enemy.
Then came the first boss of the game.  It displayed a health bar on the screen, so I figured it would be standard fare.  Then I noticed that after a few seconds, it would regain its health.  Remembering the minor enemy, I dashed at the boss.  I found out that is the only way to permanently damage them.  However, you're not invulnerable when harming the boss by dashing.  You have to dash near enough to them that it registers, but no so close that you touch them, and take damage.  This goes against decades of game design.
The beginning of the level tries to set up the world, story, and the characters.  However, it is all a shoddy copy/paste job  MegaMan story; futuristic world where robots serve mankind, and an evil scientist is trying it over.  The story is even told with a lazy news segment, with the obvious Wily-esque villain, trying to deflect the blame onto someone else.  There is a support team, but I just remember two cops, and a heavy-set guy.
As far as the visuals, they are not what was presented in the original concept art and proof-of-concept screenshots.  What we were promised was hand-drawn sprites, with the 2.5D background.  We did get the 2.5D backgrounds, but just bland 3D models for the characters.  Beck, the character you play, just barely resembles his concept art, with none of the personality.  The other models do their job, but that isn't saying much.
If you've been waiting for something to satisfy your MegaMan fix, you're better off just purchasing Capcom's MegaMan Legacy collection, or just playing the old cartridges.  Capcom may never release another game, but Comcept didn't manage this game right.
The game has a very sluggish feel to it, and it's very much a hinderance.  I hated how terrible the jumping and movement is, and since it's a jump and shoot game, it's a nightmare.  Avoid this game.

Oh boy, is this a walking simulator? It's closer to a simple adventure game as you'll be collecting things and solving puzzles, although the puzzles can really only go one way to advance the plot.
The good: the graphics are great, most of the time. The artwork style has a sort of dreamy abstraction that I really liked. I went in expecting a linear walking simulator experience and found more gameplay than I was expecting (although not much more) so that was nice.
The bad: the characters, and by that I mean how they are realized. They all lack eyes, and so look super-creepy to me. They also communicate via grunts and other simple noises. The net effect for me was to be creeped out by most conversations, and I never felt any real emotional investment in these creepy dolls. That's a problem, because the game needs you to make that connection, and I could not get past the creepiness.
Also bad: you'll be replaying the same cutscenes over and over and over and over as you trial-and-error yourself through the stages. That got old very very quickly and ultimately made the game a chore to finish. The game saves in certain spots that you cannot control, so if you get bored of trying to complete a sequence and want to come back later, you get to start over from the beginning of that sequence. There are also collectibles that are missable, and it's impossible to go back and get them - you won't know you've missed your opportunity until it's too late. The game is far too tedious to give it a second playthrough to finish this up.
On the whole, I wanted this game to click for me but it was a letdown. I'd rate it 2 out of 5: avoid unless you are absolutely in love with the artwork as presented on the store page and don't mind hollow-eyed creepy grunting characters.
Not recommended.

There's lot of talk around game being buggy. Saves are corrupted etc. Well it did not happen to me - played much later as well, so I can not comment on this.
The story.
It's quite simple and therein lies its greatness. Cute couple Carl and June are relaxing after picnic on their favourite pier and due to rising storm have to rush home. Then the gamepad starts vibrating - something happened. Death. One person has died and death wraps it’s veil around many people. Kurt Cobain’s “All in all is all we all are” came to mind and player is actually given control to use different gameworld characters to butterfly effect the moment that happened.
So you can steer the story with 6 characters total, but you still know you are doing this for Carl. Carl is interesting...I don’t know many games having wheelchair protagonist in it; he carries the darkness and hopelessness in the narrative and through him we can play deus ex machina with what happened. Sadness and regret are therefore always granted in this colourful world albeit the other characters you play do not know what’s going to happen.
I like that the developers packed pretty serious topics of death, loss, regret, emptiness etc to a nice portable package. It’s presented in-game as a gift as well, unavoidable and has to be accepted.The graphics, music and very very well done solution for voice acting all ease the creeping moments of “not again” and “I don’t want this to happen”.
Game controls are easy, I played it with controller but looked like with keyboard and mouse it’s the same. There are some things that might annoy you - you can not skip cutscenes and due to repetitiveness of the moment you are trying to alter, well they happen again and happen and…. Also some scenes made me feel rushed and too much scripted. Game is short, I don't know if it's a bad thing or not, but I don't like to keep games running to get trading cards. Just a Steam thing, not games fault.
Long story short - very well made game.

Agarest: Generations of War is a turn-based RPG, using a system of tiles as a playing field, where your characters can move and attack opposing enemies. Simple, right? Kind of. (we'll get into that later). But, for now, realize that this game is a turn-based RPG with a visual-novel story-telling method and a TON of stats to consider. (which I love).
The story in this game is interesting. I like it because of it's simplicity, yet there are mysteries to solve (if you pay attention) and lore to uncover. It takes place in a magical land where Humans and other various species (like Elves) are at war. There is a backstory about light and dark, and dark lords and such, but you read that in the beginning of the game, so you can do that.
Overall, it's not a bad story. However, since I haven't finished the game, I cannot give a complete answer. Howver so far it takes my interest.
Each character in this game is unique in their own ways (which is a must for RPG's, and any game for that matter). So far, I feel no "emotional" attatchment to any of them, and I honestly don't think I ever will. This isn't "bad", but to some it's undesirable. To me, all that matters is character interaction, personality, how they play in the story, their lore, and their designs. All of these are present in the game.
I'll explain in short: you move your characters to the desired spaces (calle the Move Phase), and make them face directions.
. Depending on their direction, certain characters can couple and attack WITH the character you move. Every character has move sets specific to them, their weapon, and their armor piece (forgot the name). Each move has an element, number of hits, range and AP cost (you regain after each cycle). So, switching weapons not only changes your stats, but it also changes your moveset with different elements. The Arts abilities are combonations of attacks, in which characters MUST be coupled. Special Arts are combos of Arts. (So you can see how much variety there can be).
This is personal, but I LOVE stat-heavy games such as this. Some people don't, but for me it adds a nice strategy element,
You would have to play the game to understand how AP and SP works, and how the battle system works. Because, in reality
. (With the exception of exploring areas and towns, which contain Blacksmiths, Item Shops, etc).
*Depending on who you marry (out of 3 girls), the next generation will have differing stats, a unique and cool feature.

Honestly, they are great and this game is the perfect starter to the series (even if Agarest Zero is the prequel). So,if you're wondering "Should I buy it? It looks kinda cool" then don't hesitate. Just get it. If your a fan of these kind of games, you won't be dissapointed.

With survival and multiplayer released and after 3 months of further development - is it worth buying now?
Graphics:
The graphics are quite good for being made from scratch and the optimisation is better than expected. The physics/destructible blocks are well done, only from time to time they behave rather wonky. All in all a visually pleasing experience.
Audio:
The music of the game is really fantastic and underlines the medieval setting. Other sounds often don't work or are not appropiate - may be placeholders though?!
Gameplay:
The construction system brings some needed innovation with it and mostly works better than it's space counterpart (Space Engineers). Those blocks that are available are nicely done, however there are so few of them even months after release.
Content:
Multiplayer seems to be the same as in Space Engineers and fulfills it's purpose. Survival however is nothing more than Creative without flying and god-mode - I really don't understand why they didn't copy the code from Space Engineers so the players at least have an inventory and can gather resources. (It seems an inventory system will be introduced later on, logs/stones have to be transported manually)
To sum it up:
After 3 months with a (for an early access) big development team one would think that many of the flaws that plagued the release version would have been fixed by now. Unfortunately the game is still glorified lego without much content. This is why I can't recommend buying the game in it's current state especially with this price tag.
P.S. Just compare it to minecraft alpha which could be bought for less than 10€ and had much more content (finished suvival/creative/multiplayer and extensive crafting/inventory system)

If you ever watched that film called the league of extraordinary gentlemen it kind of reminded me of that historical setting where the industrial revolution  meets fantasy. Its nice to see the lead characters being women as well (and posh ones at that lol).
After a few games you pick up the mechanics fairly easily. Mastering the game however is a different matter. The puzzle quest part of the game blends in brilliantly as a means of controlling your ironcast. The fights are animated as each ironcast walks, fires and powers up shields. Collecting blueprints and scraps from your victories will also enable you to upgrade your ironcast giving multiple options to how you develop it. The sounds and music accompany the game perfectly.

After playing the original Homeworld series and subsequently the remaster, this is a wonderful addition to the Homeworld universe.  While some may not like the change to terrain based RTS I found it a refreshing change while keeping the meaningful voice overs, atmospheric music, and general feel that comes from the Homeworld games.
The overall mechanics have not changed but the way the game does the airforce will keep you on your toes because of how quickly they can respond to a threat.  The land forces encourage strategic placement of your own cruisers and targetting of enemy cruiers.  That ever present threat of having to fight on multiple fronts makes a strong showing in this journey across Kharak and will have casual and veteran RTS minds mulling over how best to approach a situation.
Definitely worth the play through to experience the journey that Rachel S'Jet made across the desert before the Kushan returned to the stars.  The single criticism I have is that in the middle of battle control can be ripped away by cinematic camera shots which is very frustrating.

The devs do an excellent job of making this a true successor to the original Homeworld games (althought it is technically a prequel). It feels and plays just like the older entries. It is easily the best RTS I have played in years.

Ignore the Kickstarter drama. It's far gone now, and while Comcept and Inafune have some exmplaining to do for their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to the backers, we need to judge MN9 as a game- the drama behind it's development and release has nothing to do with how the game plays in the end. Does the game itself warrant bad score just because of an irresponsible creative team? And anime fan on prom night? People were really angry about that? Guess we do live in a generation of whiny snowflakes who can't take a joke.
First off yes, the graphics are horrible. There were cheaper crowdfunded games like Shovel Knight and Dust: An Elysian Tail, or even free games like Cave Story that look much better. sure they did 3D graphics but that was to save money and make it easier for the team, as pixel art is harder and more time consuming. No excuse for a $2-mil (after kickstarter fees) game. The cutscenes are even worse- lazily rendered through the game engine. They should've gone for pre-rendered cinematics- they definitely had enough money to.
Gameplay and audio are where MN9 succeeds. They take the dash mechanic from MMX and create an addictive mechanic out of it- weaken enemies with your attacks, then dash into them to destroy them and get a higher score. It makes MN9 extremely fast paced and fun as hell to play. Controls are great too, but I recommend a gamepad (K&M is dreadful for this game). Beck jumps and shoots with tight control, my only complaint is how Beck can stumble after climbing up a ledge while on a moving platform, which caused me to die, but its extremely rare.
Voice work is competant- the actors do what they can with their roles, and it's chidlish cheesey writing but at least everyone does a good job with some awful puns and other lines. Steve Blume is even in the game, and he's a badass in every role he does so theres a plus. Music, however, is just awesome! The MM2 composers flexed their muscle for some great and catchy tunes, which have a modern and retro setting (very nice touch).
Each stage takes around 6-7 minutes to complete, and it's extremely challenging so your play time will vary. There are challenges to complete, and if you don't feel like looking up a boss order it's yet another MM thing of experimenting with playthroughs, potentially adding more replay vale to the package.
All in all, it's a really good game and worth the $5-15 you'll pay for it depending on sale or not. The release drama was unfair- it's yet another great title developed by Inti Creates, who also made the Gunvolt series. They put out great games and this isn't an exception. I doubt we'll see a full sequel, but the fact they put Beck in Mighty Gunvolt Burst and are still working on the handheld version of MN9 gives me hope that we'll see a sequel, hopefully with the presentational issues fixed, and maybe some better level design. But as we know, our gaming community never forgives or lets up, so if a sequel does come out I doubt anyone will give it a chance.

Another game where Kickstarter fee fees get in the way of an honest review.
Apparently (and I just found this out as I was kind of out of the loop about this game for a long time), there was some kerfuffle with the kickstarter and how funding worked out for this game and there was backlash from the community.  This is wildly reminiscent of what happened to Project CARS.
However, because I don't base my opinions of a product on the person or conflict surrounding it, I have to say this is a really cool take on a modern Mega Man and not at all deserving of the bashing it gets.  It's not the masterpiece that was Mega Man X, but it's hard to compare that AAA game of its time to a modern indie game.
Even though it lacks the atmosphere and any semblance of a worthwhile story, the gameplay dynamics centered around the dash are fash and fun and almost makes it feel like if Sonic crossed over with Mega Man in a good way.  It's certainly better than any official Mega Man games we've had for the last decade, including the half-baked rehashed NES-style 9 and 10 and the Mega Man 2.5D remake for the PSP (Powered Up).
If you like Mega Man and you can check your biases and rose tinted glasses at the door, this is a perfectly acceptable modern Mega Man game and well worth experiencing.

Wow. My memory was REALLY kind to this game. I was a senior in high school when this game came out. I believe I bought the game within the first month of the original release in 2000. I still have the disks somewhere. But I am so lazy, and this was on sale so cheap that it's easier to spend a couple bucks buying it a 2nd time than it is to find my disks and figure out how to install them.
Back then, I was pretty enthralled with the White-Wolf/World of Darkness/V:tM realm. I remember being really excited about this game. And I remember my friend managed to win a treasured spot as a beta-tester and he had to sign a non-disclosure agreement and he talked about how impressed he was with it.
I remember thinking the various nitpicky details they got wrong was hilarious, and  remember that the way the medieval characters spoke was cringetastically poorly written. But I remember overall finding the game experience enjoyable.
IMPORTANT: if you have problems with everything being dark in the caves, even with brightness on high and with a torch in hand, it's a compatibility problem in DirectX. You need to get the Compatibility Administrator from Microsoft, and build a profile that activates "DxPrimaryEmulation". Without it you might as well play the game blind.
The graphics are INCREDIBLY horrible. It's from back when pologons must be minimized, and when it made more sense to prerender CG sequences on supercomputers and convert the output to highly-compressed MPEGs. Instead of the last decade where cutting to video files is long long long dead and everything gets rendered locally.
The voice acting is usually but not always HILARIOUSLY terrible. The play-control is so bad that I blocked that memory out completely. This game is from a time before we finally figured out that WASD + mouselook was a fine solution in both 1st person and 3rd person. Instead, it's sorta trying to be like 3D Bauldur's Gate. The HUD at the bottom is HUGE. it's like 1/3rd of the screen. This game was before widescreen monitors took over. It had no clue how horrible that was gonna be. The menu interaction is baffling. you can bring up multiple menus at one time...for no reason. you can leave menus up while fighting...for no reason. And while fiddling with menus, someone could sneak up behind you and beat you sensless before you could 180 and counterattack. Thankfully, the AI on this game is braindead. It's the classic "I will wait for you to kill my friend before I decide to begin attacking you" insanity.
When the game loaded, and I saw the "version 1.1" it brought back memories. I do remember being unhappy about some sort of bugs in the 1.0 release. I can't remember what. I remember being extremely grateful for the 1.1 release. But I presumed it was the first of many over the course of six months or so. And I also remember hearing when they announced that development would stop and there'd be no 1.2.
This game is now in the realm of GLORIOUSLY so bad it's good. All the struggles to adapt the RPG into the video game realm, all the compromises required to eventually get it released.
As long as it's being sold for cheap, I totally recommend this piece of junk. Once you get it working it's really entertaining.

Of what I have played of Last Day of June, I was very impressed with what I had seen. I'm not usually a fan of indie games that focus on artistic expression, but where I'm a massive fan of Steven Wilson's music, I was drawn into giving this one a try. I managed to play an hour of it and I was very impressed, the art direction is clever and engaging and the narrative is simple to follow but a (so far) powerful re-telling of a usually cliche story. There is no voice acting, only suggestive grunts and noises, but I feel that only further nails the emotion in the story.
Here's where I have to give this a "not recommended" - the game doesn't run after a save file is created and the game is closed. After an hour of play I saved the game and decided to come back to it later, however the game no longer runs and crashes on the startup screen (re-installing, verifying game cache and the usual other solutions don't work here). From looking at the Steam forums, this seems to have been a problem since launch months ago with no suggestion that a fix is incoming. Take a look at the discussions board and you'll see it's a very common problem with the devs asking people to raise tickets via their website. This would be fine, however a lot of posts and comments are also saying that their tickets have been closed without any reason or fix. The only solution that the devs are providing on the discussions is to delete the save file and start again - not a suitable fix for a problem that shouldn't happen in the first place. Until this problem is fixed, I would not have to recommend this. If the problem does get fixed, I'll happily change this recommendation as the game itself is fantastic and exceded my expectations.
TL;DR: The game itself is fantastic and would definitely be worth a recommendation, however the game itself is subject to a known issue that after the save file is created, the game crashes on startup with no fixes. Devs don't seem to have much of a desire to fix the issue and instead would rather players delete their save file and start again.

To change the events of what happened you have to play as their four neighbours. The kid, the best friend, the hunter and the old man. I recommend this game only because of its beauty and atmospheric sense of overwhelming wonder. The music sucks you right in with a finely tuned soundtrack of Scandinavian folk, oftentimes queued to things in game whether big or small. The visuals, of course, are stunning due to the animation style. The characters are equally cute, terrifying, and awe-inspiring. Everything serves to cinematically make the player feel small in this world: a part of something much larger and older. The worlds move and change and each seem to have a definite personality. A high point for me was the fire boss, Kaunan, whose design is absolutely dynamic as well as resonant with the setting.
As for gameplay, the combat is weak. The god powers system lends itself to making errors, the basic attack feels sticky, and the right click axe swing, while beautiful with its perfect glint of light and crisp sound effect, is almost useless in many fights. In a top-down adventure game like this, uncreative minion swarm happens all the time, being more frustrating and time consuming than anything else. In this sense, and the sense of exploration of unique landscapes peppered with simple combat of repetitive foes, the game reminds me of Champions of Norrath and Champions: Return to Arms.
This game is absolutely worth playing if the gummy combat system doesn't make you too impatient. Be warned, the final boss fight highlights these drawbacks, and nearly inched this game into thumbs down territory for me.

There aren't many engineering games out there, so coming across something like this is always a pleasant surprise. Most of the challenge doesn't come from the requirements of the puzzle itself, but rather trying to improve your solutions to be the most efficient possible (if you're that kinda person). This game is a pleasant upgrade from TIS-100 since it has more flexibility with the designs it can implement. However it's still kind of a pain that the instruction set has been extremely simplified. Many puzzles could have been simplified with bitwise operations (XOR, AND, NOR), and if you played TIS-100, you'll miss the JRO instruction a lot more than you'd think. But working around these limitations yields some interesting results.

Another Zachtronics masterpiece with a special flair. If you've enjoyed TIS-100, then you'll immediately fall in-love with this. The manual can get a bit confusing in some places, however. But the scenarios aren't that hard to figure out.

I picked this up knowing it was a bad game and seeing if I could marathon through it for my own amusement.  I also played the 360 version, which was also bad, and wondered if they made any improvements over it.  On both accounts I was disappointed.  This was the 360 version with no changes made, no polish, ported, and kicked out onto the PC.  I could not bother marathoning my way through this game, hell I couldn't even get past the first island before "Why the hell am I playing this crap?" blew through my head.  Without a sufficient answer I uninstalled the game.
To discuss its problems is like trying to pick apart a mountain.  The first and most obvious, as I understand Japanese, is its translation.  Since the text is in English and the voice acting is in Japanese, nothing hides this.  In fact I would encourage anyone who is bilingual to pick up this game so you can read the text as your listening to what the character says so you too can say "Who the hell translated that?"  At first the errors are small enough to only be nit-picks, a word here, they don't properly emphasize what the character is implying, only small errors.  The further you get, the more obvious the problems become, item text is word salad or bitcode since they didn't bother translating it after they changed the font, they stop using punctuation marks entirely, some things just come out as engrish jumbled together.  So, yeah the translation and localization job is terrible enough to define what poorly localized means.
This brings us to the grind, the massive grind to get skills, build up skills, make weapons, build up weapons, and on and on.  If you play through this, you will sink hundreds of hours easily into just grinding and building up your characters in order to not get crushed by the next set of fights.  Some of this grind becomes exponential where you have to grind for materials to make materials for an item you want or need.
The combat and battles are boring.  If you were expecting battles like Final Fantasy Tactics or any of your favorite squad based strategy games, prepare to be disappointed.  Much of the combat is set up to remove any depth strategy gives you and focus entirely on levels and gear, such that the story battles are a stat check.  If your stats are here or better, you can progress.  If not, grind some more.  While this would be fine for any sort of turn based JRPG, if you want to make this a strategy RPG, there needs to be some strategy involved.
The story is standard JRPG fare, an evil entity is going to destroy the world, something about the entity is relevant to the island you're on now so you get a bunch of followers to confront it.  You meet three waifus and choose one to be your true waifu to have a son who will go to a new island and be the protagonist of the next generation and repeat the process with harder enemies and better gear until you get to the generation who will confront the evil entity and bring peace to the world.  The story through each generation is rushed.  You meet several major players, kings, generals, civilizations, cities, and they are tossed out as quickly as they are introduced, leaving you with no impact or interest in the world at all.  Given how much time you spend grinding crap in this game, they could have invested a bit more into its depth so you can be interested in the time you spend in it.
I rarely say this in a review since some games I don't recommend games I enjoy and some games I don't enjoy I'll recommend, but this is a bad game.  This game is bad, there is nothing redeeming to be found here.  You should not buy it even if you are a Data Entry Technician who enjoys his job.

Awesome, underrated game. I have it on my iPad too, but PC is the best place to get this one; keyboard/mouse control works better than gamepad or touchscreen, and more importantly, there's a way to speed up the native frame-rate (you can google it) which I recommend utilizing -- the game's pace is sort of sluggish otherwise, but once you know the tweak, you can set the in-game animations as fast or slow as you like. There's also a Wikia and some FAQs online you'll want to bookmark and utilize for reference -- the game has tutorial info, but doesn't really explain all that much by itself. Some aspects of the game can be fairly mysterious if you don't investigate a bit, and there are some interesting things you'll discover as you get to know the game better.
If you like old-school, turn-based tactics-style gameplay that you can sink many hours into, and you like general JRPG weirdness and plenty of loot, this one is great. It deserved way better than the reviews it got when it was released, it's just not for all tastes. There is a dating-sim element to the game that seemed to be overmarketed -- it's a minor element to the game, and just adds a little pleasant variety to the adventure. You'll play through multiple generations of characters, breeding one of three cute anime girls in each generation to produce new characters for the next. The pathways available to play and the characters you get will depend on the girls you woo, which depends on the various multiple-choice style choices you make at various points in the game. They seem kind of superficial on the surface, but actually produce more meaningful gameplay variations than you might expect.
One thing to note: the DLC packs can massively overpower you, so you may not want to go too overboard on those. You do have the option to selectively enable/disable them when you start a new game, and kind of pick and choose what you want injected. I got a few that came with mine when I bought it and ended up disabling the majority of them. I found the balance I'm liking best so far is to play on hard, but give myself one or two advanced weapons at the onset (and maybe some extra EP and TP points, as the game is a bit stingy handing those out). Even one advanced weapon too early will make things fairly easy though, at least once you understand what you're doing, so approach DLC with caution.
If you think you might like this game, but have held back because of so-so reviews -- stop holding back. Indulge! I haven't tried the sequels yet but this one is really addictive. In summary:
+ Great turn-based combat that's complex enough to be really interesting, but not so complex it’s intimidating to learn.
+ Divergent paths and the option to focus on characters you like best, which invites multiple playthroughs.
+ Cute dating-sim/generation breeding mechanic.
+ Great graphics and art and animations if you like old-school and/or Japanese games.
+ Can tweak frame-rate and other back-end things with PC version to improve feel of gameplay.
+ Keyboard/mouse works better than gamepad/touchscreen.
+ Lots of loot and enjoyable DLC packs (but they can overpower you quickly).
+ Japanese voices (no English dubbing). To me this is a plus for this style of game.
+ Generally addictive, charming gameplay.
~ You'll probably need to do some googling and Wikia-ing to get the most out of this game; aspects of it are a bit inscrutable without a little research.
- Looks kinda crappy maxed to fullscreen on a big, high-resolution monitor -- I set mine windowed at anywhere between 720p-1080p range of resolutions, and find that feels about right for the game visually.
- Slow at first, takes some patience and getting into.
- Animations sluggish until you tweak the game settings on the back-end and bump up the framerate.

Buying Early Access Games always leave me quite concerned. There are a lot of them that promise much and deliver very few, taking too long to finish or even being released without getting finished at all. But THAT'S NOT THE CASE with Medieval Engeneers.
There has been only a few months since this game has been released in Alpha and it is ABSOLUTELY ♥♥♥♥ING AWESOME already!!
Keen Software House (the Producers) also produce Space Engeneers and both games are very well built. They are constantly being updated, mostly in a weekly basis (with bug fixes in a daily basis), and problems are very rare.
Here goes a short synopse of what you get from this, yet brute but already quite refined, Diamond:
- You get to build amazing Medieval Structures of Stone, Wood and Iron from scratch.
- You can terraform the land, raise mountains, dig deep mines and build whatever you like upon it.
- Construction is made through a very cleaver system of Stackable Blocks, which sometimes can be overlaid in order to create even more awesome composite blocks.
- Blocks are affected by real Phisics. Weight, Height and Impact affect the blocks and they even crumble when overloaded.
- EVERYTHING IS DESTRUCTABLE! You can build large fortresses just to have a lot of fun destroying it later on. And destroying it isn't only realistic as hell, but it's also very very fun!!
- You can already build a wide variety of buildings (from tiny poor villager houses to might Castles and Citadels), and every week more and more blocks are released into the game.
- The game also provides easy access to even more blocks from Steam Workshop's independant developers.
- You can build not only fixed buildings, but also complex mechanisms like Lifts, Porticulis, Draw Bridges, Catapults, Onagers, Trebuchets, Balistas, Windmills, etc. AND THEY ACTUALLY WORK!!!
This game is Heaven for your Creativity and only the sky is the Limit.

Technical details:

This is a very well polished game, and I love the deep and interesting backstory presented about the fascanating culture and history of Kharak. The gameplay is fairly solid and certainly fast-paced, thrumming with that middle-eastern "Dune" desert sci-fi that I can't get enough of. For those points, it's a solid thumbs-up. Read up on the delicious backstory and you'll love every moment of the campaign.
On the other hand, you do sometimes end up playing against the game rather than the enemy - I find the control groups are awkward to assign and clear in the heat of the particularly fast battles. Similarly, whilst I can unhappily absorb the lack of formations, it can be hard to ascertain the minutae of what exactly is going on and where: a Total War style pause button wouldn't have gone amiss for moving large intricate formations or responding to multiple distant threats. The enemy AI is reasonably good but "cheats" by not playing to the same rules as the player, at least in terms of economy and resource gathering, which makes conditions feel a little unfair in a protracted battle.
So it's got some cons, but it's a great story and interesting world to inhabit. Just make sure to read up using the backstory app and, apart from suffering through some occasionally poor gameplay design, you'll have a great time.

Disclaimer the first: I'd give it a "mixed" score, but Steam won't let me. It getsa "Recommended" from me because see below.
Disclaimer the second: I am writing this review as a player who played and eventually beat every other Homeworld game there is, including Cataclysm, because he fell in love with the universe.
gets the storytelling right - while nostalgia glasses prevent it from getting anywhere near the original
in terms of atmosphere and creating the feeling of an ancient myth rather than a science-fiction story, it still has
beat in this respect.
Gameplay-wise, however - it isn't a
game, per se, but it certainly does lack polish.
The biggest problem is, of course, AI. Cruisers that charge into battle without support despite having been given guard orders, fighters that return to carrier upon launch or refuse to return to carrier after dropping their payload, and so on.
Furthermore the game shows how much potential is left unrealised: a large part of the original Homeworld's appeal was factoring in the third dimension -
could have implemented that better by allowing aircraft to select their altitude and engage each other, and by adding more variations, such as aircraft equivalent to ground units in their movement and loitering behaviour (helicopters, for instance) or heavy transport planes capable of being loaded with light ground units.

Full Video Review:
Pros
+Weapon and ability variety gives you the ability to play your Ironcast in a large number of ways. Want to build a tanky shield Ironcast? Go for it. Want to play an Ironcast that bursts down individual systems? Definitely possible.
+Challenging not to the point of frustration, but to the point where you will constantly come back for more.

Ironcast is a combination of very different genres into something that is both unique and extremely fun. The depth of combat goes beyond what a simple RPG would usually provide by using the match board as a tool to restrict bad players from progressing and reward good players for thinking out the best way to use resources in their pool and on the board. At $15 the game provides an adequate amount of fun and wraps it up nicely in a steam punk style that is not only a theme to the game, but gives character to the abilities characters and weapons on your Ironcast. The amount of luck may frustrate you at first, but if you are like me you will be having almost too much fun to notice.

I like the Steampunk genre and still play Puzzle Quest on my PSP now and again (200+ hour play time), so when I first saw Ironcast on Kickstarter it tickled those 'back me now!' bits in my brain. Okay, so ... first off, my biggest recommendation here is to play this game when you're in a pretty chill mood.  If you're at all tense, the repetativeness of this game will get to you and drown out the overall "feels" and story as nearly happened with me.  However, in the end, I think this game is worth the ride and I do recommend it.
It's kind of a groundhog day varient; you repeat the same day over and over, from differemt perspectives, making minor adjustments to try and get the outcome your character desires.  The different perspectives interact with each-other; leave a gate unlocked from one perspective, and the other perspectives can see it.  It's not a real-tme switch; you play one character's entire day, resulting in some outcome, and only after you receive that outcome can you switch to another character.
The outcomes, together, determine the result.
Its actually a pretty cool way to tell a story.  I've never seen it done quite this way.  And the game is distinctive and reasonably pretty (the eye-less characters aren't really to my taste, but it didn't distract too much and I'm sure there's some deeper meaning there that I missed).
Here's what sucks; the little "mini cut scenes" that are repated many, many times and that you cannot fast-forward or skip.  For instance, you're going to see the little boy wake up and get his ball and kite knocked off at least 12 times in this game.  Or worse, you'll have to load the lady's damn box onto her truck and watch her poke her precariously stacked crap and examine her tie-down points about 6 times.  Each time is like 30 seconds of unskippable cut-scene.
It feels a little petty to complain about it, but it adds up.  And then, at the end of each day for each character, you're forced to watch the entire outcome.  This is a LONG cut scene, that you can't skip, and if you're going back and forth between 2 or 3 characters it adds up to a lot of get up and get a coffee time.  Unfortunately, during some of these longer cut-scenes, there's a requirement to press the 'R' key so you can't even refresh your beverage during them.
This cumulatively detracted from the experience for me a rather great deal, and I was tempted to quit when I got to the hunter's  trial-and-error minigame (with unskippable cutscenes in between each attempt).  I'm glad I stuck it through, but, this isn't a game you really want to attempt if you're liable to be frustrated.
I would have enjoyed this game a lot more if either you could skip the cutscene bits, or if they didn't make you repeat certain unnecessary parts.
The story also kind of bugged me, but in ways I can't really say without spoliing anything.  If I had to sum it up in 2 words, though, I'd say 'cumulative incompetence'.  Maybe I'm just too jaded to wax on about how sweet it is, I don't know.  I guess the point is that
Anyway :)  Bring your patience and make sure your beverages are close by cause you're going to need to press that R key,.

A bit more approachable than TIS-100, working in part like SpaceChem, allowing you to place modules and draw connections between them. Like in TIS-100 you write a custom assembler code variant to program the modules, but it's a bit easier, even having a mul operation. You have a limited space to just solve the tasks, and you can also optimize for power usage, cost, and lines of code. While niched towards programmers, it can probably be enjoyed by others who like to solve puzzles or problems.

As with other Zachtronic games (Spacechem, TIS-100), Shenzhen I/O is a programming puzzler. You play the role of a new embedded systems engineer and develop small electronics for a company based in Shenzhen, the mecca of electronics in China. You use a limited instruction set to program small chips to accomplish a variety of tasks given to you. You'll program an animated neon sign, a sandwich maker, an alarm system, and various other electronic thingamabobs. You'll rage at needing just one more line of code but having no space for it, needing just another register to store data in or needing more space on your board to place another chip. It'll feel like work, but hopefully you enjoy solving these kinds of problems.
Not recommended for everyone. If you liked past Zachtronic games, you'll likely like this as well. If you're geeky, if you know the story of Mel and wish you'd been him in a past life, if you write code and want to relax doing the same thing without real bosses or real deadlines breathing down your neck, you'll like this one. I certainly enjoy it. Thumbs up.

While EA's NHL games are losing features, this game is gaining more and more features every 2 weeks or so. Give your money to this team instead of EA, because they're converting your $17 into a much better game at a much lower cost than any of the recent NHL games.

First, this is an early access game so it is not a finished product.  It needs time and they have already made changes to the product to attempt to improve it.  I expect this to continue based on the history this team has.
Second, Some have posted that "it doesn't have the features of Football Manager" but that is a ridiculous expectation for a game that is a third of the cost of Football Manager and has not had the number of releases as that game.
Now that I got the disclaimers out of the way.  I recommend this product to any hockey fan that has always wanted to run a team.  It has some growing pains but it shows a lot of promise.
The positives:
+ It's a hockey sim, a market that is in dire need of a good product.
+ The stats are believable.  Scoring and penalties may be slightly inflated but I grew up watching hockey in teh 80's so I have no issue with the increase in scoring.  A 4-3 game is more entertaining than a 2-1 game.  :-)
+ The 2D view allows you to watch the action, or just highlighted versions of the action.  It still needs work but it has a bit of a feel like the old Gretzky Hockey days.

With the comment given I wanted to just make a note to add to the review.  I apologize for calling it a "game," because you're right, it's a much more a story ... but I think "Interaction" should mean that it requires my input not just "press x to continue" ... and I believe that I have detailed my feelings on that above.  However, I am changing my review to positive because it is a good story, even if I don't feel that the "interactive" portion was fully realized (and I wish I didn't have to bang on my keyboard just to suddenly have the game erase / reverse the choice I make; I think that's a little disingenuous)
If none of my responses actually change the ending, why give choices?  Why note if Emily will remember things if it doesn't make any difference in the overall story?  Sure, it's great not to hear her gush about Snow Patrol, but aside from some name changing I'm not seeing any difference no matter what choices I make.  It's good for a single playthrough, then, if that's the case, and the rest, given that you can't skip anything, is just typing noise.
If you decide to revise the game, this is the advice I'd give:
1) Let the game remember the choices you made.  Some of the choices are so threadbare I honestly don't remember what I've asked / responded after each chapter.  When you play through it again, have the game highlight previously-viewed choices so even if the ending won't be different, we can at least see all the text.
2) Meaningful Choices!  Maybe allow the chance to speak to other people besides Emily, or in addition to her ... maybe change at least the names of the people depending on what school you go to!  Maybe in some way not let a vague choice outcome become the turning point of the relationship between your character and Emily!?
3) (Semi-) Randomized gameplay!  Maybe Emily doesn't like Coldplay, but another band?  Maybe move the responses around a little?  Maybe offer the player the chance to introduce something?
4) Different Endings!  This goes to the heart of this review, but if you're not going to let me affect the story, why bother giving me choices at all?  Don't make me bang my keyboard to type out a response when nothing I do will change anything?  And I'm not talking about the very end where it forces me to say goodbye by deleting any response I make, but that is part of it.
You have a good concept and I have no doubt that anyone who gives it a playthrough, who grew up with IMs will understand, appreciate and emotionally connect to the story you've created ... but without more depth either on the player side (customizing details about the character you play) or the story side (being able to have meaningful choices, choices that may not get rewritten, and endings that reflect the actions you take,) all it is is a few minutes of time that use cheap emotional tactics to pull out the sorrowful response.
You may want to look at some of the other text-based stories done through other programs, where they track responses and allow or disallow certain choices based around previously-made choices or stats affected by your previous choices.  The story is sad, and shows heart, but the game could be so much more.

This is one of the best RTS games to come out in years, for several reasons.
-Large scale: You'll be fighting over great distances, but simultaneously each unit.
-Strategic zoom: Zoom out to see the entire battlefield. All modern strategy games should have this feature.
-Veterancy: Each unit has veterancy which rewards unit preservation.
-Line of Sight- Line of sight and height advantage are simulated. Use smoke screens to block line of sight for an attack or to screen your retreat. Take to the high ground with your railguns and pick off the enemy without risk.
-Combined arms: Units have very distinct roles. Most are specialists, forcing you to use combined arms to be the most effective.
-Micro: Unit types allow for lots of interesting and varied engagements. Intel and support are key to closing out the match.
-Artifact System: One way to win a match is to collect artifacts, which forces you to play aggressively. Collecting artifacts gives your carrier (basically a mobile base) a boost to its abilities. If you can manage to take your carrier on the offensive you are at a big advantage.
TLDR: This is one of the most interesting and feature full RTS games to come out in years. I'd give it a 9.5/10.

A hauntingly beautiful game with a deeply emotional story.
In Last Day of June, you'll experience the story of Carl, who is trying to cope with the loss of his wife, June.
After a tragic accident, Carl is bound to a wheelchair, coping with his loss, when suddenly he can experience the past through some paintings, and change the course of actions that led to said accident, trying to undo everything and save his beloved June.
In those flashbacks, you take control over the neighbors of Carl and June, trying to find an alternative outcome of the original happenings.
You will walk around the neighborhood, interacting with the characters and items, trying to solve some rather simplistic "puzzles" (it's not really puzzles, more like "finding the right way and order to interact with items").
Throughout the whole game, there is also no real communication through language, everything the characters do and feel is told via gesticulation and unintengible mumbling.
The visuals feel like they have been painted (which i guess fit's to the story) and the characters are quite abstract, but nevertheless it's a beautiful game, with lush colours and a very fairytale-like look.
Not just the visuals are beautiful, but the soundtrack does a great job in supporting the story and bringing out all the emotions too.
The game really took me by surprise, as i didn't really expected anything. That way, the emotional impact was maybe even bigger.
There are few games that really touched me and got me all emotional, Last Day of June is definitely one of them.
One thing that might be frustrating (depending on how you're playing) is, that there is no free saving.
So if you quit the game without hitting an autosave point you might have to replay quite a portion of the game.
Apart from that, i'd highly (!) recommended to anyone, who likes games with rather simplistic gameplay and a deeply amotional tale about love and loss.

This is the third in the series of Assassin's Creed Chronicles. They are 2.5D platformers in the vein of the superior Mark of the Ninja (developed by Klei Entertainment). I really enjoyed the first entry in the series, China, and immediately bought India when it was released. India was significantly more difficult than China, but never frustrating. I enjoyed it tremendously.
So when Russia was released, I bought it without hesitation. These games, taken as a whole, add a few things to the Mark of the Ninja formula (such as bushes you can hide in), and they are nothing but a treat as far as visuals are concerned. Russia certainly looks great and I enjoyed the story. As far as difficulty is concerns, this is on par with India with one notable exception: the chase/escape missions.
My goodness, how I hate those missions! They are an excercise in frustration. The timing is brutal and the controls sometimes are more than a little dodgy, meaning you won't got off a ledge or up from a ladder before some sniper gets you in his crosshairs. At that point, it's game over and you'll have to do the whole thing again. I was struggling to get through a sequence with spotlights, snipers, and a train, and I kept dying over and over again in a way that didn't feel like it was my fault, but rather the game instead.
Having just died for the umpteenth time, I just don't feel like continuing. I've deleted the game from my drive. Perhaps at some point in the future, I will revisit it and try if I can get further. But for now, other and better games demand my attention. As such, I recommend you check out the China and India entries in this series, but skip this one for now.
Update: so, I retried the game and actually managed to get a bit further, hoping the game would get better. I actually changed the recommendation to a (tentative) thumbs up, too, for a while, but having now reached a new level, where you are again chased (this time by a tank), with an extremely punishing difficulty (after having just played through one of the worst levels ever in the basement of the Kremlin), I'm taking another break and changing the recommendation back to a negative one, as before.
This game, man. I don't mind a challenge, but this is just almost impossible at times, and highly frustrating in a definitely-not-fun way. Who in the hell thought it would be a good decision to include so many of these god-awful chase sequences? Who thought it would be a good idea to force the player through millisecond-precision pick-pocketing (!) sequences? Who thought it would be a good idea to have the player chase a truck or be chased by a tank where a single moment (i.e. not jumping off a wall as soon as possible) results in instant failure?
Good grief, I really enjoyed the previous two instalments in this series, but this final one is as fun as smashing your head against a concrete wall repeatedly until your skull cracks and your brains ooze out. If that were in the game, you'd probably fail, not because of cracking your skull, but because you didn't do it .2 of a millisecond quicker, because now the Russian soldier saw you and it's game over. Man, in the light of the previous two games, it's like getting a polished turd for desert after having just eaten a great starter and a very enjoyable main course. Sure, it's polished, but it's still excrement.
So anyway. Assassin's Creed Chronicles: Russia -- I don't know what Ubisoft/Climax Studios were thinking, but this is definitely NOT half as good a game as the previous two entries. There are some neat ideas (the grapple thing that you can electrify, for example), and the presentation (sound and graphics) are top notch, but the level design is dreadful. What happened to the people who made the previous two games?
Long story short: do yourself a favour and skip this one.
If you like to play 1 minute, then die, retry, play 1 minute 10 seconds, die, retry, play 1 minute 20 seconds, die, retry... until you complete the game, this one is for you :)

Takes gem matching to the next level, by making the different colours represent different resources which power the shields, engines, weapon, coolant, and repair of your gloriously archaic Mech (the titular Ironcasts).  Battles are a balancing act - do I try for a quick finish attack, or go for endurance, gaining more experience but risking wasting resources on after-battle repairs?
The permadeath aspect is pretty well done - there are global unlocks which mean you'll take something away from even a crushing defeat; some of these are incremental (+15 starting health), and some have a larger effect by giving the option of choosing a different pilot (from a pleasingly PC selection), or Ironcast.   These different starting combinations  go a long way towards lessening any frustration around replaying early battles in every game.
The balancing act continues with the mission choices - Hard missions represent increased risk, but proffer tantalising additional rewards...but lose them and the game is over.
In short, the game offers me enough player agency to feel that my losses could have been avoided if I'd made better decisions.  And that's the essence of its "just one more turn/try" core.
Not an epic game, but one I think I'll keep coming back to.  A definite Kickstarter success.

Random elements are a vital element of any roguelike. They add to the unique nature of each run and surprise even the most veteran players. However, these surprises can usually be minimized with skillful play. Rogue Legacy can be conquered with careful platforming, and a master at The Binding of Issac has long since memorized enemy patterns and room layouts. Ironcast, a new steampunk roguelite from Dreadbit, combines procedural mission generation with the random boards of a gem matching puzzle game and then layers on turn based strategy on top of that. These elements form a huge balancing act that unfortunately leans heavily in favor of the random number generator at the cost of any truly tactical strategy.

SHENZHEN It takes the tried and tested formula and applies it to another slightly different set of problems. It is also a strangely strong immersive experience - considering it lacks all the "fireworks" of AAA game intros, I felt totally absorbed in the world. I even had to look out the window to check I was still at home and not in China...
The tried and tested formula is that there are puzzles with no single optimal solution. Instead, the solution to each problem has to find a balance between competing measurements - do you make it fast or do you make it cheap? This is supported by excellent leaderboards and comparisons that make competition with "the rest of the world" fun.
The problems in SHENZHEN are in the world of integrated circuits - you get a bunch of chips and several lines to program those chips. These instrcutions are very simple, but also expressive - meaning that (relatively speaking) the game is easy to play and hard to master. I say relatively speaking because, it's not "easy" in the arcade games sense - you do need to invest some time to get started, and it will continuously strain your brain, but in a very fair way.
It also comes with a great sense of humor, a relaxing card game (which would make a great standalone phone game.. please :D?), tons of puzzles and a prototyping freeform editor that lets you build all manner of crazy. I highly recommend it!

A: You got that right

Ok so first off this game should in theory appeal to me greatly.
Im a huge fan of both rpgs and VN/dating sims (dont judge me) so this should be a winner by virtue of the fact that it marries two awsome things together right?
Not so much.
The battle system in this game is so badly chosen for the genre that its hard to describe. In a huge storydriven rpg/vn story is usually the main focus of players attention right?
The battles should be little spice inbetween to keep things interesting. Well the system is certainly interesting, it has loads of customization and tactics etc but the issue is that its strategy on a grid every time.
Its VERY tedious to deal with moving all 6 characters into postion, then attacking with all of them (move and attack are seperate for some reason). Then moving them all back into position for the next turn (they have to be standing on specific tiles in relation to each other to perform combo attacks).
Now you might think "well thats ok i can just rush my guys forward and kill the enemy in normal fights and save tedium of respositioning for the hard fights! ill save heaps of time!"
No you wont.
The game preempts this by making each and every enemy a huge damage sponge that will require the full turn of 3 characters to kill AT A MINIMUM (and thats just a normal kill you need to "overkill" monsters to get item drops to craft your gear so really you need to use basically every characters moves on 1 enemy), then the game doublesdown on the tedium by making you fight 6-8 monsters at a time.
So thats 8 move turns and 8 attack turns to clear a normal run of the mill group of monsters. This takes freaking forever! like 10-15min per fight, around 50 fights per section and 5 sections in the game.
Its such a shame too singe the story/vn elements are well done and interesting for what they are.
Pity they are locked behind a massive wall of boring combat.
I mean sure these kind of fights are fine for bosses and the like but just getting my xp from the local trolls should not be an epic struggle.

Perhaps the most enjoyable sandbox I've played since Minecraft..for the 3 hours I managed to play it, at least.
The building mechanics are intuitive and for the most part easy to use, and the destruction engine is reminiscent of Red Faction: Guerrila. If you want to understand that last part, watch someones video on YouTube.
However, whilst I do recommend this game it is only in the hope that the developers will improve on this. The game is perhaps the most unoptimised I have ever played, with lag occuring almost every time you destroy something. The game also lacks a large number of objects to build with. It would be even better if it had a Besiege swing to it, with AI that actually moves, interacts etc.
My PC isn't the best, I will be using an i5 as of tomorrow, which may combat the problems with FPS drops during destruction, but what really is disappointing is I can no longer play the game. My graphics card does qualify above the recommended requirements, but now whenever I try to play the game I am given an error. After trying the troubleshoots people have come up with it still doesn't work, and I hope that the developers will get back to me with a solution. I do believe it is because my graphics card uses Nvidia's Kepler microarchitecture, which struggles to use DX11.1.
So, 7/10 in the hope that the developers grow this game, optimise it, and solve the issues people are having with DX11.1.#
Edit: 2 hours later, it's been fixed, I can now play. They've added multiplayer and sounds. Best game ever.

This is a tough one. Anomaly is a bit of a hidden gem...but also my brain hurts. Also some of it is a bit clunky. Also the graphics and presentation aren't always on point.
So TL;DR of a TL;DR: Buy it if you are okay with a
lack of polish in exchange for a fairly beautiful brain-busting 3D rotation-based puzzle solving platformer experience.
+
In the second half of the game, where individual light sources are carefully placed, there's a real beauty and variety.
+
Simple satisfying sounds, some pretty decent music, and nothing bad to speak of.
+
At what cost does one value freedom at? Is freedom the end goal?
+
Functional, rotation happening separate from the controls with 3D triggers in the world was a good call.
+
Ano's initial reactions and curiosity to everything is very cute.
+
There are multiple solutions, and the game really ups the difficulty by the end.
-
The first half of the game is primarily only blue and has more of a flat world lighting feel with fewer particle effects and other sources of different colors.
-
While the execution is decent, and the story is more of a reason/backdrop for Ano, the premise is fairly generic.
-
Never before has rotating something 90 degrees the wrong way been so easy! (This isn't 100% the fault of the game)
-
Stop or something bad will happen! Okay, wait, NOW something bad will happen...I'm warning you!
-
The puzzles in much of the first half to 3/4th of the game are a bit too easy once you grasp the mechanics.
-
No, not the ending of the game. The part where you think it's the end...then you have to do more platforming through a long hallway for no reason at all.
-

Hi everyone and welcome to this review of Anomaly 1729!
So Anomaly 1729 is a hidden gem, albeit perhaps a slightly unpolished diamond. If there was ever a sequel or a reboot in the far off future, let's say it is a title with a lot going for it that could easily be capitalized on. In Anomaly you are a humanoid...robot(?) with a very natural curiosity to explore the world around you. You quickly find that the world, however, has other ideas. It wants to keep you where you are, with your freedom and curiosity intanct. Or maybe it only wants to keep you away from the truth?
Well, the world does this by changing all around you, at first against your will. Doors close as you clear areas, new passages open, and you're often maybe not quite sure where to go first or if it's possible to get there. This makes an interesting parallel with Ano, as you the player has to have a natural curiosity to see more to drive you forward as forward is often...not forward, but in any number of places, and in all places. So the question in Anomaly, is where do you go first to progress when you have to go everywhere anyway? It's nice, because you are often left free to explore the areas that seem most interesting first.
As you progress in the game, you slowly get more ability to control the world. You can stop or start moving platforms, rotate them, or make something push instead of pull. Eventually this results in you rotating whole rooms and floors to your brain's utmost dismay. It's absolutely beautiful, but hard to keep track of. What was just the ceiling is now the floor. What is now the floor is now again that wall to the right in the room. And all of it so that you can get through that door in the left side of the room that needs to be the floor. Welcome to Anomaly 1729. The game that asks: How badly you want to get to the end while challenging you, teasing you, and inviting you in for more with it's intriguing story, simple and effective graphics, good music, and openly oppressive world ready to be conquered.
The graphics in Anomaly 1729 are simple, and I would argue effective...just not at first. Blue, blue, and more blue, with perhaps a touch of gray. Eventually you get to darker blue. To be fair, in that stage of the game, things are simple and you are learning by doing and too much variety would detract from your ability to do so. It also works well with the story, as you are early on in a more innocuous area. I challenge you to bear with it, though, as once the game opens up the graphics really start to shine, literally. Textures that were repetitive get broken up by more individual feeling light sources, there's objects and particles everywhere, the level design becomes complicated, convoluted, and labyinthine resulting in a much more diverse and beautiful experience. Later on, it even becomes more obviously thematic. The visuals do a great job of representing the state of the world and its characters. Word around the block is that it makes for a gorgeous VR experience as well, although I wouldn't know personally.
Okay, I'll come clean here: I absolutely love the sound the dialogue makes. I don't know why. It's just deeply satisfying for no other reason than some odd biological imperative or psychological effect/manipulation it was possibly designed to have. Moving on, though, there's not a whole lot to the audio of Anomaly 1729. The sounds are understated, concise, crisp, and then over. Again, this works well, as it leaves you free to think about the challenge and the world before you. That's not to say the audio feels empty or barren, although you may find yourself thinking that at a few points if you get stuck, as the music feels very dynamic and appropriately engaging if you pay attention but zen if you don't. The strength of the audio of Anomaly 1729 is that like the world, graphics, characters, etc. it all blends together to create a cohesive experience focused on solving the challenges and getting to the end of the world. So, how badly do you want to find out what's at the literal end of the world?
I am hesitantly recommending Anomaly
at:
if you want a fun 4-8 hour experience that may leave you scratching your head or:
if you are a diehard puzzle game fan, like gravity/rotation puzzles, are addicted to games like Portal/The Talos Principle, etc.
But for either category you fall into, don't expect Anomaly 1729 to have quite the same level of polish or big budget value.  Anomaly does, however, very much make up for it with it's raw and free design that clearly has some heart and soul poured in.

For weeks now on indie game sites, social media and such there seems to have been a bombardment of promotion for the game Anomaly 1729. Completing the game I understand why. I had not heard of it before and it was an easy purchase during the steam sale for $1 and its an easy recommendation to fans of puzzle platformers. Its has solid controls, platforming, story and unique mechanics that will keep you entertained for hours.
In Anomaly 1729 you play Ano a robot? Who is awakened? Created? Forced? Driven? To find meaning in the world of Phiohm and to find Yuler who is constantly warning you to stop. Why all the question ? Because completing the game it will be up to you to interpret the story. Could it be all a metaphorical interpretation  or is it simply a journey of Ano? I felt very surprised by the story and it has a satisfying conclusion with player choice at the end. However the lack of voice work and even the minimal sound for when text messages were being presented minimized the impact of the story.
As you begin the game you find yourself staring at a wall of unreadable text. As you move forward you find a small station that unlocks the ability to translate some of the letters. These messages and stations are scattered throughout the world and there are also 10 unique stations holding the pages to the story of Anomaly. I only found 5 of the story pages as they can easily be missed but fortunately new game + allows you to carry those along with any of the found translations so some of the early messages will be readable. This whole aspect is unnecessary until you start new game + and understand that not being able to interpret those early messages leaves a sense a mystery to your journey.
Anomaly 1729 does not stray too far from the puzzle platform blueprint. You enter an (hub)area, learn some mechanics, enter a puzzle room and solve the puzzle in order exit. It's all straight forward and even if you are a novice or veteran of puzzle platformers nothing will be difficult to process. While Anomaly is linear for the most part there is not an actual "go here" next sign and I found myself on numerous occasions asking where am I supposed to go. As for the puzzles themselves again a lot of it will be familiar for vets with platform moving, jumping and a few switches to interact with but the uniqueness for Anomaly 1729 lies in the ability to rotate the room left, right, forward and backward. it's a cool effect done with motion blur and it makes for some interesting puzzle solving. The only problem I encountered with this ability were some of the larger rooms, due to the number of objects and shape of the room, as it rotates you could accidentally find yourself on the ledge of a platform and able to access the exit without really solving it correctly, if that make sense? One last thing I want to mention is the absolute fantastic controls. If there has been one mechanic for indie games that has continued to improve over the years it is the controls especially when it comes to platforming.
In terms of graphics the world of Phiohm could be viewed as a part of the Minecraft universe or Supermans fortress of solitude with its abstarct block shaped world and pitch black depths. That may be a turn off for some but has no impact for me personally. Anomaly also uses a a limited bright color scheme to bring some different aesthetic to areas with some cool lighting effects and that's fine but limited use of shadows is noticeable and it can make the world seem more lifeless. It still looks OK but some more attention to small details and effects would have improved the visual experience. This lack of attention also goes to the sound which is noticeably lacking. Though the soundtrack is pretty good with its use of sci-fi tones it's the lack of and minimal use of sound effects that is obvious and again impacts the experience.
Anomaly 1729 is the first puzzle game I didn'tt have to look up (Ill grind out wrong solutions for hours before caving) a walkthrough for any of the puzzles in a long time and that itself makes it worthy of a stress free recommendation. It's not without faults due to the exclusion of some better graphical effects and sound that would have made the experience more enjoyable but it does not overall impact the gameplay. I enjoy a good puzzle game and with its unique mechanic, solid platforming and story Anomaly 1729 is just that, a good puzzle game.

Most of the puzzles involve hitting lever #1 to invert gravity or shooting lever #2 to rotate platforms.  There's a lot of trial and error in the steps but it is honestly one of the most rewarding things to beat one of the levels in the game and continue on.  Graphically the game is beautiful, although I do admit that my favorite color is blue and the game incorporates a lot of blue and purple.  There's something magical and forlorn about the art style that makes me want to continue playing the game.  Unknown words and strange structures have a enchanting effect on a game, although it is a style that many devs fall on.  That being said if you are looking for a game that focuses more on design choices, clever puzzle placement, and not too much story than I recommend Anomaly 1729 for it's safe, but somehow unique, take on the genre.
