Always been a fan of EHM and this one does not disappoint!  Best hockey sim game available

After an 8-year hiatus, EHM makes its return via early access and while the game is very similar to its most recent iteration, that does not hinder or ruin the experience in any way.  As an early access game, this is a very polished and solid initial effort.
For those who haven't played EHM, the game is a text management sim where you take complete control of a team and attempt to use your skills as a general manager to take your team to glory.  As the game is in early access mode, there are no official licenses or real players.  However,
has a very nice roster set, logos, and real team and competition names that provide that.
Unlike NHL by EA Sports, you are the General Manager and do not control the players during games.  You sign free agents, hire coaches, scouts, and of course, trade as you desire.  Additionally, you can set your lines, practices, and tactics.  You also can promote and demote players between minor leagues and choose how to build your team.  As you're unable to control your players directly, tactics are very important in helping you win games.  The games themselves can be viewed via 2d mode where the players appear as dots with the puck, similar to the initial offerings of Football Manager 8 years ago, before it went 3D.
The game engine is solid and provides a decent way to watch games and observe your players.  The minor gripe I do have with the game engine is that it does look dated especially compared with how SI has evolved its Football Manager franchise.  Having said that, the fact that this game was developed as a side project by SI mitigates that gripe somewhat.
The menus are cleaner than EHM 2007 although again, not as intuitive as the newest Football Manager games.  The other issue is that the game can only be run in one resolution which means that newer screen owners will not be able to view the game on a full screen.  Hopefully, that will be addressed in a future update.
If you love Football Manager, Out of the Park Baseball, and text sims, you owe yourself the privilege in checking this game out.  For $14,99, you simply can't go wrong.  The more people that purchase this game, the more likely we will see official licenses and future releases.  If you're an armchair hockey fan who thinks, sleeps, and drinks hockey, you definitely need to check this out.  Disappointed that your team continues to build around a questionable core?  Fix it yourself in EHM.  You won't regret it!

I'm not a programmer. I like to think I'm good at logic and critical thinking.
This game kicks my♥♥♥♥♥ It picks it up, it throws it against the wall, then it does it again...
And I love them for it, because I do not feel the game "lets" me do anything. It doesn't hand me solutions, it doesn't make it simpler if I fail... no, it lets me fail, and it lets me learn from my mistakes, and it makes me a better person for it.

Like TIS-100 before it, this is a game in which you write programs in assembly language for imaginary hardware. However, in this case the hardware is also designed by you by placing and linking components together. In this respect some aspects of SpaceChem are also brought into play here.
Like almost Zachtronics games, there are a series of histogram benchmarks that you can use to rate your solutions against others. If you're into the competitive spirit, this adds a lot of replay value as you try to best or match your friends; it can also cause premature balding as you try to figure out how someone managed to accomplish a task with fewer instructions.
Basically, if you're a fan of the genre (i.e. you're a fan of Zachtronic games) you're probably going to love the hell out of this thing. I can't help but wonder if TIS-100 was released as a smaller game just to determine if people would want to buy a game of this type, or if it's the next logical step. Either way, I'm glad that both exist.

At a discount, this is a good purchase.
DISCLAIMER:
I only played the campaign, and I played almost exclusively for the story. I had little interest in MP.
SUMMARY:
Deserts of Kharak (DoK) returns to the Homeworld formula, this time in 2d instead of 3d. This prequal returns to the time immediately prior to the original Homeworld, when the inhabitents of the desert world of Kharak are fighting amongst themselves over ideological differences-- science vs religion. While Homeworld presented a mostly united planet, set about the mission of discovering the origins of the species (for it was not their current planet, as they had long believed), DoK sets out retelling the story of the Kushan's final (?) war on Kharak prior to the unification that led to the Mothership Project being possible.
PROS:
* Persistent armies between missions, unit experience & advancement, a diverse unit list, a diverse faction list (really only useful in multiplayer), well narrated in-mission and inter-mission voice segments, an appealing aesthetic (kind of a comic-book feel to the inter-mission cutscenes), and a well scripted story that fit perfectly in to the Homeworld narrative.
CONS:
* Units are not very balanced. The solution to most fights is to mass cruisers with sufficient support to repair through all but overwhelming odds (and for that, sacrifice cruise missiles and air strikes to thin them out before crushing them underwheel.) The story is very short (8 hours to play through the first time). The artifacts that grant certain bonuses during campaign gameplay are not easily identified-- you have to scour the entire map and "shipbreak" the debris to find them all. The most valuable of the artifacts are the ones that decrease logistics costs, the rest are almost pointless on easy difficulty. However, there is no specific directive mechanic to ensure that you collect the critical relics. Additionally, towards the end of the campaign you are given 'superweapons' that reduce you to fighting defensively while your superweapons do the rest of the fighting for you-- and last, and worst, the AI is poorly written and balanced-- it will let you demolish units with artillery from afar without reprisal; it will churn out units endless, not held to any economic mechanic; The AI is not limited by line of sight and will throw endless waves of air strikes against you; the AI is not limited by unit speeds and is able to micro units to ensure squad cohension (unlike players). Lastly, technically the game does not render properly on a wide screen monitor. It has verticle bands on the left and right during inter-mission cutscenes and load scenes that show the PC desktop background sometimes (or Steam overlay may sometimes appear.) In-mission renders properly but not at the maximum resolution of my monitor.
CONCLUSION:
While I'm happy to see another addition to the Homeworld IP, and I appreciate all of the improvements over the original Homeworld UI, the game feels essentially like a retread of original Homeworld IP with a minimally updated UI. There are a number of parallels to Homeworld, including how certain scenes are presented, and how certain plot elements unfold. While I'm not opposed to formulaic stories, I could wish for a little originality when it comes to blending the formula for a new narrative. Being a prequal and on-planet is a nice spin, but by itself not sufficient to warrant unreserved praise.
I think the metacritic score is justly awarded. I would recommend any fan of the Homeworld series to purchase it, but I would recommend you wait till its on sale (or until the price comes down to <$20.)

Suggestion 3: Remove having to name a different captain if current captain is injured. Takes too much time to rename temporary captain and rename regular captain after returning, and in the NHL today, we do not see this happening. Captains stay captains through the season.
Edit 2 (November 15, 2015): Through ten years of my Tampa Bay GM Mode and winning the Cup a couple of times, there are just a few problems I've noticed that consistently occur.
1. The AI in trading is an absolute travesty as of right now. It definitely could be worked on to be more balanced, perhaps like EA's NHL AI. As of now, the AI will trade each other ridiculous things like "Dany Heatley and a 7th round pick for Patrick Kane, Jonathan Toews and a 1st round pick", but when I try grabbing a player like Mike Green, they won't even take Stamkos for him, claiming to need just a little more. Definitely an irritating aspect that needs a little time to be worked on.
2. Injuries, like EA's NHL, should have the option of being turned off at player's discretion. I've had a period of time where players such as Hedman, Stamkos, Vasilevskiy, and Drouin would all go out in the span of a week with major injuries that would take them out for 3 months or more. So for the future, either have the option to turn them off entirely, or fix it so such major injuries occur less frequently.
3. A minor, miscellaneous problem with aesthetics I've noticed is the inability to "expand your arena" at all. It's a button there, but somehow despite my near-top attendance records season after season, it never seems to stop being grayed out. If it's there, I suggest a time when we could potentially expand our arena. Could be a cool little mini-feature, going into the future.
4. Finally, player growth through practice really needs to be revamped. A player can spend 6 months on the practice screen as "working on shooting", but at the end of 4 years of that "shooting practice" their overall for that has not gone up at all. I'm not sure the logistics behind player growth, but I feel as though practice should be a factor in whether a player grows a certain stat or not.
Through 10 years however, I have had little concern to doubt buying this game. An excellent pickup, which I am sure will please all hockey fans on PC even more when the game is fixed of its tiny bugs and glitches here and there.
Edit 3 (December 31, 2015):
Noticing a very disturbing trend that my goalies keep having extremely sub-par nights, despite their overall. Yes, I understand that every goalie has an off-night some nights, but I really don't think that a 5 star goalie such as Vasilievskiy can let in a combined total of 25 goals on 78 shots in 4 consecutive games, while this no-namer with red attributes shuts me out with ease in a 33 save effort. Going back to the "practice" screen, goalies working on their "Goalie" instructions should continue to grow more consistent and more capable of stopping pucks, and perhaps just going into the coding, tweak a couple of settings here and there.

Anomaly 1729. Talk about a beautiful game. If you are into puzzle and exploration games, this is right up in your alley. In the same field as Portal, this hidden gem is easily comparable to some of the greatest puzzle games out there. Although there are some small flaws in the game, it doesn't stop it from being as great as it is.
Jumping right into the game, you are welcomed by a simplistic, yet perfect menu. It shows the title of the game and there are a very small amount of sub-menus. The rest of the screen is covered by a neat animation of one of the rotary blocks. The only issue I had with the menu was the text, and this bothered me throughout the entire game. I think it could be made more legible with the used of an outline for the letters or simply just making the text bolder.
The music in the menu was great, and is great throughout the game. One thing I did notice, and this is because I am a musician therefore am very picky with the music, but there was a lack of low end. The music could have been a little more bassy. Also, I only noticed this during the main menu, but at the end of the song, there was a crackling. This could have been intentional though, I am not too sure.
In the options menu, I wasn't able to change the graphics quality in the visual details option. It was set to low and I was trying to set it higher. This changed after a minute of hitting all the buttons on the keyboard, but the cursors were still a little messed up.
The game starts off with a beautiful cutscene showing off the environment of the game. Now I do love watching these cutscenes, but some people don't. I think the lazy gamers should be able to skip cutscenes.
Anomaly requires more thinking rather than throwing you in constant action. You will be challenged with many obstacles, and unfortunately there is no tutorial, so you will be sent out to figure the game out on your own. Now, I don't like this approach, but some people might. I think a tutorial could be implemented somehow in the game. It took me very long to figure out how to work the game.
One last small thing is the aiming. I think the sensitivity should be adjustable and I also think that the hitbox for the rotary cubes should be made bigger. The precision in your shooting sometimes has to be a little too perfect.
There isn't much to complain about when it comes to actual game play. This game plays and looks beautiful. I am very impressed by this game. I see this game becoming very successful if the developers listen to what the gamers have to say. I think also bringing down the price (in the current state that is is), or adding it to indie game bundles, could bring in some more attention to the game and maybe some critical acclaim. I give this game an 8 out of 10.

There is no such thing as strategy or skillfull gameplay in Jotun. Every boss fight, encounter you have is completely randomized and based purely on luck. The amount of health damage you take for attacks that cannot be avoided in anyway baffles me... for example, the first boss fight (Jera):
- she has a posion could that covers the entire area and the damage you take is extremely high (unavoidable)

- her fist attack has a pattern that can be worked out but the amount of damage you take from it if you are hit is very high for the amount of health you have

Aside from the stunning artwork and the lore that has been perfectly nailed, I'm having a blast with this game. Many bad reviews complain about the "empty levels" and the fighting that lacks variety and feels slow and clunky. Well, that's a feature, not a bug.
The gameplay is pretty simple at its core, but it feels spot on to me, as everything from enemy attacks to environment hazards have been tailored around the "clunkyness" of the character. In terms of hack'n'slash action I'd take Jotun over Bastion every day, and I'v finished Bastion twice.
The "empty" maps are not empty at all, it's just the fact that the game doesn't throw hordes of enemies at you. That's because the game wants you to traverse the enviroments  while avoiding hazards, enjoying the beafutiful locations and the soothing music, discovering powers and fighting every now and then. Actually, each map has its own character, layout, hazards and enemies.
Every two maps you'll have the chance to fight a Jotun. The boss battles are beautiful and challenging without being hardcore or frustrating.
I'm absolutely enjoying this game and feel rather sorry for letting the bad reviews keeping me from buying it.
The only way to find out if Jotun is the right game for you is to actually try it, so hop onboard for a round of Jotun smashing.

Is this worth £15/$20?  If you like retro games, perhaps.  The package is merely functional and has no extras apart from simple game instructions and cover art.  The games run just fine but were designed to be played with a ColecoVision controller.  It is a shame the developers did not create a newer version of this with more features and the additional games they added to the ColecoVision Flashback console they released in North America.
If this had a similar polish that
has (online play, ability to use a controller, achievements, etc), I would recommend this at the current price. Assassin's Creed Chronicles: Russia is a 2.5D side-scrolling puzzle platformer. While not altogether different from the other Assassin's Creed Chronicles games, it offers a different and unique challenge. The difficulty has been ramped up in this version to provide a bit more of a challenge, but not so much so that it'll take you longer than 5-7 hours to beat it.
At the end of the story, I'm left with more questions than answers, but I'm told that this series is a companion series to the comic books which I have not read.
You'll go through 10 memory sequences which will feel familiar if you've ever played a main series Assassin's Creed game, though these are much shorter, much less cinematic, and much more comic book-y. You'll play through a series of sequences in which you are scored based on your "style grade" and you'll earn bonuses for being extra stealthy, non-lethal, and make good use of your resources. Some of my favorite levels are the "chase and run" levels where you're racing the clock to reach the exit. Those were by far the most fun and interactive.
The controls are a little unresponsive, but no more or less responsive than the previous two Assassin's Creed Chronicles games.
All in all, I would reccommend playing Assassin's Creed Chronicles: Russia as a breather to the main AC series. While not the best game, this has inspired me to try out other 2.5D puzzle platformers and that's a good thing.

Shenzhen I/O is a really solid programming game which builds well off of mechanics established in some of the developer's earlier games, particularly TIS-100's programming and SpaceChem's multi-reactor puzzles. It's all about writing very short assembly programs in a novel assembly language, on little processors which have wires to communicate with each other. The more you can optimize the code, the fewer processors you have to use (and often you need the space), so the game becomes much more of a puzzle than simply writing code.
The game has a good level of difficulty, such that it's a reasonably difficult puzzle to complete each level without worrying about efficiency, but as your scores for number of parts and number of instructions executed are shared to the world and compared with the rest of the players, there's a drive to make your solutions as efficient as possible, which adds worlds more difficulty. If you're into that, you can spend half an hour just figuring out how to make part of your code one line shorter so that it fits into the memory of a single processor. Or you can give up and decide merely finishing the levels is enough for you.
If you like programming puzzles or open-ended puzzle games with countless ways to reach a solution, this is one of the best such games I've played.
Zachtronics continues their streak of really good games and brings fresh new ideas to Shenzhen I/O.
Really polished, really addicting puzzle game. With the in-game histograms to compare your solutions to other players, you'll spend even more time making things more efficient!

Aside from the stunning artwork and the lore that has been perfectly nailed, I'm having a blast with this game. Many bad reviews complain about the "empty levels" and the fighting that lacks variety and feels slow and clunky. Well, that's a feature, not a bug.
The gameplay is pretty simple at its core, but it feels spot on to me, as everything from enemy attacks to environment hazards have been tailored around the "clunkyness" of the character. In terms of hack'n'slash action I'd take Jotun over Bastion every day, and I'v finished Bastion twice.
The "empty" maps are not empty at all, it's just the fact that the game doesn't throw hordes of enemies at you. DISCLAIMER: I want to start out by noting a couple of things that may be relevant to people interesed in this game. First, I never played Football Manager in any form, nor did I play this game's old 2007 iteration. I had no biases coming into this game. Second, while I am a hockey fan (Go Bolts!) I was not a hardcore fan. I was (and largely am) still fairly casual in that I don't follow mundane stats, am not up to date on every player in the league and don't watch every single game.
That being said. This game is fantastic! I am having loads of fun with this gaming experience and as far as I can tell will be having lots of fun for months if not years to come.
Who would like this game?
- anyone who enjoys management games
- anyone who enjoys stats and tactical games
- any sports fans (hockey is a plus!)
PROS:
- addictive gameplay that makes you feel involved and responsible for your teams success and failure
- a "one more turn" type of pull (days are done in turns)
- a unique and highly realistic game simulator that you can watch in real time or sped up (highly entertaining)
- HEAPS of potential, this game is still in Early Access but it is very fun and playable in it's current state, updates will only launch it to new heights
- in depth stats and tactics including fully realized and modeled shot analysis for games (impressive)
CONS:
- confusing and unoptimized UI (needs streamlining)
- can't control players yourself (this should go without saying but some people don't come to grips with this concept until they're in game)
- lack of useful tutorial and helpful tooltips (had to bumble around some things before finding them out myself)
- no sounds except crowd noise (might benefit from certain ambient sounds a calm musical track)
All in all this game as it stands is great and will only continue to get better over time. It's a low price, can be played in short bursts or long stretches, has an addictive one more turn type of gameplay that makes you feel involved and connected to your team. I love it.

I've been playing this series since FHM 2005, although it was FHM 2007 that I put in hundreds of hours.  This version of the game is an iterative improvement over FHM 2007.  It appears to be a conservative migration to SI's latest app engine, but maintains a very similar flow to EHM 2007, not the latest Football Manager game.
With that said, this game is simply spectacular.  I've only played a few games into my season with this version (so I'm not an authority on the state of completeness) but what I've seen so far is fantastic.  I've had some gripes with FHM 2007, fortunately it appears that quite a few of them have been addressed.  The fact that SI is bringing this game back is astonishing considering how they unceremoniously dropped the game after pirating concerns shortly after it was released in 2006.  Those of us with the Mac version really got screwed since there were some terrible bugs that were never fixed.
Regardless, I'm really excited for the future... If this game gets half the attention FM gets, we're in for a treat.  I have a feeling what we are playing now is a wait-and-see product- see what the respose is to this conservative effort and decide if it's worth investing any additional effort.  Judging from the response so far it should be a resounding YES, this game deserves 1st class attention!
Anyway, newcomers from FM are going to need to be patient, the UI is no where near as mature as FM.  FM has had the benefit of many years of iterrative development... while EHM has been in stasis for 8 years.  Even if this release just brings EHM up to date and nothing more, we all win.  Hopefully next years release will start incorporating some of FM's ground breaking systems.
This game is worth every penny whether you are new to the series or upgrading from EHM 2007.  My favorite sports sim ever, hands down.

Update: The game is still good, but updates have been slow coming. No vegas/expansion draft yet, though and update has been in the works for awhile.
Still very recommended, but unfortunately development for this game takes a back seat to changing Football Manager just enough to slap a new year on it and sell it for full price again.

Farm Simulator 17...
What can I say about this game? Its def farming 101 if you know nothing about farming, but its def the basics of farming. I'm a bit disappointed in a game that calls itself a simulator and boasts detail of real trucks and other stuff but yet doesn't really care about anything like ground nutrient levels or the such. How about a soil sampling system that will allow you to monitor the PH levels or tell you how much bacteria is in the soil? I mean simple stuff like basic nutrient levels of your soils are key to whether or not your crops should grow.
To me this game feels more like an advertising platform for the various agricultural companies and their equipment than an ACTUAL farm simulation. Its all about the big trucks and driving around. Its more of an arcade than a sim game. I mean, plow your field, fertilize it, plant your seeds, wait some time (which is controllable by settings) then harvest your crops and deliver to the highest bidders. That's pretty much it. If you want stuff that makes it easier to do these various steps, buy bigger equipment. Can you trade to other players? Nope. Multiplayer seems more like a "helping hand" type setup where your friends can come into your game and help you farm. You give them some money to play with and they buy equipment and farm stuff for you. When they leave, everything they got or money they made (or is left over after they joined) is yours and comes back to you. There's really no point in giving them any money unless you're lazy and you don't want to buy stuff for people helping you all day long and you want to get work done on your own. Nevermind the fact that the mission system for the NPC players is disabled in multiplayer. What's up with that?? Why can't you and your friends do those missions too? Seems entirely illogical to have those missions disabled. It gives you more things to do!
Yes it looks good, and its an easy farming game. No worries about being stuck in the mud if you stick to the roads and your fields, but to me, if you're going to call yourself a simulator, how about you simulate all aspects of farming? Wheather, soil nutrients, chemical systems, different types of fertilizers, the simple ability to even clean your farm equipment after its all dirty... All of these things are part of farming that are entirely missed. Granted I haven't had much game time and maybe I just haven't seen these things. Feel free to correct me in comments, but to me these things should be more outlined in a refined simulator type game.
For them to call this a simulation of what its like to be a farmer, you get a thumbs down. This isn't a simulator for farming. Its more of an advertisment for farm equipment companies than a farming simulator. Its too late for a refund now. So hopefully if others are looking at this game they'll take heed that if they're looking for realism, look elsewhere. You won't find it here. Not even close. There is so much depth to farming its unreal. I work for an agricultural chemical company IRL. I know a thing or two about farming and they don't even come close to scratching the surface with this game.

If you watched the trailer you already know the plot: Carl and June, husband and wife, have a car accident. Carl ends up in a wheelchair and June dies.
Your purpose in this game is to prevent the accident manipulating the events caused by the characters (the kid, the lady, the hunter and the old man) and you'll discover more details about them by collecting all their memories.
At first I thought that the impossibility to skip the cutscenes was a big mistake because it makes the game too repetitive and even boring if you don't play it with the proper mindset. But then I realized that maybe it was a choice of the creators to let the player feel what Carl is feeling, being forced to watch the accident over and over.
I will definitely follow Ovosonico's updates hoping to see other games like this.
P.S I just realized, while I was writing this, that the title "Last day of June" has a double meaning and I feel very stupid not to have noticed it right away.

The AI is fked! I found one of my workers in totally different field from the one I assigned him to, jammed up with another worker. I have no idea how he even got into that field but he was in it and working. In fact, he completed the field I assigned him to and apparently took it upon himself to go work the field beside it.

I wish I'd have screenshotted the AI lining up to begin spraying an unowned field next to my own before finally stopping and giving me the notice that I didn't own that field. Customization is a joke! You can't even preview your options to see what your customization will do before you do it. I bought a new pick up truck and the God damned thing came to me looking like I pieced it together out of spare parts from a junk yard. Tough luck, I guess, because I had already paid for it.
On top of that, you can only customize a few pieces of equipment (probably due to licensing), and other than the engine sizes none of it has any effect in-game. It's just for looks. It's not even consistent! I can put dual wheels on this tractor but not that one. I can put narrow or wide tires on this one, but not that one. Can I tint the windows? Nope! Can I remove the PTO option from the front to save some money? Nope! Can I add it where it doesn't already have one? Nope! Can I remove any of the just-for-show computery BS in the cab to save some money? Nope!
And apparently all the equipment in the game is Taiwanese garbage. They've added a... lol... feature where the more hours your equipment has on it, the higher it's daily running cost. Check your starting tractors on the Goldcrest map and compare their daily cost to the daily cost of the same brand new equipment in the store. It's hilarious... no, it's not hilarious, it's idiotic! The Case 1455 brand new has a daily running cost of $260. Your starting 1455 thats a mere 67 days old has a daily running cost of a whopping $808! It's barely two months old! It has less than 40 hours of use! Are you kidding me?!
EDIT 2: I've come to the conclusion that the problem is not the equipment, but trash AI. It's completely unreliable and misses spots all over your fields with multiple pieces of equipment of varying types, loses it's path and drives in circles, or just gives up and stops working. In one instance it moved itself to a completely different field and began working again. The developers did try to make it avoid obstacles better than it did in 15 and when it works it does work, but the problem is those times when it doesn't and those times are frequent enough that the improvement over the AI of FS15 is only theoretical.
Purchasing liquid fertilizer and seeds is flat stupid. You have to buy it from the tractor dealer in small pallets or bags then haul them all to your farm. There's no 100k gallon tank out back you can fill a trailer with. There's not even a trailer in the vanilla game that will hold liquid fertilizer. You have to mod one in. You can also mod in a placeable endless tank (and one for seeds, etc) that you can put on your farm or elsewhere and buy from that but the cost is higher than buying the dumbass little pallets. This is oversimplified, arbitrary, and utterly senseless. If I want to buy 30k gallons of liquid fertilizer or 20 tons of seeds no one anywhere in the world is going to charge me MORE for it because I brought my own tank instead of buying it in 100k little bags or pallets. Even if I install a 100k gallon tank on my farm, if I buy 30k gallons of fertilizer to put it in they're going to deliver it before I can even finish writing the check and it's still going to be cheaper than clogging up their parking lot with a bunch of pallets.
How do I know this? Because my wife and I buy about 500lb of flour/week for our bakery. If we went to our supplier and said "I want you to stop delivering my flour every week. Instead I want to buy less at the time, whenever I happen to need some, and I want it all in little 5lb bags sitting on pallets in your parking lot. I also want it cheaper than what I'm paying right now." he would laugh me right out of his office!
How do I know THIS? Because we used to do something similar until the supplier told us if we bought a little more than we had been they'd deliver it to us in big plastic bins for a lot cheaper and all we had to do was return the bins to them on their next delivery. We don't even have to wash them!
Enough said! Just buy 15. END OF EDIT.
It's a good game, I guess, but I refunded it.
Why did I do that? Because I already have FS15 and the differences between the two are as shallow as the gameplay of both versions. Neither FS17 or FS15 are simulations. If they are Call of Duty is also a simulation. Really, these games may be fun but if you're looking for a farming SIMULATOR you won't find it with the Farming Simulator franchise, which is ironic considering the name.
But like I said, it's a fun game. The base game only has two maps, though, one of which is also in FS15 and the platinum expansion gives you only one more. 15 is the same way. Three measly little maps and all you do is plant and harvest, plant and harvest, plant and harvest until you have enough money to buy some new equipment. Then you do the same thing over with the new stuff. That's the entire game. You don't even need to buy more than 4 or 5 fields to get rich either, and if you're playing singleplayer it's very difficult to manage more than two at the time anyway because the worker AI is stupid and isn't programmed to do anything but beat a back and forth path across a field. You can't interact with NPCs. You can't enter buildings. There's no soil management, no  pest control, no crop rotation... Nothing. You just cultivate, spray some slurry around (or your choice of irrelevant solid or liquid fertilizer, wait for it to ripen, harvest, repeat. That is literally all these games are. Other than traffic on the road and wandering bots, the entire game world is dead and boring. At least the jobs are a little better this go 'round.
My recommendation: Just but FS15 for a fraction of the cost. Sure, 17 is graphically a LITTLE bit better but hardly enough to justify the increased cost. Besides, you're already buying the Sosnovka map from 15. Three maps... three freakin' maps and that's only if you buy the platinum edition!
What this game is is a gigantic commercial for agricultural equipment manufacturers but it is fun to play if you like to watch big machines work. It's not good for much else, though, and FS15 scratches the itch just as good as 17 for a hell of a lot less dough.

JPRGs have been a core slice of the gaming culture for as long as any of us can remember. We have the gems, and the ostracized. Our present subject leans toward the latter. Why are these kind of games not considered highly, or even forgotten? Is it poor marketing, or weak content that deserves to stay hidden in shelves, accumulating dust? Agarest: Generations of War to an extent appears to be blessed with both. Due to downright reprehensible marketing and mediocre reception from critics, this niche selection has never seen it’s time in the spotlight in NA.
Granted, “underrated” is not the best tag for this game as it’s covered in blemishes, but it would be most deceitful to say I didn’t have a blast. Agarest: GoW is a generic piece of JRPG history with merits that prove it doesn’t need to be embellished by praise or pinpoint expertise to be enjoyable.
Our 200+ hour adventure starts with the Golden Leonhardt Raglan, and his aspiration of a world filled to the brim with peace and tranquility after having enough of fighting in the ongoing war. In his efforts to save a young High Elf named Ellis, he is reduced to a state of near death. In a more habitual situation, he would have passed, but a lady named Dyshana comes to his aid (No Leo, no story, right?) with a request: his life would be saved if she is granted his progeny to be the leaders of eradicating the forces of darkness. Leo agrees to partake in the compromise, and he, Ellis and some other people begin a strenuous, five-generation journey of blood, tears, agony, hope, and... other meaningful things! A rather stimulating foundation for an extensively long story, too bad almost all the events earlier in the game hold no consequence at all. However, it does get interesting once you subject yourself to a whole 50-70 hours of insignificance.
In all seriousness though, Agarest borrows many themes and elements from your typical war drama, contrary to popular belief since this game was marketed with a bad image akin to those of harem visual novels. The five main Heroes of Agarest have their own ideals, and question these and whether their
will bear fruit. The main cast of this game adds up to over 15 characters, with each having their own quirks. From the ill-minded Winfield to the more stoic Vashtor, I never felt bored with this very colorful cast. They all get their own time to demonstrate their qualities, and even though I didn’t feel too invested into them, it was pleasant to see them whenever they’d appear. However, many of them undergo their own internal strife as a result of stored up stress from the war. It doesn’t feel as shallow as I expected, and I eventually started to care for the story as a result of this depth. The story doesn’t raise the bar for storytelling in video games, but it's memorable enough to consider it above average.
For JRPGs like this one to be separated from the rest it is imperative that its battle system is fairly accessible (as in not frustratingly complicated), paced optimally, and most of all fun. This game more or less succeeds in meeting this criteria. Agarest’s combat comprises of a grid-based layout that plays in turns, similar that found in more popular titles such as Disgaea. Party members and enemies are distributed across the grid either in chosen/fixed formation or by random (Surprise Encounters). Battles will shift from a Move Phase, self-explanatory, to an Action Phase where allies can perform actions such as attacking, buffing, or healing. There is quite a variety of actions you can perform, and more often than not you can combine two or more to execute a more advanced attack, Arts to be exact. There are a lot of these Arts, but honestly players will find themselves selecting a handful of them to use in the long-term. You can also use Special Arts when able to, and
to form Extra Arts, they’re real flashy, and feel very satisfying to pull off.
Now, my grievances with the system. There are 3 main issues with it that prevent the game from being enjoyed to its fullest potential. Sluggish pacing, exploits, and completely unfair instances. In the few times were grinding is necessary, even minimal grinding makes for such an egregious experience, as the combat itself is generally slow even when skipping attack animations on top of raising the frame cap via the ini file. Also, Running around in copy-and-paste dungeons waiting for an encounter evidently becomes tedious. Post-battle rewards such as EXP wither if you lurk in dungeons or the world map for too long because “balance”. The reward drop is justified as it does prevent extensive grinding or boosting, but there are other exploits in this game that make the pain of the learning curve omitted entirely. Even then, exploits will sometimes not help you during the occasional ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Bosses with the range of a sniper, multi-target burst attacks that nuke your team entirely, the whole nine yards, it’s a load of crap sometimes. It is around late game where Agarest starts to shine since these problems practically fade away since you are likely to have superior equipment and an improved understanding of the game. Also given the advent of a more interesting plot as the game progresses, Agarest’s core gameplay is one that is unrefined in its fundamentals but overall rewarding and thus entertaining.
There is another section of Agarest that should not go without mention as this is what established the product’s awkward reputation in the Americas, and that is the marriage aspect of the game. During your quest to defeat Summerill and the denizens of darkness, you are also in your efforts to earn the love of one of three heroines of the respective generation. Since this is a game chronicling the events across five generations, I would expect this, therefore I’m A-OK with it. How else would you acquire the protagonist for the next generation? It’s only fair. This is done for the first 4 generations of the game, and the stats and weapon the next Hero wields is determined by your choice and your bride’s affection. How will you get your waifu to love you, you may ask? There are certain events in which the MC interacts with the heroines and the player is often prompted to make a choice to advance. This choice will either increase or decrease said heroine’s affection. Some of the situations the MC can get dragged into are pretty funny too. Any more explanation about this is basically spoiler, so you better use your wits (or a guide, preferably) to charm your way into a heroine’s heart!
In-game events like these can also revolve around characters that aren’t love interests. These scenarios can vary from friendly mischief or more serious discussions having to do with their own personal matters or the war, and both of these can serve as a segue into learning more about a character’s personality. They’re somewhat tasteless to a fault, and some are absolutely superfluous fan service that break any remote sense of pacing, but it just has its own allure I find difficulty turning away from as it adds another dimension to the narrative, for better or worse.
Agarest: Generations of War is an oddball for me. It’s flawed to a point where I can’t recommend it with sufficient confidence, yet I love this game. It’s a collection of many tropes seen before, there’s no good waifus, and the first hundred hours sucked (no hyperbole). I also doubt more than a few people find the investment of up to 250 hours just to finish the damn game agreeable. But SOMEwhere, it clicked, and that’s what it really boils down to. It’s just a solid game, if not just a measly mediocre one like critics suggest. Though, I am confident in the fact there are games that people feel connected to, with the quality or lack thereof notwithstanding.

And we’re back with another thrilling review (I wish). Agarest: Generations of War is a turn-based, tactical JRPG from Idea Factory. With a bit of polishing, this game could have been very fun, but, such as it is, it was rather lackluster.
The Good
When I first started playing A:GoW I was thinking “Hey, this might be a good one.” Sadly this was not the case. That being said, there was one particular aspect of the game that I enjoyed. In battle, once you had sufficiently weakened an attacking monster, you could use spells to capture it and win it over to your side. From that point forward, you could include it in your party and use it to do battle with your enemies. Now, this is probably just the Pokemon fan in me still (Cthulhu bless those wonderful Gameboy games), but I LOVE when games have a feature like this.
Additionally, once you had captured at least two monsters, you could take them to the “Monster Guild” and combine them. This had the possibility of giving you a new monster.
The Bad
This wasn’t my first experience with a JRPG, so I knew to not expect the best translated dialogue that the world had to offer. Some of it though, was just laughably bad. Multiple scenes sounded like a pretentious play written, directed, and starred in by a high school drama club. Honestly.
Waiting for your party to appear on the battlefield also became incredibly tedious after your first few battles. Once you have six party members and you have to wait a good ten seconds for everyone to appear every battle (and there are many, many battles) you start to think of what else you could be playing right now. (For example, I found myself switching to Skyrim).
Apart from this, menus were clunky, somethings during combat would work sometimes, but then not work later, and the list goes on.
The Meh
This is another game where the art (specifically the character sprites) got me interested. Ogre Battle 64 is one of my all time favorite games and, if you’re familiar with the Ogre Battle series, the sprites are very much akin to the sprites in A:GoW. Sadly, that’s about where my interest stopped. Additional in game art was either dated 3D rendering or came straight from an anime dating sim.
Verdict: Nay

Short Answer: Boring with little real tactical strategy elements.
At first, I was really excited to play this, and during the first generation (the game's story is seperated into generations, with the main character leaving and his kid becoming a playable character every generation). I tend to enjoy grid-based, turn-based strategy games, but this one is just boring. Every battle is fought on map with no terrain. No bushes to give your guys better defence, no walls for you to limit enemy movement with, just and open field. There is a bit of positioning strategy with link squares (if you put your guys in certain squares depending on wheere your other guys are, they can attack together) so there is is some amount of thinking, you don't just run at the bad guys and stab them. Every battle, in addition to having a boring map takes about 5 minutes or so and is pretty easy. The game very well might get harder as you progress but I quit after starting the second generation because it isn't really a strategy game. The standard version gives you a bunch of stuff as free dlc. These weapons are really good in both the first and second generations but every character you doesn't use one of these weapons deals very little damage, making several of the characters you use useless because they don't have the op weapons. Shops also seem pretty useless as every signle shop, as far as I've seen, is exactly the same, progressing through the story doesn't let you buy more powerful weapons.
All in all, this game is a dating sim disguised as a tactical rpg. You can pick your own waifu every generation and then pick one for the kid in the next generation. The gameplay is very boring and not really worth time investing into, especially for 17 bucks (current price).

While Mighty No. 9 deserves all the criticism it gets for its mediocrity, I'm still kinda reluctant to give the game a negative review. Consider this slightly more neutral point of view than the usual you can expect. Hear me out...
I bought this game dirt cheap and my expectations where as low as Ubisoft's reputation. I got it out of a strange curiosity and a desperate need for a platformer, but not necessarily a good one - one that could be used as a contrast to compare with other better games from the genre. In short, I did it
I expected nothing, yet I got a game that, while being hindered in every possible aspect at every step, still got many of the basics right. There are some genuinely accurate tweaks here and there that make a basic running, jumping and dashing bearable enough to cloud my criticism, at least for a little bit. I'm impressed by this, because Mighty No. 9 constantly wants to give you a crappy part just when you got your miniscule bit of fun.
Level design is 1/3rds boring and other 1/3rds frustrating, relying on cheap enemy placement, one-hit kill obstacles and general
parts. Central dashing mechanic can often put you on disadvantage. Weapon selection system is a mess. Presentation is beyond laughable, including: awful writing with annoying characters, voice-acting that was directed by a chimpanzee, 3D Models and assets with embarrassing polygon count and fidelity. Animations as smooth as road through the Amazon rainforest. Music so quiet, it can barely show off any good that it has. Also that mistake that is a final boss of this game...
And yet, I kinda consider this game my guilty pleasure. There is some semblance of the decent game here, especially for hardcore platforming fans. Sometimes the game can be challenging in the good way, which caught me by surprise. Right now, I'm in a situation where I probably could recommend Mighty No. 9 to people like me: curious fans of the genre that are interested in experiencing the dictionary definition of
, while getting at least some enjoyment from the occasional good fragment of the level and enemy placement.. If you are that person, and you see Mighty No. 9 really cheap? Go for it! Succumb to your curiosity! Because in the end... it's just a Megaman game - it's really hard to screw it up all the way through.
Everybody else? Avoid like a plague.

It kind of feels like for every one thing Mighty No. 9 gets right, something else pops up to undo it. Mighty No. 9, in my opinion, is actually rather charming in its own right, with quirky boss characters and a story that isn't half-bad for the genre. There are gameplay innovations that the game presents that feel full of potential. And yet somehow, that good will felt squandered at nearly every turn, leaving me with a platformer that sits resolutely in the "mediocre" category.
Mighty No. 9 started off well enough and showed some nice flourishes. For instance, the main stage bosses (aka Mighty Numbers) are more than just static "boss room" personalities. A boss will often try to impede your progress through the stage, but after being rescued will often pop up in another stage as assistance. They're kind of quirky as well: I found Avi's news reporter act, for instance, to be hilarious and endearing. One might find a few annoyances here and there (*cough* Sanda *cough*) but I liked most of them, and I wish these personalities could've been a little more prevalent throughout. Then gameplay wise, you've got the fairly snappy dash mechanic for takedowns, and the form changes that replace (conceptually) simple weapon swaps a la MegaMan. The game felt new, fresh and--most importantly--enjoyable for a period of time.
But the deeper I got... ugh. Just, ugh.
Once you have like two or three form changes available, switching forms is a hassle. Its not like MegaMan where you simply swap left/right to equip something. No, in this game you have to press the swap button to open the forms dropdown, press the swap button again to cycle through the forms, then press an entirely different button to activate the form. During all this, the game doesn't stop around you until you actually go to execute the form swap. On top of that, you can't even form swap from the pause menu. Uh... really? For a platformer involving speed and finesse, this is a major annoyance. Yes,  you can bind up to three quick-swaps, but this doesn't fix the general accessibility issue. It greatly hampered my desire to be experimental with the forms: I barely touched all but one of them outside of my normal form.
The dash mechanic, though it sounds good on paper, is also counter-intuitive. Dashing and attacking are essentially two separate mechanics, and having to ping-pong between the two just doesn't feel all that satisfying. Consider this: if I'm on a ladder and "destablize" an enemy to the side, I have to jump off the ladder, dash into the enemy to kill it, and dash back to the ladder. Again, it sounds like a minor irritation, but these kind of funky situations crop up all over the place and it gets OLD. Downing foes can often feel meticulous instead of fluid.
It all just keeps adding up. The dash also has a slight amount of end-lag attached to it. Level design and enemy placement can be hit or miss. Insta-death traps feel a bit overused at times (screw the Mines level. Screw. It.) I will shamelessly admit to turning the "remaining lives" option up to 9 in the options. Putting up with some of this stuff once was enough.
But you know what REALLY "grinds my gears?" This game easily has some of the WORST boss fights I've EVER played in the genre. That's strong wording I rarely throw around, but I mean it. The fights are often paced TERRIBLY, with drawn-out seqeuences that are exceptionally sluggish and/or predictable. The game seems to be very specific about when you're "allowed" to attack which, when combined with the methodical pace, makes for yawn-worthy encounters. The dash mechanic futher disincentivizes creativity because, should you get cheeky and destablize a boss at the "wrong" time, there is a good chance you won't be able to reach him and he'll just recover the health back. Battles in this game are often far too telegraphed, tedious and SLOOOOOOOOW. And it all reaches a climax with that filthy abomination of a final boss.
Yes, I detest the final boss THAT much that I'm giving it a special mention. As far as this genre goes, that massive pile of garbage is easily the worst final boss that comes to mind. X(
Sigh...
I've struggled to post this review because its probably one of the most vitriol-infused reviews I've ever posted (by my standards, at least!) Mighty No. 9 has evoked such passionate gamer rage from me in a way most games never do, and clearly not in the "just one more time" kind of way. As a passionate platformer fan who holds the genre near and dear, this game pushed so many of my buttons. For as much promise and personality the Mighty No. 9 universe showed, the act of playing through it fell incredibly short.

Although visually and audibly an enjoyable game to play, Last Day of June has a few issues that caused me to not be able to recommend it overall. The first has to do with the story itself. The story portrays a tragic car accident very early on in the game (which can be seen in the trailer that was released,) and involves the protagonist survivor Carl going back in time to try to prevent June from dying. During the game, glimpses of their past is shown that reveal how their relationship was in the years prior to the accident. Memories of several of the other characters can also be collected as an optional part of gameplay that give additional background on them as well as for Carl and June. The problem is the lack of most of this background before the accident occurs, apart from a short flashback that briefly introduces the characters and explains why Carl and June decided to go to the dock. The player knows almost nothing about these characters when June dies, and it's difficult (in my opinion, though some may disagree) to have an emotional response about her death. Later on in the game, after discovering how their relationship had been before she passed, it's much easier to sympathize with Carl's loss. However, in my opinion, this occurs too late. Had the player been able to either see sequences of them interacting in the past in the prologue of the game, or better yet to actually play through scenes that highlight the love that they had for each other, the car accident would have been far more impactful, and the urgency of trying to save her would make the story much more enjoyable to experience. As it stands, however, the story felt a bit mediocre.
The second was game design decisions that can cause the game to feel a bit irritating. The biggest offender was the lack of a method to skip cutscenes. While most of the cutscenes were integral to the story, some of them are inevitably shown multiple times as the player figures out how to progress. This is essentially the same as an extended loading screen, and can be very frustrating to wait for. Another design flaw comes from the memory collection system. This optional part of the game was a plus, as it promoted exploration of the village as well as revealing background information for the involved characters. The issue was that although backtracking was enabled in the first three chapters, it is suddenly removed without warning once the story proceeds to the fourth chapter. This causes any player that missed one of the memories for the kid, best friend, or hunter to have to wipe their save and start the game all over in order to be able to collect them. This could have been prevented by either separating the sections for the memories of the old man from the others, or by giving a warning when the player has found the correct solution for all characters in chapter 3 that they won't be able to go back if they continue on with that choice. Another decision that the designers made was to limit the sections that the game would be saved. While the game can certainly be completed in a few short sessions, players that are forced to replay large sections of the game because they had to turn it off just before reaching a checkpoint can find the game a bit annoying. Finally, the lack of multiple save files to choose from means that players have to wipe their main save every time they want to show a friend how the game looks or to let them play it from the beginning.
Some may argue that the linearity of the game is another problem that this game suffers from. I disagree, however, as although it is certainly linear, it is not very noticeable unless one plays through the game a second time to collect any missed achievements/trophies, and honestly is fairly typical of games that put a much higher focus on storytelling than on gameplay. Additionally, some may say that the length of the game is far too short since it can be completed in just a few hours. Although I do wish it were a bit longer in the case of this story, I have played other games that did not take very long to finish either and enjoyed them quite a bit, so having a short completion time is not necessarily a problem in and of itself. Finally, some may complain about the artistic style that was used to create the character models. This shouldn't be a major concern, however, because the trailer and screenshots for the game clearly show this design and does not come as a surprise to anyone that decides to get the game. Furthermore, they make sense in light of the game being based off of Steven Wilson's song Drive Home, whose music video on YouTube shows a character that looks very similar to Carl.
This last part is not specifically a spoiler and is kept somewhat vague intentionally, but is placed inside spoiler tags in case it is viewed as such. It is intended to be better understood by those that have already completed the game, and expands a little more on the first paragraph above.
In conclusion, I do wish I could rate this as a recommended game, as it is very well done in regards to the beauty of the environment, and the music is enjoyable to listen to as well. Unfortunately, though, the problems presented in the first 2 paragraphs above are enough of a concern to cause me to not have much desire to share it with friends, and should be kept in mind in contrast to those that reviewed the game positively here when considering whether to acquire this game or not.

Just finished this astoundingly gorgeous game....but no replay chapter option or save slots is to me a huge dissapointment.

If you've spent a half hour wandering around or trying different options in gameplay, but need to quit out, it brings you back to the last checkpoint area,which in some instances is WAY back in the game. Replaying huge swaths of gameplay,even a game as enjoyable as this one, is not a pleasant thing if you're an adult and need to attend to non-gaming matters thus necessitating the need to quit out of a game.
I can't for the life of me understand why developers nowadays, especially devs of a game as complex in choices as this one, wouldn't either create more save points, an F5 (quicksave) option, or, like many games: multiple save-at-will points.
And now that I've finally gotten through this (otherwise wonderful) game, my only option is to replay the ENTIRE game from the beginning (restart)? That seems quite unfair.
To be truthful, as mentioned it is a BEAUTIFUL game, with a rich storyline, a rich soundtrack and unique graphics. But because of the complete lack of saving at will, the option to replay from the beginning doesn't entice me.
NOTE: if the almost complete lack of savepoints and/or the only end-game option being restarting from scratch the entire game doesn't bother you fellow gamers....then you're in for a treat with the game as it's beautiful and the story will leave you emotionally spent. SO: "frequent savers" beware!

Depths of Dread, is a single player dungeon crawler, with turn based battles and random encounters.
You choose your class from a choice of 12 (a heathy balance of spell casters, support, melee tanks and hybrid classes.) You can recruit up to a party of 5 (building a party completely of your choosing), using gold acquired from killing monsters in a 15 floor dungeon.
Below is a brief game review, and the pros and cons of why it may, or may not appeal to you.
Story:
There isn’t one, typical dungeon crawler.
Here are the keys to my dungeon, level up, kill monsters, save the day.
Graphics:
Minimal. Copy and paste images with no imagination, the graphics closely resemble the story.
The scenery and backgrounds are not interesting, no atmosphere, and nothing to get excited about here.
Sound: I didn’t have any problem with the sound, or music. No doubt it will get repetitive and grind on you after a while, but you can say the same for any game with minimal variation of tunes.
Gameplay: It does the job, half the job. It has almost everything I would want from building a party. If you enjoy the grind, party building and the occasional challenging encounter then this would have been so close to what you were looking for. But the game constantly stutters on the random encounter screens and takes too long to load for just the reshuffle of the same screens.
Longevity: It’s hard to say a life span isn’t there.
There are plenty of class combinations to try out, a lot of different gear and socketing combos to try, and of course each dungeon room changes every time you enter / re-enter it. But will you still be playing this after 20 hours of gameplay, probably not. I’d be surprised if many players amounted to over 10 hours of play.
Pros
- Create your own party.
- Can change class of any character to fit circumstance at no cost.
- Socketing, adding reusable gems to gear is great
- Lots of equipment, common, epic and even legendary, spot on here.
- 12 different classes, lots of combo's to play with
- The dungeon is constantly changing, not the layout but with different traps or treasures or merchants will appear or disappear, every time you enter/ leave a room.
- Simple to navigate, I found the party / equipment screens very easy to use.
- Bulletin board is a nice touch, quests for rewards.
- Honest game tittle
- Classes familiar to the genre
- If you can persevere, the battles become really fun, much later in the game
Cons
- Loading between screens, that inevitably just all look the same only reshuffled, takes the flow out of the game, and is something that should be seamless. As it stands, you spend more time waiting between screens loading than you do on the dungeon screens themselves.
- It’s a dungeon crawler, so you spend a lot of time in a dungeon with random encounters. Sadly this is ruined by constantly skipping, which again takes any real flow out of the game and frustratingly hinders progression.
- Plenty of glitches and bugs.
- Repetitive battles for the first 1/8 floors.
- May have benefitted from a talent system for your party members, just something to feel like you have some kind of input into their growth as they level.
- The dungeon levels changing every time you change screen, some may consider it to be a pro, but not for me. Enter/exit room, until treasure shows, not a productive use of time. For me, open a treasure once, then the box should be empty, unless you reset the instance or something or exit the dungeon entirely perhaps. (This particular con would be a matter of opinion, I feel)
- The sprites don’t move, the copied images just float about, bobbing up and down.
- No map / no minimap
- Bulletin board, quest objections often don’t work first time
- Very few boss battles.
Summery
You can’t help but feel slightly wronged or ripped off by this game. On paper it truly ticks a lot of boxes, 12 classes, plenty of gear and gem customisation, managing your gold to fill that last party slot and a changing dungeon. But a little extra care would have gone a long, long way.
One little patch to make the player feel like they can play through the dungeon without the game constantly stuttering, would make the world of difference. As it stands, I can’t recommend this game, sorry. There is so much potential here, but it’s completely squandered by things that could be so easily remedied. If they update it quickly, fix a few simple things then it has the potential to become an enjoyable game, and maybe a recommendation.
My final verdict is that here is another game added to the steam vault that lacks soul and any credibility or creativity, and once again seems completely rushed at the prospect of a quick sell. It’s quite simply not worth you're time.
If you’re looking for a new dungeon crawler, look away, look far away, for now. If they update the game I will be sure to update my review, and if it runs seemlessly then it could change my opinion.
Currenlty it seems that half a job was done, and perhaps they never tested the game. I cant recommened something that at present feels rushed over the finish line, tarnishing the end product and making it unworthy of being sellable goods. Not acceptable.

I know this review might not be the most useful due to my play time only being an hour, but that's all I gave it to see if I could like the game enough to continue. Unfortunately, it was not. Side note: I was able to light up 3 parts of the pentagon in The Void.
Let me get straight to the points:
-This game is excellent for people who are interested in Norse mythology.
-The visuals look great. It's always good to see a hand-drawn game. Some things reminded me of Rayman Origins.
-There is too much unnecessary running around. It's unnecessary because there's literally nothing to do in the world. There are no items or collectibles, aside from Golden Apples which lengthen your health bar. There is no interaction whatsoever with the world.
-This game lacks depth. As I said, no items. There are no levels. The only progress you'll get are the powers you acquire and the knowledge of Norse mythology. There are only 4 actions: attack, heavy attack, dodge, power. Nothing else. Attack and heavy attack have the same animations every time.
In conclusion:
-This game is good for people who are interested in the subject matter.
-The game looks absolutely great.
-The game is bad because of the gameplay itself.
-This game could have been a lot better.

I had a mixed experience with Jotun.  There was a lot that I think they did really well, so I'll start with that.  I usually don't get sucked into the story, but this game was full of interesting lore.  The world was beautiful and immersive, and every segment of the story felt unique.  I loved that the narration was done in Icelandic.  Each area had a different mechanic that the player had to learn, and they did an amazing job of introducing it organically so that I never felt like I was in a tutorial.  The experience was well thought out, and I enjoyed it overall.
My major complaints had to do with the combat.  Considering the fact that your Axe is the only tool you have to interact with the world, there were very few enemies in the game.  Each area either had no enemies or a ton of the same unit.  Fighting didn't seem necessary most of the game, and I found killing enemies to be tedious and uninteresting.
Throughout the game, the player unlocks several abilities, but none of them seem to be useful except in boss fights.  Even then, it was almost more trouble to use them than to just fight with the axe.  For example, I never used the speed boost or the arrow.  You only get to use each ability 2-3 times each checkpoint anyway.  It might've been better if they were on a cooldown.

Although early access, EHM:EA is a very polished management simulation. If you enjoy hockey, or any sports gm games, you owe it yourself to pick this game up.
From Version 15.0.1b (first early access version) here are some of my findings on the game:
Pro's:
- Has nearly all the features from the EHM 2007, meaning it already is the deepest hockey sim available.
- Nice new touches like players bio information talking about players close friends on the team.
- Nice tactical improvements like individual strategies for players
-Tactical improvements for lines including choosing who would be the playmaker on the line.
- Free Agency is much more realistic. Don't expect to always build your teams on July 1st, UFA's want money and term just ilke in real life.
-Position's of players are more in-depth, including their roles like defensive defenseman, stay-at-home defensemen, 2-way forward, skilled forward, quick forward. This adds to the fun of building cohesive forward units.
-Tons of international tournaments, take control of your favorite national team and try to build a team to bring glory to your country.
-The in game match view has been improved and is very enjoyable watching your team battle it out.
Con's:
- Interface and menus are very similar to EHM 2007 so it is missing some more modern interface options.
- Resolution needs to be improved for modern pc's
- Scoring has to be balanced a bit more to 2015 scoring levels (its a bit too high at least in NHL games).
- Missing leagues like the Swiss leagues, Russian MHL, and British Hockey leagues from 2007 version.
- Coaches and GMs get fired a little more than in the real world.
There are a few issues like the small window the game runs in and the interface definitely needs some modern touches, but the rest of the cons are minor. The positives far outweigh the negatives with this release. Please do yourself a favor and buy this game if you enjoy the sport of hockey and have ever wanted to build your dream team or test your management skill in the lower leagues and build a legendary story as you climb the ranks to finally leading your national team to world glory.

Foreword, Megaman X8 is one of my favorite games of all time. So I'm biased.
I would recommend this game to fans of Megaman and fans of the genre, or anyone that likes a fast-paced challenge but still has the patience to power through the creator's design flaws.
(If you got it on sale).
Here's what the game does right:
+Classic Megaman stage selection and ability-copying! This was all I wanted out of this game, and they did it right, so it was enough to earn my recommendation.
+Classic Megaman jump-n-gun playstyle and platforming elements!
+New dash-combat mechanic! This was very fresh. The player, Beck, has the unique ability to absorb enemies that he disables in normal combat, removing them much faster. This was all really fun!
+Point system and combos! Typically, this sort of thing would have absolutely no appeal to me. It adds nothing to the actual gameplay, however it does make big moments feel much more satisfying.
Here's what the game did wrong:
-Performance.
This needs to be my issue #1, because while I did enjoy the game, I had to play it on my gaming rig when I wanted to play it on my laptop, which isn't even particularly low-spec. It lagged furiously throughout the settings screen while I was changing everything to minimum, even distorting the resolution couldn't make the game anywhere near playable from my laptop. Once I had it installed on my rig, I set a timer to clock the rest of the 2 hours I had remaining. I was VERY VERY READY to refund.
-The art.
No where near remotely close to where it should have been, considering the budget. Colorful enough, sure, but features look as deep as a cheap sticker and some of the models are just plain stupid. Stupid enough to jarringly disturb the fun you've had to fight for.
-Readability.
Enemy and ally projectiles alike are constantly overlapping with regular textures and aesthetic effects. Tends to make combat more difficult at times than it needs to be, but not super often throughout the game.

-The Difficulty.
"Difficulty" being a friendly way to put "Lots and lots of cheap deaths." Ledge snaps fail often. During platforming-only areas, hazards have have a tendency to grow invisble hitboxes, resulting in cheap deaths and excessive swearing. Combat and Bosses were 50/50 for appropriately telegraphed attack patterns / no visible way to overcome this phase 2. It typically did a good job, though, of letting you know when phases were changed.
-The Voice Acting.
This is at best a personal grudge, perhaps. The dialogue scripts left a lot A LOT to be desired, and the execution of few, rare lines are so, so, so very poor. "Oh, I guess this murder machine is a 9-year old pretending to be batman." This qualm is low on the list, though, because occassionally they got it right enough to make me smile.

-The Music
So forgettable I almost forgot to mention it was forgettable.

Some of the level designs feel unfinished and I  wish you were able to wall jump like in MMX.  Although, the way a majority of MM fanboys were condemning this game an abortion is quite ignorant.  I am enjoying my time with this platformer.  It's challenging, has similarities to MM, and has a couple new additions that I find interesting such as the point system and absorbing enemies for combos etc etc...
All in all, I bought this game on sale for 66% off.  I definitely recommend it for anyone who is into platformers or want something similar to MM.  Again, while it may not be the Blue Bomber, it's still doing a good enough job in satisfying my thirst for some platformer gaming.

I really enjoyed it! Not as much as Brothers, but I can justify its length and price tag from where I live. Game looks nice and unique, reminiscent of an oil canvas painting, and I'm willing to forgive it for its inconsistent DOF, dropping framerates and blocky shadows. Music is appropriately subtle and not having intelligible dialogue does great for the visual storytelling. It's still pretty fun to wander around and interact with things just as it was with Brothers, though you do run out of stuff to explore as the story takes place in roughly the same few areas with but a few differences.
The groundhog day scenario did start to bother me as a large part of the middle section involves doing some things several times over and not being able to skip cutscenes. The game also breaks a few rules of cause and effect in favor of the story, but I'm willing to overlook that despite having played some other games with much better understanding of time travel. Despite the game's pacing issues, the story it sets out to tell is worth seeing through to the end and wraps up perfectly for what it's going for.
I can't say I've never seen stories like this before, but I think Last Day of June has more than enough clever ideas in gameplay and mute storytelling to warrant its existence as a short but decent time travel game. I liked it. 3.5 hours well spent.

Visually the game has undergone a bit of a facelift. It's not a complete overhaul, but a nice improvement and will be familiar to anybody who has played the EHM 2007. This has made the UI more spacious but it would be nice to see support for wider/higher resolutions in the future.

I've been waiting for this for eight years, as many of you have. I've racked up hundreds of hours getting teams of young guns to reach the mightiest of prizes, the Great Lord Stanley's Grail. And worse still, the studio responsible for my favorite sub-series of the franchise, the Zero games on GBA/DS, are somehow the same people who made THIS garbage? Factorio is a game about process design and realization.  If you don't want to read any other words, I recommend doing this test:  "Did you like to think more about the cities you made in Sim City 4 than actually building them?"  If so, Factorio is the game you've been dreaming of!  If you also like building things and see your ideas come to life, Factorio is a game you'll probably enjoy.
This is not a game that will hold your hand or always provide a path to victory.  This game wants you to think about it's problems and plan ahead, and will punish you spectacularily if you can't do that.  At the same time, it gives you enough tools and freedom to fix your mistakes and learn from them!  It's a wonderful experience with strong themes of adaptation, learning, and optimization!
The game itself is polished to a mirror shine and delivers on it's idea brilliantly.  The offspring of Zachtronics and Maxis circa 1994 is here!  It's awesome, and it's name is Factorio!

After 18 hours I unfortunately have to thumbs down this game.  While there is a lot of potential here, this game really boils down to a tedious repetitive task, merely picking what cargo contracts to select for every ship.  It is fun at first because you think that eventually you'll move to something more involved, and there are other things that need to be decided on in the game, but ultimately you're going through this exact repetition endlessly:  Open Contracts window, select cargo for a ship in port, select destination, refuel, close contract window, repeat.  While some of the other factors in the game, buying ships, buying subsidiaries, specialized ships for specialized cargo, add some flavor to this, the main game interaction isn't fun for long.  This is compounded by poor design (no hotkey for the contracts window for instance - literally have to open it every few seconds and there is no hotkey), and some bugs (often the contracts window gets glitched and doesn't load the current ship in port for instance, sometimes the ship list doesn't show which ships are stopped in port). On top of this most of the environment seems to be random rather than backed by sophisticated modelling (contract generation, ship wear and tear, etc) so it feels cheap with little player impact.  I almost think this game was designed to be a tablet game.
