If you don't care about the Kickstarter drama and just want to know if the game is fun, this review is for you.
Mighty No.9 is a solid 8/10 platform game. It has it's kinks, but is overall fun to play once you figure things out. The game is somewhat of a cross between classic megaman gameplay and the ZX Advent games that were released for Nintendo DS later. It pays homage to classic megaman in that there is no walljump and the characters look/feel like classic megaman anime characters. ( Protip: Turn on Japanese audio! ). It's similar to ZX advent in that Beck doesn't just gain new weapons from beating bosses, but absorbs their form. This is a nice decision as many of the forms have more to them than just a simple energy buster replacement, such as changes to dash or the ability to helicopter into the air. One form even lets you play as a makeshift "Zero" with a sword and various blade abilities. Graphics wise, it's a Playstation 2 game in HD -comparable to Megaman X8.
The biggest upside to Mighty No.9 is the gameplay. They didn't just straight copy megaman but tried to add an additional spin by letting you dash through enemies to destroy them, gaining buffs as you do so. You can also simply shot enemies until they die ( A few extra hits after you stun them with make them explode ) if you want. Absorbing multiple enemies in a row ramps up combos for higher score. Dashing feels fun and fluid and is the prime enjoyment factor to the game. Getting combos is fun. Rushing through stages is satisfying. Controls are smooth and the multiple forms add plenty of variety. The core of Megaman is in the game where it counts. Oh, and it's actually just as difficult too. Expect NES difficulty levels if you want to try hardmode.
Unfortunately, there are a few problems. For one, the level design isn't always top polish. Most of the levels are enjoyable, but a few made me raise an eyebrow at times. Luckily the solid gameplay somewhat alleviates the times were silly/repetitive level design becomes annoying, and again most of the game is fine. Another problem is that a lot of the extra features feel unnecessary. They should have focused more on the main game than these silly EX modes, and that may be where the biggest problem of Mighty no9 lies: Comcept overreached. They tried to cram too many different ideas and Easter eggs into the game all under an everchanging budget and regularly chaotic schedule. The result is that the game just isn't as high of quality as it could be. Mighty no9 is a solid above average game, but it certainly had the potential to be as good as it was promised to be. And that's the big downer with this game. It's enjoyable, but you can't help but see the wasted potential in many different aspects.
Overall, this is a decent game. Maybe a bit overpriced but still good. It's unfortunate that the unrealistic expectations and drama caused by the Kickstarter mess and multiple delays resulted in this game feeling overhyped. Many of the poor reviews are likely due to people overjudging Mighty no9 based on the problems faced in development. People were led to expect a masterpiece, and instead Comcept delivered a game that while good...just isn't a masterpiece. If you buy Mighty no.9 knowing what to expect, it's good fun. Had it only been slightly better and with less developer delays, we would be seeing many sequels.

SHENZHEN I/O is a game that will make you a better engineer. If this appeals to you, read further.
Unlike SpaceChem and Infinifactory, which focus on spatial reasoning, SHENZHEN (and its predecessor, TIS-100) dive into coding in assembly. What this loses in presentation, it makes up for in depth: the puzzles generally have more compact solutions, requiring more planning, and almost always require a divide-and-conquer approach to succeed.
If this is not your thing, stick to other Zachtronics titles or other puzzle games. If this _is_ your thing and you have yet to play TIS-100, play that first. Puzzles in SHENZHEN will build on the principles of sorting, searching, and solving that you'll learn there.
TIS-100 can thus be considered the 100 level course to SHENZHEN's 200 and 300 level courses. Since many of the puzzles in both games are inspired by real algorithms and computer architecture principles, you'll learn a thing or two about how professional software engineering works, too.
The biggest improvement over TIS-100 is story and scope. The story is _fantastic_, easily exceeding the writing quality of SpaceChem and Infinifactory (and providing depth and heart that would be too spoilery to describe). The language and modules give you far more freedom than any other Zachtronics title to date, even allowing you to design your own (TI Calculator-like) games within the game. Seriously, check the forums, those games are amazing.
The primary drawback to SHENZHEN I/O is its difficulty and its reliance on the manual (by design). SHENZHEN is unashamedly not a casual puzzle game -- it is a game that requires investment, paying that investment back in triplicate.
If you're a puzzle game affectionado or a programmer looking to expand the limits of what you thought yourself capable of, pick this up. If you made it through TIS-100 and hunger for more, pick this up. Otherwise, sincerely do not buy this unless you are prepared for the challenge.

There are a few different obstacles in the game - most of them just damage or instant kill you, but some of them make the car harder to control. The car is also immune to all other obstacles that break your tires which leads to some interesting choices - should you take a hit to have worse controls but have more room to drive or should you try to avoid everything? This is a neat idea, but the game doesn't use it much and there are only 15 levels in the game.
The controls are decent enough but there's a major flaw with them. Once you hit an obstacle that breaks your tires running into an obstacle makes the car go in a different direction for a few seconds. This game puts you in charge of a bacteria, virus, worm, neural worm or other biological contaminant with only one goal in mind: Infect and kill everyone on the planet.
You control the progress of your infection by evolving it's various abilities ranging from higher resistance, infectiousnous and lethality using points you collect by progressing your disease.
Of course the pesky humans won't enjoy being mass murdered by your disease so will put up a good fight by trying to develop a cure before you manage to kill the entire planet.
In general terms plague inc is a basic strategy game where you spend most of the time looking at a world map watching your plague slowly spread while you click on bubbles or kill people through your plague in order to collect points. The collected points can be invested in evolving your plague. Each plague has a different set of abilities that can be evolved and additional global abilities can be unlocked that can be used to enhance your plague in another round. Since all plagues have different abilities that can be evolved each plague requires a little bit of a different approach to eventually kill the planet making for a fun casual strategy game with a decent amount of replayability.
Plague inc is however very much a casual game with one round lasting as long as your disease isn't cured or until you kill everyone on the planet. Match that with a fitting but somewhat plain UI and you will likely end up playing a few rounds of this every now and then rather than sitting down and playing it hours on end.

Factorio is one of those rare games that has a good balance of the difficulty throughout the entire game. It is as complicated as you want it to be, and the more complicated it is, it's more efficient and compact. It is as fun as it is time consuming.
Game 9/10
Let's start with the negatives first.
Graphics.
The graphics in this game look very old and yet they somehow require more VRAM than most FPS games I play. Evidently, the team doesn't have a graphics designer. Now I did not grow up in the 90s, and perhaps if I did I would like it more.
Graphics 4/10
Combat.
It is obvious that this game was not made for fighting, and that's ok. It's just not that kind of game.The combat in this game mostly features running/driving and shooting. Combat, however, will end up being needed, as there are many alien colonies that are either blocking resources or attack you due to pollution, which is spread by mining and stuff like that. It is annoying, but it forces you to research military.
Combat 6/10
Mechanics.
This is what makes the game good. Since there are many mechanics, I will go by them one by one.
Mechanics 10/10
Mechanics - Research.
To acquire certain technology, you must research it. The tech tree is very expansive, and in order to research, there are, as of now, 8 science packs, 7 of which are valid. You must automate all of these to actually get anywhere.
Research 7/10
Mechanics - Automation.
Automation is what most of this game is about. You can automate EVERYTHING (besides destroying aliens). The machines that you use are very well coded because they will only take what they need.
Automation 10/10
Mechanics - Logistics Robots.
Logistics robots are very helpful, because they can repair things and you can request them to give you items.
Logistics Robots 8/10
Resources.
This in my opinion is one of the games problems. I feel like they should add more resources to the game. As it stands, they have
Coal, copper, iron, stone, trees, oil, and uranium.
I just feel like they should add more to it, like maybe resources that are only on the alien planet.
Over all, this is one of the best games I have ever played, and I would recommend it to developers in particular, because it involves many problems that are found in coding, such as... uh... getting stranded on an alien planet and stuff. Yeah.

I was a huge fan of the Mega Man/Mega Man X/Mega Man Legends games and unfortunately I have to say I'm not a fan of Mighty No. 9.
Above all, my #1 complaint is the "dash-to-destroy" mechanic. It makes no sense. The dash is practically required to destroy an enemy, but does no actual damage. Supposedly there is some kind of upgrade or enhancement gained when absorbing an enemy, but this is completely unexplained in the game.
Second to that is the combination of level design and enemy design. Both are horrible. The levels feel short and shallow, and enemies blend right into the backgrounds making them far too easy to miss.
My third big issue is the feeling of missing elements. This game is screaming for wall grab, wall jump, charged shots and hidden upgrades. I could understand these elements missing as not all were present in all the Mega Man games, but this game feels like it's just plain missing something without them.

A Simplified Giana Sisters: Great for Newcomers, Little Challenge for Veterans
I was extremely happy to this game added to Steam since I have never been able to get my hands on a DS copy (Someday my pretty). So much so that I sent a copy to my sister. We both played the original Giana Sisters on Commodore 64 back in the day. It was essentially our Mario.
That is probably one of the flaws I find with the game: It's very easy for seasoned players. I think it is mainly because the power-ups have been scaled back from the original and boss enemies have been removed, at least from the 'Retro' levels. I don't know how far I have to go to find a boss in the newer levels, but thus far, there are none and I haven't gotten a game over yet on these newer levels.
That is not to say I don't recommend it. Far from. This is a great little platformer for one's collection and the price on sale is not bad at all at the time of writing this. The graphics are crisp and bright, controls work well, although the camera can be jerky at times, and you can customize the controls to your liking.
Black Forest Studios also got one thing spot on: Music. Giana Sisters was very famous for its chiptune music and the remixes are a delight to the ears, even for someone that generally has music turned down when playing.
And, although simplified, I am very happy for the addition of the retro levels as it brings back a bit of nostalgia.
To those that have maybe played Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams, this is not that game, nor a sequel but a port of the DS version that many of us older Giana Sisters fans not in Europe either wished they had or had to import.
If you want a simple, cute platformer with awesome music, check this out. For veteran players such as myself, it is your call. For you, it may be more of a Giana Sisters Lite.

A bright, colourful, fun Mario clone that feels nice including a "retro" mode of the original levels released on the c64 in 1987. Title music brought a tear to the eye, sounded just how I remember playing Giana on the Amiga when I was a young grommet.

A Neat Little Gem which I'm surprised got another Remake, and for the most part it's pretty faithful to the original DS Remake. It lacks a bit of polish and Giana's Sprite (both Normal and Goth) feel a little too unnatural for my liking (it's the face), but overall if you haven't already played Giana Sisters on the DS then this port here isn't a bad place to start at all. Plus it's fairly inexpensive.
So if you haven't already played what's essentially a pretty stellar Clone of the original SMB complete with some great music, look no further. =)

GundeadliGne at first seems to be a rather competent shooter in the first 2 minutes of gameplay, however the experience gradually dminishes quickly as soon as you start getting into it.
GundeadliGne is at heart a side-scrolling bullet hell (Or danmaku) shooter where you tackle enemies and bosses in order to get a high score. Just like the original, your character is able to throw an item at enemies to slow down time (which is mandatory in many sections), also new to this game are the rechargeable bombs which can be re-used after a certain amount of time and the ability to turn around to shoot enemies behind you. Probably the best addition to this game is the 2-player Co-Op that is both offline and online (never got the online to work though)
Another thing to point out is that the game will either decrease or increase its own difficulty depending on your performance during a session, similar to other games in the genre.
Where the game absolutely fails at is absolutely everything. The game again, adjusts its difficulty depending on your performance, but the way it handles it is a joke. Basically, in order to increase it, you have to either kill a boss or mini-boss, clear waves quickly, or probably the worst of them all; OVERHEAT your weapons. Considering that the alarm that rings when you're about to overheat has a delay and the heat bar is TINY, makes this design decision absolutely atrocious. And the only way to decrease the difficulty is either by getting hit or by using up a bomb, which takes time to recharge. So it is easier to increase the difficulty rather than decreasing it, making the game too hard too fast. I was able to get to the hardest difficulty before the first boss on my first playthrough, which was just evil.
Also, the patterns in this game are pretty horrid, none feel creative or fun to dodge, in fact alot of the patterns are designed to simply kill you cheaply without any good way of relying on reflexes to dodge most stuff, and considering that you have to slowdown the time by hitting enemies with a temporary spell in order to even see what's going on, that makes the experience so much worse than it already is. On top of all this, the hit detection is even more aggravating than the original since it is hard to focus on your character's weakspot (Scarf, bell, whatever depending on the character) when the patterns fly so fast and are basically the same colour.
While Gundemonium Recollection was a really well balanced shooter with some minor flaws (Except the true last boss, he is a pain to spawn and defeat), GundeadliGne has some neat ideas but absolutely fails at implementing every single one of them.  For avid fans of the genre who love a good challenge with great patterns and excellent design, this is not for you. I can only recommend this to people who are fans of bullet-hell (danmaku) shooters no matter how well designed it truly is.

I am a long-time fan of shmups, with renewed vigor after having more recently discovered Touhou.  That being said, this is without a doubt the worst example of the genre I have ever had the displeasure of having witnessed.  The prominently-posed naked catgirl boss was enough for me.  But even if you're into that in your games, rest assured that there is plenty wrong with this game from a gameplay perspective.  Your character takes up too much of the screen, so that shots must come at you either in slow-motion or with very tight limits to the patterns that enemies can make.  You have a small but unclear hitbox, which is unfortunately imperative to use with some of the spread gaps in attacks.  Some hostile radial bursts even have no apparent gap, as though the developer didn't realize he'd made a no-health-bar shmup.  It's rather important to use the special abilities at your disposal, which the game made no attempt to explain how to use or how they work.
The ONLY good thing I can say about this game is the ability to co-op.  Combined with the ability to aim backwards along with enemies that make use of that mechanic, could lead to good teamwork moments if the game was any good.  As is, inviting another person to play is a passive-aggressive way to let them know you hate them enough to suffer along with them so long as they suffer too, but without telling them to their face.  Having Reimu as a boss is just insulting, as though this creation has any right to call itself in the same league. Farming Simulator 17 is the most unbelievably tedious gameplay experience I've ever had, where most things should be automated by a worker so you can focus on farm ownership and growth, and not farm micromanagement. This game needs to be stripped down, automated, and made way easier to play, where processes are explained and spelled out to improve the overall gameplay payoff.  I'm surprised there are DLC's to this game, when the problem is the base game, and not the equipment, because the equipment I was looking for is not available in the base game, DLC's, or in any of the mods, because swathing and rock picking is not a part of the simulation, and those two things takes up a large portion of all farm life.
In order for me to recommend this game, here is a list of things that would need to change:
⦁Land in North America is subdivided by the quarter section and is on a grid, and this game will never feel like a true farming simulation and I will never recommend it, until there is a farm out on a homestead surrounded by quarter sections of land and grid roads, and you get to put things where you want them when you buy them and don't have to go get them.  Do a random google search of anywhere in the bread basket.
⦁Fields need to be rotated with different crops due to nutrient depletion and different fields have different soils that produce certain crops better than others, and crops only grow once a year, and that should be the focus of the entire game, land management per year along with organizing staff.   This game kind of encourages destroying the land for the sake of money, instead of taking care of it, even with fertizilier and planting oilseed, and it also treats workers as though they come and go by your command instead of encouraging a team effort and the importance of maintaining a skilled labor force, which is the entire struggle with farming, getting the most value for your dollar in terms of lowest input costs in the productivity of your equipment and workers to the highest returns in the price of the grain and animals.  So, creating some sort of labor section to the game where different workers have different levels of abilities and come at different costs would really add to everything, for example, the more you get a worker to do a certain task, the better they get at it.  I'd want workers for absolutely everything that is done in this game (transport, livestock, grain, and mowing), a fully automated simulation that you could just watch play out and check your financials and adjust as you go.
⦁All crops are measured, bought, and sold by the bushel, and should be in this game. All grain is graded by quality as well, for example number 1 wheat, number 2 wheat, and feed wheat, as well as dockage from contamination, which is in relation to weather and how well you farm/enjoy gambling.  Weather is a massive part of farming, and it's all that farmers talk about next to complaining about the government.  So, the connection between a wet early spring and good yield should play into the game, along with a long or short, hot, cold or wet growing season, and temperature during harvest would really add to the gameplay, but only if everything was automated.
⦁I like the competing markets, I just don't like that I have to drive to them, that should be automated by a worker or grain should just simply sell like you sell animals, with a touch of a button.  Also, do you have any idea how much more complicated it is to transport and sell livestock than grain? There are livestock auctions and breeding problems that are totally ignored in this game.
⦁No one ever went to the retail section of an outlet mall to buy farm machinery, lol!  Farm machinery is ordered from an industrial warehouse in your local town or city and delivered to your farm; you don't even need to go pick it up in real life, so why do you have to in this game?  You only go to pick up parts that break down.  It's simulating something that doesn't even exist, and it's super tedious having to go back and forth to pick up everything over and over again, it's such a huge amount of wasted gameplay time, when again, it should be automated by a worker or simply placed on your farm.
⦁Why can't you buy feed for your animals and have a worker take care of them?
⦁Why are there no auction sales?

⦁Why are there no quonsets, no grain bins, no augers, no swathers, no grain trucks, no harrow packers, and no rock pickers?  That is the basis of all farming, and it's not even in this game hilariously enough! Or John Deere?  You can't even call it farming without John Deere.  No Versatile Tractors either? No gas and diesel tanks you can put on your farm? You can't dig a well with a pump for your animals? No hemp, camelina, peas, lentils, clover for the bee hives to make real honey, flax, mustard, canary seed, rye, or oats?
⦁Why can't you set up the parameters of the entire simulation and then watch it run very quickly to see how your simulation will play out and then stop it at parts to adjust things and then speed it up again?  I'd prefer a Sim City style simulation more, than all the running back and forth.  Cultivating, seeding, and combining is all too tedious and slow and must be sped up but there's no way to do so at all, it's all at one slow speed.  120x only speeds up the growing season and not the automated gameplay, which doesn't make any sense, simulation wise, a true simulation works very closely with time of day in order to maximize output, instead of harvesting half a field with 3 days going by in the process. As an example, when harvesting canola there's a very tight window during the day when you can harvest, as you have to check the moisture content to make sure its less than 8% before you go out to harvest in the morning and before you finish in the evening, because if it exceeds that, it will heat and spoil in the bin and will get rejected at the elevator, unless you have a dryer at your farm.
⦁The breakdown of your financials is clunky and poorly organized, which is one of the most realistic parts of this game, because that's kinda how farmers are.
⦁The zoom over a tractor with an attachment, like a tractor and cultivator, doesn't zoom over the middle of the new object, but remains zoomed over the middle of the tractor, and doesn't allow you to see behind the cultivator when zoomed in close. Adjust the center point of a unit with an attachment to the center of the newly combined unit instead of remaining centered on the vehicle.
I found this to be a frustrating gameplay experience because you have to do the jobs that are the gopher's responsibility which are tedious and annoying when you could be focusing on your plan of growth for the future.  I'd rather play a farming simulator that had a different focus and style of gameplay altogether, like Sim City, that organized the farm by the year and broke down what had to be done by the season and could speed through seasons like winter where less is happening.  Unless they created a homestead far from town surrounded by quarter sections of land, added an automated worker to go get new equipment, sell grain, and move stuff around, and made everything less tedious and less hands on, and sped up the gameplay, and allowed you to set the parameters for the simulation, showed the depletion of soil quality on your land, showed the increase in staff ability and development, had more crop varieties, and added swathers, augers, grain bins, grain trucks and rock pickers, then this would be fun for me and a more realistic simulation.  As it is, it just simulates something that doesn't happen in the real world, and I mentioned nothing about the dangers of raising animals in such confined spaces and no option for the type of cattle to be raised.
Please note, I played 80+ hours to give this game an honest shot and it's super addicting but overall, more frustrating than enjoyable gameplay, for me.

I have come to FS17 as a previous player of FS15.  I held off on buying this as the one thing that really annoyed me about FS15 was the lack of head tracking support for it.  It ws the one thing that I felt that it really needed to make it perfect and now FS17 has it!  Yay!
Having bought FS17 it is everything I had hoped that it would be and more.  Not only is head tracking enabled but several things that were enabled as slightly clunky mods in FS15 are now in FS17 as standard.
For those who are completely new to the Farming Simulator series, the game is, as the name suggests, a simulation of many aspects of farming.  The game is first- or third-person view and allows you to farm using a wide variety of farm machinery such as tractors, combine harvesters, trucks, cars, and mowers.  You also have the ability to get out and walk around your farm on foot and there are a few, limited, activities that can be carried out without a big machine to help you.
The game covers arable farming, animal farming, and forestry, and each of these go through growth and harvest cycles, each requiring different processes throughout.  Having cultivated, planted, fertilised, and harvested your crop you can then sell the harvest for cash with which to buy better equipment, more fields, pay off your bank loan, and buy seeds and other consumables to get your next crop going.
This is not a game for those who are looking for a massive adrenaline dump.  It's a slow burn, enjoyable game, that will seem fairly dull to begin with until you realised that you just lost the weekend.  I have seen some reviews that describe this game as boring and I can understand that viewpoint, but it's either something you will enjoy or you won't.  It's not for everyone.  I find it extremely relaxing (except for stacking bales, that's really quite tricky and tense).
For those who have played FS15, things that I am really impressed with in this version are such things as head-tracking having native support (that's a total winner for me), having the option to have the vehicle auto-start on getting in it or having to press a button to start/stop the engine, and working wing mirrors on vehicle.  For me the combination of working mirrors and head-tracking are superb.  I have tried reversing trailers in real life and it is really hard.  In FS17 you will have lots and lots of opportunities to practise your trailer-reversing skills and in order to do that properly you need wing mirrors and the ability to look between them quickly and easily.  With these enabled it is very, very good.  I would recommend getting a head-tracker and steering wheel with pedals for the full experience.  It is possible to customise the controls so that the steering wheel and pedals only work when in-vehicle thus removing an annoyance from GTA5 where your character would gently drift left or right if the wheel wasn't completely centred when you were on foot.
In addition to the stock elements, the game has a huge number of mods available accessible in-game.  I have not played any of the stock farms yet, I have played from the outset on a farm called Coldborough Park Farm which is based on a real farm in Herefordshire.  As a Brit I absolutely love the fact that I can play the game in the same sort of countryside I can see driving to work.  There are very few games with hedges (yeah, I know, a small thing, right?) but they are a huge feature of the English landscape and it really makes the game seem realistic.  I have 17 hours in-game on FS17 and I have not had a chance to try everything yet: I haven't tried forestry or animal husbandry, and I haven't been able to do any of the missions (as I haven't found any fields that have them yet), but from what I have played the game is superb!
There are a few flaws.  The hired help is a drunkard who frequently drives my combine harvester into a ditch and then just leaves it there, or, at best, leaves great swathes of crops un-harvested, and he charges through the nose.  The fields are huge (I'm not sure if this is really a flaw) so working them can be a daunting task.  I liked some of the smaller fields in FS15 Hagenstedt as they allowed me to do quick turn-arounds, but this is more realistic.  It's one of the reasons I am willing to hire drunken-Bob to do the harvesting.
If you liked FS15 I would say that it is definitely worth the upgrade to FS17.  The graphics are much, much better, the gameplay is better, and lots of features are enabled that made FS15 just not quite as good as it should have been.
If you fancy having a go at farming, give this a go.  I was initially put off the idea of playing a farming simulator as I could imagine my farmer friends scoffing at the idea until one of my farmer friends told me that he was pretty well addicted to it.  That was good enough for me.  Of course, it's one thing trying to wrestle the linkage of a three-ton trailer onto a tractor in freezing sleet in the middle of a muddy field in February, and another to sit at a PC in the warm, sipping coffee and doing it with the press of a button.  I know which I prefer.

Been playing Trainz since 2007 (way back to Trainz Railroad Simulator 2006).
As the newest stable release (Trainz: A New Era Community Edition has been giving me grief because my graphics card is obsolete; thanks DirectX 11!), Trainz Simulator 12 has its pros and cons.
PROS:
*Great route selection
*Nicely modeled locomotives and rolling stock
*The Download Station cleanup has updated old favorites
*The new features are all great
CONS:
*No compatibility mode like in Trainz Simulator 2010, meaning that if it shows faulty in Content Manager, you can't use it unless you repair it or update to the TS12-compatible version (build 2.9, Trainz Simulator 2009, means the item will work in TS12); this actually stopped me from getting TS12 and staying with TS2010 SP3 until now
*Content Manager still tends to freeze up (but if you ask me, it's not CM if it doesn't freeze up every once in a while; ah, memories)
*Stability issues inherent to Trainz
If you're not into simulators, go play some casual train game like TrainStation on Facebook or TrainPlayer. If you like train simulators, don't go for Train Simulator (formerly RailWorks, nee Rail Simulator). Go for this less graphically-intense, sandbox-like masterpiece of Australian game-making.

Just when I thought adventure gaming couldn’t get any more original or better than Edith Finch here comes June and Carl in what can only be described as one of the most magical gameplay experiences of the year.   Last Day of June is an emotional journey dealing with love and tragic loss and one man’s attempt to change past events using the unexplained power of being able to look into a portrait and becoming that person, and in doing so perhaps change the string of events culminating in painful disaster.
The game starts off innocently enough with Carl and June sitting on the end of the pier; June is doodling in her art book while Carl fetches her sweater from the car. These opening moments hint at a few innovative concepts that will become the norm for the following 4+ hour adventure. First is the stunning visual design that blurs the lines between stop-motion animation, a living painting, and a Pixar short story. The second is the simple fact that there is not a single spoken (intelligible) word in the entire game. We are left to interpret pantomime gestures, non-verbal vocal noises, and an emotionally charged score that never tells you how to feel, but just as easily supports your natural emotions at any single moment. The visuals of cutscene and gameplay are identical with only minimal button prompts indicating when and how to interact with the world around you. It’s so seamless you often don’t realize when you actually have control of the game.
Minor spoilers ahead, and in case the title didn’t clue you in, June dies almost immediately leaving Carl alone and wheelchair bound, full of guilt and regret, since he was behind the wheel of the fateful car crash that resulted in this painful reality. But after a bit of investigating it seems Carl has the ability to interact with some portraits left behind in June’s art studio, and by doing so he can enter those characters’ lives and relive the moments leading up to the fatal crash. It seems that everyone and anyone in the neighborhood may (or may not) have contributed to the car crash, so it’s up to you to stack the deck of fate and change history.
There are four main characters, each represented by a painting and each playing a potential key role in June’s death. You have the Kid, the Best Friend, the Hunter, and the Old Man. Without getting too spoilery, an example of how the system works is that we find out the boy ran out into the road chasing a ball, which caused the car crash, so when playing as the boy you need to take steps to make sure this event doesn’t happen. But it gets so much more complicated when each of these four characters start to overlap with the others. So, to not be playing with the ball the kid will need to find another activity – like flying a kite, but in doing this he must use a certain item that the best friend needs, and when she doesn’t have that item she becomes responsible for the car crash. And once you get the kid and the best friend sorted out here comes the Hunter to add even more puzzle-solving elements.
As you interact with the world and setup new paths of fate for each character the end results are presented in tarot card fashion leading up to a new potential timeline. You’ll often be forced to go back and play a previous character as new areas unlock. The kid can throw a soccer ball and knock over milk cans, so when the Hunter is blocked by a milk can, you’ll need to end his day, play that part as the kid, then replay as the Hunter. I was super-impressed with the way the designers shortened these replays; fading to black then taking you to the next critical part of the day, rather than forcing you to repeat lengthy puzzle elements.
There are also 20 memories; five per character, that can only be collected when playing as that character, so that lends a bit of replayable discovery to the game, since many of these memory bubbles are in locked areas that can’t be accessed until later in the game. There is a surprisingly amount of backstory locked away in these memory postcards (as well as an Achievement), so making the effort to find and collect them all is well worth it.   Between character levels Carl will also wheel around the neighborhood at night viewing various memory dioramas, which also fleshes out the backstory. Keep in mind there are no journals or spoken dialogue. Your only knowledge of the past and present is what you infer from what you see and possible feel.
We’ve all seen enough sci-fi and fantasy movies to guess where this story is headed, but the Last Day of June managed to defy my predictions. Just when I thought I knew what was going to happen I was totally blown away by the powerful and emotional ending that was revealed only in the final few moments of the game. And then the credits roll and you have time to settle down and then the post-credit stinger plays and here come all the “feels” again.
The PC version supports up to 4K visuals and has a very distinctive look.  While not as technically refined as similar genre titles, Last Day of June blasts you with saturated colors and crazy contrast along with an almost annoying depth of field when it comes to keeping things in focus.  It’s like the world around you blurs into this dream state except for anything in your immediate surroundings, which is in crisp focus.  And with no settings to adjust this I can only assume this was the intended effect from the designers.
I still have trouble understanding how this game works as well as it does. With faceless, voiceless characters right out of an unfinished Tim Burton movie, Last Day of June is as haunting as it is beautiful and without uttering a single spoken word tells a story more powerful than your best Hollywood drama. The gameplay is seamlessly overlaid into this interactive painting to create something wholly unique and totally original; a masterclass in interactive entertainment that will be studied for decades to come.

I was a big fan of Transocean I, and had been looking forward to Transocean II for a long while.

My preference was for a proper business simulation game, which I prefer to play in endless sandbox mode, and this is where TO2 is lagging behind compared to TO1. Over and over we have asked for more economic realism and complexity, but  child of 10 would be able to start TO2 and turn 20 million in 1 billion in less than a year.
The developers have been made aware of this point and of many, many other frustrations (e.g. still no full / unlimited automation). We are now 6 months after the release and have only seen patches to fix things that were clearly broken, but nothing that properly addresses the issues at hand.
Initially I had given the developers the benefit of the doubt, but the lack of communication / roadmap is simply not acceptable anymore. Don't ask for feedback if you are not willing to engage in the dialogue!
The game has the potential to be fun, but it's time for more patches, and for proactive communication about them.

I really enjoy games like that have a strong sandbox element to them.  This definitely fits into that bucket overall.  It's fun trying to come up with methods to efficiently produce reliable supply lines for parts needed to make other parts and objects, ad infinitum.
It is somewhat awkward, however, that your character must personally run up to things to place or interact with them.  Due to the story premise, there are hostile creatures running around in the world that are unhappy you are destroying their planet, and that necessitates the character arming himself and building defensive equipment around the factory structures.  For me, this clashes with the kind of creative game I wanted to play.  You can turn off the aggressiveness of the creatures and ignore the military aspects for the most part, however in the technology trees you may still need to create and build some of those military components to reach the stated goal of being able to launch a rocket into space, again due to the premise of the story.  I have been focusing mainly on finding ways to automate and optimize my production as I unlock more and more technology, but have not really been keeping the rocket launch in my mind as I play.
Overall, I definitely like the game and would recommend it either if you like the creative aspect alone or find the defensive component interesting as well.

Actual original Megaman (1-3) player review:
Not the game awaited by those who grew up with Megaman (the original 8-bit/now dubbed 'legacy' series) as the game mechanics exploit the "dash" manuever from later Megamans and the MMX series (if you couldn't tell from any previews: where it might look cool since it moves the game as a speedrun to other players, but would instead, feel akward if you are the actual player) MN9 was supposed to actually exceed the expectations of the original MM series by fixing what was wrong with that series, instead, it does the opposite by bringing out the worse from both MM and MMX.
The thing you couldn't do to be the real Megaman was run into your enemies, you also had to avoid all obstacles, and basically not be touched at all. This gameplay is so counterintuitive to the laws of Megaman, that older players will be thrown under the bus and play worse than the younger gamers who are already used to button-mashing/QTE and new to both the Megaman series and Capcom. Not that that is a bad thing, But I find the gameplay too dependent on the enemy absorption, ala dash manuever (making the gameplay cheap) This was either intentional due to the time elapsed in the era of gaming since the last official MM game was released, or naively accidental, due to it being developed by a much smaller team as a Kickstarter campaign (or both)
Whether new to the series or not, chances are, you will suck, and will need a fast and powerful, high-performance PC to play a game full of cheap deaths (a staple of classic console-exclusive games) if you don't have that, I cannot recommend this game.

I'll start by saying that I didn't back this game on kickstarter, so I can only speak from the persepective of a 25 year Mega Man fan whose curiosity got the better of him.
I really enjoyed this game.
During the first tutorial level I was trying my hardest to draw comparisons to Mega Man X (since I had just played it again hours before buying this), and it became apparent very quickly that this was not the old Mega Man games that we remembered. Once I dropped that comparison and took this game as "inspired by" rather than "a sequel to", the game became much more enjoyable
The difficulty does spike in some places, and my controller took some unfair punishment as a result, but theres nothing that can't be worked out through perserverence, after which the enemy patterns and level requirements become almost obvious. The main weapon suffices for 95% of the game, and you have little reason to explore the alternatives except for a few sections, so in this regard I suppose the game could have made better use of the wide arsenal.
In summary, I would recoomend this game to Mega Man fans, only because it gives a nice nod to the games we all loved in those golden years. I wouldn't sell it as a "spiritual successor" however since, in my opinion, the game fails in that regard. As a Mega Man game, its a no contest, but as a platformer, this game gets my vote :)

an okay 10 bucks i spent.
To expand on my joke review, like Gunvolt, it just takes inspiration from Mega Man while still being its own thing. Gunvolt, Inti Creates own Mega Man style game,  uses a tagging/weakening system to defeat enemies, just like how Beck does (Gunvolt uses electricity, Beck dash absorbs). I think this is because of Inti Creates' influence on Mighty No. 9 and their love for score-based/perfectionist gameplay, evident their own Mega Man games.
Level design is filled to the brim with insta-kill obstacles. Most of them are fine, but you will encounter some unnecessarily brutal hazards. The "spikes" in this game follow Mega Man 1 logic, killing you even with invincibility frames. That said, there's enough variety in the gimmicks to keep each stage somewhat interesting.
Thanks to the level design and emphasis on dashing to defeat enemies, the game is much more fast-paced than typical Mega Man, which I found refreshing. Sadly the enemies are pretty bland, but I guess they compliment the level design okay enough.
The bosses are all pretty fun, even with some cheap moments (fire boss, for example, has an insta-kill move). I'd say the biggest flaw with the gameplay would have to be the lack of use for your acquired weapons. Your buster does the job extremely well and can even be way better against bosses than their weaknesses.
The music is really damn great, and its a shame that I see people bog the whole soundtrack down for Dyna's song. The sound mixing is awful though, so you won't even hear tracks well. Lower the SFX volume, seriously makes the experience better.
Plot-wise its pretty similar to Mega Man Powered Up with saving your corrupted robots brethren instead of destroying them. In fact, I think Mighty No. 9 attempted to be a more realized version of that game's story. A shame that its not very well executed and comes across as more corny than it should be, but its all optional anyways. The voice acting is all over the place, but its okay enough. Never heard the Japanese VAs, but supposedly the subtitles don't match what they say.
Its kind of a messy game, but as big fan of Mega Man I'd say this game was pretty enjoyable for the 10 bucks I spent.

This games actually really good.  I think my best description for this quickly would be a more interactive visual novel.  The story without giving away too much is about the slow imminent decline of a long distance friendship.  the chat dialgue along with the chat that you sorta kinda type yourself builds you into the character while still giving you that spectator feel watching two people talk.  It takes place over six chapters or years however you see it and it's just a really good very immersive experience.  It's something like an hour long and it's free so I'd highly reccomend it.

Pros:
* Unique game, with a very good atmosphere.
* Very good at building convincing characters, making the girl of "Emily" someone we have all had a love/hate relationship with.
* Lots of replayability
* Very good ending.
* Nice pop culture references to the 2000s.
Cons (really small things):
* It would be nicer for it to be a little longer - it clocks in at around 40 minutes at most.
* It would be nice to play slightly more than every year - it's kind of unrealistic for people to only talk once every year, and a lot could happen inbetween
* It would be nice if the player was given the option to speak to some friend aside from Emily to help shape the story - lots of things that happen are out of the player's control and you're just like "oh okay whatever". Like you don't HAVE to speak to other characters as you do with Emily, but if you want to, you can.
* It would be nice if, like the other characters, you too could alter your bio and information and stuff (unless you were able to and I missed it)
* It would be nice to see multiple endings as opposed to just the one, to help feel you shaped the story.
Still, I really love the game, and the cons are more just things that I would like to see in the game, not that have to be in.

Oh Jotun
Jotun is a game that suffers from a lack of direction. It's a tremendously beautiful game (minus a few small quibbles), but doesn't seem to understand if it wants to be an atmospheric exploration game, or a slow paced dark souls / shadows of the colossus style boss slayer. In trying to do both, it sort of fails in all angles. On the plus side, it is relatively short, so the downsides of the game don't overshadow the nice bits too badly. I would say a roughly 5 hour game, depending on how much trouble you have with the bosses.
Jotun tells the tale of Thora, a viking warrior who dies at sea, who now roams Norse Purgatory, Ginnungagap, in an attempt to make her way to Valhalla. At the same time, the environment tells the tale of the Norse gods and mythos, touching on several stories very briefly, but never elaborating too much on any one particular detail. That's really the story of the entire game - 9 themed vignettes to explore, and five (plus final boss) bossfight, a mile wide, but an inch deep. It genuinely feels like the game at one point was meant to be one large connected world, but due to financial or time issues, was condensed into the nine best setpieces and connected by a void.
The art is beautiful and hand drawn, and wonderfully draws you into the world. Unfortunately, there's not a lot to do in the world you're immersed in. Each of the 9 areas has one Rune (mandatory), and one God Power and one Ithunn Apple (both optional). Some areas also have "Landmarks". which are panned out great vistas of areas where you can see the environment. That's it. Everything else is empty space. Pretty looking empty space, but empty space. Each area also generally boasts one movement puzzle and one environmental obstacle - such as a blizzard in the Nine Rivers or hostile dwarves and light-up pillars in Brokkr's Forge. These are often the only things that break up the emptiness, however. The world has a grand scale, but feels empty, and not in the good, haunting way, but in the bad, desolate way. For example, I missed the entire 'environment puzzle' in Jormundgandr's lake simply by getting the optional things and seeing the vista. The puzzle itself was contained to a small area in the middle that I would never have seen, except for the fact that I ran through on purpose trying to trigger it. Admittedly, some of the areas, such as the Forge, or Ymir's Blood, are more in your face about it. Non-boss enemies never feel like true obstacles, but rather just annoyances. The Great Nameless Eagle in Yggdrasil's Branches is reduced to 'dodge roll or lose 1/3rd of your life.' Repeat every 30 seconds. That's it. It just feels like a loss of potential.
Your character's controls don't generally help the issue. Thora plods along at a pace that would be fine for exploring, but does not give the sense of urgency that you would feel a Viking in her position might have. Dodge rolls are awkwardly animated, stopping you suddenly and ruining momentum, (though the character is still visibly rolling) and do not have any actual i-frames, making them only useful for the sudden burst of speed. Attacks are limited to a one-two swing combo, or a long charging heavy attack. Light attacks are useless for the entire game except one situation, as its almost always more useful to wind up and smash a jotun or an environment object, several of which can't even be harmed by light attacks to begin with. God Powers are all useful in jotun fights, which is a plus - I would frequently use every single one of them against bosses, though outside of boss fights, only the speed boost (to make running bearable) and the healing are really helpful. Finally, one minor nitpick - the animation for Thora is mirrored vertically. That means as she turns horizontally, her sprite switches her handedness for her axe, which always appears in front of her spite, in the bottom half, rather than behind her sprite like you'd expect in some orientations. All the Jotuns are not animated this way, so it's strange to see the level of attention given to the bosses not paid to the protagonist of the game.
Bossfights are the climactic encounters of the game, and again, while they look impressive, most of them have very little in the way of strategy, especially when the best approach to all of them is "Hit with both Gungnir magic, get on their side or behind, activate Thor and Freyja, and heavy swing", repeat until out of all magic, then keep heavy swinging (but a bit slower now) until it's dead. Two of the jotuns, the storm and the fire jotun, change this up due to their patterns but the basic strategy is still the same. Approach from a safe angle and heavy swing. The fact that all the time trials for the games state times less than 80 seconds (most are 60 or 40) should say just how swiftly a boss can be beaten with even cursory understanding of the magic.
I feel like the game would have benefitted from deciding if it wanted to be an atmospheric adventure game about wandering purgatory in search of Vahalla, focusing on Thora's story, or a thunderous jotun fight game with a focus on Valhalla and the mythos, but trying to mix both ends up with both feeling lackluster. If you're really feeling the Norse mythos (and it is done very well, with narration in Icelandic), and want to look at admittedly very pretty vistas, then pick it up, but if you're looking for an action game, then keep an eye on EITR's release, as that may be the game you're looking for.

As a real-life programmer, most of the time the code you are writing is easy, boring even. Sanitize user input and send it to the database. Made a dialog box appear when the user presses a button. There are fiddly bits for sure, but exciting problems tend to be pretty rare, because most of them are handled already by libraries written by someone else.
And then you have Shenzhen, which is entirely interesting problems (except for the first couple of puzzles). Most of them seem straightforward until you start building the solution and... oh, I don't have enough "simple" outputs on one chip. Or just as often, you have a brilliant 15 line program, except you're only allowed 14 lines. Working within these constraints makes every challenge interesting.
It's the sort of game where you will be eating breakfast the next day and suddenly have the solution to a problem that had stumped you. Or that a puzzle you had solved in a convoluted way can be solved simply with fewer components.
Of course, you're not DONE when you have a solution. You have the Zachtronis histograms to compare how well you did with all other players, and especially your Steam friends. Discovering new techniques and then going back and applying them to past puzzles to try and beat your friends adds a lot to it, and is a nice break when you feel stuck on a later challenge.
It's humorous and weird in the way Zachtronics games always are. And there's a really good solitaire game in there too for some reason.

Like other titles of the same studio, it's again a success !
If you loved TIS, this goes a bit beyond because you will also design the board with some simplified processors or components.
If you loved Spacechem, then you might like the same kind of targets to the puzzles where you either have to optimise power consumption (number of instructions during a run), Design cost (each component on your board) or lines of code (size of your code).
The atmosphere of the game is also quite great because you’ll feel like a proper employee designing electronics in a Chinese company. Lots of funny situation where you’ll be asked to design stuffs for a very dubious usage… but hey… who asks questions when you’re given money ;-)
I do not recommend this game for casual gamers though. It is indeed really frustrating when you can’t get a design right because your code is one line too big to fit in a chip or when adding more stuff on the board to solve a problem actually makes it worth. And the worse is seeing your friends outsmarting you with a very clever design that they will never disclose and you’ll feel depressed until suddenly a great idea pops in your mind and you’re back in the race for the best virtual designer.
Also Checking for solutions online is definitely gonna ruin your experience, don’t do that !
Otherwise, if you can deal with this… Oh boy, go ahead ! This game is great !
Finding clues in the manual to understand what instruction or what component could make you completely rethink your design. Understanding a pattern in the puzzle that can allow you to make big shortcuts (engineering cheat you could say, yes).
Where also the game is smart, it is due to the fact you will often fin the best design in a category, let’s say cost but rarely the 3 measures at the same time (cost, power, code). Therefore, you will probably have to find 3 different designs to optimize each one of these and that is where the replayability of the game is great. More to that : you will unlock new components later in the game, so… why not revisiting your design when you can save a Yen ?

Bottom line: Only buy it if you like Zachtronics games. If you don't, you're in for a frustrating and questionably designed experience.
Having completed a couple of dozen levels, I have been left feeling frustrated and cheated by the game design. You're always one register, or one pin, or one line of code off from the solution -- making it feel like a grind to rearrange board pieces (for no reason other than to frustrate you), make the code more dense and illegible, etc.
The instruction set is absolutely awful -- you are given a bare minimum number of instructions, and conditions work terribly. There are no logic operators. You are given two registers and a very limited number of lines of code.
In my opinion, this is just awful, frustrating game design. It feels more like a chore and a grind than a fun experience. I'd stay away unless you know what you're getting into, unless the game changes out of Early Access. Sorry, Zach, but you need to work on making your games less tedious if you want to keep doing this.

I have been playing simualtors like these for many years, so here's my review:
This game is Alright, it's very balanced in nature, quite flexible orders and rule system, while having a mid-range graphics capabilities, with very friendly, yet stupid AI system.
The forums have been very good to me over the years.
CMP is alright for keeping track of content, it is very friendly for the beginner for managing and sorting content, but it gets less and less flexible as your experiance grows.
The thing I like most aobut CMP, would be its "Content Creator Plus", it gives you the tools to create content pretty nicely, CMP also sorts content for you into diferent catagories
I do like the concept of CMP as a whole, but what I don't like, is the trainz database, if it gets corrupt, it has to do an "Asset repair", which fixs all of the descrepencies within the database, which is why I'd prefer Windows Explorer to do it, and trainz to just load the content in.
The lack of beginner tutorials, espechially route creating / steam locomotive tutorials really doesn't help beginners get used to driving driving steam locomotives for the first time.
Creating routes is hard without advanced DEM tools (Digitally Elevated Maps), which is sold seperately, so what you're left is oversimplified terrain tools, which doesn't really give enough flexibility when creating rotues.
I'd much prefer an external tool handle DEM maps, such as L3DT.
Creating routes using the default tools makes route creating tedious and it doesn't really give a realsitic feel when it comes to the finsihed product.
The inability to create vertical structures using the default game grid restricts multiple players and forces them to build models which gives the effect.
The 10M grid is way too low resolution, the 5M resolution is too big as well.
Soo, I have to ask this, if trainz can support models which have so many polygons, why does trainz baseboards lag so badly with anything below 10 or even 5?
I can almost guarrantee that the baseboards are going to be lower poly compared to rolling stock and locomotives.
I bought this game because of the "Multiplayer" aspect of it, which everyone wanted since 2007, which, at the time, the thread had 800 replies to it, Unfortunitely, when multiplayer came out, all of the data was routed through Auran / N3V's servers, causing lag for practically everyone, which sort of continues today.
Now you rarely ever see more then 5 players playing on multiplayer at a time, compared to the thousonds of people playing Garry's mod.
It's a shame that multiplayer turned out to be less popular then anyone at the time would have anticipated.
I admit, trainz isn't going to be everyone's cup of tea, and it has its pros and cons, but I feel this game is okay. I'd recommend it for the beginners and seasoned players, because of its ease of use and the concept of the game is moderately easy to learn, but again, the lack of tutorials is a let down for the game.

Chicken Little is a 2005 American 3D computer-animated science fiction comedy film, produced by Walt Disney Feature Animation and loosely based on the original fable of the same name. The 46th Disney animated feature film, it was directed by Mark Dindal from a screenplay by Steve Bencich, Ron J. Friedman, and Ron Anderson, based on a story by Mark Kennedy and Dindal. The film is dedicated to Disney artist and writer Joe Grant, who died before the film's release.
Chicken Little was animated in-house at Walt Disney Feature Animation's main headquarters in Burbank, California and released by Walt Disney Pictures on November 4, 2005, in Disney Digital 3-D (the first film to be released in this format) along with the standard 2-D version. It is Disney's first fully computer animated feature film, as Pixar's films were distributed, but not produced by Disney, and Dinosaur (2000) was a combination of live-action and computer animation.
Chicken Little was Disney's second adaptation of the fable after a propaganda cartoon made during World War II.[5] The film is also the last Disney animated film made before Pixar executive John Lasseter was named chief creative officer of Disney Animation and the last Disney film produced by Walt Disney Feature Animation before the studio was renamed Walt Disney Animation Studios.[6] Chicken Little grossed $314 million worldwide.

This game is immensely emotional. Don't expect to play it without crying.
The artwork is gorgeous and nothing needs to be said about Steven Wilson's music - as a huge fan I already knew what I was getting myself into... even his music videos can make me cry.
I think it's fantastic how the faces are drawn - every character is uniquely identifiable by a particular trait but because all of them are "faceless" it's easy to empathise with them; put yourself in their shoes if you will. Each character has their own (sad) backstory so there's something for everyone who's been down and out in life. This makes the game so much more relatable and emotional, especially if one has been through emotional trauma. The soft art style makes it so much more aesthetically pleasing and palatable to the eye as well.
A game about experiencing life, loving and letting go... sometimes this is just what we need given the stresses of modern life. It's absolutely worth the money.
One gripe though: if you don't get all the achievements in one playthrough it seems like the game forces you to restart at the end which can make it tedious.

The story is based off this music video:

Last Day Of June is a slightly frustrating, repetitive, arty puzzle game with a slightly Groundhog Day theme. Thanks to its distinctive visual style (with saturated colours and doll-like characters) the game is good-looking, and a soundtrack based on instrumental passages by Steven Wilson means it sounds good too. The reason to play this, though, is not the visuals, the puzzles or the music but the emotional payoff of the sombre tale of a widower trying to fix the past so his wife survives a car accident. If you like games that make you feel something, Last Day of June will do that, and it repays the small time investment of 3-4 hours to take that journey.

Factorio is one of those games that fits a niche market. On the surface, gameplay is very simple once the basics are learned. The depth comes not from the content itself, but from the complex systems a player must design to fully automate progression. it can be fun to take systems and try to improve them slightly to increase efficiency, but once you find the way to automate processes most efficiently, I find the challenge drops sharply. If you are an achievement hunter, be prepared for quite a tedious grind. Worst grind example is likely making 20 million electronic circuits, and yes they are produced one at a time. If you don't mind the grind, it is fun to try to create a modular automation system to increase production speed, but that is the game in a nutshell.
I have played the game on Windows and Mac systems and have yet to run into any serious performance issues. For gamers of any supported platform who are just a little bit masochistic, this title can be used to pass time in short sessions.
Very addictive.

I was so incredibly hyped for this game, I have watched the development from the day it was first announced, that being said I've struggled with debating if this game is a good, short answer yes long answer: not till they fix a few things. For starters what is new? New vessels such as bulk and tanker vessels, however, they all play the same have very different benefits, The region points system, this system allows you to get benefits from a region by building subsidies and collecting a profit share off of those buildings. There is also now multiplayer which in itself is a mixed bag of nuts, on one hand, I love being able to take on my friends and see who can make the biggest company, however, dont expect to build a shipping empire on multiplayer(ill get into that later). Now what is all the fuss about, well there are a lot of drawbacks from the first game for example in the first game managing a fleet of over 10 vessels was possible (now not as much) the automation system shuts off after running one pattern and doesn't make money so you'll be stuck with notifications that ships need orders. The next system is the sabotaged system which consists of 3 options: bribe subsidies, call in a notification of contraband, freeze bank account. In multiplayer the only real useful one is the contraband call, freezing bank accounts is annoying but does literally nothing to the player other than waste money. Speaking of multiplayer here is where a lot of shortcoming with the game show them multiplayer is great, sorta... the fact that we can to take on other humans makes planning and competing for more fun and more challenging HOWEVER multiplayer is incredibly restricted and I've yet to have a game where I'm able to buy a tier 5 ship by the end of the match, another issue is even while hosting you can't control any of the settings other then sabotage on or off, and game time at 1hr,1.5hr, 2hr this time restriction make 0 sense why cant we play endless or set better goals a good way they could make multiplayer 100x better is by allowing the host to set the goals of the game, by setting the victory conditions such as first company to own X amount of ships, first company to hold X amount of regions, first company to hit X value will win. This would make multiplayer not feel like such a crapshoot another thing would be able to join a game mid game allowing the multiplayer menu not to look like a Gamespy server. The last to MAJOR drawbacks are the UI everything from TO1 that worked so well got completely screwed up the UI is annoying and confusing even for a returning player. The last thing that I have no doubt in my mind will end up changing is the price 25$ is a way to steep for this game currently with all the bugs and drawbacks however if the devs listen to the community and change a lot of the problems it would be worth 25$ easily. However even if the devs don't fix a lot of the drawback the game is still worth picking up on a sale for around 5-10$.

EDIT: My old review got obsolete after the patch so this is a new one, and I have to give game developers some credit for listening to user feedback.
My old biggest complaint about the game was that it had no in game pause function to be able to plan your route properly. Now it is fixed as well as some bugs. Now it more resembles a tycoon game it is supposed to be and is marketed as. Some of my complaints remain unfixed like being able to repair ships only in designated ports (I think it would make more sense to make it possible to repair your ship in any port, just make prices different), but it seems this game now is going to direction it is supposed to be. It still has some technical issues (like resolutions over 1920x1200 are not supported so if you have 4K or 2560x1440 monitor – you are out of luck, play in windowed mode or not fully use your resolution). There still is no easy way to quickly get to the port that your ship is standing in from list of ships menu.
Now I can give it a careful recommendation if you are into tycoon or management games. It still has some issues, so I would recommend to wait for some more patches to come out before buying it. If you did not played the earlier game this might be more friendly to you, because it has a tutorial and should be more easy to learn for newcomers. If you played the earlier game this is not much different, but it contains new types of ships and campaign missions, so it is upon you to decide if it is worth the asking price for you.

Pros:
* Unique game, with a very good atmosphere.
* Very good at building convincing characters, making the girl of "Emily" someone we have all had a love/hate relationship with.
* Lots of replayability
* Very good ending.
* Nice pop culture references to the 2000s.
Cons (really small things):
* It would be nicer for it to be a little longer - it clocks in at around 40 minutes at most.
* It would be nice to play slightly more than every year - it's kind of unrealistic for people to only talk once every year, and a lot could happen inbetween
* It would be nice if the player was given the option to speak to some friend aside from Emily to help shape the story - lots of things that happen are out of the player's control and you're just like "oh okay whatever". Like you don't HAVE to speak to other characters as you do with Emily, but if you want to, you can.
* It would be nice if, like the other characters, you too could alter your bio and information and stuff (unless you were able to and I missed it)
* It would be nice to see multiple endings as opposed to just the one, to help feel you shaped the story.
Still, I really love the game, and the cons are more just things that I would like to see in the game, not that have to be in.

Although I got the game for free, this game is underdeveloped and leaves you hanging with a feeling of emptiness, like nothing was accomplished.
This game has 3 facets:
[Areas]
Most zones are walking simulators with linear puzzles that are supposed to give you a sense of exploration, guess what you don't get given the linearity and dull visuals presented by the near-sighted camera that make everything feel washed out. You will just be trekking through hoping for anything interesting to happen, spoiler, nothing does except moving to the next area.
[Bosses]
The next highlight is the bosses with well crafted drawings/animations but each only having 1 to 3 different attack move, this extends even to the final boss which has a wooping 2 different attack move(1w and 3w lightning spear attacks since the other abilities are re-used)! I had no trouble beating any of them as it doesn't seem like they're fighting you, rather they use their abilities and you might happen to be in the way. Don't even get me started on the hitboxes.
The unresponsive gameplay is going to try its damn hardest to keep you down though.
Can't say they're memorable and I find it funny that some consider the skeleton at the beginning to be a boss when I thought it was going to be the staple enemy, boy was I wrong.
[Story]
Let's not forget the norse mythology-based storyline, which goes for the deep voice of wisdom narrating approach far better executed in games like Ori or Bastion, the drivel spouted is as cursory as one would expect given the short length of the game. I appreciate all mythology normally, but they didn't go out of their way to create a world, they only introduce bosses or other concepts whenever need be. It didn't feel like any of it was tied together since they opted for a "choose your path" gameplay. I guess the icelandic voice was nice.
[Conclusion]
By the time you question why you're playing this game that feels like an unfinished product, you got to the end.
What dissapoints me greatly is the fact that there's like 20 people who worked on this title when the controls and gameplay feel like a flash game from newgrounds, furthermore there's practically no content thus the game can be easily completed in 1 sitting. That's with dragging out certain areas as well like the swamp/lava pit/constellation area.
I appreciate the free weekend, but the game wasn't worthwhile.
To compare to other indie titles like Hyper Light Drifter or Bastion which are very similar but accomplished significantly more in exploration/puzzle-solving and bosses, can't say I recommend.

So far I had a lot of fun with this game, so I have no other option than to click on "recommend", even though I doubt that this game is for everybody. I had an easy start because I had played the predecessor TIS-100. And back then, it didn't take me long to learn TIS-100, so I guess it would have been similar if I had started with Shenzhen I/O right away. However, I am a physics student and had learned some programming at university, even though never assembly programming. More importantly, as physics student I am used to problem solving, and this is something that you should enjoy for Shenzhen I/O. It is a puzzle game after all. Read the manual, look at the example, if you want look at some online tutorials. But even without prior experience, all that shouldn't take to long and you should be quickly able to solve your first puzzles.
The presentation and the story I well done, the soundtrack is enjoyable. The learning curve seems not quite as steep as in TIS-100, none of the puzzles that I have done yet seemed like it needs some magic to be solved. The puzzles are awesome, as always. And there is solitaire, which is the only way to get achievements in the game, at the moment at least.

SHENZHEN I/O is the latest masterpiece from Zachtronics. It builds and expands from TIS-100 by giving you different kinds of parts to work with, with heavy focus on the microcontroller chips in between. The familiar elements of problem-solving, discovery and optimization define their own puzzle subgenre, a "zachlike".
The game starts with an optional real-world quest of assembling your own manual by going to a supply store and buying a three-ring binder and a 5-part divider. Then you print the 40+ page manual and divide the pages according to the instructions. I absolutely loved this part, bringing back memories from my youth when games shipped with real manuals.
The game starts with easy puzzles, which jog you through the assembly language the game uses. Real-world programming experience helps tremendously here. As you progress through the puzzles the difficulty curve picks up delightfully, although I felt the suggested order was somewhat off for a few of them. Luckily the game always offers multiple puzzle options for progression, so you can make progress even if you get stuck on a puzzle.
I've seen some confused opinions about whether the programming in this game is real or not, so take it from a professional software developer: this is real low-level programming, albeit in a very limited fictional environment. This game tickled my brain just like a good programming task does. Too bad it often doesn't make sense to optimize my real world code to this degree!
The game is still listed as early access, although there is already tons of puzzles to solve. I have high hopes for future content, including new chips and parts to play with! The only thing that's sorely missing so far is an editor for building and sharing our own puzzles. It feels like this game was tailormade for Steam Workshop. I'd love to author a few puzzles for my programming friends!

TL;DR - You'll need to like coding and making friends to improve your enjoyment.
I have played this game for a while and I have several friends that have varied experiences in this game. I'll break down them into three separate and simplified categories:
1) Optimisers. These people compete within their circle for better scores, and will get the most out of this game.
People who are good at code and have competed in other zachtronics games will generally be in this category.
2) General. People who played through the game, but do not have much incentive to optimise any of their code due to lack of interest.
Most of the community is here.
3) Casual. People who played through part of the game but has stopped due to it having a steep learning curve or disinterest in the gameplay.
A lot of people are here, and bought the game without enough research, has expectations from previous games, or just do not enjoy the gameplay.
I'll say this much: this game requires you to make friends to have a good time. Yes, in this single player game, having friends helps.
(1) will have many people competing and constantly interacting, (2) will have some friends, but in the same category, they will not have enough incentive to keep going. If you have a lot of friends that have quit or stopped, then some of the experience will be less enjoyable.
I personally fall in category (2). I don't have enough desire to optimise, or desires to keep up with the top. I did not enjoy some of the later puzzles. One of the only reasons I am still here is because I am waiting for the level editor.
I'd place myself in my own separate category that focuses on creating the experience and puzzles I want, as opposed to playing through the campaign that I may not enjoy. I have created several puzzles for the past 2 games, and hopefully for this as well.
Purely singleplayer, it is a mediocre experience. The more you engage with the community on steam and reddit, the better it will be. This is my recommendation.
