This game has good bones but it's a serious departure from TransOcean 1. Where its predecessor was a careful, intricate, satisfying management sim, TO2 is an uncontrollable mess. I attribute this almost exclusively to the lack of pause in the time controller. I get what they were trying to do, but because time never stops you're just frantically pushing through the game mechanics instead of actually enjoying them. It's supposed to be about selecting the best contracts, planning the most efficient routes, building and managing a fleet, and keeping up with objectives and rivals - but when a day goes by every 10 seconds you can't afford to stop and spend a GD second to think about any of it. It plays like a reactionary mobile game instead of a sim. Not to mention the fact that time continues even when you're docking/undocking or in a port loading screen. The hell is that about.
I just feel totally detached from the many great things this game offers. I can only afford two seconds to look at the helpful economic graphs and variety of well-modeled ships. TO1 felt like so much more of a realized world - TO2 might be even better in that regard but I was too busy manically trying to keep up with the game to tell. I severely recommend this series - it is an astounding piece of work as a story (as it is not a game).
There is that strong burst and subsequent emptiness of emotion you get from going through a very captivating ending after a subtle build up you didnt even notice. I felt drawn to the intensity of things in the Visual Novel - from its usual cold, calculating money-talk, to the very sparse burst of vehemently avid emotion. If you've gone through the first episode, you would somehow understand what I mean when I say that you're not captured by the emotions and that the series' selling point isn't any sort of feels; there are some, yes, but there's more to it than that - it's this grasping impact that you cant fully comprehend but can appreciate.
It is, by no means, an easy read if you intend to learn things about the stock market using this material (it covers newer concepts from the first episode), but at the same time this isn't one of those series that just uses a setting as a simple given; all the talk about flow of money and stocks, even if the finer aspects allude you, build the atmosphere and successfully convince you of the importance of the situation via its brevity and complexity.
As with the last one, I find myself rather unreasonably attached to the character and series, taking home a handful of wisdoms I already knew or heard from others but didnt sink in the same way as they did when it was told here. I can acknowledge that a very thinking-heavy novel might not be to everybody's taste, but I am very impressed by this series and would happily recommend it.

tl;dr: If you like Mega Man games you
like this game
Playing through this game the one thing that I kept wondering was, why did people hate it so much?
I've been playing Mega Man games all my life, Mega Man 2 was like my second or third videogame, ever, and the MMX series is one of my all time favorites,  maybe that colors my opinion, but as a fan of this type of game I can say that Mighty No. 9 was exactly what I was looking for when I started playing it.
It plays like a Mega Man with infinitte dashes that can absorb stunned enemies to power up your abilities, this gives it a fast pace that I particularly enjoyed myself to be honest.
Besides the infitnite dashes there are ffew other innovations to the classic formula, but Mighty No. 9 is a classic Mega Man game at its core, it changes enough things to be its own game, but it still retains everything that made the Mega Man games fun and addictive.
Now I got the game on sale and I wasnt a backer, I also encountered but one glitch through the entire game, so, again, that may color my opinion, but after having played through the game I can say I would have been ok with paying full price for it, its just what I had expected the game to be when I first heard about it, and in my opinion any fan of the Mega Man series gameplay should like it, whatever controversy might have come around the game, the game itself is a solid Mega Man game, fun, fast, tight gameplay, classic gameplay, new features, its got everything for a Mega Man fan to enjoy the game.
The game is not groundbreaking, nor are the graphics last gen, and I personally would have enjoyed a longer ending, if any of those are a deal breaker for you, or if you have some personal grievance against the game, then it might best to pass on it, but if you just enjoy Mega Man gameplay, with fast pace, and good controls, then you should definitely give it a try, its worth it.

Wanted to also mention that I backed the kickstarter for this game and waited some time after launch for Inafune's team to patch it.
This is also my first negative review and it's a shame it had to be the spiritual successor to Megaman, so I'll delve deep into this one.
The music is 'ok' and the plot is enough to wrap this new world together, other mighty's make cameo's in levels making you feel like there's more going on than just you jumping from level to level. That's it really.
The general look of the game and the move to 3D (this is subjective I realise that, however it takes away from the charm of all previous Megaman titles), the weak gameplay mechanics (combo's, dashing), really and I mean really poor dialogue and lazy cutscenes/animations take away from what made the old games so amazing and fails at setting this game up as a noteworthy contender in recent times.
Beck's base movement speed is really slow so you'll to have to rely on the "dash" ability for speed.
See, if the dash was there purely for movement purposes then it could be tolerated, but unfortunately the added mechanic for Beck is to use it to get near weakened enemies to either destroy them or damage them (bosses). This simply adds to the general awkwardness in some levels and is the cause of many deaths due to poor handling and timing of the dash. You'll very often plough straight into an enemy when trying to absorb them then get hit by them/an attack (as any contact with an enemy damages you), dash into the many one-hit kill zones or overshoot ledges which in some levels is an insta-death. The dash acts as intended and by design but I feel other games implemented this better.
I also feel they took on more of a speed run approach to this game rather than an actual platformer.
Combo meters? Racking up kills? Performing the fastest most efficient level run? This doesn't feel like a megaman successor but more a Supermeat Boy meets SpeedRunners type of game, level knowledge is key to your success and expect to die many times over as you learn each level in order to get your best 'run' and level rating.
The learning curve is also very steep on each level, and I don't mean the difficulty in particular, but the rate at which new features are introduced which mostly result in Beck's demise, topple that with Beck's awkward movement and you get some really frustrating levels. The game almost expects you to memorise where everything is in order to enjoy it. The thing is that for most of us we won't be going back to play through a level again for a better time so the bitter experience of each level stays with the player.
The MegamanX series also had hidden armour elements which actually created a purpose to re-visit levels, to explore hidden nooks and cranies. Might No.9 instead rewards players with temporary damage/speed/armour buffs and health pickups which add nothing other than boost your score.
The lack of being able to charge your basic attack also feels like an attempt to force the player to move faster through a level. The developers don't seem to want the player to linger around chipping away at enemies and pre-charging your attacks to kill a tough enemy or boss faster, you have to constantly dash. I can appreciate what they wanted to achieve with this, but by doing so it moves the game into the extreme gamer category rather than the casual gamer one.
I really enjoyed seeing each boss have their own personality, voice acting for some of them was even tolerable and especially how they assist you in future levels.
This is a dynamic I wish they'd explored more of because it actually felt unique.
However the boss fights themselves were really dissapointing. Learning patterns is one thing, but having each attack take a quarter of your life away (some hit sequences hitting you twice) in a single hit is not my idea of a good time nor does it reward the player in any way. I never felt like I achieved anything by defeating a boss, there was no sense of accomplishment. Instead I felt like I simply persevered long enough to outlast a boss or manage to do enough damage during being hit (invincible time) to make it even matter. Even the original Megaman wasn't this brutal when it came to learning boss patterns. Bosses in Might No.9 move laughingly faster than you and in some instances simply run at you to give you damage by touch and not an actual attack.
Special mention is the Ice boss which is downright frustrating at even the best of attempts and the reason why?
Being frozen by an enemy lasts a ridiculous amount of time, wish to reduce that by only a second? Mash every key for a few seconds and this might be enough for you to get out just in the nick of time - and only that, you won't get an edge. Being frozen feels like a chore in Might No.9.
The Ice boss fight includes this and it is infuriating each time to have your effort in weakening an enemy taken away by a single frozen moment as the boss regenerates their health back and robs you of yet another attempt. I've played through a number of 'platformers' such as this, I can accept a hard boss fight, but a poorly designed game mechanic does not make for an entertaining boss encounter.
I managed to last through 5 Mighty boss encounters/levels before the constant dying to new bosses swayed me to quit. It's a pretty dissapointing way to end a game, with a frown rather than a smile.
I think what it really comes down to is that this game is missing the 'fun' factor and instead strives to be a hardcore speedrun platform for the extremists. Don't bother with this and instead go to any number of the existing indie games that manage the megaman-esque gamplay better, that or get the Megaman Legacy Collection and take a trip down memory lane.
At no point did I feel like something 'awesome' happened while playing Might No.9, the bad things chipped away at my enjoyment and that's all that remains in the end, a sour and bitter taste because you're more likely to quit the game mid-level than with a sense of accomplishment at its completion.

This game is a wonderful logistic puzzle simulator.
There are a lot of machines to build and technologies to research. As you climb higher on the tech tree, the resources needed to craft each part increase exponentially (because they're made of some number of parts from lower in the tree). Each part needs to be crafted, so you'll have to build machines to do the crafting for you. Then you'll build machines to build the machines.
You will need a LOT of resources to craft into a victory, so you'll need to build trains to haul resources from remote patches back to your assembly line. When the assembly line gets too complex, you'll build robots to haul parts around.
Endgame parts require tens of thousands of tier 1 parts, so you will need to build a huge factory to win in a reasonable time. Watching my factory process multiple tons of raw material per minute is enough to give me the nerd chills.

WORLD END ECONOMiCA episode.02 is a kinetic visual novel which is a continuation of episode.01. It is written by the same author who wrote Spice and Wolf. Unlike the first episode, the story does not mention too much about economics, thus a basic understanding of economic concepts is not required to fully enjoy the novel.
Story: The story for this episode is okay. It talks about the events that happen four years after Haru, the main character, had suffered from the events from the previous episode. Not too much happens, mainly character development. The plot is mostly about how Haru struggles to conquer his past, and how he tries his hardest to help others so that he does not make the same mistakes as he had done in the past. I really missed the heavy amount of economics which is in the first episode, although this episode did talk about market bubbles and accounting scandals. I would rate the story 7/10.
Characters: Other than Haru, a few of the characters from the previous episode, Cerrow, Risa and Chris, returned to in this episode. I really like how the characters changed and matured after four years. Haru is a lot more mature and considerate, Chris is less shy, Cerrow has a job as an actual programmer now. A new main character, Eleanor, was introduced. Eleanor's character design was okay. I feel the princess/rich girl side of her was too cliche though. A few minor characters, Le Geoff, Marco and Rena, where introduced, but they did not really add to the plot. Rena helped Haru with his inner turmoil and helped him with some task after, but the other characters did not really do anything. Overall, I would rate the characters 8/10
Music: The music is okay. About the same quality as the previous episode. Some tracks were reused from the previous episode. I would rate it 7.5/10.
Artwork: The artwork is pretty nice. I still feel there are a bit too many reused scenes, and too many times when the background was blank/just all black. It is an improvement from the previous episode though. I would rate it 7/10.
Overall: I would rate it 7/10. Maybe it is because this is the second episode out of three episodes, but I feel nothing too significant happened, other than the introduction of the new character, Eleanor. The plot is still well done, tying up some loose ends from the previous episode. There are a lot more typos, and grammatical errors in this episode. I really hate how some of the names changed from the previous episode. I hope the developers fix the names and the typos/grammatical errors in the future.

This is my first building game I've given a try. Yes, I've tried Minecraft but it didn't do it for me. This however...boy, 20 hours in just a couple of days.
The building is in a simplistic manner but the structures you can create with it are phenomenal. If I browse the workshop and see Edoras and Helsmdeep popping up then I really applaud those that have taken the time to work on that.
Which brings me to one of the, for me, stronger points of Medieval Engineers, and that is the Structural Integrity. Most building games allow you to build stuff, despite what physics would say. The game would give the finger to physics in order for the player, to achieve a creative structure. Medieval Engineers has the possibility to turn physics off so that buildings might be build according to player creativity.
Yet, building a structure with Structural Integrity on, has given me that edge to go and create. Is it physically possible to build this? If not, the building will crumble before your eyes!
Which brings me to the next part, the destruction. It's great to see a structure take shape over the hours of building, but it's even more rewarding, I'd say, to see them crumble down into tiny little pieces when you throw a cannonball at it. It's just magnificent to see and behold how an entire tower crumbles into nothingness. Plus you can test how your structure would fair in an assault!
There are still many things missing, the amount of blocks for example are, good enough to create many structures, but sometimes you lack specific blocks to really create the structure you want. I do think, that more blocks will be added in the future.
Another strong point of the game is terraforming, creating the land in order to suit your building. If you want a mountainstronghold with paths through the mountain, you can go and shape that mountain, shape the paths and, endless possibilities in that regard.
In contrast to other games, on which I have little knowledge, I find this one to be peacefull, thanks to the music which is really  awesome and lets time fly by. Definately a must play if you like building games such as Minecraft

AVSEQ is weird. WEIRD. It is an audio-visual sequencer puzzle game. That much is obvious once you look at any screenshots of it. It is bright, it is nice, it is confusing. Yes, confusing. See, the aim of the game is to add the required number of notes using these steps:
1) to connect falling atoms of the same color
2) using the white atoms to bridge different colors together (optional but longer strings equals higher points and more chances of notes to appear)
3) detonate them before any of the atoms in the string touches the bottom (failing which the entire string goes *poof* and some notes disappear)
4) chain up notes when they appear (notes act like white atoms) and reach the target
The confusing part? The background is nice and all but sometimes you can't see a thing and speed is of the essence here. There is 9 different stages and when beat, every stage unlock an infinite mode. However if you are aiming for the note achievements, take note that playing infinite mode refreshes your note count. Also, the game doesn't track progress for achievements so you have to do it in one sitting.

There is some minimal music generation using this game, but mainly, you are playing a tetris-like game combined with color matching.
The later levels get very difficult very fast.
I wish it had a sandbox mode we could compose music in.

This is a simple game, but I'm not really sure how to categorize it.  It's kind of a mix of rhythm, skill, and puzzle.  It's definitely unique, and I enjoy playing it during down time.  Basially, each level starts with a beat and fragments of notes will fall from the sky.  You match togetehr similarlly colored fragments into a chain of up to 8 pieces, and then release the chain to gather points.  However, the skill comes in as the notes are falling quickly and the chain isn't released instantly, so you need to time it out to make sure you don't lose the note fragments.
As the game goes on and you gather more fragments you gain "notes" that change the song of the level, slowly climaxing until the entire song is revealed, which I found to be quite well done.
As said, it's deceptively simple, easy to pick up, hard to master, and a lot of fun for down-time gaming.  It's not something you can play constantly for weeks on end, but as far as a "puzzle" game or other little skill game that sits in your library where you pick it up every once in awhile AVSEQ certainly fits the bill.  I would recommend any type of gamer to pick it up if you're looking for something to break the monotony every once in awhile.

Factorio is one of those games that fits a niche market. On the surface, gameplay is very simple once the basics are learned. The depth comes not from the content itself, but from the complex systems a player must design to fully automate progression. it can be fun to take systems and try to improve them slightly to increase efficiency, but once you find the way to automate processes most efficiently, I find the challenge drops sharply. If you are an achievement hunter, be prepared for quite a tedious grind. Worst grind example is likely making 20 million electronic circuits, and yes they are produced one at a time. If you don't mind the grind, it is fun to try to create a modular automation system to increase production speed, but that is the game in a nutshell.
I have played the game on Windows and Mac systems and have yet to run into any serious performance issues. For gamers of any supported platform who are just a little bit masochistic, this title can be used to pass time in short sessions.

In spite of the rocky and now-infamous Kickstarter history surrounding this game, I came into as a $20 experience of a Megaman-like game. Megaman was never a particularly large or perfect game series to me, and so I can't say I was disappointed in Mighty Number 9.
It's a fun run-and-jump shooter using a dash mechanic to mix it up and introduce a bit more depth and movement capability than in traditional Megaman games (if anything, it's a mix of the Megaman Zero design with some of the traditional games). When I discovered that I could continuously dash in mid-air and didn't need to directly hit an enemy to absorb it, it felt like there was a new amount of energy to the experience and gave me a number of options to dealing with the challenges. The main story mode is short, and lacks in production values, but has some good touches to it that lends personality to the Mighty Numbers and kicks off a universe that I would be interested in seeing grow.
Replayability helps this game a lot, and I'd say your enjoyment stems from how much you like pushing yourself to complete challenges and perfect various stages. There are various things that pull the game back, but the most egregious ones are surface level; if the look of the game doesn't bug you, then give it a shot. I've only completed the game once so far and put time into boss rush mode, but I can see myself playing Mighty Number 9 again and again.

On the contrary of Megaman fans, I like this game a lot. It brought an interesting redesign of Megaman into the ring again. Of course, I am judging this gameplay wise over how Megaman-ish it is. Granted, it is quite unoriginal to reskin Megaman and go from there, but this game is still fun.

The second installment of WORLD END ECONOMiCA is an improvement over the first in almost every regard. The story picks up four years after the end of the first episode, and we're once again placed in appropriately renamed protagonist Haru's shoes. Where the first episode was in many ways a confrontation of Neoliberal logic and an educational piece about modern finance, the second episode is far more of a personal story, it's not quite about the vagaries of market logic and people's place within it as the first one was; instead, it is in many ways about living with guilt & regret, dealing with loss and what it means to struggle from a position of powerlessness.
Compared to the first episode, the visuals in ep. 2 are better in every way - the character art in particular is much improved, especially in terms of proportions, and the backgrounds & CG scenes are well done and do a much better job of giving a more distinct feel to the sci-fi setting. In terms of sound and music, everything is still quite adequate (only adequate, mind you), but there could still be more variety & restraint in terms of music. Silence would have served the VN quite well in some moments. As for the story, it is, as expected, quite good: interesting and informative as always, and the emotional tone is something of a long slow burn, compared to the bipolar highs and lows and emotional gut punches of the first episode.
As before, I'd continue to recommend this series to its intended audience of political economy/anime nerds, as well as anyone else who might be interested. Really, the only black mark on this installment as compared to the first is a distinct and shocking absence of any autistic Jewish waifus.

Brutal singleplayer deckbuilder with a unique and beautiful art style. It's really its own beast- it doesn't play like your typical deckbuilder, but has its own ebb and flow that I find very satisfying.
Here's the basic game flow- you start with a handful of food and wood, and a couple survivors. You use your survivors to gain more resources, which you'll need to gain idea cards and to pass the area. Ideas are extremely useful and give you better access to resources, thin your deck, or remove negative cards. On the other hand, you only have a limited amount of time total to bypass a certain number of areas, so you can't usually dawdle around and just build a lot of ideas. But if you don't build enough ideas, then you'll be doomed when a particularly difficult area arises.
Each area also has an encounter- sometimes friendly, sometimes not. Not all encounters are difficult, but they always throw a wrinkle in your plan.
You're always pushed forwards, but additional ideas are unlocked for each turn you stay in an area. It's often a difficult decision- do I stall for a turn or two to gain an excellent card, or do I forge onwards and hope it doesn't matter? The right choice isn't always obvious for a couple of areas, so learning what sorts of threats are likely to be ahead of you matters.
Additionally, more interesting cards and obstacles and areas are unlocked as you play. It's really a fascinating game, and there's nothing quite like it.

The artwork looks simple, but it's quite beautiful. The entire atmosphere of the game is oddly relaxing, like a quiet day in the woods (or, given the theme, a snowy woods).

Frost is a rogue-lite deck management (NOT building) game where you have to juggle your hand and deck, which contain a number of resources, against the environment, which you need a number of resources to do. There are wrenches thrown in, like idea cards where you can sacrifice resources to now for various benefits later, and fatigue, which decreases your maximum hand size until you find ways to deal with it.
The game has various win and lose objectives, and a "death wall" turn timer that constantly pushes you forward so you don't farm a nice region for too long. It works really well. There are a variety of options you can select to customize your custom game, like how far you have to travel and how many epic regions (more difficult) are in the deck. Plus there then are specially-defined scenarios to challenge you with once you have mastered the base game.
The main downside of the game for me is that you can't customize the deck, thus why this is a "deck management" game and not a "deck builder" game. This camouflages another downside - that there aren't that many different cards of each type. There are 54 idea cards, 28 event cards, and some unknown number of region cards, probably around 20-30 or so. You unlock more cards by completing games, win or lose.
They are selected randomly each game and the issue with that is that there are some cards that are almost entirely superceded by a stronger version of the card (like Story Stone vs Shelter), Therefore when the weaker version comes up in a draw it is usually a waste, because I know the stronger version exists, and have so many other things to buy with my resources.
Still, overall, the game is fun. If you enjoy card games, what is currently in the game should be good for 10-20 hours of gameplay if you are attempting to complete all the scenarios. Each successfully completed game should take you around 20-40 minutes, with failed games depending on how long you survive. Also as other reviews have pointed out, there is a demo available on Steam, and trying that is ultimately what influenced my decision to buy it.

If you can look past the antiquated, cartoonish graphics, this flight sim will provide you with hours of challenging fun. One of my personal all-time favorites, F-117A Nighthawk Stealth Fighter 2.0 is the sequel to the ground-breaking 1988 stealth flight simulator F-19 Stealth Fighter. If you like stealth games, this one's for you. Attack Saddam Hussein's palace in the Desert Storm campaign, blow up a submarine pen in the North Cape, take off from Key West, Florida and attack targets in Cuba, storm the Iron Curtain in the Central European campaign, take out (virtual) targets in North Korea, Vietnam, and many other scenarios. Each mission is different; no two missions are alike. Choose between the more realistic Lockheed version, or play Microprose's version (bullets, two more weapons bays, and Sidewinder and AMRAAM air-to-air missiles).
The game comes with the manual (for free) in PDF format. The manual will automatically be downloaded into your "\SteamLibrary\SteamApps\common\F-117A NightHawk Stealth Fighter" folder when you download the main game itself. You will need the free Adobe Reader to view it.
Also, the control instructions are included. The file is called F-177A Key Control Card.PDF and is located in the "Bonus Content" folder. It is a necessity for people who are unfamiliar with the game's controls.
You can use the DosBox DAUM mode for better compatibility with more modern computers. Press Ctrl+V to turn off the shrill engine sound, if it bothers you. Also, to get the game to perform smoother and play faster, go into windowed mode (Alt+Enter) and press Ctrl+F12 several times until it gets up to 15,000 cycles. Make sure you do this before you calibrate your joystick at the game's startup menu. Then you can go back into fullscreen mode (Alt+Enter), if you wish.
Buy this game. Seriously, it's worth every penny. Plus, you'll have it on your Steam account forever.

Jotun is a beautiful but incredibly simple game. The controls are kinda clunky and slow, but the focus is mostly on exploring the maps and solving puzzles involving the environment to unlock all landmarks and upgrades.
For a game about vikings and combat, however, the combat is arguably the weakest aspect of the game. For the most part it's not too terrible as the maps typically account for its clunkiness, but your basic attack is incredibly slow, and your heavy attack is even slower. You have powers you can use to assist you with the combat, providing really basic buffs like more movement / attack speed, or healing, but combat mostly consists of 'attack, attack, attack, roll, attack.' There are no variants on your moves so attacking feels very repetitive and stale. It does not feel fun or satisfying to fight, or to even control your character in combat sequences, and that's a major let down. Walking is slow, and rolling has a pause added in that just doesn't feel good, especially when fighting.
Fighting sections are few and far between. Most of the maps involve navigating hazards, not foes. If it were first person it'd definitely be a walking simulator--that said, I still found the maps interesting, and as they made up a good majority of the game, the exploration is why I still have to recommend it. While some maps have enemies, your attacks in most others are used for activating switches or opening pathways. The artwork is superb, including bits of Norse lore with matching art upon finding landmarks, and a lot of the puzzles or even just the exploration elements were pleasing to solve.
The lackluster combat is also made up for slightly by the bosses at least having interesting mechanics that require more a focus on your positioning. I learned about some of the environmental hazards the bosses can bring upon themselves in the middle of combat which felt incredibly satisfying to turn on them, and as a result most of the bosses were pretty enjoyable despite how overly simple fighting was. Environmental weapons proved to do a huge chunk of my damage, as the basic attacks are so slow and only do a minor amount of damage.
Unfortunately, and this might be slightly spoilery, but the very final boss however is incredibly rage inducing and I pity anyone who attempts it without getting all health and power upgrades first. He's not challenging, just frustrating and dull, with only one actual attack. There are no environmental elements you can turn against him, it's mostly just a fight of you dodging his homing projectiles that have a very large (too large probably, it felt like it extended outside of the graphic) hitbox by rolling at the last second at a perpendicular angle. As artificially hard as this fight is, it's also boring for this reason, as there is only one strategy you can adopt, and it's the simplest one available. The last boss is frustratingly and lazily designed, and was a huge let down compared to the prior ones, both visually and mechanically.
It's fine to rely on player skill, such as their ability to dodge for a fight's mechanics, but with how slow it is to chip away at a boss's health due to the poor attack handling, there should be some reward for good play. E.g., maybe have the projectiles deal damage back to him if you successfully dodge? For the latter part of the fight it becomes a mess as well for reasons I won't spoil, but it becomes majorily dependent on luck, hoping you don't get screwed over by the arena layout.
Honestly, the final fight was almost enough to flip my opinion on this game. However, I still think if you know what you're getting into you'll still enjoy it. Don't expect anything revolutionary, and aside from the bosses it'll be a pretty laid back, slow-and-steady experience.

I mostly read negative comments about it. Nevertheless, I wanted to try the game out myself. After months of waiting with fading expectations in light of the destructive reviews and comments, it was finally released for Mac.
Well, okay, it took very long. I could be upset about it, but I’m not. Too often I have seen and experienced things thrown on the market prematurely (e.g. Microsoft software, music…), just because people asked for them.
Comcept & the others have taken their time instead. In my opinion, this was the right decision. Firstly, anticipation is the greatest joy, secondly, in spite of many opinions, they created a well working product. Of course there are always some smaller bugs, but the game’s perfectly running on my MacBook Pro. That’s how I expect it to be. I simply would not benefit from an unfinished product.
Whew, it’s hard and really challenging! At least for me as a person who has not played for a longer while. I guess that’s its problem. Gamers today are not patient as they used to be 25 years ago, when Mega Man was created. It was normal to try, fail, retry, fail again and so on at the time. I can remember my friends and myself smashing the NES controllers on the floor, because we f***ed it up again and again, but we were so ambitious to make it, and we made progresses until we made it in the end.
So from this point of view, Mighty No. 9 is a really worthy successor of my beloved Mega Man series!
Although it is that hard, the controls are so simple and intuitive! You get used to them very fast, and that makes the game more fun in my opinion. As soon as you get used to the elements displayed on the screen and their meanings, there’s a lot less distraction so that you can focus on the actual game.
The graphics are not bad at all. Okay, they are not the state-of-the-art kind of graphics and if you ask me, the characters’ faces could have been less “flat” - but for this type of game, they are quite impressive and colorful.
The soundtrack is probably not as memorable as those from the Mega Man series, but still there is the one or the other really good piece of music! What I find a bit disturbing is that Beck, the character you play, is permanently commenting your actions, as well as all the other talking during the game. Especially if you’re not a native Japanese, English or French speaker, because then you might be distracted by reading the subtitles, if you want to fully understand what is being said. It would be cool if at least the commenting could be muted.
Overall, I am quite happy with the game and I’m looking forward to getting my new gamepad, as my current one has terribly loud buttons. When that problem is solved, I’ll be pretty happy playing Mighty No. 9, as I have already become a bit addicted to it.
Be patient, learn from mistakes, develop a system to defeat enemies and bosses – that’s the core of the game and what makes it cool for me! If you can’t, this would probably be the wrong game for you.

How do I explain Mighty No. 9? To put it simply, it's like that kid at school who goes around saying he's ♥♥♥♥ed the hottest girls, but really hes a ugly little♥♥♥♥♥♥with no game. Mighty No. 9 tries so hard to be good and "modern", and thats its weakness. It's supposed to be a spiritual succesor to megaman, yet it focuses so much on being modern that it pulls away from the retro aspects of the megaman games that made them fun. Now, let me clarify, while the game is bad, that doesnt mean it doesnt have good areas. It controls really well, and with the abilities you're given, it fits perfectly for a shoot-em-up platformer, but it lacks the proper level design to go with the control style and abilities it gives you. The amount of times I've died on a level because I was moving way too fast in the air and ended up hitting spikes that were on the wall is countless, and and once you get moving, it becomes hard to slow down, which is mainly due to how tight the areas can be sometimes. This game is a wonderful logistic puzzle simulator.
There are a lot of machines to build and technologies to research. As you climb higher on the tech tree, the resources needed to craft each part increase exponentially (because they're made of some number of parts from lower in the tree). Each part needs to be crafted, so you'll have to build machines to do the crafting for you. Then you'll build machines to build the machines.
You will need a LOT of resources to craft into a victory, so you'll need to build trains to haul resources from remote patches back to your assembly line. When the assembly line gets too complex, you'll build robots to haul parts around.
Endgame parts require tens of thousands of tier 1 parts, so you will need to build a huge factory to win in a reasonable time. Watching my factory process multiple tons of raw material per minute is enough to give me the nerd chills.

WEE Episode 2 begins 4 years after the ending events of Episode 1. In the time between the main character has changed from the punk with attitude to a respectable young man who has learned his limits, and along with those changes he also learned how little he truly knew about the world back then. There is a clear schism between how this one plays out from the first. While the first episode felt fairly childish and cliched, falling back on common tropes a number of times, this one is focused on telling the more mature story the first one set up. The childish dreams were shattered, and in the place of those dreams the protagonist was forced by the world to mature. Not the arrogant "I'm more mature than you" mature that he was in the first, but legitimate personal growth. Because he was forced into that growth he was still not able to cope with his actions though, and the reader will get to see how that still affects him 4 years after the fact.
In this episode you can expect a few less walls of text attempting to inform the reader about stocks, and in the place of infodumps the reader is treated to a lot more character development and relationship building than the first. This isn't to say the infodumps that (fairly poorly) attempt to teach the reader about different aspects of the stock market don't exist, but rather that aspect of the storytelling has definitely been dialed down for the better.
In place of the explanations readers are instead treated with a continuation of the plot that started developing wonderfully toward the end of Episode 1 regarding all of the corruption going on. There are many victories and defeats for the protagonists along their journey along with a pace that accelerates towards the end leaving you begging for more as the credits roll. Unfortunately (fortunately?) the ending of this one leaves on a great cliffhanger (thankfully not wheelchairs and missing tsundere) that will have you waiting impatiently for the final episode to release.
Improvements all around make this a must try for any fan of visual novels, but this is still WEE so if the first wasn't your fancy this probably won't catch your fancy either.
Overall:
8.5/10

World End Economica episode.02 is a kinetic visual novel, meaning the player faces no choices during the story. It continues the story-telling method of the previous episode with no voice acting, thematic background music and overlaying effects without other animation to the graphics. The engine has faced some improvements with font choice and text log (not rewinding as in the previous episode).
It continues four years after the events of the first episode. Stock trading takes more of a backseat this time around and while the world of economics is still the backdrop, more focus is had on the characters and their struggles. First, if you’d like to see gameplay footage and a bit of review, check out my video here:
If you’d rather do that whole reading thing, well, keep reading.
Frost is a deck building-ish game that board gamers will feel right at home with; it provides an interesting take on the genre, at a great price, with many interesting decisions to make as you play. It’s mechanically solid and definitely entertaining though I’m not sure how much longevity it will have in the long run. That being said, I’ve enjoyed my time with it and will certainly boot it up from time to time.
If you’ve seen any of my videos before this, you know I’m a huge nerd and lover of board games. I was initially drawn to Frost exactly because of that; a deckbuilding game that only exists in digital form. As much as I love board games (especially cool solo games) it can be a hassle to actually get the damn things out and play them (not to mention time consuming). So this seemed right up my alley, a cool card game to pick up and play easily on my laptop.
Let’s just get the production value/graphics/sound out of the way; if you’re someone who likes super-slick graphic design and sound, you’re going to have a hard time getting into it. I find the art and (very minimal) sound kind of charming and enjoyed it. In no way did it detract from my experience, but I’m also the kind of guy that still periodically boots up the original X-Com and has no problem diving into that game. So yes, the art and minimal soundtrack/effects are functional but remember, this is an indie game and it shows. Functionally though, it’s great; there are very few things that are unclear how to interact with so UI wise, pretty rock solid.
That leaves us with the gameplay and experience. Every game has you basically trying to get to the refuge (or completing other objectives depending on difficulty) with very limited resources while a wall of cold chases you; think Day After Tomorrow but, you know, actually entertaining.
I call it a “deck building-ish” game because it does break considerably from the genre. Most deck building games have you purchasing more powerful cards and adding them to your deck. Although there ARE cards you “purchase” by permanently discarding resources, the majority of cards you add to your deck come instead from searching for resources using your people (also a resource).
And boy do you need every last resource. Besides balancing your deck “construction” (and trying to remember what the hell you have in there) every region you move through has different resource requirements. They’re not permanently discarded, just used for the region and reshuffled into your deck afterward; but gain too much of any one resource and you might find yourself out of luck trying to draw the right cards. But hey, you’ve got plenty of time to get it right, right?
Noooope. There is the constant threat of the frost wall. You’re always under pressure to keep moving towards your goal but there is always so much to accomplish. You have to carefully weigh whether it’s worth sticking around to try and acquire some sweet cards that come up, or take a turn to rest and get rid of your fatigue (cards that do literally nothing…a lot like me in real life). Several cards also have multiple uses, so there’s another layer of choice to how you want to use what you’ve already got. But at least all you have to do is get through the regions, right? RIGHT?
Double noooope. On top of all that, there are event cards that come up for every region (and sometimes the weather is so cold that you draw less cards). Granted, not all of these cards are bad, in fact, several are very beneficial and either allow you to heal or give you a chance to acquire more resources. But there are plenty that can damage you or your people or are just generally scary.
So what does this all add up to? A pretty damn entertaining game. There are plenty of decisions, it’s well paced and the UI is fantastic; it’s easy to play and know what you’re doing. Besides, cool theme bro.
Its simplicity may ultimately be its downfall though; after you’ve played the game several times, you know exactly what you’re getting. It does help that as you play you unlock new cards and new scenarios (which I haven’t touched yet, just been playing the base game). As a frequent board game player, honestly this doesn’t bother me; I’m used to learning a game, figuring out all it has to offer and then using the knowledge to play it better and better.
Which is also part of the beauty of it all; you learn. This game isn’t insanely hard but it is difficult, and as you play you learn how to better manipulate your deck and improve your gameplay. You learn what’s important and how to survive in the long run.
As a fun board game like diversion, I’d definitely recommend this game. You get a lot for your money and much like any other solo board game, it’s something you can pick up from time to time and just enjoy without having to commit to hours and hours of gameplay. Also, if you’ve never played a deck building-ish game, it’s not a bad place to start.

If you love deck-building games like Dominion and Ascension, then this game is for you! Try the demo, you'll probably be hooked like me! There is a lot going on during the tutorial, but once you get the mechanics down this game is loads of fun! You are playing a traveler through the white wastes of the north, with a storm known as the Frost always at your back. Each time you achieve your objective in a region (by collecting a certain number as determined by the region), you progress, and the Frost gets one step further behind. Each time you dawdle in a region, the Frost gets one step closer. If the Frost catches you, you die! There are three kinds of resource cards: Survivors (people, who can gather more supplies), wood, and food, which are used to progress through the regions. There are also "Idea" cards that you can buy with resources, making more powerful versions of the resources with added benefits. As you play more games, you unlock variations of these resources (like a card that sets the Frost counter back by one, giving you another turn, or a trader who can trade food into wood, etc.). You build your hand, make a strategy, and try to stay alive.
That's just the basic game! A "temperature" gage dictated by the region's weather, alters the number of cards you draw in each turn, and there are fights with wolves and scavengers that can cause health damage if you don't fend them off. There are also trade opportunities that come up at random, giving you a chance to get rid of a surplus of one resource in favor of that one you really need. There are also scenarios where you play as a special character with unique powers. (Ex. the hunter can give up heath for attack, or create food by hunting; the tracker walks a lonely path and therefore doesn't have any survivor resources). You have a specific goal for each character that you must achieve under their limitations (Ex: The hunter must fight the tough-to-beat Bear God; the tracker must defeat the enemy that killed her father then travel to a certain area to deliver her father's talisman). Once you beat (some of) these scenarios, you can play the regular game with the unlocked characters. There's also an endless mode, where you just try to survive as long as possible.
I've unlocked all the characters, beaten all the scenarios, unlocked all the cards, and spent something like 36 hours playing and I'm not even sick of it! For $6.99 at full price, you can't say no!

Yeah, not a big fan. This game isn't really bad, it's just mediocre enough for me, having gotten it free for it's free to keep weekend (thanks for that BTW devs, even if I didn't enjoy your game it's a pretty good practice and a nice show of faith if you're giving away a game that you know not everyone's gonna enjoy), to not want to continue playing it after my first playsession of beating 3 of the Jotun avaliable.
Elephant in the room, the art's great. You should be able to tell that by just looking at screenshots. Voice acting's also pretty good as far as I can tell.
Now, for the problems I personally experienced that turned me off:
They have 2 optional upgrades hidden in each zone, as well as the rune to show you've beat it so you can progress to the Jotun, and that's it. In most games that use a gameplay format comparable to this (Megaman or Dark Souls would be the ones I'd relate most), the levels are, while not necessarily as iconic as the bosses, very important and pretty memorable parts of the game. Jotun's levels aren't that, and I feel like I just want to get to the boss already.
The simple problem I can state with the levels are that they drag on for too long for too little content. The introductory level is fine enough because its length allows players to get used to the game before fighting their first boss, but later levels are far too monotonous because they stick around longer than they're welcome. The Roots of Yggdrasil level introduces the idea of sliding on roots, for example. This is used at the end of the level for a gigantic slide sequence, but not before the game wastes about 10-15 minutes of your time with you repeatedly sliding down roots, potentially even using geysers to bounce back up to do it again looking for secrets- And there's ONE collectable in this entire timewaster with no enemies to fight or anything else for me to be looking out for (some stalactites fell a couple of times, that was it).
That level's mechanical value is one collectable, and one mechanic that as far as I could tell won't be used again. And because they can't have a level that lasts around 2 minutes, they add a crapton of filler into it before the level's actual content which is the slide secret. A similar thing goes for the Crater level, which introduces rock-throwing enemies, keeps them around longer than I was willing to fight them and therefore I got bored fast, then introduced the idea of using their rocks to build bridges in lava, which interested me at first, but then that mechanic also got over-used, and once again because there's only 1-2 collectables each level, I once again got bored fast.
If there's one thing I can criticise Jotun's level design for, it's telling the player things through level design is done very, very wrong. Jotun appears to be almost incapable of it, and when it does do it, it gives you information that's outright not correct.
For example, the crater level. During Chris Redfield's bridge building classes, I realized according to the map a shrine was pretty far away. I had noticed up until this point that sword icons in the ground made from lava seemed to be indicating where I should be building bridges up until this point, so when I saw one pointing roughly in the direction of the shrine, and the game dropped a huge number of rock-throwers near me, I assumed "Okay, the game's trusting me to build a really big bridge here in the rough direction of the shrine". I was completely wrong and I'm not the only person to make a similar mistake. Turns out, the sword icons are meaningless decoration.
Similar thing goes with the intro level. When I started, I ended up seeing giant roots blocking my path, attacking them didn't work, and heard Odin say something along the lines of me needing seals to progress. I assumed that the roots were blockages to stop me from going further and assumed I had missed a level entrance. Once again, wrong, you need to POWER ATTACK the roots (which the game never tells you how to do, so players have no idea that's what they're meant to do in this situation) and I ended up wasting time- But I maintain that's the game's fault here. Involved playtesting would have discovered this problem, and it's easily fixed by only playing this dialogue after you destroy at least one root- Me trying to see if I had a stronger attack would have been my natural reaction had the game not told me I needed seals to go any further.
These wouldn't be too major problems if Jotun didn't try to teach players through smart level design instead of straight-up tutorials. If you take the "Let players figure it out" approach, you CANNOT make mistakes like the ones demonstrated above, and considering 2/3 of the zones I experienced had one of these issues (one of which including the Ymir's Blood level, which I've heard good things about and I enjoyed a fair bit despite also being a long level with minimal gameplay elements for the amount of distance I was travelling. The story sprinkled in actually made the level feel worth it to some extent.) I'd say it's unlikely the other levels have a drastic improvement I haven't heard about.
Other stuff I'd list would probably be considered more on the side of nitpicks (The game's combat is very stiff FYI. For me that wasn't much of an issue, some will hate it), so I'll just summarise: Jotun's levels drag the game down to a snail's pace even if you're just casually going for a few collectables, and they're very poorly made all around due to being extended longer than they're worth, having poor design and simply not being very fun as opposed to the bosses, and the bosses, while fine, were not enough to motivate me to keep going. Had they been back-to-back bosses, or if I was actually enjoying the levels I would almost certainly have continued playing further, but Jotun can't really decide which it wants to go for.

A great TRPG based on Fire Emblem and more specifically FE9 and FE10. If you are familiar with this genre I strongly recommend playing on hard mode. I haven't enjoyed a FE this much since FE10. The whole game is very tightly designed and does not pull ANY punches, you will need to use all of your resources carefully and more often than not beating a map was such a close call that waiting one more turn would have meant losing or a character getting killed.
+Most maps allow you to draft your whole army, making every unit important, even your measly thief
+No permadeath, instead, a unit dying means they will be unable to fight on the next level. This is a great middle ground as losing a unit does not mean "instant reset" but instead a decision like "can I afford not using this guy and not giving him any EXP for one map"
+Renewable weapons. Every unit's basic weapon's durability is restored to full at the beginning of each map, but not the rarer, more powerful weapons. Interesting addition that prevents the bronze or iron weapons from becoming the most valuable item like in Fire Emblem.
+The trap gimmick makes your lord character unique in a way different from being overpowered in combat (in which he instead is thief-tier in this game), and encourages observing and exploiting the AI in creative ways
+No unit is invincible. There is no Sety or Haar to carry you here. Every unit has clear weaknesses, and enemy diversity means that your units NEED to work together to cover them. Dodge-tanking everything is also impossible in this game, as the AVD stat always stays at reasonable levels : both yours and the enemy's precision is often in the 90s, and rarely lower than the 80s.
+Good level design with varied objectives. I don't think I ever had to create so many walls and control so many choke points, as well as baiting invincible enemies. If you were afraid of the Black Knight in FE9, you're in for a treat in this game.
+Characters and dialogue are adorable
-As a result of the first positive, the playable cast is smaller than your typical Fire Emblem
-No class change or branching promotions
-Support bonuses are often useless (luck on healers, mag on fighters, offensive stats on dancers...) and the viable pairings become very few if you want them to be good in combat
-The soundtrack is hit or miss, I loved most of it, but a couple tracks are kind of annoying to listen to, especially since maps can be hours-long
-The final chapter is amazing, but the extra chapter is somewhat disappointing (where's my "VS Desunoya"?!)
Overall a very fun game with a lot of charm, in which you can try your best at all times without being afraid of it becoming too easy or plowing through everything.

While not a top-quality game by any means, this is still a decent followup to the legendary Fire Emblem series.
You can tell this game is build for FE veterans, but Fire Emblem isn't particularly complicated to begin with so newcomers should have no problem learning this. There are some minor chages here and there to fit what changes the devs wanted to the tried-and-true formula, including the stroke of genius of having basic-tier weapons repair themselves after each level so you don't have to redistribute 20 damaged iron swords after every battle. The levels themselves are competently designed if nothing spectacular.
My main complaint is oddly enough the plot. It is rather random and entirely too light-hearted for a game about battlefield tactics and should be just a shade darker. Where are the card carrying villians? Where are the pillaging bandits, the heartless tyrants, the constant plotting and scheming against the heroes? The Fire Emblem games have consistently managed above-average quality plots using these tropes. This just disappoints in that regard.
Even so this is still a worthwhile SRPG even if is not the greatest and does not truly attempt to do anything new.

Really fast-paced old-school fun. It takes a little bit to get a hang of the controls, but it's smooth as butter once you do. It's difficult, but not super difficult (I did better at it than I do at any of the NES Megaman games), and setting your lives to 9 via the options menu is highly reccommended (There are some cheap insta-deaths, but when you have 9 tries to make it through a stage, it's a non-issue).
Boss battles are really tense, fun endeavours, and the level design is pretty interesting - one stage is jumping between moving cars on a highway, another is a chase through a building while dodging sniper fire from the boss you face at the end, another is a climb up a tower against strong winds. You interact a little with the bosses during the stage, which is a touch I really like - they end up having a bit more personality than usual sidescroller bosses.
It's certainly rough around the edges. It's not pretty, the voice acting isn't good, etc etc. But it's definitely a really satisfying sidescroller if you take a step back from the 'controversy' and appreciate it for what it is. I'd replay it anytime I have an urge for a good 2D platformer.

TL;DR
If you are wanting a game that is exactly like the classic Megaman or Megaman X/Zero games, this game isn't for you.
If you are looking for a Megaman like game that has its own spin on how to play, I would recommend checking this game out.
Pros:
Megaman style: beat the boss of each level without losing all your levels otherwise restart the level, get weapons from bosses, bosses are week against another boss's weapon
Good controls
Good graphics (although they are rather cartoon like, but are well made in that style)
Dashing mechanic is fun
Bosses are good
Weapons are good (although I ended up only using my top 3 favorite weapons, and only switched to use the others when they were needed)
When a boss is beaten, that boss will help out in the stage where his/her weapon is effective against the boss
Call level is fun and different change of pace compared to Beck
Ray DLC is fun and provides a different game style compared to Beck and Call
Good story
Decent voice overs
Cons:
No invincibility frames: you can get hit by an enemy, pushed back into spikes and instantly die
Overuse of instant death spikes/electrical traps, makes some stages harder without being more creative about the level
Retro Hero DLC only shows in Maniac mode, should be an option to switch to it, regardless of mode
One Hit KO for maniac mode, is too difficult imo. Health items are useless in this mode
Only one Call level. Would have been cool to have a couple more stages for her.
Floating enemies are hard to hit with Becks normal weapon, since they are either just out of range of jumping to hit
My Thoughts
I really enjoyed playing this game. It was fun playing a game in the style of Megaman but with the added mechanic of needing to dash into enemies to get points and bonuses. Each level I thought was fun to play, although some levels could have been a little better designed. The bosses were fun to fight against, and the weapons were all fun to use. However, I quickly only starting using a couple of the boss weapons because some of the boss weapons are only really good in certain situations that didn't come up very often. I would consider this game a good game, but nothing more than good due to the Cons list.
I recommend buying this game if you are interested in a Megaman like game with its own mechanic of how to play.
If a sequel for this game comes out, I hope the developers take into consideration of my Cons list, because I feel like that would have made this game a great game, instead of just a good game.

Disclaimer: I was given an early copy of the second novel by a friend who is a kickstarter backer.
An incredible follow-up to episode 1. A well-balanced sequel about love, intrigue, introspection, and of course - economics!
New characters help the story progress forward in a new, broader direction, however Eleanor and her particular group all look quite striking compared to the overall art style of the novel. So much so that the novel itself pokes fun at said characters, but it's something you quickly get used to, due to how well-written they are, which helps them fit in immensely. Unfortunately, some new faces get a *lot* more face time than others, which is a shame considering how human all the other ones feel.
There are more places to visit on the lunar surface, but the lack of CG's in the first novel is compounded this time by the fact that, not only are there not enough of them still, but the ones that are there fail to stand up to the grandiose writing that describes these places. It's a bit jarring hearing a description of how truly massive the hotel in Clapton Square is, and actually seeing the single-CG they present to you. The novel still truly does suffer from what seems to be either a creative or budget issue in the art department.
The music score is expanded with some new tracks, most of them somber piano pieces which go with the game's now more grown-up, adult-ish theme. While they're good at setting up the mood, they sometimes unnecessarily bring it down for long periods of time. Some catchy tunes from the previous novel still make a comeback however.
The writing, like in the first novel, is what truly makes this one shine as well, so much so that it obfuscates everything else. This is not a bad thing: you're constantly left pondering about the emotional state of the characters (though this may be a bit overbearing by the end of the novel), and the intrigue that they're involved in at large. The one bad part of this is that you're no longer in the small-scale enviorment of the first novel, following the exploits of Hal as he tangles with the stock market. Part of the fun of the first novel was the scenes where Hal frantically performed trades and explained at the same time how he was doing them. The player could relate somewhat and experience the thrills Hal had at the time. This takes a backstep in the second novel - it's still present, but much less so, which is ultimately a bit dissapointing.
Isuna Hasekura pulls another powerful story about economics, and throws in another engaging ending in as a bonus. A must-buy for fans of the first novel. Newcomers to the series are encouraged to purchase the first novel, as it is necessary reading to understand the second one.

Better than the first, but if you haven't played episode one, stop reading this review and go play it, because I'm going to spoil some things about the first game.  You've been warned.
Like WEE1, this is a 'kinetic' visual novel, meaning no choices.  It takes place four years after the first game, with Hal (now translated as "Haru" for some reason, but whatever) trying to pick himself up from the ruins of his self-inflicted catastrophe from the last time we saw him.  Hagana is nowhere to be found, much to his chagrin--he's not over her by any means--but other familiar faces abound, along with some new faces who are well worth getting to know.
What I loved about this game was the obvious growth in the characters.  Their decisions had consequences.  They changed a great deal not just from the first game, but over the course of this one.
WEE2 is also better on the artistic front.  The backgrounds and character art are more detailed and polished, and there are fewer blank screens with only text.
I won't spoil anything about the ending except to say that this is obviously the second part of a trilogy.  Don't expect anything to be resolved yet--you'll have to wait for WEE3 for that.
But it's well worth your time if you like stories about economics, society, and most of all lovable, flawed characters who try their best to overcome their foibles.

(Long Review - TL,DR: pros and cons at the bottom)
We’ve had more than our fair share of survival games in recent years; similarly, there’s been more than an ample outpouring of card games into the gaming market too. However, the survival card game ‘Frost’ takes the two and puts them together into something unique and special that we haven’t quite been witness to before.
In Frost, instead of running around a landscape and grinding away at rocks and trees for resources, the player plays a card to send one of his party members out to scavenge for desperately-needed supplies on his behalf. Instead of playing cards from his hand to inflict damage upon the enemy, or its minions, the player judiciously lays out cards against mother nature herself where the only true nemesis is the ever-approaching frost.
The goal of Frost is to make the treacherous journey through the ever-dangerous and frigid wastelands to the sanctuary beyond – a place where the deadly cold cannot touch you. At each stage during this journey the party, which you lead, will have to stop in a region and fulfil the area’s requirements before being allowed to proceed again. Such requisites include having enough food, fuel, and personnel to be able to survive, regroup, and voyage forth again by pressing the ‘travel’ button and thus ending the turn.
The main mechanic of the game is the eponymous frost, which pursues you relentlessly from start to finish. At the beginning of the game your tribe starts 8 turns away from the frost, and you can end each turn either by resting, travelling, or merely just ending the turn if you have no other available option. Each turn that ends without you setting forth again results in a decrement of the frost counter. When the counter reaches zero, you succumb to the devouring blizzard and lose the game. On the other hand, every time you travel onwards you put that extra bit of distance between the freezing menace and yourself, leading to an increment in the frost counter – up to the maximum starting value of 8 turns. Your choice of the three end-turning actions (rest, end turn, and travel) will depend on the cards you have in your hand, whether you meet that area’s criteria for passing onwards, and what actions you have or haven’t performed that turn. Depending on the hands you’re dealt it’s quite possible to spend several turns stuck in the same region. So when planning your strategy you always need to be mindful of the approaching danger, and to keep travelling forwards quickly to keep it as far at bay as is possible.
Extra challenges will come your way in the form of hungry animals, and hostile natives. These can either be placated with food, or can be fought off with crudely formed spears and axes – at the potential expense of removing these from your deck. Another alternative is simply to run away from them by pressing the ‘travel’ button at the end of your turn. This has the advantage of not consuming any precious food or weapons, but does inflict damage on your party. Now this is where one of Frost’s very neat mechanics comes into play – you can choose where to impose this damage on your party. Picking yourself means that you’ll lose one of your four hit points, but victimising one of your party members means that they’ll die immediately and will be removed from your deck straight away.
Fatigue is another very intriguing mechanic that Frost has to offer and has a particularly interesting and relevant role in the game. Each time you send a party member out scouting for resources they have the chance to come back with food, fire wood, or even another survivor. However, there is always the risk that they’ll return empty-handed and exhausted from their exertion – this ‘exhaustion’ adds a fatigue card to your deck. Consequently, every turn when you draw your cards there’s a chance that you’ll end up drawing fatigue cards, which are essentially useless, in place of other (useful) cards such as a party members or food.
Removing fatigue cards from your deck requires that you and your party rest for the entire duration of the turn. The difference between a mere ‘end turn’ and ‘rest’ is that to rest you must not have played any cards at all during the turn prior to resting. This consumes valuable time so you have to be very strategic about when offering respite to your weary group. Spend too many turns in one area scavenging for the needed requirements or resting the fatigue cards out of your hands, and you’ll find the ever-approaching frost gaining ground with alarming speed.
The game presents you with additional planning and management challenges in the form of events. These are random cards played at the top of the screen, which give you the opportunity to perform specific tasks, providing you with extra strategic options. They basically equate to trading one thing for another, making you try to decide what will be most useful to you many turns later into your journey. As with everything else in Frost, choosing poorly or just plain falling foul to the RNG could spell doom for your survivors later down the line. With these stakes hinging on such decisions you will be left debating whether you’d want to spend scarce resources to craft a potentially life-saving weapon such as a spear or trading them for alternative bare necessities. It truly is surprising how much choice and planning there is available every turn with randomly drawn cards.
On a negative note, some of the special effects are very basic, to the extent that they distract the player and break the immersion of the atmosphere. These are built up of a series of diagonal, zig-zag lines that flutter about on screen either when you remove a card from the deck or on the turn when the frost is about to catch up with your party. The latter is far more egregious, as it involves these distracting lines criss-crossing pretty much the entire screen in a rather intense cyan hue. The former is red zig-zagging of lines covering just the area of the cards in question.
One thing I truly believe that Frost could benefit from is some sort of campaign. It’s nice to have a game that can be picked up, played, and even completed in about 10-20 minutes (depending how you play). But then it would be great to have some longer-term strategy involved that spanned the equivalent of multiple play-throughs - forcing the player to focus on very acute needs and even more chronic ones.
+ An excellent hybrid of survival and card game genres.
+ A very nice mix of (surprisingly deep) strategy and RNG.
+ New cards are unlocked as you play through the game, thereby enhancing subsequent sessions.
+ You get to indulge in cannibalism...if you want to.
+ Some good sound effects, and cold and bleak music adds a sense of scarcity and vulnerability to the atmosphere.
+ A good challenge – even on easy mode.
+ Nicely animated cards.
- No strategic deck building over an extended period as in other digital card games, sadly. When you start a fresh game, you start anew with the standard basic deck.
- Some of the visual effects are too basic and detract from the atmosphere.
- No window mode or resolutions available in the options menu.
- Music can end rather abruptly without a smooth transition from one piece to another.
- Whereas most sound effects are appropriately atmospheric, others feel below par.
- Unsure about Frost’s longevity at this time.

Somewhere in an eternal winter, your band of chill-bitten survivors pushes on towards safety with a deadly storm clawing at your backs. As starving wolves and lurking feral cannibals lurch from the mountainside, your meagre resources succumb to the cruel hunger of the cold. Your numbers dwindle, many lost to fruitless scavenging expeditions. Fatigue sets in. You must rest for just a while... but the frost never sleeps and the frost marches for you.
Speaking as somebody that's never touched a deck-building game in their life, I may or may not be rating
higher than it deserves but I can tell you that it has served as a perfect introduction to the genre for me. The excellent tutorial lays out the simple framework of the game: use your food, materials and survivors to successfully pass through each location on your journey before the frost counter rolls down to zero and you are consumed by the storm. Move to a new area and the counter rolls back one. Spend any longer than a single turn there and it advances.
Complicating matters are the area events that can range from benevolent farmers willing to trade wood for food to vicious wolf attacks that must be dealt with before moving, lest you face a blow to your health meter. A range of helpful optional 'Idea cards' populate the top of your screen with various effects but come at a cost to your resources, forcing you to make tough decisions on what is likely to benefit you long-term.
is an incredibly unforgiving game, even on the so-called easy difficulty. A good run can be torn to shreds in a matter of two or three bad rounds but a lot of the blame will fall squarely on the player's shoulders rather than those of the game itself. Inescapably, there is a degree of RNG to be considered that will test even the most well prepared survivalist but
scorns those who relax in the opening half of their campaigns with brutality, punishing frivolous resource management with a swift death as the run grinds on.
Although it could do with more deck variety and some degree of player customisation,
is solid for the asking price. The game does a fine job of incentivising extended play by unlocking new cards and unique scenarios with every run you complete and the combination of the minimalist interface and eerie soundtrack do wonders for immersing players in the wintry theme. Well worth a try for newcomers to the genre but the easily frustrated will be quickly turned off.
