I can not understand how this game is currently at 99% positive. Don't get me wrong: This game is great! But this is not a simple game to get into. A game about writing assembler? Yeah, this won't be for everyone and unless there is more added tutorial hand holding I suspect it sadly will scare away plenty of people who otherwise could get in to it.
So, if you look at a video of game play and think it looks wonderfully nerdy and something for you, it probably is. If you look at it and think "This looks strange and difficult." then you are probably also right. I'm very happy that this game exists and that it's finding its target audience, but you should not take its high %-rating to mean that it's accessible. You *will* have to RTFM to get far in this game.

Highly recommended for anyone with any interest in assembly programming. The game assumes a degree of familiarity or interest, so don't expect to come into the game with no programming knowledge and walk out as an assembly pro. It could help sharpen your tools, but you need that toolset going in. There's enough here to get you started but you may need to supplement the manual if you have no idea at all how a processor works. Thankfully we live in an age where that sort of information is readily available to anyone who is inclined to look for it. If that sounds like a unique form of torture to you, it may not be the game for you.
The UX of the game also deserves a special mention. From launching the program to physically thumbing through the manual to checking emails to completing assignments to wasting time playing Chinese Solitaire, it really makes you feel like an expat wage slave in the Pearl River Delta of the future. I haven't lived in Shenzhen in 2026, but the characters in the game really match up with similar experiences in other nearby parts of the world. It's great. 10/10
Very challenging and interesting game.

tl;dr: 10/10 if you are a perfectionist who enjoys programming. Basically, a modern and shiny TIS-100, minus lonely/creepy part, plus the "corporate atmosphere" part.
Basic gameplay: you get puzzles, you solve them, then you see some metrics for your solution, then you spend an hour trying to optimize stuff to beat everyone else.
You can skip this part and just rush forward, but it's amazingly satisfying to find the solution that is better than your friend's solution.
What makes this game unique compared to many other puzzle games (even the nerdy ones) is the anmosphere. You don't get a tutorial, you get a 40-page-long manual. Wild, unreliable, with some marketing BS (not the real one, it's just for the flavor) and the part of it is in Chinese (10/10 for realism), and you need to dig into it to solve your problems. You don't just get normal levels: you get emails that contain a lot more than just your task. You don't get just "scores" for the solution, you get the cost and energy consumption metrics that you are trying to minimize.
Remember that time when programming was fun for you? If you do, try this game, it's totally worth it even in the current EA state. If you don't (or if you don't get it why some people go ecstatic after making their program 2% more optimal), than this game may not be for you, unfortunately. But you are totally encouraged to try: there are no "frustrating" parts that can make this game unaccessible if you are not familiar with programming.
Game helps you everywhere it can (Ctrl+Z totally works, you can clone you solutions to fiddle with them without any risk of destroying the original, etc.), and it's unlikely that you will hit a brick wall that you can't overcome no matter what you do. It's always possible to make a "terrible" solution (slow and expensive), and revisit it later, when you'll get better (or unlock new elements). Yes, there is a progression system that unlocks new stuff as you go. You won't get immediately overhelmed with all these micro-controllers that you see on screenshots. Game has a very comfortable learning curve (at least so far, I haven't finished the EA version yet), and it's a lot more novice-friendly than TIS-100, for example. It doesn't mean that this game is "shallow" though. While I think that TIS-100 had a lot more room for optimizations (so you could spend more time on finding the best possible solution), these optimizations sometimese where quite exhausting if you was trying to minimize the runtime (you had to write a lot of code to make it marginally faster). Here the game uses different metrics that encourage you to write compact code, and this just feels nice. Best solutions don't feel "bulky". They feel "clever".
The only complaint I have right now is that the information about other players' solutions is very unprecise (it's just a clunky histogram). I mean, the whole game is about optimizations, why can't I see if I found the best known solution or not? You do have precise metrics for your friends' solutions, though, which is nice.
Read esoteric datasheets.  Write tiny chunks of assembly.  Have nerdy fun!

Not for casual fun as you really have to think, read and learn. Nevertheless doing something right is a great and rewarding experience.
Programming language is simple but limited in functionality (because it's assembly language), so past experience with coding is recommended. You don't have to be an expert though.

Ok so not sure why people are bashing on this game so hard. I hear the graphics are fuzzy the sound is bad and voice acting is terrible. I didnt find any of that to be bad.
GOOD STUFF: Its lots of fun. Game play can be very fast at times. Thats how the game was made. Its not so fast that people cant beat it.

The graphics: They are not fuzzy. Maybe other people have the settings wrong or they have an older graphics card than I do. (MSI Lightning II ATI R5870) I did not see any fuzzy or blury graphics in the game.

The sound / music: I did not find the sounds or music to be bad or too loud or too quiet or even annoying. The voice acting is not bad. I have heard far worse and I enjoyed almost all of this games voice acting.
The controls: My game pad is old and worn out the L3 / R3 analog buttons do not work and the right analog stick is breaking and its not reliable so I was not able to calibrate my controller. But I beat the game anyway. I did not have any issues with the controls even with my controller uncalibrated and partly broken. For a "Megaman" type game I would say its a very nice ballance between old school Megaman and the Megaman X series. That said this is NOT Megaman or Megaman X. You can set the buttons how you want them to be set. You cant change the weapon your using if you have the game paused I think this is how they want the game to be played just learn the controlls and git gud lol.
The content: This game is short. I beat it in about 5 hours. But I did not expect it to be a very long game. The story is not epic or even great but I would not say its bad. I did enjoy the story. The game does have a nice amount of challenges for people to play around with. They range from very easy to very difficult. I did not play the multi player stuff but it looks fun if you play with friends. I hope they keep adding more to the game. I think the game has a good replay value.
BAD STUFF: Some people might find it to be too difficult at times. Some of the levels have parts that are far more difficult than the rest. I thought this was fine for me but I could see other people having a lot of issues with it. I would love to have an easy mode.
The weapons: Some of the weapons are very situational and not very useful in combat. Others might be a bit broken and or over powered. The game does not have a charge attack for your main weapon... this aggravates me to no end! Its one of the few things about this game I really hate. I dont know if this was a copyright issue and they simply could not add it in or they just didnt want to add it but I think it hurt the game play a bit. The game has a lack of upgrades that could have added a lot to the game play. Maybe they just have plans to add more stuff or use it for another game but I think the game is less than it could be without them. The only other thing I hate about the game is when you find and or get a recovery item that you can carry with you and you die without a game over you will loose all of them. I dont know if this was done to make it more difficult or if its a mistake but its super aggravating!
OTHER STUFF: I found an issue where if I did try to use the left analog stick I would get lots of lag I think this could be from me not being able to calibrate my partly broken controller im not sure. But it didnt matter to me anyway because I did not need the analog stick to play the game but others might.
I did see some very minor lag at times but Im sure its from my older system and not the game. Or my lol controller.
Over all I would give this game 8 out of 10. I had lots of fun playing it and look forward to playing it several more times. I do wish it was longer and hope they add lots more to it.

I love a good old-school point 'n' click adventure game, and The Charnel House Trilogy seemed to fit the bill when I purchased it. It's a relatively short experience, taking me around two hours to finish up and earn all the achievements too. What you get here is a fun, interesting little mystery, split into three 'chapters' that vary in length. The first two are pretty brief, and the third is the longest, with most of the plot twists and developments happening there. There's a horror element to the game, but also a bit of humour and some nods and winks to the gaming community.
The voice acting is decent, particularly from the two lead characters - Alex and Harry. Jim Sterling voices a character here too, and he's suitably over-the-top and impassioned. He's clearly having a lot of fun with the role. The weakness in the voice acting is mainly that they were all clearly recorded separately, possibly over Skype, so there's a difference in quality that I found a bit distracting. It's the nature of the game and how it was made, however, and I found it easy to forgive those issues. You work with what you've got to hand.
I think what some people who have left negative reviews are struggling with is the fact that this is more of a narrative experience. Sure, you're pointing and clicking, but the game very much pushes you in the right direction throughout. There are a couple of puzzles, but they're very, very easy and only really serve to push the plot along. It's a pretty captivating plot too, although I felt like most of my questions went unanswered by the time I reached the end. There will almost certainly be a sequel that fleshes out some of what we see here, but I wasn't disappointed by what I saw. There's some real promise here in terms of where the story could go. A bit more gameplay and some clearer answers would be great in the future, but this is a good starting point and a decent little game to boot.

Charnel house has none, you are basically herded into one train cabin, where you pickup single item and a herded towards next cabin where you use the very same item you've picked up earlier.
Charnel house plays like an interactive novel where you know exactly how it ends by the time you finish chapter and 2 and just just click away for the next 30-40 minutes to see the very ending you've been expecting all along.

You're presented with a series of events out of your control, and your choices determine how those events develop. Simple enough, right? But as time goes by you realize just how deep and important each of these questions asked is, and soon you begin to be really invested in the story and where it all goes. It presents you with your life, you decide where you go, how you act, and these actions are not without consequence.
All in all, it's a text based game with an emphasis on your own choices, your own beliefs, and while quite broad at first, slowly narrow down towards the end of the story to become more and more personal. The game is definitely worth the buy in my opinion, but I would say that you should play this game alone and with as few breaks as possible in order to maintain the attachment to the story and characters.

TL;DR - It's not as horrible as some people would have you believe, but it's a far cry from being a good game. It's okay at best, bad at worst, thus the negative recommendation. It has too many bad design choices to make me consider it anywhere near good.
I say this as a Megaman fan, I say this as a backer (Mighty Number 66298), and I say this as a gamer. This game suffers so much from trying to emulate Megaman, and trying to be it's own thing. Let's go over the three main design decisions that hurt this game way too much for it to be considered good:
This is fine, except that the game isn't well designed around it. Consider other platformer games that include dashing or airdashing as a core gameplay mechanic - there's either obstacles or some form of limit to how much you can dash in midair, so to prevent you from bypassing stages almost entirely.
The game isn't well balanced around the dash. You have unlimited dashes midair, plus you also can just bypass scores of enemies by dashing through them altogether. There's also the option of fighting enemies in the way, but I'll cover that in the below point.
To MN9's credit, the obstacles come in the form of instant death spikes or enemies, but the enemies are mostly bland and the spikes can range from being obnoxiously placed (Dyna and Cryo's stages come to mind) or negligible.
The enemies point is important, because...
In game design, there's a point to be had with viscerality. What I mean by this is that impacts or hitting enemies should feel satisfying and thus have that extra "oomph" or juice to it. I have a link below to demonstrate what I mean about this.
Why am I pointing this out? Not only does Mighty Number 9 lack the said viscerality that I mention that most games do have, the sounds that do pop up are either annoying or not very satisfying. Having "good moments" in the game end up being rather mundane and boring is not fun. The sound effects and the particle effects for eliminating enemies are not satisfying.
This isn't even getting into the fundamentals of the combat itself. The dash centric gameplay means that enemies must have enough space to avoid dashing into one (unless you want to shoot an enemy enough until it disappears, not even explode), or you'll hurt yourself by dashing into the enemy behind the one you absorb, unless you have the red Xel powerup. But even then, the dash centric gameplay means that - unless you're playing for score, which seems odd considering this game seems catered toward speedrunners - you'd be avoiding combat unless you love this style.
That also doesn't include the many instances in the game where you're locked in a room and are forced to eliminate enemies before being allowed to proceed. I'd forgive this lazy attempt at padding the game's length if the game was well designed around combat...
...but it is not. The combat is dull for all the reasons I mentioned above and I made every effort to look for ways to avoid it after the first hour.
What I mean here is that aside from the tutorial - which seems odd considering this is on the heels of games like Shovel Knight - the game's stages do very little to teach you about the obstacles or gimmicks and how to get used to them, then be challenged with them.
Instead, the game expects you to be able to react to them the instant they appear without any learning curve. Let's go over a few examples from Megaman, since it's a relevant franchise to cover regarding this game, for examples of what I find Mighty Number 9 is lacking:
There are multiple other examples of gameplay design like this in Mario and Metroid.
My point is that Mighty Number 9 fails at doing this (and the Megaman series has been consistent with this sort of game design since it's inception!), and instead wants to fill the game with pointless chatter that I don't care about for the most part, almost like the characters are just talking to fill in the dead air (especially looking at you, Sanda).

First of all let me say that I enjoy the Megaman series, and I donated to this game back during the kickstarter and then completely forgot about it until release, so maybe I just didn't get ridiculously hyped for something that would be impossible to deliver, unlike most people it seems. THIS GAME WAS NEVER GOING TO BE ANYTHING MORE THAN A PSEUDO REMAKE OF MEGAMAN WITH 8 "ROBOT MASTERS" ALONG WITH A FEW LAST LEVELS AND A FINAL BOSS EXPECTING ANYTHING MORE THAN THAT IS BEYOND IDIOTIC.
I'm not a slave to popular mass opinion, this game was awesome through and through with some minor flaws (most of which were brought over from the flaws of the original Megaman series which this game is a remake of.) like the graphics being quite a bit lower quality than was originally advertised (which is a sacrifice that was made when they tried to release the game on ten different systems at once instead of just PC which is what they should have focused on instead.), and unlike Megaman which had only one battle capable female out of ten games (which is just plain disgraceful unless you count Megaman powered up but that doesn't exactly do much to help cure the sausage fest that is the Megaman franchise) Mighty No 9 has quite a few awesome and powerful female characters (even Call who is the Roll of this game can hold her own), with Ray standing out as quite possibly being my favorite character in the entire Megaman series. She also has her own challenging story mode with a completely different playstyle and weapons than Beck. I should also mention the robots in the game which have a pretty interesting concept behind them. They consist of a core which contains their essence, surrounded by a colony of nanomachines called "Xell" that comprise their body. The basic gameplay consists of shooting enemies until their Xell become destabilized and then dashing into them to absorb them and the bonus that they give you (extra firepower, speed, defense, and health tanks) it's a really fun mechanic and makes the game fast paced and unrestrictive (unlike the original Megaman series, which although I greatly enjoy I also don't have the near idolic reverence for it that most people in the fandom seem to have.)
Also I think this game has much better character design than the original Megaman series. Call for example is obviously a robot (and has a personality like one to play her off of Beck's more human personality) whereas with Roll in the original series I didn't know until the games outright said that she was a robot since she looked nothing like one. Also in my opinion Beck has a better outfit than Megaman's which was a very simple and very basic blue jumpsuit, some blue tighty whities over it, and a weird looking helmet (I should mention that the later Megaman incarnations fixed this though with more complex and better designed outfits.) Beck's outfit has more going on and looks obviously mechanical. The "Robot Masters" in this game also all have designs that I love, whereas in the original Megaman games I only liked about 2 or 3 out of every 8 Robot Masters and even then they barely had any character or personality to them. Some of the voice acting is a little annoying (Dr. Sanda overreacts to nearly everything and makes puns like "don't count your atoms before they're smashed!" but I warmed to his goofy nerdiness eventually), but even the worst of it has a charm that sort of cancels out the annoyance to me, and you can change the language to French or Japanese if you wish also.
The main problems are the abundance of one hit kill death traps (think of a narrow corrider of spikes which instantly kill you if so much as the tip of your pinky toe touches one  that you have to carefully float or fall through), add to that several bosses having one hit kill moves, and the fact that the game uses the painfully outdated and draconic "lives" system and you have a recipe for frustration, but all of those were in the original Megaman games so it isn't like it's anything new, and you can get through with a good deal of trial and error (and luck).
I already mentioned the graphics quality which I don't consider to be a problem at all, to me the art style is much more important, and the game completely delivers on that front. And isn't it funny that Megaman 9 and 10 despite being released recently and having  "pseudo 8 bit"  graphics get a free pass from the critics and fans despite the fact that Mighty No 9 has far better graphics? I guess having the name "megaman" just gives them a free pass. Another problem that "fans" bring up is that the game and it's controls aren't "tight" which I don't give a rats left buttcheek about, I searched and searched for a definition on what "tight" means in relation to video game controls and all I found was about a hundred discussions where even the game developers themselves couldn't give a concrete answer (the closest being that it means the character stops on a dime) so it seems to just be a word that the "fans" use to make Megaman seem superior to Mighty No 9 (and to make Mighty No 9 into their strawman) despite being pretty much the exact same repetitive game released 10 times in a row with very few changes to the formula (Mighty No 9's dash mechanic and female characters push it far over Megaman as far as I'm concerned) because heaven forbid a remake of Megaman not using the exact same movement as it's predecessors! I don't care what anybody says, the game controls fine, and the combat and platforming are extremely fun.
I should also mention that Mighty No 9 FINALLY got rid of that awful, sickening, cheap, artificially game lengthening Robot Master/Boss gauntlet that EVERY SINGLE FREAKING GAME IN THE ORIGNAL MEGAMAN SERIES HAD. And I say good riddance to it!
I should mention that the only truly horrendous problem I had with the game was Dr. White's hair which I find to be personally offensive but it wasn't enough to ruin the experience (unlike seeing videos railing against this game from the talking heads on youtube)
Anyways I've ranted for long enough, I doubt anybody cares (I've certainly stopped caring about what the rest of the fandom thinks since they just want a Megaman 11 that's a carbon copy of the previous games and another sausage fest where the only female is a secondary character who never does anything, so as with most series that I'm a fan of, I reject the fandom almost completely) but the bottom line is, Megaman is great, Mighty No 9 is great, play what you want, but don't reject a game just because it got delayed a few times and doesn't have the exact same controls and name as its predecessors.
And yes I'm "salty" about how the community has treated this game, DEAL WITH IT

In Factorio you are a single engineer stranded on a planet infested with giant insects. Like so many other games you must build yourself bases and weapons to defend yourself, except unlike every other game involving crafting, you automate the crafting in Factorio. You build yourself a factory. Build and manage your power, figure out how you're going to move the massive amount of material you need to a conveniently defended place (Hint, it's probably with trains.) You set up gatling, laser, and flamethrower turrets to defend your factory as you work to launch rockets and continue to research more efficient technologies.
There are few games more hypnotizing than Factorio. Sure it all starts out simple, mine some coal, iron, and copper. Move the coal and ores around manually to get things going. Then build some inserters and belts so you don't have to do too much. Then build a steam power set up and get started on science. Research assemblers and set those up. This is a game that you either hate or love. There is no middle ground. While the puzzle aspect of this game is strong and the interface is great, the fact that you have to scratch your head and dig into manuals everytime something is introduced to you can be little bit off putting to say the least. In addition to the fact that the game requiring you to read through 41 page manual, it also require you to debug your chip if anything goes wrong. Sounds familiar, right? Yeah, this is exactly how you process through the actual project, if you ever have programmed something. The only difference is, this is much simplified and less infuriating because "it's just a game."
As for the engineer wannabes like me (well, to be fair I am an engineer but majored in chemicals), the game is fun and pushes your mind in a right way for a challenge. However, for everyone else, the game can be bit overwhelming. So Shenzhen I/O is more like OOP for the dummies instead of a game in a traditional sense. Yes, it's a puzzle, but at the same time it's bunch of engineering projects that requires you to actually carefully plan and think hard before you do anything.
So If you're up for time-killing fun or puzzle that only requires you to think within the set of mechanics it directly introduces to you, then look for something else. The game is great but it also is impossible to grasp without (really) basic understanding of programming. But, if you loved TIS-100 and love to torture your brain even when you're resting, then you chose the right game. I highly recommend this game to people who constantly seek for challenges, but I cannot recommend to the others who just want simple fun.

It took me a while to realise where the title is coming from. After all, for many of us the 2nd Encounter is considered Serious Sam 2. But no! Sam crash-lands on Earth and continues his journey to find a spaceship with which he can finally travel to Mental's homeworld. Essentially, the 2nd Encounter was identical to the 1st - there was just a change in scenery.
So, there comes Serious Sam 2 where Sam's blast-off is successful and he finally finds himself on a distant planet. He is, in fact, summoned by extraterrestrials. This aid he receives from the Sirians helps him understand what objects are required so that he can defeat Mental once and for all. It is not that much different from the artefact collecting approach we had the last time, however, instead of Sam's A.I. companion it is the Sirian natives that provide more feedback on the story.
This is now a whole different setting. We meet different races on different planets and the cutscenes are now a regular thing (there are usually 2 for each level). The game is significantly longer, however, the story is still simplistic, so there's no added value here since you still make sure all of the waves of enemies thrown at you end up in gibs. The assortment of weapons available does not change significantly; the favourite guns remain the same such as the grenade or rocket launcher.
My problem with the game was its "cuteness" factor. I felt the cartoonish look was too unnecessary. The many cutscenes with the smurf-like aliens explaining the peril they are in and how Sam must help felt annoying very early on. I know the word "serious" is meant to be a pun in the title since the gameplay is as simplistic as possible (it is an homage to Doom) but the game was always very hard (especially on higher difficulty settings). Sam's one-liners after eliminating a throng of headless kamikaze guys came like a godsend.
And now it's cute little aliens, cartoonish graphics and a cartoonish (quite horribly looking) Sam. Vehicle use is a regular thing (we can also mount turrets) which gives the game a more arcade-like approach. We also have lives available (they increase as we hit score milestones) which I never got to understand as quick-saving was still an option. The grenades that can be thrown by just the press of a right-mouse button are very helpful (and here will be used frequently) as they fly fast ahead and explode upon impact.
I do not know what to make of this sequel, really. I was happy to see how the creators reverted to the old gameplay formula in Serious Sam 3 as the inclusion of adorable little aliens did not have any appeal for me. Imagine Duke Nukem going to the alien planet once the Earth is cleared and along the way he meets Pig Cops, Enforcers and Octrabrains just in a more "enchanted" form. Albeit long and just as adrenaline-fulled as its predecessors, Serious Sam 2 deviates too much in terms of story and graphics. Since neither was an expectation for a sequel I cannot recommend the game.

I can not actually recommend this title for players looking for a deep, point & click, atmospheric game.  It isn't a terrible experience, and I really liked the beginning of the game, but there are some points which seem misleading from the get go.  The store page advertizes this as "Three thrilling, horrifying adventure games in one" and that is just not true.  Not only is this not three adventures, it doesn't even feel like ONE whole and complete adventure.
This title contains three short scenes, which are loosely related and leave an open-ended interpretation of what actually has occured during the course of the story presented.  The first scene is excellently narrated, introduces the main character and piques the player's interest and, although very short, draws the player into the world.  The second scene is a bit surreal, does not exactly correlate to the first scene, but does still allude to it, and brings a bit of a psychological teasing to the narrative.  The third and longest scene is best described as "meh" and kind of diffuses the interest that was piqued in the first and second scenes with a haphazardly thrown out, cliched type of story.  And the very end of the game is an allusion to that fact that another game may come in the future which will bring the player back to learn more of what may or may not have happened in the course of this game.
And "game" is used in the loosest sense of the word here.  There is hardly any game at all.  This is more of a psychological experience where the story is narrated (with some excellent voice acting for the most part) and the player is allowed to click on a few icons for added description while the story unfolds itself.
I actually enjoyed most of this title, but as this is being billed as multiple point&click adventures rolled into one, I think that many people who are going to purchase this title are going to end up with something that they feel disappointed with when they have finished.  Also the rushed and unfinished story that the third scene leaves the player with just doesn't lead to a satisfied feeling upon completion.  I am 100% for a psychologically baffling story that people can have long dialogues about long after they are over, but more of the picture should have been presented at the ending rather than forcing people to purchase a different game at a different time to get the satisfaction that completing a game should give.  And for these reasons, I would not recommend this title to fans of the point & click genre.

A mercifully brief, on-rails (pun) point-'n-click with uneven execution. Since I purchased the game at under $2 USD, I can't really complain much. For the retail price of $6 USD, I'd save your money for a longer, more interesting game. I had really hoped for more game and less grinding narrative.
Too few real puzzles and a mediocre reveal make this one a don't-buy at full price.
Nevertheless, the score is quite good because it instills deadful foreboding. I think it's easily the best element in the entire game, and if (as the climax hints) they intend on making more in this series, they should continue with their current composition.
The art, despite being extremely limited in scope, is on par with modern p-n-c's. My estimate of the actual places you can visit includes: one apartment, a train station, and a train interior with between 6-8 largely identical compartments that alter in presentation as you progress. So, in total, there are maybe 2 dozen individually constructed environments. One additonal room pops up for narrative purposes, but it isn't interactive. Plenty of good stories have taken place in a small arena, but this is one tale that would benefit from more depth of milieu. The cramped quarters of Charnel House don't derail the game (pun), but they don't give us much variety, either. The game ends up feeling claustrophobic, though not in a good way.
The voice acting (by a handful of game professionals, no less) is technically proficient, though not particularly impressive. Sterling's addition seems like a mis-cast, perhaps. His voice is off-putting, no doubt, but it doesn't quite fit. A couple characters sound like they are talking through tin cans. Some moments that require "Oh, God, no!" sound more like "oh, gawd, noes..." These potentially exciting crescendos could have been intense and gripping, but they lose their weight when offered up in unenthusiastic, uneven presentation.
Perhaps I've been spoiled by the far above-average voice direction in Wadjet Eye games, but I believe those gems are the industry standard.
A great deal of the horror lies in tropetastic reveals-- for instance, sometimes the lights go out, something spooky is shown, and  the lights come back on. Some of the scary is more than mild, but it's lost in a slew of teen-horror shlock padded by the ramblings of an incoherent raconteur.
Charnel House would be so much more compelling if it were simply more interactive.You will be shuttled from one room to the next, sometimes solving extremely easy puzzles, sometimes just using the right item on the right environmental object. You will find yourself with no options to explore, and you are shackled with unsubtle directions to a paint-by-numbers game.
Example:
Walk into train cabin.
Creepy but not exactly scary thing is going on.
Collect an item.
Leave cabin.
Use collected item to solve a "puzzle."
Hear a noise in the next train car.
"Oh, maybe I should go there," narrates the viewpoint character.
Go there.
Lights go out.
Creepy thing happens.
Repeat.
I'm not sure why the game is divided into chapters, since it is neither long enough nor diverse enough to require compartments (pun). I understand that the viewpoint character changes, but there are better, stronger methods of offering cliffhangers than sending the player back to the main menu every 30 minutes.
In the first and third chapters, you play the same character, a snarky lady with a penchant for cigarettes and bad relationships. In the second chapter you play an archaeology professor with a drinking problem who constanly loses his train of thought (pun). Each chapter will last you about 30-45 minutes, and since I only paid $2 for ~2 hours of mildly interesting, slightly spooky game, I'm not unhappy. But, I'm not really satisfied.
I wanted to jump on the train and love this game, but I think I'd rather throw myself on the tracks.
P.S. "Sepulchre" is definitely pronounced [sep.əl.kər], not [se.po͝ol.kər], New York Times Bestselling Author Madeline Roux.

There's a truckload and more things to be mentioned, but that's enough for now.
My personal score for this Farming Sim would be a strong 9 out of 10, developers put a lot of effort into production of this game, became more open with the modding community and also gave them an opportunity to participate in contests and create official and fully licensed DLC's.

99 Spirits is a very charming Japanese indie game. It combines elements from a few genres including Visual Novels, Turn based battles, lite character progression elements and even monster collecting.
The first half of 99 Spirits consists of the Visual Novel cutscenes that progress the games story - developing the characters and allowing the plot to progress. There is no voice acting for these cutscenes but this didn't bother me because characters only ever speak in short sentances so it makes it very easy to read. As the game progresses, the story and characters develop in some unexpected ways. The premise starts off fairly simple: the world is inhabited by demons called 'Tsukumogami' that possess everyday objects and attack humans. You play as a swordswomen called Hanabusa who is trying to destroy them. However, over the course of the game the story explores many different themes like love, family, loss, betrayal and more. I was very surprised at how dark the game becomes towards the final few chapters. Throughout the course of the game you will have a few choices that can even change the ending depending on these choices. It's a good story overall and there are a lot of optional conversations and characters that add depth to the world and characters.
I liked the majority of the characters in the game. The main cast all have interesting personalities, if a bit cliched. My favourite thing about the characters is when they interact with each other in humourous ways. There is some funny dialogue between characters such Komiya (the protagonists sidekick) and female characters he is always perving on. My favourites are Hanabusa's (the protagonist) conversation with the Gods and Godesses in the game, they are vey funny and sometimes endearing. The anatagonists on the other hand, I didn't like. All of them - except for one - are just badly written and have very questionable motivations in the game. Furthermore, none of them - except for the aformentioned one - go through any real developmeant or change like the other characters in the game do. Ultimately, they are just very boring.
The second half of 99 Spirits involves combat and exploring the overworld. Outside of the cutscenes, you progress by exploring different locations in the world that are represented as grids. Unfortunately, each location uses the same grid look so you never really feel like you are exploring a Shrine, a field that had a war fought on it or a bustling city. While on the grid, you can battle enemies or pick up items as you make your way towards the objective. Some grids have lite puzzles, like a tree blocking a path or secret passage that can be interacted with using the 'Tsukumogami' you encounter.
When you pick up items, you can take these back to the main hub world to be sold for money to buy other items. Finally, there are random encounters where you might encounter a trader who will trade one of your items or a stone statue that can replenish your stats (Health, money, hunger, sword condition).
When you encounter an enemy on the grid, you enter into a battle. The battle system in 99 Spirits is fairly unique. There's a few mechanics to fighting an enemy but unfortunately they lack depth and become repetitive as the game progresses. Each time you encounter an enemy, the enemies identity is hidden and you cannot defeat them. The only way to defeat enemies is to reveal their identity. So your first ability allows you to reveal traits and characters about the enemy (a spoon  may reveal 'food' or a katana may reveal 'sharp'). At first, it's really fun trying to guess what an enemy is and you can only reveal very little so you have to actually think about what an enemy could be. It's almost like every enemy is a puzzle. Once you reveal an enemies identity, you can defeat it. Defeating enemies will gain you EXP that will increase you health, attack power and sword condition. You level up fairly quickly so you don't have to grind just to finish the game.
As the game progresses you gain new abilities and power them up. You gain the ability to capture enemies and use their skills in battles and in puzzle solving (such as using a lantern Tsukumogami to light a candle and unlock and secret passage or using food related Tsukumogami to preapre a feast). I thought this was actually really clever and made good use of the fact all your enemies are just everyday items. The skills you unlock to use in battle are also very useful allowing you to deal more damage, heal yourself, increase defense or evasion and more.
So essentially the game falls into a loop of Watch of cutscene > explore the map/battle enemies > watch the next cutscene. It works well and it keeps the pacing very tight. There is a bit of optional content to break things up. There are the conversations with the many characters in the game to further develop them, there is a minor side quest to destroy skulls on each of the maps, you can go about completing your 'Spirit Index' (essentially a monster encyclopidia) and learning every enemies skills. You can even be crazy like me a level all the way up to level 99, becoming massively overpowered.
I really have to praise the games artstyle and music. The visuals are beautiful, supposedly inspired by watercolour paintings. The characters and backgrounds are wonderfully designed and have a soft, simple texture that really does look like a painting instead of the sharp, clean anime look seen in most visual novels. I purchased the art book because I loved it so much. The music is also a highlight. It's a mix of traditional Japanese music using Koto's and harp's but mixes in some modern instruments in certain tracks to enhance the sound. The majority of music plays on a short loop but it never really bothered me and mostly added ambience.
I have praised the game up to this point but I have to mention some flaws. Firstly, the game is not very technically stable. During my playtime I experienced multiple crashes. It seemed that the longer the game ran for the more likely a crash would occur. It's fine if you play in shot bursts but since the game has no autosave I cannot stress enough how important it is to save frequently. Some of the cutscenes are quite long so it was frustrating when the game would crash and I would have to watch them all over again because I hadn't saved. Secondly, a lot of the animations in the game are tied to frame rates. This meant that while playing the frame rate would rise and fall very frequently and gave off a certain stuttering effect. This only really occured in battles but I could never find a solution.
On the gameplay side of flaws, the battles in the game become very repetitive after a while. Once you have all the abilities almost every battle plays out the same way. This is made worse by the fact that there is only a small pool of enemies on every map so you will run into the same enemy frequently. Regarding balance, there are certain abilities you can acquire that are extremely overpowered to the point where I fought the final boss and took almost no damage because I had so many buffs in effect. You may have to set self imposed restrictions. Also, there is a New Game + that allows you to carry over your level and spirit index to a new game but the game does not adjust the difficulty or balance at all so you will essentially be starting a new game at a very high level and will one hit kill every early game enemy. This does at least allow you to achieve every ending quickly. Finally, there are two chapters in this game that mess up your abilities to reveal clues about enemies and reveal their identity. These chapters make the battles much, much worse and so you should rush through them quickly.
Overall I really enjoyed 99 Sprits, so much so that I completed the game 3 times and unlocked every achivement. It's got a beautiful artstyle, nice music and a lovely story backed up by an interesting if a bit repetitive battle system.

As a huge fan of the classic Mega Man series let down by Capcom's complete disavowment of it, I was one of the first to back Keiji Inafune's spiritual successor on Kickstarter.  Then came the announcements of anime and animated movie spinoffs, and merchandise, and a Mega Man Legends spiritual reboot, with all being announced well before Mighty No. 9's release and getting fans more and more worried that Comcept were spreading themselves too thin and misappropriating the nearly $4 million their Kickstarter had received.  I remained optimistic nonetheless, steadfast in giving the game a chance before panning it, which I eventually did after nearly three years of delays, setbacks, terrible trailers and harebrained developer quotes that quickly turned into memes.
After all that, and as much as I hate to say it, the speculation about the game not getting its due attention was entirely correct.  Mighty No. 9 looks very low-budget, comprised of garish colors with minimal shading and low-poly models that don't even move their mouths or change facial expressions in cutscenes.  The music is entirely forgettable, the sound effects are flaccid and the repeated voice samples get grating in a hurry.  The camera is awkward and collision detection is often spotty, making platforming messy and unintuitive.  Weapon changing is also puzzling, requiring the player to toggle between weapons with the shoulder buttons and then complete the switch by pressing Triangle, rather than simply letting them pause and select from a menu or quick-switch via shoulder buttons.  All of these things contribute to an experience that, while it superficially resembles classic Mega Man, comes across as a poor imitation of the formula on par with some of the lesser games in the X franchise instead.  If you really want the classic Mega Man experience, then do the right thing: Save your money for the Legacy Collections instead.  Because whatever problems the Mega Man games had, none of them qualified their developers for a one-way trip to Kickscammed!

Plague Inc. I remember playing it on my phone and tablet a year or two ago. It was fun. Now it is on Steam. And by now I mean it has been there for 10 months.
The game costs 15 euros but it is free on mobile. Is it worth it? It makes me think about Fruit Ninja Kinect. Is it worth it? Well... do you want to play it on PC? Are you a streamer or a Youtuber? Did you get it from the Plague Inc boardgame for free? Then yes.
Alot hasn't changed from the orginal game. Sure, it looks alot better. Not just graphics vice, but it overall feels more PC. It isn't just a game slapped on PC with the developer saying "GIVE ME MONEY. But does it have 15€ worth of improvements? Lets see how the game works first:
You start off by selecting a disease. When you win with that disease on normal or above, you unlock the next disease. Each one has its unique play style but they all basically work the same. Once you have selected your disease, you can move on to choose your starting country. WHY IS ALASKA PART OF CANADA? Once you have chosen a country, the game begins. You can upgrade your disease by giving it more killing power, more infectivity or making people think it is dangeous. Your disease then speads over the world etiher by land, boat or plane. Once people start dying and see "Hey, theres this new disease going around! Lets deal with it!".
Now there will be a country that will be the main or the head of the research that tries to find a cure to your disease. The more damage you do, the more they invest in research. They can also block you from entering a nation and infecting it by closing the borders or executing the infected. There are many ways they can block you but a disease always finds a way, like infecting via birds, rodents, bats, water, air or livestock. They send these planes to get DNA or something, burst their bubble and kill each and every last one of them!. One match can easily last 30 minutes and its really fun.
Thats the game in a nutshell. Theres also this very unique mode, the... the disease from The Rise of the Planet of the Apes. That SImean flu thing. It is very fun, you should check it out. Infecting apes and humans. It is a bucket of fun.
But back to the main issue, is it worth 15 euros? Well you can go to the leaderboards or make your own custom scenarios, speed runs, CO-OP? This game has Co-Op!? Unfortunately I have no friends who own this game, so I can't really talk about it. Is it wort 15 euros though?
I wouldn't say so. I have to say that this game isn't an game you will play actively. It is a phone game. It is a fun distraction, it is a game designed to be played while waiting for the buss or when you nothing to do. Despite all these new updates, it isn't worth 15 euros to me. Maybe to you. But I recommend you buy it on sale, like I did. I got it for 7,50. I think it was barely worth 7,50. 5 euros? Must buy. 7,50? Eh, I mean it is a fun little game to play. So I think I will give it a pass.

This is one of those cases where I really wish there was a more neutral option for recommendations, as it pains me to bring down the score of a Zachtronics game, and for people who already know how to code this is a game I would 100% recommend. Personally I found it overwhelming in the extreme, because the way in which the manual is written assumes you already have a base level of competence with programming, and there is absolutely no effort made within the game to familiarise you with practical implementations of the functions the manual describes. If you're after a game that might teach you a bit about programming, this is not it.
Spacechem is my favourite game of all time, and Infinifactory is not far behind, but if Zach intends to make his future projects as unwelcoming and opaquely explained as TIS-100 and SHENZHEN I/O, this is simply a path down which I cannot follow him. I very much hope that his next game might cut neophytes like myself some slack, otherwise I guess I'm done with my favourite developer.
Edit: I deliberately kept my playtime low to keep the possibility of a refund open (one I've since taken up), however I spent at least an hour poring over the manual before even booting the game up, and closed and restarted the game many times after consulting the manual to try and come up with a solution. I gave it much more than 30 minutes of my time, but it just didn't click with me.
And before giving this a thumbs down, please keep in mind that 'Did you find this helpful?' is not synonymous with 'Do you share this person's assessment of the product and find that the level of enjoyment they derived from it closely matches your own?'
Edit 2: This review has attracted way more attention than I had anticipated. It was written quickly on a first-and-last-impressions sort of basis, so I didn't go into much detail. At this stage I feel I have a duty to provide more context about myself and how this affects my enjoyment of the game.
An argument could be made that I was stupid for buying this after having difficulty with TIS-100. I bought SHENZHEN I/O because it was made clear that TIS-100 was a side project created for a very niche audience, and the visually dreary interface itself reinforced this. From the trailer, SHENZHEN I/O seemed like it would have much broader appeal - an attractive interface that made use of the mouse, the usual great Zachtronics music, actual promotion in the lead-up to its release. I thought that, while employing similar concepts to TIS-100, it would make them more accessible. I was wrong. And it's possible that assembly programming mightn't ever be something I find accessible.
Personally, I suck with numbers. I hate them. As it turns out, assembly programming deals with almost nothing but numbers. I didn't go into this blind, however - I had a quick look at what assembly programming looked like, and, true to my username, I made an erroneous assumption: I assumed that the numbers were not used in the sense of
but, rather, purely as
. For example, in a sudoku puzzle, the numeral 9 doesn't actually represent a quantity of nine units, it's just a symbol interchangeable with any other character which simply represents a guarantee that there are certain other places in the grid within which it cannot appear. In the context of assembly, I assumed it would work on the basis of 0 representing an off position and 1 representing an on, and similarly simple functions. Numbers
function in this way, however they also often need to be used in a quantitative context, functioning within complex, infinitely repeating algorithms. If this doesn't sound like your cup of tea, don't bother with SHENZHEN I/O, or assembly programming in general.
I got along with Spacechem and Infinifactory because their circuits used sensors which worked on the basis of 'if x = true then do y'. Simple stuff, with which you can make extremely complex devices. Assembly works more on the basis of 'if x = more than n squared divided by acc then do y, else do z'. Complex stuff, with which you can make even more complex devices. I'm sure that someone more experienced could give a far better explanation than that, but I think I at least have the nuts and bolts correct. SHENZHEN I/O requires not just the purely visual logic of Infini/chem (i.e. how do I combine and transport these ready-made products) but numeric logic as well (i.e. how do I make these ready-made products function differently by playing with the digits within them). One works with objects, while the other works with concepts.
I have to reiterate, there is no problem with the game - its standard of presentation is right up there with any other commercial release from Zachtronics and it plays just fine. That said, there is a portion of the Zachtronics audience to whom this game will not appeal, and for whom this game was not made, so I've written this for their benefit. I put it into the 'not recommended' category, not to disparage it, but because I truly would not recommend the game to a person with my tastes. My abilities with programming and numbers in general are not of such a standard that I could write a 'recommended' review which would offer anything more than uselessly facile, vague praise, directed towards an audience I'm unfamiliar with. I instead put it into the category where I could offer honest opinions of my own.

Plague Inc. I remember playing it on my phone and tablet a year or two ago. It was fun. Now it is on Steam. And by now I mean it has been there for 10 months.
The game costs 15 euros but it is free on mobile. Is it worth it? It makes me think about Fruit Ninja Kinect. Is it worth it? Well... do you want to play it on PC? Are you a streamer or a Youtuber? Did you get it from the Plague Inc boardgame for free? Then yes.
Alot hasn't changed from the orginal game. Sure, it looks alot better. Not just graphics vice, but it overall feels more PC. It isn't just a game slapped on PC with the developer saying "GIVE ME MONEY. But does it have 15€ worth of improvements? Lets see how the game works first:
You start off by selecting a disease. When you win with that disease on normal or above, you unlock the next disease. Each one has its unique play style but they all basically work the same. Once you have selected your disease, you can move on to choose your starting country. WHY IS ALASKA PART OF CANADA? Once you have chosen a country, the game begins. You can upgrade your disease by giving it more killing power, more infectivity or making people think it is dangeous. Your disease then speads over the world etiher by land, boat or plane. Once people start dying and see "Hey, theres this new disease going around! Lets deal with it!".
Now there will be a country that will be the main or the head of the research that tries to find a cure to your disease. The more damage you do, the more they invest in research. They can also block you from entering a nation and infecting it by closing the borders or executing the infected. There are many ways they can block you but a disease always finds a way, like infecting via birds, rodents, bats, water, air or livestock. They send these planes to get DNA or something, burst their bubble and kill each and every last one of them!. One match can easily last 30 minutes and its really fun.
Thats the game in a nutshell. Theres also this very unique mode, the... the disease from The Rise of the Planet of the Apes. That SImean flu thing. It is very fun, you should check it out. Infecting apes and humans. It is a bucket of fun.
But back to the main issue, is it worth 15 euros? Well you can go to the leaderboards or make your own custom scenarios, speed runs, CO-OP? This game has Co-Op!? Unfortunately I have no friends who own this game, so I can't really talk about it. Is it wort 15 euros though?
I wouldn't say so. I have to say that this game isn't an game you will play actively. It is a phone game. It is a fun distraction, it is a game designed to be played while waiting for the buss or when you nothing to do. Despite all these new updates, it isn't worth 15 euros to me. Maybe to you. But I recommend you buy it on sale, like I did. I got it for 7,50. I think it was barely worth 7,50. 5 euros? Must buy. 7,50? Eh, I mean it is a fun little game to play. So I think I will give it a pass.

This is the best Megaman game I've played in years, with all the pros and cons that go along with that series.
First off, if you're reading this and haven't followed the kickstarter campaign and delays leading up to this game's release, please realize that many of the negative reviews and hate-infused commentary surrounding this game are due to a legitimately dismal kickstarter campaign and numerous ups and downs surrounding a release date that seemed like it would never come and the game constantly being pushed back for features that nobody really cared about.  And then all of that followed by thousands of people not receiving steam keys right away (including myself) due to confusion with Humble Bundle and other shenanegans.
This review is about the game we have, not about the way we got it.  And I believe you should only seriously consider any review that treats the subject in this way.  And i fyou're one of the people that hate this game for it's terrible launch (and it was terrible), then I urge you to take a week -better yet, a month- and just put the game out of your mind before finally coming back and giving it an honest try.
The good:
What IS great about this game is that it effectively recreates some of the best feelings you could get form old Megaman sidescrolling games.  Like modern games such as Dark Souls, you play the stages and fight the bosses at the end and for a lot of it, things feel pretty damn difficult.  But then you learn the stages hazards and you memorize the boss's patterns and next thing you know, you're breezing through the level and trumping the boss with minimal damage.  And that feeling is and always will be a great feeling.
Better yet, this game genuinely evolves the old megaman formula by allowing you to bind multiple keys (or gamepad buttons preferably) to other powers you have at your disposal.  Many of which are just plain fun and some of which are actually useful in more than one boss fight.  For example, during the boss fight against Mighty No. 3, I actually utilized multiple different powers to efficiently clear the metal devices she spread throughout the stage in order to create damaging lightning tethers. I also used the another boss's fiery explosion power to hit all of the weakpoints on a shield she creates at once.  And the game even boosted my score for using these powers in this way.  I legitimately felt like the Megaman fantasy had been achieved, swapping powers based on the need, constantly growing in power and versatility as the game progressed.
Traditionally, Megaman powers are useful for the boss they were designed for and basically little else (with one of the notable exceptions being Megaman 2's metal saw power, which was just good against everything ever).  They either were the single correct weapon for the boss you were fighting or they weren't.  Might No. 9 allows you to absorb the special powers from each boss and potentially even use that as your primary play style if you felt inclined, or to easily switch between powers based on the situation.   As many reviewers have stated, once you unlock Brandish's power, for example, you can just stick with that one if you like and play the game like it's Megaman Zero or Strider all over again if you like (which shows the amazing Inticreates development teams involvement more than any other detail).
The dash allows you to quickly and skillfully speed through levels even more fluidly than Megaman X once you know what you're up against, and absorbing the Xel from normal enemies mid stage lets you keep your special weapons constantly charged if you play well.  There's even a rewarding scoring and ranking system much like the also poplular Azure Striker Gunvolt series (also made by Inticreates) which I thoroughly enjoyed playing with.
Once you finally beat the game, there's plenty of extra challenges and difficulty modes to play with as well as those online features that delayed the game so terribly, such as a versus mode and cooperative VR missions.
Lastly, the story itself is actually not bad.  I say "not bad" by Megaman standards, which are honestly pretty low, but as you play through more and more levels, the universe becomes less and less shallow.  The other Mighty Numbers seem a little bit more believable.  And the plot feels more satisfying.  As you free your comrade robots from the affliction of the
mysterious problem causing them to run amock, they will actually show up to help you on the stage that their power is designed to help you with.  An "advice" button will even show up when selecting a stage, letting you know if you currently have the power designed to fight against the boss in that level.  Even
Dr. White and
Dr. Blackwell become a bit more interesting characters by the end than their predecessors in the Megaman universe.
The Bad:
As a hardcore megaman fan, most of the bad points of this game I wasn't bothered by, but you may be.  There are unforgiving instant death spikes that will drain your remaining lives and force you to eventually continue at the beginning of a level.  If you aren't used to this retro gameplay, it might be tough to deal with the few stages that have these.  If you ARE used to it, it might take a few tries to get back in the groove of handling this old-school game mechanic.  You will get past it, but it might be a bit frustrating at first.
Some of the voice acting is mediocre (although much of it is honestly just fine) and the graphics look like they are 3DS quality models and textures.  The worst of this is the graphics.  Likely because the game was being ported to so many different consoles, the visuals were probably compromised to some extent.  Much of the music is also par for the course for a numbered Megaman title, but some of it does feel a bit uninspired.  I still have tunes stuck in my head from old NES Megaman games that will probably still be stuck there by the time these melodies fade from my mind.
In Conclusion:
This game is a good game.  It's a hard game.  It's a rewarding game to play.  It has some flaws, some of which are inherited from Megaman's legacy (some of which may not bother fans of those games, assuming you haven't already been enraged by the kickstarter campaign).  Some voice acting is a little mediocre but most of it is fine (none of it is as bad as Megaman 8's voice acting).  The story and universe seem very shallow at first but after a little time start to feel more believable and a little fuller.
But more than anything, the gameplay is Rock(man) solid.  Comcept, and probably more specifically Inticreates, achieved that much if nothing else.  And if you like difficult 2D sidescrollers, this game is absolutely worth it.

This is pretty much the best Mega Man game we're going to get for the time being, and I'm okay with that. I'm more than glad that I backed this game. I'm going to write an honest review.
To start, there were certainly some issues with the delays and and bad press releases stemming from those delays, and that is essentially what many bad reviews are stemming from. On its own, if you take the delay issues and the forum issues out of it completely, this is a decent game. I have yet to find a reasonable facsimile that's as good on Steam as MN9.
Controls are tight and consistent, which is as you would expect from a Mega Man style game. Level design is challenging, and I enjoy the challenge. Most games these days basically place you wherever you die with infinite lives or infinite continues, which defeats the challenge and purpose. Music was catchy, but not overbearing, and fit the overall theme of the game very well.
Story was what you'd expect from a game like this, and doesn't require it to be well thought out with a bunch of plot twists to get the point across. I also don't have any problem with the graphics. I would compare the graphics to Mega Man Powered Up on the PSP, not bad, but certainly won't blow your mind. Again, it didn't detract from my enjoyment of the game.
Basically, people that had their feelings hurt over the delays should probably do something better with their time if they're going to allow that to ruin the game for them. Good game. Buy it if it's on sale if you're unsure.

Let me start by saying that I don't normally write reviews for games because I'm lazy, but this game deserves medals and accolades beyond which I am able to vocalise.
My friend bought me this game for my birthday... It is the greatest gift a man (or woman) can receive!
I can't quite explain why I love this game, but it makes my brain happy.

Factorio is an automated factory logistical production and resource harvesting survival* building game, if any of these things please you, then Factorio is for you.
(* - Aliens can be tweaked to be off completely or ramped up into lil' evolving killing machines)
8-bit style graphics and animation, VERY low PC requirements, extremely fast save/load times.
Factorio however is not without its faults, mostly in the form of balancing issues, which for a solo player can be extremely steep in costs, both time and resources.
Automating production is a must, an absolute MUST, there is no way around this (aside from mods) and as your technology becomes more and more advanced, the factories needed to automate production become vastly more complex, this isn't a bad thing, but it can get very tedious to set-up solo, truth be told it's satisfying at first but quickly becomes a burden when producing the next tier up requires production of a product which requires an entire production facility of their own, and the next tier requires exponentially more automation of their own as well, arguably this is the whole point of Factorio, and where the enjoyment is.
Don't even bother crafting in-hand, it's the slowest thing in the universe, and the more complex (and needed) things cannot be crafted in-hand at all.
TL;DR
Great game with satisfying gameplay which can become repetative quickly, especially solo, so bring friends if that bothers you!
Has some recipe cost balance issues.

I was very excited for this game considering all the positive reviews. After an hour of "gameplay", I decided to refund it. I can feel that this game was someone's love child, and that someone (or group of someones) really tried for this to succeed. But I just couldn't bring myself to "play" this "game" any further. It hurts a little to give this a negative review, but I'll have to be honest.
To be clear: The concept of this game seems very promising, especially since I personally love the SciFi genre. I expected something like "Ex Machina" or the unfortunately not very well known TV series "Humans". Sadly, my expectations were not met.
As someone else already mentioned, the writing style was that of a mediocre fan fiction. If you know what I mean by that, you'll know what I mean.
Relating to that, the characters were extremely one-dimensional, and no identification took place. Neither with the main character (me) nor with any of the other characters. They kind of just existed, but had no personality. All in all, the writing was bad. Considering this is a purely writing based game, this is a major issue. There was no immersion. When I felt something interesting was happening, I raised my hope only to be let down, because this topic was so quickly dropped again. I finally didn't even care for the text anymore, and just read the answers. That was when I decided to end the game because it had simply lost me.
And relating to that, there is a lot of wasted potential (as seems to be a common theme with this game). I chose Josh's story path. My character and Josh knew each other for years now, and my character was secretly in love with him. In the context of building my robot, my character finally came out to Josh, and saw that Josh felt the same for him. This could have been a major theme. Instead they very anti-climactically just kiss, spend the night together, and from then on are a couple. And the writing is not much more excited about this than I am in this review. And that is bad. I would like to compare this to Pam's and Jim's romance in The Office. They loved eachother, but couldn't be together. When they finally kissed, Jim didn't simply say "ok cool", but there was so much emotion going on. This was totally lacking here.
The author is clearly forcing a certain POV that I really don't agree with. As someone who is very much into ethics, I would have loved to decide my approach for myself. But generally, I could only decide between different POVs the author had, not my own.
The choices were way too specific so that there was no real immersion. Someone else wrote a review where they critizised this. Or I didn't agree with any of the choices, but I still had to chose one. Again, those were the author's choices, and not my own. With choices a little more general and not that specific, this could have been avoided, probably.
Everything seems a little bit too easy and convenient. There was no twist, no sense for reality, but simply:
->
,
->
.
As someone else has pointed out, the story sometimes doesn't add up. At some time I decide to go to a party with Josh, my significant other. Later, when he calls me, it is as if that never happened. And instead I can either go without him, or with him to a monster truck show (and not to the party). So my previous choice didn't matter. And not in a narratological sense, but simply based on the programming itself. This is frustrating.
I get that this game is based on writing alone, but the complete absence of anything visual besides the text was making the experience bland and uninteresting. I don't expect cut scenes or anything, but some kind of graphical design would have been nice.
I will have to give this game a "no". But, of course, everyone should see for themselves. I didn't like this "game", but apparently some people do. I was disappointed, but ultimately, this game is not trash. It's only lacking. Lacking very hard.

Yellow: The Yellow Artifact is a short platformer game where you have to collect a key (and coins) and reach a door. There are ~20 levels total and each level can be completed in less than 1 minute.
I recognize some of the graphics from
asset (yes, they are free, in case you're wondering) and i actually love it. Sadly, the fonts doesn't match with the graphic at all and the coin counter uses a plain black font.
This game has a good set of relaxing music. I really love listening to it while playing the game.
The game loads very slowly after you press "start" button to start a new game. There is no tutorial so people have to figure out that you have to walk using arrow keys (no wasd control and you can't rebind the keys). You also have to learn (by yourself) that you can't kill the enemy (not even by jumping at them) and you have a limited amount of heart that will be reduced when you touch the enemies (might be different at a certain level, but it's usually 3 hearts). The character can "jump" which looks like floating in the air (because it jumps very slowly), although you can't "jump" down to the platform below you. The game collisions aren't too great either; sometimes, you can fall down when you're walking on a straight platform with a little gap on it (even though you didn't fall on the previous gap) and while you'll hardly fall down if you're on the edge of the platform.
You'll have to collect a key to go to the next level by going through a door. Before you proceed to the next level, you can also collect some coins to increase your score (which i don't know what the purpose is since the score doesn't even displayed after you finish the game). There are some enemies which will move left and right (or up and down) and you have to time yourself to not getting hit. Your heart will be replenished when you run out of health and/or proceed to the next level, so you can force your way through the enemies as long as you have enough heart to reach the door.
There is a menu button on the top left or right of the game (the location changed in a certain level). However, this button will throw you back to the main menu without confirmation at all and the worse part is, the game doesn't save. You have to redo the game if you accidentally pushed the button out of curiosity.
While most of the levels are different from each other, the levels become quite similar starting from level 15. It's like the same world with a slightly different platform placement and key location.
Pros:
- ~20 levels
Cons:
- Slow load after starting the game
- No tutorial
- Bad collision
- Similar levels in latter level
- No save

The Charnel House Trilogy is a game I had my eye on for a while, recently I played through all three games and here is my opinion on them all.
The Charnel House Trilogy is a collection of three games: Inhale, Sepulchre and Exhale. In Inhale we play as Alex Davenport and we try to find our ticket for a train heading to Auger Peak.  In Sepulchre we play as Doctor Lang, a man also heading to the same island and with him we explore the train and then in Exhale we again play as Alex who also has to explore the mysterious train.
The Charnel House is a weird title and I will try to explain it the best I can. The game is more or less story driven, so don't expect that many puzzles and when you do get a puzzle now and then, they are so simple to solve you shouldn't even break a sweat.  I wish the puzzles were a  bit more complex are had some layer of difficulty, but I found myself breezing through the entire game without even having to stop and think on what I'm supposed to do.
The graphics are great and shows that if you want to make a great pixel adventure game, the adventure game engine is the way to do it.
The soundtrack is also really good, It helps build mood and tension and also brings out atmosphere in some of the darker moments in the game.
The voice acting is also really good. Everyone does a great job including Jim ♥♥♥♥ing sterling son who portrays his character in a very creepy manor. If Jim is reading this (which of course he isn't) he should do more voice work in the future.
The game however has a few negatives.
The story has a very rough start. The first chapter is so slow I thought to myself that this game will bore me to death and I've heard so much good stuff about it. But once the♥♥♥♥♥♥starts hitting the fan it get's really good, not to mention the final bit is really disturbing in it's own way.
The puzzles as mentioned previously are way too easy and I wish they could have come up with a better way to do them, but even then some of the puzzles are very fun to do.
The game is not filled with jumpscares, so if you're wondering about that you don't have to worry, you are safe from jumpscares, but you're not safe from disturbing voice acting by Jim Sterling and disturbing material.
Overall I can safely say The Charnel House Trilogy is a great game and definitely worth your time. The game is spooky good time and if you like adventure games or horror in general I highly recommend picking this gem up.

8.5/10 - Great

Medieval Engineers is a medieval (duh) based building game.
Now having said that, the building is very similar to Space Engineers, but with a few twists. I will be making a few comparisons to Space Engineers and Medieval Engineers in this review.
Gravity is always present, and has a huge role in building structures. The structure of any building you make has to be built with a certain amount of structural support. Players can not build a an over the top tall tower and expect it to sustain that height for long. More than likely, it will come crashing to the ground. Just remember when building, you will need to keep in mind on how well it holds up. Currently, the way the game handles structural integrity may be disabled by the player.
All of the building assets that are in Medieval Engineers can be fitted together. One thing unique to Medieval Engineers over Space Engineers is that many assets can be fitted together in the space of one block. Unlike in Space Engineers at the moment, you can put, for example, 2 walls and a bed in the space of one block. This can be very useful when you need to build compact structures.
There are, at the moment, a few objects that allow interaction with structures. Ropes, wheels are probably the most apparent, but they get a lot done. You can build retractible bridges, gates, and many other structures.
There is quite a bit to be seen in Medieval Engineers, but...
TL;DR: Medieval Engineers is a highly indepth building game, but be wary of small lag issues and somewhat rare jumpy physics.

Choice of Robots is the game I always wanted. It's deep, punishing, joyous, and so very genuine. I love that this story is as much about who you are, and who you become, as it is about the world you inevitably change in very real ways.
We sit back and judge triple A games on it's 3 endings with different colored cutscenes; but CoR is so much deeper and enjoyable for it's design. I'm torn between describing it as a game, as much as it is a novel that unfolds to your hopes and inclinations. Every decision made creates a very real impact in your story, and I respect the design choice not to allow for backtracking; as now everything you do has weight.
If I might make a recommendation beyond 'buy this game now!'; it's that you don't try to min-max things. I'll confess I'm guilty of always trying to get 'the best' outcome in most games I play; but Choice of Robots drew me away from that direction. It rewards your mistakes as often as it punishes or ignores your wisdom, and like life; makes you wonder if you made the right choice at every turn.
