Imagine the bleakness of the man versus giant creatures gameplay of Shadow of the Colossus as a definitively Nordic tale, and you have a general idea of what Jotun is. Sprinkle in a little bit of Dark Souls’ difficulty and a malevolent sense of challenge, and you’re closer to hitting the bullseye. Now imagine all of that hand-drawn in a style somewhere between Dragon’s Lair and Princess Mononoke, and you’ve got Jotun.
Boiling the game down to its disparate parts does the game a mild disservice, though. In execution, Jotun is a perfect storybook, a game that seems ripped from the imagination of a Viking child being told tales of warriors of old facing down their gods. It’s a wonderfully wild, vibrant bedtime story told with fire and verve, even when the game is at its most stark and lonely.
Jotun tells the tale of Thora, a Viking shield maiden who falls from her boat during a voyage and drowns. Because passage to Valhalla is only granted to those who fall in battle, Thora is given the chance to earn her way into the golden halls by finding and killing the Jotun, the Titans of Norse mythology. Along the way, the gods assist her, granting her new power when she finds their shrines and pays her respects. Otherwise, all she has is an iron axe and an iron will. We learn between stages where Thora’s determination comes from in a fantastic, steely narration performed in Icelandic. Each new piece of her story would be worth it on its own, revealing years of underestimation, neglect, and later, a sibling jealousy that turns tragic. Even if the gameplay wasn’t as good as it was, being able to help Thora achieve glory would be more than worth the effort.
Gameplay is 16-bit levels of simple, and yes, that is a compliment. You have a light attack with Thora’s axe, a hard-hitting heavy attack with a major delay, and a dodge. Thora can find massive shrines to the Gods in each stage, and by praying there, she earns new magical powers specific to each one--Thor allows her to use Mjolnir for a short time, Frigg allows her to heal at will, Loki creates a decoy that eventually explodes after a time--but all six of the powers have limited uses, and none are what you would call a guaranteed solution to any sticky situation. Primarily, timing, cunning, and luck will get Thora to Valhalla.
For most of the game, that cunning involves mastery of the environment. Jotun’s six stages, which can be tackled in any order, are impeccably designed. They are deceptively linear, laid out in such a way that gives the impression of vast, stunning tableaus in places dwarfed in size by your typical Diablo III dungeon. The illusion works. Grand, breathtaking vistas are the norm in Jotun, and they often serve as a wicked distraction from the dangers mere inches away. They’re also often rather desolate places, dark locales that no mortal has tread upon in ages. The game isn’t swarming with enemies, except for one particular stage that sends a veritable legion of dwarves your way. This bolsters the comparisons to Shadow of the Colossus, where the loneliness of what Thora has to do makes the sheer distance between each new obstacle feel like a greater journey. The real problem with that desolation is that more than a few times, you’ll need to backtrack through some of these areas to find much needed power ups, or because you’ve missed a crucial switch in order to get to said power ups, or because you’ve ended up in an area and the game’s obtuse pause screen map didn’t help you.
The main events of the game, however, are the Jotun themselves as bosses. The Jotun are simply awe-inspiring enemy design, taking the rather threadbare descriptions from Norse lore, and extrapolating them to the nth degree, with each one several times Thora’s size onscreen.
The best is still the first: A nature giant that feels like Ursula from The Little Mermaid made entirely out of living trees and vines. Still, each of the bosses are just wonderfully realized, and you get maybe a good minute to marvel at them before the pain starts. A terrifying shield-swinging giant can summon a legion of dwarves out of the ground to rush at Thora with a scream. Halfway through the frost giant’s fight, the playing field turns into a sheet of slippery ice; when it’s down to a quarter bar of life, a white-out blizzard starts. A blacksmith giant has you fighting in a neverending firestorm. What the Jotun typically lack in speed, they make up for in power, where being in the wrong place at the wrong time during a fight will mean your end in two hits. The Jotuns’ patterns and weak points aren’t hard to suss out whatsoever, it’s simply a matter of using your limited arsenal to deal with them, and often with the horde of peripheral obstacles/enemies each Jotun will throw at you during, and quite often it will still not be enough. The game gives Thora infinite tries, and will start her right at the boss with each of her powers replenished each time she dies. Persistence and learning from the numerous failures will lead to success, but the game will not coddle, and every victory will be well-earned beyond a shadow of a doubt.
The PS4 and Xbox One ports of Jotun are very much on par with the PC version. The only major difference is the addition of Valhalla Mode, a boss rush that opens up after you beat the campaign. Aside from expanded health bars, an extra element of danger has been added to each boss battle taken from the campaign, forcing you to alter your attack strategy. The first stage's plant boss now has poisonous spores surrounding her weak points, making it a game of hit and run rather than patient strikes. Alternately, a sword-wielding forge boss has a much shorter window in which to strike. Valhalla Mode is a small addition, but a welcome one.
Jotun is a short game, and good players can probably plow through it in about 3 or 4 hours, but even with the ending behind me, I find myself dying to witness some images again and wanting to try different strategies. I want to hear Thora tell her tale again. Any good bedtime story that makes you want to hear it again right after it’s over is one for the ages.
The Good
Beautiful hand drawn art
Tough but mostly fair challenge
Wonderfully imagined take on Norse mythology
Fantastic boss battles
The Bad
Some mild, tedious backtracking

In a time of horror games that rely more on monster closets or cheap jump scares than they do any sort of atmosphere or dread, The Charnel House Trilogy is a welcome creep-out that matches its building darkness with its point-and-click pace. Following a fateful encounter, a man and a young woman separated by fewer degrees than they realize board a train for a rather peculiar and rather disturbing journey.
Despite being dubbed a trilogy, the game on the whole is rather short. This is not a disadvantage, however, as it keeps the plot tight and keeps things moving along at a pretty good clip, so long as you don't get stuck on any of the puzzles. In the first segment, we learn about Alex, still infuriated by a relatively recent breakup and not having the best evening in her apartment before an impending train trip. This is mostly establishment, though we are introduced to the other playable character, Dr. Harold Lang, and the train central to the plot, at the end.
In the second segment, Dr. Lang is highlighted, left alone to interact with the train's mysterious but friendly conductor, who sends him roaming among every cabin -but- Alex's for some reason to chat (or try to chat) with some other peculiar passengers. Strangeness accelerates rapidly, eventually leading to some grim discoveries regarding Dr. Lang's fate and, possibly, his present as well.
Alex returns in the third chapter, similarly left to roam the train and avoid Alex despite wondering what he's up to. Alex meets a greater number of passengers than Lang did, and eventually starts inexplicably stumbling her way through her past. Reliving several events from her more recent months, she discovers the truth behind what drove her to take this trip in the first place, and some things about people she thought she knew better.
Despite the short length and the low price, The Charnel House Trilogy is a beautiful game. The sprite work is great, the animation fluid, and the voice work is fantastic. I did have some mild beef with Alex's monologue toward the end of the first chapter sounding rather flat in its delivery, but this was not an issue that repeated itself later on. It was also great to hear Abe Goldfarb again, as he's quite a familiar earful from his regular appearances in other point-and-clicks. Jim Sterling also delivers what is arguably his creepiest performance to date, which is saying quite a bit if you're familiar with his Podtoid, Fistshark, Dismal Jesters, or Podquisition history.
If it wasn't clear already, I highly recommend picking this up. It seems there may be a follow-up down the line as well, and I cannot wait to see more.

The word "ruthless" used in the description of the game is just a euphemism for minimal game development and lazy programming. I rank this worst than Coldfire Keep. For $10 USD I didn't expect much, but I got less than that. Maybe this is one of those games that's meant to be played on mobile device. Here are the pros and cons as I see them:
PROS:
1) Nice graphics for still scenes
2) Interface is pretty straight forward and intuitive
CONS:
1) Saving game.
a) quits the game and not back to main menu.
b) If you die, and you will, you go to the main menu. If you choose Continue you go to the point where you died and go into an endless loop. Start a new game.
2) If you get poisoned by a snake, unless you have a Cure Poison potion (50gp), you will die. You die because, even if you sell the two mana potions you start with you only get 30gp. If you get poisoned you CANNOT leave the dungeon to get cured back in town. Since you don't have a Cure Poison potion, YOU DIE!
3) No resting or camping. No regeneration of health unless you find food. Good luck on finding potions as the dungeon is randomly generated, so the map changes in each game. If you get poisoned, YOU DIE!
4) There is not enough money or junk to be gathered to afford buying/upgrading gear or a single Cure Poison potion. And, we know what happens if you get poisoned....

Ok, move forward to the next room, and dammit another snake. CRAP, the character got poisoned! Guess what? That's right, YOU DIE!
This could have been a fun and interesting game, but the developer didn't seem to want to be bothered including a few features to allow the game to be interesting and challenging versus just ridiculous to the point of why should I spend anymore time on a unenjoyable $10 game.

Transistor is Supergiant Games' followup to their indie hit, Bastion. It's easy to spot similarities between the two regarding the setup of their worlds and their awesome narrators but Transistor steps out often on its own, even though this means certain areas in Transistor play second fiddle to Bastion.
The game opens with the protagonist - a singer called Red, who takes a mysterious weapon called Transistor that is impaled through her friend. She has lost her voice, and her friend's soul is transferred to the Transistor. The world she lives in is called Cloudbank, a world where robotic entities called the Process repurpose the environment based on people's votes through terminals called the OVC. Red is hunted by the Camerata for unknown reasons before the game starts, but her position from prey changes to predator the moment she is armed with the Transistor. With nothing more than the voice of her friend to guide her, her goals are clear - find out why the Process are going berserk and why she's being hunted by taking the fight straight to the Camerata, and to restore her friend's soul back into his body.
Most of the story is told through the voice of the Transistor and through brief tidbits you get through the OVC, and Traces. You'll have to make do with bread crumbs leading you all the way to the finish, but even after the credits scroll, you'll wonder what exactly happened. Not every question is answered, and even when answered, one has to ask whether that's what the devs intended.
Transistor is a 2D isometric, single-player only, action-RPG. You make use of various Functions() gained by absorbing 'Traces' - the souls of fallen people, and by leveling up. You have 4 active slots, 2 upgrade slots for each active slot, and 4 passive slots. Every Function() performs differently depending on which slot they've been put into. This is reminiscent of the Materia system in Final Fantasy VII so with a little planning, you'll be able to pull off huge combos that not only pummel your foes into submission using various debuffs, but also end up healing you or temporarily having enemies switch to protecting you. Functions can be executed in real time and have short cool-down times but if you want to stop time temporarily and plan out your actions, you can do so by making use of Turn().
The downside to using Turn() is that the cool-down time is much longer, and aside from a few Functions() like the quick dash called Jaunt(), you'll be essentially unable to be on both the defensive and offensive.
Word of advice - don't spam Turn() unless you are facing the last boss in the game. Use Turn() sparingly or to dispose certain high value targets. In all other situations, it's best you use your Functions() in real-time. You can also use various 'Limiters' that grant you experience bonuses at the risk of increasing the game's difficulty.
The game is mostly linear with the occasional branching with hidden OVC terminals or Back Doors (special areas where you do side-missions like disposing foes in a single turn, or a time-attack mode, fighting a gauntlet of enemies etc).
What I did not like about Transistor is the fact that most of the stuff I've mentioned is not explained. I had no idea what the Passive and Upgrade slots looked like till 3/4th of the game and I still cannot fathom the in-game use of flourishing (a fancy animation where Red throws the Transistor and grabs it in mid-air) and humming. The UI is clunky and you need to swap between various sub-menus to make sense what the various Function() setups will do. When your health drops to zero, you lose Functions() that you've frequently used but don't fret - you can recover them again from Access Points that functions as your savepoint and menu to switch skill setups. The game does not mention this so first time users may freak out when their health bar is depleted.
Words don't do this game justice. The visuals are pure 2D sex for the eyes with luscious colors, cool shades and a very fitting artstyle. Props need to do be given to the art department. The animation work is stellar and is in perfect sync with the rest of the visuals. This game is a visual feast.
In-game graphical settings are surprisingly bleak with only a screen resolution setting. The game also seems to have some technical issues because when I first ran the game, I got a shockingly disappointing 20 FPS. Checking the forums, I saw that even users with hardcore setups were getting huge frame drops. Fortunately, I was able to fix this by doing the following.
Open Steam --> Library --> Right click Transistor --> Properties --> Set Launch Options.
Paste the line below in the field and then hit OK :
/Bloom=false /DrawRecursivePaths=false /SwapInterval=0
The music in Transistor is decent. The tracks are kinda light and ambient but there are a few standout tracks like 'Paper Boats'. Supergiant Games has uploaded the entire OST of the game on YouTube so give it a listen.
The voice acting in this game is really good. But the real star is Logan Cunningham, the voice actor for the Transistor. SO. DAMN. GOOD.
Transistor is a nice, short game of about 6-10 hours that is well worth the money. Is it better than Bastion? No, but it is still a good game and one worth owning and playing.
Transistor is a 2.5 GB download from Steam.
The game is stable and I've not encountered any crash while playing this game.
Transistor has Steam Trading Cards and there are a total of 5 cards.
There are 33 achievements and the game will require at least 2 playthroughs to 100%.

Owned Space Engineers and played it for quite a bit and so far I like what I see in Medieval Engineers. It has several useful mechanics that we will hopefully see implemented into Space Engineers but also has a few things that need to be addressed, that one would of thought wouldn't be a problem.
Let's start off simple:
Medieval Engineers is a branch off of Space Engineers developed by an entirely seperate team within the same studio so that both games can continue to grow and be improved without splitting the time and effort between one game or the other. This is an exceptionally good thing because it means we won't have to deal with prolonged update times or glitches having to be put on hold as they alternate. Another good thing from this is that as one development team comes up with a great concept within their own, it will then eventually be transplanted into the other essentially improving both games at the same time, a double bonus for us who own both.
I enjoy the fact it is a lot easier to place blocks within the same tile now so that you can easily fix wall placement and/or fortifications that would otherwise have some very weird looking repairs/modifications to themselves and it also allows you to merge blocks that would normally not have been placed together to create even more interesting designs. Since this game released roughly a little over a month ago now, it is already impressive.
The implementation of the structural integrity build adds much to the "Engineering" aspect of this game which many had claimed had been missing from Space Engineers. Sure we get to build things, but they aren't always sound nor well thought out and now we're forced to do both. We experiment and build a design and then when it falls apart, we take it apart and see what went wrong so we can fix it or build it even better the next time. When it comes to designing structures and defenses, this is a great mechanic at seeing what is already weak and needs to be reinforced instead of having to destroy it first. However, this mechanic is still very much a prototype of the final feature. There are bugs with this and as it is only in Alpha Stage so far even with the public release. Where one time it can function properly, other times things will fall apart even when they're sound. It can be annoying but then this is an Alpha, don't expect everything to be working properly.
Many people complain the price of the game at $19.99 or $14.99 USD for those who already own Space Engineers is a bit much. For those just coming in, I can see why you would think that as there have been many cash grabs in the past but these developers have already been around for over a year with Space Engineers and it has come a remarkably long way. With the quality, care, and dedication they've put in their other version, I would easily pay more for this kind of game even though it's far from release because they keep re-polishing it, the workshop is a major source of custom mods and/or net-code UI, and better yet, it fits my favorite time frame of the Medieval Period in general.
Multiplayer hasn't been fully implemented yet but then in Space Engineers, it took over four months for that to come out and when it did, it was working with very few bugs and overall was very enjoyable. It gave people time to experiment and plan ahead on what worked and what didn't so that way when you and your friends decide to have a battle-royale, you could make it work the way you imagined it (maybe, depends on your creativity).
Overall, with just a few minutes of gameplay experimenting with the new features, I can safely say that this game has brought several much needed changes to the table and can only get better from here on out. (Knock on wood, don't want to jinx the unimaginable happening).
Overall Score: 9.1/10
The game is in Alpha mode so I respect that there are still some bugs/features that don't work properly but overall, the game has a steady framerate, the destruction engine doesn't lag as much as it used to, better building interface and UI, somewhat functioning AI which is a great hint at what is to come.
For those of you who don't already own it, I suggest also getting Space Engineers. For tips, help, and general improvements to those starting out, try watching some videoes from LastStandGamers. They're a tremendous help to the community and also take out shoutouts for things people want to try but can't build on their own yet.

I got this game as part of a donation bundle and despite it not being the main reason for donating in the first place - or secondary motivation either - this game had me positively surprised and took my main attention of the bundle in the aftermath. As I am sure many will have told you in here, this game is an edutainment game done right. You identify enemies through a clue game. If you can't speak English well, you might be able to do it a little better afterwards. And even if you don't know the right monster, with the spirit index you can obtain, solving the puzzle is more than possible and may teach you one or two things you didn't know about the English language yet. I consider myself not native, but well educated, and I learned several new things. Not about Heian Japan, I knew that much. There are some nice things you might only notice on your second run and a lot sense for detail, although I found some places where that detail sadly lacked. For example if you didn't save a certain character, if you haven't been up to date with the talk of another, that person regards the other person as still alive. Some kind of event trigger would have been nice and several altered text. If you act 'evil', the other characters should at least shortly react to it on the next visit. But those are minor immersion problems I only suffer from as a roleplayer.
I got it in both, English and Japanese, and if my motivation ever reaches its peak to learn Japanese fully, I will use it as some kind of final test to complete it yet again. For now since I only donated half the bundle price to the creators - and 99 spirits was one of many games - I decided to support these games by buying the sidestory content DLCs. These 10€ are well earned.

I honestly don't get why this game has such "mixed" reviews. So let me start explaining why this game is worth playing.
Pros:
+ Good plot
+ Original gameplay
+ Good artwork
+ Nice soundtrack
+ You can capture Tsukumogami, like Pokèmons!
+ Bonus white fox
+ Bonus skirt-chasing monk
+ Bonus armor you see in some screenshots and you can actually get for yourself
+ Three different endings
+ If English is not your main language, guessing the Tsukumogami's name can actually be a good exercise for your vocabulary
+ Every Tsukumogami has different skills, and you may choose your party according to your needs and preferences
+ The characters are fun to interact with and overall well-written
Cons:
- Sometimes, it's gonna crash, and you're gonna rage
- Sometimes your save gets corrupted
- I personally found looking for new Tsukumogami relaxing, but it might not be the same for everyone, the encounters are random and it may get somewhat tedious. (I found 5 pots while looking for something else. 5 pots. In a row.)
- After a while the combat system may tire you, because it's always the same
I recommend getting this game on a good sale or a bundle because of its "crashy" behaviour. The only real thing you can do to somehow prevent the legendary crash-rage is saving often, changing slots from time to time so you don't have to start over, should your save get corrupted.
Combat system is completely awful, well beyond ruining the game for me.  Be certain you're interested in that style before purchasing.

Personally I really enjoyed the game. It's not perfect, but a fun experience.
Pros:
- Tight gameplay controls
- Fun fast paced action controls (besides when there are the occassional cutscenes)
- Really satisfying to finally beat a level/boss after struggling for a few attempts.
- Fun characters for the most part, especially for kids I imagine.
- Some of the boss powerups are fun and interesting to learn to use, although some like Battalions are a bit overpowered, but still really fun to use.
Cons:
- Too many insant deaths. This was really the main frustration for me. A few here and there aren't too bad, but it felt like a large part of the levels difficulty was getting around the instant kills, as opposed to fighting enemies themselves.
- The lives system, although it probably would have been better without the numerous instant deaths previously mentioned.
Overall:
Regardless of what all the haters say, this is a fun game. I wouldn't consider it better than the best MMgames, my 2 favorits being MMX and MMX4. However, I will say that I enjoyed it overall moreso than X5, so I would also say that it is better than some MM games, and really that's about what I would have expected. I doubt any MM styled action platformer will get me to think that it is better than MMX, but that's okay. The game is still fun and I am happy with my purchase. I havn't played the Ray DLC yet, but I plan to buy and play it soon.
I would definitely recommend this to fans of the action platformer genre, but I do have to say, don't expect it to be the next best Megaman game. It isn't, but if you keep your expectations at reasonable levels, then you should find yourself having an enjoyable time zipping through levels blowing up robots, and hopefully avoiding 1 hit kills.

mechanics feel sluggish and incomplete :

- shooting doesn't feel that good

x You can't shoot two arrows at the same time, the first has to reach something before you can shoot the second
x Her shield only works on small bullets
x her gliding feels weird
x dashing with her is useless and WILL make you die

I ain't sure they needed even one million for this part, too....
- Storytelling :
It's basically Megaman & Megaman Zero plots mixed :
Something happens at "the robot colosseum" & every Mighty N° are crazy. Some say the game is shorter than the credits.
It's true.
I died & had several game over. Still took me less than 4 hours to beat the game.
Credits are 4H long.
And a lot of backers are called "Generous Backers", I'm pretty sure they asked another name (like "refund pl0x")
CONCLUSION :
Not recommended.

I went into MN9 like alot of people, hoping for something like a modern Mega Man from a legend in the industry.  I was sorely disapointed.  Check the bottom for a summary if you aint got time for my ranting.
Let me get a few of my biggest beefs out of the way.
1: This is NOT Mega Man.
While MN9 has some similar basic aspects to the blue bomber, it stands seperatly but still trapped in its shadow.  Namely there is no wall jumping from the X series and no standard charge shot to take out larger enemies, at least not that I found.  The wall jumping I can understand, but when I'm trying to keep a flow going and I need to stop to peck at my enemies with a pea shooter the game can become a slog early on.
2: The assimilation mechanic is MN9's biggest strength and weakness.
MN9 (or Beck) can absorb enemies by dashing into them after weakening them to gain additional score points and buffs.  The buffs can be useful increasing speed, filling a standby healing tank (somewhat like Mega Man's sub tanks), or granting you a flame shot that passes through enemies.  Since it can be used to more quickly eliminate enemies, this mechanic encourages you to charge directly into them, even while they are still functional and attacking.  Couple this with my next point.
3:  Healing items are rare and assimilation does not heal.  Mega Man X had a great rhythem of shooting enemies to grab health and keep moving.  MN9 from my experience only drops healing items at checkpoints, which drop more aids the more you die.  So while I was charging into enemy fire and taking damage near constantly I wouldnt get to heal untill much later if at all.
4. The learning curve is too sharp for new players and borderline for vetarans.  Some sections can turn the game into a bullet hell.  Mighty Number 1's level had a section with so many enemies in the foreground and background that realistically dodging it all was just infuriating.  It was near impossible to get through remotely unscathed.  Sometimes the platforming can bring your flow to a screaching halt and other times borders on just unfair.  Every level had a point where I went from a smooth flow to a controller dropping brick wall way too quickly.  I never felt like the game was teaching me to master it, only that it was trying to get in my way.
5. Characters are WAY too chatty.  The most anoying sin of the late Mega Man games lives on.  That's all I have to say.
With MN9's budget, pedigree, numerous delays, and general fan expectation it was almost doomed to fail.  At the very least it is not a total failure.  It's just.....meh.  To quote the game's designer "it's better than nothing."  In the generation of Shovel Knight, Axiom Verge, and Undertail "better than nothing" just doesn't cut it.  At the very least it made me dust off my old Mega Man X cartridge.

Shenzhen I/O follows the strong Zachtronics tradition of extracting the _fun_ part of an engineering job and placing it into a game; if you enjoyed TIS-100 or Spacechem, you'll very likely enjoy this game.
Of note, both of the scoring metrics are different than what players have seen in the past:
- Parts Cost: Instead of just counting the number of reactors or cores used, there are varying qualities of parts to consider, each with their own price. If you can manage to squeeze your program down from the ¥5 microcontroller to tiny variant that costs just ¥3, you'll have incredibly constraints to work with, but you'll be at the top of the cost-leaderboard.
- Energy Usage: Thankfully program-size itself is no longer scored (that's already paid for in the parts-cost), but instead the number of executed instructions during each "turn" is. This not only is more interesting from a real-world applications point of view (sleeping is essential for battery-life), but it means the game fundamentally provides synchronization-points between the processors in each puzzle, since they now *must* sleep at some point.
Oh, and Shenzhen also offers Zachtronic's best story-telling structure to date. It's both quick to read and stays relevent to the puzzles on hand, since each puzzle is embedded in a short email-chain that describes both the setup and consequences of each product being engineered. Another nice touch is that most of the puzzles come with context-appropriate output animations that help make it feel all the more like you're actually engineering a product.
This is a game I look forward to playing with friends, both cooperatively on the couch, and competitively through the leaderboards. :)

Just requested a REFUND. The dev seriously needs to re-think how certain aspects of the game should work.
As for being a difficult game, I can live with that,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥I grew up playing Wizardry I on the Apple IIe and then the PC, talk about unforgiving and difficult? I beat that game multiple times and it was very difficult compared to today’s games.
The problem with Verlies II is NOT it's gameplay difficulty, but the ridiculous and annoying controls, plus highly illogical rules that limit the player. Let me explain.
1. Using the 'F' key to move forward instead of the standard 'W' key as in most games, you know the WASD control.
When you are in the dungeon, you face one of four possible directions just like in most other games of this type, yet to move forward you HAVE to focus your cursor over the opening and then press F and not W, that is ridiculous! Now, saying that... IF the opening in front of the hero had something like a shut, or locked door, then placing the cursor over it, and pressing 'F' to unlock (if you have a key), or to turn the knob to open a door would be understandable, but so far in the time I played, all the openings are simple black passages to simulate the darkness leading into the next chamber. Since the openings are unobstructed and as easy as walking from one room in your house to the next via an arch or opening, a simple press of the 'W' key to move forward would suffice. Also, if perhaps a single direction had more than a single exit, or path/door then placing the cursor over the proper door, or opening you wish to exit through makes sense, but in all the time I've played I've only seen a single opening/path in any one direction. Again a simple press of 'W' would suffice.
2. Exiting the Dungeon
When you enter the dungeon, you CAN NOT simply turn around and exit, even though when you do turn around, you see the cavern exit and the forest (trees, grass, etc..) on the other side of the exit. Essentially, there is nothing to keep you from simply turning around and walking out, especially if you've wandered around a bit and took a beating and need to get back to town for supplies or to heal. When you try to leave you get some BS excuse that you have too much pride to leave the dungeon. COME ON! If you are really set on such a ridiculous rule (not allowing the hero to exit via the opening they just entered from, use a little imagination and get creative. For example... "You enter the dungeon and look about the first chamber. As you are examining the chamber you hear a deep, rumble... the room begins to shake and then a loud crash... then darkness! You spin around to see the entrance to the dungeon/cave has caved in and there is no amount of digging that would allow you to leave this place from whence you came! Tis up to thee hero to find another means of escaping this dunjon!" Wala, instant logical explanation and more realistic method for keeping a player from leaving the dunjon whenever he, or she wishes to.
3. No control customization!
How many games have you played where they use a modified WASD control scheme where Q and E actually turn you left, or right? Well, in this game, the 'E' key = drink a health potion. Do you know how many times I've been in the dunjon and tried to turn and my sub-conscious simply hit the 'E' key because two of the other games I play use the 'E' key to turn right? Well, it's safe to say I've wasted countless potions by accidentally hitting E instead of D to turn right. This can be simply remedied by allowing the user to customize their movement and function keys.
There are a few other issues that irk me... Here is one more...
4. Using a shield to block.
This game's combat is not turn based, but real time. The monster moves from left to right, and vice versa all the time you must position your cursor over the creature before swinging your weapon or you'll end up missing the target. Combat is really a timing game because you need to see how many strikes you can get in before you must press the other mouse button to raise your shield and defend the monster's attack. This so far is fine and can be quite enjoyable, but there is a problem in that even using the shield properly doesn't negate the damage taken by the monsters attack. It may lessen it, but if you are low on health, have no more health potions, and a simple hit or two is going to kill you, then you might as well restart because there is NOTHING you can do to survive the next encounter, and you aren;t going to move more than a room or two before that next encounter happens. Remember as per issue #2 above, you also can't turn around and head back to town and rest, heal, or stock up on supplies, so once you are in the situation just mentioned, your game is OVER even though you aren't quite dead yet. The next fight and a single hit or two regardless of whether blocked or not, ends up killing you. A better way to have implemented the shield would be one of the following...
A) Have the monsters movement and strike timing alternate between 1 or 2 speeds during a battle, so you can't simply get used to a creatures timing and then strike/block without danger of harm. With this method, you can have a shield block all damage from a strike that is successfully blocked with the shield. The slight randomness to a monster's attack pattern can trip up a player who may miss a block with the shield and thus the monster makes a hit that realistically kills the hero. That would be acceptable.
B) Have the shield only able to block a certain amount of strikes before the hero MUST repair it himself in the dunjon, or purchase a replacement shield to replace the now broken one. For this to work, the dev needs to either a) allow the hero to repair a shield with materials found in the dungeon, or b) Allow the hero the option of exiting the dunjon when he needs to go to town to have the smith repair or sell the hero a new shield.
Well, there are a few other things not worth mentioning because they will make this already long review even worse. I have requested a REFUND and will not purchase this game until some changes are made. I only hope the dev listens to this review and similar complaints in the forums and makes the right choices. I know I would have no problem returning to Verlies II, if these issues are remedied. As it is i would NOT recommend this game to anyone.

When you rage quit from a game and you immediately want to give it another try, you know you've got something special.
Verlies II is a first person dungeon crawler, with real-time combat and grid based deplacement.
And it wants you dead.
Yep, according to the Master, death is the only thing you rightly deserve.
Let's prove him wrong, shall we?
In order to do that, you'll have to master combat precision, actively aiming at the monsters, and timing, to block with your shield and manage breath/endurance. It's a fun and solid system and you may soon try to block "frame perfect" in the vain hope it will mitigate more damage :p or you will die miserably for it was obvious this 5th strike in a row was dumb.
You'll have to master the odds in a game of dice for you'll need tons of money to buy keys, health potions, repair your so fragile stuff, cure poison, sharpen a blade, ID artefacts way too high level for you but rejoice! The smith can "standardize" it (remove the level restriction) for a mere 30 gold coins, less than a night at the inn! That's one of the only "gift" in an otherwise harsh and tight economy.
You'll have to take lots of risks. The boss is down, should you delve deeper straight away for an XP boost or should you take the chance to go back to town as it's the only moment it's free of charge? On the brink of death, do you tail back in the middle of a floor with XP loss or do you pick up that probably trapped healing basket? Yeah, you should have trekked back...
You'll have to die, over an over, for there's no tutorial and the game is mean and nasty. But like in the best rogue-likes where exploration and experimentation are key, it wraps up in the long run and I dare say Verlies really shines, carrying the torch of classics with strength.
You'll probably have to specialize. There's not so many level ups and there's a lot of skills, actives and passives. Classics like shield bashing or alchemy for instance, and not so classic ones, like a heal paid by XP or an instant kill spell that eats up your total mana pool.
Floors layout, monster population, loot and traps are all randomly (procedurally?) generated. Level tone and design change every 3 floors and while there's no lush vistas nor DX12 features, the comic-style graphics are lovely (though I miss the naked blacksmith from the first opus^^)! Sound is good, atmospheric and creepy, or dumb and funny like that cash register trading sound.
So, this review's a mess... I hope it stills shows of much I enjoy this love letter to the genre!

Initially I only purchased this game because I heard that Jim ♥♥♥♥ing Sterling, Son was involved, and I generally enjoy his work. However, once I got sucked into it, a whole new aspect opened up to me.
Remember that time when you were little, and your parents left you alone in the house for the first time? You felt oddly excited, even a little courageous... until you heard a bump in the next room. At first you were sure it was nothing, but then your little childish brain began to run wild, and told you that there was something wrong. You couldn't put your finger on it, but there was something about it that all of a sudden made you want to rush to your parents, but they weren't there. You were alone, and your only recourse was to curl up in a corner and wait out the storm.
Charnel House is the video game equivalent of that memory. Although it doesn't assault you with blood and guts, there's something about it that's just... off. As you work to unravel the mystery, the entire story begins a subtle, but noticable descent into madness. It gets to the point that you'd rather a monster did jump out and try to tear off your face, because then you'd have a definite answer to the question of what's out there.
It's short, but every gosh-darn second is packed with atmosphere and tension. Slowly but surely, an overwhelming sense of hopelessness seeps over you, and the plan becomes not to survive, but to figure out what's going on before you die.
It's definitely one of the better games to come out this year so far. Sure, it doesn't have guns and explosions, but who needs that when you're slowly urinating down your own leg?

Now, Don't mistake this game to be anything like space engineers, The people over at Keen have done an amazing job at making this game vary from space engineers, Those of you who have Space Engineers will have to re-think everything you thought you knew about engineering. The Physics complexity, The Graphical beauty and the absolutely
soundtrack make this game completely worth the cost! The soundtrack alone is worth buying this game!
The downside's are that the game so far has not been completed, so flaws are to be expected, and the structural integrity can crash the game at some point and because it's newer there's a distinct lack of mod's compared to its space-themed counterpart.
To sum it all up;
Pro's:
+Graphically stunning, very good for an alpha, But atleast on my PC, Not too taxing.
+Eargasm! The soundtrack is both soothing, and uplifting. If you like medieval themed orchestra, Then the music alone is reason enough to buy this game!
+Complex physics.  Something that is hardly ever seen in most games is the formation of rubble in such a believable manner. Your building's will have to stand up to the test of gravity and it really makes you need to think outside the box!
+Scroll n' roll. Scrolling with select blocks will give you varients of that block type. This is something i love about Medieval Engineers. Nuff said.
+Blockception. You can place a block withing a block withing a block within a bl- (etc.)
Con's:
-Physics! Y U DO THIS?! Like I said, Amazingly complex and glorious physics and destruction, But these attributes are also a downfall if you build too big! The very structural integrity this game is heralded for is its greatest downfall, requiring you to bear with the limitations of the current engine. Remember, This will probably be changed in later updates.
-So, No real weapons? Well, Not yet. You can shoot canonballs but let's be honest. We're all waiting for swords, shields, bows and arrows! The recent addition of Barbarians (destructive A.I.) can't be killed very easily and appear to have their own spiked club as a weapon, which is not available to the player at this time. This will mostlikely change in future updates.
Now there are probably some other things, but that's a summary. Also, some blocks are missing from the trailer, My guess is over at Keen, They are fixing up some block dynamics, Checking viability and tweaking the physics engine a bit. The lack of mod's in the steam workshop should be temporary too, as the more people get this, the more modder's will come and grace this gem of a game. You dont even need to own this game to mod it! :D
In the end, I give it a 9.5/10. Good job Keen and thanks for this wonderful addition to my Steam library!

I was a bit skeptical at the beginning, but after playing it for one evening in the coop, I had to change my mind.
I usually don't bother playing early access titles - low amount of contents, bugs, unpolished gameplay, poor optimization, etc. But this one is completely different. It's already bug-free, has polished and captivating gameplay, runs great on almost any PC, got enough contents to make you entertained for at least 100 hours.
Also, I usually don't like base building sandboxes. The absence of goals, "entertain yourself" style gameplay gets boring pretty fast. But this one is very opposite.
First, it has different modes enough to get you busy for some time.
Second, it has coop, that works surprisingly well.
Third, the sandbox mode has a real goal and ending, unlike the most early-access titles out there. You will have things to do all the time.
Fourth, the amount of technologies and techniques in the game is overwhelming. Building electricity network, mine metals, craft weapons, defend your base and attack monster dens, harvest oil, create nuclear power stations and there's still tons of more activities to do! And each one has its own gameplay mechanics you will have to learn.
So, if you like this kind of game, just buy it already. But even if you usually don't like them, just like me, there's still a big chance you will enjoy it a lot. Just download the demo and give it a shot.
The only ones who will not enjoy this game are the ones who can't stand any logic or strategy games at all. This game contains action moments and gameplay, but still probably it's not for you.

Developers of Factorio are among the most irresponsible game devs there is. They apparently don't care that we gamers have lives to live, that our bodies need 8 hours of sleep or that we are still required to maintain our relationships with other human beings. No they are the scourge of gamers everywhere.
Seriously my first computer game was Pong in 1976. And today at 51, I play Civilization VI, City SkyLines, Starcraft II, World of Warcraft, Withcher III, etc. While I cannot compare apples and oranges, Factorio tops them all when it comes to addictiveness. Within the first 2 weeks my average nightly sleep was about 5 hours per night. In one of the reviews someone called it digital heroin. God damn right.
I initially was hesitant to buy it because 1) the graphics were crude (reminded me of 2D platyform games, and 2) it was only $20! What self-respecting game would charge $20?! Unless it is just crap - that was my thinking. What turned me was thousands of raving reviews. Surely these are some♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy fanatics, right? A $20 game with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics like this?
I bought Factorio to prove to myself that I am right and this game will prove to be crap. And all I lose for the glory of feeling I am right is $20. I was wrong. Thank goodness I was so wrong so bad.
And as if the basic game was not good enough, there are so many mods that make the game varied in so many different ways. You want more resourc variatio? You got it. Want more industry option? Got it. More aliens? More wars? Got it. No war, more planning? Got it. Want to play trains? Got it. WOW WOW WOW, this game is awesome.
Some pros and cons:
Pros
What? Wre you kidding me? you want pros from me? Go read 20,000 other reviews. No, No. Go read the negative reviews. I did that one night for an hour. Even the negative reviews make you want to buy and play the game.
Cons
Oh yeah, there is always room for improvement. Because we live in an imperfect world and Factorio itself teaches you to do, then to automate, then to improve.
1. I still find the research tree needs improvement.
There is a concept of toolbelt that gives you a row of icon shrtcuts at the bottom of the screen. With research you can have two rows. With more moded research you can get 4 rows. Why oh why I ask. Why do I need research to extend and improve the game's UI? Imagine in RTS games there was no keyboard shortcut for creating a combat group but you could research the shortcut within the game. What?! That's crazy. Give me a UI that I deserve. Lock in-game features not software features.
Good research areas are new tech but bad ones are numbered research. I have nothing against abstract numbers (Turret speed 1, turret speed 2, turret speed 3) but I don't get why there ahs to be so many. Not a biggy. Just too monotenous, maybe for the sake of having more research items there.
2. Quality of resource icons is not homogenous. A lot of them need improvement in quality. Some of them look too similar. But then the game is still in Beta.
3. While the devs have gone out of their way to get realistic in some respects, they are bypassing reality all together in other respects. For example early in the game I realise to mine resources or place facilities I (my tiny man on the screen) need to be in the proximity of the physical point or he can't reach it. I wished it was like city building games so you place things where your mouse can go. Why the need to move this little guy all the time? I thought this is enforced UI awkwardness and clumsiness with the good intentions of enforcing reality of the story line. (By the way don't worry there are mods that allow you to access the screen freely just as I described).
But then they go against reality when the player can load and unload boxes full of resources from his bag/pouch onto anything. Imagine your train comes to unload some iron ore that it has brough from some far away place. You got 6 or 12 inserters pumping ore out of the train at blazing spped. So fast your eyes can barely catch the movement. And yet one human, YOU, can open the train's cargo wagon and in one click of the mouse unload the amount that would take those 12 super-fast robots at lease 1 minute to do. Oh come on!
OK OK. So the game needs this. So we sacrifice representation of reality for the sake of a better flowing game. Yes? Then why in other places are we sacrificing UI functionality for the sake of achieving game reality? Why does my UI have to suffer?
4. Generated maps are too monotenous. But the good devs are working on it. BTW the weekly blog updates are good and how fast the devs respond to the community is legend... - wait for it - ...dary!
OK I am tired now, so I'll stop. I close by saying never in my life have I enjoyed so many hours of fun for so little money. Not to give the devs any ideas but this game is better than most games that I have paid upwards of $70 for.

I absolutely loved the first two Serious Sam encounters, and adore Serious Sam 3, however, the feelings of sheer inextricable joy I gain from the first and third installment in the Serious Sam series are not felt in Serious Sam 2.
From the start Serious Sam lovers will notice a stark difference in the pacing of the game. Enemies have become more generic, the pacing of the combat has slowed, and due to the tight inclosed areas you will often get ambushed without anyway of escaping. Furthermore, the speed that's normally associated with his lightning feet is also gone, reducing the pacing even further. This feels like Croteam tried to emulate period games like Halo, but took barely anything that made the orignal Serious Sam games fantastic with it.
Give this game a miss, and go buy the First and second encounter, or the third installment.

The battles play like Kindom Hearts meets Ratchet and Clank, with an element of a tactical turn-based role playing game when the Transistor's time freezing feature is used (which is somewhat overpowered and gives you the upper hand). New game+ is awesome, and it would be awesome to have a feature where New Game+ is played with a randomized preset weapon assingment (instead of always using the easier "I already know this works" combination of weapons). Lots of people say that this game is terrible but I really like it. I'm going to prove this game is good.
1. People say that this game is lot like the Megaman games that it is based on, but if someone who didn't know Megaman so a game exactly like Megaman in modern day they would think that it is terrible because all the ideas and gameplay are not very creative or interesting. Megaman is a GREAT series but it's not a modern day game. We just have to accept that.
2. Everyone says this game is WAY to hard. I agree. But that isn't a bad thing. Older SNES games are really hard. Example: Battletoads. The Megaman games vary in difficulty. Megaman 2 is so easy, I can beat this game without any special weapons and gameovers. (I've done it before) Although Megaman and Bass is really hard! I can't beat it once! Now compare that to Mighty No. 9. I've been doing okay at Mighty No. 9. The more you beat bosses the stronger you get. If you are having trouble with a stage, try a different one. When I first tried I refused to try another stage than Brandish's stage. (My logic: That guy has a sword, I will beat him and steal the sword) I got 3 gameovers. I was terrible at the game back then. If I tried to beat that stage now I may get 1 gameover. Yes the game can be hard if die over and over, but the stages are really short you can get back to where you were in a couple of minutes. Even if you arn't too good it will take an hour or two at most to beat one level. Key to beat this game, don't give up just keep on trying, you are getting better each time. This game is made for people who are ready for a challenge. I think that normal difficulty is pretty hard, and I've had a lot of experience in Megaman. I hope that they could make an easy difficulty too help people who havn't played Megaman. Key to make the game easier: There is a setting in the options to turn on a helper robot. He gives you health and sometimes extra lives. I feel so sorry for people who are willing to try instant kills mode, good luck.
Want me to go on and talk more? I didn't think so. Closing paragraph! I hear so many people say this game is bad. I think the main cause of people not liking the game is the difficulty. I got probably 15+ gameovers. (I havn't beat the final boss yet, but I'm going to keep trying) You may say 15+ gameovers is a lot, but Mighty No 9. isn't that long. The lenth of the game is all about difficulty. Just like Megaman the game can be beaten in a little more than an hour if you are really good. If I told you for $20 you would have an indie game with PS2 era level visuals, tight challenging retro gameplay from the 8 bit/16bit era, and would play a lot like Megaman, depending on what your tastes on gaming were, you might be interested. Shovel Knight and Undertale went retro style, even Capcom's own Megaman 9 and 10 went 8 bit. Yet I keep reading and hearing absurdly unfair criticism of this game?
The backstory on how the game was made, funded, and delayed has nothing to do with what the game actually is, exactly what it set out to be, a Megaman spinoff/unofficial sequel/successor. For what the game was intended to be it is very good. Not perfect, there are instances of framerate issues, the extras are kinda boring, but the main game? The main game is my favorite Megaman game since 1993 with the very first Megaman X.
The art design, animations, music all are more reminiscent of the Megaman X series than the original Megaman series. The dash attack is a novel fun idea that is the biggest game changer since the wall climb in the X games. Of the 8 robot master stages, 6 of them are flat out throwbacks that any Megaman fan should feel at home with, it is more challenging than the MM games of the 80's and the early Megaman X games, but it is old school in you memorize timing, patterns and learn when to shoot/jump/dodge/dash.
The most original level and biggest departure from the Megaman formula is the sniper stage where you are chasing down a robot master from room to room while he targets you in a stage inspired by the White House. I liked that stage that it broke from the MM formula.
The Aviator tower, wind level is not the first time we have seen a level like that in a Megaman game, but I feel it is executed better than it ever was in this game. Fire and Ice levels are also nothing new to MM games, here it maybe more run of the mill but still not bad. The cave level with something chasing you has also been done before, but it is done well here too.
Beat the 8 main robot masters and its like going to Wily/Sigma's castles again where you are expected to use all your abilities to beat the final parts. There is a break from this where you use Call (which she is obviously Roll) and that is a nice break from the rest of the main Beck levels.
The music is catchy (8bit mode is a fun option too), its the best looking MM game ever (I know that wouldn't be tough since MM hasn't had hardware to work with in a very long time), the gameplay is fast paced, fun, and does take chances at times while still staying at its core a really good Megaman game.
If I was to score it, I would give it a 8 out of 10. If you are an older gamer that grew up with Megaman, you will like this game. A lot of hate by those that funded it and the business of making a game, but now that its out judge it for what it is, a Megaman type game, on that it is one of the better MM games I have ever played.

If you've played previous Zachitronics games (Spacechem, Infinifactory, TIS-100, or KOHCTPYKTOP for the old school fans) you'll know exactly what you're getting into. This is an excellent addition to the collection, and I would recommend getting it immediately.
If you're new to the niche of games Zach and Co. have built, you should know that this isn't a "puzzle game" so much as it a "problem solving" game. As opposed to some puzzle games (portal, talos principal, etc.) which have more or less one "expected" solution laid out, in this game each challenge can be solved a multitude of ways. As such it is immensely replayable- you can always challenge yourself to improve the efficiency of your solutions. (Each puzzle is followed by a histogram showing how your solutions stack up to other players for added incentives.) Fair warning- these "puzzles" become very difficult. These games admittedly aren't for everyone, but if you're looking for a challenge I'd highly recommend trying it out.
The story of this game is probably my favorite so far of Zach's games. Set in the near future, you're an engineer who's moved to China seeking employment. The "game" is your computer you log on, and you recieve assignments and story updates through "emails". It comes with a 40 page "manual" which is is well designed and adds depth/flavor to the story, with printouts of emails, visa applications, a 90's web page, and more. The music in the game is also great and on point for working on these problems.
Regarding early access- as someone who purchased TIS-100 and Infinifactory in early access, I can vouch for the devs statements. This isn't some buggy zombie survival pipedream. Like the previous releases, it is already highly polished, story complete, and as it stands currently, I feel like I got my money's worth.

is a hardcore dungeon crawler with a very interesting art style and an addictive combat system.
You must attack, defend, use skills and potions at the right time, as each enemy has its own attack timing, and mastering this is very important to survive. If you make any mistake, it's almost a certain death! Having a good build is also very important, so keep it in mind when leveling up and choose the right skills.
This game is very challenging: if you die, it's over, you lose all your gold, XP, skills and items, and you'll have to start over again, in a new randomly generated dungeon. Also, there are some puzzles that you must solve to progress further in the dungeon.
If you like challenging games, VERLIES II is very recommended!

Este jogo é muito desafiador: se você morrer, já era, você perde todo o seu ouro, XP, habilidades e itens, e você vai ter que começar tudo de novo, em uma nova dungeon gerada aleatoriamente. Além disso, existem alguns quebra-cabeças que você deve resolver para avançar.
Se você gosta de jogos desafiadores, VERLIES II é muito recomendado!

A great story driven point-and-click adventure.  Here's my full video review:
Video Transcript:
Hello viewers!  Welcome to another episode of A Bird's Eye View.  My name is Endeavor, and today we are reviewing The Charnel House Trilogy.  Developed by Owl Cave and published by Mastertronic,  this game was released on April 16, 2015.
The Charnel House Trilogy is a point-and-click adventure with a horror twist.  The story is told over three parts and revolves around two protagonists taking a train to Augur Peak.  Alex Davenport is the first character we follow.  She’s a seemingly average woman in her twenties that has just experienced a bad breakup.  She meets Doctor Harold Lang, our second main character, as they depart the station.
In the beginning, the ambiance and feel of the game gives the impression of a slice-of-life story, albeit with a few darker notes.  As the story progresses, the game reminds us of its true genre.  While the first two parts introduce us to the elements at play, it is the final chapter when everything comes together.
The storytelling in The Charnel House Trilogy is superb.  The themes, writing, and plot are more than strong enough to earn a recommendation on their own.  This is not a horror game that relies on jump scares and gore to shock the player.  Instead, expect to be slowly unnerved by the atmosphere as the game presents seemingly innocuous things-- things revealed over time to be far more sinister than it at first appeared.
The game leaves you with many unanswered questions.  How much of what Alex and Harold see on the train is real?  Are we to take what happens metaphorically, or is the train granting the protagonists an insight into their lives?  These questions lingered in my mind long after I finished playing.
As for the gameplay, it is similar to other point-and-click adventures.  The player has an inventory to store found items.  We walk around, talk to people, and interact with the environment with mouse clicks.  The puzzles in the game are not very complicated, and most can be thought through logically (unlike other point-and-click adventures which can require an almost compulsory level of trial-and-error).  I found the simplicity of the puzzles to be in the game's favor, as the central focus was on the story.
Each episode of the game averages about forty minutes long, so the whole thing can easily be completed in two hours.  This is mostly due to the limited scenes and the ease with which the puzzles can be solved.  While the game left me wanting more, I feel that my time playing it was well spent, so the shortness of the story is only a minor criticism.
The voice acting was great for the most part.  The actors sold their roles well, and the audio was good for the major characters.  There were only a few spots where things could have been better (which had more to do with sound quality than actor performance).
The game's retail price is $5.99.  For a short but well put together horror story, I give The Charnel House Trilogy a strong recommendation.  It's currently available on Steam for Windows computers.
And with that, my review draws to a close.  Thank you for watching, and don't forget to hit the “like” button if you enjoyed my video.  For updates on our upcoming content, follow us on Twitter at Rookery Gamers.

The Charnel House Trilogy is a psychological horror point and click adventure surrounding a female lead character. This game has terrific music that really makes you feel as if you are there. The game is short, a few hours of gameplay, but the adventure element and the story are tied together very well.
The adventuring aspect of the game is nothing overly complicated; the puzzles and choices are not that complex, which can be appealing to those new to the genre, or looking for a not to heavy experience. What is especially well done with this game, however, is
how well the story ties into the mechanics of the game.
The story is astonishingly good; well done, and backed up by well by the music and  atmosphere. You play as a young female traveling on a train to see a friend, and sort out your life. The story takes more of a dark turn however, and becomes an adventure of oneself through the darkest parts of what they may fear to face. To come out on top and try to realize who they are if they are able to. You never feel like you are lost; if by some chance you get confused in the story, you are easily able to get back on track. The story and adventure draw you into the experience, and by the end of the game, I was ready to do whatever was necessary to fight in my own way to help the heroine. I felt connected, I wanted her to succeed.
Whether you are a hard core adventurer genre player, or crave a more casual experience, this game does an excellent job of bridging the gap between both. The story is great, the simplicity of the graphics and the music weave together seamlessly to create an amazing game.

99 Spirits is an overwhelmingly anime game. It even includes the untranslated Japanese version! The game is divided into visual novel, and turn based strategy segments.
While I am not an anime or visual novel fan, the gameplay half of 99 Spirits is what had me intrigued. Basically the player moves their character around on a chessboard sort of thing, trying to reach objectives, stores that sell items to improve stats, or dialog scenes. This phase of the game is turn based, and enemies will move as the player moves, making it possible to sometimes avoid combat through careful navigation.
Once a battle is initiated, the player uses a turn based system to attack and defend against the enemy. When enough damage is done, the player receives a hint to the enemy's name. This will be something like ‘Sh’ or ‘Digging’, to hint that it is a possessed shovel. When the player guesses the proper name, it can be defeated. This made 99 Spirits a lot more intellectual in its gameplay than most visual novels can offer.
I did not finish 99 Spirits, but I have been told it is worth completing for the story.

begins with you selecting a country to begin your disease. There can be a lot of strategy involved even at this stage as you’ll gain resistances to certain effects, but at the same time you may have trouble infecting other countries. There are numerous factors to take into account such as airports and harbours, the climate of the country, if the country is rich or poor – poorer countries will be less capable of dealing with disease – and if the country is an island.
You gain DNA points periodically over the course of the game and you’ll gain more by infecting new countries, popping DNA bubbles on the map and generally just spreading your disease. Devolving certain symptoms also yields a refund of DNA points if you need them. Symptoms, transmissions and abilities (such as resistances to drugs and certain weather) all cost DNA points.
Each pathogen is distinctly different and each one require different strategies. Bacteria is the most basic pathogen which is easy to master, viruses can mutate very quickly and can quickly get out of control and funguses are hard to spread. Some pathogens also have unique gameplay modifiers to them such as the neurax worm – which can manipulate minds. The neurax worm is able to develop a trait that allows you to fly infected planes to uninfected countries. The necroa virus allows you to control zombie hordes and send them into other countries.
can also be played on 4 difficulty levels – casual, normal, brutal and mega brutal. Normal mode is the most realistic interpretation of how a disease might spread as the game treats 67% of the world’s population as regularly washing their hands and doctors only work a standard amount of days per week. Sick people will also be ignored.
Higher difficulties have 100% of people washing their hands, doctors working non-stop and sick people will be locked up in prison.

Definitely more fun and addicting than you would think.  Farming, after all, is not the most exciting thing to do hour after hour.  I was sceptical but bought the game on a rainy weekend for "something different". Now 300+ hours later I still love it.
More properly, the game is a tractor and implement simulator. The tedium of droning up and down the fields have been replaced with lots of different tractors and implements to try out in the basic game and tons more in easy to install mods.    Giants got the balance right.  Enough variety to keep a person interested in all the different facets and operations on a farm and just enough work to make a good harvest very satisfying.  Several different crops requiring different types of machinery and a few animals  having varyious needs provide even more opportunities to try out new equipment and provide clear goals for your crop farming activities.  If these are not enough there is also logging equipment in the game that can provide some rewarding challenge.
Farm Simulator 17 also offers enough flexibility to satisfy many different types of gameplay.  You can be very serious and plan out your crops for maximum yeilds and most efficient operations or just "play" with different equipment and see how it all works out.
The physics model is quite "generous" and playful.  You won't have to worry about getting stuck too often.    The game definitely does not punish you for being a bit sloppy with your driving.  The graphics are great and sunsets on some of the maps are simply beautiful.
A very well rounded and adaptable game that provides more entertainment than it should. You might even find yourself curious about how a combine really works under the hood or browsing a tractor dealerships website "just to look"...
Highly recomended.

The long wait is over. After many delay's the "megaman" spiritual successor from Keiji Inafune finally arrives. Does it live up to the hype that fans have been waiting for? Well...not really.
First off the graphics. While there definitely not the worst ever, very unremarkable is what I would say about them. Nothing about the style or art direction stands out. A least some of the boss designs and stage colors stand out. All in all its the biggest issue for me and I usually don't care about graphics that much.
Next up is gameplay and controls.
Shooting enemies then dashing into them "assimilating" as it were, can be quite fun. It's the usual megaman type gameplay otherwise. Run, jump, shoot, beat boss gain a new weapon. The usual walk in the park. If you've played megaman you know what to expect. It's quite good in that respect. Not a fan of some enemies after assimilating them giving you a speed boost or powered up shot but that's just my opinion.
Music and sound. Pretty unremarkable. Unfortunately there's not alot of catchy tunes here. Mostly forgettable and uninspired. There's a few that stand out (last boss theme is one of em) but other than that it's mediocre city.

Give this a pass or buy when it's on sale.

Might No. 9 is an interesting mixed bag of what could be considered the next generation of the Mega Man / Rockman series. To start off, I did help kickstart this game based on what was being presented to us backers at the time. While I do feel that the game we received was true to what Kenji Inafune sold us on, I feel that he has much to learn in terms of finding a balance between challenging and downright annoying.
Let's start off with the graphics. They're decent. Many people go back and complain that the concept art we were provided with looks nothing like the final game, and that's true. It's exactly what it is, concept art. The actual in-stage levels go from being visually moderately interesting, to being plain bland. Considering how much time it took to bring this game out, there should have been more attention to detail in stages such as Might No 1 where canisters fall down smashing, but then vanish from the ground after impact. It looks very amaturish. The characters in this game are fairly well designed each with unique features that separates them from the others.
The music I have no complaints about. The soundtrack composed by Manami Matsumae, fits everything quite well with catchy fast paced tunes. In terms of voice acting, the English voices are a mixed bag, while the Japanese actors are far better. In terms of translation, the dialogue between the English and Japanese script is night and day.
Gameplay is also where things go from classic Mega Man style to an annoyance factor due to the new dashing system. One of the biggest complaints I have is when you encounter multiple enemies in a row and only being able to hit one of them; and to destroy them, you need to dash and collect their Xel. Only issue is, that you'll end up hitting the enemy behind them taking damage. This makes it extremely unfair and often ends up with Beck getting killed. There's many other scenarios such as this, but it would take too long to write every single one of them. Let's just say, you'll be cursing every 5 minutes on just how unfair certain situations are... especially against the other Mighty No's. However, once you beat your first Mighty No, you'll find that things get easier due to the weapon you acquire. These are pretty much needed as some bosses are insanely hard to defeat.
If you do end up picking this game up, my only recommendation is to have some patience. It's not a horrible game by any means, but Inafune has a lot to learn in terms of making a true spiritual successor to the Mega Man / Rockman series.

Once upon a time, there was a man named Keiji Inafune. He made a game, called Mega Man. Mega Man was good, until Capcpom decided they'd rather make other games instead of a beloved series that many fans loved.
Inafune eventually left the company and made a kickstarter for another game, called Mighty No. 9. This game raised over $4,000,000. That made Inafune happy, so he took $20 of that and made a game, then spent the rest of the money on hookers and a jelly bean wall for his suburban house.
The game eventually released, but due to the production budget of $20, the game took several years longer than planned to make, as Inafune couldn't find enough programming slaves, especially when he only gave each one a single packet of instant ramen a week, so each slave only had a lifespan of about one month. The game released and was bashed by critics, but Inafune still had his hookers and jelly beans. The End.
Moral of the story: If you get $4,000,000 from Kickstarter, you better buy yourself some hookers.

Now, before I say anything, I feel I must preface this: if you bought this game looking for a pound-for-pound Megaman clone, you will be disappointed, so I wouldn't bother with buying this game.
Now, that being said, I am glad I got this game.  It's fun, it's challenging, it's characters are interesting most of the time,  and the best part is, this game knows it's Megaman roots and embraces them, but still tries to be it's own thing where it can.  The dash mechanic is well implemented by both characters, and I fail to see where people's issues with the controls lie.  The default works just fine and if you don't like the default setup, you can just change them to something you do like.  The graphics look like they belong on the PS2, which is impressive for a game like this, and are very reminiscent of Megaman X8, but in a more cartoony style which, rather than being a detriment, gives the game it's own almost cutesy charm.
I have little in the ways of complaints with this game.  Most notably is the simple fact of a lack of extra things to do and find, but considering it's roots, this isn't really surprising.  And I also wish Beck could charge his Buster, but again, that can be written off for the same reason the lack of real secrets is.
All in all, this is a much better game than people give it credit for.  It's challenging, it's fun, and for anyone looking for a burst of Megaman nostalgia while still experiencing something new, it's well worth the buy.
(Especially when playing Ray, MY WORD!  She makes this game infinitely harder, and that just makes it better.  :)  )
Overall score: 3.5/5

I have to say, I'm really surprised! Perhaps I'm just early, that no other bad reviews (aside from those reporting about technical issues, mainly game crashes and loading times) have been written as of this moment.
Let's get to the main issue I have with the game: This game is simply unable to be able to compete with many other MMORPGs in (possibly nearly) EVERY aspect.
1. There nearly isn't any tutorial, or starting help that aids a new player (which pretty much includes everyone right now). No automatic tool tips (aside from the HELP section, which should only be secondary), no mini-map, no quest helper (that helps you locate the next NPC involved in a quest chain). This leaves nearly everyone absolutely lost (and frustrated) at the start of the game.
2. The graphics and animations are among the worst I've seen. It would be (somewhat) forgivable if it were 2002, but it isn't. There isn't even an animation for stationary characters.
Any good parts to the game? Perhaps there are. Unfortunately, I will likely never find out, whether or not the storyline is interesting and engaging, whether the in-game skill mechanics are unique, etc etc. Because getting a player started is almost always the most important part of every game; if you can't hook players within a relatively short period of time, and players have not invested (financially-wise) into the game, they are likely better off finding just another MMORPG that's better.

Recommended, for a certain type of player.  If you'd rather read a Lovecraft story than watch Paranormal Activity, The Charnel House Trilogy may be for you.
The gameplay is simple point-and-click, optionally using arrow keys to move your character.  The plot is laid out in a very linear fashion, with very simple puzzles to advance the story.  It's a slow-burn, dialogue-driven horror experience without cheap jump scares.  There are rare moments where something disturbing may flash onscreen, but there's nothing designed to launch you out of your seat.  The gore is rare and mild, even more so with the low-fi graphics.
The voice acting is done well (including Jim f'ing Sterling, son), and the music usually is effective at setting the mood.  In the later acts it tends to switch from room to room which can be a bit jarring, especially if one area is meant to be creepy and the next one not.
My only real gripe with the game is the way it leaves things unresolved - the credits promise a sequel next year, which will hopefully complete the story.  Throughout the game there's a strong sense that you never know what is going on.  This makes sense as it mirrors your character's confusion, but without answers at the finish, the game's ending feels a bit rushed and unsatisfying.
Worth picking up at its current price.
