Having recently played The Cat Lady (amazing game) I was looking to play something with a similar vibe - I love horror/the macabre and I love point and click games, and this seemed to fit the bill pretty well.
+ Story moves you along well - at no point are you stuck, wandering around wondering what to do, endlessly talking to the same people again and clicking on things randomly in case you missed something. This is something that seems to happen in a lot of point and click games, but not here.
+ Decent pixel art graphics (if you like that sort of thing)
+ Great story which has chilling moments - it's a subtle terror, though
+ Liberal dose of swearing (I realise some may see this as a con, but this isn't a game for kids, and it fitted the situation and situation)
+ Voice acting is OK (not brilliant though).
- Very short. Calling it a 'trilogy' really does give the impression you're getting three games here, which isn't the case at all. There's 3 short chapters in an overarching story and is one of the shortest games I've played for a while. (It probably goes without saying that there's no real replayability here either)
- A few minor irritants - for example, in chapter two, for most of the hotspots you can interact with, the dialogue is the same whether you select 'examine' or 'interact/use'. In the context of gameplay the responses you get therefore don't always make sense. This isn't the case in the other chapters, so although it's a small thing it just seems like a weird thing to cut corners on
- Gameplay is very easy/basic - although I play a lot of point and clicks, I'm pretty rubbish at them and usually have to refer to a walkthrough at least point during a game. Definitely not the case here - the game actually drops heavy handed hints even when you don't need them, basically telling you what to do in places. I know other games tend to give you hints after you've been pootling around for a while and are clearly stuck - I'm not sure why this game tells you pretty much what you should be doing before you even have a chance to try anything (example scene - 'I could kill for a cigarette right now')
- Story is a little more ambiguous than I would like in places.
The pros outweigh the cons - this is is a great little game that's worth a look if you like point and clicks or horror themed games.

My, my! Wasn't this an astonishing experience? When I decided to give this one a go, I wasn't expecting neither that much spiritual depth, nor such qualitative narrative.
- one game with separate acts, actually - is an incredibly well arranged psychological horror adventure.
I'd try to give you the baseline for the story, but the events, the characters that they are surrounding and their in-depth meanings are completely dependent on a perspective, and it is near impossible to define any character that we encounter within the game without pure speculation. Charnel House is what you get from Charnel House. Thus, I'll only present you some facts.
You begin the game as playing Alex Davenport, a young woman who is trying to recover from a bad break up. For some reason, she decides to go on a long train journey, in hopes of reaching the Island of Augur Peak at the end. During this odd journey, she encounters an odd British gentleman, Dr. Harold Lang, who is the curator of a museum and visiting the same island for an archeological expedition. The only seeming bond between them, is their lonely destination, and a series of uncanny encounters they shall endure during their journey.
consists of three separate acts, as if taken from carefully planned scenes from a theatrical performance: Inhale, Sepulchre and Exhale. Inhale is tied to reality, with a bitter taste of past experience. It feels old, dysfunctional and hurt. Sepulchre is the sublime passage between the real and that shadow on the corner of your eye, descending into the very Heart of Darkness, the horror itself. Exhale is the triumphant delusion, breaking the barrier between the reality that we coddle ourselves with and the cruel fact that logic doesn't work anymore. It is weaved with pure manifestation of raw emotions, raising more questions than it answers.
Three acts come together to compose an elaborate setting of carefully chosen subliminal details. The story is full of literary references, thrilling anecdotes, grave yet elegant symbolisms and interrelated details that will give a shiver down your spine when you realize their relevance. Don't expect your common jump horror. The art of absurd is the game's primary weapon against your psyche. This is a great psychological thriller.
The gameplay is no different than your casual adventure. There are some very minor puzzles, but nothing that would hinder your progress. As long as you keep exploring, the story reveals itself. Graphics are nothing extraordinary, nearly same as Blackwell series themselves, familiar and simple. Encountering something this eerie in this basic environment is probably down right uncanny compared to facing a grotesque enemy in full HD. This is one is a tough one to review
This game has the unique mechanic of having you try and defeat enemies by guessing what type of object they are by typing/inputing the correct spelling of their name.
While many of these objects have basic names like "pants" others have a japenese name which makes sense given the setting of feudal japan, which is fine.................if you know japanese words and culture.
The problem is that this is a translation of a japanese game (obviously) with the main gamplay being featured around language and spelling. Otherwise translation would not be such a problem.
Non japanesese people/speakers are at disadvantage as it is but the real problem is there is no compensation for this fact in the translation (at least in english) or gameplay.
So unless you are VERY knowledgeable of japanese words and culture (feudal japan no less) it stops being a fun game of trying to guess the word/item from the hints/letters given to you and becomes a game of "well what is the japansese word/english equivalent for it.............sigh better go look it up or cheat".
In conclusion i just can not recommend the translation of this game with these problems unless you are big into japansese culture (in which case you probably already own this). That being said i did rather enjoy it when it was mostly english words and japansese words i already knew or could see in the index. It does start getting rather repetive after a while though but this would be tolarable if it were not for the above mentioned problem. If this problem was not present i might rate this as average (IF STEAM HAD SUCH A OPTION )♥♥♥♥♥♥maybe more given it's unique gamplay feature but as it stands it has a problem that can not be overlooked.

Definitely more fun and addicting than you would think.  Farming, after all, is not the most exciting thing to do hour after hour.  I was sceptical but bought the game on a rainy weekend for "something different". Now 300+ hours later I still love it.
More properly, the game is a tractor and implement simulator. The tedium of droning up and down the fields have been replaced with lots of different tractors and implements to try out in the basic game and tons more in easy to install mods.    Giants got the balance right.  Enough variety to keep a person interested in all the different facets and operations on a farm and just enough work to make a good harvest very satisfying.  Several different crops requiring different types of machinery and a few animals  having varyious needs provide even more opportunities to try out new equipment and provide clear goals for your crop farming activities.  If these are not enough there is also logging equipment in the game that can provide some rewarding challenge.
Farm Simulator 17 also offers enough flexibility to satisfy many different types of gameplay.  You can be very serious and plan out your crops for maximum yeilds and most efficient operations or just "play" with different equipment and see how it all works out.
The physics model is quite "generous" and playful.  You won't have to worry about getting stuck too often.    The game definitely does not punish you for being a bit sloppy with your driving.  The graphics are great and sunsets on some of the maps are simply beautiful.
A very well rounded and adaptable game that provides more entertainment than it should. You might even find yourself curious about how a combine really works under the hood or browsing a tractor dealerships website "just to look"...
Highly recomended.

Having not bought into the hype surrounding Bastion, I passed on Transistor when it was released in 2014. Sure, the reviews (both critically and from us "normal" folk) was incredibly positive, but so were the reviews for Bastion. That game just failed to grab me. Still, every time Transistor popped up on sale I would be  tempted. The cyberpunk art style appealed to me a lot, and I kept reading "the music in Transistor is REALLY good!"
And then comes the Thanksgiving sale of 2017. I click on Transistor's store page yet again, but smething different transpires this time. I watch the launch trailer. It's the first time I see and hear the sights and sounds of Transistor. The song hooks me. The seemingly fast-paced combat interests me. I want to be in.
And I was in. I started playing a month ago, but the allure of other Black Friday AAA game sales pulled me away for awhile. I platinumed one AAA game, beat another. But Transistor was calling me back. "You liked what you played," my brain told me. "Don't let it become another Steam game you don't finish." And so I went back to it. And then I fell in love with this game.
What makes it such a great game is its aesthetic. Without it, this game would be merely good. But like a few of my favorite games of all-time, mood plays a big part in the game's success. It looks like an art nouveau painting come to life. And the music... well, the people were right. The music is great. I feel like it drives the narrative forward just as much as actually progressing through the game does. That's quite a feat for a soundtrack that is still mostly instrumental. And even though I just stated the game would be merely good without its unique visual and aural flair, the game is still great fun to play. It might not be the most unique or fun system out there, but I applaud any game that encourages you to try different things. If you fail, you're forced to do something different. That failure could end up being a blessing because then you discover some different ability combination you might like more.
And to wrap it all up, what would a great game be without a divisive ending? Anytime you beat a game and want to see what other people thought about how it all ends and what it all means then I think the makers accomplished their goal of what they set out to do. It got people talking. Some people hated it, some people didn't. That was probably what they planned all along. Me? It kind of just makes me want to try Bastion again, after all these years...

An okay port of a very good mobile game.
If you go in expecting a hyper-realistic epidemiological model like the game blurb promises, you're going to be disappointed. You can, for example, infect every single person in China before your disease reaches the US, or Europe, or Southeast Asia. This is wildly unrealistic. In Normal difficulty and below the world is also weirdly chill about this one mild disease showing up suddenly in billions of people within a year.
However, it is an excellent casual game. It is a fun game to play moment to moment - seeing the disease reach critical mass of infection within a country; executing the sudden coup de grace with Total Organ Failure et al; the tense race against the cure, then the relief when the cure ETA slips away from humanity because so many governments have collapsed - all these little moments are incredibly satisfying. Petting an ugly cat while laughing evilly is not mandatory when playing the game, but will probably greatly enhance the experience.
If you already own the mobile version, I'd recommend against buying this. Aside from a few minor UI changes, this is pretty much the same game as the mobile version, down to the busywork bubble-clicking (more annoying with a mouse than a touchscreen). I would like to have seen the developer be more ambitious and add more depth to the core game. As is, it's barely deserving of its "Evolved" subtitle. PC additions like a minimap showing which countries are infected are nice, but not really enough to justify its price.
If you're new to Plague Inc however (and possess a megalomaniacal streak), I recommend checking it out, particularly on sale.
Note: the Android version of the game is free on the Play Store. If you're undecided, you might want to check it out there first.

One of the best games that you should never buy.
The only issue with this game - and by issue I mean MASSIVE ISSUE - is that you cannot speed up time. The game gives you objectives to reach on each map, and in order to unlock the new maps to play you must reach the objectives of the previous maps. However, you will often find that you reach the objectives well before the deadline, but because you cannot speed up time you cannot move forward and hand in your objective to complete the map.
This is kind of a really big deal because you will often find that your objective has been met, but it will be anywhere from 1-2 hours of real time before your objetive is due... I have 22 hours worth of playtime, but I think I've only spend 4 hours of time actually playing the game - I ususally just minimize the game and have it run in the background until the objective date is met.
With this said - this is a fantastic game with one major major flaw. To some people, this isn't a big deal as they just play the scenario and keep building the park. but for me, I'm super objective oriented and I want to progress once I have achieved a goal... To be stuck in the map knowing I've already beaten it is super annoying.

Erm, what do I say about this game really? The Kenney's game assets I could sort of forgive, considering there was at least an effort to make things yellow. The 1% steam store discount I can see for the joke it was intended to be. Considering how low the price is, then it doesn't really need anything other than publicity. The android-like setup of the score and menu is also somewhat laxidaisical though I guess enough for what this game needs. I'll be honest, I was willing to give this game a try. I really was expecting a 1 hour runthrough of a somewhat enjoyable game.
Unfortunately, this game just screamed "meh". You cannot damage enemies as far as I could see - one touch and you lose a hitpoint. At that point, you have a temporary invulnerability by way of flashing. You lose three hitpoints, you reset the level. When a game this simple can't even include a death transition effect (you just appear at the start of the screen. Not even a You Died - Try Again?) and has barely any enjoyment, it gets stale fast. There is just generally not a whole lot here to be anywhere near entertaining. I know that game development takes time and effort. This, however, seems to have neither. A simple hue alteration, if it even needed that - Kenney has so many assets - is not enough to call this game your own without at least including him as an artist on the About page. That would have at least been something.
I was literally bored within two minutes... there just isn't enough here to merit a pricetag. I actually went back to the game a second time in case I was being too critical, but I can't really say that I am. If it were free, I would possibly recommend to children aged 3-11. At that price, you can get plenty of alternatives out there much more worth your time. Simple as that really... Sorry to be harsh, there needs to be a lot more done than this for it to be available to the public.

The premise is real solid, with a weird Lovecraftian adherence to the weird and unexplained, but sadly that's where the enjoyment for me ended.
The first biggest problem for me is the dialogue. It feels like every character was written to sound slightly tired and distant, to showcase a dreariness to the world, yet unfortunately no-one seems to be able to sound like anything more than entirely bored and disconnected to the project. I made me skip ALL of the dialogue in act 3 because I couldn't bear to listen to a cast of people who seemed like they didn't want to be there.

I like some really key things about this game, but for $6.50 I would rather have gotten myself a burger.

The Charnel House Trilogy is a short 3 part point and click mystery game of intertwined stories.
*Fully voice acted by some known people.
*Linear play with limited options to keep the game moving onwards.
*Took me 2hours playing it, clicking on everything I could find.
The game begins off mundane enough, then takes a spin for the strange.
While The Charnel House Trilogy offers an interesting story for Alex, there are aspects that are never explained and a lot of vague supernatural psudo-real segments that look like they matter but fail to connect to anything.
The second chapter, focused on Harold, certainly felt like a waste of time with no relevence to Alex's tale. An entire chapter about random unnatural happenings and characters with alzheimer's, none of it making any coherent sense. You could skip this "commercial?" entirely without any loss to what the main story.
Thankfully the first and the last chapters provide a conclusive mystery story concerning Alex and Robert, on a sad yet disturbing note. There was a character, Grub, who felt like it was supposed to be more important in some way, but probably just a backdrop distraction along with all the unnatural occurances and other strange characters.
It has come to my attention there will be sequel to possibley fill in holes left in this finished trillogy; which doesn't make it a trillogy if there's more than three, if I am not mistaken.
So the story being held financally ransome, with a forth installment. Then again, there are no garantees any questions about this game will get answered. The Charnel House Trilogy is, after all, supposed to be a "complete" trillogy.
I'd recommend it would it not have too many pointless aspects, most notably the entire second chapter, the luggage bags, and Grub.
I have four words to say about this game:

The Charnel House Trilogy is a little horror gem: you'll be playing as Alex Davenport, a young woman who is fighting depression and apathy after a breakup, and Harold Lang, a museum curator boarding the same train as Alex in chapter two. Soon things turn weird with the train crew openly talking about the characters' past as they were old friends and  long-lost acquaintances suddendly appearing on the train.
-good pixel art
-great soundtrack, expecially the minimalistic piano songs
-fully voice acted by a great cast
-the story is creepy, unsettling and surreal
-the characters are very well-written and with quite alot of depth
-the fact the overall story isn't fully explained might be a letdown for some
-the slow-burn horror might not appeal to everyone
-very short at one hour and a half
-puzzles are very easy
-might be a bit too cryptic for its own good
I called the game a little horror gem and I did so due to its truly interesting story where you soon find yourself deep down into what I'd properly describe as a nightmare you can't wake up from where the characters' worst fears and guilts come to life to haunt them. It feels like one of those weird episodes of The Twilight Zone or a novel by Poe and it's truly surreal at times not to mention quite unsettling. On the other hand the gameplay sadly is only functional to the story and not much else, the puzzles are easy and even novices of the genre will probably never find them challenging or get stuck.
Last but not least do know that the overall story is never fully explained but only hinted at: this spawned a lively debate in the game forums with some interesting theories on what happened and why. There'll be another game coming out in 2016 and it'd clear things up a bit.
To sum things up I really enjoyed The Charnel House Trilogy and I recommend it to anyone wanting to experience a true and deep horror story, you can easily find it for 2,5$ if you peek around and at that price it's a steal.

Emily Is Away is a game set on a desktop of your average American teenage boy (or girl though if honest it feels like a boy when you get deeper into conversation). You have Windows XP in the background and two windows open, one is a chat with Emily, our wily and often aggravating antagonist to our seemingly desperate protagonist who’s sole purpose is to make Emily fall in love with or at least get some semblance of a happy life over a period of five long years.
To do this you have conversations with Emily about various aspects of yours and her life, from music to video games, movies to social anxieties and more. The game is a simple one to play. Emily pops up in AIM and says hello, which leads you to a multiple choice of answers. By picking your answer you then ‘converse’ to Emily by pressing random keys on your keyboard. It may sound overly simple and even dull but rest assured, it is not. It feels like you are having a conversation with a real person and in this the developer, Kyle Seeley, really must be praised. Emily will annoy, tempt, tease and laugh along with you for all of its 45 minutes average gameplay per session.
Emily feels so real that at the end of my second playthrough I was desperate to make her fall in love with me but by the end of the fifth I was content to insult her and be as cold as a man in love can be to a woman that constantly scorns him no matter how hard he tries! Come my sixth attempt I just wanted to be loved by anyone and was quite relieved and happy to know that it was all just a game.
Emily Is Away is a game that pushes buttons, your own emotional ones and for something consisting of basic text and very little else it does a surprisingly good job of it. Sure, it may not work for everyone but anyone out there that enjoys interactive fiction, choice and consequence this will no doubt bring more than one emotion to the fore once you really get into the game and determine your goal.

Fantastic programming/puzzle game. Very well polished. You can safely ignore the 'Early Access' label.
Comes with a 40+ page, authentic looking manual containing references and documentation for the various components you will be using in the devices you design.
I particularly like how much world-building and ambient story telling is going on. There are email exchanges with your colleagues, quirky contracts, even the components you place on the board each have a unique character. At the same time, all of this is completely optional. You never have to read through a wall of text or follow the bantering of your co-workers. If you just want to focus on the puzzles, you can totally do that.
I found the puzzles very diverse, and there are often many different ways to solve them. You are being judged on two scales on each puzzle: power-consumption (number of executed instructions) and cost-effectiveness (how expensive your design is). Often there is a lot of optimization potential between a solution that just gets the job done and a beautiful design that is cheap AND efficient.
This game is fantastic, I can't seem to stop playing this game and making circuits. Highly Recommended!

The Choice of Games franchise nails the Choose Your Own Adventure format, and this is one of the strongest entries in their catalogue. The beauty about Choice of Robots is that it explores deep themes like war, the ethics of wealth and relationships, both romantic or platonic; but it explores these themes in a fun way. It caters for everyone, from those who hold the simple ambition of raising a merciless army of robots to conquer the world, all the way to those who have the natural urge of inseminating a fembot. So let me get this straight, you happened to be a young swordswoman who is traveling across Japan with a fox demon of some sort in order to find her dad while killing other demons possessing common household objects. I guess that sums up the basis of the story. I don't remember how long I have spent with 99 Spirits because I mostly played it offline when my internet was down for a period of time, but I still have not finish my first play through so keep that in mind.
The combat system pretty much consists of guessing a word through hints given to you when you attack the enemy and after you have successfully guessed the word, you are able to kill the enemy or capture the soul when given the opportunity, but guess the word incorrectly and you will take damage with no chance to negate it. Other than that, it is really just a QTE. In theory, it sounds like a good idea, but in practice, it gets repetitive pretty quickly because you are guessing the same enemy over and over again due to the limited enemy variety in each region, not to mention all the enemies feel very similar to one another. The boss fights completely enforces the idea of sitting through QTEs because they behave just like the normal enemies you have faced for the umpteenth time except they have maybe 10 to 20 times more health, has the ability to kill you in maybe 2 hits at most throwing in unblockable attacks every so often forcing you to stay in the defense stance around 80% of the time, and heal very frequently to extend the length of the battle. The movement for the world map is pretty standard with nothing special to make note of except for the hunger meter that does nothing except makes moving around the map slower than normal. Even if the hunger system did something to impact the game, it does not tell you what it even does and even if they do tell you, the game does a pretty bad job at it.
The soundtrack is, in my opinion, ok at best, but the battleground music can get really repetitive sometimes and you can even hear the where the track loops.
Perhaps the worst offender this game has is that it crashes very often if you don't know what is causing it to crash in the first place so if you are going to play this game, I suggest you head to the forums to look up on other people's experience so you hopefully won't have to deal with them too much.
I am really having a hard time on whether or not I should give a recommendation for 99 Spirits because it's game play feels lackluster in some areas in addition to the frequent crashing and a fairly iffy story, but it has an interesting idea with the combat system despite on its shaky execution and has some fairly interesting characters to meet. For $15, I think it's a hard sell for those who are skeptical about the gimmicky combat system, but if it goes on sale for maybe $10 or less, it's possible to take it into consideration. At the end of the day, I can't recommend 99 Spirits despite that fact that I had a decent time with 99 Spirits due to all of the problems I have stated before, but then again, it's probably a game that is best played in short bursts. If you do happen to take an interest in 99 Spirits, try the demo first before pulling the trigger.

Mighty No. 9, despite its troubled development and negative press, is not a bad game. Developed by the newly-formed Comcept and the talented folks at Inti Creates (previous work including the Megaman Zero series, and Megaman 9 and 10), it aims to bring classic Megaman to an era where the Blue Bomber is little more than a recognizable icon. Having backed this and several other games over time, one in particular releasing in an upsetting state, I struggle to see where all the disappointment is coming from. For fans of the later Megaman spinoffs which take the basis of classic Megaman and modernize it, this game will be hit or miss. However, for those who grew up with the classic series, and adore its careful balance of memorization and dexterity, this is likely a game you will enjoy from start to finish.
At its core, Mighty No. 9 is a Megaman game. Basing itself around the same roots Megaman 9 and 10 did, and refining these standards, the game accomplishes what it sets out to do rather nicely. The big addition to the formula is a neat twist on Megaman X's dash; enemies are now stunned after a set amount of damage, and can be absorbed with a dash (dubbed AcXelerate in-game) while in this state. When played like a traditional Megaman game, the elongated health bars will frustrate you. However, this is done intentionally; the game wants the player to water down groups and absorb them all in chunks with a dash, and when played properly, this works surprisingly well. Not only does it allow you to do quick work of enemies, but it also sends you forward, allowing you to keep momentum as you move through a level. Replaying a level you've memorized (which will happen often) and blasting through it is incredibly satisfying.
The abilities are alright, though I barely found myself using them unless a hazard required it (which is done often in neat ways). Though I do want to note that I naturally stick to the buster in Megaman games, so it's moreso due to my style of play. Several have advantages to the buster, like Dynatron's seeds having a spread and hold on the enemy, and Cryosphere's ice cannon reaching over ledges. Battalion's missile in particular has a large blast radius and deals a ton of damage, which can make certain segments a breeze, but where's the fun in that? A proper weapon wheel rather than three shortcut buttons might've made me use them more, but overall I hardly used them, which was worth the challenge. One thing I did find neat is that regular enemies can give a stat boost when absorbed, sort of like sub-abilities. There are three types, one raising speed, one raising damage, and one lowering bar consumption for specials, and are a nice addition!
Levels are a lot of fun, and feel carefully designed around the style of gameplay. Through my playthrough, I never felt any to be rushed or overly cheap, just punishing if you don't take your time, which is a Megaman staple. If you are used to the Megaman flow, you'll notice muscle memory often saving you before you fall to your death. Not every time, but when it happens, it feels great. A few levels even twist typical platformer conventions! Countershade's level, for example, cuts out linearity and has you roaming around the building in search of him, as he attempts to snipe you down from a distance. There is also a later level with Call that is stealth-based, but still manages to fit in with the rest of the game, and has some fun encounters. I have seen people wince at these segments, but I personally found them refreshing. They manage to do some really unique things with the formula, and don't overstay their welcome.
Boss encounters are a huge staple of the Megaman series, and I have seen a lot of mixed thoughts on the fights in this game. One thing worth noting is that bosses that react based on your input (Cut Man, Metal Man) are seemingly unpresent here. Instead, they've opted for three/four-phase bosses that cycle through patterns either at random or in order, with no reaction to player input. This is an odd omission, but the boss fights are still no pushover. Cryosphere, Dynatron and Battalion in particular have segments in their fight where you have to cut corners around their attacks, which I found pretty fun! The only real fight that disappointed was Countershade; as awesome as his level was, he leaves himself open far too often, and doesn't really position himself based on your location, which makes his fight a bit easy. Though overall, I really enjoyed them. The final fight in particular stands right up with some of the best Wily fights, in my opinion.
There is a lot of pessimism towards the game's visuals, but it really isn't ugly. It's about as unpleasant as the NSMB games, and personally, I don't buy platformers for state-of-the-art visuals. They're definitely not distracting or low-quality in any way, just simple. Textures pop out really nicely over the simple geometry in a cartoony style, and although games released long ago like Megaman Legends had more dynamic facial expressions within this same style, that's about all there is to complain about. There isn't as much post-processing and complex lighting as shown in early builds, but that may have been cut out to account for the lower-tier console ports. On PC, the former is probably something third-party injectors could get around, and it's definitely worth looking into. However, I don't feel it's going to detract from the experience, especially if you're just looking to play some Megaman.
On the subject of presentation, sound should probably be addressed. I found the music to be generally catchy and well within the spirit of classic Megaman tunes. There is also an 8-bit version of the soundtrack, which I have not tried, but many recommend turning on. I felt the default music works fine. Generally the sound design feels great against the gameplay, as there is a lot of feedback that adds to the experience. One of the more negatively received aspects is the voice acting, and while I can tell some will be turned off by it, I found it charming in its own cheesy way. The voice acting itself isn't awful, it's just very energetic, like a saturday morning cartoon. Some boss cues I can admit overdo it, but at the end, voices can be disabled, and cutscenes skipped if it isn't your style. Either way, you have to give credit to the music and SFX. Definitely retains that Megaman feel we all know and love.
Having backed this at the 80$ tier, I am not disappointed with what I got, especially reflecting on other KS projects I've been involved in. Mighty No. 9 is a return to form; classic Megaman running and gunning, carefully built, with no overbloat. It took me a good six hours to beat the main campaign (you may be looking at less if you raise the life counter, which I do not recommend), with some extra content that may or may not keep you busy (personally, I resent their decision to delay the game over these online features, as they aren't that great, and really hurt the game's reception). At full price, I can only recommend it if you adore the Classic and X games. On sale, I can definitely recommend it a lot more. Despite the general reaction throughout social media, this is a solid first installment, and I'd love to see Comcept and Inti have another go at Beck eventually.

tl;dr Little less Serious, but still Sam
Serious Sam 2 has a very vivid palette, even compared to the originals with its colourful pickups and enemies. This game manages to make it even more colourful, to the point of making you want to reduce the brightness/contrast of your display. One of the arguable gameplay decisions is the inclusion of lives system in a game that has a save/load feature anyway. Every 10'000 points you get an EEEXTRAAA LIIIIIFEEE *cash register sound*, which do not traverse across levels, and if you lose all of them, you can continue playing, just with your current level score frozen. There are vehicles, aircraft, human-sized hamster balls (*gasp* I'M HUMAN SIZED!), and even a fire-breathing dinosaur to ride. This replaces the Serious Speed pickup, and gives you extra firepower. There's no point of conserving ammo or serious bombs - pick one up and use it as soon as a too menacing horde appears, since you may lose them when you die (or sometimes respawn with more) and some levels end unexpectedly.
The weapons are your usual Serious Sam arsenal: you start every act (regardless of your previous acquisitions) with a melee weapon, two revolvers, and... some energy pistol from nowhere. The circular saw has little use, I only used it once on a crate (then I switched to shotguns or explosives to open them) and a second time on a horde of pathetic Hell Chicks on Kleer planet. The revolvers are deadly accurate and reload after 6 shots each. They reuse the original anims, making them the only weapons to have an idle "inspect" animation. The energy pistol fires weak homing projectiles, and can be charged up to fire a stronger homing projectile, good for shooting behind corners. The pump shotgun is replaced by a HIDEOUS multi-barreled shotgun, which is as slow as the pumpgun was. The double-barreled shotgun is a sawn-off now with weird shell windows, this is gonna be THE weapon you will use all the time. The 5,56mm Thompson is replaced with dual Mini-Uzis, while all other guns feature different models. There is no flamethrower, but there is a homing bomb called Klodovik, it also has an idle animation. Most of the guns feature displays, which were most likely going to be ammo counters. In the end, some have broken screens, while others show the Serious Sam logo.
The enemies in the game do not have the NETRICSA biographies and tips-n-tricks, unlike in the original games or BFE. That means you don't even know what you're fighting (if you even care), until its model and name appears in one of the loading screens, when you have most likely already encountered these foes couple of planets earlier - the Levitator is a good example. From the remixed stock female scream I suspected this enemy to be female (and the 3d mesh in a loading screen confirmed it), but no further backstory is given. Most enemies also have pretty generic names, so instead of names like "Scythian Witch Harpy" or "Sirian Were-bull" we get "Lizard" and "Tank". The Kleer skeletons are surprisingly easy in this game, to the point that their home planet can be considered the easiest (and shortest) act. The worst enemies, as usual, are those armed with hitscan weaponry - especially the shotgun zombie. At least the arachoids (or whoever their replacements are) are armed with projectile weapons and do not spawn on the high ground. The rolling spiked balls are nasty too, being a tougher version of bulls. The Gnaar are only featured in cutscenes and some secrets. And the scariest monsters in the game are friendly NPCs, period.
The gameplay is the same: slay some hordes, pick stuff up, find a secret, slay another horde, fight a boss... watch a cutscene which makes little sense and has weird jokes. The problem of cutscenes is mostly the animations and, of course, the voice acting. They ARE funny, at least some of them cause you to expel the air from your lungs faster than usual, while others leave you in "Wha.." shock at the utter nonsense you've just witnessed. Sam himself cracks his usual jokes (and laughs himself sometimes), belches, scratches balls, and makes shout-outs to movies/games/whatever. NETRICSA got a voice, and her Captain Obvious tendencies annoy even Sam. Can't say that slaying hordes with a minigun or an oversized cannon (maxigun?) isn't fun, especially since most enemies explode in a lot of gibs, bones, teeth (!), and spill impossible amounts of blood of all possible colours.
In the end, this is just a wackier Serious Sam. If you liked the original, you will like this one, even if you disagree with the shotgun models. Just shoot everything that moves and explore the areas to find secrets and watch with glee how odd some people's sense of humour can be.

I have over 750 hours on the multiplayer for this game on PC during 2017 alone, not to mention my time on Xbox 360 and PS3 in 2009 and beyond.  The meager playtime you see is just for single-player.  I realize that this is an absurd amount of time spent on a game like this -- but if anyone's qualified to review this, it's this guy here.  Clearly, this review will be mostly multiplayer oriented.  However, I did finally check out the story mode in 2018, so here goes.
Here's my impression of the single-player story: SENSORY OVERLOAD.  This game has no pacing whatsoever, in that there is literally no downtime to kind of recollect yourself.  There are explosions non-stop, motion blur and shellshock effects everywhere, enemies swarming all over the place like the story itself, and so on.  From start to finish, it is non-stop action.  The levels are mostly decent, albeit the psychic enemies with perfect aim (along with the absurd viewkick) on harder difficulties can frustrate.  The only level I truly despised was the first favela mission, as dealing with the infinite enemies was a chore.  The optimization is mostly fine, except this is a straight console port.  No FOV slider, no PC specific adjustments, etc.  This game also seems to be CPU focused, so anyone with a weaker CPU (or especially streaming on 1 PC with OBS Studio) may face challenges.  However, this game's single-player is perfect for those who just want an obscene amount of mindless action.  I dig it.
This review's focus is on the multiplayer, though, as that seems to be what most people are curious about.  And after wading through the highest of the highs MW2 offers with the lowest of the lows, there are things people should know about this game in 2018, should they consider buying it.
I've played most other CoDs, and personally, this game's gunplay feels the best out of all the games in the series.  Guns shoot where you aim, even on most lag, and the player can use a lot of different guns and perk combinations while still being functional.  It really is true in this game that, "If every gun is OP, nothing is OP."  There are, say, only a few guns and perks I would advise against using, although the UMP/Famas/Intervention is king.  The former is true if you're like me, and staunchly refuse to use the dirtbag One Man Army/Grenade Launcher/Danger Close exploit.
This is the perfect segway to speak about the playerbase that still plays this game.  Let's get this out of the way.  Yes, there are a lot of players that will use the noobtube nonsense 100% of the time.  Couple with that, there are quite a lot of cheaters in this game, too.  They only serve to frustrate and get reactions from others players, who are just looking to have fun.  However, fortunately, there are also a lot of players just looking to play and get a few games in for that 2009 nostalgia.  The lobbies in this game truly are run by jungle law, as Activision (unsurprisingly, since they don't even seem to care about CoD WW2) doesn't moderate cheating in MW2.  Therefore, your experience in this game will be based simply on the other players in your game.  If they're not cheating, not tubing, and the host isn't on Dollar Tree internet, this game is still fantastic online.
Keep in mind -- this is a straight-up console port.  The optimization here is quite a mixed bag.  On one hand, the framerate is capped at 90fps, no FOV slider, ONE slider for audio, and so on.   However, the game does still run smooth on max settings (i7 CPU and a 1080ti), and I've only encountered a handful of crashes.  Not necessarily exclusive to console games, but just as important to mention, MW2 IS P2P-CONNECTION BASED.  This is a deal breaker for a lot of PC gamers, sometimes moreso than the 90fps cap.  If anyone is looking for a CoD with dedicated servers, MW2 isn't your game.  For others not put off by this, though, this game runs smooth enough.
The only other complaint I have is the DLC, which completely fragments the playerbase.  I truly wish Activision would do what they did with CoD4 and World at War, and package in the 10 DLC maps with the base game.  I happen to like playing the DLC maps, but the playerbase expectedly drops off significantly.  The silver lining here is that there aren't nearly as many cheaters that play in DLC lobbies, but at the expense of proportionately more noobtubers.  The dilemma here is this: do I play in regular lobbies with more players but more cheaters, or do I play in DLC lobbies with less people but less cheaters?  I ultimately have been choosing to take my chances with the regular lobbies, so I cannot recommend the DLC at this point in time.
But, really, this game is just so much fun online when everything breaks right.  MW2 comes with 16 maps in the base game (almost double what CoD WW2 gave us at launch!), tons of guns to unlock, perks to improve, classes to experiment with, and so on.  Although it's a mystery that people don't play Ground War on PC (unlike on Xbox 360, where there's usually a full lobby up), as well as some other modes, there still are many games with TDM, some Domination, and even some S&D too.  There's three conditions to having a fantastic time in MW2 multiplayer, in my opinion: no cheaters, no tubers, and no bad hosts.  Should these conditions be met, I can absolutely still recommend this game.
One disclaimer: I have not played the Spec Ops portion of this game, although I guess it's a good co-op diversion to sink some time into.  I guess.  I have no idea, so I would look elsewhere for opinions for this game mode.
Although I really love this game, I realize that MW2 isn't for absolutely everyone.  The player may need to have the patience of a buddhist monk at times to await the right lobby to actually play the game on fair terms.  However, when that happens, MW2 is FPS nirvana online.  And if the player doesn't care about multiplayer, then their experience gets a whole lot more reliable with the over-the-top single-player story.  Either way, MW2 is a flawed classic, but it's still a classic.

This game gets hated on a lot because the port is terrible, and I can't really fault the community on that logic, because this port is pretty terrible. It's unstable, it's unoptimized and it's unnecessarily huge (really, 30GB for this 8hour game from 2008?!). It needs tweaking for higher resolutions and needs a patch for 60FPS. Yeah, 30FPS cap on PC, let that sink in. It's a shame, because visually, this game is pretty damn good, and while there are some (very rare) cringeworthy voice acting moments, all in all, the story is pretty good (more engaging than Rogue One, at least) and the voice actors do their job - especially the guys doing Vader and ol Palpy, I never would've guessed they're not the original actors. When everything clicks, it's awesome. I mean, you're Darth Vader's secret apprentice for Hutt's sake, how much more awesome do you need?
Gameplay-wise, it's also good for the most part, with some fairly annoying design decisions, but unlike the cartoony Clone Wars game, here I'd say the good does outweigh the bad all things considered.
The start of the game is fairly bland and irritating, and getting to know how to play the game is a bit frustrating if you're new to 3rd person hack and slash games (I'm not really *new* to them, having played a lot of PoP games and Batman Arhkam games, but it's not what I play most of the time). Until you get lightning upgraded and some other powers/perks, you feel pretty weak, it's around the halfway mark that things really start to kick in. Little by little you upgrade your sorry Sith 4ss and by the end of it, you feel like a total Forcewielding God (of War?). The upgrade system is very simple, but oh-so-satisfying, upgrade points are divided into Force (for Force Powers), Combo (for various Force and Lightsaber combos) and Talent (passive health/force pool/defense/offense buffs) spheres, and they drip fairly slowly, meaning you don't get too powerful too quickly, but like I said, it does lend itself to a bit of a rough start. There are collectibles (Jedi Holocrons) that help you along the way, and unlocking lightsaber crystals (another upgrade and also an aesthetic item) is also extremely rewarding. Too bad there aren't any achievements, another thing the PC port was robbed of.
The environments and missions are done well, I enjoyed the level design, which is fairly linear, but still very polished. I like the fact that there are secondary objectives in almost every mission and collectibles/challenges as well, which adds some more replay value (my actual time needed to complete the story was half of what my total time is).
All in all, the combos are intuitive enough, they're mostly effective and not unecessarily complex, and the force powers are well balanced with the exception of Lightning, which is a tad OP at least on "Sith Warrior". Throwing Jawas around never gets old, hehe. It works, when it works, and it took me a long time to get into this game, but when I did, I enjoyed it thoroughly minus a few gripes.
So there, the bulk, the bones and flesh are good, but man, oh, man does this game have zits and warts.
My least favourite thing are the UNSKIPPABLE CUTSCENES. WHY? WHY DO THESE EXIIIIST?!? The reason I'm b1tching so hard about this is because this makes replaying levels to find collectibles or just to play them again because some of them are, you know, ACTUALLY FUN LEVELS that you WANT TO BE IN and INTERACT WITH, ever so freaking annoying. I know the intro level cutscenes are there to disguise the loading time, but GOD, I swear I'd rather stare at that loading bar than watch the same cutscene n-times.
Another rather annoying thing which makes some boss battles annoyingly annoying (I hope I am making it clear how *annoying* this is) is the knockdown downtime/vulnerability. If so powerful you are, why take 5 seconds to get off yer ruddy feet?! Bosses are not really that easy, and the fact that some of them just pummel your weak 4$$ to the ground without any way of blocking or fighting back or recovering makes them controller-throw-worthy. They really should've incorporated some kind of "recover" button (there's a dash button, why not use that?). It's hard to feel like this ultra powerful Sith dude if you're rolling around like a whiny football player because you got dinged by a Stormtrooper. Some Sith Lord, jeez.
Also, there's DLC, comes with the "Ultimate Sith" Edition. It's 3 maps that last around 35-45minutes (or more if you're stupid and OCD like me and you need to complete the secondary "get 600 000 Force Points" objective, which you need to... grind for... ugh...). Pathetic.
In conclusion, this game is not worth full price by a long shot, and it has its fair share of problems. However, it's still a damn good Star Wars title and if you're a SW fan, you'll definitely enjoy it, if you can swallow a few drops of lemon juice.

First Impression Gameplay:
A great little horror game that suffers from minor problems and could use a bit of polish.  The horror element of this game is on target, with a creepy atmosphere and a feeling of suspense.  The changing level design keeps things unpredictable, which adds to the element of surprise.  Graphics are great, and I like that this is on the Unreal engine.  Audio is well done and certainly adds to that layer of uneasiness.
Unfortunately, the game does suffer from a few issues.  As far as bugs are concerned, it could use some polish.  In one specific room, a sliding chair pushed me into the world and I was stuck and unable to continue.  Which brings up another point: no saves.  Makes this very frustrating, especially when you have to reload due to no fault of your own.  The game also suffers from massive frame drops and stuttering from unknown causes.  Apart from that, the game is fun.  It's a really solid horror game, the developer just needs to tighten the bolts.
All in all, the negatives seem to be general release issues.  Nothing seriously wrong with the core game-play.  If the developer can push out some hot-fixes, this will be a very solid addition to the horror genre.  I will recommend.
-Solid concept of the horror genre
-Beautiful graphics
-Great sound work
-Good horror atmosphere
-The beginning menu is unique and I like it a lot
-Puzzle game-play is simplistic, but fun
-Good price
-Needs optimization, frames drop horribly and there's a lot of stuttering
-No saves
-General glitches (like getting stuck in the environment and having to restart)
-Just needs some overall polish

A fun little JRPG with some distinctive mechanics.  Word guessing is one of them, as is a timed-hits-like feature.  Occasionally, some enemies or obstacles may even be integrated with the plot, such as "puzzle" bosses that query the details of a mystery.  Mechanics are pretty solid, plot is reasonably interesting, music is quite decent too.  It's a little tedious having to discard gemstones one by one when you run out of inventory space, but that's about my only complaint.  This game's not the most epic of adventure tales, but it's definitely surprisingly fun to play.
Just make sure you use the gem upgrades to make the C command reveal a ton more hints at once.  Four is good.  If you're paying attention, you should rarely need more than that.  And also get the Escape upgrades, so that you can stop attacking/defending immediately once a gem becomes available for use.  And if the clues go by too fast, there's another upgrade for that.  The game would probably be more tedious if I didn't get those, so I'm glad I got them.  Oh, and buy the Spirit Indexes from the store -- if a spirit is in the list, you can just click the name and be done with it.
(Right-click to cancel if you don't want to upgrade a gem, by the way.  I'm not sure the game makes that clear, but it's there.  Though you can always redistribute all your upgrade points anyway.)
The game comes with both Japanese and English voicework (which is just battle grunts/lines anyway), as well as the fully Japanese original version.
(Disclosure: I acquired this game as part of the Groupees Indie Bundle.)

This game is a very interesting oddity, with a unique way of doing combat and and a very grand story. Taking place in medevial Japan, it's up to you to destroy all the pottery, tableware and clothing articles for justice. By that, I mean possessed objects, just like the start of Mother 1.

Lengthy story
No two people will ever have the same loadout
Multiple endings
Quite a few bosses which put a twist on the combat system
Shizuru is hilarious.
Cons:
The combat system is a love it or hate it affair, which the hours I put in you already know what I think
An inperfect translation, there's a few typos here and there. This is a very minor nitpick.
Saving a certain person who can't keep their chest contained is easily missable on your first run
If you can't identify a boss even though you've seen all the hints, yeah, good luck buddy.
Overall, I believe this game is rather grand and will provide you with at least 20 or so hours of enjoyment. This can go to 60 hours depending on what kind of run you'd like to do. However, it's a game that you'll love or you'll hate, so keep that in mind if you decide to purchase it.

I purchased on sale for £5.99, though it is well worth the full price £11.99 on the basis you’ll get hours of entertainment out of this over time.  I bought as a casual game I was half interested in, but it turned out to be a huge surprise in just how good this game is. I thought it would be a basic strategy game; and the controls are exceptionally easy (basic) to learn.  But, for a game that looks easy, the underlying strategy is deep.  The idea in the game is to create a virus and spread it around the world, all the while the world governments’ tries to cure their citizens.  It sounds easy and basic, but the complexity comes from knowing where to spend your limited DNA points – do you focus on improving how well the virus spreads between countries, how well it spreads within countries, how strongly it makes people ill, or how fatal the disease is. But you also need to spend DNA points on ensuring cures take longer, and making your disease resistant to the cures. Then, add the complexity, that you need to focus on shutting down countries in order – focus on those that are most quickly developing cure research against you.  Each country could have many unique needs; is the country wealthy, poor, hot, cold, arid, humid, etc.  Each DNA choice affects how well the disease spreads in an individual combination of country. And to make matters worse for you, you have to know how well your disease will spread via boat or airline.  Warning: some islands will simply shut off their ports if they notice the disease is strong. Greenland is particularly isolated, so is Iceland. So if you can’t spread your disease you will lose the game.  You’ll also lose if you kill off people too quickly (doesn’t make sense at first), but you’ll realise you can’t simply spread a horrid disease as there’s a risk people could be killed before transmitting the disease to other people.  A potentially better strategy, you want to spread a mild disease first, and then ratchet up the symptoms so they kill, without leaving it too late that the population can make a cure.  Good luck!  This looks a simple game, but it is a fun, exciting challenge, that is very addictive with one more turn (try/game) feel.
The game is real time, but has a pause button and pauses on important news. I thought in the tutorial the game played too quick even on the slowest level, but in my first game I got used to this speed and see why it works. The interface is very nice and adequate for a value game, providing news flashes from around the World, country data, cure progress data, your virus data, and shows planes and ships moving around the World from port to port.
Oh, and if you master all this with a standard disease, try the scenarios. Fancy running a group of infected apes against the population? The scenarios add NEW features: Managing ape colonies, building them into a human fighting force and disease spreader. The “Planet Of The Apes” scenario may be for you.  No doubt they’ll be Zombie symptoms to create as I progress the game.
There is also variety in starting standard games as there are “loads of bonuses” you can unlock to start games with, so viruses are unique for each game.  And there are over 100 achievements to strive for, from relatively easy to very challenging – hours of fun trying to get them all done.
Because this was cheap, is unique, fun, addictive strategy, deep for how simple the game seems on the surface from its UI, it’s a 10/10, for a game you can enjoy over an hour or two each evening. MUST BUY for strategy fans.  You will know (if) you like it after 2 hours, so no risk if buying through steam – just get a refund if you don’t like it. I’m sure you will love it though and see this is a keeper to come back to again and again.

Jotun is a game that suffers from a lack of direction. It's a tremendously beautiful game (minus a few small quibbles), but doesn't seem to understand if it wants to be an atmospheric exploration game, or a slow paced dark souls / shadows of the colossus style boss slayer. In trying to do both, it sort of fails in all angles. On the plus side, it is relatively short, so the downsides of the game don't overshadow the nice bits too badly. I would say a roughly 5 hour game, depending on how much trouble you have with the bosses.
Jotun tells the tale of Thora, a viking warrior who dies at sea, who now roams Norse Purgatory, Ginnungagap, in an attempt to make her way to Valhalla. At the same time, the environment tells the tale of the Norse gods and mythos, touching on several stories very briefly, but never elaborating too much on any one particular detail. That's really the story of the entire game - 9 themed vignettes to explore, and five (plus final boss) bossfight, a mile wide, but an inch deep. It genuinely feels like the game at one point was meant to be one large connected world, but due to financial or time issues, was condensed into the nine best setpieces and connected by a void.
The art is beautiful and hand drawn, and wonderfully draws you into the world. Unfortunately, there's not a lot to do in the world you're immersed in. Each of the 9 areas has one Rune (mandatory), and one God Power and one Ithunn Apple (both optional). Some areas also have "Landmarks". which are panned out great vistas of areas where you can see the environment. That's it. Everything else is empty space. Pretty looking empty space, but empty space. Each area also generally boasts one movement puzzle and one environmental obstacle - such as a blizzard in the Nine Rivers or hostile dwarves and light-up pillars in Brokkr's Forge. These are often the only things that break up the emptiness, however. The world has a grand scale, but feels empty, and not in the good, haunting way, but in the bad, desolate way. For example, I missed the entire 'environment puzzle' in Jormundgandr's lake simply by getting the optional things and seeing the vista. The puzzle itself was contained to a small area in the middle that I would never have seen, except for the fact that I ran through on purpose trying to trigger it. Admittedly, some of the areas, such as the Forge, or Ymir's Blood, are more in your face about it. Non-boss enemies never feel like true obstacles, but rather just annoyances. The Great Nameless Eagle in Yggdrasil's Branches is reduced to 'dodge roll or lose 1/3rd of your life.' Repeat every 30 seconds. That's it. It just feels like a loss of potential.
Your character's controls don't generally help the issue. Thora plods along at a pace that would be fine for exploring, but does not give the sense of urgency that you would feel a Viking in her position might have. Dodge rolls are awkwardly animated, stopping you suddenly and ruining momentum, (though the character is still visibly rolling) and do not have any actual i-frames, making them only useful for the sudden burst of speed. Attacks are limited to a one-two swing combo, or  a long charging heavy attack. Light attacks are useless for the entire game except one situation, as its almost always more useful to wind up and smash a jotun or an environment object, several of which can't even be harmed by light attacks to begin with. God Powers are all useful in jotun fights, which is a plus - I would frequently use every single one of them against bosses, though outside of boss fights, only the speed boost (to make running bearable) and the healing are really helpful. Finally, one minor nitpick - the animation for Thora is mirrored vertically. That means as she turns horizontally, her sprite switches her handedness for her axe, which always appears in front of her spite, in the bottom half, rather than behind her sprite like you'd expect in some orientations. All the Jotuns are not animated this way, so it's strange to see the level of attention given to the bosses not paid to the protagonist of the game.
Bossfights are the climactic encounters of the game, and again, while they look impressive, most of them have very little in the way of strategy, especially when the best approach to all of them is "Hit with both Gungnir magic, get on their side or behind, activate Thor and Freyja, and heavy swing", repeat until out of all magic, then keep heavy swinging (but a bit slower now) until it's dead. Two of the jotuns, the storm and the fire jotun, change this up due to their patterns but the basic strategy is still the same. Approach from a safe angle and heavy swing. The fact that all the time trials for the games state times less than 80 seconds (most are 60 or 40) should say just how swiftly a boss can be beaten with even cursory understanding of the magic.
I feel like the game would have benefitted from deciding if it wanted to be an atmospheric adventure game about wandering purgatory in search of Vahalla, focusing on Thora's story, or a thunderous jotun fight game with a focus on Valhalla and the mythos, but trying to mix both ends up with both feeling lackluster. If you're really feeling the Norse mythos (and it is done very well, with narration in Icelandic), and want to look at admittedly very pretty vistas, then pick it up, but if you're looking for an action game, then keep an eye on EITR's release, as that may be the game you're looking for.

I realize this is a contrary opinion, but Mighty No. 9 is not a bad game. In fact, it manages to reinvent the Mega Man series in a way that won't please every fan. But if it does scratch your particular itch, then it will reinvigorate your enjoyment of the franchise.
Like many of these 0.2 Hour "reviewers", I despised my initial hours. It wasn't until the final boss when all the subtle mechanics came together that won me over. If you are willing to read about your abilities (and controls) that are not obvious and if you play the way the game wants you to play, then you'll find a great game that suffers by going against what is expected.
Before someone claims that I'm don't get Mega Man, I have played every Classic, X and Zero game, and I have even dabbled into a few spin-offs. Each series has their own particular gameplay and tempo, and Mighty No. 9 is no exception.
If I had to describe MN9 in a sentence, it's classic style gameplay of short, linear obstacle courses with the emphasis of speed from the X series. Like with games such as Bloodborne and Street Fighter V, I think MN9's greatest problem is how it tries to reinvent its difficulty/appeal for non-casual fans while leaving more casual fans unsatisfied.
People are exaggerating how MN9 has soiled Kickstarter forever. While I am familiar to the numerous sketchy aspects of its development--from the Red Ash projects, to the politics, and to the announced Deep Silver publisher deal--I don't think the game suffered as a direct result.
For the sake of transparency, I did pledge the minimum tier which gave me access to a free copy of Mighty Gunvolt and the demo. A former significant-other also backed the Kickstarter and gave me a free copy.
So I essentially got the $25 reward of the game and all the DLC with paying $5 out of my own pocket. I don't think this influences my perception, but it's relevant when you have many backers who paid the full price (or who paid more) and didn't enjoy the experience. Take it as you will.
(FYI my name in the credits is wrong, so I'm a little peeved about backing the game as well.)
There are two problems with the classic series' that will be familiar: 1.) Boss weapons are a must on specific enemies (either the Robot Masters or a specific Wily boss) and 2) they only provide a different weapon. MN9 surprised me in how it addresses both, and it succeeds--for the most part.
For starters, when fighting bosses you can fight ANY boss using your standard weapon. This means you can play the game in any order of your choice without the game requiring you to have a boss-weapon for that one boss (ex. Fireman from MM1). This change doesn't compromise the difficulty, and even if you have the "weakness" the battle still requires your skill as the battle tends to be build to counter it.
Second, in regard to weaknesses, they are not OP anymore. You will find that multiple forms are often more viable than the obvious weakness. Boss forms in MN9 rely on their utility and skill than what works the best, and it leads to a wonderful feeling of discovery. And because forms have recharging ammo, you are encouraged to use them more before and during boss-fights.
Examples of this:
-Mighty No. 3 : You can blow away her shield with one missile.
-Mighty No. 5 : You can deflect projectiles with your sword.
-Mighty No. 1: In his stage, you can use the bulldozer to speed through the falling towers section.
Not every form offers the same ultilty for combat and non-combat, but this is a great step in the right direction that I would like to see more. (I found only one form I'd avoid using: Pyro.) And with how you can map your forms to specific buttons (3 total), you can transition between your favorites and keep the pace of the battle.
When you get to the point of using both Beck's abilities with various boss-forms on the fly is when you get to see the game at its best. There are no pause-menus or cycles to shift through (you can shift through them on the fly but it's definitely not how you are meant to play).
And as much as people complain about the dash ability, its implementation is actually quite good. You can cancel out of dashes with a short-dash or a downwards dash, so you don't have to dash off a ledge all the time, and with its generous hit-box you can absorb two or three bots with one dash. The mechanic also makes boss-fights a little more hectic because they can regain their health if you don't absorb it quickly. (I only wish the bosses had an offensive/defense phase to work with this mechanic.)
The story is another thing MN9 has done right, though it's nothing to praise either. The plot wasn't as melodramatic as the X series (and thankfully Beck doesn't whine as much as X like an anime fan-girl on prom night). However, it was slightly more complicated from the "Stop Bad-Guy" of the classic games with some extra plot-threads. The only downside of its execution is how the ending quickly resolves itself with many unanswered questions.
Before I address why I think more casual fans may not enjoy this game as much as MN9's intended audience, I do want to point out the aspects of MN9 that are undeniably abysmal.
Lastly, and perhaps the most infurious problem with the game is its atrocious level design.
Its worst offender are those one pixel-perfect moments in the level--and each stage has one of these like the saw-blades of MN3 and the jet-pack section in Roll's mission--that require so specific of a response that it not only breaks the flow of its speedy gameplay but makes the game feel unfair. The platforming will kill you more often then enemies will.
The less extreme problem is how level gimmicks are never introduced long enough to make each stage unique or offer a fair challenge. One only needs to play Shovel Knight to see how modern level gimmicks should be handled. MN9 stages are too simple and straightforward, a result of its speedrunner design.
MM games have always rewarded patience, and MN9 is the exception. It is this change that will make-or-break the game for you. Temporary buffs from absoring enemies, the scoring system, and the announcer all emphasize a speedy recklessness for how you play. And aside from those pixel-perfect moments, the level-design is meant for speed.
While I am not a speedrunner fan, I can appreciate a game subverting difficulty for fans. Only I don't think the game succeeded in pleasing its more casual base. In the end, I can only share Blacknell's final words:
"Time will tell if this Mighty No. 9 -- this "Beck"-- is a blessing... or a curse."

This game doesn't utilize of anything that made Megaman good. It decides to go on the frustrating way of Megaman 1 and make it worse. Now, don't get me wrong, there's nothing wrong with difficulty. I love Megaman 1, but there's a difference between frustrating difficulty and good difficulty.
Yup, they're back and they're worse than ever. Now, instant kill sprites are nothing new to Megaman, but in this game they're noticeably atrocious. You can't beat a level without running into one at least once. Even the original megaman didn't have spikes all over the place like this. In one of the stages, there's a part where you have to slide through an instant kill spinning object, and it's one of the most frustrating parts I have ever played in a video game.
If you didn't know, this game has a little mechanic where in order to kill enemies, you have to weaken them with your buster and then charge into them. While the idea sounds ok on paper and I admit, dashing into multiple enemies after beating them can be pretty satesfying, the overall execution is terrible if they're near a bottomless pit or an instant kill spikes (Which isn't not common). It becomes worse during bosses, since if you don't dash into them fast enough, they regain their health and you have to do it all over again. Now, yes, it is possible to shoot enemies to death (not bosses, you HAVE to dash into them), but if you do that, you won't get any power boost you could be getting if you dash into them, it takes wayy longer, you won't get any score and you won't have a chance to get an energy tank (Or Axel Recovery as the game likes to call them). Speaking of energy tanks...
Ooooh boy, remember in the original megaman games where you could use an energy tank to save you from death? That was fun right? Remember willing to take challenges on to get them right? Well in this game, they're completely ruined! There are two ways to get energy tanks.
1. Dash into as many enemies as you can with a 100% score (Which you can only get if you dash into them RIGHT AFTER you weaken them) and get as many combos to charge one up.
2. Get lucky and have one of the helping robots spit one out for you.
Here's the problem. You can only have 2 energy tanks at a time, and both of those ways are ways to get one of them. Which means you can't do the second method twice and get two energy tanks. You can do both methods and get them, however, once you die,
The energy tanks dissappear when you die and then you have to get them again. Which again,
. That can lead up to so many frustrating times and overall annoyance.
The story of this game is terrible and is full of plot holes and I don't want to talk about it.
Now, this game isn't completely terrible. I admit, I did enjoy playing through parts of it. Once you memorize the levels, this game can be pretty fun (Friendly reminder memorizing the levels can take thousands of lost lives and frustration). Some of the bosses for this game are pretty clever and are pretty fun to play against with their weakness (Assuming you don't die due to half of their midway-through-battle ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t attack). The graphics are alright and it runs pretty smoothly if you have the specs for it. The music is pretty nice too, so at least someone did their job right. The game has a system where if you beat a robot master before beating another robot master who'se weakness is the robot master you already cleared, the robot master you already beat will come and help you to get rid of frustrating parts of the level. Unfortunately this is a wasted potential half of the time seeing as they only help at parts which are pretty easy, but some of the times it's a lifesaver, so I'll thank the game for that.
I haven't really touched that much on this game's level design, so let's talk about that real quick.
It's overall pretty bad and frustrating until you fully learn it. Remember in past megaman games when you could find secret parts and other ways to clear a level thanks to using a robot master's power? Well there's only one stage that uses that in this game and it's only for an extra life and places you can go without it. I'd talk more about it but there's not much I can say about it without you playing it to understand.
Don't worry, I'm not spoiling anything, but this game's final boss is one of the worst bosses I have ever played. It's Yellow devil frustration for half of it and the other half if just plain terrible. Never have I ever played a video game boss that actually gave me an anxiety attack. And this game successfully did it. Good job.
Well, here's a short list of the cons and pros.
CONS:
Bad level design.
Instant kill spikes everywhere.
Energy tanks are handled horribly.
Terrible plot.
Dashing mechanic can be pretty frustrating at times.
This game is overall frustrating.
Final boss is one of the worst in any video game ever.
PROS:
Game can be enjoyable when learning how the level is structured.
Music is pretty good.
Some bosses are well done.
The robot-helping system is pretty nice sometimes.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game unless you like to play really difficult games and you're not that frustrated by them. And even then, I'd say wait until this goes on sale. If you're just a megaman fan like me that like the fair difficulty in most games, don't get this game unless it goes on a 1$ sale.

This is the natural evolution of TIS-100, you can now place a variety of modules, from the standard 9 line MC4000 to the opulent MC6000 (14 lines should be enough for everybody). This game is fantastic. I've never been disappointed by a Zachtronics game yet, and Shenzhen I/O adds elements from several other Zachtronics titles while still feeling like a completely fresh and awesome experience.
If you've ever taken a Computer Architecture class or know anything about Assembly or Computer Engineering, Shenzhen I/O is a gamified version of it. The puzzles involve creating a program that runs across several microchips; you are given digital inputs, program requirements, an empty board, and several different types of microchips, and then are tasked with matching the outputs with their expected values.
The manual is basically a requirement; I got the limited edition, which comes with a physical copy of the manual in a fancy little binder. If you get the digital copy, it still comes with the manual, but I'd strongly recommend printing it out. It's very nice to just have it in front of me because I've had to refer to it / flip through it frequently.
If you like Puzzles, Hacking, Low-Level Programming, Hardware, Raspberry Pi's or Arduinos, Reading Manuals, Circuitry, and/or challenging games, definitely check it out.

The parts of RCT that have aged poorly:
-- The visuals
-- The audio quality
-- The UI and menus
-- The animations (which were gorgeous for their time btw)
-- Just about everything that has to do with how the game looks.
The parts of RCT that have aged extremely well:
-- Building roller coasters is still a blast, with simple controls and lots of trial and error that legitimately pays off.
-- The management part of the game is still brilliant and engrossing.
-- The variety of maps and scenarios means hours of content.
-- Plenty of options for personalising your park.
-- Picking up customers who complain and dropping them in the water to drown them, or making them go on an unfinished or otherwise dangerous ride so they crash to their death, is still morbidly satisfying.
-- Just about everything that has to do with how the game feels.
In short, an immense amount of nostalgia and happy memories of playing RCT is what led me to buying and playing this in 2016. The fact that the game is still a ton of fun is what led me to play it for more than 100 happy hours in 2016. This is one of the best simulation/management games ever made, and THE definitive amusement park game, and it's a testament to its greatness that unlike many dinosaurs of turn-of-the-century PC gaming, it's still great today.
