I picked this game up for $ 3.75 because I'm into choice-based games and because AI is an important part of my research.  After two hours I finished my first playthrough. I don't think there is going to be a second one.
The reason I won't play through Choice of Robots a second time isn't because it's bad – quite the contrary. It's just that this one playthrough did everything that I wanted it to.
My choices felt like they had real weight. My AI evolved in a manner consistent with my play style. At times, the options presented by the dialogue tree system felt a bit ambiguous (what does it mean for my character to refuse to shake someone's hand?), but the author of the game and I seemed to be in complete agreement about the implication of each choice, which is amazing now that I think about it. I got 2 hours of stellar entertainment for $ 3.75 – I'm a happy customer.
Of course there's another reason I shy away from a second runthrough: Immersion. I completely identified with my character. In a weird way, I felt like I really had no choice at all – I NEEDED to follow my own moral compass. To do anything else would have been... uncomfortable. Sure, I'd be interested to find out how a total gung-ho military playthrough would have turned out, but I know it couldn't possibly grip me in quite the same way – they just wouldn't be MY choices.
In the end I didn't destroy the world, nor did I save it. But the game always made me believe that either outcome was possible. That's just good writing, folks.

Let me just begin by saying that I don't hate this game like other people do. The gunning actually feels fine. Too bad this game has some major flaws that just destroy the fun.
positives:
+ jumping and shooting feels good.
+ the robot masters have some nice designs
negatives:
- Leveldesign is either bland or unfair, especially when you have to navigate falling down a small hole filled with spikes
- the game is horrible at describing what all the power-ups and robot powers do. It also doesn't describe certain features like shooting diagonally down.
- the whole dashing-into-enemies-to-kill-them is just flawed. You never know how many hits you need to land until you can absorb them. Even a health-bar for the bosses doesn't make it better because every boss has another point at which you can deal the damage to them. If you dash into an enemy when he isn't absorbable, you just fly all over the place - most of the time into instant death spikes
- because of that, your effective range that your weapon has is limited to your dash range. If you just want to shoot until the enemy disappears into an unsatisfying blob of data, you have to shoot it twice or even thrice as much, slowing you down.
- the game is horrible at descirbing anything, really. You have health-items that you can use when absorbing enough blue enemies, but it doesn't tell you about that. You just have to know.
- there is a tip-section, yes, but even those don't explain enough.
- bossfights are slow and boring. Pretty much the only good boss fights are MN 1 and MN 2. You will still die often because you try to dash into the enemy before he is available to be dashed into.
- boss weaknesses are almost useless - your normal mighty buster kills the bosses just as fast.
- The prison stage is the worst thing ever.
- the final boss is a bullet sponge that you have to retry from phase 1 if you fail.
All in all, this game is a mixed bag. If you like Megaman, this game is like a 6/10. If you don't... just stay away. Get the Megaman Collection on Steam.

A great set of short ghost stories as videogame.
Unnerving and with more than a slightly wicked sense of humour, The Charnel House Trilogy is a sort of classic Amicus style portmanteau with a deep understanding that horror works best when it's about the gaps, what's unsaid and what can never really be understood. That mix of the unexplainable within the eveyday mundane.
It's magical, preposterous and at times hilariously willing to have fun along with the player instead of using the player as a prop for cheap jump scares or gross out horror, trusting enough that the player knows the beats as well as the author does and willing to have fun with that without making it impenetrable or offputting.
I think this is the closest a horror game has got to my tastes, it made me wriggle in my seat in parts, left me curious as to where it was going to turn next, smirking at the turns it did take and on more than one occasion, left me laughing like a drain at some of its more absurd moments.
A horror game for your more classical horror appreciating folks but also smart enough and tales well told enough for everyone else.

You will get answers but perhaps not the answers you want.

This is the type of horror adventure game I just love.
The story is strong, engaging, and satisfyingly creepy. I quickly became sucked in to the gloomy world depicted and remained transfixed until I completed the game. I think what impresses me most about the narrative is what great job they did with the balancing and pacing of mystery. In a story like this, if too much is left unknown for too long things tend to become overly abstract and tedious, but if the story explains too much the 'magic' of not knowing is gone and things start to feel artificial. This game hits the mark perfectly, by the end of the game you will have some idea of what is going on, but enough unanswered question to leave you wanting more (and trying to construct you own theories in the meantime.)
Beyond excellent storytelling, this game sports a solid cast of voice actors in all its lead rolls. A few of the minor characters are a little underwhelming, but altogether everything is passable and doesn't take you out of the story.
The graphics take the form of the classic adventure 2D style and are beautiful and well-crafted for the purposes of this game. Likewise the music is atmospheric, haunting, and fits the created world perfectly.
In terms of adventure game gameplay, things are fairly simple and straight forward. Not much in the way of puzzles beyond the usual "What do I do with this object?" If you are looking for a challenge this wouldn't be my first recommendation. The game is also fairly short, it took me about 2 hours to finish it, but considering its overall quality and the lower price I am fully satisfied with my purchase.

update: It appears there is a possibility that I've missed some optional story content. So take my main criticism with a further grain of salt until I investigate it and update my review accordingly.
I haven't been this conflicted about a game in a while. Let's see, what it does well? The presentation, the music, the atmosphere are all excellent. This is a horror-ish game and the mood, pacing, suspense are superb. There are some banal elements here and there but oh boy, do I genuinely wish all horror developers learned from this game. The game is more focused on being unsettling than trying to be outright scary and that works out amazingly. The unique mood the game immerses you in is hard to forget.
The writing is solid, and the game tells some interesting stories, both explicit and vague. The characters are vibrant, distinct and interesting. The personal stories presented here are a very decent and satisfying part of this work. A certain theme is prominently present in the game, and while it can be considered technically kinda thrilling, it can also just as well be considered mundane. The metaphors and symbolisms surrounding the theme are probably some of the best I've seen, which is both impressive and slightly disappointing as a waste of potential. But wait, there is some intriguing underlying lore that can possibly redeem this if it's interesting enough. The whole Charnel House thing, yeah? If only the game actually told you, well, anything substantial about this story branch.
Which also happens to be titular. Oops. And that's the major shortcoming of the game as far as I'm concerned. It merely teases you with its titular story branch, only giving some bare hints at what it might be about. And look, I'm all for mystery but here the game leaves me in the dark about even whether I really like it or not since for me a significant portion of judgement depends on how interesting the underlying context is. But I can't evaluate it because the game doesn't expand on it that much. It does somewhat openly promise a sequel, and while I don't see anything wrong with that per se, it depends on the sequel a bit too much for my liking, remaining a very unfinished work on its own. Which also isn't inherently wrong, but it becomes hard to judge for me because of it. And well, there simply are better, more satisfying ways to present a mysterious unfinished narrative. There got to be. Also it's worth pointing out that I found Alex definitely sympathetic and I absolutely enjoyed learning about her life, but also I honestly can't say I like her enough to prefer that to some cool intriguing supernatural storyline. And since the game isn't called "Alex's Life" I dare to suggest this imbalance of story branch reveals favoring hers is a bit of an actual flaw.
So yeah, if you can tolerate vagueness, unfinishedness and merciless cliffhangers then by all means go for it. There is a lot to enjoy here and it does horror differently from how everybody else does horror. As you can see, I definitely enjoyed it enough for this to remain a cautious but positive recommendation. But if not, then I suppose you should wait for the sequel first. Because if the sequel provides a satisfying explanation, or a more satisfying mystery at least, then this was all very good apparently.

The actual meat of the game, the story, is kind of what I have the most issues with. Without getting too spoilery, I'll just say that it leaves a little to be desired. I enjoyed it thematically, but there was really no resolution or conclusion. There's all kinds of really interesting story bits and hooks... but none of them really LEAD anywhere. They're just kinda sprinkled in there, for you to look at, I guess.
Like a modern abstract painting, you get the feeling like it means SOMETHING to someone, but it's really just kind of lost on you. It feels like if I were watching a movie and it just ended halfway through. It honestly kind of feels like this game is just a preview for the sequel coming in 2016, which was hinted/teased at in the ending. Which, at this point, I'd be a little hesitant about buying it.
Again, it's hard to recommend simply because the story really doesn't GO anywhere. But it only cost me 4 bucks, and it was interesting enough to hold my attention. Give it a go if you like adventure games and dark/horror theming, I guess.

99 Spirits introduces a unique new type of rpg. There are many good, as well as bad points to it.
First of, it is very extremist on difficulty, it is either really easy, or pretty hard. However the difficulty to it doesn't rely on lack of skill, it is mostly because of a low level. The game is pretty easy itself, but going too fast through it may cause it to be a headache. I remember that when I got to certain boss on my first playthough I had absolutely no skills or support from monsters, and I couldn't go back to catch more because I HAD to defeat the boss. Took me MANY tries to beat, so hear my advice ALWAYS be ready with a nice or decent "party".
Second, it is the gameplay itself, it can get really repetitive once you find all monsters of an area. And sometimes, when finding a monster for the first time, you have absolutely no idea what the monster is. Has anyone ever heard of a Torii? or a Naginata? Well it was the first time for me.
Also, there are some features of the game that are never explained to you, for example Starve and Food, the only thing these two do, is make your character move slower on the map the hungrier you are and viceversa, you can't die from starving though.
It has a very nice amount of characters, each different from the other (in the sense each NPC has her/his own personality). If something, I'd say this game is like a visual novel + a puzzle RPG style. In addition the soundtrack in the game is actually really good, but you might get tired of it as it will repeat itself several times on different areas (Same that happens with any song, the longer you hear it over and over, the more likely you'll start to hate it).
It is a very nice overall game, I don't really suggest it for its story, but for the experience of the game itself. And again, the game is easy to beat, but a little time consuming (especially if you want all achievements).
However, the game does fall short for the full price ($15). So if you can get it with discount or on a bundle, I'd say go for it. The best advice I can give you, is to try out the demo, that is the best way to tell if this game is or isn't for you.

I greatly enjoy the game and there are literally thousands of mods available both public and private mods that can keep it interesting enjoyable.
However there is much about this particular series of simulators that needs improvement. I have played every single release in the farming simulator series and there are some things that are always lacking. There is no dynamic ground effects from the tire tracks and many games already have that implemented so it shouldn't be too much to ask for a farming game to include it because afterall working in less than ideal conditions is a big part of farming. Also except for not being able to harvest while it's raining there are no weather effects in the base game and again that is a big part of farming.
On another note the helper system....has always and most likely will always be complete garbage. If the field isn't perfectly square they are utterly useless and end up wasting you more time than they save. It simply cannot be that difficult to scan each field on a map and put that information into a helper code so they are able to actually do their jobs in the fields properly.
The developers of this series need to seriously sit down and work on some of the main aspects of farming and make these games more of a simulator and less of an arcade style game. They seriously are going to have an extremely difficult time surpassing Cattle and Crops when it's released and they may not win fans back when it's time to release FS 2019 if they don't make some drastic improvements.
Also I would like to add a word about their DLC content.....In the past and with this particular version of the game the content is not at all worth what they charge for it. Yes the big bud content has some large equipment in it but is nowhere near the $15 they think it is. The other dlc isn't even worth $5 honestly. These dlc's should come free with the game as included equipment and not a simple money drain from the customers. There are hundreds of mods that include the same or better equipment and are available on the public sites.....for free!
Overall the game is very enjoyable, especially with a few friends, I would and do recomend it to friends however as I mentioned there is vast room for improvement.

I would highly recommend Choice of Robots both as a solid example of the "Choice of..." body of work and as a solid sci-fi (or, in this day and age, science future?) choose-your-own-adventure game. Wonderfully written with thought put into both actions and consequences, Dr. Kevin Gold weaves a tale of a computer science student pursuing greatness who's driven by you, the reader, to live a life worth remembering. With no shortage of characters, choices, and scenarios to learn and explore, Choice of Robots is a solid read the first time through - then an adventure in exploring "what if?" in the following playthroughs.

It's only my my first time through, and perhaps it's better if I try to take over the world, etc. But mostly it comes across as badly written and clumsly. As a person who is about to receive an MSc. in robotics, I enjoyed this game. I only went through one story line in which I played as if I would make the choices in real life. The game seems to be created by a computer-science phd that actually worked on learning and robotics. The game includes many aspects of the robotics domain, design considerations, ethics as well as real world trade-offs. The game seems to be very detailed and grows in deep. Yet I enjoyed the first half of the story more and felt that the story somehow pushes your choices. Also the events felt a bit jumpy and unrelated. For example, a war between US and China has started in my story out of nowhere and at some step it ended just like that and everybody continued their lives. Yet overall I really liked the game and willing to play it with many other choices.
Pros:
- Realistic features and terminology, it is not like ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sci-fi story with made up random scientific words
- Nice emphasize on robotics domain and its possible effects on ethics, human interaction, law regulation...
- Detailed storyline with rich and realistic components such as politics and its effects on market, bussiness management
Cons:
- Game being biased on US politics
- Story sometimes pushes your choices to make you something, for example it constantly wanted me to have a romantic relationship with my male robot

I am going to compare it with Tell Tales games and Life is Strange in that aspect, since those games too let the player take action. But Tell Tale and Dontnod Entertainment still narrated a linear story where your actions only affected the whole story as a general a tiny bit.
Since I have played Choice of Robots only once I can't tell whether the story is changing too much when you take different actions, or if Chloe will die in the end no matter what you do. But judging by the sheer amount of achievements this game has for different scenarios it seems to be a really variable story.

I tend not to review a game until I have beaten it, but I'm a little over an hour in and I just can't force myself to play it any longer. Whatever the Kickstarter project I put $20 into back in 2013 was, it certainly wasn't this.
Aside from numerous delays, a cringe-inducing marketing campaign and a clear graphical downgrade, the game just doesn't feel good to play.
The dash mechanic is a nice idea, but the levels feel like they weren't designed for it, meaning that spamming the dash button can overcome most of the platforming challenges. Beck's hitbox also feels wonky, and combined with several insta-death traps can make for a very frustrating experience.
I know I'm just beating a dead horse at the point but for a $4,000,000 project, its total embarrassment.
I really wanted this game to be a return to greatness for Mega Man style platformers.
I wanted it to succeed.
I wish I could be recommending it to everyone.
But I can't.
But hey, at least it's "better than nothing", right?
-Kickstarter Backer #6,446

A game that's cursed by it's name, Mighty No.9 hit the market (late) admist a cloud of negative perceptions, people didn't like the change in art style, delays in production, and a horribly tone deaf advertising campaign.
So after all that I'm reccomending this game.
Why?
Because it's been fun to play. As simple as that. If this title had shown up on steam without the press, or developer associated with it, I have no doubt it would have become a sleeper hit.
Enough soap boxing what I liked
+ Old school game play, its not new or innovative, but it hits the points of the original MM series well
+ Bosses, You will run into them midway through a stage and launches  a mini challenge, also when you do fight them, its
old school pattern recognition. These guys you need learn how they attack and how they move in order to forumlate a winning strategy.
+ A full game, you get a campaign (w. bous ray missions) that calls back to MM games of old by letting you choose the order you take on  levels/bosses.  In addition you can play on a mode that exchanges the health bar for 1 hit kills. Also there is an Ex mode comprised of several "VR" minicourses that are timed forays into sharpening a particluar skill (ie dashing,accelerating etc...)
What I didn't like:
- Janky cutscenes, not that I play a game like this for its plot, but putting a picture place holder  on view while randomly voicing some of the text and not others is just poorly done, and smacks of running out of time or money. Its like the place holder sketches you find in some early access titles.
-This is more personal taste but would have like a Charged shot mechanic, I was always a MMX fan more than just plain MM and liked the veristilty  that and other moves added to play. The game makes up for this some with a wide variety of powers claimed from defeated bosses, so its not a huge neg, but would have preferred it.
So there you have it, overall I found it a fun if conventional game that fills the niche of modern mega man like titles.

The Force Unleashed lets you play as Vader's apprentice and minion, as you weed out resistance members on assassination missions. After playing a series of clunky old Star Wars games, I was happy to find one that was more player-friendly than say, Jedi Outcast 2.
The Dark Force oriented combat is well developed, though not totally perfect. The button mapping is simple to learn and combos work relatively well. Quick-Time-Events are cool at first, but like all QTEs, they get old fast. During boss fights, it’s easy to miss the action as you wait for the button prompts. The only real complaint I have stems from the schizophrenic targeting and lock system for the much needed force grip power.
Another complaint is that maps are recycled, as are enemies from these areas. For me, it's no big deal, but I imagine for people who bought this when it came out for $50, that would have been a huge disappointment.
The story is okay, cheesy and predictable, but serviceable. I’m interested enough to try out the sequel, so I’ll give this a recommendation.
edit: oh, and at least two hours of this game are AFK. Beat it in about seven hours.
The opening sequence involves you cruelly mowing down Wookies with a lightsabre. It felt like 20 minutes of kicking puppies. I'm still in rehab and haven't progressed any further since.

I saw this on my steam suggestions, and almost passed by it. It's by pure chance that I actually clicked on this game, and I am really glad I did. The game has a very simple design to it. It's all click based, there are almost no puzzles to solve, and for the most part it's more of a story than a game. However, the story is amazing, with many "holy crap!" moments, and epiphanies. At several points in the game I though that I figured out exactly what is happening, just to be told several moments later how wrong I was. This is definitely a game worth checking out.

Full disclosure: I received a code for this game from Mastertronic for review, however, all opinions expressed here are my own
I had no idea what the game was about prior to playing it tonight, but I was pretty quickly invested in the games story and played through the game in one sitting.
Game-play style is point and click, so you can expect heavy story focus with some logic puzzles mixed in. The puzzles aren't terribly difficult, so this should be accessible to those new to playing this genre, or anyone looking to for more of a story than a challenge.

The Charnel House trilogy, a classic style point-and-click adventure game by Owl Cave, succeeds at telling a great story. In the first chapter, Inhale, we meet Alex, a 20-something woman who seems to be working to overcome some hardships – a recent break-up that’s still in the forefront of her mind, a sick father.  Alex will be going on a journey. This first act functions mainly as a set-up for the rest of the game, and introduces us to the characters and themes that will be explored more deeply later on. Act 2, Sepulchre, was actually available as a standalone game for a while and is made stronger by the bookending chapters. Sepulchre focuses on Harold, who boarded a train with Alex, and has to deal with strange events that are happening. While Harold seems to be in an almost fugue-like state, Alex is plagued by her memories, which weigh heavily on her. Act 3, Exhale, goes back to Alex and does an amazing job at tying everything together.
It’s hard to say a lot about the story without giving things away, but the titles (Charnel House, Sepulchre) should certainly give you an idea of the direction it takes. While it is a horror game, it’s not scary in the traditional sense, but provides a gradually increasing sense of unease that worms its way in and turns into dread. The writing by Ashton Raze is on point. Dialogue goes from sounding completely natural to Lynchian levels of bizarre. The best praise I can give is that from Act 2 on, no line is wasted. Everything has a purpose, and is building towards something. It’s a very well constructed story with a self-aware script, and it gets better as it goes.
For a game that maxes out at a 320 x 200 resolution, not a pixel is out of place. The style is very reminiscent of the Blackwell series (Ben Chandler did work on both this and The Blackwell Epiphany). The character portraits that pop up during conversations are lovely and the backgrounds, few that they are, are attractive.
The soundtrack often blends seamlessly into the background, but when it becomes more prominent, it’s really quite great. I highly recommend playing this with headphones, I put them on halfway through and was immediately impressed by how great it sounded. The voice acting is competent. Madeleine Roux’s Alex started off a little flat, but got better as the game went on. I have no complaints about the rest of the main players. Jim Sterling did well in his turn as a too-friendly neighbour, and the smaller parts were also generally well done. Though to be honest, I can’t hear Abe Goldfarb without thinking of Joey Malone.
The game is light on puzzles, but since the story is the star, that works out. There’s no mindless combining of inventory items or pixel-hunting for objects. Gameplay is quite straightforward, and I think more challenging puzzles would have been a distraction.
I only have one real complaint about the game. Inhale is peppered with in-jokes and nods to the voice actors. In-jokes are okay, but the first 10 or so minutes of the game consisted of little else, so that it was a bit of a turn-off.  Once the game got that out of its system, the story started steaming ahead and I was more than happy to go along for the ride.

It's OKAY. Just okay. I would still say give it a play, but it feels kind of rushed and simplified compared to other point and click adventures. I'd say Alex is a really unlikable character.Why does she have to swear in every single sentence? It seems like the writers tried very hard to portray a young woman. I honestly thought she was a teenager from how she spoke, then you find out later she's actually in her mid to late 20's. Completely unbelievable, especially as a 29 year old myself.
Harold Lang is a lot better and all the other characters are pretty cool. Lang's reactions are more believable and realistic. I like the train conductor Ol' Don the best though. I will say I love the old pixelated style a lot and the concept of being on a train where everything goes wrong.

The Charnel House Trilogy is an atmospheric and stylish point and click adventure set on a beautiful retro 2D backdrop. The simple mechanics and powerful narrative make this a truly enjoyable title with a very attractive price. It is also supported by a fantastic musical score and full character dialogue audio.
In this 3 chapter game; you begin by playing the role of Alex Davenport - a young woman who has to embark on a personal journey to Augur Peak by train after receiving some bad news. En route, you meet Dr. Harold Lang and this is where a routine train trip becomes an incredibly eerie experience. I wont elaborate on this because it will spoil the chilling and absorbing events that follow, but it will leave you deeeply engrossed throughout.
The game mechanics are fairly basic which makes this a title that you can pick up and play straight away. Each chapter is fairly short though and solving the occasional 'puzzle' or what to do next to progress isn't all that challenging. These aren't criticisms though - the way the narrative champions itself outweighs any depth or difficulty concerns.
The only real disappointment surrounding the game is the length - it will take you about two and a half to 3 hours to complete and the first two chapters are fairly limited although everything you accomplish has some bearing as the game flows nicely. You aren't walking around or searching aimlessly at any time so you feel you are always engaged in the product and everything has some merit. Despite the completion time; you will certainly get your money's worth for what is on offer and the intriguing writing.
Overall, The Charnel House Triolgy is a terrific game that delivers a powerful and absorbing story supported with a truly unique art style. If you're a fan of the genre or are just looking for a great story; it's highly recommended.

Full disclosure: I worked on a game with one of
game's developers, Ashton Raze, and we had a grand old time doing it, so my opinion on this is probably a little bit skewed.
That being said, this trilogy of bespoke hand-crafted adventure games is terrifically creepy and absolutely worth your time. The voice acting is almost always on-point (especially Cara Ellison's in Inhale), and the puzzles are totally solvable, even for a huge idiot like me.
My recommendation: buy it, and play it at three in the morning with the lights off and a light rain pattering on the roof, like I did. Proper creepy.
Also, just to note, if you're still hesitating on a purchase, the middle episode
is available for free separately, you can find it
.

All things considered, The Charnel House Trilogy is a very interesting game that will give any fans of point-and-click adventures and horror stories a run for their money. While it lacks the complexity and length of luminaries of the genre, it makes up for it with relatable main characters, smart dialogues and storytelling and masterful voice acting.  I will seriously be paying attention to all new releases from Owl Cave from now on. Hitch a ride on Old Gloria and prepare for a macabre trip.

I greatly enjoy the game and there are literally thousands of mods available both public and private mods that can keep it interesting enjoyable.
However there is much about this particular series of simulators that needs improvement. I have played every single release in the farming simulator series and there are some things that are always lacking. There is no dynamic ground effects from the tire tracks and many games already have that implemented so it shouldn't be too much to ask for a farming game to include it because afterall working in less than ideal conditions is a big part of farming. Also except for not being able to harvest while it's raining there are no weather effects in the base game and again that is a big part of farming.
On another note the helper system....has always and most likely will always be complete garbage. If the field isn't perfectly square they are utterly useless and end up wasting you more time than they save. It simply cannot be that difficult to scan each field on a map and put that information into a helper code so they are able to actually do their jobs in the fields properly.
The developers of this series need to seriously sit down and work on some of the main aspects of farming and make these games more of a simulator and less of an arcade style game. They seriously are going to have an extremely difficult time surpassing Cattle and Crops when it's released and they may not win fans back when it's time to release FS 2019 if they don't make some drastic improvements.
Also I would like to add a word about their DLC content.....In the past and with this particular version of the game the content is not at all worth what they charge for it. Yes the big bud content has some large equipment in it but is nowhere near the $15 they think it is. The other dlc isn't even worth $5 honestly. These dlc's should come free with the game as included equipment and not a simple money drain from the customers. There are hundreds of mods that include the same or better equipment and are available on the public sites.....for free!
Overall the game is very enjoyable, especially with a few friends, I would and do recomend it to friends however as I mentioned there is vast room for improvement.

text:
So, I got this from kickstarting it around two years ago. I was already dissapointed due to the 1.5 year delays, but let's get to what Comcept did with Megaman's legacy, with the metaphor of the legacy being a dog:
After getting it away from capcom, who was brutalizing it, they then tried to nurse it back to health. Seeing as they had no idea how to feed a living being, they then began beating it with a stale bread stick. Afterwards, they began to attempt to clean off the bruises from its previous beatings, and instead accidently used Japanese water torture on it. When trying to bandage it, they instead axphixiated it, nearly suffocating it several times. Giving up, they cut it up into meat chunks and used the four million dollars that backers gave to them in order to start a meat packaging plant.
Now, on to the pros and cons:
Pros:
+Decent gameplay
+Good ost
Cons:
-Buggy as Sonic '06
-Over a year of delays in release
-Graphics have the same quality as early PS2 games
-Graphics are nothing like the concept art
-Voice acting is worse than Megaman X4 and X7 could ever be
-Launch day DLC when Comcept was trying not to be like Capcom
-Somehow laggy even with bad graphics (something that should run fine on a 2.0 GHz processor with no video card lags with a 3.5 GHz processor + 2GB video card)
-Easiest game I've played in years (even easier than Kirby games)
-Trailers insult the main audience
-Enemy invincibility and player invincibility apparently assigned to the same variable (meaning that an enemy may randomly become invincible when you should)
-Extremely strange controls (tight as Megaman when grounded, slippery as Super Meat Boy when airborne)
-Any challenge is removed by infinite airdashes (and thus flight)

It's basically a classic Mega Man game, with few departures from the formula.  In fact the first six Mighty Numbers are basically reimagined versions of the six Robot Masters of the first Mega Man.
The gameplay is very typical of Mega Man games - you will platform and you will shoot straight horizontally.  There are a few new moves, like a backwards jump combined with a diagonal downwards attack, but it's very situational.
The stages and the bosses are fairly challenging - like the original Mega Man, which was one of the reasons that "Nintendo Hard" was a trope.  Like with most of the Mega Man games, the idea is to find whichever Mighty Number is the easiest to kill with your default weapon, and then leverage boss weaknesses to take out the rest in order.  Mighty No. 9 actually makes that piece fairly easy - each defeated Mighty Number will give you advice about one stage, not coincidentally being the stage whose boss is weak to that Mighty Number's weapon.  So once you get one special weapon, you can go in sequence through whichever stage has an "advice" option, using the last special weapon you acquired.
I'm not yet sure how I feel about the Ray DLC.  I like the melee-based attacks of Ray, basically a Zero-expy, but the vampiric nature of Ray makes all of her stages feel extremely frantic as there's an overwhelming need to kill quickly.  I think once I get past how some of her stages are just crazy hard I'll enjoy it a lot.

If you're a huge fan of Mega Man, you'll like the play style of this game.  I really enjoy the gameplay, personality of the characters, as well as the simple story you'd see in old NES and SNES games.  Music suits every stage, and the game is a nice challenge.
It's had a lot of hate drawn towards it due to development, but I think it's a good game none the less.  Just as good as Gunvolt.

Initially, I despised the game. It wasn't fun. It was frustrating, cheap, annoying, etc.
Then, I stopped thinking of it as Mega Man.
It was still frustrating, cheap, and annoying, but more fun than not. The phrase 'Nintendo hard' applies here, if only for the INCREDIBLE number of cheap or nearly unavoidable deaths you *WILL* encounter. I'm not a massive fan of the Xel absorption mechanic. Sometimes it's cool, but when stuck against a boss with a massively-OP attack or two -- and they can *HEAL* if you don't dash into them in time -- it's kind of BS. Or, when you're going through a stage that actually *REQUIRES* that you still have a power from some enemies a while back or you're trapped and have to die to try it again faster... (I'm *NOT* a speedrunner, damnit!). This, coming from someone that could do Quickman's stage blindfolded. ...almost 30 years ago, granted, but hey. >.>
Oh, and I hope you like button-mashing and waggling the stick/control pad. You'll do that a *LOT* to 'free' yourself from trap attacks. I think it's about 50 mashes to get out of an ice block. Maybe more.
Was it worth the wait? Absolutely not.
Is it worth the $20? If you're a masochist and want a frustrating, but *DECENT* (not *GREAT*) platformer, then yes.
I'd like to see a sequel, so it gets (some) of my support. I've already returned my PS4 versions (hey, I pre-ordered it a few times, apparently. Ambien.), so......... I don't have the option of 'complete and total ambivalence', so 'yes'. I guess.

So I review this game with conflicted feelings.
Overall the game is pretty solid but I would not pay 20 bucks for it. Probably 10 at most.
Gameplay and movement is pretty solid with minor kinks that cause major annoyances. Specifically the dash mechanic allows for quick gameplay but suffers in the fact that enemies often soak up bullets when you try to clear a line of them. This is solved with the bullet buff but you don't get it often enough to be able to avoid the issue. There is also a huge hassle in changing weapons but it's probably solved pretty easily with a pad as opposed to controller. Funnily enough when you get Brandish's weapon the gameplay turns into Megaman Zero which was more enjoyable in my opinion.
The problem with the game lies in the stage design and bosses. Most of the bosses are designed pretty well despite some being easier than other. Three bosses however stand out with some significant problems. On the final boss the game actually bugged out on me three times and I was unable to do anything and had to restart the stage. Stage design is abysmal for the majority of the stages as spike placement is often in terrible places. Spikes often pop up in places you cannot see and as a result cause some cheap deaths.
I ended up doing a buster only run and enjoyed most of the boss fights. As a Megaman fan I'm satisfied with this product but I feel like much more could have been done. The environments and explosion effects look like♥♥♥♥♥♥and cheap death mechanics are often in super annoying places. The weapon buffs often cause issues as well as you can only have 3 bullets on the screen.
The game is decent but it was obvious that Inafune was not the one responsible for the success of Megaman.

This game is not for everyone. There is a great amount of exploration between the bosses for the runes you must collect, which can really bore some people, and the attacks in this game are much slower to what one might find in games like Hyper Light Drifter or Hotline Miami. So if you would want to quit a game because there was too much exploration and puzzle solving between each boss or you don't like games that take combat in a slower way than normal, I'd give this game a pass and look elsewhere.
However, with all that being said, I had a great time playing Jotun. The levels in between bosses, while can be tedious at times, still manages to keep you entertained enough by the enviornment around you and some puzzles here and there. The art within the game helps build an interesting world which is enough to keep you going even if you start to get tired of the tasks within each level. The speed of your attacks take some getting used to for sure, but after a while, they are not noticed too much and become of little concern. But where this game really shines is with the boss fights. Every boss fight in this game is amazing. Each one provides a nice amount of challenge which gets you engaged within the fight. They are also very interesting with attacks that differ from each one, making each boss more memerable and interesting. And the soundtrack that is composed by Max LL makes the fights unbelievably epic.
While this game isn't for all types of people out there, those who enjoy a fair amount of exploration and are able to accept the slower paced combat Jotun has to offer will not be dissapointed.

The Charnel House Trilogy is a point and click pixelated adventure game that caught my attention because of how it looked, the design and quality is similar to what’s been coming out in the past couple of years, but is the visuals the only thing it has to offer? Far from it.
The story of the game is your journey to Augur Peak, going there in the middle of the night ridding in a train that would change, explain, confuse and reveal everything to the main character that you play as, Alex, a young charming woman with a troubling life.
Along your fateful journey you meet all sorts of interesting characters from who knows when or where, and each of those characters have their own story to tell but all of them come back connecting to the main character, and to the destination Augur Peak.
The gameplay is like any other point and click of recent years, click on anything that is of interest, one that you can interact with, and the character you play as would then give her / his thoughts on the interacted object or person. Collect items whenever you think you can or need so that it can be used to solve a problem / issue later on, which aren’t that difficult and mainly goes with the flow of the game.
The game is rightfully creepy, the story is mysterious and grabs your interest and attention in the first five minutes of playing it. The story progresses as I’m in a fateful train, keeping me intrigued as more characters appear and nicely written dialogue backing it up. After entering the train I found myself playing as a different character, one with a.. somewhat confusing but still understandable and nice end.
As I walk through the hallway of the shadow of death in the train Playing as the first main character again, exploring and progressing through the game in the train and meeting yet new and old unexpected characters, revealing twists and turns throughout the end of the game. Speaking of the ending, it’s a great one as it left me hanging and excited to see and play the sequel, and it did it in a common sense and satisfying way.
The Charnel House Trilogy is a fine piece of point and click adventure game, one that looks great, plays good, and sounds wonderful, a game that I’d rank up high along side games like Blackwell Epiphany, but what I really loved about the game, aside from the soundtrack, is how dark and twisted it is, and how it has the balls to be dark and give dialogue that we barely see in other games, if there is any with such dialogue. It is a short game but a damn interesting and entertaining one, and gave me an experience that I I’ll never forget any time soon. After playing this game, I can’t wait to see what comes up next in 2016.

Due disclosure: I am on friendly terms with Ashton Raze, developer at Owlcave. There is no conflict of interests making this disclosure necessary, but please bear this in mind when judging the balance of objectivity to subjectivity in my assessment of this product. It is because of this and the inherent flaws in a numerical rating system that I give no score.
The Charnel House Trilogy may not be a game in the conventional sense, lacking a challenge to overcome, but the alternative genre and take on point and click do not at all detract from the interactive narrative. And this is what sets it apart from so many of its would be peers on the digital shelves. Owlcave didn't make this choice vainly, in a gratuitous or vacuous manner; the genre and narrative serve each other well.
Mechanically, the game is competentently executed but not without flaws. The voice work seems recited rather than acted at times, a flaw that Exhale seems to soundly move away from. Variable resolutions would be appreciated, but my main complaint lies in that there is no option to mute sound on focus loss — resulting in rare sound artifacts and looping glitches while tabbed out if you happen to alt+tab at an inoportune time. This appears to be purely an inescapable glitch with the engine rather than an overight.
Narratively, I'm quite frankly astonished. Whether it be the genre's saturation or my own expectations, I expected quality but not quite this much.
The trilogy was originally Sepulchre, an installation in which doctor Lang, an archaeologist on his way to conduct research on Augur Peak and experiences a series of increasingly surreal events of a symbolism he is clueless about. Inhale and Exhale later completed the trilogy, more fleshed out installations that give the original context and bring it into the build up to what is setting out to be an intriguing canon by adding a fresh perspective to an uncanny journey. A journey where time, memory and identity are warped beyond the boundaries of sanity; a burden each protagonist deals with differently.
Alex Davenport, protagonist of Inhale and Exhale, is a well rounded character that significantly strays from horror and alternative storytelling conventions by retaining a degree of roots to the mundane but not deluding herself into denying that she is departed from it. What sets her apart in this regard is that Exhale features a very well written transition from being suitably shocked by to actively partaking in the disturbing ride that something more twisted than fate conspired to involve her in.
Neither losing itself in the esoteric for the sake of padding its dialogue nor playing it safe, The Charnel House Trilogy is a short but oh so sweet breath of fresh air for the genre.

This game is a decade old and it shows. I constantly felt frustrated while playing this game. Issues range from archaic camera management to sluggish controls, all of which combine to make a game that could have been great but instead turns out to be really annoying.
My biggest three complaints:
- Camera seems to constantly position itself in a way that is not helpful, or it prohibits you from actually looking where you need to look (like upward).
- Your character becomes immobile when hit with an enemy attack, forcing you to take hit after hit until the enemy stops attacking. Multiple enemies attacking simultaneously can kill you while you're force to stand by and watch. Some enemies can knock you down, then attack as soon as you get back up, knocking you down again... and repeat until you die.
- Sometimes you can input a control command and it simply won't happen. I had this occur several times, particularly with double jumps. There seems to be a forced delay between inputs, but it effectively just makes the controls feel sluggish or feel like they don't work at all.
If these three issues were fixed, I still probably wouldn't like this game. Force Unleashed is pretty much exclusively a combat game, and I really didn't like the combat. The combat is of the memorize-a-ton-of-combos genre, which I have never really enjoyed. The fancy combo attacks seem too tedious to use and difficult to remember the proper timing, especially with the control issues, but the basic attacks all have lag between attacks, leaving you vulnerable. I found myself in a type of Catch 22 situation, but it turned out I could win nearly every combat with just two special attacks memorized and completely ignore the rest of the attack options. The whole system feels clumsy and poorly implemented. Boss battles and larger enemies also threw in QTEs, which never serve to improve the situation.
I also don't like that you can run out of force powers, or be punished for using them too quickly. That ultimately just makes the combat even less fluid as it instills mandatory breaks into your flow of attacks while you run away and wait for force to replenish.
About halfway through the game I realized that nearly all the combat was optional and I could literally just run past the enemies to the next area. This certainly made the game faster, but also made me realize just how much this game relies on the combat to provide any meaningful game experience. Yet the combat isn't any good, so there really isn't anything meaningful here to find...

Transistor is an exciting new style of game that brings joy to us turn based RPG fans. Transistor has many RPG aspects as well as a minor hack and slash game. The main pros about this game have to be the battle system. The battle system is a real time as well as a freeze time strategy system. You battle using a skill that allows you to freeze time so that you can use your other abilities that you have equipped to do damage and stratgize how do maximize your damage within the frozen time lapse. When the battle is not frozen, you are usually running around planning your next move on the enemy while its their turn to attack you. This game is really challenging and can be a turn off for anyone who doesn't like turn based games. The story is more of a romance/revenge story that for the most part was a little bland for me. The artwork is really amazing and the environments look like nothing I've ever seen which make this game beautiful to look at. The sound effects are really nice during the battles along with the soothing environmental music while outside of battle. I will say that the villians in this game are forgettable. I would reccomend this game for anyone who likes turn based battle systems with a twist (like Final Fantasy, XCOM, etc.) but if you're someone who doesn't like those kind of games, I don't think this game will be for you.

I normally don't have the patience for turn-based combat. Transistor lets you take your time with it's mechanics or disregard the turn-based style combat system in favour of a more action based one. Aesthetics and music are great as per tradition of a Supergiant game. Story wraps up very nicely and there's a New Game+ mode to keep you playing. For a short game, it will definitely be stuck in my head for awhile.

Mighty No. 9 is a grind. It's not the worst 2-d platformer, in fact just playing the game can feel really good. The dash and the combo system in this game make for some really great moments but these moments are ruined in an instant by terrible level design and an awful narrative. The level design relies heavily upon mechanical execution and rote memorization of the maps to proceed and often punishes the slightest misstep with instant death. While this design isn't inherently bad, other games such as Super Meatboy will present a gradual increase in difficulty throughout the game. This feels more like a flat line punctuated with spikes in difficulty and that means that you're more likely to slam your head into these challenges and grind them rather than flow into them and refine these actions upon replaying.
The second issue with this game is the narrative. Usually I can play through a 2-d platformer and simply ignore the narrative if I want, however Mighty No. 9 decided to go with a more theatrical approach and failed. Miserably. The plot and voice acting is so ham handed it would put Charlie Chaplin to shame. Seriously, the plot hits every single entry on
. The final shot screams sequel at you and at the end of all this you really just feel like slapping Dr. White and asking him why he even exists as a character at all.

If you were looking for a Megaman style game where the enemies are all nearly invincable except for a newly invented dashing melee attack, this is the game for you. This game is a major dissapointment.

I love Mighty No. 9. I think people will agree that it's not Mega Man but I'm glad to see games like this coming out. Good music, plenty of action and well worth the 20 dollar price tag. If you enjoy Mega Man or Gunvolt, I think you should pick this  up. It will only set you pack 2 packs of smokes. I'm giving this 7/10.

I backed this project at $40, but seeing what it is now, I would not have even given them $0.40.
The project brought in over 4 million USD, and everything after that has been a complete disgrace. The community manager was apparently terrible (I was never on the forums, though), the game was delayed multiple times, the game was delayed for multiplayer features I could not care less about, backers (like me) got our keys late (if at all), one of the DLC's for the backers didn't even have a proper key for a while, Comcept was silent during time when they said the game was going to be released and then was delayed, and that Deep Silver trailer is its own atrocity.
On to the game itself. The player character, NPC's, enemies, and bosses look like cheap plastic figures. Character's mouths do not move when talking. The voice acting is a special kind of terrible I would hear in a free Flash game, not some indie game, and I've yet to find a way to mute said voice acting. Cheap deaths are everywhere. Instant death spikes, instant death pits, instant death bullets, instant death electrified wires, junk that freezes the player character in place for several seconds, etc. Instant death traps were bulls**t in the 90's and they are still bulls**t now. The dash mechanic could have been decent, but it has been hampered by stupid decisions. Shoot a robot a few times, they flash, then you dash forward to absorb them, but does this give you health back? NOPE. Shoot the 1st robot into an absorbable state, and do your bullets go through them and into the next bot in line? NOPE, unless you have a limited time powerup. Even with that insta death crap, the levels are far too short compared to several of the Megaman games. There is also a lot of foreground junk in the way to obscure your screen, in addition to subtitled text of the awful voice acting. The weapons you can get from bosses have too little ammo to be of much use, and the explosions look like cheap frozen pizza. I almost wish I got a physical copy, just so I could smash it with a sledgehammer in a fit of rage, or toss it into a woodchipper.
There is only 1 very short level for Call, and it is just terrible. Call cannot absorb enemies, cannot recharge her own energy bar over time, she can only fire one shot at a time, and her voice acting is so annoying. While the additional enemies in her stage would be a welcome change, several of them can't be directly killed by her. Finally, the boss section is a mess. You have a rather small target to shoot (it's eye) with a weak gun, and once that target is destroyed, you have to wait for boxes to drop to either feed the boss an explosive, or an enemy that restores the boss's sight. Shooting the boss anywhere but its eye is pointless.
I have yet to beat the game, and yet, the game has already succeeded in ticking me off.

To preface this review, I'm a Kickstarter backer at the all-digital tier and perhaps one of the more thorough beta testers since I got over half the game's achievements in the pre-release demo.
The game is a Mega Man esque game. Your character by default jumps and shoots up to three lemon pellets on screen at a time, meaning there are benefits to standing in an enemy's face rattling off shots faster. There are eight bosses which grant diverse powers in place of these shots, and these bring navigational and combat benefits as well as effectiveness against one of the other bosses in a cycle of exploitable weakness.
The regular levels generally introduce mechanics one at a time, and then combine them to increase the challenge. Towards the end of each level is a challenging segment often containing various sources of instant death. After beating all of these levels there are a couple of ending levels that require the use and combination of your newfound powers in a slightly longer gauntlet of challenges before the final boss which will kill you a few times before you figure it out.
So the whole basic Mega Man formula is still there. The main divergence from this is the use of a dash mechanic which a few people come to like and a lot of people expect they will always hate. The complaint is that it's too much of a departure from the idea of sitting back and shooting all enemies to death, and that physically ramming enemies when physical contact otherwise causes you damage is too contradictory for gameplay.
Personally, I can understand these complaints, especially as the game sometimes forces you to dash through tunnels of instant death spikes twice in succession with tunnels that I feel are a little too thin. The complaint I can't understand is about how this dash allows you to travel in the air infinitely. For one thing, it doesn't as Beck always falls between dashes. For another, the levels are always structured to prevent a long air time being of much use.
The level design itself is the next complaint, and that has more merit to it. A lot of the level layouts do seem fairly bland with uninspired corridor sections. Probably this was handicapped by not wanting to allow the dash to become too powerful. There are a few secret areas reminiscent of Mega Man 1, but complaints about the lack of exploration or the linearity of levels are somewhat justified.
Following on from that, the visuals are often said to be bland. This I separate into two elements. Firstly there are complaints about the detail or depth of backgrounds and I find this a disagreeable point. Take a look at the highway and construction tower screenshots in the store page. I believe that if those were considerably more detailed, it would become a distraction and make the gameplay harder. When concentrating on the foreground during play, the detail is fine.
However the detail of character models and other foreground objects could definitely be improved on, and the obvious criticism here is the model Beck himself. Rather than being complicated, too much of his detail such as the chest rivets are just painted onto a flat surface which brings no gameplay benefit and just looks bad. I suspect this was done to keep parity between all the different versions of the game but I feel they really should have made better versions for the better consoles and PC.
But the Mega Man model of game has always been about gameplay, so while I do feel the lack of detail is a shame, I also think it's nitpicking and easier to think about when the game isn't running. When it is running, I'm too busy thinking about how to beat the levels or how to improve on levels already beat, and despite the linearity there's a lot to the game. Beck has a diverse range of useful controls and combinations, and the powers he acquires prove to be unexpectedly useful more than I was expecting.
I find myself dying a lot until I learn how to beat various portions of the levels, or at least until I can work out the timing of various actions in the instant-death sections, and it feels great to discover an effective new way to use an acquired power to make something tough easier. That is the heart of what Mega Man gameplay has always been about and it can be found here.

This game caught my attention a while ago, mostly because of the lore, but also because of its unique artstyle.
Having finished the main content, now, I'm not too impressed, but it's not all faults!
The game is essentially a boss-rush type of experience. Except the rush part. Instead, you're forced through different levels between boss fights, to collect "runes".
You have a central hub with 5 different Jotun to defeat. The first one is fixed, as the introduction to the game. The other 4 you're free to tackle in any order you please. To open the Jotun's gate, you need to collect 2 runes. Each Boss has 2 distinct areas (levels), each with one rune for you to collect. There is also one HP upgrade and one skill in each area.
Each level will have a different "mechanic". However, they're very simple, so calling them "mechanics" is pushing it a bit.
For example, in one level you'll have to hit certain marked trees to create bridges. In another you'll have to taunt enemies into throwing rocks at you, which you can then hit into the lava to... create bridges, once again. Now that I'm writing this I realize that there are lots of bridges in the game. They're not very important though, except as gates. Anyway...
The game does an okay job of teaching you how each level works by starting you off with simple examples.
Unfortunately, the levels aren't very interesting. It's just about walking until you find the rune, without much else going on in those. The reason for this is that your character doesn't do much.
You can walk around, do a light attack, and a heavy attack. Also, roll! That's important. Now imagine that every action had an additional "heavy" modifier. That's how it works. Everything is very slow (intentionally so, I assume). While that isn't a negative, necessarilly, it does make the levels feel like a drag. Especially the running speed, since each area is fairly big and also fairly empty, you'll get tired to just walking around very quickly.
I'll talk about combat later.
The character also has skills. These include healing, a speed boost, spear throw, etc. You can only use each twice, unless you find a checkpoint to replenish your health and skill points. These abilities are completely fine in the context of the boss fights. In the levels, however, they're mostly useless. And I have to say the speed boost would have been very welcome (to battle tedium)! Unfortunately, since you have maybe 5-10 seconds of a slight boost,
, it's rather useless. Healing was the only usefull skill in the levels, honestly.
Ok, here's a cool idea, but that ended up being very superficial and not very good in the end. You have a map for the levels. A "real" map. Not a GPS, but a semi-fixed thing. You don't know exactly where you are, but you can deduce it (you know where you start) by the paths you've taken or some landmarks.
This is cool! Not many games require you to read a map. Unfortunately, it's rather awkward, in this game. There aren't real landmarks, except the checkpoints, or the rune/skill locations that you can see on the map before you find them. The rest is an exercise in linking (bridging hehe) the bridges you see on the level with the ones of the map.
The map isn't very useful, and not very acurate either. There are levels for which it is almost impossible to read the map, since the drawing doesn't really match the level.
Heh. A bit of a missed opportunity, but hey...
Now, let me talk about the artstyle. Again, the problem I have is in the levels. The perspective seems very off, to me. The art is also very flat coloured, which makes it difficult to figure out what ground is higher than another.
The levels aren't built of game objects, as I've come to expect. Instead, they're like a drawing. Then, they add collisions with invisible objects that match the drawing. Well, in principle.
I suppose this would be fine, except that it didn't seem very well made, to me. The hitboxes aren't very precise, and combined with the flatness and the perspective, things don't really connect very well.
The screenshots aren't very revealing, but look at the game in action to see what I mean.
Ok, so far, this is a bit too negative. It has also been all about the levels.
And I think that's fair, since the levels seem to be mostly filler. Having the game consist of 6 boss fights probably seemed insufficient, so they added a bunch of level to stretch that game's length. That's mostly how it felt, to me.
Again, they tried to keep things fresh with different mechanics per area, but then lost the opportunity to build upon anything, and the levels ended up very superficial and uninteresting.
The artstyle, aside for the weird perspective and somewhat disfunctional aspects, is beautiful. Especially when they setup the scenes in parts of the levels, zooming it out quite a lot and showing a much vaster background than you could see before. That's cool. Not original, but they still look very cool! There are some scenes of this type throughout the levels, where you encounter some important animals to the mythology and whatnot.
So there are pretty things to look at!
The music is also fairly good. Well, fitting. It wasn't very memorable or anything, but it was good as a background thing.
Nothing surprising, really, but I can't fault them too much for it.
Ok, the main part of the game, now. The Jotun fights. This is very clearly the developer's idea for the game all along. The limited skill use, the slow attacks, etc. It was all to fight against the giants, not to run around fetching a rune for 20 minutes.
How is it? Pretty good! Not as striking, perhaps, since the fights are shorter than the levels... It's unfortunate, since the impression I'm left it is mostly about the levels than the bosses.
Each Boss is very different from one another, but all follow a multi-phased structure. They start off fairly forgiving, for you to learn their attacks, and then they start becoming meaner.
I've seen people complain about impossible to dodge damage, but that's not true. You'll have to do some clutch dodges, most of the time, but you can avoid stuff!
Some bosses were abit too easy, but others compensated for it by requiring very timely skill use to defeat them!
The gameplay mostly revolves around... rolling. The heavy attack is a bit too slow to be reliable (although the bosses have appropriate pauses to let you use it), so you'll mostly be trying to do some damage to the boss between attack, and then rolling out of their huge attacks.
Positioning and timing are everything, and this part of the game is cool, once you get the patterns down! Choosing when to use the abilities is also crucial.
The game also has a "Valhalla Mode", which you unlock after beating the game. I guess it's a pure boss fight mode, in which they get stronger.
Maybe I'll give it a shot later, but I didn't really feel like trying it right after beating the game.
Ok, to finish this rambling thing, the best (?) part of the game: the lore and voice-acting. The game has 2 stories, more or less. One, is about your character and why you're doing what you're doing. It's okay, fitting, but not very inspiring. Two, much cooler, is about norse mythology. As you go through the levels, you'll see some creatures, followed by a short narration of what they are and their role in the mythology.
One level in specific was far heavier in exposition, and it was much cooler than the rest. You won't learn a lot about the mythology through casually playing this game (since the levels are a bit too disjointed and these bits are quite spread apart), but it seems to convey the general ideas about the creation of the world pretty well!
Finally, the voice-acting is awesome and I didn't understand a word of it. Well, maybe a couple. I'm not sure if it is Icelandic or Swedish or what, but it sounds really good, and makes the whole thing far more convincing than most game where you hear accented english.

I AM CRUSHED by my feelings upon completing The Force Unleashed. I had played some on the Xbox years ago, in college, and really liked it. For one reason or another, I never finished it, but the fondness of the experience, the first three levels or so, stuck with me. Returning to it for my podcast project, I was completely blindsided by how utterly terrible this PC port it.
I'll keep it short. The controls are horrendous. Whatever joker tried to convert the QTE events from the traditional controller to the keyboard missed the really obvious translation of ABXY on the controller to the WASD on the keyboard, and instead force you to use q, e, space, and left click. And no they're not spacially arranged in a way that makes sense. Moreoever, there are many combos that require you to move your hand back and forth on the board, but because you're pinned to WASD for movement, the more visually interesting and powerful combos languish for lack of motivation to bother breaking my own hand to make them work. Or using my genitals as an extra finger.
Mechanically, on the whole, the game is exciting, except that it is riddled with bugs. When Starkiller isn't falling through the world, enemies aren't falling out of range, or progression isn't triggering because the AI is asleep at the wheel, it can be a really compelling experience, wrapped in an excellent, really engaging Star Wars story. Until you get to the boss battles, which are horrendous, from the first to the last. I have rarely been aggirvated to the point of shouting at my computer by a videogame. I spent a LOT of time shouting incoherent profanity at the screen during the ridiculous boss battles, which layer a terrible "action cam" the player suddenly has no control over on top of the bugs and bad controls. All around terrible, nearly amateur design.
To short circuit "but then why'd you play it for X hour" concerns: I played it for a podcast project, and because I agreed to. If I had not given my word to get it done, I would have quit by the end of the second level. This game is INCREDIBLY disappointing. Stay away, and if you want the story, watch a Let's Play, or readon the novelization. (I actually think that may be worth it.)

"A JRPG, you say?"
Well, yeah, sure, but not in the traditional sense of the term. This is a strange one indeed, but (mostly) in a good way.
This game has a very strong japanese mythology theme. You play a swordswoman, whose main goal is to fight Tsukumogami, strange creatures which take shapes of common everyday items, such as a jacket, a broom and so on.
When you get to fight a Tsukumogami, instead of one of the traditional RPG battle systems, you need to zap the enemy with your special Gokon Sword in order to get clues about its identity and expose it. Once you exposed its identity (i.e. what item it really is), you need to hack it a few more times to finish it.
The thing is - all the clues are literal, in english and based on the japanese lore. For example, if you're fighting a broom Tsukumogami, the clues you get could be either letters from the item's name in uppercase (B or OO, for example), or details about the item itself, what it's being used for, what it's made of and so on ("wood", "cleaning" for example). Once you think you know the name, you "call it out" either by typing it on a virtual in-game keyboard, or by choosing it from a list you can get (and later upgrade for a price) as a part of the story.
If you're wrong, the enemy gets a bonus attack and you lose HP. If you got it right, the shroud is lifted and you get to see the enemy for what it really is. A few more hacks and slashes, and it's usually gone.
I've only been playing the game for 3-4 hours so far, so there might be more complicated stuff I haven't reached yet, but this is what it looks like, so far, and while it gets a little repetitive, it is fun.

99 Spirits is a Japanese indie game localized into English. The gameplay itself contains mostly turn-based fighting, JRPG style but with just one character, and with blocks and counters requiring quick reflexes.
The battle system is the main novelty here: the character must first find out clues of the enemy's name, then guess its name (an English noun, such as "beads", "hatchet" or "hat"), and only then can the player deal damage to the opponent. As the game progresses, the combat gains more complexity with the enemies guarding against attacks and the player capturing the monsters to do her (Hanabusa's) bidding.
There's not much progression in the way of gear - the only gear the player can change are the Tsukumogami (the monsters). By identifying more different Tsukumogami, the player can boost some abilities that will make the battles less of a chore later down the line.
The translation itself is mostly competent. Especially the monster names - that the player has to guess properly - use English words known to most, with the only exception being "Torii". The puzzles are simple and usually require only a specific type of Tsukumogami to accompany the player to a marked spot. Again, there's only one problem and it is knowing that the "wand" Tsukumogami is used to purge evil spirits. Then again, these aren't a problem due to the translation itself.
Visually, the game is bare-bones. It's functional, but in the battles the enemies are not animated at all and in the "walking" mode Hanabusa and the Tsukumogami just "teleport" from one tile to another. There's nothing wrong with the character portraits displayed as they do a lot of their talking in the game.
As for the plot - there's a lot of dialogue, some tropes, and some branching points between which the game progresses with nary a sidequest. A sandbox game of any description this is not, and there's about only one sidequest in the whole game.
The battles have some voice acting, with separate tracks in English and Japanese. The dialogue itself is not voice acted at all. The music is a curious blend of modern and old - you might want to check it out (and not only the game's theme song).
Bottom line: 99 Spirits is a bit different game. The visuals are a bit underwhelming and eventually, the game gets a bit monotonous in spite of how the new features are added for several chapters from the start of the game.
Give the demo a go and see if you like the concept and how it was handled.

Emily is Away is a short game, where you (re)live the good old time of the instant messaging with icons, with horrible sounds. You play Emily's best friend and for 5 or 6 years, you're going to see this relationship evolve depending on your choices during the discussions. You begin at the end of high school until finishing college.
If there is something that you should know is that there is no happy ending. Well, I mean, you can be as nice as you, as much as responsible, trying to please Emily and the result will be always the same: she'll call on you. At the end, you can see that life changed you both.
You can clearly see that your character was crushing on Emily, however, you don't know if she's feeling the same. You don't have any control on outside events, like Travis's party or what happened between you and her during the week-end after she broke up with her boyfriend.
However, it's frustrating to try different routes. Each end of the discussion is Emily is away. You tell her that you can miss a group project reunion, a party with your friends, etc.. so that you can listen to her and she's rejecting this offer for example.
The fact is that Emily is Away is just a game made for nostalgic people. You just press enter to see the text you're writing (even correcting faults) and you choose your answer just before among three proposed. Some of them will not change the course of the discussion, others are important.
The only real fun thing to do is to try many usernames, to unlock new icons. I would even say that some may be not belonging to this era at all (Portal, Undertale and others). Another funny thing is to look at everyone's profile and remember when you were putting quotes or lyrics everywhere.
But it's not because it may become boring after a while that Emily is Away isn't worth a shot. It's reflecting life as it can happen, missed opportunities and relationships. It's always interesting to see that and besides, like I've said, it's also for nostalgic people, though I'm not feeling a nostalgia wave.
The graphics aren't bad at all. It's really well-chosen for what the game will want to do. As for the soundtrack, apart the infamous Windows sound and the ping, you don't have anything.
My only problem is that the cursor isn't pointing on where you want, I needed to click on the left of a button to manage to play - it has caused me a problem the first time I've played it as I thought it was stuck. I suppose it's a problem due to the a wider monitor than the game can handle.
Emily is Away is a good little game in the end and as it's free, your wallet will not cry for money.

Bought this game cheaper than dirt and it still wasn't worth it. Absolutely awful. The in-game performance is fine, even on max settings (and it does look fairly nice), but for some reason there's MASSIVE slowdown on the menus - any menu I tried to access was nearly unusable as the game rendered one frame every few seconds.
The controls are awful. I haven't tried it with a controller, but with a keyboard, WASD was a horrible choice. The maps are placed diagonally, yet you move on standard XY axes. The maps aren't even at a 45 degree angle, so you'll have to juggle between one direction and another to travel down, say, a long canal. Also, most "rooms" are small boxes, so you'll have to awkwardly switch from one misaligned direction to another. The developer should have added an option for this control scheme: W - Forward, S - Backward, A & D - Turn left and right, respectively. If I remember right, that's what Battleship: Surface Thunder did, and that game is a hundred times better than this terrible clone.
The game, for the short time I played it, seemed like it had the potential to be fun, but trying to actually play it was such a terrible chore, I decided it really wasn't worth the time to get used to the bad controls or the small amount of space it took up out of 2.5 TB available on my computer. Waste of even 79 cents. If I could go back and stop myself from buying it, I might decide to buy it later on anyway if it went on sale for, say, a penny. Sitting uninstalled in my library, it isn't worth anything anyway, except as a warning to others.

As you can tell from my avatar, I'm a big Megaman fan. This game isn't perfeect by any means, but overall, I feel that it has been reviewed a little harshly.
Pros:
1. Good boss and weapon design
2. The dash mechanic leads to fluid movement and allows for level design that requires taking advantage of it
3. Fast paced movement compared to MM without feeling too "hack and slashy"
4. The levels are challenging to get through, but never feal unfair (so far)
5. Challenge mode! Something that MM needed for a while and got a little of in MM9/10, so this is always welcome.
Cons:
1. Cut scenes are too lengthy (but skippable)
2. Voice acting (English) is not particularly good
3. Some enemies are very annoying to deal with (guys that float just out of reach dropping endless bombs on highway stage come to mind).
Nuetral:
1. Graphics aren't amazing, but not amazingly bad either, their just "ok"
2. Once you have defeated one boss, there is a means to KNOW which stage to use that weapon on next in game. I kinda liked the trial and error of MM.
Overall:
I think the trouble with this game is the hype that's been building for so long. Frankly, I'm not sure anything would have met expectations by the time it came out. I think it's worth noting that none of the cons that I experienced were gameplay related, and to me, gameplay is the biggest part of any game.
Is it the mind blowing successor to MM that takes things to a whole 'nother level? No. But if you like tough platforming and the classic MM idea of stealing weapons to take advantage of boss weasknesses, then you'll probably enjoy this game.
