Note: My recommendation comes with an asterisk, since I cannot give something a Maybe recommendation.
So, I've read a few other reviews, and one thing that some people say is that you will enjoy every minute of this game. While that was true for me, you need to understand that there are very few minutes to enjoy.
Let's start with the good stuff. First, this game looks great. The art style is probably my favorite part of the game. Second, the music is quite pleasent, while not particularly memorable. The boss fights are really fun, and I would say are the highlight of the gameplay. Just don't expect them to require much strategy. The variation of environments and incorportation of norse mythology are both well done, too. There are lots of instances where you will stop to take in the views and Thora will give some nice exposition about what you are looking at.
And now the bad stuff. Probably my least favorite thing about this game is it's short length. I beat the game and got all of the collectables and powers in six hours, which isn't a lot of time when comparing this to similar games. Second, Thora is slow. Not a big deal, but yeah, she's no sprinter. The combat also doesn't have much variety. You have a a vertical slash, a horizontal slash, and a charged slash. And that's it. The combat isn't really the focus, and it works when it needs to, but it does leave something to be desired. And finally, while you you get tons of nice views of landscapes and battlefields, you cannot explore many of them, which is kind of sad considering how beautiful they are.
So would I recommend this game? Well, I would recommend something like Hyper Light Drifter over this in a heartbeat, but if that's too hard for you, then yeah, give this one a shot. If you want a relaxing and beautiful experience that will last you a few hours, then yes. If you want a glimpse into norse mythology, then yes. If this game is on sale, then yes. Otherwise, I think you'd be better off looking elsewhere. Which is a shame considering how amazing the art is.

Yellow: The Yellow Artifact is an absolutely horrible platformer. I only have negative things to say about it.
This is a basic need for any good platformer, and this game leaves it out.
It took me a whole 10 minutes to complete this game. That was with collecting all the coins and dying several times. The extra time spent in-game was me idling for the trading cards from this game.
For some reason, the game loads all of the levels when you click play (which is why it takes so long). If it loaded each level individually, when you got to them, then there wouldn't even be any loading screens needed.
The levels are as big as the screen; they don't scroll. Enemies are placed in odd spots, which are sometimes unreachable or awkwardly positioned. Some levels are reused and the coins and enemies are the only things that are rearranged.
The only option the game has is to toggle fullscreen mode, which is on the main menu. However, you can't change the volume of the music or sound effects.
I'm not sure how many tracks there are, but in my 10 minute of playtime, I only heard two. One of them was just looping and sounded horrible. The other one, although not looping, sounded horrible as well.
The sound effects are 8-bit style and don't sound. There is a way to make good sounding 8-bit effects, but this game doesn't do that. Also, some things don't have sound effects while others do (ex. no effect for taking damage or completing a level).
Although I like when games implement Steam achievements, I don't necessarily mind when they don't. However, the description of this game on Steam says that it includes achievements, when it actually doesn't.
There is a button with 3 horizontal slashes in the top right of the game screen. Buttons like that are common in mobile games and usually take you to a pause menu. Instead, the button in this game takes you to the main menu. If you click play again, you have to restart the game.
An example of this is when your character runs into a door. He will run a little in the door and then teleport back out.
When you press the jump button, your character stops moving for a short period of time. It makes jumping feel awkward and can cause you to miscalculate some jumps.
Most of Kenney's CC0 graphics are good for placeholders, but have no place in a published title.
You get 3 hearts per level. If you lose a heart, you become invincible for a short time. If you lose all of your hearts, you restart the level. You can just run through the entire level and win because of the invincibility.

I've logged quite a lot hours into FS17 so its about time I done a review. I've owned every version since FS2011 (This is the first I got via Steam). Its truly great game from Giants Software and with many improvements over FS15. New features that improve the gameplay include the a option to lease machinery as well as buy, the ability to pick small objects by hand which is great picking up those fiddly small bits of trees when logging. There's also new crops in sunflowers and soybeans as well as a new animal type, pigs which seem to breed like rabbits. In one of the vanilla maps theres even drivable trains to transport large amount of crops and logs around.
The missions are now more meaningful and related to farming. Instead of before where you just transported pallets around the map, you now do work on fields that are not owned by you. This has the added benefit of having crops growing in all fields rather than having them empty until you buy them which gives the map a more dynamic feel.
The game with its two maps is great fun to play as it is out of the box but you would be missing out on one of the best aspects of this game; the mods. There is a continuously growing number of mods that are available, most of which are very simple to install. Theres the mods that add extra maps and machinery which improve the variety and choice in the game. Then there's the gameplay mods such as GPS mod, courseplay, and 'follow me' mod that help make tasks that little bit easier. Then there's ones like the seasons mod than make  the game more realistic. Best of all these mods don't cost a cent unlike a certain train game where you have to get the credit card out when you want more content.
There are many other Farming games appearing but FS17 is still the best so far. Nice graphics and runs flawlessly for me with no issues. Definitely worth a buy.

The current game development model is releaseing a very early vision of a game the developer wishes to make.  By giving early access, the developers can use the feedback from players throughout development to shape the game into something much greater.
Keen Software House delivers.  Based on their work with Space Engineers, the weekly patches are more than just bug fixes, but they truely bring new content.
Medieval Engineers is a great idea with lots of potential.  I look forward to the coming months and hopefully years of fun that this game has to offer.

Keen Software House has come crashing down to Earth, it seems. Hot off the heels of their success with Space Engineers, the studio has taken a decidedly different approach to its next game. Yes, they’ve swapped the dark, lonely nothingness of outer space for the green and pleasant fields on Terra Firma. And whilst the core gameplay of Medieval Engineers is, in essence, no different from Space Engineers – build stuff, destroy stuff – it goes that extra mile to engross you in its twee setting. Medieval Engineers, like Space Engineers before it, launched as an Early Access title with a solid amount of content, and whilst its current incarnation only lets you build stuff just to knock it down, it gives an exciting glimpse at the possible shape the game might take in the future.
Before you can indulge in senseless destruction you’ve got to build something first and, even at this early stage, the creation tools on offer are surprisingly slick. You can choose from a different number of fields to start out in, be it a rocky hill terrain, or a plain with a castle town already in it. Building your own castles using the various building blocks available to you is a cinch, and the auto-snap grid means that you will line everything up correctly – almost every time! I say “almost” because, at present it can be a real pain the undersatchel to line up floor panels. That’s before I have even touched on the terraforming tools.
So, you’ve started building that ridiculously oversized mountain fortress and want to even out the ground a little, well it isn’t  going to be that easy. Terraforming, in theory, should be easy: you pick your brush shape, give it a width, height and depth, and can set about adding or subtracting ground blocks to the scene. There’s a bit of an art to it though, meaning you need a steady hand to keep things smooth – otherwise you end up with ground that has the texture of artex. Indeed, my inability to use the tool effectively saw me creating underground caverns that had an eerily beautiful quality to them, but I couldn’t get out! Hopefully, future releases will see these tools tweaked a bit for people like myself (idiots, basically).
You needn’t build alone, either! Get a buddy or two in on the action and you’ll be up and running with a serviceable castle in no time; the system really is just that astonishingly easy to use. Think of it like minecraft where each block looks different and has different properties – except they aren’t cubes, of course. There are all sorts of different blocks at your disposal, from round-edged  walls for turrets, battlement attachments, and windmill blades for the show-offs.
Humans will be human and it’s in our nature to tear down and destroy, and Medieval Engineers has you well covered in that department. Technical dunces like myself can equip small and large cannonballs to their hotbar and let rip a volley of shots on their structures, watching them crumble to the ground in a cloud of smoke and dust. There’s a perverse pleasure to be had in seeing your time-consuming efforts reduced to nought but rubble within a few minutes,  a feeling which is amplified by the warming celtic soundtrack that plays throughout. It’s a highly incongruous matchup, but also very enjoyable. You can further amplify the destruction by kicking your map’s maximum fracture pieces all the way to the top – your PC won’t thank you for it, but it sure as hell looks amazing! If you have the technical cojones to create catapults, trebuchets and other machines of war you can also set your mind free to think up the most dastardly creations it can. When you are done you can upload them to the Steam Workshop for others to enjoy – a feature that will no doubt become inundated with cool items I only wish I had the skills to create.
There is so much untapped potential waiting to come out of Medieval Engineers that it’s difficult to see what form the final game will take. Keen have recently released an update featuring barbarians so who knows, maybe we will see a full-on medieval war simulator, with massive castle-vs-castle battles? I’ll see you all there when I manage to get out of this damn hole!

Finally it's here, after about three years of development. And what a disappointment. This is the first kickstarter project that I baked, and I'm sad to say that I wasted money.
The game is just...bland, I can't find other words.
For the levels, they went with the "all retro" way, so, as in the old Mega Man games, you need to fight your way through a bunch of levels, in the order that you prefer, and for each attempt you will have a limited number of lives. Every level has several checkpoints, but if you lose all your lives you will restart from the beginning. You will find yourself having to replay through the entire level several times, probably thanks to all the fu**ing instant kill pits or walls. I think that this is the major problem of the game, lives should disappear from every game now; even in Mario and DK games, wich are way better than this, they became only a useless and annoying number at the top of the screen. This worked back in the '80s and '90s, where this was one of the few ways to increase longevity, because you had to keep all your lives from the beginning to the end of the game, but here you only lose your progress trough the level. To say the truth, even a lot of old Mega Man games had challenging and unforgiving levels, but their design was way better, so they were less frustrating. The problem is that in this game the enemies hardly represents a real threat, and the 95% of the times you will die by the aformentioned pits and walls. This is probably due to the new "shot and dash to absorb" mechanic. This new introduction in the gameplay is funny at times, but the enemies doesn't seem to be designed around that, and most of the times they are way too easy to take down. In old Mega Man games a lot of enemies needed different strategies, making them more part of the levels. In this game they only seems to be scattered around randomly instead. The fact that you will have to replay through them more and more, due to limited lives, worsen the things out. You know, I think that Shovel Knight isn't all that better in terms of level design. Yeah, you heard me, I finished that game too, and the levels weren't that memorable to me, but the fact that you got unlimited tries after each checkpoint changed the things completely. It tunred down the global difficulty too much on the other hand, but at least the games was a way better experience.
Bosses are a different story. I have to say that they did a good job here. The attack patterns of each one of them seems well studied, and it seems like they came straight from a real Mega Man game. The only problems are that here the hit and dash thing dosen't fit very well, and that the weapons often feels useless against them, even if you are using the right one for the specific boss; I wasn't expecting something like Metal Blade from Mega Man 2, but at least something that doesn't feel useless. Bosses are actually the only moment where you are gonna die by losing your entire health bar, and here I want to poit out another stupid problem: energy tanks. In the old Mega Man you could find and replenish energy tanks in your progress, here there is a similar thing, because by absorbing certain enemies you will charge up to 2 recoveries, but the problem is that you willlose them when you die. This doesn't make any sense to me, because at the bosses you will be able to use them only in the first attempt, and probably you won't start with a full health bar to begin with.
The story is stupid and full of annoying characters. Beck lacks of personality, Sanda is stupid, Call is useless, and I could go on and on. Only some other "mighties" are well done, in terms of personality, but they are exceptions. Obviously, with a cast like this, you can't expect much from the plot, and in fact it doesn't even deserve a single line of this review. I know, even the old Mega Man games' plots were lame and predictable, but, as I said before, it's 2016. Inafune made even the Zero games for GBA, and they had a really good plot. I wasn't pretending something like that, but at least a little bit more than this. You know, old characters and games can go that way because they have always been like that; if you think about recent Super Mario games, they basically have all the same plot, but it's fu**ing Mario, it's like a tradition, and once you play you'll forgive him every time. Here we are talking about a new IP, they had to try harder than this.
Do I even have to talk about the visuals and audio? You probably saw videos of this games. It's bland and uninspired. I saw this coming from the first "concepts" shown after the kickstarter, cause I never liked any single character that much. Again, only some Mighties are ok, but all the other character and enemies feels made out in 5 minutes. The graphics simply sucks. it seems like a bad PS2 game. Everything from models, textures and animations is incredibly low detailed, and I can't even find words for some effects, like the explosions. I know that they had to adapt the game even on the 3DS, but they had almost three years to fine tune it on other platforms.
At least we could expect a pretty good soundtrack...you know it's Mega Man heir. But no, think again. They had the composer from the first megaman, which, guess what, was the less memorable in terms of music, but this is even worse. When I heard the main theme, I thaught: "this is boring", and sadly, almost every other tune is like that. They went with the Battle Network style, both for designs and music style, and to me that was the less memorable Mega Man serie technically. Then there's the voice "acting"; decent at best, in few cases, but generally amateur level, wich sounds out of place, for a project that earned 4 million dollars on kickstarter. You'll find yourself hating characters like Dr. Sanda for their intermissions during the playthrough.
Overall, it's mediocre, really. With some more attention it could have been at least fun to play, but like this is only a waste of money. I never trusted Kickstarter that much, but I thaught that, with a personality like Inafune behind the project, I could trust this one, but I was wrong, sadly. I don't know if it's Inafune's fault, or Deep Silver's, or what else, but I still hope that I'm not the only one that will learn something from this mistake.

The game looks pretty enjoyable in the trailer, and I like what they were trying to go for, but there are some major hang-ups with it, most notably the control scheme.  The controls are mostly just infuriating, as you might think they would've elected to go for something closer to Asteroid-type controls, but instead they've gone for something closer to Zelda games.  Zelda-type controls probably would've worked OK, except that when you go from left to right, up to down, or vice-versa, instead of just going the other direction, it does this little rotation maneuver that sort of makes it impossible to know where you'll end up.  Aside from that, I could barely see the cursor on the screen when using a mouse, all of which makes it seem like it could only be played using a gamepad.
The graphics are adequate for this type of game and the storyline seems moderately interesting, but I personally just couldn't get passed the frustrating control scheme.
I think the game could've easily been salvaged with some other/better control scheme choices, but as it stands there are better places to spend your time.

I'm not the kind of guy who plays hack and slash games. I usually find them boring and repetitive, but because this one was star wars themed, I figured I'd give it a shot.
A quick for New Players:
1. Get some combos as fast as you can, especially sith flurry, lightsaber damage and health absorbed from kills. Getting those will make the game more enjoyable faster.
2. After the Cloud City level, save your game, and play the "Jedi Temple" campaign. It's a short, 30ish min level that will greatly add to what is going on in the story. In it, Starkiller goes to the desecrated Jedi Temple on Corusant, where he faces something he was not ready for...
Do not play "hoth," it's boring. Also,
play Tatooine, although it does not fit in to what happens in the story.
Now for the actual Review
I should start off by saying that most of the reviews of this game really don't hit the right notes. You could read a few here or there,
I plan to fix that with this review.
The highlight of this game is truly the gameplay itself. The gameplay is intense in most areas and boring in others. As the game goes on, you feel that your powers have grown over time. For example, some enemies which were once difficult to beat mini bosses regularly show up in combat, really emphasizing the learning curve that this game puts you through. For example, what was once a huge armored stormtrooper mini boss is now something you can take on
It truly does make you feel like a more powerful force wielder as you go on, dodging rockets and slaying armies of storm troopers and rebels.
I should say that the beginning of the game is the most boring part by far. With almost no combinations, the gameplay feels lacking at first. A few beginner tips I'd give are to: get some combos as fast as you can, especially sith flurry, lightsaber damage and health absorbed from kills. Getting those will make the game more enjoyable faster.
Since we're on the topic of gameplay, I should say that most combinations are to master, which is a good thing for people who don't play a lot of hack and slash games. There's also more complicated combos if you feel like learning them, so in that respect there's something for players of all skill levels.
In terms of difficulty, the game can be surprisingly hard. I'm the kind of gamer who really likes a challenge, but I felt like leaving the games difficulty on Sith Apprentice was more than a challenge. So in that respect again, the game is able to cater to both new and experienced gamers, which is frankly unexpected and impressive.
The story is meh, although it gets better as the game goes on. Some people say they really liked it, I didn't see too much going on that was notable, but it definitely wasn't bad. It's kind of hard to tell what exactly is going on with Starkiller throughout the story, but maybe it was meant to be that way. In any case, the story felt weak, but again, wasn't so bad that it took anything away from the game.
Graphics wise, the game has aged fairly well, things don't look bad enough to take away from the story, but some levels do look noticeably better than others.
The level design was dissapointing. Some of the levels felt a little different than others, but mostly it all felt like the same things with a few differences thrown in here or there. I have to say though,
The game devs were fully capable of making a better game than they actually made. After playing the actual campaign and then experiencing the Jedi Temple and Tatooine levels, it becomes clear that the potential to make a better game was fully there. Jedi Temple allowed players to understand more of what is going on with Starkiller, and frankly I think that Jedi Temple should be
(Which is why I told players to actually play it in the middle of their campaign.) Maybe it's just my enthusiasm for the series, but those two levels carried a heavier and more intsense feel than the actual game itself.
To conclude, this game is probably worth playing if you're a star wars fan, can deal with a difficult learning curve, and have the patience slow to start story. It's definitely
worth playing if you can't handle those things. In the end though, the game
and it has many entertaining, rapid, intense fights that make the game enjoyable and worth playing.
PS. If you need help with a certain part of this game that's particularly difficult (you'll know it when you get to it) reference the Steam discussions on how to beat it, people are willing to give you some sound advice.

To start with massive automation engineering is not for everyone.  Even me, apparently.  But I love this game anyway.
Like my review of FTL, I find my enjoyment in the complexity behind the simplicity.
Factorio is a game about building automated factories in order to construct a satellite and phone home from a surprisingly Earth like world covered in murderious alien super critters.
As Doctor Ivo Robotnic (Not really), you must race to build your military industrial complex up from literally scratch.  Starting with a few plates of steel and a stick, and making it all the way to the space age.
The vanilla game isn't overly complicated in its tech tree, and speed runs can get it done in hours.  But with the game open to mods, there's so much depth available from the community to all but teach you how truly epic a full industrial process becomes to support even the most simple of products.
The game thrusts you into a world where you can build your dream (or nightmare) factory one part at a time (or a million parts at a time if you're doing it right) and lets you do your thing.  A short campaign gives you the basics, and after that, it's all in the free play.
Graphically, the map feels like Age of Empires.  Something about the textures just reminds me of that.  But the deceptive simplicity of the graphics and sprites hides how much graphics card you'll truly need to run a huge fab.  It's simple 2D, but there are innumeral moving parts.  The engine takes simple graphics, and pushes them to the edge.
On the audio frount, it's kind of skeletal.  The soundtrack is okay in my personal opinion.  Unfortunately track diversity doesn't really exist, and in a game where you can really get into the 'I've been working this fab for six weeks and counting' category, the same couple of 3 to 5 minute ambient tracks kind of gets very, VERY stale.  For sound effects, they're simple, and sink into the subconscious after a while, providing just enough to keep you aware the game is running if you close your eyes.  But honestly, outside of alarms and gunshots, you could turn the audio completely off and not even realize it.
The controls are acceptable, and don't require much thought before you just fall into the right commands.  Interfaces are easy to discern, if a little bland.  But the game doesn't need flashy interfaces.  The game's about building your factory, not staring at menues.
To further emphasize what thig game can do.  Not only do you have factories to build, you can design automation with logic.  The logic system is in fact so robust, people have made TETRIS out of the logic system and game lights.  (Look it up on youtube).
Overall, the game is an engineer's toybox.  Build, optimize, capitalize, and brutalize all in one package.  Play a relaxing sandbox experience of making your dream factory, or exploit limited resources in survival mode while space murder bugs hem you in on all sides.  And then hit them with a train.  Because I should mention the train system in this.  Quite good.
If you have not given this game's dev your money yet, well, get to it!

I bought it in the recent sale, and coming from a Spintires background and enjoying mud-running massive trucks this was a natural progression for me, so you might be able to relate to me.  It is quite fun working through the farming and tech trees, and feels challenging even on easy mode.  I've earned and spent probably half a million dollars and am still dead-flat broke.  I am working less than half the crops on the original paddocks...
If you buy in
and the community  forum open, because the learning curve is quite sharp and punishing, especially if you have no farming background.  What is a tedder for?  Do I need to windrow?  Is silage like planking or  the ice bucket challenge?  There are dozens upon dozens of expensive(!) equipment options for the dozen harvestable crops, and multiple brands of gears, which are (mostly) incompatible with each other.  Just bought a new $200K forage harvester?  Great, your old header combs don't work with this, you must buy more hardware.  Too bad if you spent all your money... (yes, you can get more through missions, or sell updated gear, or get a loan, or lease...)
I will say that patience is key in this game, and it's a lot of fun inching toward long-term goals, upgrading your gear and buying more to try out new cropping techniques.  Be prepared for a LOT of mind-numbing rumbling back and forth over the same paddocks again and again and again, and getting frustrated when your attention wanders and your coverage is less than perfect.  I took on one mission not realising it was est. 110min sowing 3ha @ 9m swath, succeed or you get nothing.  OMG.  I think I did it half the time, but still, 55mins
without pause rolling up and down a paddock in the dark looking for dark brown on darker brown patches is not fun.  Time compression doesn't actually seem to speed the game up, just the time of day.  I did like the built-in internet radio channels which is a neat and logical feature (these can be customised and you can also load your own music files).
Against the boring parts, it runs beautifully even on old computers like mine (mostly 60FPS on ultra-highest settings), is very pretty and there's always things to do, even if it's just mowing the lawns, cleaning up your vehicles and stacking your bales neatly.  Cruise control, AI helpers, intuitive simple controls, multiplayer and peripheral support make farming a lot easier and fun.  Good difficulty settings and custom configurations extend the playability.
Modding appears to be very big, at least as big as it is Spintires or even bigger, but it doesn't have Steam Workshop.  It does have it's own in-game mod interface and it's easy to add 3rd=party mods (just drop zipfiles into MyDocs game folder)
Overall, if you're a persistent person that enjoys 'growing' your success and overcoming complicated longwinded challenges, you should enjoy this.  Or you could just blow all your money on grown-up Tonka trucks and tool around the countryside posing for screenshots, then restart. :)

This game is going to be brilliant. Already it is incredibly fun, despite it being a very early and unfinished game. There are quite a few bugs (to be expected from early access), so if dealing with that is something you absolutely loathe I recommend waiting a bit before trying it. Knowing the developer after playing a lot of Space Engineers, they make patches and improvements all the time. Normally I am skeptical to all early access games, because you always fear it will turn into vapor ware and be abandoned, but I had no such reservations about this one.
Since release there have already been several patches and hotfixes, including one today that gave us more blocks to play with, including more catch blocks (essentially hinges), round timber logs, as well as "barbarian" bots that basically run around the map looking for king statues to destroy. This is excellent news for those of us who enjoy making horrible medieval traps of all kinds (dev has a hilarious video showing this). The bots can be turned on or off depending on what you want to do, so they don't mess up your perfect dream castle if you don't want to.
Even with all the current limitations and bugs, the game is already amazingly fun to play. Keep in mind though that it does require a bit powerful pc to run properly. Especially destruction of blocks can slow down the computer.
Finally, a tip: If ropes, rope drums, hinges or physics in general start acting strange, try saving and going out to main menu and reloading the game. It sorts out most problems.

I can't belive that my Windows 10 likes this as much as I do. This classic of the classics had no argument with my system and I can announce that I am hooked into it again. Roller Coaster Tycoon is like a theme park version of Sim City or Cities: Skylines and the thing which keeps me getting back to it over and over again is complicated but yet relatively simple design and controls, with which you design, create and manage your park.
There is dozens of different maps and challenges to play and the key feature is that every playtrough is more or less different than the last because you get exact freedom to plan the overall layout and architecture and create Roller Coasters from tiny joy rides to most extreme coasters beyond this world (if you can afford it). The another cool thing is that the parks can be decorated by creating some beautiful sceneries to make your park even better experience for your customers. The management is the thing that assures that player won't feel bored at anytime - if there is not anything to build you can check that do quests have something to complain about: rides will get broken, streets need more handymen to clean up some vomits next to roller coaster ride's exit, some ride has gotten old and thus over priced etc. You also must take care that visitors have always something to eat or drink close-by.
All these and various other tasks must be handled well enough to pass the maps and unlock some new ones. While all this may sound hard it is not, thanks to the ultimately successful user interface, which lets you solve things by few clicks without getting lost in hell of management windows. In my opinion this is the very feature that makes RCT1 and RCT2 better then the third installment.

I'm very unsure whether I should recommend the game or not. I own it both on PC and Xbox. and have re-purchased the Steam Version to remember how the game was (I got and finished the xbox version immediately on release).
My opinion is very mixed. In short you should buy this only if you are either very skilled in action games and are comfortable with a console controller which you can connect to your desktop/laptop; or if you REALLY love the Star Wars universe and have a lot of patience. All these four things combined or any other combination of at least two should provide you with some resilience and allow you to complete the game... What happened to me is that I only have one of the mentioned perks: being a Star Wars fan. So I finished the story with a lot of cursing, one rage-quit and a headache.
I'll put first what I hated the most, because I chose to recommend the game, but am all but sure about it. What I disliked was:
-Most of the boss fights. The camera angle is often fixed to a position and only rotates as you move around. This is terrible, it's really a pain, and I think the average player shall find this very annoying. The boss fights are in fact not hard because the enemy AI is skilled and well designed, but because you are forced to fight with a terrible visual which prevents you from properly and quickly avoid attacks. I noticed how bad the boss fights are designed when it took me maybe 15 minutes to beat Vader and only 5 (With no deaths) to take out Palpatine. Ridiculous. Sometimes bosses even spam repeteadly one of their abilities, it feels like some glitch, or again really poor design. My hardest boss ever was the second one at the Jedi Enclave, and after it I turned the game to easy difficulty and continued that way.
-The controls: they are a mess. I think the game is a port, but I'm not sure and don't feel like looking up. The controls are simple and badly designed, making playing with mouse and keyboard a bit annoying. It's not like they bothered me through all the game, but you easily end up using the same 3 moves because the rest feels so inefficient and bothersome. Along with this I must add that in the boss fight with Vader, resisting his force stroke by pressing E multiple times is almost always failed. No matter how fast you press, you almost always fail and get tossed, often onto the lava-like radiation or whatever it is (Taking damage). Lastly beware the Star Destroyer scene, look up some youtube videos, it's really a pain to work it out on PC unless you see how it's done first. Terrible design here.
What I liked was:
-The story: the writing is decent, the chracter depth, the dialogues with a bit of humour, some romanticism, heroism etc, not different from the movies in my opinion. It doesn't match at all with my own personal taste, but I never expected a quick action game to have the same story and character development of Knights of the Old Rebublic, to give an example.
-The design of the enemies and the worlds: The scenarios aren't exactly enjoyable and truly fascinating, because the game is fast, linear and I feel it does not make the player "wow" at the lanscape too often; and yet I think for an action game they are good. At least a handful of them. The enemies are of many different types and each pose a different challenge and resist your force powers and combos differently. I found this interesting and it made the game more challenging without hassling the player in any way.
EDIT ABOUT THE THREE DLC LEVELS:
I found the two sith assassin missions on Tatooine and Hoth very fun and playable, way better than the whole base game to be honest. They are absolutely against all canon as you get to kill some major movie characters and are replacing Vader as Sidious's apprentice, however despite the humours way in which some scenes are designed (Luke turning to the dark side in 5 seconds and whimpering like a girl), it plays nicely.

Kazden Paratus, you cheap son-of-a-♥♥♥♥♥! I've finally killed you, haven't I? You're dead! You're finally dead! I've finally paid you back for the humiliating defeat you put me through so many years ago...
A-hem.
I have only ever played Star Wars The Force Unleashed on PC. And only ever with a keyboard. So, I couldn't honestly say how it compares with the original console game (which I'm assuming it was, considering how few options there are. I can say that the Steam edition is a lot better than the version I'd played years ago in that it actually allows some level of customization for controls, and mentions those controls during the endless Quick-Time-Events in this game.
I think this game is nearly 10 years old now. This was back when Star Wars Expanded Universe existed, and before they decided to look into making yet more movies. There are nods to the prequels (including a very welcome cameo by Jar Jar Binks), and set ups to the original trilogy. I don't know if it's still a part of the Star Wars Universe or not, but then I've never been a big Star Wars fan.
Star Wars The Force Unleashed is a third-person fighting game with an appropriately overpowered Sith apprentice fighting his way through the Jedi remnants of Order 66. You get your lightsaber, your force powers, and combos, and of course, your QTEs, because simply killing people isn't enough. I really hate QTEs, because you can't enjoy the cinematic fights while you're anxiously waiting for the stupid button prompts. And Force Unleashed has so many QTEs.
The combat is good, and most of the battles are against trash mobs who'll die in one or two hits. There are no health packs; all healing is vampiric, so if you're not constantly attacking, you're doing it wrong. Enemies are a mix of melee and ranged, and you need to prioritize whom to go after during a battle. Most of the stages are good, with a mix of corridors and wide-open arenas, but Raxus Prime is awful because of how uneven it is, and how awful, awful the boss is.
You get a few large enemies whom you have to take out using powers and then finish off during QTEs. Each stage has a multi-level enemy with Force powers, and occasional "nope, you can't damage me while I'm doing this" BS.
The graphics overall are pretty good, though some of the animations (during cutscenes, oddly enough) are very awkward looking, especially when characters are just walking. This is early Havoc, which looked good at the time it came out, but now looks very hokey and over-done. But the in-game graphics are pretty nice for a nearly 10-year-old game. No wonder it used to make my PC chug.
Sound is great. There's excellent voice-acting all around, and there are some nuanced dialog, especially from the main character. It's better than the movies, I think. The obligatory droid companion is probably the best out of the series, including the new BB-8.
The Ultimate Sith Edition (the only version out on PC) comes with a few extra campaigns, all but one set in a what-if timeline where Vader is killed. It's pretty dope, but does have a few technical problems.
I think it's a good game, even if it's no longer canon (rather a pointless measurement in any case, considering that all that I like about Star Wars is now non-canon anyway). It's old, somewhat hokey, but a fun way of visiting the Star Wars Universe. Just watch out for the second mission, and see if you prefer mouse+keyboard, or controller.

Okay before I do this review I want to make something perfectly clear:
KICKSTARTER IS NOT A PREORDER PLATFORM. IT IS AN INVESTMENT PLATFORM. ANYBODY WHO SAYS OTHERWISE IS LYING OR SORELY MISTAKEN.
With that said, I also backed this game on Kickstarter. I mourned the loss of the megaman series at the time and wanted to see what Keiji Inafune could do if given creative freedom to make the game he wanted to, and without Capcom's interference.
WELL BOY HOWDY I GUESS I GOT TO SEE THAT :|
sigh. Pizza explosions: Real.
Terrible voice acting: Real.
A cute character utterly gutted of any personality and interesting details: Real.
Floaty controls: Real.
Terrible animations: Real.
Godawful stage backgrounds (no wonder they had the embargo not to show stages like the oil refinery. christ...): Real.
Kinda naffy music that wouldn't have been out of place in the 90s but feels really dated here: Real.
Placeholder/alpha looking assets that are sadly final: Real.
I suppose if you strip away all those elements there's the potential for a good game. The absorbtion mechanic is pretty cool, the shot powerup you can get from absorbing certain enemies is pretty cool too.
Turns out it is actually set what powerups you get from certain enemies. I didn't see a tutorial on this however, or any indication which ones give what powerups and under what conditions though, and personally I find the icons a little hard to distinguish at times. Others may find it easier, and with time you'll probably get used to the mechanic.
I wanted to give this more time to play and get to grips with this game, maybe find the good points of it, but given how grating everything you are assaulted with WITHIN THE FIRST FORTY MINUTES, I can fully understand why people aren't recommending this...
And that's why i can't recommend it either.
If this is the best that Inafune can come up with, with the huge budget KS gave him, and without Capcom's interference... maybe they were right to can all the megaman games.

After some hours of gameplay I thought maybe I could do a little review of CoD Modern Warfare 2.
I'll focusing the multiplayer, because I can't say much about the single.
I've played it, also on the highest diffcult for the achivments, but all in all it's just a normal CoD Campaign and the direct sequel to Modern Warfare.
I'm just talking about whether the game is still playable in 2017 or not.
Let's start to talk about the multiplayer.
Some people maybe think this game is dead, but there still round about 1000 people who playing it. The disadvantage sadly is you'll find those people most in following game mods: Teamdeathmatch (and Hardcore as well), Free For All, Domination or Search and Destroy. Most of the other game mods like Groundwar or Capture the Flag are dead, or you'll find only 4 players who are searching for... whatever.
And if you find a lobby? How is the gameplay in 2017?
It's okay. On the one side you have some people who played the game since it came out and dropping killstreaks one by one, on the other you have people who just playing with the easiest mechanics to play the game, playing with the overpowered grenade launcher or in everyday language Noob Tubing.
But is it playable?
Yes it is. You have the playertypes mentions above, but the lobby isn't full of them. There are still enough normal players around who just enjoy to play some rounds to feel the nostalic or just have some fun with friends. I've never heard someone using the voicechat, so theres no one who screams in your ear how bad you are. Just sit back, play some rounds alone or with your friends and have fun.
But what's about the hackers?
Yes, there are a few hackers still in MW2. But in my whole playtime I met less then 5 who hacked very
obviously and if you're joining a hacked lobby, just quit and search for a new one.
All in all I recommend this game, when it's on sale.  I think 20€ are to much, maybe 15 or 10 would be better. Also it's not a game that you can play 24/7. But some rounds on the weekend with a couple of friends, messing around in Teamdeathmatch or Search and Destroy can be very funny.

This game has an interesting structure: you explore levels that have little to no combat in them, but you do find combat abilities for bosses later. Most players probably choose to beat the boss after each stage, but I did all the stages first to collect as much as I could (health upgrades + powers) and then tackled all the bosses. So first Jotun felt like a relaxing exploration game, to culminate in one long boss rush... and I really liked that.
It's a good idea to find as many upgrades as possible, because the bosses are no pushovers. There are 2 in particular that could take a few tries.
There's also a great soundtrack and the Norse narration is really well done. Aside from a few nitpicks (main character is pretty slow, hitboxes on bosses) I loved this game.
Bonus point: no padding! Game doesn't overstay its welcome and can be completed in about 5 hours.

This game falls under the catagory of Minecraft-like, but not for the reason that you would have imagined. Despite a mostly "gather resources, and build with the resources" style gameplay, the main similarity between the two is the necessity to have a wiki on a second monitor.
One would imagine the lack of in-game documentation would encourage the player to expirament, and learn how the logic of the game is put together, and for the most part this is true, but there are a couple instances where this is untrue.
Figuring out how to make piping and chemicals come together in a way that is efficient is woefully difficult without some kind of guide.  Things like how many boilers does a steam engine actually need?  These questions may be answered deep in the game, but it is much easier to find on the internet.
It is up to you weather or not you actually want to jump down the rabbit hole of this game. Whatever time you give to it, it will hungrilly eat up and demand more. But sometimes this comes to a screeching halt when the game stonewalls you with a specific resource.
I played the game online with a pair of  friends. We built up a massive facility and were doing fine until we hit the "Oil wall."
Unlike a real wall, the "Oil wall" is completely invisible until you have your face squarely in the middle of it. Everything needs it, all your friends want it.
So what's the big deal? just go out and get it.
Unless you played on "normal settings" and oil is harder to come by than silence in a barbershop
So there we were, sitting on a whole bunch of normal, now mostly useless materials, using the radar to scan for oil.
and we waited
and waited
and waited for that bright pink dot to show up on the map.
.... "is that it?"
"I don't know, maybe?"
"Go check it out"
So Rhett, in all of his infinite glory and sacrifice, took one of our hundreds of cars, and drove out to the pink dot.
We held our breaths in anticipation as he swerved the car around like a drunken frat boy
around the enemy spawners, past the grunts
"ITS OIL" he shouted over the mic
the tension broke
we had done it, we knew where the oil was.
A pit worm then destroyed what was  left of the flaming car, and rhett's sacrafice was complete.
We studied the map, searching for the best course to make it to the new found oil.
The number of enemy spawns from our base to the oil was obscene, but we would try.
We created an arms factory, whose sole purpose was to make turrets and bullets.
We built a railroad, to take the turrets there.
We made our push, and made it further and further in, the worms destroying our turrets faster than we could load them.
We were desperate, we couldn't make better weapons because we didn't have the oil yet.
We started ramming our cars into the large worms, destroying our own lives but for the better or the company
we pushed like this through the night, and as the sun crested the horizon we were met with our greatest challenge yet
It was a whole bunch of big worms. Enough to slaughter our cars before we could ram them.
It was a military disaster.
We were pushed back, our dreams of making it to the oil dashed by the massive worms.
We had to sleep
We did
And we let the company fail
It's still there
Waiting for it's oil, but it will never come
I won't be playing the worm's game anymore
Never again
Ever

Factorio focuses on crafting and building very similar to Minecraft. However, it focuses on logically coming up with intricate solutions to automation of crafting. They cut out a lot of the nuance such as mining around for materials, which can be fun, but that isn't what Factorio is about. Its about building an effecient factory. If someone told me that this game was about that, I'd think it sounds like a chore. However, Factorio makes it incredibly simple to get into by unlocking things slowly (using a technology tree), and Factorio gets much, much harder as you go. You will usually have a "next step" to your factory, and find yourself having to innovate previous parts of it in order to achieve the goals that you make for yourself. This innovation process involves complex logical puzzles that you can take at your own pace. You can play around with your currently unlocked gadgets to see what works, and actually see things moving around in real-time. Eventually, you start to build a whole factory, and the game allows you to zoom out and see your work. The feeling of awe as you see everything working together perfectly is awesome. This game is basically a must-try for anyone who liked Rollercoaster Tycoon, Sim City, or building in Minecraft even a little bit. Don't forget to play with friends!

Game had great potential. It felt a lot like deja vu in a good way for me in some parts when it came to messaging a girl in high school, but it took a hard left turn at the end when the game started making choices for me. That's not how it's supposed to go... Bait and switch much? Look, this game presented itself as a free to play messenger story between you and a mysterious girl named Emily in which you get to choose what to say to her, and she responds in her own way. The entire last chapter ignored every response I chose and put a different one instead. I'll give it points since that's how I probably would've acted in real life, but this isn't real life; this a GAME where I'm told I'm allowed CHOICES that I have direct control over, but I don't have any. What kind of interactive story doesn't allow interaction?
I'll give the game another go later and update my review if anything catches my eye that makes the game more worthwhile in playtime, but the dev killed it for me by making choices for me on the final chapter. Bold move there, dev. If it's seriously because of how I handled the story, that's no excuse to immaturely rip the dialogue choices away from me because I didn't play the way you wanted me to. "Play my way or you don't play at all."
Keep in mind I played every chapter of this game, so hours don't mean a whole lot because you will finish it in under an hour. Not much thought you can put into the three welcoming greeting replies of: 1. hey, 2. hello, or 3. how's it shaking? (really?)

This game is part of a lost art. A genre of online novel all but abandoned. One without pretty pictures for the minors to look at. Choice of Games is a bastion, the rebuilders of a crumpling art. And Choice of Robots is a good example of their contributions.
Story:
I was drawn into the world, as a story properly ought to. I kept reading, flowing with the river of words that i saw. The characters had meaning, were not merely static figures of humanity. The trials and tribulations of building your robot, raising it as you saw fit, eneamored me. Some endings fall flat, a few concepts feel rushed, but what story dosen't have those flaws? I give this segment a 9/10.
Gameplay:
There is no gameplay in the traditional sense. No guns to shoot, no swordighting to be had, no mystical magic. Instead, you make a variety of choices, which, despite all games with this mechanic failing to make it so, actually matter. The characteristics of your robot that you build over time; Autonomy, Grace, Military, and Empathy, directly impact the story, the choices you make, and the lifes of the characters. Its barely has gameplay, but it makes the few things it has work.
10/10
Sound:
There is no sound. Some may complain about this, but when you read a book, do you really expect it to make a noise? To belt out some fresh tunes? No, you do not. Except audiobooks, perhaps. This game does not need a sound; the words provide all the stimulation you need. I remain neutral on this aspect of the game.
Replayability:
The game enagles you. It draws you in with its story, an amalgamate of choices. Each one has an impact, each one leads down a different path. There are trials, multiple endings, moments of small pleasure among the characters, and a seemingly infinite number of ways to play. There are multiple endings to strive for, and a chievment hunters will find plenty to do. I rate this aspect 9/10.
In short, play the damn game.

Plague Inc Evolved is a strategy game about creating and evolving a disease that will infect and ultimately destroy the whole world. Upon discovering your disease, scientists of the world will attempt to cure it.
Breakdown:
Great things:
-This is the biggest pro in my opinion: there is something for everyone here. It is a great casual experience for people who aren't big strategy gamers. My friend who claims to dislike "map games" loves this game. Hardcore strategy gamers and fans of the genre will also find fun here. I, for example, play tons of 4X and grand strategy games, and I love this one as well. The harder difficulties and scenarios (custom and official) can provide great challenges and interesting strategical situations.
-Fantastic difficulty curve. The game is very easy to learn, and provides a fun challenge to master it at the hardest difficulties. The jump from Brutal to Mega Brutal is pretty big, but that gap can be filled by harder plagues or scenarios. The game never has to feel too easy or too difficult.
Good things:
-Good variety with the main plagues, official scenarios and custom scenarios. I will say that the "normal" plagues (bacteria, fungus, parasite, and prion) all feel very similar to each other, but even with that in mind, there is still a good amount of variety in the main game. Some of the official scenarios are very interesting, and can provide a large or small shake-up to your normal strategy. However, I will say a large portion of the scenarios don't feel all that different from the main game or each other, which is why I put this under "good things" instead of "great things." But there are so many scenarios, you will definitely find something interesting.
-Custom scenarios are great. The game allows community members to create their own scenarios and customize the world, events, and the plague itself to create a unique experience. When you start to get a bit bored of the normal stuff, there are basically ENDLESS custom scenarios to play. True, not ALL custom scenarios are good, but custom scenarios are produced so often, that is is viable to only have to play really good ones. And the editor is very intuitive and explains everything very well, so it easy and quite to fun to create your own custom scenario. I rank this as "good" instead of "great" because the editor doesn't provide THAT much variety, and (last time I checked) TRULY unique plagues like the Necroa virus and the Neurax worm, cannot be created in the editor. Granted, they would be difficult to create, but many communities have dedicated creators who put time and effort into creating cool content for the game, and I have no reason to believe this one is any different. Anyway, you may feel that none or few of the custom scenarios feel meaningfully different from anything else.
-Clean and intuitive UI. You will never be befuddled by this game's UI. It is not over-complicated, while still providing all the information you might ever want. As well, it looks very nice, and has some nice aesthetic but not distracting touches, such as a cool picture of your pathogen, and what an infected body might look like.
-Concept: It is a very cool and interesting concept to manufacture a plague to infect and kill the whole world. The only other game I know of that has a similar concept is Pandemic, but Plague Inc has much more depth I would say.
-Sound effects are pretty cool and fit the theme of the game rather well. There are enough to feel satisfying, but not so many that you get annoyed.
Okay things:
-Main graphics on the map are pretty good, if simple. You can zoom in quite far and see some detail. However, you would never want to do this, as there is never a reason to not look at the whole map, as you might miss something, so you might get a little tired of looking at the same thing all the time (besides the UI screens), although admittedly it is satifying to see everything slowly turn red!
-Music is a bit lacking, but not bad. The main "music" creates the feel the game is going for, and is mostly ambient noises. I'm not sure if actual music would fit this game well, but nevertheless, I cannot rate the sound here as "good." It is a short loop, and there is not much to it, but since it is just ambient, it won't annoy you, I wouldn't recommend muting it.
-Multiplayer is pretty meh. There are two multiplayer modes: Co-op and competitive, which I really like. They are pretty different, so I will start with Co-op.
-Co-op mode involves two players controlling separate plagues on the same map, and they can work on separate regions, or the same, and they can buff each other. However, multiplayer seems to function very differently than singleplayer with changed mechanics, and yet the game doesn't seem to tell you this, so we floundered a lot in this mode, despite both being very good at the singleplayer modes. Even when we won, most of the time, one of the plagues got eliminated early on and the other one did all the work. Also, pop-ups don't seem to appear as much in multiplayer, so I had my plague 50% cured without even noticing that the cure started.
-Competitive is fine, but it feels like a race, like we might as well just play singleplayer and see who wins first. Interactions are limited to several evolutions that can "sabotage" the other player. Some of these are very major and can change the whole game, but usually the other player will just do the same to you, as they are pretty much forced to, so it still feels like a race, just under different conditions. Also, the victory conditions are changed a bit: you don't have to kill everyone, just infect everyone, which is a big negative for me, as it feels like half the game is just missing. You can also win if the other plague is eliminated. As mentioned, you can sabotage the other player, but this victory condition almost always feels like you won because the other player messed up, and not because you did well, so can be a bit unsatisfying. I have mostly mentioned negative things, but that's not to say that multiplayer isn't fun. It is still Plague Inc, and all the previously mentioned positives still apply, it just isn't quite as fun as the singleplayer mode for me. However, big disclaimer: I don't have many friends who play this game, so I haven't actually played that many multiplayer games, so my opinion on them might improve as I come to understand them a bit better.
Bad Things:
-This game's only real con is that it can get a bit repetitive, but that can be a big con.
-The game lacks any real variety in its events, and doesn't have that many to start with, so there is very little variety created by in-game events, and even the ones that do happen seem to barely affect anything in the game.
-For many of the plagues, the EXACT same strategy can be used, and it can feel very repetitive. However, this isn't a huge con, as many of the more unique plagues and scenarios can change it up quite a bit, but it will still feel prevalent as you try out different things.
-This is sort of a subset of the repetitiveness, but it is the biggest issue for me: Most of the symptoms feel the same. There are many symptoms in the game, but for most plagues, they consist of: Increases infection rate, increase death rate, or slow down cure research. Different tiers of symptoms will do this at different levels, but still feel the same. It can be fun to think about how people are affected by the actual symptoms you are adding, but from an actual gameplay perspective, many feel exactly the same.
OVERALL RATING: 8/10 - Worth buying at full price.
The pros heavily outweigh the cons, and you will definitely get some fun from this game.

It is quite fun working through the farming and tech trees, and feels challenging even on easy mode.  I've earned and spent probably half a million dollars and am still dead-flat broke.  I am working less than half the crops on the original paddocks...
If you buy in
and the community  forum open, because the learning curve is quite sharp and punishing, especially if you have no farming background.  What is a tedder for?  Do I need to windrow?  Is silage like planking or  the ice bucket challenge?  There are dozens upon dozens of expensive(!) equipment options for the dozen harvestable crops, and multiple brands of gears, which are (mostly) incompatible with each other.  Just bought a new $200K forage harvester?  Great, your old header combs don't work with this, you must buy more hardware.  Too bad if you spent all your money... (yes, you can get more through missions, or sell updated gear, or get a loan, or lease...)
I will say that patience is key in this game, and it's a lot of fun inching toward long-term goals, upgrading your gear and buying more to try out new cropping techniques.  Be prepared for a LOT of mind-numbing rumbling back and forth over the same paddocks again and again and again, and getting frustrated when your attention wanders and your coverage is less than perfect.  I took on one mission not realising it was est. 110min sowing 3ha @ 9m swath, succeed or you get nothing.  OMG.  I think I did it half the time, but still, 55mins
without pause rolling up and down a paddock in the dark looking for dark brown on darker brown patches is not fun.  Time compression doesn't actually seem to speed the game up, just the time of day.  I did like the built-in internet radio channels which is a neat and logical feature (these can be customised and you can also load your own music files).
Against the boring parts, it runs beautifully even on old computers like mine (mostly 60FPS on ultra-highest settings), is very pretty and there's always things to do, even if it's just mowing the lawns, cleaning up your vehicles and stacking your bales neatly.  Cruise control, AI helpers, intuitive simple controls, multiplayer and peripheral support make farming a lot easier and fun.  Good difficulty settings and custom configurations extend the playability.
Modding appears to be very big, at least as big as it is Spintires or even bigger, but it doesn't have Steam Workshop.  It does have it's own in-game mod interface and it's easy to add 3rd=party mods (just drop zipfiles into MyDocs game folder)
Overall, if you're a persistent person that enjoys 'growing' your success and overcoming complicated longwinded challenges, you should enjoy this.  Or you could just blow all your money on grown-up Tonka trucks and tool around the countryside posing for screenshots, then restart. :)
(I haven't played any FS games before so no opinion on earlier versions or DLC)

Overall, a very good sim with very few bugs that make you want to punch someone in the face.
Pro:
- Pretty good AI; does a fairly impressive job pathfinding even when you've modified the edges of your field
- Game flows at a good rate; things happen predictably, when you expect them to happen; very few surprises
Con:
- occasional AI boners; AI sometimes likes to turn around in the middle of a row and go back down the next row, or just ignore the end of the row
- the clamps of every tool used in forestry is coated with some kind of "super Teflon" and will literally launch logs out of the grip randomly.  Hilarious the first 40,000 times it happens, annoying AF after that
- the steering likes to behave oddly... you'll be turning left, and all of a sudden your steering wheel jams over there and you crash.
- I was adding 3-4 windmills every day, and my property income was going down every day.  How???  Is it supposed to be "wear and tear" on the turbines?  A little too much realism there, particularly since I couldn't figure out if I could repair them.
But definitely a decent game; one of those games that you can play while also watching tv, talking on the phone, IM'ing, *and* playing another game.
Also: skip the DLC, not worth it.  There's enough content already and tons of mods.

Factorio is, in a sense, the game that I've been waiting for my whole life.
There's been a ton of resource management  / base building games out there, but not in the sense I've been longing for. In those games resource management is a means to an end, usually to build an army and destroy your opponent. Typically you're restricted in some way, be it time, resources, or ultimately, space. And after your opponent is crushed, the base you spent hours building and perfecting is meaningless. You won. Go along.
Not in Factorio. Here, the resource management and base building are both the means and the end. You build a factory to get stuff, and you use that stuff to build a bigger, better factory. Why? To get more stuff of course, for the bigger and better factory. There's always bottlenecks to unravel, production lines to boost, conveyor belts to draw. And you are limited in only your amount of imagination and dedication. In an endlessly generated 2D world you just take your train track a bit further for the next iron ore patch. Eventually you will consume the forests, drain the oceans, choke the air - hell, if Factorio had elevation, you bet you would grind the mountains to concrete flats. When Alien Artifacts were still around, even the enemies that tried to kill you were just resources. You didn't fight them because they were evil aliens - you fought them because you wanted their biomass. (Actually, in this sense, the evil alien is you.)
I'm an engineer and I go to work to take time off Factorio.

Short review-amazing.  Well worth 20 bucks if you enjoy building castles.
Long Review-
Pros
Hard game to stop playing.  There is always one more build to attempt and one more looky-loo at your creation.  After spending 3-4 hours messing around, learing the controls, I have been putting together an imense mountain castle that includes a drawbridge, portculi, dozens of towers, houses, and catapults.  It is easy to get lost in your work while hours pass by.  The graphics are beautiful, and on my new Alienware, I see the grass and trees sway in the breeze.  I get the same feeling playing this game that I got as a kid playing with legos nonstop, oblivious to the world.
But, there are a few problems that can be frustrating.
It's Alpha.  There is clunkiness to the controls, especially in clearing debris.
As others have mentioned, the buildings you constuct need to be over-engineered or they will tumble down.  There is a lack of variety of materials to flesh out your castle: a bed, table, dresser, and a chair is all you get for now.
Roofs can be very anoying to place correctly and if you misplace, you often delete the walls underneath in addition to the section of roof.
You also have only a half a dozen maps to choose from, none of which are overly large.  There is no water as of yet, so no moats.  Smoothing terrain is perhaps the most frustrating part of the game for me so far.  Instead of pushing down on terrain, you add up.  The controls are clunky, awkward, and no way to take away or delete terrain.  No food, crops, animals, resources, blacksmithing, or fine crafting of any type.
Flying can test your nerves as well.  Gravity doesn't exist if flying mode, so inertia sends you at mach 1 with just a touch of the controls.  You often need to be in the perfect spot to place a block, and the inertia controls require fine little pushes in the direction you want to travel in.  Plus, you are invulnerable and if you send yourself flying into a wall, if often comes tumbling down as cuss words tumble out of your mouth.

Plague Inc Evolved is a strategy game about creating and evolving a disease that will infect and ultimately destroy the whole world. Upon discovering your disease, scientists of the world will attempt to cure it.
Breakdown:
Great things:
-This is the biggest pro in my opinion: there is something for everyone here. It is a great casual experience for people who aren't big strategy gamers. My friend who claims to dislike "map games" loves this game. Hardcore strategy gamers and fans of the genre will also find fun here. I, for example, play tons of 4X and grand strategy games, and I love this one as well. The harder difficulties and scenarios (custom and official) can provide great challenges and interesting strategical situations.
-Fantastic difficulty curve. The game is very easy to learn, and provides a fun challenge to master it at the hardest difficulties. The jump from Brutal to Mega Brutal is pretty big, but that gap can be filled by harder plagues or scenarios. The game never has to feel too easy or too difficult.
Good things:
-Good variety with the main plagues, official scenarios and custom scenarios. I will say that the "normal" plagues (bacteria, fungus, parasite, and prion) all feel very similar to each other, but even with that in mind, there is still a good amount of variety in the main game. Some of the official scenarios are very interesting, and can provide a large or small shake-up to your normal strategy. However, I will say a large portion of the scenarios don't feel all that different from the main game or each other, which is why I put this under "good things" instead of "great things." But there are so many scenarios, you will definitely find something interesting.
-Custom scenarios are great. The game allows community members to create their own scenarios and customize the world, events, and the plague itself to create a unique experience. When you start to get a bit bored of the normal stuff, there are basically ENDLESS custom scenarios to play. True, not ALL custom scenarios are good, but custom scenarios are produced so often, that is is viable to only have to play really good ones. And the editor is very intuitive and explains everything very well, so it easy and quite to fun to create your own custom scenario. I rank this as "good" instead of "great" because the editor doesn't provide THAT much variety, and (last time I checked) TRULY unique plagues like the Necroa virus and the Neurax worm, cannot be created in the editor. Granted, they would be difficult to create, but many communities have dedicated creators who put time and effort into creating cool content for the game, and I have no reason to believe this one is any different. Anyway, you may feel that none or few of the custom scenarios feel meaningfully different from anything else.
-Clean and intuitive UI. You will never be befuddled by this game's UI. It is not over-complicated, while still providing all the information you might ever want. As well, it looks very nice, and has some nice aesthetic but not distracting touches, such as a cool picture of your pathogen, and what an infected body might look like.
-Concept: It is a very cool and interesting concept to manufacture a plague to infect and kill the whole world. The only other game I know of that has a similar concept is Pandemic, but Plague Inc has much more depth I would say.
-Sound effects are pretty cool and fit the theme of the game rather well. There are enough to feel satisfying, but not so many that you get annoyed.
Okay things:
-Main graphics on the map are pretty good, if simple. You can zoom in quite far and see some detail. However, you would never want to do this, as there is never a reason to not look at the whole map, as you might miss something, so you might get a little tired of looking at the same thing all the time (besides the UI screens), although admittedly it is satifying to see everything slowly turn red!
-Music is a bit lacking, but not bad. The main "music" creates the feel the game is going for, and is mostly ambient noises. I'm not sure if actual music would fit this game well, but nevertheless, I cannot rate the sound here as "good." It is a short loop, and there is not much to it, but since it is just ambient, it won't annoy you, I wouldn't recommend muting it.
-Multiplayer is pretty meh. There are two multiplayer modes: Co-op and competitive, which I really like. They are pretty different, so I will start with Co-op.
-Co-op mode involves two players controlling separate plagues on the same map, and they can work on separate regions, or the same, and they can buff each other. However, multiplayer seems to function very differently than singleplayer with changed mechanics, and yet the game doesn't seem to tell you this, so we floundered a lot in this mode, despite both being very good at the singleplayer modes. Even when we won, most of the time, one of the plagues got eliminated early on and the other one did all the work. Also, pop-ups don't seem to appear as much in multiplayer, so I had my plague 50% cured without even noticing that the cure started.
-Competitive is fine, but it feels like a race, like we might as well just play singleplayer and see who wins first. Interactions are limited to several evolutions that can "sabotage" the other player. Some of these are very major and can change the whole game, but usually the other player will just do the same to you, as they are pretty much forced to, so it still feels like a race, just under different conditions. Also, the victory conditions are changed a bit: you don't have to kill everyone, just infect everyone, which is a big negative for me, as it feels like half the game is just missing. You can also win if the other plague is eliminated. As mentioned, you can sabotage the other player, but this victory condition almost always feels like you won because the other player messed up, and not because you did well, so can be a bit unsatisfying. I have mostly mentioned negative things, but that's not to say that multiplayer isn't fun. It is still Plague Inc, and all the previously mentioned positives still apply, it just isn't quite as fun as the singleplayer mode for me. However, big disclaimer: I don't have many friends who play this game, so I haven't actually played that many multiplayer games, so my opinion on them might improve as I come to understand them a bit better.
Bad Things:
-This game's only real con is that it can get a bit repetitive, but that can be a big con.
-The game lacks any real variety in its events, and doesn't have that many to start with, so there is very little variety created by in-game events, and even the ones that do happen seem to barely affect anything in the game.
-For many of the plagues, the EXACT same strategy can be used, and it can feel very repetitive. However, this isn't a huge con, as many of the more unique plagues and scenarios can change it up quite a bit, but it will still feel prevalent as you try out different things.
-This is sort of a subset of the repetitiveness, but it is the biggest issue for me: Most of the symptoms feel the same. There are many symptoms in the game, but for most plagues, they consist of: Increases infection rate, increase death rate, or slow down cure research. Different tiers of symptoms will do this at different levels, but still feel the same. It can be fun to think about how people are affected by the actual symptoms you are adding, but from an actual gameplay perspective, many feel exactly the same.
OVERALL RATING: 8/10 - Worth buying at full price.
The pros heavily outweigh the cons, and you will definitely get some fun from this game.
This review went way longer than I intended, but hopefully it was helpful to you!

From what I have read, there are four main problems that everyone seems to be having. The graphics suck, the controls are loose, the level design is uninspired and the music isn't up to par with the rest of the Megaman franchise.
Firstly, I'll have to agree that the music isn't as memorable or as catchy as the music in the earlier Megaman games, there is no Dr Wily's Castle Theme or Storm Eagle Stage Theme to be found here. Not to say the soundtrack is bad by any measure, there was just no particular theme which stuck in my mind after finishing the game. As for the graphics, they are bright and colourful with lots of interesting robot designs, but if the Dreamcast-era 3D isn't your thing, this game isn't going to suddenly change your mind.
Moreso than any other Megaman game, Mighty No. 9 emphasises speed in its controls, a lot of the level sections (especially those in No 1's stage) require you to quickly dash through areas while either avoiding or collecting the assorted enemies along the way, it reminds me a lot of the Megaman Zero games and their emphasis on running and cutting through your foes to get to the end as fast as possible. This is something that the controls loan themselves well to, with the ability to dash multiple times in the air and with most enemies only requiring one or two hits with your buster to become vulnerable, blitzing through the tropey stages feels satisfying.
The levels themselves have similar platforming challenges, but with one or two interesting gimmicks thrown in to mix them up, one particular level that stands out is one where you are stripped of all your collected powers and are forced to play the Roll-like sidekick to infiltrate a prison complex. It is particularly interesting since your weak stungun forces you to evade and think around the enemy patterns instead of just blindly shooting everything dead, it was an interesting change of pace which I wish the game had explored more.
It seems like a lot of hate for this game has stemmed from the poor way the kickstarter campaign was managed, although if you can manage to look past the flood of negative press, Mighty No. 9 is well worth picking up, especially if you want an interesting take on the old Megaman formula.

I had to completely finish playing this game to aquire the full experience before writing this and boy... it left me disappointed.  What was going on in their heads while developing this game? Did Inafune suffered from amnesia when he left Capcom because what I was playing isn't what made mega man great.  Does anyone remember how in each stage there was a new gaming mechanic and tricky platforming that we had to learn figure out and when entering the final stages of the games, those mechanics come back, but more devious?  Well kiss all that goodbye becuase that doesn't exist in this game at all.  In fact, Beck, the main character of this game can easier dash right over obstacles with his overpowered dashing ability making platforming almost useless.
Oh that right, pardom my matters, I'm suppose to take about is the game fun.  Fun um that's a hard one guys since what's fun for me could be painful to others.  The game itself is bland with its vanilla gameplay, stages, artstyle, graphics, story, characters, etc.  I wasn't sure if this was suppose to be funny but the human characters in the game are just as or more mechanical than their mechanized counterparts.  One human character in particular looked like a union between an old macintosh, a dog toy and human to give birth to a scientist name Dr. William White.  I'm mean seriously look at his mouth; i always felt compelled to find an old floppy disc and slide it into his mouth.  Yeah, with all that voice acting, no lips movements, lack of personality, lack of character motivation and list keeps going.
