To be brutally honest, I really don't hate this game at all, but I do hate how overly hyped this game is and hate even more how the backers were treated like cattle.  It's almost as if nobody really cared at all what they went through and rather swipe it all under some rug somewhere and slap the word drama on it make easier to gloss over the whole ordeal.  I'm not going to get into the details of it since the discussion board pretty much covers that, so find them, read them if you have the patience and venture through them with an opened mind because there's alot to unpack in regards to this game's histoy.  I'm a backer too, so I definitely know this game 's histroy very well and boy I wasn't surprised how this game turned out.
I wanted Comcept to prove the naysayers (that includes me) wrong by backing it up with all that money they got to create something good after 3 deleys, but no dice.  Jesus it's so hard to recommend this game without them first playing at least some mega man and mega man x games first to give them some idea why many are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and then play the game or its demo to form you're own thoughts on the game.  But I implore all of you, don't believe the hype, don't confuse constructive criticism with hate and really try to distinglish the ones with well thought out reason why this game isn't good versus the ones how barely played it t all. Feels like playing a new spin-off series for a certain Classic Robot Platformer game:  lots of classic tricks, and just enough new stuff to be a new game.  It's not any more revolutionary than another X interation would be, but like those games just having more is, it turns out, still pretty fun.  The Ray DLC adds some interesting twists on the gameplay as well, so that's a plus.
I have a lot of issues with the localization, and it's not graphically all that compelling in general (although it has its moments), but overall pretty much exactly what you'd expect it to be given its pedigree.

Ignore the absurd hate-train of the easily-offended sheeple, this is a legit Megaman game.
Fast paced and challenging, you get the classic precision-based levels, without being too lengthy to be frustrating.  The boss-battles are skillful and unique, requiring you to recognize their tells before you can master them.  And they managed to give the bosses some personality and decent voice-acting, giving the game a bit more character.
The dash-finishing mechanic is new, and definitely not like oldschool megaman, and clearly is geared more towards the perfectionist, score-attack, speedrun style, which it does well, but even if that's not your fancy, it doesn't distract too much from your jumping and shooting.
On the downsides, while the Ray playthrough is different enough from Beck and challenging, the little Call section feels lackluster, and kinda thrown in.  In addition, there are a few typos in the text here and there, and while I dig the Boss's voice acting, the human's talky segments are kinda mediocre, to a lil annoying, annnd Beck kinda repeats lines pretty rapid-pace on everything you do.
Overall, a great addition to the Megaman series, and if you want it to be, it's a great Mastery game to cut your teeth on.  It's only a shame that the belligerent hatetrain has gone way off the tracks.  I kickstarted it, and am satisfied.

I originally wasn't gonna review this game, but I had some time to play the game and had no reason not to.  First of all, the game itself isn't bad.  Sure, it's not as hard as say Megaman, but I wouldn't call it terrible.  My issue with the game is that for nearly four million dollars, it looks terrible.  Now, I don't usually argue about graphics, but there is a bit more than meets the eye.  First of all, this game looks like a PS2 game, a comparison I barely make, and the textures, for the most part, or rather low res.  Take that with cutscenes that barely have animations, and you got a basic looking game.  I can understand wanting anime/cartoonish characters, and I'm all for it, but did it bother them to animate the mouths at least, instead of having them hang their mouths open like idiots?  Even budget Roll, I mean Call, looks like she doesn't want to be there, as she stares blankly into your soul as if she's saying "just exit the game.  You don't want to play it."
Speaking of Call, the sound is mixed.  The voice acting ranges from cheesy, if lucky, to boring as all hell, like Call.  Music is also mixed, as there is a small chance you'll get a likable tune.  Retro BGM helps, but it's still meh.
My biggest problem with the game is the optimization, and believe or not, this is the best version of the game in that regard, and even that isn't saying much.  I can run the game at 60 FPS just fine most of the time, which is to be expected with a bland looking game like this, but there are still times where it will take, for example, Mighty No 1's level.  Remember that "epic" pizza explosion in the trailer?  Well, there's a part you navigate in a hallway engulfed with it, after it ignites the oil on the ground, and my framerates tank to the 30s on this one part, and this is on a PC with a FX 8350 and a GTX 960, a build that can run many intense games at 60 FPS.  How is this happening?
Overall, it's a game that had the potential to be good, but giving the rocky development, along with trying to fund a second project before this game came out and numerous delays including for dumb reasons like Online Play, I can't say I was surprised.  Deep down, you can find a decent game, but this is the case of a Kickstarter campaign going bad, and even with games like Yooka Laylee, Bloodstained, and many other titles coming out and looking good, it doesn't help the outlook of crowdfunding at all.  If you still plan on buying the game, I say less than $10 is the best price for it.  At least that's better than nothing.

Then I got to the final boss. The big climax for the game. And I got stuck. I couldn't figure out why. At a certain point it became invincible and I could do nothing except reset. And then it happened again. Frustrated, I tried to figure out what was going on.
At a certain point in the boss fight, there's four separate towers you have to destroy. The boss fight is designed in such a way that you're meant to only be able to destroy one at a time. But you can destroy more than one. I found it very easy to do so. Apparently the developers never considered this as destroying more than one at a time caused the invincibility bug.
I was not impressed.
It was never an amazing game to begin with, just some simple mindless fun. But when the final boss is so buggy, that's a serious issue. I have no doubt if I looked into it I'd find countless other problems throughout. Releasing a game in such a state is inexcusable. Even when it's on sale at massive discount, I cannot recommend this. Recommended, with caveats:
- Pro: Amazing art direction! Just look at the trailer and the screenshots. Sprite animations aren't always as smooth as you'd like, however, and looks like they could have been improved with a few more frames.
- Pro: Great bosses! Fighting giant bosses (quite literally Giant bosses, here) and somehow winning is always fun. These bosses are also well-designed, and not one of them feels like a rehash of any of the others. My one criticism with the boss battles would be how tiny you are next to the giants, especially when the camera zooms out so you can see a larger section of the boss arena -- it can be a little tricky to see what you are doing and whether you're attacking in the right direction, especially when your sprite is standing behind the boss.
- Pro/Con: The map design isn't perfect. Before boss battles, you have to explore environments to unlock keys - runes - that allow you to transport to each boss arena. One for the first, two for all the rest excepting the final boss. These environments are well-designed and fun to navigate, presenting unique atmospheres and challenging you in different ways. However, to have a good chance in the boss battles you'll want to step off the beaten path to collect power-ups and health boosts - the latter of which aren't marked on the map - which, after the first few worlds, can start to feel like a drag. The joy of exploration gives way to the feeling of wadding through padding keeping you from getting to the good stuff.
That said, similarly to the bosses themselves, every world is different -- in one map, you'll climb the branches of Yggdrasil while an eagle swoops down from you as you get closer to her nest, in another, you'll connect the dots in the clouds to form constellations or dash through the snow inbetween bursts of wind as blizzards periodically ravage the land. While each world starts to outstay its welcome if you try to collect everything, they all feel unique from eachother.
- Con: The controls are somewhat sluggish and slow in all areas -- it's only when you activate the speed boost power that you feel like you're actually moving and acting quickly. I feel like the game would have felt a lot more dynamic if both your own and your enemies' movement and actions were sped up somewhat.
- Con: It's not every long at all. You can go for achievements (defeat gods without powers, without taking damage), and there's Valhalla Mode (NG+) which toughens the bosses up and changes up their patterns somewhat, but a run where you make a dash for each power-up and take down the bosses without limiting yourself won't take more than an evening's worth of gaming.
In summary, I'd only recommend getting it on full price if you really wanted to support the developers (and I'd recommend looking at the Sundered kickstarter before that), but it's definitely worth getting if you can get it on sale.

(Please take mind of the first paragraph of thie review before commenting on it)
+ Some of the best gameplay of the series
+ Proper Rush maps
- Poor server population (at least in Europe)
- No new wave of players to provide some breathing space for begginers
+ All-kit weapons balance out all the classes, preventing one class from dominating the game
- Most of your opponents are going to be level 50 Generals of the Army, who have been playing the game
since launch.
While I still believe that Bad Company 2 is the mechanically best game in the Battlefield series with its implementation of classes, weapons, all-kit weapon balance, and map design, as a "playing" game, it has not stood the test of time, so please take note that I am giving a negative review of the game in the state it is in now.
If you're interested in the Battlefield series and in general online shooters with a modern military theme, I'd recommend going for the next instalment in the series proper -- Battlefield 3, which still has, three years after its release, a somewhat lively mid-level population, something that Bad Company does not. And that's the very first wall you will run into playing BD2.
True, there are many people coming back to BD2 and you will run into low-level players from time to time, but the *vast* majority of players on most, if not all, servers are level 50 Generals of the Army, who have been playing the game for years and know every map like the back of their hand, and all the various expliots in the game proper. As such, it is next to impossible to compete with these players.
Since sniper rifles in BD2 do not have scope glint to give away their position and scope sway to balance out the amazing killing ponential of bolt-action sniper rifles, camping is pathological and prevelent on the few remaining populated servers. Most matches quickly disintergrate into sniper team vs sniper team situations, which makes arming MCOMs and capturing flags extremely difficult for both teams, resulting that most matches simply run out with the first team to capture flags as the winners.
In some such situations it is impossible for Attackers in Rush to advance beyond their deploy, because the whole of the other team is keeping them in the proverbial pen with sniping and camping next to exits out of the deploy, and there are only a handful of servers with active admins that stop such behaviour with kicks and bans.
In short: the game has reached the end of its play cycle, and is no longer the game it was in back in the "glory" days of 2010-2012.

It's very much in that vein (Stardew in particular) except instead of farming, you are amassing the world's largest collection of black hares while trying to avoid getting beat up by the Mountain domain.
For those of us who were Warrior Cats nerds back in 2008 and still foster love and nostalgia towards that world, this is the game you would have procrastinated on your geometry homework for. Cattails is very much its own thing, but it maintains that spirit of exploration, survival, family loyalty....and fighting for territorial hunting rights. As you do.
Things I like:
- Pretty pixel art and music
- Hunting is actually tricky
- THERE ARE FRIGGIN POLITICS
- You're a cat. Duh.
Things I want:
- More dialogue depth with everyone (potential mates in particular)
- Longer days
- Generational play, or at least multiple litters of kittens
It is a fairly simple game, but at only two hours in I have already seen so much depth -- and so much potential for growth. My understanding is that the developer is going to continue to update Cattails, and I hope to see even more complexity packed in to this little gem. I can't wait. Meanwhile, there are mice to catch!

Having grown up in the dark ages and cut my teeth playing such text based games as The Zork Trilogy and every other Infocom game before graduating to the likes of Monkey Island; I expected to find myself back in the 1980's when playing Choice of Robots. How wrong I was.
CoR certainly has the text based spirit of its earlier predecessors but is more specifically a decedent of the Choose Your Own Adventure style of game books that also stole much of my youth. Even though the linage is obvious the result is something much deeper and more beautifully crafted than any of its ancestors could have hoped for.
Its claims of 300,000+ words would not mean a dime if the story itself was rubbish and thankfully CoR is far from a lame story. Each word and paragraph that leads to detailed and well-structured choices is expertly transposed to the screen. That these choices then have real consequence makes for an even greater experience. Real choices are often trumpeted by modern AAA games as the headline banner, few could hope to accomplish the impact that the choices in CoR provide.
I expect I will continue to feed those choices for a long time yet and has me looking forward to exploring the catalogue of Choice of Games.
In a word brilliant.

So I have played a decent number of megaman games in my time, ranging from the entire megaman classic series to a good chunk of the X series, even some of the other titles like ZX and ZX Advent, so when I heard this game was coming out, I was excited. Then I completely forgot this game was coming out because of all its delays. nevertheless, I still remembered to download it.
Mighty No. 9 was boasted as a "spiritual successor" to the megaman games. Sure there are some elements of megaman in it, such as absorbing the bosses' special abilities, I really didn't feel like it was a megaman game. If you go into this thinking its just another version of megaman, you would be dissapointed.
But what if you just take the game for what it is, just a standalone game? You would get a quite enjoyable experience.
PROS
the dashing mechanic is pretty cool. it takes a while to get used to it if your used to the megaman way of shooting until said enemy dies, but once you do get used to the mechanic it feels smooth. Thats another thing as well. I felt that the controls were quite nice, but can be problematic at times (i'll go over this in the cons section).
I feel that the bosses themselves were designed well enough. All of them have visual or vocal ques on when they are going to do their attacks, which forces you to pay attention to what they are doing.
After defeating a boss, you get a special ability from them called ReXelections. Most of them are pretty useless aside from damaging the boss that they are weak against, but some of them are really cool (Cryospheres especially, her ReXelection is the whole reason I could beat the final boss lol :P)
Playing as Call (not roll) was a nice touch too (it helps that I thnk shes pretty cute)
Anyways, now onto what I feel the game is bad at:
CONS
remember when I said that the controls could get problematic at times? what I mean is that when you stop moving on the controller, Beck (the character you play for 99% of the game) will slide. This isn't very noticeable when on the ground, but is SUPER ANNOYING when in the air. There were many times where I had unwarranted deaths because of this (stupid death spikes).
Another issue that I have with this game is that it doesn't explain ANYTHING you get in-game. For example, the ReXelections (the abilities you get when defeating a boss). It is never explained on how to use them in-game. Instead, you have to go to the tips menu on the stage select screen. This appies to almost everything, from those special abilities I mentioned earlier to the buffs you can get from time to time. I literally didn't realize this until halfway through the game, so most of the time I had to learn on the fly, which I feel is uneccesary. Why should I have to do the homework on a brand spanking new ability I just got? Why not just give me a denonstration on what it does right then and there?
The last issue that I have with the main game is the ridiculous difficulty spikes that occur from time to time. They dont happen often, but when they do, they hit HARD. If you aren't ready for the said difficulty spikes (especially during Brandish's level), it could mean redoing the entire level again, which becomes EXTREMELY annoying after some time.
CONCLUSION
Overall, regardless of whether or not Mighty No. 9 is truly a "spiritual successor" to megaman, I still enjoyed myself quite a bit. Its a decent challenge the first time through but its still a fun game in my opinion. If your on the fence on getting this game, I'd say pick it up. I paid full price for it, which was $20, and I feel I got my moneys worth. I'd definitely reccomend picking this game up though if it is on a discount (25% is a perfect discount)

This game is in a weird space where it wants to be both a Sonic-style game and a Mega Man-style game. Sometimes it works - the intro stage is fantastic in showing you the ropes, and there's a few stages that really make you think, "this works, this is great, this is fun!" That's because in those instances, it's true. It's fun to switch between shooting and zipping around. This core idea is great!
It's just not true all the time, and that's a real shame. In fact, in a lot of places it feels like they're pretending they're back in the eighties and nineties. A time where people had neat ideas for a video game, but little to comapre it to in order to see what works or what doesn't. It's made even more strange when one considers the developer's pedigree in developing similar games. It's a feigned innocence that is somewhat endearing, but only if you have the patience for some of the sillier mistakes you'd more readily attribute to novice fan-game makers than hardened professionals. The highs and lows are extreme, thanks to this lack of consistency and discipline in the overall design.
The presentation is weak in terms of graphical prowess, though in most circumstances it does a good job of conveying to the player a lot of information you need to know (where you are, what's an enemy, what's scenery, can this enemy be dashed into, etc). This makes the times where it isn't all the more glaring! The game can and will sometimes blindside you with enemies you could not have seen nor heard coming, and give you precious little time to work with even if you know when they appear. Sometimes it boils down to memorization as opposed to actual skill. Some levels don't seem to consider your amazing horizontal mobility at all, leading to a number of level stretches being easily skipped without missing a thing.
Boss fights have an interesting balance between fleeing and chasing. After a certain point, bosses have to be rammed into with your dash in order to "keep" the damage, which is an exciting way to stop the player from trying to be on the opposite side of the screen at all times. The balance is not always maintained, however - some bosses spend way too much time being invulnerable, which grinds the careful pacing between these two concepts into a zone that simply becomes not fun. There still manages to be one, possibly two, bosses whose tricks are so easily mastered that fighting them becomes a chore out of sheer tedium. The ones who maintain this balance are worthwhile experiences, for sure, and I'm happy to say the good outweighs the bad among the boss designs.
The core moveset is just so good for both fighting and movement that it often feels - and is, in the heat of the moment! - cumbersome to switch to and use the weapons you've earned from defeating bosses. A few may be worth experimenting with, maybe even as part of a self-imposed challenge thanks to how easy it is to collect and maintain weapon energy. The extra challenges make a genuine attempt to expand on them a little more, but odds are good you'll only use a few outside of being a means to take down specific bosses faster.
Unless you are a very big platforming genre fan and have simply run out of things to play, it's a bit tough to recommend this whole-heartedly. When the design works, it works with confidence and the potential for something more that this project never quite realizes. I give it a thumbs up only on grounds that if you're interested in game design, there's a lot to learn! Many lessons for developers, players, and donators, both good and bad. It's an experience worth witnessing - though ideally playing - at some point or another.
The most tragic thing about this whole picture is that the very feature that got the release delayed for many months in the name of fulfilling baseline Kickstarter promises - co-op play - is one I just cannot get to enjoy, as nobody seems to want to play it!

This is my first review, as a general rule I usually let you guys handle this kinda thing, but in this case I felt I had to. First off, I love the game as you can probably tell by my hours played. I enjoy games that allow me to build slowly over time, and I don't like easy quick gratification games. I spent prolly the first 100 hours just trying new maps, learning the game, basically just getting a plan together. Finally I settle on Westbridge Hills, I spent the next 300 hours building a business, no money mods, just hard work and time. I like that I can come home from work, spend an hour baleing hay, feeding animals or whatever, save the game and log out, no strings attached like a MMO, which is my normal sort of game. As all gamers know, it is very important to save regularly in this sort of game, one power flicker from a storm or whatever, and you just lost an hours work, or even more if you're not careful, so I save on a regular basis. So this is where the bad comes in. I get up on Saturday and start my normal deal, let's get this field mowed before I have to leave for the day,  I get it done, save the game, and leave. I come home later that day, log into the game and POOF!!,, all placables, as well as equipment is GONE!!,, just gone..  I still have my money, but everything, and I mean everything else is just gone. I don't want to give the game a bad review, I feel that I certainly got my monies worth if you figure the hours of play time that I enjoyed, but I still had big plans for that farm. I tried to just say the heck with it and start a new one, on a new map, but it went from a fun process, to just plain work.  I'm sure you smart computer guys know a way to have a back up save, so you could have gotten around this, but I just counted on the game save alone. I don't want to spend more time learning to hack game files, than I do enjoying a game. I'm gonna leave a thumbs up, since it really is a cool game, but with a warning. If you lose all those hours, well that's just to damn bad.

Recommended, with caveats:
- Pro: Amazing art direction! Just look at the trailer and the screenshots. Sprite animations aren't always as smooth as you'd like, however, and looks like they could have been improved with a few more frames.
- Pro: Great bosses! Fighting giant bosses (quite literally Giant bosses, here) and somehow winning is always fun. These bosses are also well-designed, and not one of them feels like a rehash of any of the others. My one criticism with the boss battles would be how tiny you are next to the giants, especially when the camera zooms out so you can see a larger section of the boss arena -- it can be a little tricky to see what you are doing and whether you're attacking in the right direction, especially when your sprite is standing behind the boss.
- Pro/Con: The map design isn't perfect. Before boss battles, you have to explore environments to unlock keys - runes - that allow you to transport to each boss arena. One for the first, two for all the rest excepting the final boss. These environments are well-designed and fun to navigate, presenting unique atmospheres and challenging you in different ways. However, to have a good chance in the boss battles you'll want to step off the beaten path to collect power-ups and health boosts - the latter of which aren't marked on the map - which, after the first few worlds, can start to feel like a drag. The joy of exploration gives way to the feeling of wadding through padding keeping you from getting to the good stuff.
That said, similarly to the bosses themselves, every world is different -- in one map, you'll climb the branches of Yggdrasil while an eagle swoops down from you as you get closer to her nest, in another, you'll connect the dots in the clouds to form constellations or dash through the snow inbetween bursts of wind as blizzards periodically ravage the land. While each world starts to outstay its welcome if you try to collect everything, they all feel unique from eachother.
- Con: The controls are somewhat sluggish and slow in all areas -- it's only when you activate the speed boost power that you feel like you're actually moving and acting quickly. I feel like the game would have felt a lot more dynamic if both your own and your enemies' movement and actions were sped up somewhat.
- Con: It's not every long at all. You can go for achievements (defeat gods without powers, without taking damage), and there's Valhalla Mode (NG+) which toughens the bosses up and changes up their patterns somewhat, but a run where you make a dash for each power-up and take down the bosses without limiting yourself won't take more than an evening's worth of gaming.
In summary, I'd only recommend getting it on full price if you really wanted to support the developers (and I'd recommend looking at the Sundered kickstarter before that), but it's definitely worth getting if you can get it on sale.

Cat or Bread is one of the most innovative games I have ever played. On the surface it looks like a simple clicker game, but everything goes so much deeper than that. The game begins with a Unity logo which quickly becomes the intro screen, written in russian no less. Some people would be put off by the russian language, but it rewards persistant players with a somewhat happy chiptune song. The hardest challenge in "Cat or Bread?" is navigating the menus, among the other soul crushing features "Cat or Bread?" is a game mode that is akin to dark souls. It seems a little too similar to games such as sakura clicker, or Clicker Heros. For an indefinite period of time you are able to click a button, which increases your score by one, and allows your timer bar to become larger, and another button, that increases your score my ten, but decreases your timer bar. I have yet to see a similar system implemented within another game, besides dark sales of course.
All in all "Cat or Bread" is a shameless rip off of Space Waifu 2: Waifus in Space, which is by far, the greatest video game ever created.

I don't write reviews much, if at all, but I'm willing to for this masterpiece!
I've been looking for a fun, calm, and relaxing game centered around animals and that's what I got. I love this game and I've barely dived into it.
I started off as a stray cat on on the side of a road. I went through some tutorial stuff and chose one of the three clans. (Forest Clan, Mystic Clan, and I believe the Mountain Colony.) I went about my buisness. Meeting my local clan members, hunted, fought, etc. I also encountered some interesting story quest that I'm currently working hard on. I'm curious as to where these story quests are leading and I hope to get back on in a minute to continue my journey to find out. I can't wait to see what else this game offers as it seems pretty deep in a sense.
Let's break down all the good points I personally found with game.
Music: Great. Not annoying and very nice to the ears. Excellent job to the musicians.
Graphics: To the level of RPG Maker's graphics with a little hint of DS styled graphics tossed in too. I personally like it and thinks it suites the game.
Story: Not much to it at the start, but you tend to get the general idea. Nothing too gripping, but good enough to get you started. The game is designed for you to make your own story, so that's mostly what you do. (Like Skyrim, Minecraft, etc.) Story quests do show up later and they are interesting.
Gameplay: This is where the game shines. The menu interface is nice and simple, while the movement, hunting, and fighting work like a charm. The skill based level system is a nice touch, as it keeps the gameplay from feeling too stale and it also helps that you get XP for almost anything. (Outside the colonies.) You can also decorate your house which is pretty cool, and you even have a friendship mechanic with the citizens. (Still not sure how it works completely though. I'm still experimenting.) The hunger system that's in the game is nice and doesn't feel too intrusive. On a side note, hunting takes practice. So expect to take a good bit trying to figure out the hunting mechanic.
Conclusion: If you want a realistic cat simulator, then this game ain't for you. But if you want a game simular to Harvest Moon, Sims, or Animcal Crossing, then here you go. I do have one issue and that there's lag in the section with pruple rock pillars, even with fancy lighting turned off , but that's minor.
Making games in Game Maker is not easy. (I should know.) But this small team showed what you can do with the program when you know what your doing. Makes me rethink games I used to work on.
Anyways, I love this game and I hope to see more for this game in the future. Great job Falcon Team. :)

I'm writing this review, as if it was a book. If it was a book, it would be a helluva great one. From the beautifully crafted story, to the intelligence behind it. The characters are constructed with such complexity, and truthfulness, that you feel immersed as if you were in the story. Every moment feels like it matters, like you are crafting this beautiful story.
The best part? You choose what story you want. Essentially, there are routes to go within the story, autonomy, grace, empathy, and military. You build a robot choosing to go down any of these four routs, and anything inbetween. So essentially, you have
endless stories. Now obviously you don't have as much as I just said, but it is certainly enough to satisfy, being that each route can be somewhere between 1-3 hours. 3 being a take-your-time kind of feel, and 1 being rush through the dialouge, i've already seen this.
Each of the stories are so radically different that you can truly choose the type of story you want. From creating robots of mass destruction to bend the world to your will. To creating a peaceful movement that preaches robot equality, you can do it all. All of the routes you choose are all made with serious depth, so that, no matter which path you choose, you will almost certainly enjoy it. It all follows a baseline of how things go, so that most opportunities are available throughout most playthoughs, but each playthrough has it's own special traits that the others do not.
To summarize: This game is essentially the perfected version of a choose-your-own-path adventure game. It has the depth and charm of a short book, yet it keeps the individuality of choosing your story. I encourage you to get this game, wether you plan on playing one singular story, or all. It is very enjoyable and you should play it.
I don't know how to review games that well, but I can review stories, and this is a ♥♥♥♥ing good one. Buy it.

Factorio is, in a sense, the game that I've been waiting for my whole life.
There's been a ton of resource management  / base building games out there, but not in the sense I've been longing for. In those games resource management is a means to an end, usually to build an army and destroy your opponent. Typically you're restricted in some way, be it time, resources, or ultimately, space. And after your opponent is crushed, the base you spent hours building and perfecting is meaningless. You won. Go along.
Not in Factorio. Here, the resource management and base building are both the means and the end. You build a factory to get stuff, and you use that stuff to build a bigger, better factory. Why? To get more stuff of course, for the bigger and better factory. There's always bottlenecks to unravel, production lines to boost, conveyor belts to draw. And you are limited in only your amount of imagination and dedication. In an endlessly generated 2D world you just take your train track a bit further for the next iron ore patch. Eventually you will consume the forests, drain the oceans, choke the air - hell, if Factorio had elevation, you bet you would grind the mountains to concrete flats. When Alien Artifacts were still around, even the enemies that tried to kill you were just resources. You didn't fight them because they were evil aliens - you fought them because you wanted their biomass. (Actually, in this sense, the evil alien is you.)
I'm an engineer and I go to work to take time off Factorio.

Man, what a deal this is -- I paid $50 or so for this when it was new over a decade ago, and then bought the expansions separately after that. Fast forward to now and while I can find the discs, they're scratched up and my computer won't read them properly half the time. I got this for $2.49 on sale and it is very much worth that price. Hell, I'd say it's worth ten times that when you look at the amount of scenarios and content this game has.
For the uninitiated, you build a theme park... sometimes from scratch, sometimes adding on to an existing park. Some scenarios require you to have a certain amount of guests, a certain park rating, or increase the value of the park by a certain amount before a year or more has passed in the game. There are dozens of attractions, coasters, rides, and shops to place into your park and quite a few besides just the roller coasters allow you to construct a ride of your own design (other "build your own" rides include a boat hire, train, monorail, car ride, log flume, and water slides), and there are a dozen or so types of coasters on top of that.
Building and running a successful park is a balancing act of proper pricing, layout, marketing, and well-designed custom rides. You can't just make a coaster with a 90 foot drop that sends your patrons through all kinds of madness at 80 mph -- they won't get on it because it's too scary. A successful coaster has lots of different elements (hills, banked turns, helixes, tunnels, loops, and what have you), goes through those elements at the proper speed, and has scenery and theming that add to the ride's excitement (like rushing through a row of trees after a big drop, or a loop that has a track going through it).
I feel like I could talk about this game forever... in short, if you like building things, buy this game. If you like theme park sims, buy this game. If you are put off by the dated graphics (which still look pretty darn good to me), buy this game anyway and be surprised at the depth and amount of content there is.
I can't recommend this game enough.

Alien Swarm is a free, top-down, fast-paced shooter in which you [and a team of up to 3 other players] gun down. . . Well, swarms of aliens.
And let me tell you, it will be a team of up to 3 other players. To try and fight your way through this alone is a near impossible task, Alien Swarm is a very difficult game. It's great. The aliens alone aren't strong. They are limited to melee or incredibly slow ranged missiles and are dispatched easily. But of course, there are swarms of them. Without quick manoeuvring and teamwork you can become easily surrounded and you'll soon discover that the player characters are about as hardy as the aliens you've been gunning down.
Personally, I've been playing it with only one friend of mine and, frankly, we've got stuck. We'll need to rope in a third if we hope to have enough medkits and ammo packs to beat this damned level.
It's a very fun game, and at no point does the difficulty feel frustrating. The game doesn't feel unfair in its harshness. When the player dies it is the players fault, it isn't due to any random or unpredictable events. This makes it all the more satisfying when you finally overcome the level that has up until that point been kicking your♥♥♥♥♥
Each player can choose 1 of 4 classes to suit their playstyle, though in practice the only differences are available weapons and load-outs. And also the Tech class is often required to complete a level via hacking mini-games. The hacking mini-games themselves aren't particularly challenging, but can be quite intense when your team or partner are relying on you doing them quickly as the alien swarms won't stop for your convenience.
The medic class is also a must, any small mistake can be severely damaging to a squad-mates health bar.
As well as choosing your own class, there are a surprising amount of weapons and extra items to equip yourself with before charging into battle, most of which require the player to level up before using.
Which brings us onto the short campaign.
The official campaign of Alien Swarm is far too short for the player to actually unlock the content by levelling up by playing through it. This is where the community comes in. Alien Swarm was released with the source code of the game for free. This means that there are plenty of custom campaigns created for the game and a quick glance at the Steam community forums will point you in the right direction of finding those.
There is not a lot else to say about Alien Swarm, it's a free, fun [and difficult!] co-op shooter and does an excellent job at keeping the players on their toes. Rarely is there a moment of downtime for the players to prepare themselves for the next attack, indeed if the players stop moving then the game will send a small but steady stream of aliens their way.
It's free, so I can't not recommend it. But I do highly recommend having at least one other person play it with you. Even if you have the skills to survive on your own, you won't have the ammo. Also, I totally recommend it.

Honestly I would say this game is worth 60$, not that I want it to be 60$, because less people would buy it. 15 dollars is a very good price, you should get it even if you don't like warriors. This game might seem intimidatingly complex at first, but has a really nice curve to it. I love the technical mod packs for Minecraft, but the problem with those is that there's no clear path to take; it's just one big jumble of resources, machines and crafting recipes. Factorio solves that problem by implementing a technology tree. For instance: in order to build a diesel locomotive, you first need to understand logistics, automation and engines. This way, you won't get overwhelmed with choices and can take your time understanding each new tech you unlock.
If you're looking for a solid game to really sink some time into, look no further.

This will be my very first review, so let me begin by saying that I'm seeing a whole lot of whining and b!tching about this game from reviewers who bought it knowing it's state of development. It's early access. Anyone who's bought an early access title before should know what that entails.
If you don't have the patience for long waits then you have no buisiness buying this or any other early access title. Just because you pay for an incomplete product (and knowingly doing so) does not mean they are required to build a game on YOUR acceptable time frame. This game (as far as I'm aware of) is being built by one man. Not a small crew, but one man. Make your choice of purchase while being aware of this.
Now. Lets get to the facts of this game and clear up some of the half truths and misleading information.
First, yes this game has been in development for a while now. And yes it's still in an Alpha state. What does this mean for you? If you purchase this as is then you will be getting a game that's missing a lot, and likely become very bugy from time to time. Despite this, there are still a great many things to do for someone who is willing to learn without having their hand held like it was when they played WoW.
Next, I've seen reviews saying that there is no tutorial, this is false. There is a playable tutorial that will show you the very basics of this game without holding your little WoW hand and telling you every little thing about the game.
Now, about the updates, yes they are few and far between. Apparently people are still under the impression that one person, that one man, is required to release updates every week or hold their hand and take time away from what is most likely his real world life, job, and family to tell each and every one of them (personally, as they are special little snow flakes) what's going on and when things will be done. While I agree that his lack of communication is very unprofessional, again, this is one man who likely has a life. Like a few of us. And this is most likely his first attempt at build and selling a game. Keep this in mind before purchasing.
I've also seen reviews stating that there is no new content. This is very much false. While some of these reviews are old enough to have somewhat of an excuse, I've actually seen newer reviews claiming this. Again, it's false. This game was released bare bones. There was almost nothing to it. There has been a significant amount of small content added that most would likely miss while they were busying wiping their eyes and lamenting on how they missed the good old handholding days of WoW when they'd get into trouble with their Pally and just bubble and Hearth. And a little complaining got all the drop rates adjusted to drop for them. I know. You are upset there is no bubble and hearth for when you are about to die and you are upset that you actually have to look for parts to build a decent gun instead of handing you a nuke. Yes, it's very sad, but you will live. But in all seriousness, there are a lot of items that I've heard about that I've not even found yet myself. Also, the last update just released a new area that appears to be an instanced zone that will have something to do with the upcoming storyline. So to finish this story, yes, there is new content. Yes, there are new things to do. The real problem is people not satisfied with how far apart the updates are. Again, if you don't have the patience for it then don't buy this game.
I've also seen reviews about the graphics and gameplay saying they have not recieved any updates or improvements. This is, again, false. The AI had a big overhaul. The spawning system recieved a very big overhaul. There is no longer Enemies walking through walls, or standing at the base of the building that you are bravely cowering on waiting for them to kill eachother so you can escape. I know, you are angry that he took away your exploit and you now have to fight. You're♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that you now have to worry about the enemy jumping up to your floor and spray painting your oily parts all over the wall from a close range shottyng  blast. Yes, it's sad.
As for the graphics and optimization, yes, they can use a tweaking, but they have been tweaked already. I was originally getting around 12-16 ish fps. After the recent update I now get around 20-40 ish fps. On a 4 year old laptop running a 2.4 cpu, 8 gigs of ram, and a GTX 840m. I feel pretty certain that your gaming rig will likely do better.
To finish up this little book I'll close with this: If you're not a spoiled little manchild missing your WoW days of having everything handed to your little Alliance pally and can actually LEARN to play something new that ISN'T finished yet and are capable of understanding that concept then you MIGHT just like this game. It's not for everyone. But if you have the maturity to understand that not everything has to be Witcher 3 quality just because you demand it, then you just might enjoy this for what it is. It's different. It's going to be slow and watching the growth could be enjoyable.

Full disclosure: I have like 0 hours played because I played the DRM-free version. I was a $15-tier Kickstarter backer.
MN9 is an OK game. It's not offensively awful and there are certainly worse games out there. It's got some bugs and the presentation overall is fairly lackluster, but it's still playable.
The difficulty in reviewing this game is that nothing stands out about it. All of it is very simply mediocre. There are no highs and no lows. It is the feeling of "meh" manifested into game form.
Let's be very clear about one thing: There are plenty of "meh" Megaman games out there. But MN9 is trying to be a spiritual sequel to Megaman, so one wishes that it had captured the spirit of the essential Megaman games rather than the "meh" ones. MN9 does not do this, and if one were to rank it against the vast continuum of Megaman games it is quite squarely in the league of the more mediocre Megaman games.
The question in a Steam review however is "Would I recommend this game" and the answer to that is a very solid no. There are plenty of more satisfying and fun Megaman clones out there such as Shovel Knight and 20XX to name a few. There is also no shortage of Megaman titles to explore.
Ultimately what I am saying is this: Mighty No. 9 is an absolutely mediocre Megaman clone, and there is no need to settle for it when there are much better and more satisfying options out there.

I'm very happy with how this game turned out. The gameplay is really fun, and the voice acting is just the right kind of goofy that you'd expect from a game that doesn't take itself too seriously. The graphics are fine at max settings and the game is a good challenge if you like old school platformers.

Despite all the talent and all the delays and all the money, the resulting game is an utter failure.  Glitchy and imprecise controls combined with levels covered in instant death and bosses that require precise timing make the game frustrating and unenjoyable.
I grew up playing Mega Man, and this is a travesty.  As much as I want to recommend it because it's a spiritual successor to Mega Man... I just can't.  The game is terrible, and I'm very disappointed.

Despite the backlash this game has gotten, it isn't a bad game.  Mediocre, yes, but certainly not bad.  The powers are all useful in their own ways, and give a few different ways to solve the different puzzles.  The missile power from Battalion obliterates everything, however.  While I can't say I was terribly impressed by this game, I don't find it as offensive as other do.
And yes, I was a backer.

I am a huge fan of Megaman, so when I first heard that Mighty No. 9 was being made, my brain exploded. I pre-ordered it! And I went to steam on it's realese date and! Delayed. 'Okay', I thought. 'They might be fixing a few glitches, it will be out soon!' And then I waited. And waited. And waited. I thought it was cancelled. Then... just a couple days ago I saw it. It was ready to be installed! I was so hyped. I was ready to have fen and then!...
It Crashed. It turnes out I needed to change something in the game's code! That's a good sign! Then, I played it and... well... How do I say this? The graphics are hit-or-miss, the story is lack-luster, most of the boss weapons are useless, the boss designs are pretty crappy, the dash feature can be very glitchy, and there is day one DLC. Also, I pre-ordered the game, and it didn't come with the pre-order stuff. I would have rather they had just done a slight over-haul of a Megaman game rather than try to force inovation where it wasn't needed. Finally, it is quite hard. Even on normal mode (Yes, there isn't an easy mode) and 9 lives per round, it took me a while to get through the first boss level I took on!
If you want a better Megaman style game, get 20XX, a Megaman x rouge-like game! Or Megaman Legacy Collecton. That one is great as well! If you want a mobile Megaman game, get Rockbot. It's okay for a first project. Or, if you wan't a non steam Megaman Game, get the FPS Megaman 8-BIT Deathmatch! It has a campaign and Multiplayer (Made on Zandorum)! But buying this isn't worth the price tag. Wait for a sale or something.
Overall, 4/10, Meaning it CAN be fun and fairly challenging, but it's not worth the cost... This was probably the most dissopointing game for me. I mean, I have seen some crap, I have seen some bull crap, but I will NOT bealive that 4 MILLION USD and over 3 years went into this. Maybe some of the money was stored for later, but I would rather have it all be used for one potentially good game, instead of many potentially crappy ones. Upsides: I love the design, gameplay, and role of call, the game itself can be very fun sometimes, the DLC was great, And some of the weapons are really cool.
However, if your not a Megaman fanatic like I am, it will probably be a 5/10, or if you are a bit more cynical, 3/10.

When I first heard that this game had a story mode, I wasn't expecting a whole lot out of it. I've heard many times developers bragging about a story full of difficult choices, and they almost always end up being sub-par. While there are only a few to be found here, each one had me pausing and thinking for a good while after each game day had ended. The consequences of each decision can be grand or small, and while little may change other than your acquired ending, it's all about making the morally correct choices in a morally corrupt world.
The gameplay starts out fairly complicated, and gets even more and more convoluted towards the end. While it doesn't stray far from checking the same documents over and over again, it's the story that keeps you curious as to what happens next. Not to say the gameplay is boring, I certainly don't think it is, but the story is the focus, and rightly so.
You will likely only get a few hours out of this game, but I would say they are a few hours well spent on a unique game that deserves your attention.

This should have been an animated movie. As a game, it is slow and boring. 8/20.
Obviously it's core feature, all "hand drawn". Okay, that's nice, it does have a nice particular touch to it. But that doesn't mean it is good (It's not bad either. It's far from both, right in the middle). Here's what's what : only a few recurring things are actually well animated, otherwise, it's pretty much a bunch .png moving or not moving, and most of the time, the only thing we see besides the character is the ground... Nice backgrounds are rare and zoomed out bits feel very cheap because it oftens underlines a very rough level design.
This is also very "meh". The story is simple and uses bits of mythology. Though the narrative experience is extremely good, as both voice acting and atmosphere fit perfectly, the story in itself is plain as white paper. As a writer myself, this is not even remotely good. It never got beyond the concept phase : Warrior and bosses. We just stumble across more or less random mythologic elements or facts. Some are very well told and drawn, and some are about a cow and a celestial shrimp ? I'm sorry, but for the very few elements they chose to put in the game, there are way more interesting things to consider before those. It's just out of context. They do not matter in the story anyway. So, what they have here is a good start that never got beyond that, supported by a powerful voice acting and ambiance. Again, it's right in the middle of good or bad.
Now this is the real deal breaker here... I don't even know why it is a game. Jotun is all about art, but it forgot the art of its own support : a video-game. The gameplay is simply bad. It's not "super bad", just bad. First off, the controls does not feel right nor good. Everything is heavy and slow... The only 3 possible attacks reacts on a different timeline from your mind and your input, so if you want to react to something, you have to take the time to adapt to it. Not only it is counter-intuitive, but it also feels heavy and plain as you know what's gonna happen, and you know you're gonna do this seconds before it actually happens. Basically, you live the game twice : in your mind, then seconds later, depending on the pattern or the attack, in the game... It makes it all feel even slower. I do have to mention that I had to get back to the "oldversion" because the latest one made my Xbox One controller bug, and I found this solution in a thread from someone with a similar issue, so it's not on my end.
Now, as I was saying, a whole 95% of the game is spent walking around staring at the empty ground... It's like they drawed the maps and were too lazy to add gameplay to it. You find the same falling trees you can cut in different levels... And that's pretty much it.
Now, I want the name of the guy who thought a story about a Viking Warrior fighting Gods to enter Valhalla had to be about cereal-boxes level labyrinths and (that's a big word for it) puzzles ! It's so out of place and out of purpose. I'd rather walk a straigth pathway while a story is being told and artworks go by rather than that. It's full of nothing ! You have to find, or not, 3-4-ish things per levels while trying to understand why the map reflects so bad the actual environment. You cannot lose yourself, and actually, it is pretty much straigth paths to the end, and when you spot a different path, it will surely leads to something. There is no work done there.
The second part of the game, the last remaining 5% of playtime, are bosses. This is what the actual main part of gameplay is about : fighting gigantic bosses. Some are nice, some are not. None of them have any originality in their patterns. They are nicely drawn and, sometimes, nicely animated too (when they're not just idle or locked in a frame waiting for something to trigger in their code). There are only 6 of them... And, sadly, because you gain unbalanced powerups as you move on, the difficulty goes down so while you may find it challenging to fight the first one, you can pretty much rekt the 3 last ones while scratching your balls. Only if you go for the annoying "beat the following bosses without using half of the gameplay features of the game" achievements may it be challenging.
One last thing... Putting stones busts of the devs right before the final boss is the most idiotic thing of all in a narrative game. It completely ruins immersion and what should be the peak of the story gets completely evapoared and becomes simply "a final boss".
The ambiance is good. The music is not great but it does its job and fits the rest perfectly.
It is a rough. It is barely a game actually. This is a symphony of visual, sound and narrative art. Though it is still far from good and deserves a proper storyline, I believe this would have make a very memorable movie to keep, a very good one, with a particular hand-drawn style and ambiance. Thinking of it, to be honest, it's the same exact base as Dante's Inferno : A Warrior figthing mythological dieties to deserve the after-life, but Dante's Inferno has a tremendous amount of design and research and it adapted the mythology for its support and ambiance and story. Jotun does nothing of that. It's as plain as it could have been, which is sad, for with more work, it would have been a powerful piece of art.
In the end, it's not.
I love mythology and I did not waste my time playing it. It has its enjoyable moments, though they are very rare. If you can get your hands on it in a bundle or for a couple of €/$, try it out.
And don't forget : Wether we like something or not has nothing to do with the quality of it. You can find yourself to like it even if it's not good, same as you can dislike good games ☺

I wasn't expecting much out of this game when I saw it in the Steam store, but I like Harvest Moon, Stardew Valley, and cats, so I figured why not. Well...I've actually been playing this today as much as I would my favorite Harvest Moon games. The pixel artwork is gorgeous, the dialog is so endearing, and the music is REALLY great (I absolutely love the hints of jazziness in several of the tracks). There's a surprising amount of depth to this game and you can just tell that the devs are thoughtful people. The only thing I don't like is the amount of killing lol. It seems a little out of place for such a cute game. One minute you're getting attached to an irrelevant NPC from your colony as they talk about their secret pet mouse that they couldn't bear to kill, and the next minute you hear sounds of the rival colony slashing them to death. I would definitely suggest this game to anyone who likes cute, laid-back games (if you can get past the murdering of cute little pixelated cats with equally cute names). It starts off a little slow, but it's very fun overall.

I think I would consider this game like another Stardew Valley or World's Dawn but without the farming side. In this game you become a cat and you get to experience its life in the wild. When you start the game, you get to choose between three colonies of different cats and that colony becomes your new home. Some of the things you are able to do in the game is hunt, forage, mine, have a romance, and do a short story. The mechanics for the same are simple enough to get the hang of and if for some reason you do not like the placement of the keys, then you can change them. I haven't played around with the mining mechanic too much but it's like Stardew Valley. There are a hundred levels and the farther you go down the better gems you find.
For the romance option, for each colony you join there are three romance options in each colony. I have not tested it but I believe that even if you are in colony A but like one of the cats in colony B, you can still romance that cat. It's just out of your way to visit them. When you join a colony the romanceable cat starts with two stars and once you reach five stars you can date and then that cat gains a heart. Once that heart turns red then you can marry. Eventually you can have kittens and I believe you can have four. I haven't reach that part yet so I can not say what happens after you get the kittens. I believe you can name them and build your relationship with them. Also if you do not like your partner cat then you can get a black rose and break up with them.
The story/quest of the game isn't too difficult. It's pretty much a fetch quest of different plants, animals, and bugs that you can find in the game. Its taken me about three years in the game to really find everything. Some things are more rare then others and you could buy some of the items if you don't have the patience to look. The story doesn't have very much depth and they try and cover that up with the fetch quests but this game is not really big enough for a large story so the quest length wasn't too bad in my opinion.
They let you customize your cat at the beginning of the story. Through out the game, you can buy differant colors of fur for your cat and accessories at different colonies. One thing I like that the game does is that they allow you to recustomise your cat at any time in the game. You could be blue one day and white the next, with different colored eyes. The game also has an experience system where you upgrade four skills to level ten such as hunting, swimming, foraging, and fighting. The game also has festivals at the end of each season where you can play mini games and get tokens. The tokens let you buy quest items, furniture, accessories and even pets for your cat like butterflies and fireflies.
The seasons are ten days long and there are four seasons. The last day of the season is the festival where all the colonies gather. Another thing you can do in the game is upgrade your den/home. You can add a storage room, garden (kinda), nursery, and two additional rooms to put random stuff in.
Overall I think this game is cute but there is a lot of grinding for the game and the main story is a fetch quest. If you do not mind that and even enjoy that type of game then you will have a blast. I think the customising of your cat in the game is well done and they give you a ton of options and the map is cute/pretty. The music in the game is also well done. There is a huge cat book series I read as a kid called "Warriors" by Erin Hunter and this game brought back major memories of that book series. So over all I like the game, I personally think 15$ is a bit much and would wait for the game to go on sale. The game is very grindy but other then that I had no issues with it and thought it was fun and brought back memories of my childhood.

This game is very simple; it's just one hidden object scene after another, with a minimal story and a few easy puzzles to solve along the way. If you like the artwork in the screenshots, then you'll probably like the game (I did).

Season of Mystery may be old and outdated for a hidden object game, but the accompanying murder mystery visual novel is worth the gameplay inconveniences.
Season of Mystery: The Cherry Blossom Murders was made in 2010, but it feels more like a hidden object game from late 2007: gameplay is nothing but hidden object scenes, of which several have to be replayed up to three times. The low-resolution graphics and some of the incredibly cheap tricks to hide some items also point to outdated mechanics.
I still would wholeheartedly recommend it, because the story is strong enough to carry the game through those ancient HOG mechanics.
The writing and presentation follow the style of a visual novel, where we play as the wife of a recently murdered American embassy worker stationed in Japan. Interestingly, the cultural differences play only a small role, as the plot focuses mostly on the investigation. Since this put the emphasis on the dialogue and characters, Season of Mystery almost feels like a classic British whodunit, which is a wonderful change of pace compared to the standard fantasy adventure stories most HOGs offer.

The most morbid RTS I have yet seen. An RTS where you cannot command units. You are a disease. You are fighting against a simulation of disease response by human organizations. Your goal is to kill all humans before being cured. Your methods are choosing Transmision vector, Symptoms, and resistance to climate/drugs/research mutations. The choice of when to mutate how is interesting and fun to experiment with as you interact with the simulated global population. Expect to lose often as you feel out how the game responds to stimuli. Games can be very short, and there's a mild clicker aspect to keep you engaged in what would otherwise be a very hands off game. Pause often to keep up with clicking things and to spend mutation points at precise times.
This game's mobile origins show, but its enjoyable enough to spend a few hours on trying to wipe out humanity.

I'd like to clarify that I was one of the people waiting for this game from the moment I heard it was announced, several months ago, by an email that told me the developed of Warrior Cats: Untold Tales was working on a new game. However, I also didn't follow the news on this game aside from its release date, so I could have an experience without more expectations than necessary.
I'd also like to clarify this is my first attempt at a more in-depth review of a game, so I apologize if I'm not really up to par.
Also, this review may contain spoilers for events throughout parts of the game, if you consider things like characters and details on recurring events to be spoilers.
As someone who still plays Untold Tales today because I find it fun and familiar, I was hoping for an experience that wasn't a carbon copy of Untold Tales' simple formula, but took the parts that are still fun even now and remixed them into something even better, and something new, and, well... I wasn't disappointed. Cattails is altogether a very different experience from Untold Tales, that's something I can tell just by playing the small amount I have. It feels a lot more like Stardew Valley, which... I personally don't mind. Probably because I love Stardew Valley.
The hunting system from Untold Tales is here, but far better executed - probably because this game actually has a budget to work with and a more experienced developer, but I digress. There's also a lot more variety in the prey you can catch, and the general distance from which you can do so. Some prey even has variants, such as the three types of mice I've come across so far - there might be more, I don't know. I really like it, even though I spent about ten minutes in the tutorial because I didn't realize I had to press the spacebar to pounce rather than just releasing shift like in Untold Tales. Another cool thing that I'll put here is that what seem like uninteractable set pieces, like butterflies and fireflies, can be attacked and collected. I've been collecting butterflies myself.
There are three colonies, and after the tutorial you're given the option to join any one of them. Coco, the tutorial cat, pushes the Forest Colony but I'm a rebel, so I picked the Mystic Colony. They live in the wetlands and are led by Alisa. I haven't played with either of the other colonies yet, so my experience is 100% a Mystic experience.
Every colony has a few datable cats. After looking over my options - the older-than-you Slip, the leader Alisa who I haven't had a chance to get to know, and Nil, who needs higher self-esteem - I went for Nil. Mostly because I gave him catnip one time and he told me he didn't believe he was worthy of it, and I can relate to that.
Cat relationships are another place where it falls into being a lot like Stardew Valley. For one, it's not locked by gender - the player doesn't have an established gender. Secondly, you have a relationship level, one to five stars, with each cat. (The datable cats have hearts instead of green arrows in their dialogue boxes.) At four or higher, I think (I'm not sure?) the tutorial wizard Coco will appear in front of your den and instruct you to go get a red rose and ask the object of your affections out already.
Once you've been dating long enough and have a relationship of five stars, you can buy a certain item that allows you to ask another cat's paw in marriage. Holy catrimony, if you will. Once married, your spouse moves into your den and you can have kittens. I haven't had any luck with my many, many proposals to Nil so far, so that's about as far as my knowledge extends.
Something I do know more about, though, is dens! You start with a smallish den, but partway through your first winter Molby the Construction Mole will show up in front of it, install his calling card without your consent, and offer to expand your home for money. Some of these upgrades are useful! I've only got two so far, the nursery (required to have kittens) and the herb garden, which lets you grow the plants you forage from around the world, even out of season. You can decorate your den with items from all your exploring. The items don't disappear, which is nice. I've started a stockpile of prey next to my nest.
On that note, let's talk about skills! Hunting, foraging, and fighting, and probably other things I haven't noticed, all help earn you experience points that you can use to upgrade your skills. Unlike Stardew Valley, your skills don't just level up on their own when you do things - you can apply your experience points to any of the skills, which can be useful if you want to level up something like swimming. I haven't reached the cap (level 10) on any of my skills yet, so that's a bonus.
The seasons change, too. They're each ten days long, with a festival on the tenth day of each. A festival is where cats gather at the Sacred Temple, the center of the map, to just kinda chill and compete in festival games. You can earn special currency to spend on items like special colorings for your cat or hard-to-catch prey if you need it for something or decorations for your den or even a pet butterfly.
There's a lot more things that I can't really talk about because I haven't gotten very far in them - like relationships between colonies, and the mines, and even the main questline. I haven't spent a lot of time on any of those things, so anything I could say would be extremely limited and hasn't come up much in my experience. But that's a big part of this game.
TL;DR: A unique experience, but if you came here looking for the sequel to Untold Tales because of the developer you'll be disappointed. If you really like Stardew Valley or other similar games, though, and are looking for something kind of similar but also different - this might be a good game to check out.

Im an alpha tester as well as a lover of Falcon's last games. I have played this game on and off for quite a while and i have a lot to say about it. I havent played as much as my best friend (an alpha tester and backer), but i've been involved in the communities discord and heard many opinions about this game! Now, here goes my review!
Gameplay:
The gameplay consists of living your life out in a colony as a wild cat. Your main task is hunting to gain food so your cat does not starve. Your cat can catch many wild critters by holding shift and sneaking up on the prey. It feels a bit unbalanced, because hunting is surprisingly challenging at first, but at high levels the prey basically walks into your paws.  The hunting feature is fun although leaves a bit to be desired.
The next mechanic is foraging. Your cat can pick berries and roots that will restore a tiny bit of hunger, and certain plants to heal you. There are also misc plants with effects like growing territory and giving your cat a boost. Its a cute mechanic and i dont have much to complain about it.
Although, it feels a little unrealistic for cats to eat berries, but i wont complain. One of my cats in real life loves to eat people things sometimes, I caught her eating noodles the other day! It was hilarious!
Battling is a major part of the game, and the thing i was most excited for.  The battle system is pressing spacebar for attack, and there are a couple special skills you can get, such as one that drains health overtime. But i have to say, the battle system could be much improved. Its repetitive, and at high levels, you can defeat patrols of 7 cats at once with ease, which is quite unrealistic. I believe developing the battle system offers a LOT of potential!
Now, here are my main issues regarding gameplay. As people said, it is incredibly fun. Also as people said, it can get really repetitive. My main issue is the game has a lack of balance. When you level up, it becomes so easy (even on hard mode) the game loses a portion of its fun. Prey and items are able to be spotted up on the minimap at high levels, and defeating patrols is extremely easy. The game goes into a cycle of waking your cat, catching prey, talking to  the cats, Maybe mining or some misc activity, but it is not a fun long term game.
Its good to play in short bursts, but i find a lack of incentive to be an issue. The game suffers because it does not have a very good quest or event system that can help you feel like you want to find items for a goal. There is a main quest where you can catch items and bring them to certain statues, which is something, but it is very simple and underwhelming, and seems to just be a continuation of the daily grind. It justs asks you to hunt items and bring them like usual, and does not offer anything unique, like a rescue quest, or a time quest, or maybe a special skill or reward for each quest.
In conclusion, the game is amazing, but i reccomend the following to improve the gameplay:
A random event system where you may have to find certain items, another cat, or maybe that plays out a little bit of story. Or, a quest system where you can find and bring back rewards. Something that keeps you motivated to play! Maybe some special accessory or event when you collect certain items. There should be something to break that repitition cycle so many people speak of, making it a true wilderness adventure.
But, thats my take on it.
Story:
Ill say that there is not quite a story in this game that is very developed. We have many cats we can talk to in our colonies, and they are quite cute characters. I like the uniqueness of the characters designs, and seeing my friends backer cats has made me very happy. You can give them items for dialogue, a fun system. Marriage and kits are great, and i have no suggestions on those.
Now, i know falcon has heard this a lot, but a suggested improvement has been to have marriage eligibility for every cat. You cannot marry many of the cats, including some of the communities favorite felines in the game. I do think that would be a positive change.
Coco, our mysterious helper, also has their own gamemode. Its the gameplay with the statues, where you give the statues items, the forest guardian quest. Now, my best friend, also an alpha tester, has said it leaves room for improvement, and i must agree. It was not very engaging to get the statues items, and it did not reap satisfying enough rewards for the effort. Now, why would i not like the system when i suggested quests and events? Well, it eases the repetitive grind. You are still looking out for the same items and living the same day, though, and it just did not seem any more interesting then your daily cat life.
Music:
The music? Well, it is what it is. Not amazing, but it has its moments. There are a couple tracks that play during seasons, which are nice, though i only really like the winter soundtrack. I still am satisfied with it, as music isnt a big deal for me, though it can get repetitive. I just realized I have the whole soundtrack too apparently, being an alpha backer, hehe.
Art:
I have a lot to say about the art of the game. Simply, I love it. The cats and enviroments look wonderful and natural. I have to say, this was a huge selling point of the game for me. Sure, you could say some of the cats profiles look a bit awkward, but the sheer effort that was put into it makes me unable to say anything bad about it. I love the charm of the leaves and bugs flying through the air, and the winter snow is beautiful. Thanks for making me feel like a real cat, falcon.
Conclusion:
Im going to end by saying that I really love cattails. I know it seems like i gave it some negative comments, but i want the game to improve. I love the potential, direction, art, everything. This game is important to me and im very thankful to falcon for this amazing game yet again.  It suffers from repetition, a bit of ability imbalance, and a oversimplified battle mechanic, but succeeds in aesthetic and design, adorable and unique direction and customization, and charming characters. I have met many wonderful friends who play this game, mainly through the discord.Thanks for letting me live life like how it goes in my cats wildest dreams!

This is a pretty decent game, and I think it's worth $15. Essentially it's a lot like Stardew Valley, but you- well, you're a cat. You hunt, forage, fight cats from other colonies to establish territorial dominance, do a little dungeon mining, collect item sets, and establish relationships with other cats.
The problem is that the gameplay mechanics themselves are rather basic, and after a few hours it definitely starts to feel repetitive. Stardew Valley sidestepped this problem by having a farm you could customize in almost every single way, along with stuff like fishing which made what could have been a throw-away mechanic engaging and lucrative. In Cattails, you're given character customization options, and you can eventually upgrade your home den to have stuff like a nursery or garden or aesthetic props, but none of it goes as far as Stardew does.
Combat consists of pressing the attack button until your opponent is dead, occasionally using some special powers you unlock through XP gains. You can, sort of, dodge attacks by moving away from enemies, and you can usually run from any fight if it's too tough or you're being mobbed. Stardew Valley's combat wasn't very good or focal either, but there was at least some variety in enemy types and a certain satisfaction in destroying a bug with a sword. As far as I can tell, Cattails has two enemy types: cats and dungeon bats of varying degrees of HP and attack strength; both attack or run away if their health is low. Considering that you can partake in optional battles every day, the system just doesn't have staying power.
The dungeon stuff is also underwhelming. You collect ores and gems to trade in for tokens. I may not just be going down deep enough, but at level 20 of the mines, all there was to do was break open rocks and fight the occasional bat. If there's any collectibles or unique things to be found there, I haven't gotten to it yet.
To hunt, you sneak up to prey (but not too close), until a circle fills up above their heads and you pounce. This is done for animals on land as well as fish. You can forage a moderate variety of plants that do several things, from healing to nourishment to applying poison damage on enemies to cementing your colony's control of a region.
The relationship system is well done, but also comparatively limited in content. There are about a handful or so of interactible NPCs in each colony/faction, and AFAIK only through festivals do you interact meaningfully with other colonies outside of battles. You can date NPCs from your colony and eventually marry them and have kittens if you want. The writing is well done, amusing and cute, though characters tend to repeat themselves as the days go by.
Despite its problems, though, I like Cattails. It needs more content put into it (after glancing at their website forums it looks like the devs are working on custom colony building) and it doesn't have nearly the same effortlessly addicting quality that Stardew Valley does, but it's bursting with charm. You could do a lot worse for fifteen bucks, and if it's ever on sale for less I'd call it a no-brainer if you're a fan of Harvest Moon/Stardew life simulation games.
