This is one of my top favorite Star Wars Games. You feel like an actual Jedi/Sith slashing through waves of enemies, and you feel like a master when you can pull off advanced combos. The storyline is pretty great, in my opinion, even if it might not be considered canon (welcome to Post-Disney takeover). Boss battles are intense enough to keep you engaged, but not so tough (at least at lower difficulties) that you'll completely rage quit (unless you're that bad, like I was when I tried this on my cousin's Wii). Speaking of which, the Wii version had a lot more sidequests and backstory, mostly involving the Jedi Temple on Coruscant. This version lacks those extra parts, but still maintains the primary plot and bosses. And it adds in the (spoilers) alternate timeline if Starkiller killed Vader, which was a nice touch.
Any issues I've had are mostly do to my own skill (or lack thereof) and my machine's capabilities (Macbook Pro). Some objects and scenes appear as nothing but black, glittery shapes with nothing to define where they are. This makes it difficult to navigate areas and know which object you're supposed to Force Push/Grab. I can only presume that when I get this onto a proper Windows machine, those graphical errors will hopefully disappear.
Overall, though, it is a fantastic game with hours of replay value trying to collect all of the holocrons and attempting to beat the game on harder difficulties. Great game for the Star Wars enthusiast.

Note that I think the game runs in 256-color mode, so it probably will not display correctly in Windows 7 or Windows 8, as those operating systems handled 256-color palettes differently than earlier or later versions of Windows.

Please read this review as to why I don't recommend this game. Honestly, I loved it but the cons outweigh the pros here.
SEASON OF MYSTERY: The Cherry Blossom Murders is a hidden-object game in a mystery genre that takes place in the 1890s of Japan.
First...I'll start with the good: The story.
Story: The story follows Irene, an american woman who came to Japan with her husband. Irene's husband was murdered and deemed to be suicide from the police. However, Irene believed that it wasn't suicide. This opens up to something bigger: kidnapping, staged suicides, and blackmail.
Now for the story, I don't wish to reveal more about it, as there will be spoilers. I can say what kept me playing the game was the constant contradicitons and strange evidence come across.
Graphics: I admit the graphics are beautiful and capture the feel of traditional Japan. There are zen gardens and traditional japanese buildings and services.
Now...here comes the bad below.
Graphics of hidden objects: Now I'm not sure if this would count as a pro or con...but I guess a pro for those who are beginners and a con for those who like challenge. Thing is, there are A LOT of hidden objects that look the same in many stages, that it isn't much of a challenge to look for them. For example, one stage you have to look for a cracker (edible form but the game doesn't mention what kind). You find it in one stage...a stage or so later, it asks you to find it again and guess what? It looks exactly the same! I know there are some hidden objects that look different such as birds, fishes, cats, and fans but it becomes tiring.
Stages: The stages are repetitive. You basically keep retracing your steps back and forth. So much that it becomes easy to find the items.
Music: I wish they had more variety of music playing. I mean the music sounds beautiful, but having the same few tracks of music looping over and over gets boring.
Gameplay: The game has some minigames other than just the hidden object. They have matching puzzles, a "spot the difference," and puzzles to unlock stuff. While it does add variety, again, there are two or more instances of the same game that it gets boring.
Overall: This game should have been a bit more polished before it was released. It could have shine a bit more if they improved on the problems I've listed. While I've enjoyed the story a lot, the cons seem to outweigh the pros here. If you don't mind the bad things above and enjoy a good story with some good graphics, then get it. Otherwise, to the majority of the crowd, this can be a pass (unless you want easy achievements).

If you like Simulation games, this is a great one to add to your collection. It's a great family and cooperative game that is both fairly relaxing and deceptively challenging. You can certainly play the game casually, but playing it as intended means a fair dedication of time. It will take a long time to do everything there is to do, and there is a lot of it. Farming ranges from the typical grains to the more involved root crops. You also have animal husbandry available and it goes well when done side-by-side with regular farming. The last major job available is Forestry, which is one of the most engaging tasks available in the game, although it can be frustrating due to in-game physics.
Each map starts you with a couple of fields, farming equipment, and a loan of varying amounts depending on the difficulty. From there on, you make your decisions as to how to play and what to do. You can sell all your equipment right from the start and do whatever you like. Fields you don't yet own are "owned" by NPCs who will offer you jobs to work that field and is a great way to make early money. Just don't spend too much time on other fields and not your own. Each job raises your reputation for that field and in turn lowers the price to purchase. Jobs are unfortunately but understandably not available in multiplayer. You can take a bigger loan to expand your business, make money from selling crops when the price is high, or even hunt hidden "nuggets" for a big cash bonus and an achievement.
The amount of vehicles and tools available to help you in your chosen roles is astounding and here might be one of the drawbacks. It can take a while to fully understand what they all do and what the advantages of each are. You are likely to have a whole selection of these that you will just never use unless you purposely try them all. With more tools and attachments come more key bindings to remember. The F1 help menu is great at listing the main keyboard shorcuts, but many are only learned if you dig deep. The game is not difficult to play by any means, but it is difficult to master. Parents who play with their kids should definitely aim for about 6-7 yrs and up unless your child is very familiar with these type of games.
Graphics are great for what the game is looking to achieve. Most of the game engine power will be dedicated to tracking your crop and equipment status and you'll grow to have a lot. The equipment is incredibly detailed with great animations of moving parts all realistically working. Older computers can still play the game but will be forced to lower settings and limit the amount of equipment on the screen. Forestry may be very difficult with slower PCs as the tree rendering and physics will cause lag. Sound design is decent but some of the machines do not feel powerful. Sounds are also shared across some equipment which leaves little to tell them apart sound-wise. I imagine some of these tractors and harvesters have very unique engine notes that sadly do not stand out. There is a built-in game radio that your can tune to online music streams and comes with some basic "radio stations" with a few songs each. You'll likely listen to your favorite music separately and never use the in-game offerings.
If you like downloading add-ons or "mods" for games, you will find a wealthy offering by the community. The game features a built-in mod browsers which is a huge step up over previous versions. The mods available here pale in comparison to those available at many online sites, however. Do be warned that some of these sites may have ads or even malware, so be careful when browsing. The community mods can vastly add and transform the game, making it more realistic, larger, adding more vehicles, crops and even jobs like mining. Giants also has DLC avaliable, but nothing that you really need. Kuhn DLC has extra tools but nothing spectacular except the square bale wrapper. The Big Bud DLC requires a large map and you won't have the need for big tractors unless you're later in the game and made some money for bigger fields.
All in all there is a lot to do here. If a job gets too boring there are other ways to do it or other jobs to do to keep it different. There's multiple approaches to almost all jobs and money making is fairly balanced if you're playing it as designed, so just do what you like. You'll obviously have to like the sim genre, but the game offer the best farming simulation out there. With several major releases under their belt, this latest release really does have a complete package. Not entirely without faults, but it is by far the best of its type out there, and a fantastic investment in terms of play value; especially with friends. Highly Recommended.

I rather enjoy becoming a cat! (Disclosure: Backed this on Kickstarter, for what that's worth.)
Cattails falls into a genre of relaxed, daily-rhythm games that used to be Harvest Moon-like but is now Stardew Valley-like. (Though I'd say that this has the most similarity to Survival Kids/Lost in Blue with a tough of Cube and Star: An Arbitrary Love.)
The world is open before you, but as it goes through seasonal changes, it opens up to you like a puzzle box. Plants to forage for and animals to prey upon move in and out of the world according to rhythms that just barely elude you, since you are a cat. You murder them all, often for experience points. There's a central MacGuffen that imposes a modicum of order and direction on all this murder, but while it's welcome, it's not really the point.
There are also cat politics which I haven't quite worked out yet (though again, systems that you haven't quite worked out yet are part of the joy of this sort of game). There's a mining section stapled on, which is fine. But mostly you walk around the landscape to murder small animals and to get slightly better at murdering small animals with practice.
Ant it does take practice--there's an awkward rhythm to the pounce that is quite satisfying when you get it right, but the kill never feels guaranteed. I imagine that there's a lot of math happening in the background generating random-feeling pounce radii and the like based on the temperature and the time of day and how hungry your cat is, and so on. Fighting other cats is similarly fidgety and awkward, but in that good way, where getting into any fight at all is a fearsome proposition. You feel like you're part of an ecosystem rather than The Player Character in an important way.
I could make some criticisms that are more like dev notes. (Menus are pretty bad: If you want to sell and then buy a commodity, you need to talk to a character, complete the sell transaction, leave the dialogue tree, talk to the character again and complete a separate buy transaction. There doesn't seem to be a way to assign special abilities to particular keys/buttons, so you're stuck with the default assignments until you have enough skills unlocked to strategically enable and disable them. There are some contextual situations where the game reads your inventory to see what you most likely want to do, and you go through "Is this what you wanted? Y/N" until it guesses right.)
But the rhythm is there. The core mechanic of wandering around and happening upon things and killing them because you are just an adorable murder-baby is there. It's a good time!

There are two kinds of gamers: those who can enjoy life sims, and those who cannot. Some people need the game to show them "this is what your goal is," and others are very happy to invent their own goals regardless of whether or not the game gives you one. If you're in that latter category, then by all means, I recommend this game to you. Especially if you like cats. Otherwise... you'll probably find yourself growing bored right after the tutorial.
Although I feel like this was pretty ingenious--
you have no goal at first. You're a housecat that was dumped off into the middle of nowhere! Your first few days should be spent learning how to survive. THEN you can come up with something to do. (And the game provides you with a main quest a few days later, so there's that.)
What I like:
>The festival games are fun.
>Unlike stardew valley, this game feels more polished, code-wise. SV had a lot of glitches, and that's not to mention that some parts of the game (looking at you, dumb festival with the slingshot minigame!) are virtually unplayable. In Cattails, I haven't run into a single thing that felt like shoddy programming.
>You can get married and have kittens
>Your kittens inherit their looks from their parents, and can be a mix of the two coat colors. Later on, they can join you in your adventures!
>You can decorate your den, and move about as you please.
>You can expand your den
>Tons of coat colors to choose from and/or collect.
>Arthur is the most adorkable cat I've ever seen and I love him to bits
>Main Quest quite like that of SV's.
>Sliding on ice is ridiculously fun
What I dislike:
>Fighting is lame. It basically boils down to "who has the most numbers?"
>Getting money can be rather hard. Lots of things costs ridiculous amounts of money (nursery expansion is 500 mews! The highest thing I've been able to sell was somewhere around 15 mews)
>A couple of the cats have slightly wonky portraits
>THE MUSIC. OMG
This is probably the first time I've ever muted a game's soundtrack, because I prefer to play the devs' intended experience. Each season seems to start off with one song, which is usually pretty good, but then it gets replaced by this dumb jazz-like tune that starts grating your nerves after a while. Thankfully, you can turn the music off. (Or at least make it nearly inaudible.)
All in all, though, I fully recommend this game if you're a fan of life simulation games and cats.

As many people already mentioned this is an action-exploration game, just as the description of the game already says. If you expect a hack and slay adventure game, this is not for you.
I love the artwork of the game and it's totally fitting to a sometimes slow-paced game like Jotun. You will find long, looong bridges to cross so you find the time to admire the illustration of the levels and the story they tell.
I'm a fan of old myths and therefore I was already in love with the overall topic of Jotun. Each level told a little piece of Norse myths, and even the character got a nice, touching story that was concluded in the end.
Working with the minimap is hard since your current position is not shown. I don't see this as a downside, since you simply have to keep track of where you might be. In some levels I got lost. In some levels I had no problem to find my way at all. The feature of not showing the player's position makes it not only an exploration game but also a little maze, which I find amazing.
Combat is very interesting and diverse. The levels before a boss introduce core mechanics of the boss fight while giving the level itself an obstacle to overcome -> insanely good approach to game design! The bosses themselves have their own abilities and mechanics and I can assure you that you will need at least 2 attempts for each boss to beat them. These fights are about learning and how you can counter specific abilities.
All in all I extremely enjoyed Jotun and I definitely recommend this game to everyone who is looking for a puzzle-like exploration game with cunning combats, a fascinating story and beautiful artwork.

When I first backed Mighty No. 9, I was excited to see what Keiji Inafune would come up with. Through all the twists and turns of development, I think the end result is pretty decent.
The game is fast paced, and really starts to open up once you get a few Might Numbers beaten, though getting to that point can be a bit frustrating at first: there is pretty liberal usage of instant death traps, and there's no ability to recover from falling down a pit. The lack of wall-kicking feels especially weird and obnoxious, as you want to maintain speed, which sometimes results in dashing off a ledge accidentally; this means several levels feel a bit "trial and error," as you try to figure out how to best maintain your speed.
The "trial and error" bit is made a bit more annoying by the use of lives and stage restarts - I'm not sure why this was needed, as it forces you to redo the entire level after dying to the boss. There were a few time where I just put the game down for the night, because I didn't want to do an already frustrating level
just to make it to a boss fight I'm stuck on.
While all this sounds pretty damning, Mighty No. 9 does improve in quality the further you get - by the time you reach the final stages, you have a decent set of abilities, the level design has gotten better (and the writing improves as well, in my opinion), and the instant death traps become less of a problem as you master the dashing mechanism (though I still kinda hate them).
Overall, I recommend this game for anyone who wants an interesting, but not brilliant, side scrolling platformer. There are certainly better 2D platformers on Steam, but Mighty No. 9 is a pretty decent pick up if you're willing to put up with a few frustrations in the beginning.

After getting this game unlocked in my region on 2016/06/24 , I've played around a bit and  reached (what I assume) is the final stage. With that in mind, here's the break down of my  first impressions so far:
1). Gameplay.
+ The basic movement of the main character is pretty precise and responsive.
- The 'crouch dash' is basically what the actual dash was supposed to be, but now you have to  manage timing for an additional button press to avoid lower projectiles and instakill spikes.  The 'downwards dash' is maybe useful in one room ever. The 'backwards jump' and 'backwards  jump and shoot' moves require more windup than is practical; on top of that, most of the  situations that looked like they would be useful in seem to be deliberately designed to  disallow these two moves.
+ Dashing through or near the stunned enemies to progress encourages you to go fast. And with  your basic dash move, you can go pretty fast.
- It also makes it very easy to lose health to enemy contact to a slightest mistiming.  Coupled with a bunch of enemy placements prone to knocking you into instant death and several  segments seemingly deliberately designed to punish you for going too fast, it... kind of  doesn't jive well together.
- Speaking of losing health, there are very few ways to replenish it. Scoring enemy kill  combos can apparently grant you a medkit you can use instantly on a button press, but the  requirements are way too long, in my opinion, and the damn thing disappears on death and  doesn't carry over between stages on top of that. You basically have to rely on random drops  at predetrmined locations to have any surplus health for that upcoming boss battle. You are  limited to static health recovery items scattered around the stages beyond that.
- There are powerups that can increase your movement speed, weapon damage, defense, etc. The  problem is that they drop randomly sometimes from enemy deaths combos and at certain points  of a stage if the game thinks you've been dying too much. They last for a very short period  of time, they disappear on death and they very much cannot be taken with you to another  stage.
Considering all the ways you can die instantly via a single wrong move, all they end up doing  in practice is throw you off from how your character handles normally around all the  instakill hazards this game is littered with.
+ There are some nice ideas for stage concepts and gimmicks.
- ... which are bogged down by said stages being full of instakill hazards requiring  memorization to beat more than anything else.
- They are also short and severely lacking in exploration, secrets to find and meaningful  sideroutes to go through.
- The way the game goes about 'compensating' for it includes sparse checkpoint placement and  a life limit that forces you to start the stage from the beginning if you run out. There was  never a good justification for this kind of game design and there is even less so in 2016.
+ The powersets the player character gets from defeating the bosses are pretty interesting.
+- Special weapon energy can regenerate on its own and (apparently) be replenished by getting  enemy kill combos. It only does so for the weapon currently equipped, however. And there are  no pickups or items you can carry with you that can speed up the process. Can be a bit too  slow in boss battles.
- You can't change forms while hanging from a ledge or a hook. If you happen to hang above a  botomless pit with a strong sidewind and there is an enemy impeding your progress your  current weapon can't reach? You need to get airborne or back to solid ground in order to  change it.
+- The game has a strong emphasis on your score and all the various multipliers for it. I  personally didn't care one whit about it, but it is not an automatic negative just by itself.
+ The stage you play as Call on is a nice break from the rest of the game and tries to go for  something different.
+- The bosses require you to dash through or near them after you take off a certain  percentage of their health; they regenerate the health lost otherwise. It's not necessarily a  bad break from the usual formula by itself, but coupled with some of them frequently dancing  out of your weapons' reach for prolonged periods of time and your extremely limited health  recovery options, it tends to create more frustration than fun, in my experience.
- The boss moves that damage you for over half of your health and at least in one case  require to perform a QTE seemingly designed to break your controller and fingers, however,  can go screw themeselves.
- The mook enemy variety is lacking.
2). Audio.
+- The music can be switched from the default to the retro style arrangement. I didn't like  any single track I've heard in the game, but the feature itself is certainly nice and the  music is, at the very least, not annoying or painful to listen to.
+- I understand that audio cues for various actions are important, but I can't honestly say  that tying voiced lines to (very) often repeated actions was ever a good idea. It's not as  bad as it could be, but that doesn't make it good.
+- Some voice lines appear to be mistimed or peter off into something too quiet to hear at  times, so VA direction could probably use some work. Some roles go for outright hammy  delivery, which you may or may not like. It's far from bad though.
3). Visuals.
+ Some levels manage to look really nice and make use of the chosen '2.5D' perspective well  to enhance their presentation.
- There are, however, swathes of low detailed textures, lacking doodad placement and  backgrounds of the 'murky all concealing fog with a couple vaguely detailed objects sticking  out' kind to go with the above.
+- The models themselves could work quite nicely (and indeed do for the enemy mooks), if all  the close up shots in cutscenes didn't shove their lacking animations front and centre all  the time.
+ The 2D portrait art and stills used in some scenes look nice.
- Flame and explosion effects are just bad.
4). UI.
- The 'Press A to start' prompt before you are given a chance to look up and customize your  controls is the first thing the game greets you with. No mouse support for the menu  navigation for the PC version as well. The default control layout without using a gamepad is  counterintuitive. Switching between transformations requires operating two separate buttons  or juggling a set of three shortcuts (which is really not enough).
+- You /can/ turn off the score update notifications that take up almost a quarter of your  screen with oversized brightly colored junk  and the announcer voice that goes with it. I  have to question why it is turned on by default or even in the game to begin with though. And  the options that do this are labeled extremely vaguely.
+- The tutorial popups don't stop your movement beyond the intro stage. But they also tend to  be less than useful when it comes to anything but weapon functionality. The MMX dash jump is  in the game, but it is not documented anywhere.
5). References.
+- There are a lot of them, most from various things Megaman, including room layouts, enemy  types and one-off character cameos. There is not a whole lot to the game beyond them though.
6). Narrative.
+- Unobtrusive and manages to make me curious about some things. It doesn't wanna give out  much in the way of answers though. Which may or may not be a good thing.
7). Technical issues.
- There are quite a lot of them. Look up the steam community page if you are interested.
In conclsusion, I believe that a serious opportunity to breathe something new into the  Megaman formula was completely blown by this game. And it isn't a 'Megaman 11' either. I give  it a tentative thumbs up because I still enjoyed it despite everything, but it feels like an  incomplete game and probably isn't worth the full price.

"The first installment of the RollerCoaster Tycoon franchise is a true example of an instant classic."
A genre I play and like a lot are the simulation games: the SimCity series, Theme Park and Transport Tycoon Deluxe are good examples of the early games in this genre. Transport Tycoon was Chris Sawyer's first simulation game created in 1994 and obsessed by roller coasters, he created RollerCoaster Tycoon. And still after more than 20 years this game is great and for me the best in the series.
The goal of the game is simple: built an amusement park including the biggest, fastest and baddest roller coasters you have ever seen. This goal repeats itself 21 times, but the different surroundings and kinds of rides and roller coasters make it a very addictive game. Each scenario, you start with a budget and a loan for building the first rides of your theme park to attract people. You can give each ride a name, price and different colours which is fun to do. When building a ride you can choose from a few standard designs, but building and designing a custom design is the way for having a real challenge.
Besides placing rides, you have to have personnel to watch over your theme park. You will need handymen, mechanics, security guards and entertainers for every issue that may occur with the hundreds of sloppy visitors. They vomit, throw garbage, demolish the rides and scenery and are not happy. Well, not always. You can hire enough personnel placing them in your park and they will walk just around or you can hire less personnel and then assign a route to them. The last option has the advantage that for example the mechanics are on time to inspect and/or repair a ride, but it takes more time planning the routes. It is up to you.
As I am not a roller coaster fanatic and therefore do not know all the sorts and names of the turns and stuff, building one is so much fun. How good your coaster is going to be, depends on the amount of money you have to spend. That is an easy rule, but there 3 ratings that can make or kill your coaster. These are the nausea, excitement and intensity rating. A good score on all three, extreme not included, will attract lots of visitors. And a good score on these ratings will cost you. Building above and undergrounds is possible. Building undergrounds is pretty difficult, because it is sometimes hard to see where your entrance path or coaster is.
The graphics and sound are great. The lovely tiny people walking around, the rides and coasters you see are detailed and colourful. Menus are easy to use: the different sorts of rides and the flora and fauna are categorized into tabs.
Overall it is a true fun and very addictive game.

Choice of Robots is purely text Choose Your Own Adventure (CYOA) game. It features plenty of choices and some nasty consequences. You can end up incredibly rich, creating enemies, losing everything, dating humans or making the ideal companion, advancing medicine, making meaningful moral choices, and more. It's a pretty wild, contemplative ride where you start off by building your first intelligent creation and going from there. I had some sad tales and some hopeful ones. The replay value is pretty high as you can explore the different branching paths for very different results. I greatly enjoyed my time with this game and finally spent some time reading words instead of blasting pixels. Ohoho.
How will you define the future of humanity and robot kind?

When it comes to games, I'm usually a 4X player, but the Steam Summer Sale prompted my first foray into choose-your-own-adventure style text games/interactive novels. I bought and played this particular one based on a recommendation, and the fact that I ended up buying the entire Choice of Games library as a bundle during the sale is probably the best indication of how much I enjoyed it. Having tried this, Choice of Alexandria, Affairs of the Court, A Study in Steampunk, The Last Hero, and The Hero of Kendrickstone, Choice of Robots remains my favorite.
I was always a sucker for choose-your-own-adventure books as a kid, and this is basically exactly that, sans illustrations. I really love how Choice of Robots actually writes out a summary of your story as you go, divided into chapters (I ended up being really disappointed that none of the other CoG games I've played thus far do this); that it displays your stats as you gain or lose them; and that the choices are so varied. Choice of Robots has had the best replayability, because the choices veer off in so many different directions - some of the other games in the genre will drive you into the same path no matter what, but here, each playthrough can result in wildly different branches.
It's a different kind of game than I usually play - ultimately, it's not going to have the replayability of Alpha Centauri or Civ, but for the price, it doesn't have to be. It's a fun several hours of entertainment, and, as I said, I really like Choice of Robots for how varied the story can become, and how long it actually is. 10/10 would recommend.

People consistantly comparing it to the creator's previous endeavors "Megaman". at first I was very upset, because although I dont play the traditional games of Megaman, I was a very big fan of Megaman Battle Network. Anyhow, when getting this game, here were my first impessions.
The controls on a controler were very clunky at first, and honestly? I wouldnt recommend it. The controller (At least, the Steam controller is a bit large for this game, you need to do very quick and precise maneuverability, so when you attempt to do that on the very new, very large steam controller, you tend to mistake controls a bit. However, if you circumvent the controller and just remain on keyboard, the game handles fairly well.
The gameplay, although very pretty to look at, doesnt really do all too much in the long run. Comperable to your old car, sure it's not beautiful, but you could pull of drifting on the dang thing without much trouble at all. thats how I feel about the Gameplay Control, it's not super amazing, and earthshattering, but it wasnt broken, and it didnt need to be fixed.
Around the concept of the dash? I feel like it fell short in one area. Making Mighty dash into enemies wasnt a very smart design choice in all honesty. As much as it feels nice to get buffs? it tends to launch me into the face of an enemy that I could have sworn only took 2 shots, but was still standing after 2. Perhaps im making mistakes in calculation but with casual play, it seems like it's a detriment. I love the dash when im traversing, it helps when I need to go fast, and when I need to be careful, I simply move my finger away from the Button. I hope if a continuing of this game is released, please get rid of the absorbtion mechanic. It's not very good, and I am left very dissapointed on that front.
This game also features something mentioned earlier in this review, Buffs. Yes, buffs are in this game. Although I cant place the yellow one as easily by name, it seems like it goes like this: Red buff will allow your shots to pierce enemies, as well as doubling your damage, its very useful when going against a boss if you've died once to it, and you've finally mustered up the courage to try to go all out. The Yellow Buff is either Shot speed, Number of Bullets allowed on screen, or both. I havent really tested this buff effect as this game is very fast paced. Though I notice that I am able to shoot faster, and perhaps put more pellets on screen. The green buff allows you to go quicker, a very lovely addition in long enemy filled corridors and you're very low health. These buffs can save you, or break you honestly, it depends on the level design to decide if absorbing the enemy to get the buff is recomended.
This game has a tendancy to go with the route Trial By Fire with it's gameplay I feel like having only 2 lives, is very uncomfortable, and a little too difficult for me, I could go with six lives, but for Irony sakes I went with 9. If you're going to get this game, you really need to be careful. this game will put your skills to think on the fly and adapt to new situations on overclocking levels. Just be ready for any jumps you think are comming, and you should be fine. Do not feel bad about dying in this game. Part of me feels like this was intended in some way as there's no significant penalty to my view of dying.
Overall I was astounded to realize at the end of the day I was having a lot of fun with this game. Is it perfect? No, is it worldbreaking like Inafune "promised"? No, and I understand some of the sour feelings from that, but this is a rather fun game to play, and I would very much recommend it to you. I havent tried the DLC, but im very excited to. For now, this is what im giving it. 8.9/10 A very good game.

I wanted to like this game I really did, when I booted it up I felt a wave of nostalgia for the old megaman x games. That nostalgia soon turned into dread as I realized they took away some of the most important parts of megaman. They removed the charge beam making it so you had to fire rapid shots into enemies instead of strategically saving a charge to wipe out enemies ahead. I could live with that.
They gave you the dash and I could quickly see there would be no hidden upgrades to your suit or life. I could live with that though I would miss them.
they made every enemy be able to be absorbed for different buffs, this sounds like a fun thing till you realize that after they start flashing you still have to unload a dozen bullets or so to take out the enemy while it is flashing, that doesn't mean too much till you find out that multiple enemies spawn together so it becomes a game of what will damage me more, dashing into this enemy and getting hurt by the one behind it or taking down this enemy while his ally shoots/spins/ damages me in some way from behind his meat shield of an ally.
There are parts I enjoyed, it does give you the power ups from the bosses you defeat but even that gets extremly frustrating as you have to dash through them multiple times in the battle when they start flashing purple to keep injuring them. This wouldn't be so bad apart from the fact that the bosses continue moving while you are doing this so quite often you dash through them then stop dashing in the square they ran to meaning you get hurt by them unless you have split second reactions.

Cheap pitfalls everywhere, leaps of faith, and general screwing abound. The scoring and ranking system doesn't make sense, and messing up your controls during a boss fight? Seriously? That wasn't funny or original 20 years ago, and it sure isn't now either. I can understand wanting some difficult segments, given the original games being infamous for the platforming challenges, but some parts just feel downright cheap, or they punish you for not having played the levels before.
Some of the weapons are somewhat fun to use, while others feel gimmicky and almost useless except for specific niche situations. The absortion system doesn't really do anything for the game. It doesn't feel rewarding or interesting. It feels like something you're forced to do, especially during boss fights or when trying to recharge weapon energy. It doesn't help that the way you get awarded regeneration charges from absortions feels completely random. In addition, the options menus feel very PC unfriendly, and clearly meant for consoles and controllers. This being the PC version, and release having been delayed so many times on flimsy excuses, is simply unacceptable.
The only good thing I can say about this is that some of the characters are well designed and likable, despite some people's attempts to alter them to suit their own personal agenda (see: SJW PR manager and related ♥♥♥♥♥torm, not touching that subject here) . The rest of the game, I cannot recommend on good conscience in its current state unless you're an absolute diehard Mega Man fan and/or Inafune fan (the latter might change after you've played this, too).
The saddest part about all this is, this game had all the elements it needed to be absolutely great. You can see great care was put into some design elements and the game itself is quite nice to see and hear. But as soon as you step into the actual levels, you start getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by all the random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

I'd recommend this game, but it has some major problems.
1. WAY WAY too much smoke and dust clouds. Even a short spray of bullets will cause a cloud of dust that takes awhile to disappear, even when you shot at something like a window frame, wall corner, door frame, etc.
2. The vehicles suck, for the most part.
3. No option for team deathmatch, only Squad Deathmatch. (4 teams of 4 against each other)
4. No option for free for all deathmatch.
5. Every Squad Deathmatch map has one tank that continues to spawn. It's annoying and wasn't a good choice of vehicle for Squad Deathmatch. Humvees or 4-wheelers would have worked better. Maybe a few boats on the maps that have water.
6. Only sniper rifles can be equipped with a sniper scope.
7. Heli control(s) suck, and minigun control (that the heli's are equipped with) also suck.
8. Way too few maps for Squad Deathmatch option, and the maps for the other gametypes are often large with not enough buildings/cover/good landscape for a battle. Why not just spawn us all in an open field?
9. Extreme lack of good urban environment maps.
10. This is one of the worst things about the game. Accuracy is ridiculously crappy when you aren't looking through your sights/optics. You can fire at a stationary guy 20 feet away and maybe get 3-6 out of 30 of your shots to actually hit him. If you need to be looking down your sights to get more than 1/10-1/5 accuracy from 20 feet away, then you probably shouldn't be anywhere near a battlefield. In real life if I was shooting from that distance, every one of the those shots would have met their target. Seeming as how most of the assault rifles used by assault class are chambered in 5.56mm, they should by little to no issue with recoil. The game's designers, however, thought that it best to give rifles chambered in 5.56mm the accuracy and recoil of an automatic shotgun being fired by a small child with Muscular Dystrophy.
11. This one isn't as big of a deal to me, but there's no option to go prone.

I played this game a ton back in the day on Xbox 360. I put several hundred hours into it (it was one of two games I had at the time), but my 360 is currently buried in the attic somewhere, so I figured I'd play the PC version... except the PC version is virtually unplayable due to control issues, EVEN WITH A 360 CONTROLLER. There seems to be a bit of input lag so some actions that require a quick sequence of button-presses are hard to pull off. The enemy hitboxes are weird, so some attacks that auto-target enemies (aerial strike and throwing explosive barrels for instance) stop just shy of the enemy without doing any damage, the lock-on controls are terrible ("toggle" leaves you stuck orbiting a tiny piece of scrap when the selector locks onto a bit of junk from the environment, but "hold" requires you to play through entire fights holding down the shoulder-button because if you aren't locked on,  your attacks miss the target even if you're aiming at them. The selector- indicator is fainter than I remember, and just to add insult to injury, you can't see if you're locked onto an enemy when they're A) too close to you, or B) too large (in a game where you fight a Star Destroyer) because in both cases, the lock-on indicator fades out until you can't discern it from the background. I suspect that anyone reading this review without having experienced these problems first-hand will be thinking something along the lines of "Git Gud", because these sound like the complaints of someone who hasn't learned to play the game yet, but after all the hours I spent playing it on console, I still have plenty of muscle-memory for the controls... they just don't WORK on the PC version .

A must-play classic. Many would say its sequel RCT2 is superior with more rides, scenery, scenario editor etc, but RCT1 has the vastly better learning curve and scenario structure. The challenges are more interesting and is a much better sense of progression over the sequels. While in RCT2 you are often presented with empty landscapes to build a fresh park, most of the RCT1 scenarios involve picking up an existing park (with a few really cool starting rides) and fixing its unique problems.
The challenge progression also takes you through the history of theme park rides (up until the late 90s). The first available rides tend to be wooden or small coasters, but eventually you are introduced to the 70s classic Arrows and Schwartzkopfs, and the later parks include the more modern (at the time) B&Ms.

Is this game worth buying? Yes and no.

The only real complaint I have right now is that there are a few promised features that aren't here just yet.  The create-your-own colony feature is the most obvious one. I've heard it can get repetative, and I somewhat agree.  It can get dull.  You hunt, fight, forage, swim, and mine.  Do any of them too much, especally on an easier mode, and it gets old after a few hours.  I've found bumping up the difficulty helps make it more interesting.
The music also has started to irriate me.  I often play without sound now, and that's really helped.  The music just feels overly cheerful and energetic at some points.
I also must mention the puzzles in the game.  I'm not a fan, mainly because I wasn't expecting them.  I love puzzles normally, but these felt like they came out of nowhere.  So be prepared if you do Coco's quests, bring food and healing herbs.
One thing I do love is having kits. Right now each cat can only have one litter. But the kits are adorable.  Mine are kinda ugly though, but adorably ugly. Kind of like pugs.  The genetics in the game are by far my favorite thing. I am defineity going to be playing around with it to see what horrifying and adorable kittens I can create.
It's not a perfect game.  But it's still a fun game for a select group of people.  I happen to be one.  If you like games like Stardew Valley, and other similar simulation titles, you'll probably like this one.

Short game, well priced for the time. Great art and animation, very atmospheric music. Generic story, horrible gameplay.
As for the story, makes no sense, is not properly telegraphed to the player, no reason for it to be there really. The game is also sexist technically. Every character is female, not a single male human character. Why, probably because none of the developers were homosexual, so what pubescent wants to devote time to something that isn't a waifu candidate for them.
On the gameplay side.
Yet another two dimensional game where touching, some, enemies hurts the player. So in a game where the player can only attack with short range melee, and both the player and many enemies move quite fast, you also take full damage if you touch the enemy. Some enemies, most enemies. It's great, when half the difficulty is trying to hit a target that is running at you while you run towards it without simultaneously ever making direct contact with it.
Some other random obnoxious elements include, having to skip through a bosses dialogue every time you go to fight it. Having to fight a boss then complete another area all without saving. Having it so that dying flat resets the players progress back to the last checkpoint, this including boss fights, item pick ups and mini boss fights. Having a secret alternate entrance to a boss fight, the secret entrance having multiple possible ways to get into it all but one leading to instant death. This secret entrance, when you finally get into it after over ten minutes of trial and error; and replaying the map to get back to that point, literally leads the player to a boss they will fight if they just progress two more screens ahead; these screens not even having any real threats in them anyways.
What a pointless, stupid waste of time that was. What was the actual point developer, you made a shortcut to a boss which skips the player over a checkpoint in the process; this shortcut requiring obscene effort to use even though it handicaps the player. Whoever designed that, incompetent. Utterly incompetent. Should not be a game developer.
In general, the best way to play this game is to equip the item that heals for each kill, equip the item that increases defense and invulnerability frames; and then just rush spam everything. That's it. Not only does it work, but it is more effective then actually trying to be methodical because so many obstacles spam the player and require stupid amounts of precision and luck to counter; it's better to just ram through them with invulnerability frames while healing from the kills.
Many enemies have very little telegraphs for their attacks, many enemies have projectiles with hyper tracking, many enemies have attacks with oversized hit-boxes. It is so overbearing, it's better to just spam through. This works, and is highly suggested, for beating the final boss as well because they are literally just all of the above in boss form.
Probably the best part is the bosses. They have either one attack, or two attacks. Fighting them is literally just trial and error pattern memorization mixed with human error. Better yet, almost all of them are generic humans. Better yet, the humans are so small; the players attacking visual effect is so large, and the bosses damage recieve splash effect is so large; while attacking the boss it's almost impossible to see it. So you can't even tell when it starts attacking, which often it has little telegraph for anyways, because all the visual effects block it. Bosses also have so much health, and the player attacks so fast that mashing the button is mandatory to fight bosses. Which again, constantly keeps the fighting particle effects active which constantly obscures the actual boss besides being spammy and annoying to uphold in general.
Wasn't fun, at all, because the options are; play recklessly and actually progress through shear brute force, or try to be methodical and actually fight but take triple more damage because the combat system is spammy so not spamming back just leads to you getting hit a whole lot.
Cheap and short, you can play through this in 20 minutes or less if you just run through it but the first time around you I guess an hour. It's simple, clean and fun

I rate the game Choice of Robots 4/5. Good.
While this is merely a text-based game in a similar style as the old Choose Your Own Adventure books it is an extremely extensive one which has a lot more to say and a lot of lessons to potentially teach. Most of the endings are interesting and meaningful and the ideas presented and the choices you get (on almost every page) are very interesting. It is a shame that more games with actual, visual graphics could not have the amazing freedom of choice and the sheer number of possible endings which this game allows. Though it is a mere text-based game, I ended up playing through about 6 or 7 times and I am certain this story has many other potential endings I have not yet discovered.
However, this game does have some serious weaknesses beyond the fact that it has no graphics. The writing seems more like an outline of a story rather than an actual story with very few visceral or sensory details though this does allow the reader to skim through sections which have already been read very, very easily. The characters seem a little 2 dimensional or slightly shallow at times as it's far too easy to classify or figure out the different characters and their motivations, underlying emotional conflicts and agendas.
Indeed, emotion is not described very well in this book/game at all as the text often seems to have a very egocentric focus on whatever you, the player/reader-character might be feeling at any given moment instead (when emotion is described much at all). Still, despite this shortcoming, just from the situations which are described, the story can still manage to feel very touching anyhow.
This story was particularly touching when I played through the game trying to be the worse, most selfish, scheming ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I could possibly try to be. This game will let you know you are being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in some very touching ways and will give you results that would logically spring from being that way. Does that mean that the story will kill you off if you act badly? Not necessarily. But you will get realistically punished. You may even become a zillionaire captain of industry which no one loves or wants to be around, for example. If you act in an apathetic way to your created robots they will in turn become more apathetic towards everyone. In this game, your robots are an nth degree reflection of your actions and inactions. Unfortunately the narration feels cold apathetic regardless. It is good that it does not push you in one direction or another but it is unbiased to the extent that it is cold and clinical. Robotic even.
And while it is excellent that this story/game will let you make truly stupid, rash and irrational decisions too with seemingly realistic results, the bare-bones writing style does feel like it often falls short and that every single passage could have been even better with more detail. Visceral and emotional details are the "graphics" of a text-based experience and this experience doesn't have anywhere near as much of it as it should. As in an outline of a story, there is probably too much left to the imagination causing every situation to not be quite as fleshed out as it should be. With more detail this story/game could have been more funny, felt more tragic or felt more awe-inspiring with just the addition of a few more details; The good experience that it is could have easily been a great one, a masterpiece of multiple-ending choice-based fiction. Perhaps a newer, enhanced version could still be written to achieve this.
English literary details aside, perhaps the most glaring problem with this story/book/game is how there is no back button which allows you to undo any choice you just made. Indeed, you cannot even flip back to an earlier page. As a result, unlike the Choose Your Own Adventure books of old you cannot easily figure out how the story/plot/game is structured and learn all the different options and endings which exist. While this maintains the sense of the book's mystery and forces you to live with any mistakes you made (which is more realistic) it more often seems frustrating and nonsensical that you, as a reader of a story, cannot turn back to a previous page. While this frustrating lack of a feature allows for massive amounts of replayability (or re-readability), it also means that much of that replayability will inevitably consist of carefully skimming through increasingly repetitive passages to get back to some critical choice or another which may lead you on to a different ending. The game should give you an option of being able to go back to a previous page or not and should have put that option in a menu somewhere.
Despite its weaknesses this story/game will give a sci-fi robot fiction fan many hours of enjoyment. Indeed I found that I was often captivated by the plot and adventure of trying to find out what would happen next. I read this on a computer which has a GTX 780 graphics card installed in it and is capable of easily running Far Cry 3 with all of its graphics settings turned to maximum. It's not like I don't have a choice of which games I want to play and so I read this instead. No. Truly, this game was interesting and for me, and at least initially was able compete on an even playing field with the most graphically intense games on the market.
With a choice on nearly every page the old young adult choose your own adventure stories of the 1980s and early 90's cannot hold a candle to the number of possibilities which this game presents. Indeed, most other adventure games, (most of which have just one to three possible endings) can barely keep up with the amazing variation of possible endings which this story gives you. A character who is your chief love interest in one play-through of Choice of Robots may end up being your archenemy in another play-through. In many ways this game further realizes the potential of the ideas in that old movie Butterfly Effect while at once being set in a I-Robot, Isaac Asimov science fiction situation dealing with the moral pitfalls and potentials of the advent of robotic AI sentience. The number of different potential messages and meanings which this kind of interactive fiction can hold in store for any given reader is truly staggering.
Despite its literary flaws and the absence of a back button, this is a work of art worthy of being discussed and studied in any forward-thinking university (or high-school rather due to the relatively simplistic language) English department in the nation due to its amazing potential and amazing re-readibility.

The animations are nice, and the boss designs are cool...and that's about it.
As for the game itself, the exploration is utterly boring, with really empty and far too big places to go through. The enemies can be bypass 99% of the time so except running slugishly, there's not much to do. And the layouts you're in are not that pretty to look at: when the game shows its background like it's supposed to be a masterpiece, I just wondered why it wasn't detailed at all. You can see that there is some level of mastery and quality in the art overall, but it's not detailed and varied enough. Especially when you have ONE type of enemy for each sub-level repeated ad-nauseam just with a swap color (sometimes just ONE swap color).
The only interest you might have lies in the bosses that can have some fun patterns but can equally be frustrating due to unintuitive hitboxes; it seems like the devs didn't choose between having the entire boss sprite being the hitbox and having some parts of the boss, that makes sense in 3D, being the hitbox.
This inconsistancy in the combat combines with the short range of the axe, the amazingly wick main attack (that takes like one percent of a boss' lifebar) and the amazingly slow hard attack that takes forever to land (seriously WHY is it so slow?!). All that makes for a really tedious combat system that doesn't feel too bad, but never feels really good. Oh...I didn't even mentionned the boss with dwarves everywhere that pretty much consists of playing "where is Waldo?" (Waldo being the main character) while being slowly but surely pummeled to death. Sometimes, it's hard to see what is going on because you are far away from the camera.
TL;DR
It could be really good looking, thanks to the design and the animation, but lacks details in the environment. It could be fun to play, but lacks attention to the hitboxes and actual fun things to smash, aside from some bosses some times. A bit too tedious to really enjoy the game, event though you can see the devs worked hard on it.

Jotun is almost exclusively a boss battle game. While you will be spending a significant amount of time in the side areas, this is mostly because of how slow your main character feels. Both in running speed and also in her attacks. While it makes sense if you look at the weapon she is wielding it still makes for some frustrating moments. You really need to get used to the overall slower speed of your character.
The art style is pretty fantastic, although I must say that the perspective can cause some problems in boss fights as it is not always clear where the attacks will land. The animated style they have chosen is really well made and the boss's design is top notch. It really gives the feeling of walking in the land of the giants and fighting against such overwhelming foes.
The boss fights are well designed and enjoyable, however they might be a bit too easy since I managed to beat every one within the first few tries. Once you figure out their moves it becomes quite easy to predict what they will do. And with a game so focused on boss battles you would expect more stages for at least a couple of the boss fights. I guess the difficulty will come from self emposed rules, such as not using any powers, or not getting hit.
If you have any interest in norse mythology then I think you will find the story quite interesting. And all of the story is narrated in Icelandic which really furthers your immersion in the world. Although I wish the story was more detailed, as it stands it gives you just enough to understand what is going on, but if you don't know the background beforehand then quite a bit of the awesomeness of the game will sadly be lost on you.
If you just want to go through the main game then it will take you anywhere from 2-4 hours to complete it, depending on how thoroughly you want to explore the side areas.
Jotun is a good game with an awesome setting and an incredible visual style. It is hampered by some peculiarities of its gameplay, namely the overall slowness, not always interesting side areas and issues with perspective. It's still an easy recommendation for me, despite the quite short main campaign.
7 / 10

As a backer, I can't recomend this game to anyone. Especially not as to merely progress through early game there are quite a few pixel perfect dashes you have to do. Add to the fact that this dash needs to be a "crouch dash", something that the game doesn't give any indication of you being able to do, especially as all other narrow passages you have to "crouch dash" through automatically makes you dash through without an issue.
There's also some quite severe fps issues in the game still.
Another stage has you chasing a sniper through a stage. However, if you die to any of the myriad of one-shot kill things, you have to start over from the start. There's also no indication of what you actually have to do against the sniper to progress.
Also, if you don't dash through the bosses when they are dashable they regain their life. There's also only the particle glow indicating that you even can dash absorb their power, in comparison to all normal enemies that get stunned for a short while to indicate that you can absorb them with the dash.
While the game would have been punishing but reasonably fun if it stood on its own legs, it's leaning towards Megaman far to much in order to not make the comparison. Anyone who hasn't played Megaman games wouldn't have the skills to make it through the platforming sequences. Especially as the game breaks its design paterns at quite a few different places.
Examples of this would be the inability to grap onto platforms that are covered with ice, as well as the previously mentioned "crouch dash" under a huge fan that will insta-kill you.
In short, avoid. If you are a megaman fan, there's better games out there. If your not, then chances are that your going to be frustrated from the horrible level design and punishing boss battles. Most of the bosses have atleast one attack that will eat half your life or more and not all of them give a good indication of how high an area they will hit.

This game is bad regardless of trying to be a Spiritual Successor of the Mega Man series (I think we can ALL agree on that if you ever play ANY Mega Man game)
I come from a long history of Mega Man games, so naturally I was excited to see this; however, after hearing its 2nd delay, I kinda gave up hope with this game, but considering I did give this game 40 dollars to help towards the fund I feel the need to play it.
Mighty No 9 suffers from a lot of problems even not counting the whole “This is not a Mega Man game meme” and honestly, I could write a college thesis on how Nostalgia could misinterpret the gamers perception; however, I will keep this bare as possible but still being effective
Gameplay
The gameplay feels very stale, the fact you have to use the dash to kill your enemies is a bit redundant. The whole point of a “Jump and Shoot” shooter is to utilize your accuracy of jumping and shooting to eliminate your foes. With this dashing feature being a key role in killing your foes, it kinda defeats the purpose of the whole genre. In Mighty No 9, your goal is to shoot your opponent until he is able to dash through and get your “Points”. In fact, most of the time I usually dash over them if I have the chance to since shooting them takes longer/infective than to just dash around them. For the bosses it’s even worse. You shouldn’t have to dash through bosses even after using the weapon that counters them, the dashing thing is unnecessary in its perspective, sure if it was just a dash I would be ok with it, but considering that it is a key role in attacking EVERYTHING gets really old really fast. The fact also that I get “Combos” if I dash through more than one enemy makes me feel like I’m playing a mobile game designed for people that only care about getting a high score and rubbing it in your friends face (Aka Candy Crush or Temple Run)
Graphics/Level Design
I want to coup with them and understand that the graphics are what they are because of an outdated version of Unreal Engine, but considering that it took them 3 YEARS to release a game that is very to the point, I would imagine they would switch over. The graphics look worse than King of Fighters XIV ALPHA Footage. Everything is Muddy and not shaded well and I can actually see sharp corners on the models in somewhat rare cases.
The Level Design is another problem. In a game where you are given limited levels to impress your viewers, they did a poor job in doing so. In most side scroller “Jump N Shoot” games, you can remember what the levels are from the second you enter in the level. Sure, you may not remember the whole level, but you can remember key events or a general design. In Mighty No 9, all the levels look stale and generic. You have your beginning platform that introduces the gimmick of the level, followed up by a sub boss of some sort (which most of the time are a pain than actual fun) then combining them near the end of the level before the boss fight. Same formula for ALL levels and because of this it feels like the game is one Giant level of tofu, generic and not really memorable. Also these levels are unnecessary long and tedious. You get halfway through a level and you feel like you should be at the boss is a VERY common theme throughout the game.
Overall Mighty No 9 does not only fail at making a Mega Man successor, but as well as a side scroller “Jump N Shoot” game.  Yes, there are many reasons to it behind the games development, but that’s for another time. Even if you don’t like Mega Man games, please don’t pick this up. It’s very generic and you’ll end up dashing through ¾ of the game because at Boss number 5, it will feel like a chore at that point rather than a source of entrainment.

It's just as bad as many people say it is.
- Grafic quality is from 15 years ago (low res textures, coloration/saturration remind of dreamcast games, lighting and shadowing is practically non-existant and why the hell did they decide to use 2.5D instead of nice 2D pixel-art?)
- Gameplay just feels strange (thanks to the infinite dash mechanic platforming is non-existant. You can easily reach everything and if you fail, you can dash back - mid-air! Also this whole highscore hunting doesn't really fit into such a game. And since the platforming is so easy, they implemented dozens of instant-death traps.)
- Story is extremely bad and non-original (a story a child could have written in 5 minutes. It feels like they developed the game and decided in the last minutes what kind of story the game will have)
This is what I think about the game when I'm not trying to compare it to the Mega Man Franchise. If I also take into consideration, that this game is/was supposed to be a spiritual successor to the Mega Man franchise, then it gets even worse.
This game is developed by the man (Inafune) who developed most of the Mega Man games and is the one who created Mega Man in the first place. He always delivered great quality Mega Man games and the name Mega Man was like 4 times mentioned in in the Kickstarter campaign. Also the design of the first artworks reminded alot of Mega Man. Naturally, many people expected it to be a game with a slightly different world and characters, but other then that, a 1to1 copy of Megaman (gameplaywise), maybe with little innovations. So to say: A real spiritual successor to the MM franchise (since Capcom refuses to make a new one). That's why people backed 4 million dollars for this project. When I see what other developers from Kickstarter did with much less money (Shovel Knight = 400,000$), you really wonder where those 4 million $ went into. Like I said above, grafic quality, story and gameplay are all in a really terrible state and lets not forget, that the games release got sheduled at least 3 times. They had the money, they had the time and it is still what we see today.
But that's not all. I was an active forum member in the backer forum and made a thread 8 month ago, pointing all those things out. I told them the game will get roasted at release if it comes out in this state. I never received an answer from the devs and the few tryhard fans defended MN9 until the end. It was a useless effort from my side to think that the devs would actually listen to an honest backer, especially when all the real MM fans already left the forum and therefore I didn't have any support for my arguments from others. Well, now the game is what it is and is not really liked by the community. Even the positive votings are often sarcastic.
So all in all I can't recommend the game. Just go for another plattformer (Shovel Knight or 20XX for example) and forget about this game, unless you can manage to forget, that this is supposed to be a spiritual successor to MM and you're looking only for a real mediocre experience. Then you MAY enjoy it, but I wouldn't buy it at full price...

++My Way Of Thinking When I Play Games++
"Now that we have countless games to try, we do not experience the same feeling of having a game for ourselves, and nothing else than that, that is why we find the negative aspects quicker than when we were young, games were fun, even the now called ''Bad Games''. If you give this game a try, do not be afraid and play it like you did when you were young."
++Quick Intro Containing Information Of How Much This Game Means To Me++
-Before I give my opinions of this game, I really have to go back to when I was a child. I was in love with Megaman X games, from 4 to 8,
I didn't really like the Megaman games without X, but when I got older I tried Megaman 1 to 6. Oh how I loved them, it was such a great experience to get through them as they were tough to beat and fun to play.
So It is quite obvious that I felt hyped when I heard about this Mighty No 9,
I was hyped, but the delays came, I do believe that they were Four delays in a row.
Which got me thinking. . .Should I really even buy it?
But when It got finally released I quickly took notice of the Reviews, people saying that the game was trash, bad optimized, short and so many things.
There also was the message of the Mighty No 9 Team, saying something like "Here you go, It's Better Than Nothing". . .
There were other things that got me into wondering if this game was worth buying or not. I actually despised this game just because of the reviews and all the proof that this game wasn't as good as people expected. . .What did I do?.-
++Important Words That Got Me Into Playing This Game++
I cleared my mind of all those reviews, and bought the game, saying to myself that I was going to get through the whole game even if it was bad, and then, right at the end, I would have to give it the veredict.
++The Review++
//Positive Aspects\\ Hey Look A  Clown  --->                     :O)
[+] Mighty No 9 controls: they are really well done, I only had issues at the beginning, as it all felt different to me. And the character itself it has that feeling of a cool character that just like in the Trailer he justwants to be Fun, the game itself isn't trying to get Fans angry or isn't doing anything bad to the extreme, like Devil May Cry did a few times in the saga.
1[+] They kept some of the classic Megaman Ideas in place, but they were in my opinion "Upgraded", such as:
2[+] The ability to select any level that you want.
3[+] To be able to use the Bosses's Powers. + There is a huge level of interaction you have with those Boss's Powers, they aren't just there to be used against Bosses.
4[+] The classic unfair Instant Kills from Megaman on the Nes. +The Uprade here is that you are the game doesn't put you in an unfair situation, you put yourself into it by going quickly, as in the game you have infinite dashes in the air
5[+] The Dash was finally a weapon in the Megaman Series, +As previously Zero in Megaman X4 was the only Character to be able to Dash and Hit in that way
6[+]  The game will has multiplayer when you beat it.
7[+] You can choose 8 Bit music or the Standard one, plus English or Japanese. +I recommend English as I had some laughs with "The Flying Boss"
8[+] The Bosses are not easy at all. +There's now the use of "Fine Play" Which is to pretty much Stop/Parry an enemy's attack for bonus stylish points, and you'll need to make use of it a lot to get through the game
9[+] There are places in some stages that make you think "It is impossible to get through there!" Like in Megaman X6 Gate's Levels
10[+] The Most Important of them all you can choose your own gameplay with Mighty No 9's "Lemon Bullets" Or the Power of a Boss, and it feels really unique when you learn how to use each. +Although I do not remember playing any megaman using only the Bosses's Powers
//Negative Aspects\\ Hey Look A Duck --->             :V   "KILL HIM BEFORE HE LAYS EGGS!!"
[-] Mighty No 9 isn't a game for everyone, as the controls are quite different than what we all are used to from Megaman X to Megaman on the Nes, as there will be a lot of things that will distract us from having fun in the game. Some of these are easily avoided and some are not, Here is a list:
1[-] By playing a game that was made from the original creator of Megaman, it feels weird not being able to charge your shot, or getting confused with the controls
2[-] I felt like the concept of fighting enemies in a room/locked camera place, got tedious as I wanted continue the level but they took quite a lot
3[-] Some Powers block your View, or mess you up in some way that you will regret equiping them at first, like one of them stuns you for 1 second , the other doesn't do damage, and then another one requieres you  to be in a specific place to hit your target.
4[-] The Song was not as memorable as the other Megaman games, I had to actually lower the volume of the Voices and FX to 50% to be able to listen to the Music
5[-] The Bosses help you when you finish a stage, showing you who's the next boss that can exploit their weakness and it takes some difficulty off of you when you are playing, making the game easier
6[-] When you die quite a lot of times you receive more healing items and sometimes revive items making the game easier
7[-] The only secrets that you will find won't be armors, they would be Revives, healing or energy Items , the only useful ones are Revives, since the bosses are quite hard
8[-] Sometimes the game explains you more than it should making the game easier accidently, showing you what to do or where to exactly hit an enemy to be able to deal damage
9[-] The online sucks at the moment as it's laggy and buggy, the only way to play it correctly is if you and your friend are close and have no Ping
10[-] The most important one is that the game forces you to have to redo the entire stage again like the old megamans when you lose all your lives, as you only have 2 (Or 5 if you modify that in the options menu)
Overall: With all it's flaws I had a blast playing this game, and I still do, as I'm currently playing the entire story mode again in One Hit Death Mode, it is really fun and I have never experienced something like this in a Megaman Game,
Because this isn't a Megaman game at all, it is a game that tried to look like Megaman, while also giving a new story, a new way of playing and a new main character with endless possibilities on how to start a new saga.
Because that is what this is, a game that is trying to revive a dead saga. We have to be thankful that we have this and as they said,
"It really is better than nothing" . . .
We have to be thankful to experience a fast game like this one. And if you can't , just try, I'm sure we can all change our way of thinking about this game, together as a community!.

This game is a whole lot of wonderful nostolgia.  I would sink endless hours into this game as a kid, and as computers got newer getting the thing to work was harder and harder. Then steam came out with this! Completely worth the 6 bucks! And it even has the 2 expansion packs to boot!
This game is old, so bear in mind it's isometic rather than 3D so if you are used to a free-form camera you may need a moment to adjust to having it locked at 90 degree angles. However, I never found myself struggling to place objects because of the camera.
The AI is.... not the best.  Your park layout has to be, for the most part, a strait line or a large circle.  Otherwise your park guests get lost. However, I don't find this takes away from the game. Placing information kiosks and using monorails or chairlifts help with this "guest 102 is lost and can't find the park exit" nonsense.
A great feature is any alert it gives you, good or bad, you can bring the camera to that spot. Lost guest? pick him up and show him the park exit.
Despite it's age the coaster design part of the game is still my favorite.  A good variety of coasters, options, designs, I can truly build the monster coasts of my dreams. And make incomplete ones that rocket guests to their dooms like a total sadist.
If you were a fan of the game a a kid, totally dive back in it's a wonderful game.  And to anyone curious about trying it for the first time, it's an excellent simulation game and you really can let your creativity shine.
ONLY issue I ever encountered: The game will strobe if you have the program F.lux running. This is a program to dim your monitor to yellow-toned colors at night to reduce eye strain.  But it's incompatible with this game. All you need to do is disable F.lux before firing up the game and you will have zero issues.

When it comes to hidden objects, this game has a lot of them. Unfortunately, it's random each time as to what objects you're looking for. And after two playthoughs (just to get all the achievements), there were still tons of hidden objects that I had seen that the game had not picked out for me to find. So this is my biggest complaint about this game. If you want to replay it at all, you have to create a new profile, which is also a negative.
This game would have been better if after your first completion, there was a sort of unlimited hunting mode where you could just go through the locations and find objects from a larger list.
There was only one puzzle that I found to be any kind of real challenge near the end, so if you don't like doing a lot of puzzles or tough puzzles, I recommend.
When it comes to the objects you're looking for, I found this game to be a nice mix of hard and easy. Some items blend in so well, you don't notice them for several minutes sometimes. (Which this could be a positive or negative.)
Overall, I do recommend this game if you like hidden objects games, despite the complaints I have about it. I did enjoy it, but the biggest thing with me is I wish it had a slightly higher replayability.

I wish I could give this a half yes half no recommendation, honestly. I was a kickstarter backer--so I may be blinded by my own purchase a little--but this is a really cute harvest moon-like with cats and without a true farming or ranching mechanic. That said, without the ability to rule your own territory implimented yet, there's really nothing to do after you've collected all the shrine gewgaws. Granted, I've only started on training my two kits, but I think I'm going to hold off playing any more until I can make my own colony.
And even then, will having my own colony make a difference? As far as I've seen, the only difference between territory owned by your faction and territory owned by another is that you're more likely to be attacked in the other's. There's no restriction on harvesting herbs or hunting prey outside my territory. I'm not totally confident that there will suddenly be court drama once I'm my own ruler, either.
I really wish that there was an abundance of npcs (some non-colony ones perhaps?), and that some would try to trick you. As it stands, every cat except the faceless npc fighters is basically friendly, and none will attack you outright. I think there's room for a really solid plot here, but it seems to be going for a really kid-friendly bright and cheery atmosphere, after the touching opening sequence. I wish there was a plot that involved finding humans, whether or not they were your original humans, and/or dogs and cars to watch out for. The only combat is bats and cats (and in just one segment, ghosts), and I would like more enemies. Maybe even a Hardcore mode with permadeath.
I know I've really only talked trash about it so far, and I think that's because I WANT it to be really good! Right now (and possibly forever?) it's cute and solid and a little grindy, but I've enjoyed my time with it. I just don't know if the average harvest moon-type gamer would be satisfied with how few mechanics there are, and if the average warriors cats fan would be satisfied with how mild and gentle it is.
Huge plus is that the cats are ungendered, though.
