I've been enjoying this game for the most part. I do wish there was a bit more substance to it, and perhaps at it's full price, it's not worth it for everyone (although, some people will definitely get their money's worth), but it's a fairly relaxing game. There's enough to do that if you set your own goals, you'll enjoy the experience. It would be nice if the developers continue to add content, and I believe there may be some still to come (at least according to features in the Kickstart stretch goals, although they're mostly there from what I've experienced), so hopefully it gets a little more fleshed out.
My only real gripe so far is that during the Winter season, the game basically stagnates as there's very little to do. Thankfully, the seasons are quite short and if you're really struggling you can just sleep through it, but it is a little disappointing that your only option during winter is to hunt, as foraging becomes very limited and you're quite restricted in what you can do if you're not already prepared for it. There may be more to do once you're further into the game, but at least for the first winter, prepare to be bored.
It's a bit like playing Stardew Valley, except without farming, and also you're a cat. There's less to do and fewer NPCs to interact with, but it feels very much inspired by Stardew's style and play. That said, comparison aside, it stands on it's own two feet and if you're a fan of that casual "do your own thing" style game, with a cute pixel art presentation, relaxing music, and no real pressure on you to do more than what you want to do, you'll enjoy Cattails.

I got Momodora III because I was very interested in getting Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight and I wanted to try out this game first. While I am still interested in getting Reverie Under the Moonlight and I DO recommend this game, it didn't feel like anything that spectacular at times.
The combat is very basic and apart from spamming your melee attack or shooting a few ranged attacks, there's not much you can do in terms of combat.
The characters weren't that memorable because they are introduced very quickly and are rather rushed. The story isn't a key part of this game, however, so that can pass.
While the soundtrack to this game isn't as amazing as Shovel Knight's or Undertale's, I enjoyed it. The music was, at times, very relaxing. My favorite track was the track to the final level in
Most of them weren't really that interesting or engaging. The combat is very basic so it the bosses can all be defeated the same way.
The artstyle is extremely cute and I really love it. The enemy and NPC designs are very cute and unique and I love it. This is probably the greatest part of the game. This is probably what compels most players.
Although I've been complaining a lot, my final complaint is about the final level. I put a spoiler notice when I talked about it before, and I'll do that again.
Okay, so... What did I enjoy about the game?
Well, I thought the atmospheres were very nice and, like I said before, I thought the soundtrack was very relaxing. The NPCs were, while rushed in their introductions, at least likeable. The game doesn't give you a defined purpose, which is nice. You can make any predictions or guesses, which I wish more games would do sometimes. You can also occasionally find secret items, which I wish there had been more focus on. The game feels like 25% of a Metroidvania style game. The artstyle is, as I said before, wonderful. You can tell the developer obviously put a lot of time into it and that's what I admire most about the game.
Overall...
Sure, I would recommend Momodora III. No, it's not the greatest game I've ever played, but it's worth playing and is a nice way to pass an hour or two when you're bored.

Jotun is a top-down action adventure with beautiful hand-drawn art and pretty bad gameplay.
The game is split in two parts, exploration and bosses. The exploration levels are extremely tedious and boring. Most of them don't have any enemies, the only threat is usually the environment itself. The main annoyance comes from the horrible map system, however. I really don't understand why the developer chose not to display the player's location on the map.
Boss fights fare a little better as they at least offer some half decent gameplay. Unfortunately they suffer from rather clumsy and sluggish controls. On a positive note the difficulty level was pretty good, most bosses took a few attempts to figure out but once you work out their attack patterns and weaknesses they are not too difficult to defeat.
Despite the beautiful hand-drawn art I can't really recommend Jotun as the gameplay is just too tedious and plain unfun.
I did finish the game but there's no way I would even bother attempting the harder Valhalla mode with the poor controls.
The good:
- Nice art style
- Good use of Norse sagas
- Narrator speaking in Icelandic was a nice touch
The bad:
- Clumsy and sluggish controls (I was playing on a gamepad, I don't think keyboard would be any better)
- Exploration is boring and tedious
- Poor animations
- Terrible map system
- The perspective is an issue on some bosses

So there is a lot of hate for this game on the internet, but I can't really figure out why. Even more so when you compare it to actual megaman games.
People complain that the story is bland and boring with a boring level design. Well I'm not going to say it's not but have you ever played megaman 1-5 and walked away thinking boy that was riveting story full of emotion and passion. No. You haven't.
Mechanically the game plays itself off as very hard, but no more hard than megaman games. Insta death pits, and scenery that can kill you, however it's constant in it's  placement of said insta death forcing the player to quickly learn the pattern/background to adapt. Now people have critizied the first stage (Pyrogen) for having mechanics that feel unfair or cheap. However if you go back and play them you can easily see there is a auto cue (Call warns you) and a game play cue that tell you to avoid the insta death mechanics. You actually get to watch robots be destoried by a falling building, a clear sign that you should avoid that because you'll be destoried.
Boss wise, the bosses I've beaten all have Audio cue's and mechanical cue's as well. Once again you learn their patterns and you can defeat them rather easily. My first 5-7 deaths on Pyrogen was a struggle to progressively due better til my final fight vs him where I  barely took damage because I had memorized his attack patterns. Like previous games bosses have weapons that they are weak against, though the buster proves to be effective vs any boss which makes the game less linear about starting points and what boss to tackle next.
The dash mechanic is interesting and in some ways good and others bad. Enemies get stunned after being hit a bit which allows you to dash into them get a random power up and instantly kill them for loads of points. However on the other hand the dazed enemies can still be hit by bullets so they body block excessively, and merely walking into them causes damage to beck. They also shoe horned the ability in vs bosses where after a certain percentage of damage you have to dash into them to lock the bosses health down this however also allows them to add phases to the bosses where their attacks change slight or get more powerful.
While the random power ups are good, enemies in this game don't tend to drop health making taking damage much more punishing, this is offset by checkpoints with a helper robot sometimes throwing you temporary power ups and some times help but feels far to random to be actually helpful. One bit of advice i'd say to players if that you can turn up your maximum starting lives in options, it makes the game a much more enjoyable experience even while dying because you have more time to learn the bosses
The final thing I like about the game is that on stage select you can see an "Advice" tab on the stage if you've beaten the previous boss that the current is weak to. They will come to the stage with you and wreck it up a bit, often helping you bypass minor parts of the level, and let you know which weapon to use though as I said earlier weapons are not required as your buster is pretty useful all  together.
Overall I remember Megaman games to have very poor story, very tough challenges that you overcome by memorization and a lot of jumping and shooting. All things that mighty No 9 have, I recommend for the die hard megaman fans but maybe less so to the casual gamer.

This is not Megaman, keep that in mind while playing.
That being said it is not a game I could recommend as it falls squarely into mediocrity. The shoot and dash mechanic felt pretty clunky, it would've been nice if they pushed the dash and speed running angle more. Level design doesn't really push any limits other than your patience as falling platforms don't respawn, enemy placement is annoying and insta-kill mechanics slows down what should be fast paced game play. Boss fights are pretty meh as well, at certain heath they have an enrage type mechanic where a boss skill gets changed. Sounds cool but falls flat, most of the bosses just feel cheap instead of challenging at that point.
There are other issues such as no control mapping and how clunky some of the basic controls feel. Not game breakingly bad, but doesn't feel great by anymeans. The visuals are hard to read at times as they often put similar colors together, and some things aren't clear enough the explosions hit box being the biggest example. Overall the graphics aren't great- noticing a trend :P I think 2d would've worked much better with the cartoon appearance and may have cleared up the visual readability of the game.
Music and voice acting isn't all the good either. I've heard much worse in both aspects but that also means nothing so bad its funny- 'sup Resident Evil :) The story is on par with most platformers- not hard to reach that goal, if they managed to pull off worse I would be legit impressed - just enough to make conflict to clean up and just that.
Overall this game is meh, If they fix the crashes and framerate drops I could say grab if for the cheap you might have fun. It isn't 20$ of fun though, maybe 10$ if/when the bugs get cleaned up.

I remember purchasing this game when it came out, and ever subsequent expansion pack and sequel. From the beginning, RCT invites you to take full control of a world of theme parks and encourages you to not only manage a successful business, but to design the coasters of your dreams along with a great selection of theming, scenery, music and other fun rides. While RCT2 added much more control of scenery and added a lot of new rides, its merely another expansion for this one (in my opinion).
For the time, the isometric graphics were great and many games since have copied the Railroad/RC Tycoon game's ability to easily convey to the user how things should look. While not incredibly realistic, the game does introduce you to other parts of the world and how they view theme parks and attractions. It wasn't until this game's release did I ever hear about free admission to parks and paying for riding the rides, but thats how a lot places in Europe go about it. By the way, this team was based out of the UK which is why some things are surprising for US audiences.
If you're going to buy a version of this game, I highly encourage RCT2 for the added scenery and construction options as well as the Six Flags park packs. RCT 3 is also very fun, it came out not long after SIM Theme Park and SIMcoaster which (both borrowed tons from this game) and adds the ability to ride nearly every single attraction. It's still a classic to me, and I will never be able to get the music out of my head.

I was on the fence with this game. I ended up giving it a "yes" since the storyline is nice and the graphics and sound were good. This is a Hidden Object game with a lot of hidden object scenes and a few other games (such as memory). For the price, it's worth the buy, especially if you enjoy Hidden Object games. However, I did find a few things with the game I didn't really like. For one, (and for me) I don't see a lot of replay value with this game beyond trying to get all the steam achievements. With all the scenes, none of the items within the scene are changed. The only thing that changes are the items you have to find (for the most part). After a bit, it doesn't take that long to get the general location for items in each scene.
OK, I do like when game makers for this genre use a word that could be various items (such as bow, it could be a hairpiece, weapon, or a musical bow). However, there was a few times (given, not a lot) where the game would require an item found and there were a couple items it could be (in one instance, it asked for a hat and there was one in the painting and another one on a statue). Given, it's not a huge deal, but when trying not to make any mistakes, it makes it a bit hard. Also, there was one scene where it asked for 3 x brush, and one item was a broom (which for my crazy self, annoyed me a bit since I don't really consider a broom a brush).
However, despite what I found annoying, I would still recommend this game for all the Hidden Object game fans out there.

It's been a couple years now since I first played this game. After finishing Bastion I needed something like the experience it gave me again, and then Transistor was released. I honestly don't know how to start talking about this game. How each song in the soundtrack perfectly reflects the situation you are in at the time, or how the voice actors absolutely NAILED their respective performances. How the man in the Transistor talks to you during every moment, supporting you, or how at the end I found myself physically crying because it could not have ended in a more correct way. The art style is magnificent, and if it weren't for the events of the story, you would totally want to live there, were it real.
If you aren't one for those parts of a game, then let me tell you that the gameplay is remarkably tight and intuitive. Every ability you recieve synergizes with any other. You can use an ability as an active attack or move, or you can augment and active ability with it, OR you may use it as a passive that augments your own abilities. Enemies grow and change, and so must you. If you are having to easy a time, the game also presents you with challenge you can impose on yourself, called limiters. They make the game harder in small, or larger ways, in return for more level XP, which helps you unlock new things faster.
I'm doing my best to hold out on any information on the story, as this is a game that is meant to go in blind. Do not read any story spoilers, or listen to the soundtrack before playing. Expereince it like it is supposed to. I almost want to say I want the game to be longer, as you can easily complete it in about 4-5 hours on a slow day, but to be honest, it's the perfect length. It tells you what it wants to say, and then leaves. It's perfect, all of it. Play it, and tell Supergiant Games thank you for letting us play.
This game is aesthatically beautiful and mechanically interesting at the same time. Another product of Supergiant's love, from the soundtrack to the gameplay.

I love a lot of things about Transistor, but its combat just might be my favorite part; it's unique, wonderfully animated and, although the player needs at least a couple of hours of gameplay to really get comfortable with it, figuring it out definitely pays off. I finished the game and the new game +, and I still come back to Transistor because it's just so much fun. The storytelling and worldbuilding is amazing and the artstyle and soundtrack really play a crucial part in the storyline -- which is to be expected from a Supergiant Game after all. I highly recommend it!

Momodora III was a dissapointment to say the least. Having played through the first two one after the other I was excited to see how 3 would improve on 2 considering the huge jump in quality from the first to the second but I feel like that didn't happen here.
Pros:
x Dora is cute!
x The animations are very nice, definitely better than the previous two
x The colors are very vivid and areas a lot more varied than before
x Multiple bosses instead of just an endgame one
x Having bosses do dark souls-y large, damaging but telegraphed attacks is neat, though I feel like it doesn't work like it's supposed to
Cons:
x Almost entire removal of all metroidvania elements. No more map or hidden health items, or a secret thing you have to get to get the good ending
x Around halfway or 3/4 through the game I got sick of it and decided to just rush through everything to progress...and it worked
x Holding S to shoot feels a lot more awkward than pressing up S, which made me rarely want to use projectiles (though perhaps this was on purpose?)
x I found that most bosses could easily be beaten by just standing next to them and spamming attack while tanking any damage...and this is on the normal difficulty
x It feels like I missed a lot but apparently I got 89% completion so I guess not! Though seeing the npcs again definitely would've made things less confusing
x No more upgrades like double jump or dash, just items that I feel like didn't so much to mix things up when equipped

x The last boss felt pretty anticlimactic, I only figured they must be the last one while I was fighting them because they had multiple forms

Conclusion:  Not recommended (limited replayability)
------------------------------------------------
A novel premise, but the execution is quite limiting.
At first glance, the game seems varied and interesting, but in reality the gameplay is quite simplistic.  Once you play a single game there is little to do beyond beating your previous score.
Also, note the voice acting is not present in the game (only in the advertising movie).  This removes a fair bit of the anticipated immersion.
The single player experience offers only few hours of enjoyment (2 - 3 game sessions).
Multiplayer may offer a bit more enjoyment time, but given the game design limitations it is likely to be shorter than mp experiences in other games.
Overall, a fun game the first time, but the limited enjoyment of replayability is why I could not recommend this game.
If you are still set on purchasing the game, my final bit of advice is to recommend that potential buyers wait for the game to go on sale for at least a 50% discount before purchasing.

After 8.3hrs into the game and have beaten all bosses in normal mode, I think I have some say to the experience that Jotun can offer.
The first thing i want to say is, if you are a fan of Dark Souls frachise, I bet you would fall in love with Jotun instantly. I myself am a expierenced player to the Dark Souls franchise (over 300+ hrs in game time) who was trying to find some game similar to Dark souls that can refresh my mind. Jotun, which is a 2D game with norse mythology background caught my eye instantly. In this game the player character, Thora,  who died an unhonorable death, needs to prove her worthness to the gods by beating the jotuns, so she can ascend to vahalla. Very much alike a 2D version Dark Souls game, Thora has light melee attack, heavy melee attack, dodge rolling, and a few unlockable combat spells that either heals, buffs herself or damages her foes. The key to beat many bosses lies on timing on dodging. The feel of controlling the character is exactly like that of darks souls, and any souls fan can pick up playing instantly.
The con is, this game offers far less combat variety than Dark souls, as Thora wields one weapon only(a two-hand axe), compared with hundreds of weapons that are offered to players in Dark souls.
Visual Effect:
On the screen, Thora is often dwarfed by the colossius Jotuns she fights, and her moves and attacks felt powerless in front of the godly power the Jotuns wield. However Thora always emerges victorious through her courage and wit. This contrast is astounding both visually and mentally.
Boss fight:
Each boss fight essentially has a learning curve, and players have to learn the boss patterns through trial and error until they can eventualy beat the boss. All boss fights have serveral stages, and each stage is triggered by boss's remaining health. The boss will use more abilities and become more and more dangerous to the player with further progression into the fight. Quite often in the final stage players need to finish off the boss as quickly as possible through the burst of DPS, otherwise things will get out of control.
Difficulty:
All bosses have interesting abilities and  most of them are fun to fight. However, I have to point out that diffculty of each boss fight is not linear, some has a much larger difficulty spike than others. For example, The ice giant in normal mode feels like face roll while Odin feels way too hard (even for a Dark Souls fan like me). Took me 1 try to kill the ice giant and around 20 tries to beat Odin. Timing your dodging wrong,  or dodging in a wrong direction will cause you hit by Odin's thunder lance and lose a big chunk of your health, which typically results in failure in later combat stage. From the 3rd stage onwards, Oden will summon the shadow of one or a few Jotun that you previously beat ramdomly to aid him in combat, who throw their characteristic ability at you. As some Jotuns has abilitys that is much easier to dodge than others, whether we can beat Odin or not some feels luck based rather than skill based. I personally dislike this type of design very much.
Summary:
In general, Jotun is a hard and fun game. If you are not used to this type of game and expect to beat each boss in one go, I don't recommend this game to you at all. If you are into the souls game like me, or if you wanna give yourself a challenge, I am pretty sure you will enjoy this game very much.

I find a want to compare this game to Dark Souls (a Series I love and have hundreds of hours in for each game) like many others probably have. This game has the same sort of difficulty curve, gives the same kind of satisfaction on defeating a tough enemy, and, at first, feels as though it sratches the itch for more Dark Souls, but it has one MASSIVE difference. The defining principle of any Dark Souls game, what distinguishes the good bosses vs the bad bosses, and why Dark Souls fans don't mind repeatedly dying on the same boss is a concept termed "fair damage." Fair damage means that when you take damage and ultimately die because of it, every bit of that damage was because of a mistake made by you or because you were not skilled enough. There is no such thing as an undodgeble attack. Now the reason I am talking so much on fair damage in Dark Souls is because Jotun is full of the oppisite, "unfair damage." Unfair damage is when a random lightning bolt falls from the sky and kills you, unfair damage is when your screen flashes white for a second because the boss is changing stages and you get hit in that moment because you couldn't see anything, unfair damage is when your dodge roll ability is too worthlessly short to dodge an attack because you just happenend to be in the wrong area, an area that would normally have been safe.
I would not recommend this game to anyone unless you are a masicist who enjoys being punished for doing nothing wrong, like boring, repetitive and inanely simple puzzles (added in order to pad game length), and getting less information on ancient viking mythology than you would get by skimming through the Wikipedia page on it for 15 min.

TL;DR:  "Mighty No. 9" isnt the "mighty no. 2" that so many people are making it out to be, but its nothing we havent played before. Its not bad, its not amazing, but its good fun.
TL;DR2:  Haters gonna hate.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Wow, this game sure is causing a real ruckus, eh? Honestly I dont see what the fuss is about. Lets go over some of the issues people are having.
-Mighty no 9 doesnt NEED a deep story.
"9" is meant to be a "love letter" to retro games like Mega Man-- a series which never had much of a "plot", "character development" ETC. Why did people expect this one to? Its the exact same story weve seen in every MM title that ever came out- "good scientist makes robots, bad scientist takes em over, good robot must fight bad robots. the end." We never had a problem with that story for 20+ years, but suddenly its a huge issue to a lot of people. WHY???
-Voiceacting woes?
Im just gonna put it on the table-- VA work (ESPECIALLY Capcom games), generally sucks. It probably does in this game too, I would not be surprised. However this is an issue which does not affect me, and shouldnt affect you, because you can set the audio to Japanese, which sounds fine, or even turn the voice off altogether. No problem!
-Bland music?
Ill admit, the 'normal' OST really does define "BACKGROUND" music. Its pretty generic sounding. However, in the options you can change it to "retro" music, making it sound 8-bit and honestly not bad. The compositions wont hold up to classics like "Metal Man" etc, but theyre good, and the game sounds a TON better on retro. The music volume seems to be drowned out by the sound and voice, even at 100%, so I would recommend setting FX/voice to 50% so you can actually HEAR the music.
-The Dash
Ahhh, the dash. The move which lets you absorb other foes' powers and zoom around the map.
Im sure youve read peoples opinions on this ability. Heres mine: Remember Mega Man 3's slide move? That was pretty awesome after 2 titles without it, and so great they let the Blue Bomber keep it in other games. The dash is much like the slide, only it can be used in mid-air, which is loads of fun once youve mastered the controls. The dash is the true core of this game's fighting mechanic and is used everywhere including boss battles, so Id say if you dont like the dash, youre not gonna like this game. I love it myself- it makes combat super-zippy and heightens your reflexes as you attempt to blaze a path through everything. While its true that the ability can be spammed eternally with no cooldown, the game -encourages- you to spam the move and zoom through areas like youre that *other* blue guy (you know, the one that goes fast), so I dont view it as some game-breaking problem. Besides, there REALLY arent as many flat, wide open areas that you can "fly over and avoid" like some people think. Try it and most of the time youll get bot-slapped out of the air.
-Graphics, level layout ETC
The graphics may be what suffers most in this game. I would have preferred this to be a 2d pixel shooter, or even hand-animated. Regardless, the 2.5D graphics arent anything amazing. They get the job done, they look good enough, the robots look like their illustrated concept work.... but its all very generic and for the most part, pretty low in polycount (that is, &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥looks blocky"). Still, the gameplay makes up for the average look.
Level design is pretty straightforward- youre generally running right, sometimes climbing ladders, sometimes dropping down pits, similar to MM games. Some spots can be tricky with their classic "1-touch kill" objects about the levels, but overall its nowhere as tough as retro MM platforming. You wont be hopping on crumbling blocks midair while trying to fight a robotic dragon, ETC.
The most disappointing part about the level design is lack of replayability. Other than pickups, there are no real secrets to be found. There are little to no walls/doors/ETC that can be interacted with via robot master powers (IE, blow up a wall to find a bunch of 1-ups), so once you have beaten a level theres really no reason to go back through it again other than for the sake of it.
One thing I found neat though, when you beat a robot master, not only do you get their power like always, but instead of destroying them, the other Mighty units get REPAIRED- and certain ones will join you in certain stages to help clear out tougher areas. The first time I saw another Mighty unit jump into the level and start taking out obstacles and foes with me, I got a big goofy grin. That was pretty cool.
-Overall....
Im having a good time with it. The gameplay is zippy and fun, and thats what really counts in a platformer-shooter game. Not the lack of a story, or crappy voice work, or average looking graphics...but the game itself. Sure, it could have been better, and I can see how some folks may not like it, but its enough fun to me that Ill certainly play it through in full. And then, much like the old, classic, groundbreaking MM games I grew up with since the 80s, it will sit on my digital shelf and collect dust until I pop it in for a couple hours a year, cuz sometimes you just want to blow up some robots.

Papers please is a game that does so much right that it's just shocking.
I played the entirety of Papers please twice back to back trying to chase down a few achievements and both play throughs were pure brilliance in video game form.  I've never had a game made me think even half as much as Papers please did in just 16 hours.
I started to question how immigration really works.  What would I value in an immigration agents, speed or efficiency?  Was the goal of an immigration officer to move the line or properly admit people?   Should I investigate transgender people or just turn them away?  Is taking pictures of people as part of immigration acceptable and so much more.
I mean the depth of my thoughts while playing the game was quite astonishing, but the fact that such a simplistic looking game can develop these thoughts was impressive.
The game's game play loop is pretty simple, you take passports and documents and choose to admit or reject people based on the simple information given.  You're not graded on catching people but rather graded on if you get a correct result from the official procedure, but much of the game is left up to the player's discretion.  It's actually not only possible but acceptable to reject people based on information that isn't fully acquired.  If someone seems has the incorrect sex on their ID, you can reject them or scan them to get the correct answer.
The entire game though doesn't exactly tell you how to play it 'properly' it's acceptable to deep dive on people to assist them, it's also acceptable to reject them as fast as possible.  I have a feeling the latter is the better way to play, but it's really up to the user to figure out how to play it.
It would probably be a pretty dull game just to examine the passports but the game does two things to change up the experience.  Almost every day there are some small rules that change.  Early on you need to get entry tickets and then entry passes.  ignoring these rules will result in penalties, so you're forced to follow the rules, but almost every day adds a new twist or complication you have to remember, and over time it gets more complicated but also parts of it becomes second nature.
The second feature is the story.  Almost every day there is some story go on.  Usually it's a single person or a pair of people., but there's always a little mini story to play with, as well as a larger story that spans the game's time line.
The only down side is that after someone plays the game there's not much difference in the game, the game does tell a compelling story but it's not a long story or overly involved.  There's only one problem with it.  Once you've played the game you've seen every event in the game.   There's only a handful of events that have follow ups and the main story continues to matter what.
There's also a few achievements to earn as well, at least two require a full play through specifically for them, but the majority of them are one offs on special days or even just three day spans.  None are particularly hard.
What I'm trying to say however is there's minimal replayability.  You will get to the end of the end of the game in a few hours and may need a few more hours to beat the game a different way, but once you've finished it, there's only a few things to go finish up.
However there are issues with the game.  The game's play area is about half the screen, and the extra area isn't really used that often.  There is a number of quality of life improvements that I wish the developer made, such as allowing me to return documents once I finished going over them to the applicant.   Also a better way to investigate the issuing cities, as a real inspector should be able to memorize local cities of neighboring countries  the player has a tendency to forget them.
In fact there's a few issues.  Pictures can look similar but be different, or look different and be similar,  Fingerprints also sometimes look the same.  When an official seal is wrong it's VERY subtle and rarely wrong, Heights are nebulous, and certain tasks take long (And others are pointless such as giving the wrong entry reason or length of time.  They always correct themselves yet you MUST ask or reject them because of it)
However many of these are because otherwise the game would be too easy, and I rather enjoy the game as it is.  It's just I wish the game had just a few QoL improvements.   I can live with the game as it is, but it's frustrating at times.   Perhaps intentionally so.   I can totally buy the smaller play area is made to be annoying to people, the difficulty of the detection is to challenge the player and the seal issues are because otherwise it'd be simple to notice issues.
Overall though I enjoyed the game, I loved how it told it's story, I love how it made me think, and what it made me think about.  The fact that it somehow found a story about a western bloc nation relevant today, and that fact that the game just brilliantly works is impressive.
Actually there's one other problem.  It's been 4 years since Papers please came out.  I want another Lucas Pope game.  Not a sequel as I agree with him that there's not a sequel to be made, but Papers Please is just a unique breath of fresh air, I want another breath, and hopefully soon we'll get it.

I played this when I was 7, and it's still very good. Enough said.
In all seriousness, nostalgia does cloud our perception, and I don't play a lot of simulation games, so I may not be the best person to review this game since I don't have much to compare it to. I haven't played more than a few minutes of the sequels and games by other companies inspired by the series like Planet Coaster. Those are probably a better option if you're looking for a modern experience, as this game definitely is a bit dated. Still, for its age, I don't feel that the UI is too clunky or the learning curve is too steep. Fun to pick up for a couple hours exactly once, or to dump days into, if you have that kind of time.
I never did fully understand a lot of the roller coaster-specific mechanics, like intensity and excitement, which can be limiting when I'm trying to make a park the best it can be. The track builder is a bit clunky, too. Still, I'm a lot better at the budgeting and management aspects than I was when I was a kid, and the game can still be easy or challenging depending on the scenario. The quirks and flaws are a drop in the bucket of nostalgic goodness. Or lake. Lake of goodness, which your guests can fall into and drown.

Bastion was reasonably fun, but this was a BIG step down from that.  The whole combat system is just a mess of failed pseudo-turnbased, and the story this time just doesn't click at all.

Transistor does things that I didn't expect from a game that make the fantasy of a world made of data come to life.  While the overall plot gets hard to follow, the moment to moment jabs of the story hit well.  The mix of action and planned strategy really appealed to me personally, though I imagine trying to take too strictly an action approach might leave some confused.  All together, it's a smart design that bakes puzzles into combat while allowing for different approaches to the main game.  It's everything I could have hoped for from a successor to Bastion.
Perfect sound design, beautiful graphics, and interesting gameplay all tied together with a compelling story. A must play

Beautifully rendered game with gorgeous artwork. Love the sound track, narration and story. Facing enemies never grows old, new powers and combos evolve your strategies. One of my all time favorites from Super Giant Games.
Excellent story and great skill combination mechanic for the action combat.

I came into the game not entirely sure what to expect, but the aesthetic, the art style, and the sound design is incredibly on point. I haven't played their previous entry, Bastion (which I heard has very similar gameplay), but Transistor kept my attention for a good while with the gradual unveiling and unraveling of the world of the story.
Granted, combat is simplistic enough to grasp, and a few clearly superior build will be all that you will end up using, but experimenting to find that out for yourself, and to unlock the backstory of the world is a good implementation of story and gameplay progression (though I resent the idea of your program being destroyed if you lose a life).
Definitely check it out for its very low price tag.
